AR, SAC, and VC are currently being edited by Horst Lasic and myself. These files are not reproductions of the text as printed in JNA, but already incorporate a number of corrections based on the manuscripts. Due to technical difficulties, these corrections are not yet marked—the footnotes have not yet been added to the files.

More useful files will be provided once the critical editions are completed. *KBhA.txt* was originally produced by Tadashi Tani and kindly converted to ASCII by Kyō Kanō. I have subsequently converted this file—which utilized the Kyoto-Harvard convention for encoding diacritics—to conform with the @-convention used consistently across all other files.

The file contains several footnotes within the text that include abbreviations for textual editions; some of these abbreviations may have been erroneously converted and currently appear irregular (e.g., RNA > r@n@a@). In any case, this demonstrates the limitations of Kyoto-Harvard.

With the exception of this file, wherein the use of brackets and other formatting devices is as yet inconsistent (I shall attend to this in the near future), all other files adhere to the following standard:
page and line numbers are given in square brackets [ ],
while the folio numbers of the manuscript are given in round brackets ( ).

Notes from the editor or from the typist are given in fuzzy brackets ( ). Pointed brackets are used to indicate emendations to the text. NOTE: A more comprehensive list of specifications that should be observed in Sanskrit e-texts is provided on my home-page, http://www.ipc.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/~kellner/etext.htm. These specifications are subjective and have grown out of my personal experience.

I hope that these files prove useful, notwithstanding their current limitations. Any suggestions regarding how to enhance their utility would be greatly appreciated. Birgit Kellner, 01-06-1997. Notes from the editor or the typist have been excluded for the sake of practical use.

The Chapter on Momentary Destruction, titled the First Section: The Topic of the Property of the Subject.
The text of the first section is from Kyuma’s dissertation (September 7, 1999).
[Namo Buddhāya. While the world, which lasts but a moment, is being stretched out by the rays of the Kinsman of the Sun as if by others,
let those who lament over what is undesirable awaken, as if from sleep, by means of a blow to the palm of the hand.
Whatever exists is momentary, like a rain-cloud; and these entities exist.
Here, existence is the capacity for causal efficiency, and that [capacity] is established by means of valid cognition in those things already proven.
Nor is this capacity of a single uniform nature at all times, for otherwise there would be neither the production of another thing nor the absence of action.

Thus, in both ways, the application of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) rests upon the probandum (*sādhya*). Here, the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) presented in the first quarter-verse is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For even if there is indeed a difference in the definition of existence (*sattva*) according to each philosophical system, nevertheless, it is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) that is intended here as "existence" and employed as the reason. And this [capacity] is not impossible to state in every respect, nor is it something that could be claimed by anyone [to be absent].

For those who cannot tolerate such definitions might at most allege that our reason is too narrow (*avyāpti*). In that case, since only those very entities whose specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has been established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are made the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no suspicion of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) either in terms of the essential nature of the reason or its locus (*āśraya*).

Furthermore, as for those things which, despite the possibility of their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), have not been determined to possess that nature in reality—should a subsequent observation of causal efficiency occur when one examines them later, even though they were previously excluded from the subject (*pakṣa*), another inference will arise. However, in the absence of such [efficiency], the non-apprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*) is precisely what is intended, just as in the case of other logical marks (*liṅga*).

If it is argued that, in this way, the proof of momentariness is not all-pervasive, we say no; for it is established that whatever is anywhere and at any time useful for some purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), all of that possesses that nature [of momentariness]. Furthermore, this is accepted because the investigation into specific details is only appropriate when directed toward that which is indeed useful in some context. Therefore, there is no exclusion of undesirable forms, nor is there an inability to determine the logical reason (*hetu*).

Nor is the partiality of the establishment of the probandum caused by the absence of a single simultaneous application of inference across all subjects possessing the property to be proven, as is the case with the inference of God and so forth. By this, it is demonstrated that the various entities whose capacity for causal efficiency is certain are the subjects (*dharmin*), while the general capacity for causal efficiency is the logical reason (*hetu*).

Alternatively, all these entities that fall within the scope of perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the subjects (*dharmin*). "Causal efficacy" (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). This is because it is impossible to make anything that is not an object of a *pramāṇa* the subject in an inference that establishes a positive entity (*vidhisādhana*), whereas inference operates everywhere with respect to what is an object of a *pramāṇa*. What further pervasion (*vyāpti*) is needed for the establishment of the probandum? Thus, since the subject is within the range of a *pramāṇa*, there is no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the reason.

Nor is there a lack of establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), because regarding those things where the perception of external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is beyond dispute, there is no need for further deliberation. Even in cases where that [efficiency] is not directly determined, the determination of the capacity for causal efficiency is faultless simply because it produces a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this occurs directly in the case of perception and indirectly through its effect in the case of inference.

On this point, some say: "How is the existence of that very cause established, whose causal efficacy consists in its capacity to produce an effect? If that [capacity] is not established, then the primary entity itself lacks causal efficacy. Alternatively, just as the seed has efficacy in relation to the sprout, so too let the sprout have efficacy in relation to the leaf, the stalk, and so forth; and likewise, let cognition have efficacy in relation to another cognition, memory, verbal expression, purposeful activity, and so on, as well as in relation to its own and others' benefit."

It might be argued as follows: If there is no finality in tracing the succession of effects, then the proof of momentary destruction—which proceeds by postulating that even a single thing possesses some causal efficiency—would be impossible. Alternatively, if at the conclusion of the causal series there is something that lacks causal efficiency, then by the same logic, all preceding things would also result in being non-existent; thus, not even a single thing capable of causal efficiency would be established, and therefore this does not avoid the charge of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Furthermore, as for the claim that even if existence (*sattā*) is not established due to a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is no impairment of its being an effect (*kāryatva*), that too is incorrect. For if existence is not established despite a difference in exclusion, how can "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) be established? Indeed, being produced consists in coming into existence after not having existed. And for you, coming into existence is precisely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Therefore, when there is doubt regarding causal efficiency, it is impossible even to say "it comes into existence."

The state of depending on the operation of another for the completion of its own nature is what constitutes being "produced" (*kṛtakatva*); this too is not a property of a non-existent thing. Furthermore, existence (*sattā*) is precisely causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, properties such as "being differentiated by a difference in conditions" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*) and so forth, which are properties of existent things, cannot be predicated for the purpose of determining existence.

To this it is replied: First of all, sprouts and the like, which manifest clearly in a perceptual consciousness that has attained proficiency through specific practice and in which the suspicion of error has been entirely dispelled, cannot be said to be non-existent simply because their result is not seen. Otherwise, there would be no confidence even regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and consequently, due to the absence of any discourse concerning what is real or otherwise, the world would become motionless.

Now, if you argue that the very capacity of an object (*arthasāmarthya*) is the definition of existence (*sattvalakṣaṇa*), then why should a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) be asserted on the basis of a definition established by mere convention? If it is your intention to state a flaw in the definition itself through this sequence, then let it be stated. For us, however, there is no preparation for the sake of establishing that definition; rather, our aim is to establish momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of that definition.

Therefore, the failure to ascertain that characteristic would create an obstacle to the proof of momentary destruction regarding the effect. However, if another effect is observed, who could prevent the subsequent inference of that [momentary nature] there as well, occurring in due course? But now, since only that which is capable of causal efficiency is made the subject (*pakṣa*), it has already been explained that there is no fault whatsoever even if the probandum and the probans are unestablished with respect to what lies outside the subject.

Therefore, even when there is a breach of the conventional definition [of a cause], how much more so in the case of mere non-ascertainment? Since the nature of a thing—such as a sprout—is supported by the force of a more acute perception, there is no contradiction in the property of being an effect belonging to that thing. With respect to that, the seed and so forth are indeed capable of sustaining the proof of their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*); how, then, could there be a lack of proof (*asiddhi*)?

Now, it might be argued: "How can sensory cognition, which does not touch upon the definition of a real entity—whether that be the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) or something else—establish its status as a real entity? This too is trivial, because when there is direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no room for considering other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is observed that even without the application of technical definitions from the treatises, an activity undertaken after determining the reality of an object through the mere arising of perception refined by habituation (*abhyāsa*) is accompanied by non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*). What can be done about this? It would be thus.

If, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), being a real entity (*vastutva*) consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), then when perception delineates a real entity as the locus of arising—expressing that "this arises from that"—it necessarily delineates causal efficiency itself, even if it does not explicitly mention the word for it. Alternatively, if the definition of a real entity is something else entirely, then that [other characteristic] is what is delineated; just as when perceiving blue, the grasper of blue apprehends that which is not external to it, such as its consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇīmaya*) or some other property, even if it does not explicitly delineate those.

Thus it is established that, even when there is no observation of other effects despite the conformity of the sprout and so forth with their status as effects, perception establishes the causal efficiency (*arthasāmarthya*) of causes such as seeds through the fact of their being real entities.

If it is argued that seeds and the like should also be considered real entities simply because they arise through perception—just like an effect—what is the point of investigating causal efficiency? We do not, in our practical engagement with real entities, bypass the acuity of perception to follow after causal power, for even that [efficiency] is dependent upon perception. Rather, we do so to compel the acceptance of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). For practical engagement with real entities produced by perception, being common to both what possesses and what lacks the aforementioned characteristics, is not invariably capable of proving momentariness.

However, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), which is the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*), does not enter into its own existence without necessarily bringing that [efficiency] along with it wherever it exists. Therefore, it is established that this [capacity] is introduced here as a means of proof (*sādhana*), and not as the defining characteristic of a real entity.

Thus, in the case of cognition as well, self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is invariably concomitant with existence; everything is as previously stated. Therefore, it should be understood that by this too, the establishment of the object through its own causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) remains unimpeded. For when one thing is known by another, there is room for the suspicion of error; but in the case of self-awareness, such [error] is altogether absent.

Now, if one were to object regarding self-awareness (*svavedana*), [we reply: if cognition is admitted as being known even by a consciousness that inheres in the same object, then—just as in the case of a sprout and so forth—there is no fault whatsoever, since its own nature is presented [to itself] by another [cognition]. Otherwise, the loss of all practical activity (*vyavahāra*) regarding perceived objects would result in every respect. [Objection: But how is the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*) between the object and the cognition to be understood, given that the object is not perceived prior to its apprehension? [Reply: We say it is through the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And when an external object exists, there begins the investigation into whether it is stable or otherwise.

Therefore, just as in the case of taking the collection of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as the subject of the argument, even when taking the entire range of objects of valid cognition (*pramāṇagocara*) as the subject, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*)—of either kind—of the unstable probans by way of the nature of its locus (*āśrayasvarūpa*).

Now, if it is argued that because the power of an object cannot withstand scrutiny in every respect, "everything is incapable" (*aśaktaṃ sarvam*), then where is the subject (*pakṣa*) for this proposition, or what is the proof (*sādhana*)? [We reply: Indeed, the capacity of seeds and the like toward sprouts and so forth is observed. For there is no such thing as an impossibility regarding what is actually perceived.

For experience alone is the ultimate limit of every means of valid cognition known as investigation. Furthermore, if one does not accept this, how could a person who regards themselves as authoritative infer fire from smoke? Afflicted by wind, heat, cold, or rain, would such a person act toward both water and fire in the same way, or perhaps refrain from acting altogether?

How is it that you yourself, while knowing the absence of a probans when another has put forward a proof by falsely attributing a power to it, are eager to offer a refutation out of a desire for victory over him? Even there, you take care to state only "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) and so forth, rather than a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*). Thus it follows that there is no conviction even regarding oneself. Therefore, you must say something, having been deceived by someone; for the power [of words] with respect to objects is impossible to deny.
If that [existence] is held to be conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and not ultimate (*paramārtha*), then let it be so—whether conventionally or ultimately; what is the point of insistence here?

Now, if the thought is that momentariness, being endowed with conventional power, must also be conventional and not ultimate, to that too it is replied: Here, virtuous persons undertake the investigation into permanence, impermanence, and so forth, because the practice of reality is the cause for the fruits of higher status and the supreme good; for such practice is impossible if there is no certainty regarding that [reality]. And as to whether that practice—assisted by a permanent God and so forth, or independent of Him—is the cause of those fruits, the introduction of the doctrine of momentary flux occurs in such a context for those who are skilled in the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In this regard, if conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) alone is the means for achieving the supreme human goal by way of the necessary concomitance of the avoidance of what is undesirable and the preservation of one's capacity, then let this momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*) also be merely conventional reality, since it is precisely through its utility for the supreme human goal that we have such regard for momentariness. What need have we for an investigation into ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), wherein there is no distinction between means of valid cognition and their objects, nor any conventional practice of probandum and proof?

Now, if such [momentariness] is possible even in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), then the occurrence of power drawn forth by that [ultimate reality], or momentary destruction as its consequence, does not transcend ultimate reality. However, in the absence of the distinction between means and objects of knowledge, whether through the total exclusion of consciousness or through the establishment of mere self-awareness, the non-establishment of momentary destruction—just as during the time of ascertaining the absence of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—does not cause any distress.

In this regard, as for one who is alarmed by the claim that the proof of momentariness is not ultimately real (*atāttvika*), why is he not likewise alarmed by the claim that the attainment of the fruits of heaven and liberation is not ultimately real? Therefore, as long as there is the conventional usage of the relationship between the probandum and the probans, so long does that which withstands critical examination possess ultimate reality; for, from the perspective of one who speaks of the fruit, further subtle analysis is as good as non-existent. Enough with this prolixity.

By this, it has been demonstrated that everything described by the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, who clings to an untenable position, after raising a series of arguments to refute the commentator’s [Udayana’s] theory of causality, is entirely useless. For instance, if this much effort serves no purpose other than pointing out a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), what is to be gained by it? Furthermore, the lack of proof has already been refuted; for one who engages in the investigation of the true nature of things with the desire to achieve a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the establishment of causal capacity (*śakti*) is an inseparable concomitant of that activity.

Therefore, the claim that the production of an effect by means of either succession or simultaneity is necessarily pervaded [by those two] is likewise unestablished. Furthermore, what was stated—that this [argument] is without scope—is also unfounded. Moreover, whatever he has suspected there and offered as a rebuttal out of conceit, [we reply: ultimately, that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) is what is here considered *paramārthasat* (ultimately real).

Having raised the objection that such a statement is redundant, [the author] wrote: "If you argue that whatever is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) conventionally is thus ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), then why is existence not likewise accepted for universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), and so forth? If you claim that these lack causal efficiency even conventionally, we say no; for the appearance of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is equal in both cases."

For instance, wherever the eye operates, there the appearance of a pillar or the like does not occur in the manner of the hair-phantoms seen by one with ophthalmia; thus, the capacity of the pillar and so forth is understood. Likewise, among buffaloes and the like, there is no cognition of the recurrence (anvaya) of [the universal] "cow" and so forth. Furthermore, in mere atoms—which lack conjunction and the like—there is no cognition of the conjunction of a composite whole (avayavin); thus, the capacity of the universal (sāmānya) and other categories is also understood.

That too is without substance. For it is not the case that mere conventionality is what is to be accepted or rejected; otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of accepting even the conventions of the ignorant, and the absurd consequence of rejecting even the conventions of the wise which are directed toward accomplishing the supreme human goal. For conventionality is simply a cognition that is pleasing so long as it is not subjected to critical analysis.

Furthermore, there is the child’s grasping at a face reflected in the surface of a mirror as being real—a grasping devoid of inquiry—or the grasping of the wise for the means to achieve the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), which is rendered futile by your analysis; yet this [latter] is not to be abandoned, because its abandonment would imply a lack of concern for the investigation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).

If you argue: "This investigation belongs only to the Buddhist; for me, however, there is simply no acceptance [of it]. Therefore, the contradiction with the Buddhist's own tenets and the fault of the probans being unestablished for the proponent belong only to the Buddhist," then we reply: Is this investigation a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, the distinction that "this is yours, not mine" is untenable. On the contrary, by accepting its inclusion within valid means of knowledge, it follows that you have no standing even in the role of an opponent (*prativādin*).

Now, if it is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), then even if some matter set forth in a portion of scripture is not valid, there is no harm to the subject at hand; for this follows:
"If something in a certain treatise is not logical, it is refuted—provided one says that another thing is also logical. This is the established practice of the royal court.

Thus, for one who abides by the Sautrāntika tenet and establishes momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the contradiction with another state of duration (*sthityantara*) is not a subverting objection. Otherwise, [it would contradict the teaching that] "space and the two cessations—these three unconditioned things (*asaṃskṛta*) are eternal."

By this [statement], why is there no mention of sublation? Furthermore, for the Naiyāyika who accepts comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how is there no contradiction with his own tenet (*siddhānta*) when compared to the Vaiśeṣika? However, their having different systems (*bhinnaprasthānatva*) is the same [in both cases]. Moreover, the reliance on causal capacity (*śakti*) does not overstep the Sautrāntika method. If even there were no establishment of causal capacity, then one would merely be describing one's own mental representation (*svapratibhāsamātra*) and would not be abiding by the Buddhist tenet.

Therefore, even when there is a contradiction with another system (*nayāntara*), there is no possibility of contradicting the established tenet (*siddhānta*), nor is there a failure of the proponent's proof (*vādyasiddhi*). Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*), there is no conformity whatsoever to a treatise (*śāstra*).

If, however, that investigation is valid, then even though it is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), the causal capacity of the object must necessarily be admitted. Consequently, the conceptualization of universals, inherence, and so forth—which are held to be eternal—is sublated by the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) brought about by that very capacity; thus, being a lower conventionality, such conceptualization is not to be accepted as having causal efficiency, just like the conventions of children. If there is no such capacity, let the admission of existence for that which is incapable of producing a cognition of itself be merely a conventionality; however, it is certain that this is a conventionality even lower than the lower.

For this very reason, since each successive level is established as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) in relation to the preceding conventional level, one must necessarily admit that the conventionality which possesses unsurpassed causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is indeed the ultimate reality. Thus, that which exists by virtue of such [causal efficacy] is called "ultimately existent" (*paramārthasat*). To illustrate: for an ordinary person, in relation to the perception of a face in a mirror, the face appearing there is said to be the "ultimate reality" because it is actually non-existent.

And with respect to that, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that the rays of the eye, reflected back by the mirror, perceive one's own face itself. Thus, among successive conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*), when they are powerful, each preceding one is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and each succeeding one is the ultimate, as long as there is the stability of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). For if that is transcended, since the distinction between the grasped and the grasper collapses, there results the establishment of mere appearance (*pratibhāsamātra*); so where would there be any talk of the conventional?

Therefore, it is precisely the capacity for ultimate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) that is denoted by the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*). Consequently, universals (*sāmānya*) and other such conventionalities do not reach the status of the ultimate merely by virtue of being conventionalities. [This is because] the validity of the analysis of those [conventionalities] is disregarded—like one closing one's eyes like an elephant—and thus it is said that in various contexts, power alone is the ultimate reality in truth, while universals and so forth are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛti-sat*).

In this way, the whole (*avayavin*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth, are also conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*); they are to be understood in both ways [as conventional and ultimate] because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, power (*śakti*) is admitted to have the nature of momentary existence (*kṣaṇasthitidharmatā*). For it is merely atoms produced in a specific state, or two substances devoid of conjunction, that serve as the basis for those respective cognitions; what is the use of postulating a "whole"? How then can the inclusion of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth be equated with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by virtue of being mere convention?

And if their similarity were based on that alone, what would be the point of proclaiming this logical proof? Let it not be the case that they are merely conventional (*adharasaṃvṛti*); such is the application of the principle. However, that [status] is difficult to avoid for that which is endowed with causal capacity or its substratum, due to their connection with momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), as was stated previously. If there is an absence of the endowment with causal capacity, then even if its substratum is conventionally real, how could one avoid the status of being a mere lower convention for its properties, such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth? Therefore, their similarity consists precisely in being mere conventionality. And in that regard, the fault has already been stated.
Furthermore, this argument regarding "arising" which consists in the exclusion of cognition (*buddhi-vyatireka*) will also be examined in the discussion on *apoha*.

As for what was said: "Moreover, if conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is a cognition whose true nature is not determined, then for that very reason the establishment of cause and effect is accepted; if that is so, one must admit that the causal relationship between non-momentary things alone is what is well-known among all worldly practitioners. What is the use of subtle analysis in that regard?"—that too is incorrect.

For instance, when a Sautrāntika states a proof (*sādhana*) to establish in reality the collection of entities that are momentary by nature—since there is no application of proof or refutation when one abides solely in one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—and since its capacity is indeed real and is apprehended through the three types of perception and non-perception (*trividhapratyakṣānupalambha*), how can this [criticism] be leveled against him?

Or, having set aside an object established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) belonging to another’s domain, how could he possibly remain [in his position]? And if that much suffices to establish real momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), then it simply demonstrates that non-momentary things possess a conventional causal relationship (*sāṃvṛta-kāryakāraṇabhāva*); so what is the point of this effort to accept [the opponent's view]? Furthermore, an investigation cannot be avoided merely because it is flashing before one's mind; for if it could, then one would also have to disregard the refutations of the substantiality of shadows and so forth, as well as the proofs for a Creator God (*Īśvara*) and other such arguments.

Regarding those who speak against that [position], even that analysis is subtle; therefore, enough now with this laborious study of the succession of treatises. And so, what is the use of such subtle analysis there? This analysis is not "beautiful" (cārur) in the sense that it is appropriate to say "there is a rejection of non-momentariness. Furthermore, that [rejection] is not established by mere assertion alone. We, however, have presented a proof to overcome [the notion of] permanence, and there is no fault in that.

Furthermore, if there were the undesirable consequence of allowing room for another subtle investigation when one is already intent upon the subtle investigation at hand, that would indeed be a fault.

As for the claim that "by means of subtle scrutiny, the very relation of cause and effect would be destroyed, according to the logic you have stated," this too is only fitting for one who is dull-witted by faith alone. For as long as we do not tolerate the abandonment of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) of entities, our acceptance of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and our refutation of permanence remain unassailable.

But when the mind proceeds toward another powerful investigation that discriminates capacity (*śakti*), then we shall also abandon the conviction in momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*), for the logic of the stick is the same. Furthermore, the acceptance of capacity in this way cannot revive both permanence and impermanence simultaneously, because it is not common to both. For indeed, the conviction that "capacity exists somewhere, at some time" is not based on a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What then? [It is based on valid cognition.]

"This [seed] and so forth is capable of producing the sprout and so forth"—it is by means of this very form that [the capacity] is known through perception itself. And just as that perception is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too is it a means of knowledge regarding the sequential or non-sequential nature of effects. By such a line of reasoning, the capacity, when it comes to rest in momentariness, is not common to permanent entities; how, then, could there be a revival of both [momentariness and permanence]?

Thus, when an investigation that strongly indicates the collapse of the causal relationship is underway, it must be stated that momentariness alone—which is established by its own capacity—is the ultimate conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), whereas permanence is merely an inferior conventionality, like [the categories of] universals and so forth. However, once that investigation has been shaken, there is no ground for any doubt; thus, capacity is indeed established.

How, then, can it be said that "nevertheless, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), momentariness is not proven by way of existence, nor is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by succession and simultaneity established"? For it has already been shown that [the argument] is sustainable even under the view that power (*śakti*) is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).

Now, one might object: just as for one who, within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), seeks the supreme human goal and engages in the search for its means, there is no possibility of remaining without relying on the power of the object, so too, because of the search for means based on the thought "I must become a possessor of that fruit," the grasping at permanence necessarily follows. Therefore, let even the permanent [self] exist as a true conventionality; why then would it be an object of an inferior conventionality? True. First of all, the grasping at a permanent self is the motivator for the search for means, and that [grasping] is not prohibited.

A permanent self, however, deserves further investigation. Nor is it appropriate to accept it on that basis alone, because it would then have as its object a specific conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Thus, let the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*) be the motivator for inquiry; one may indeed say, "What is to be done with this capacity? But by these words, no transgression of capacity is shown, since the apprehension of capacity is accepted as the cause for seeking the means [to knowledge]. However, this is not possible regarding a self.

If it is argued that the apprehension of causal capacity (*śakti*) is also a motivator only conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), let it be so, whether conventionally or in reality (*tattvena*). For once the capacity is established, the fact that the apprehension of a self (*ātman*) is also a motivator is likewise established; thus, there is no necessary implication of the establishment of a self. It has already been stated that if a definitive determination is required, the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) would be its sublation.
As for the claim that the apprehension of cause and effect establishes a fixed synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*), that will be discussed later in the *Anekāntacintā*.

Furthermore, as for this which was stated—that even through subtle analysis, the apprehension of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is impossible according to your own view because you do not admit the apprehension of one thing by another that is not connected—[we reply: since a connection (*pratibandha*) resides in two things, it cannot be grasped by perception, which apprehends only a single [object] at a time; thus, inference does not operate therein.

In our view, however, there is no impossibility of apprehending even the relation of cause and effect, because we do not accept the restrictive rule that perception must have only a single moment as its object. Accordingly, in the context of establishing the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it was demonstrated that even the perception of persons like us can sometimes operate with respect to objects such as the past and the future by the force of causes such as [clairvoyant] observation.

For it is not possible for the cognition of the relation between cause and effect and so forth to occur otherwise; thus, that [objection] is also entirely trivial. To explain: first of all, the perception of one thing by another is accepted by both proponents—those who maintain that things are momentary and those who maintain otherwise. In that regard, if you claim that there is a grasping of non-duality through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this contradicts reason. It is only logical that there is a grasping of duality. And this being the case, there is no contradiction in the grasping of the causal relationship.

Even one who maintains the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga) would incur only a minor loss by accepting [the opponent's position] in that way; for this is not something unseen or undesirable to him.
Previously, he too adopted his own philosophical tenet solely according to his own will;
why then should he not be able to adopt another at some point?

Now, if it is somehow logical that only the apprehension of non-duality is correct, then its opposite—the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect—which inclines toward [the reality of] causal efficiency, would be merely a matter of your own preference; where, then, would it be useful? If your intention is that, according to the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), the apprehension of the causal relation itself is impossible, then let the contradiction be pointed out: "The causal relation exists," for this is not a case of unestablished evidence (*asiddhi*). And we shall address that point later.

As for what was said—"If it is argued that this cognition arises solely from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), we say no; because even in this case there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*)"—in that regard too, he [the opponent] is unable to present any such valid evidence that establishes a quality characterized as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*), which is a distinct entity inherent in a substantial self (*ātman-dravya*) separate from body and mind; nor is there any other specific power of the mind or action that can establish this.

Thus, there is great faith [in this]. For it is the very power of the mind (*citta-śakti*) that is designated as "latent impression" (*vāsanā*). Therefore, for one who maintains the doctrine of the perception of mere unconnected moments, the beginningless practice of conventional discourse, the resulting latent impression, and the subsequent false cognition—all of this is like a succession of blind men and lacks any valid authority; thus, it should be understood as the mere prattle of the dull-witted.

The meaning is that the one under discussion is the Sautrāntika proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), who asserts the cognition of moments as being entirely unmixed. For him, the perception of a causal relationship is a false perception; thus, there is a great delusion. However, it is more appropriate to describe the Yogācāra, who denies the existence of a causal relationship, as a proponent of the cognition of mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanamātra*). And the refutation of that [Yogācāra] does not affect the proponent of momentary flux in the least.

Even for those who deny cause and effect, if there is a logical possibility for such a denial, then that too is not far-fetched; what then is the point of this persistence? Thus it is established: whether the capacity for causal activity is real or otherwise, in either case, the fault of "unestablished" (asiddhi) does not apply.
This concludes the first section, titled "The Section on the Property of the Subject" (pakṣadharmatā). [The second section: The Section on Positive Concomitance (anvaya)]

Nor is this a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*), because it is observed in the "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*)—the rain cloud; for a contradictory reason, characterized by pervasion with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), cannot possibly be observed in that which possesses the probandum. But is this not a rash assertion? For nowhere has the capacity of cognition to take momentary destruction as its object been perceived, nor is there any such determination. Furthermore, the establishment of momentary destruction in a rain cloud does not result from relying on the force of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is through perception that the recognition "this is that very same cloud" establishes its persistence over a period of time. Since inference is sublated by this [perception], it finds no scope; nor is there any other inference [to support it]. Furthermore, if one were to resort to an inference based on existence (*sattva*), then upon examining another instance for that inference, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, because it is not observed in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the contradiction is not resolved.

Furthermore, because [the reason] exists in the cloud—which is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—there is indeed no contradiction with the inconclusiveness of the non-existence [of the probandum]. Moreover, there is sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) regarding the thesis of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). As Śaṅkara said: "Because by perception itself the absence of the reversal of stability is established. Nor is this apprehension of identity between earlier and later times invalid, for it is reliable (*saṃvāditva*).

And likewise, the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* states: "Just as the validity of the cognition 'this is its effect' is accepted solely because of the absence of contradiction, so too the validity of the cognition 'these were produced by him in succession, not simultaneously,' as well as that of recognition such as 'I am that very same person' and 'this is that very same crystal,' must be accepted solely because of the absence of contradiction, since they share an identical status regarding their logical security (*yogakṣema*). This, however, is inconsistent.

For a conceptual construction that lacks a real objective basis (*aliṅga*), what is called "discrepancy" would have to consist either in the failure to attain purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) or in its lack of correspondence with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, since there is merely a mental determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "it is that very thing," no further operation of a [separate] means of valid cognition occurs here.

Nor is any causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) established as being tied to a single [cause], because there is no contradiction in such causal efficiency being produced even by something different, provided it possesses an equivalent capacity. For instance, just as one jar holds water, another jar existing at that same time does not necessarily hold water; likewise, if another [jar] were to hold water in the second moment, what fault would there be? As for dissimilar actions, there is no question at all.
Therefore, just as the action of cooking and so forth is established as being tied to fire and the like, and is thus experienced...

[12] One attains corroboration regarding the cognition of burning; however, no action is found within the range of perception that is bound to a unity between the initial and final moments, such that even the apprehension of a single entity would be corroborated.

If it is argued that because there is always a uniformity of single determination for all [cognizers], what further need is there for corroboration? We say no, because this is unproven (*asiddhatvāt*). For even if unity is to be determined by those of equal capacity, it cannot be established by "all" unless one is omniscient. There is no contradiction if some among the gods, sages, or yogis—who perceive what is beyond the senses—should occasionally be perceivers of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), since such superior powers are the seed of possibility.

If, however, this very nature called "momentary destruction" does not exist, then there would be no apprehension of it by those [means]; this is logical. And that [nature] has begun to be examined. Therefore, as long as its establishment as an intrinsic nature is not achieved, so long is the determination of the negation of momentary destruction for all things not established. For those who hate the perception of supersensible objects are not virtuous when they assert a negation based on mere non-apprehension, because that leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, let us set aside for now the fact that non-apprehension of a suitable object is incapable [of establishing existence] when the object is remote in terms of space and so forth. Furthermore, mere agreement among a few people—even in the case of hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia—is possible, yet it cannot establish a true correspondence with reality. And this is said with reference to perception (*pratyakṣa*).

But since people perceive a difference in entities based on a difference in moments through inference, how can they be prevented even here in this assembly, given that the practice of proving such [differences] cannot be barred in some cases? Therefore, for all people, there is no single determinative cognition—whether produced by perception or consisting of inference—that necessarily negates the determination of difference; nor is its validity established by correspondence with another means of valid cognition, as it is subject to deviation in the case of things like grass, kuśa-grass, plantain stalks, and the like, which grow again after being cut.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by this person who takes pride in his specialized terminology: "Now, recognition is seen even when it is non-concordant (*visaṃvādin*). Is the cognition of the relation between cause and effect not also seen to be non-concordant? If you say, "That which is non-concordant is not indeed a cognition of cause and effect, because it lacks validity (*apramāṇatva*)," [we reply] that the same applies here as well: that which is non-concordant is not indeed recognition, because it is a mere semblance (*ābhāsa*) of it.

It might be argued as follows: if the distinction between definitions could be established in the same manner as the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). For instance, even in the cognition of the causal relation, if one were to apprehend the production of smoke and so forth merely by the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*), one would have to abandon all caution regarding fire even when a donkey or the like is present, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). In the same way, it should be understood accordingly whether there is mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Furthermore, when the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—which consists of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) and is inclined toward grasping positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*)—is brought forward, as we have established in our *Trikapañcakacintā*:
"It does not abide therein, it is not born from another, nor has it come from elsewhere;
for if an effect were to exist when something is present, and not when that thing is absent, then it would belong to no one."

"In the case of establishing the relation of cause and effect," it is then that there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Thus, if even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), a difference in characteristics were shown—or could be shown—that is relevant to deviation and non-deviation, then this would be logical. But this is not the case, because in all instances of objects that are absolutely similar, the recognition of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) possesses a single uniform nature.

If there were a temporal restriction such that the delusion must necessarily cease after this much time, then this would be appropriate. However, in the case of a mass of hair that has been cut and regrown, even with the exhaustion of a human lifespan, the cessation of the delusion of oneness does not necessarily occur for one who exerts effort. If you argue [that it must], we say no; for even in that case, there is no such restriction. For even for one who is striving, mere verbal assertion is not authoritative, and another logical proof is difficult to find.

And if another argument were to subvert the unity established by recognition, why would such a thing not be accepted in the present case as well? It is a great power of discernment that while the wretched inference based on past recognition alone was now incapable [of proving anything], your mere word is now sufficient regarding hair and the like.

If it is argued that since a non-differentiation is observed even when hair and the like are distinct, one may somehow maintain a cognition of difference in those cases, we say no; for such [non-differentiation] is frequently observed elsewhere as well. Indeed, when one pillar is removed and another similar pillar is placed in its stead, recognition does not fail to occur. This principle applies likewise to jars, cloths, crystals, and so forth, as long as an object of extreme similarity is obtained. And this same logic holds for perceptions occurring at different times.

However, even when two iron balls are perceived at the same time, there certainly occurs a determination of their difference. Therefore, regarding a pillar or the like—which is intended to be one—there arises a doubt: "Is this determination of oneness actually distinct [from the object], just as it is with another pillar, due to a difference in time; or is it non-distinct? How can such a doubt, which subverts the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), be refuted? If it is argued that no such doubt arises because a non-difference across moments has never been observed before, this too is not correct.

For it cannot be said that something does not exist simply because it is unperceived, since even an existing thing may go unnoticed due to its subtlety—just as the momentary arising and passing away [of moments] is not perceived despite the growth and decay of the body. Therefore, even when there is no perception, doubt remains unavoidable, characterized by the inclusion of the possibility of existence despite the difference. However, in the absence of such reflection, an ordinary person would have a firm and singular conviction; yet what they call such certainty is itself merely doubt. Furthermore, difference even through the distinction of moments is indeed "seen," because it is observed by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[14] Just as, for example, in the case of a stream and so forth, even though drops of water fall one after another in a certain portion of space, there occurs both the possibility of the determination "this is that very same water" and the possibility of its opposite.

If it is argued that the apprehension of oneness occurs where there is no perception of repetition—as in the case of a pillar and so forth, whereas it does not occur for one who perceives repetition—[we reply: indeed, it has already been established that in every instance involving a particularity arising from the difference between moments, our lack of perception constitutes a non-repetition. However, in the case of water, a pillar, and so forth, there is everywhere a repetition based upon a commonality consisting of the collection of those activities, which takes a gross object as its domain. Therefore, it is impossible to accept that perception functions to establish non-difference between two moments.
Even if a mere determination of oneness exists, it is incapable [of proving such non-difference] due to its fallibility.

[Objection: Surely, in all cases such as [the perception of] blue and so forth, the validity of perception is established because its operation is followed by a subsequent conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*). Therefore, let even the determination of their identity illuminate the validity of this [perception] precisely because it has a single object. [Reply: This is not so; for the sense-cognition does not possess validity with respect to the object of every subsequent conceptual cognition. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even a cognition whose object is a mirage would have validity regarding water, since it is determined as water.

The logical principle is that validity depends upon conceptual determination; therefore, in the absence of such determination, there is no validity. However, when that determination arises, validity depends solely upon corroboration (*saṃvāda*). And it has already been explained that this [corroboration] is not the same as the conceptual determination of a single [object]. Now, one might object: "In cases where there is sublation (*bādha*), there is invalidity; where there is no sublation, there is validity—is this not sufficient? This approach is applicable even to the appearance of a sky that seems to be bending down, as it extends across different places, times, and persons; yet, when scrutinized, it falls apart. This is the same in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as well.

Furthermore, regarding this so-called "non-sublation" (*abādha*), there are two alternatives: is it the absence of sublation, or the non-perception of sublation? In these two cases, respectively, [the arguments] are unproven (*asiddhi*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), which are difficult to refute. This is because negation cannot be established by mere non-perception, and because a subverting inference (*bādhaka-anumāna*) will be stated later.

Now, if this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is designated as being of the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it be sublated by an inference? Moreover, by the very assertion that it is not subject to sublation, one has already granted an opening for the inference itself at the moment when the possibility of a subverting factor is being considered.

If it is argued that since the establishment or sublation of validity itself is the subject at hand, perception alone should be its sublater—then what can even a hundred perceptions do to this [validity] when its firmness is established through corroboration? Therefore, even by means of perception, the sublation of this [validity] brings to mind the possibility of a weakening of corroboration, which in turn calls inference into play.

Furthermore, has it not been observed that the recognition—"the magician is drawing out with his mouth the ball submerged in his head"—is sublated by an inference based on the contingency of there being a hole in his head? Let it be granted that even in the case at hand, what is sublated is not perception. Therefore, the claim that this [recognition] is perception is merely a borrowed ornament, providing no protection.

Just as the appearance of a downward-bent sky, despite being universally acknowledged, is certainly not uncontradicted, so too it is clear that it is not non-discrepant either. In exactly the same way, the apprehension of oneness, despite being universally acknowledged, is not non-discrepant. For, without the arising of a determination of that [oneness], there can be no further corroboration—consisting in the nature of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and so forth—in the cognition "this is that very same [thing]" regarding the perception of the curved sky.

Therefore, even in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is impossible to establish the conventional designation of non-validity. Just as that is so, for one who maintains that validity is determined by correspondence (*saṃvāda*), how can there be a conventional designation of validity for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) in the absence of such correspondence? Furthermore, when both [validity and non-validity] are unascertained, doubt (*saṃśaya*) based on both is established. Moreover, since its definition is seen to deviate (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of plantain trunks and the like, it is also deficient in both desired and undesired factors. How, then, could it possess validity?

Furthermore, one who says that a cognition which is thus contradictory is not actually recognition at all because it is a mere semblance of it, must also necessarily say: "That 'knowability' (*prameyatva*) which, when used as a reason for sound and so forth, deviates from the probandum, is not truly knowability at all because it is a mere semblance of it."

Now, if "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is merely the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that [property] remains unimpaired even in the case of what is errant (*vyabhicārin*). If that is so, then the purpose of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is merely the non-merging of what was previously perceived; and that exists even for what is errant. Whether recognition is called an action or not, one must simply say that it is not a means of valid cognition at all. You should also say that whatever possesses knowability yet is errant is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) at all.

Since a deviation [of the reason] in one case is not prevented because it might likewise occur elsewhere due to the fact that [all things] possess a single characteristic, it is not impossible even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Furthermore, as for one who says: "That which is non-concordant is not indeed a recognition at all, because it is a mere semblance of it," he must also say: "In the case of sound and so forth, that which is the probans 'knowability' (prameyatva) and which deviates from the probandum—that very knowability is not actually knowability at all, because it is a mere semblance of it."

Now, if "knowability" (*prameyatva*) consists merely in being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that property is not lacking even in the case of a deviant [reason]. If that is so, then the purpose of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is merely the non-separation from what was previously perceived; and that [purpose] exists even for a deviant [reason]. Whether one calls it "recognition" or not, one must simply say that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). You should also say this regarding knowability: that which is deviant is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) at all.

Since there is no deviation in one case due to the fact that [the cognition] has a single characteristic, it cannot be ruled out even in other cases where such [deviation] is possible; thus, this is not impossible even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). [Objection: But surely, at the time when there is a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), the inference "there is fire here" and a non-inference are identical in form. How then can there be confidence in one case and not in the other? [Reply: Because of the distinction made by way of the reason (*hetu*).

For just as one [cognition] is produced by the ascertainment of a three-fold mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) while another is otherwise—as it has been shown that the cognition of the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is sometimes perfectly pure, being established through perception and non-perception (*adhyakṣānupalabdhi*), while at other times it is otherwise—so too, because their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are distinct, there is no confusion between reliability (*āśvāsa*) and unreliability (*anāśvāsa*). Likewise, this is not possible in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), because even when the object is deceptive, that cognition functions just like the cognition of one whose sense faculties are unimpaired.
Nor is there any other distinction pointed out by others; for [recognition] is merely a persistence over a long period of time, which is [often] intense...

[16] Due to delusion, even when there is a delay in the convergence of the causal complex for error caused by factors such as the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), it is still logically possible, as was stated previously. Alternatively, if one accepts that inference is the cognition of an imperceptible object based on any [mark] whatsoever, then that which is subject to deviation cannot be a logical mark (*liṅga*) or an inference; thus, one who maintains this cessation [of error] would ask: for what purpose would one state the definition of a logical mark—such as its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—or the inference arising from it?

Furthermore, even if one observes deviation, it is incapable of [establishing] deviation; for if deviation were to occur despite the mere non-observation of it due to a delay in obtaining the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it would follow that anything could serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, the definition must indeed be stated—that by the observation of which certainty arises, and by the non-observation of which lack of confidence is produced. Otherwise, a discerning person would not undertake an action corresponding to that [mark].

For there certainly exist proofs for those who maintain opposing views—proofs that, due to long-term habituation, have their validity manifested by the power of meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), yet whose objects of perception are subject to deviation, just like the proofs for momentariness and so forth. Therefore, on the grounds of such deviation, should one now abandon all proofs merely because they are not perceived? Or, since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the existence of] future things would be untenable, should a discerning person enter into a fruitless exertion of effort in accordance with those [opposing] proofs?

However, regarding the definition of the reason as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, if that [definition] is not attained when one examines its characteristics, then at that very moment, by abandoning the hand [of inquiry], one does not enter into the path of reasoning. Or, if that definition is attained, one should simply adopt it. Therefore, resorting to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not sound, because the undertaking of this discrimination is precisely for the sake of refuting deviation (*vyatireka*).

If it is asked how the definition can be inexpressible, consider all of this even in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*): as long as you do not perceive a difference in the definitions, you—failing to observe any deviation in one case—should not, merely by the non-observation of deviation, place absolute confidence in the other. Therefore, if sublation were possible for that which possesses the definition, the definition itself would be refuted; thus, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases.

Therefore, let this recognition dispel the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for, being stained by that suspicion, it is neither able to establish the persistence of an object over time, nor is it able to preclude inference. How then can the thesis be said to be contradicted by perception in dependence upon it? Or how could there be an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the "cloud," which serves as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)?

Now, let it be that recognition lacks validity, or that the certainty of stability following from it does not exist; however, how can the determination of momentariness be established in what has been made the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), such that the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the similar instance is possible? It is said: here, the capacity for the act of holding water on the part of a cloud necessarily entails a single functional nature (*ekārthasvabhāva*) that cannot be avoided.

And in the subsequent moments, such as the second and so forth, because that action has already been performed and cannot be performed again, one might perform another action of the same kind or of a different kind; or else, one might not perform any action at all—this is the position. Thus, it is also the case prior to the moment of performing that action.

[17] It must be stated: in that case, if the cloud possesses an intrinsic nature capable of producing that [rain], why would there ever be an interruption of its activity even at another moment, just as there is at the moment [of production]? Alternatively, if its intrinsic nature were capable of producing an activity to be brought about at another moment, then—just as at that other moment—it would follow that it would produce an activity of the same or a different kind even at that [present] moment. For since that capacity exists even at the other moment, production would occur; and that [capacity] is not diminished at other times either. Indeed, effects are delayed only due to the absence of their causes.

"When the efficient cause is present, why is there a delay for them? (TS 395). By this, the position that [the cause] does not act is also refuted. When even a delay is intolerable, then non-action is cast far away. Or, if there were incapacity, it would follow that it would not act even at the desired time, because it possesses a single, constant nature. And if there were a change in its nature, the momentary destruction of the cloud is established. In this regard, the formal argument is: whatever is capable of producing something at a certain time, that necessarily produces it at that time.

Just as the final causal complex [produces] its own effect, or that very rain-cloud while holding water performs the function of being a festival for the eyes of the farmers, or at the time of discharging water performs that action—since this [cloud] is capable of accomplishing both effects in both states, this is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). If capacity were established without actual production, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of everyone having the designation of "capacity" for everything everywhere; yet this conventional usage is recognized as restricted.

And no cause other than its production is possible for this [capacity]. Therefore, since it is necessarily present in the absence of production—that is, in the counter-example—it is deprived of its own existence through the loss of that which pervades its definition; thus, it must rest in production itself. Consequently, the state of being a producer is established as being invariably concomitant with the mere status of being the object of the conventional usage "capable"; hence, the pervasion is established.

Thus, whenever something is capable of performing a certain action, it necessarily performs that action at that time; for example, the final causal complex. And this [agent] is capable even at a time when all activity has been transcended. This [argument] should be applied to the alternative position that [the agent] never acts at any other time.

But if its nature were incapable, then whatever is incapable of performing a certain action does not perform it—just as *kodrava* grain does not produce a rice sprout. And this cloud is incapable in other moments just as it is in the moment when it does not act; thus, because of the perception of the opposite of the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*), the meaning of the reason is that it would never act at any time. The formulation of the contrapositive (*viparyaya-prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not perform a certain action is not capable of it, just as *kodrava* grain, which does not produce a rice sprout, is not capable of producing one. And [the cloud] does not perform in the second and subsequent moments the action accomplished in the first moment, nor the action accomplished in the second and subsequent moments [in the first moment].

Or, regarding the first moment: thus, through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), the fact that a cloud possesses a nature that is both capable and incapable with respect to its various actions produces a distinction [between them] at every moment. In this way, with respect to non-performance in every respect: whatever does not perform a certain action is not capable of it, just as *kodrava* grain, when not producing a rice sprout, is not capable of it; and [the cloud], at the time of non-performance, does not perform the action which is the effect of the time of performance. This is with respect to capability (*sāmarthya*).

Whatever performs an action is not incapable in that regard, like the final causal complex (*antyasāmagrī*). And this cloud performs the holding of water; thus, the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) distinguishes that which is capable of acting from the moment that is incapable.

For just as the capacity for effective existence is pervaded by production, so too is production pervaded by that [capacity]. That efficacy which is opposed to inefficacy pervades the causal operation; thus, it renders nugatory the perceived efficacy [of the cloud at one moment]. Therefore, due to its nature of being both efficacious and inefficacious, a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is established for the rain-cloud. How then can it be said that there is no inference other than that based on existence (*sattva*)?

In this context, the objection raised by some—that because "capacity" (*samartha*) and "fitness for causal operation" (*vyavahārayogyatā*) have distinct exclusions (*bhinnavyāvṛtti*), the logical reason (*hetu*) is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*)—is to be understood as having no application. Therefore, since a momentary entity that performs a single function possesses a nature that is either capable or otherwise in relation to subsequent moments, there is indeed a distinction; thus, by virtue of its momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), it attains the status of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*). Consequently, the establishment of existence (*sattva*) in a cloud is not contradictory.

Now, one might object: even for an entity that remains identical throughout its successive moments, the production or non-production of an effect is possible depending on its dependence upon the encounter with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); how, then, can this establish a difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)? Consequently, the fundamental reasons for the aforementioned reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, what could these auxiliaries possibly do for this entity that already possesses a capable nature, such that it would not otherwise proceed to perform its own function without depending on them? For dependence upon that which provides no assistance is logically impossible.

It is logical that one who is himself incapable, yet desires capability, must depend upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). However, it is contradictory to claim that these auxiliaries are both ineffective and yet objects of dependence. Regarding this, Śaṅkara [argues]: "The absence of auxiliaries is indeed what is called its incapacity. And that [incapacity] is removed by the causes of the totality of auxiliaries, because there is a contradiction between those two [incapacity and totality] existing together in one place. Furthermore, from the causes of totality, there is the exclusion of deficiency alone, not of that which possesses it [the entity]; for the totality is of the nature of the exclusion of the absence of auxiliaries."

Nor is the existence of that which possesses [the auxiliary causes] established by the appearance and disappearance of the completeness or deficiency of those auxiliaries, because it is distinct from them. For this very reason, the disappearance of that which possesses [the auxiliaries] cannot be established on the grounds of the exclusion of the absence of auxiliaries.

The author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* has said exactly this: "If it is asked what assistance the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) provide to that [primary cause], such that it does not act without them, [the answer is: they produce the very effect itself. For if they were to provide assistance to something other than that, they would not be auxiliaries at all. To explain: if they produced that [primary cause] itself, then they would be its producers, not its auxiliaries. Indeed, those who produce a single effect together with it are designated as its auxiliaries."

[The opponent] might object: "Let it be granted that even one who provides no assistance can be a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*). Nevertheless, if its capacity (*śakti*) existed previously, why does it not act then? If it did not exist, how can it act later when it is incapable? And if it becomes capable later, how can there not be a difference between the capable and the incapable states? For the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) constitutes a distinction. Anticipating this, [the author] replies: "Indeed, its capacity consists in the completeness of the cooperative causes (*sahakārisākalya*), while its incapacity consists in their deficiency (*vaikalya*). Therefore, due to the deficiency of the cooperative causes, it is said to be incapable beforehand."

Furthermore, [the cause] is capable of producing the whole; moreover, the distinction between the property (dharma) and the property-bearer (dharmin) has been established. Therefore, even when the capacity arises, it does not necessarily follow that the [entity] itself arises. Likewise, even upon the cessation of incapacity, there is no necessary cessation of that which possesses it, because there is no necessary connection (pratibandha).

All of this should be understood as already refuted in the discussion on *apoha* by the demonstration of the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), because the substratum itself exists in such a state through the manifestation and disappearance of its completeness or deficiency. Or, let there indeed be a difference between the property and the substratum; nor do we dispute that auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are ineffective in themselves. We maintain only that those [auxiliaries] alone are not the producers of the effect.

Nor does it produce the effect in its entirety; rather, that entity itself [produces it]. Since they exert effort for that very purpose, there is no need for further elaboration. And if the nature of that entity—which possesses the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā*) in its final moment—is exactly the same as it was in the first moment, then being compelled to act at that very time, it cannot be thwarted even by the curse of the gods.

But what is the point of this mere distressed outcry of yours, born from the pain of a vital wound? For just as, in order to avoid the consequence of [the entity's] being either capable or incapable, one postulates that capability and incapacity—which are characterized by completeness and deficiency—are distinct natures, so too it cannot be maintained that this nature of non-delayed action is anything other than the entity itself; for if it were, it would follow that the entity is not an agent.

Now, just as we maintain that capacity and incapacity are two distinct properties, and yet the entity itself is not affected in any way by their arising and passing away, so too, the property of non-delayed action and the property of delayed action are simply other properties. These arise and pass away according to the presence of auxiliary conditions and the non-delayed production of the effect; in that very same way, it is said that there is no change whatsoever to the entity itself.

Let it be said: let there simply be no production of an effect at this time, because that which is considered the cause remains in its original state. For it is not the case that only the auxiliary factors are the producers, nor is it the case that only the completeness [of conditions] is the producer; such being the case, even when completeness exists—

[20,1] Even the state of having the property of non-delayed action (*akṣepakriyā-dharmatva*), once arisen, does not produce the entity in question independently; for even if it were a producer, one would have to admit that the entity itself is the producer. However, the entity in question must also be accepted as the agent. And since its form is not distinct from its previous state, if it performs the action while being that [same] entity, it should have performed it previously as well; or, if it does not perform it, it should not perform it later either—thus the same refutation remains in force.

If, however, some other distinct entity such as "completeness" (*sākalya*) and so forth, which occurs only occasionally, is the cause, then it is logical that the effect, depending upon that [cause], should also be occasional. Thus, for every further conceptualization of additional properties, the entity remains indifferent [to the production of the effect]. Now, if the property of "unimpeded activity" has arisen, what logic is there for the effect not being produced from that? Therefore, the effect must necessarily be produced.

Furthermore, since that property of non-delayed action did not previously exist, there would be no occasion for the arising of the effect either. If that were the case, then non-delayed action would be inseparable from the production of the effect, and the production of the effect would be inseparable from non-delayed action; thus, mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is evident. Otherwise, if non-delayed action were not inseparable from the production of the effect, the emergence of the effect would not be necessitated by non-delayed action.

Furthermore, if the production of the effect were not invariably concomitant with non-delayed operation, then it would have to occur even prior to that [operation], because of its non-delayed nature. But if they share a single essence, then once completeness (*sākalya*) has arisen, a distinct property (*dharmāntara*), namely non-delayed operation, has come into being; what, then, has been stated by this terminology other than that "the effect has arisen"? And if that were the case, there would be no avoidance of the original fault. For there is no dispute regarding the birth of the effect itself; rather, the question is raised as to how the arising of the effect—which depends upon its own essential nature—can be occasional, given that that nature remains eternally the same.
