Therefore, if this designation "that which has the property of non-delayed action" or "that which produces" is applied by virtue of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), how could it ever fail to produce [the effect] if that nature existed even previously? Or, if a prior entity possessing a nature contrary to "non-delayed action" were to persist later, how could the production of an effect ever occur? Now, if that single entity alone were the agent, this would be logical; however, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer, and in the absence of its other auxiliary factors, [the effect does not arise] even for one that is otherwise powerful.

What contradiction is there in the production of an effect? It has been stated that cooperation (*sahakāritva*) consists in performing a single purpose, not in providing assistance. To this it is replied: if they perform the effect while being combined, then let them have cooperation characterized by the performance of a single purpose; who would forbid this? But from what source is it obtained that that effect must be produced by the combined [causes] alone? For if the preceding and succeeding effects were identical, then the impossibility of avoiding the consequence that an entity would necessarily be subject to either constant production or constant non-production would be unavoidable.

Therefore, it is the totality (*sāmagrī*) that is the producer, not a single factor; thus, the desire of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence (*sthiravādin*) has a different object. If it is argued that "it is indeed observed to be so," we reply that for this very reason the position of permanence is untenable. For every reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) culminates in its opposite. Consequently, if the producer were eternal, the produced effect would either exist at all times or never at all. But this is not the case; since the production of an effect occurs only when there is completeness [of conditions], the inherent nature [of a permanent entity] is destroyed by this restriction.

Now, if a cause were ever observed to be eternal at some place, then the consequence that it would always be an agent—given the admission of its eternity in that case—would be logical. However, since such a thing never exists, how can such a consequence be urged?

(9b) This too is vulgar. For instance, regarding the phrase "if [the entity] were eternal": this is its meaning. If that very nature of an entity which exists at a later time and is productive were to exist at an earlier time; or if that very nature which exists at an earlier time and is non-productive were to exist at a later time—then either production or non-production would necessarily be perceived. And that being the case, by superimposing identity upon two established states, it would follow that what is already established as production or non-production must indeed be so.
Since the identity of prior and posterior intrinsic natures is impossible, it is stated that "this being eternal"; what contradiction is there in this?

Now, one might ask: "If the identity between the preceding and succeeding states has not been perceived, how can it be superimposed? If that were the case, there should likewise be no superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl; for mother-of-pearl never comes within the range of perception as having the nature of silver. However, it is your own established conclusion that since the silver being superimposed was indeed perceived at some time, there is no flaw in the theory of superimposition. Likewise, even when such a situation arises, I do not perceive any identity between the natures of the preceding and succeeding states.

However, the prior and posterior natures being superimposed upon one another are already established. Therefore, the performance or non-performance of that superimposition is entirely consistent, just as there is burning when fire is superimposed upon a cluster of *guñjā* seeds.

Thus, Śaṅkara has revealed his own extreme lack of sophistication; this negation by the Buddhists—who assert that "non-momentary things do not exist"—is as irrelevant as the denial of blue and other colors to those born blind.

Therefore, this is established: if there were a permanent self-nature, the restriction of cause and effect could only exist through their conjunction; yet [your argument] merely nourishes the daydreams of the unfortunate by deluding others through the mention of irrelevant and useless matters. For the proponent of momentariness—who, by superimposing a distinction based on contradiction between the capacities and incapacities of things, attempts to establish his position—has not thought it necessary to provide a rebuttal to the specific kind of capacity and incapacity we have intended. Having abandoned that, he has instead fabricated [his own version].

[22,1] To construct a rebuttal by means of convention (*saṅketa*) demonstrates the great skill of this preeminent Naiyāyika. For even when one says, "Because there is smoke here, fire must be present," if someone were to assign the word "smoke" to a donkey or the like and thereby deny the existence of fire, there would be no fault. Indeed, the proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) states that whatever effect arises immediately after a cause—by virtue of its designation as "produced"—is capable of being that very thing. And this is not merely a novel convention.

For even in the world, the conventional usage of "capacity" (śakti) is based solely on the fact of producing [an effect]. Although production occurs only when there is completeness (*sākalya*), one does not call something "capable" by way of that completeness; rather, it is called so because of its production. This is because, even when completeness is present, if there is a delay, the conventional usage of "capacity" is not straightforwardly applied. Furthermore, even when the completeness of specific auxiliary factors has not been definitively ascertained, if production is observed, there arises the conventional usage: "this is capable in this respect. And such an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is what is called "capacity."

Even though there is a designation of difference in the phrase "its power" (*asya śaktiḥ*), [the power] is non-different [from the entity], just like its own nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, since that generative nature exists even prior [to the action], yet it does not generate [at that time], it follows as a certainty that the mother is also barren. In this context, even if you have employed the word "power" (*śakti*) somewhere, nothing is gained or lost for the entity through its manifestation or disappearance.

What follows from this being introduced? Since [the effect] is indeed non-different from the producer and the form of the producer due to their identity as producers, if there were no arising and passing away for those two, how could the effect be occasional? Or, if it possesses arising and passing away, its difference in intrinsic nature remains just as before.

But if even that [non-producer] does not produce a distinct form, then its existence would also be severed by arising and passing away. It would simply be a non-producing entity, which is the destruction of its very root. Therefore, you must say: for one who produces something to some extent, there is indeed a difference [between the producer and the non-producer], because of the imposition of contradictory properties—namely, the natures of being capable and incapable—at different times relative to the effect.

For this very reason, as the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* stated: "Because there is no contradiction due to the difference in time; just as a crystal is motionless prior to the arising of an action, and that same [crystal] is subsequently possessed of motion. If it is argued that this is not a valid example because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*), we say no, for that which is established by valid means of cognition cannot be considered "to be proven.

For if one were to argue that even the distinction [between entities] is unestablished due to the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsāt*), how could such a person be refuted? Therefore, in whatever manner a contradiction between two properties is observed, they must be accepted in exactly that way.

Just as that very same cause is capable with respect to its own effect but incapable with respect to another effect—so that the capacity and incapacity of a single entity toward different objects are not contradictory—likewise, even if there is a difference in capacity due to a difference in time, there is no distinction between the two cases because the non-difference of the possessor of the capacity is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This too is without substance; for by this [argument], one merely mimics the grandiosity of a mass of foam.

For indeed, it is certainly not possible to assert the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while disregarding perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). And in that regard, what is called "perception" is nothing other than conceptual recognition (*pratyabhijñā-vikalpa*), and that has already been refuted. As for the inference stated by Śaṅkara in his *Sthirasiddhi*: "An entity does not perish immediately after its arising, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatvāt*), like the exclusion of a thing (*vastuvyāvṛtti*)," this reason is purely positive (*anvayin*) because there exists no counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

If it is argued that there is a "doubtful negative concomitance" (*sandigdhavyatireka*) because there is no contradiction between being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), we reply: no, for indeed, the status of being an object of cognition cannot be established for anything in the case of momentariness. This is because that which has the property of existing for only a single moment (*kṣaṇasthitidharman*) has already passed away by the time of its apprehension through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and furthermore, if the past were perceptible, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). That [argument] is merely a fantasy. For instance: let there be no apprehension of the past; the apprehension of the present, even if it is momentary, will occur by means of a momentary cognition. Therefore, there is indeed no contradiction between being an object of cognition and momentariness.

Now, if it is argued that because an object is the cause [of cognition], an entity whose existence is required prior to the cognition would not be graspable at all if it did not persist into the subsequent moment; or, if it were to persist into the subsequent moment, it would simply be non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*)—then what is this royal decree that a graspable object must not be non-productive? If you say, "This is merely his convention (*samaya*)," then this is an occasion for logic (*nyāya*), not for convention. Therefore, one who is addicted to debate should instruct the opponent by presenting logic, without relying on convention.
For if convention (*samaya*) were the means of proof, there would be no such thing as "reasoning" (*nyāya*), since all things would be established [merely by it].
But how could reasoning, which exists precisely for the purpose of subverting convention, ever take refuge in that very convention?

If it is argued that there can be no apprehension by what has not yet arisen, and that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then how is there apprehension even by what has already arisen? For a cognition arises while experiencing its object; and that [arising] must be either produced by the object itself or produced by something else—what is the difference? As for the charge of over-extension, it applies equally [to both views], since the cognition is also produced by the eyes and other sense organs.

If it is argued that this is because it does not have the nature of being an object (*aviṣaya-svabhāvatvāt*), [we reply: surely an object is designated as such only when it is being perceived; there is no such thing as an "object" restricted by its genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the response "because it is not an object" means "it is not perceived because it is not being perceived"—where does this answer lead? If you say, "For the same reason, the sense organ itself is not perceived due to its very nature," we say no, because the perception of it by yogins is accepted. If you argue that this restriction is only with respect to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), then even subtle things and the like would be perceived by their very nature from the perspective of ordinary persons, and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Or else:
However, that very same causal complex, like light and visible form, produces both the cognition and the momentary object, such that they are experienced together.

Alternatively, the cognition produced by that [object], being restricted to its own object, grasps only that; or, it is produced as restricted to that by the totality of its causes (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). Thus, there is no difference. Therefore, how could those two—the object and the cognition—be subject to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of having a fixed birth in the state of the grasped and the grasper? Now, for the proponent of the theory of cognition with form (*sākāravijñānavādin*), the arising of the awareness of that [object's] own nature is held to proceed from the object itself. In that case, if there were the grasping of what is past, there would be an over-extension; and if there were a persistence into the moment of grasping, the establishment of permanence (*sthirasiddhi*) would follow—this is what is intended.

Is this, then, a *prasaṅga* argument (reductio ad absurdum), such that [the cognition] does not occur without depending on the approach of another [object]? If that were the case, because it would result in the opposite conclusion, either the permanence [of the object] would be established for you, or there would be the apprehension of what has already passed; thus, the arising of the knowledge of the object's own nature from the object itself would be impossible. And this being so, the maxim applies: "one thing is clearly eaten and another is vomited. Having set out to establish permanence, one instead undermines the theory of cognition with forms (*sākāravijñāna*) by means of its opposite.

Now, if it is merely said that for the Sautrāntika both of these [positions] are inconsistent, that too is not the case. For, according to the position that sensation arises with a form (*sākāra*), even if there is a persistence into a second moment, because the object is insentient (*jaḍa*), its manifestation is impossible; thus, the cognition of the object by the consciousness is simply the self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) of a nature that conforms to the opposite [form]. And in this way, there is no adherence to the present, since the proximity to that [object] has not ceased even in the past.

Nor is there an over-extension [of the argument], because similarity is established by means of another object; nor is the upholding of that [opponent's] view the subject at hand. For you, however, even by resorting to that view, the reason "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva) does not suffice to prove stability, because it fails to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika).

Furthermore, since a stable entity cannot be established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even a diamond (*vajra*) is included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*); how much more so the wretched crystal? Thus, since this [diamond] is undergoing change between its states of being capable and incapable, how can it serve as an example for the absence of contradiction despite a difference in capacity? Moreover, the attempt to demonstrate that there is no contradiction between capacity and incapacity through a difference in time, just as there is through a difference in object, is also ineffective; for in all cases, it is the counter-correlative property (*pratiyogin*) that constitutes the contradicting factor.

Furthermore, the non-performance of its own function is not the opposite of the performance of another's function; rather, it is simply the non-performance of its own function. Likewise, the performance of another's function is the opposite of the non-performance of that other's function, not of the performance of one's own function. For it is precisely to exclude [the possibility] that "it does not perform its own function" that it is said "it performs its own function. Moreover, the operation of perception establishes the distinction between entities as those that perform their own functions and those that perform the functions of others.

However, perception is not an absolute determiner regarding the difference in time, because recognition has already been refuted. Consequently, the performance of its own effect—which remains as the only alternative—is insufficient to resolve the contradiction. If it is argued that "the production of its own effect in dependence upon a plurality of moments is contradictory," this might be so if there were a functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing non-difference for that which possesses successive parts, just as there is for the distinction of objects; however, this has essentially been stated before. If you ask, "What is the proof for your position that it exists without depending on that [recognition]? [the answer follows].

It has already been stated that whatever is capable of producing something at a certain time must necessarily produce it at that time, and so forth; furthermore, the dependence on auxiliary causes has been refuted by the consequence that the effect would either always arise or never arise, regardless of the presence or absence of those auxiliaries. Therefore, for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), "capacity" is intended to mean nothing other than the very nature of producing. And if there were a difference in that [nature], how could there not be a loss of the entity's identity?

And as for what was prattled by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa: "Even if a power distinct from the possessor of power is admitted, nevertheless, a distinction between the potent and the non-potent is not necessarily established. Why? Because even in your own system, the rule that a difference in attributes necessitates a difference in the substratum is unproven. Furthermore, while demonstrating the separate utility of auxiliary causes even when the effect is a single entity, he wrote in the *Hetubindu*: "From the clay-lump and so forth, [the effects arise] from those things whose nature is clay," and so on.

And just as in that case there is no difference in the effect despite the difference in the nature of the clay and so forth, so too there will be non-difference despite the difference in the nature of being capable or incapable, because the uncontradicted determination is the same.

That too has been refuted by this [argument]. For there are indeed phenomena (*dharmas*) that are mutually contradictory and those that are not; however, contradiction or non-contradiction does not follow merely from the fact that they are *dharmas*. Indeed, it cannot be asserted that because being a Brahmin is not contradicted by being a grammarian, it must likewise not be contradicted by being an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*). Nor is it the case here that being an outcaste is pervaded by being a Brahmin, nor is it contradicted even by being a grammarian.

And just as in this case, it is "otherness" (*anyatva*) with respect to its own counter-correlate, Brahman, that constitutes the contradiction, and not [the property] of being a grammarian; likewise, the nature of being a producer is contradictory only to non-production, and not to a difference in the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of the entity. However, properties such as blueness or squareness may encounter contradiction with whiteness or circularity, but never with [properties such as] cause and effect.

Therefore, if—due to the impossibility of even a scent of contradiction—the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and the nature of earth must exist as non-different from a single substratum (*dharmin*), then what conscious person could conceive that this would also apply to two things that are absolutely opposed, such as that which produces a certain effect and its opposite? Furthermore, how is it to be understood whether something is contradictory or not?

When there is the affirmation of one thing through the exclusion of another, or the exclusion of one thing through the affirmation of another, those two are contradictory. Furthermore, there is not even the possibility of suspecting that the affirmation "made of clay" excludes "having a large belly. By the mention of its producer, the non-production of that [effect] is indeed excluded; and by the non-production of that [effect], its production of that [effect] is excluded. For even the negative compound sentence "it is not a producer of that" means simply "it is a non-producer of that"—this has surely not been forgotten.

Therefore, the contradiction between two phenomena must be accepted exactly as it is observed; it is appropriate to intend this specific distinction, and not merely with respect to a single time, because two things of equal validity do not function simultaneously.

For it is logical that a single entity itself could be endowed with activity and inactivity, blueness and non-blueness, and so forth, depending on a difference in time; or, for one who has applied a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward its very nature, it is reasonable that there is no contradiction regarding a difference in time when a dispute might arise in some respect. But it is clear that neither of these two cases exists. Therefore, the qualification "having an uncontradicted object" for the determination of unity (*ekatvādhyavasāya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, the mere determination of unity is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it depends entirely upon a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

Otherwise, one would not require a subverting argument even in the case of [illusory] hair and the like; yet a subverting argument has indeed been stated. Furthermore, if this [subject] were to undergo a distortion as if dreaming, and if no difference in nature is admitted for anything that is of a non-different essence, then the statement regarding the distinct utility of the causal factors would be the prattle of a child or a madman. Therefore, if you merely intend to establish a difference between the property and the substratum by disregarding their identity, that is of no use to the present context.

For instance, let properties (dharma) be either distinct from the substratum (dharmin) or not; at any rate, there exist certain mutually contradictory [properties] which, according to the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin), cannot even subsist without splitting their own locus. In that case, it is only logical for him to say either that such properties do not exist at all, or that even if they exist, they establish distinction only by depending on conditions (upādhi) such as time.
What is the point of this [argument], since those [properties] are already distinct from the substratum due to the separate application of auxiliary causes (sahakārin)?

If, however, his position were that only those things possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are differentiators, while those being differentiated themselves are not, then this would be logical. But since even forces (*bala*) and the like are observed to be differentiators from what lacks force, and these are indeed distinct because they consist of the nature of action (*kriyā*) and so forth; therefore, whether according to the Buddhist view or your own view, let the distinctions be constructed by conceptualization (*kalpanā*). Why then is there not an absolute real distinction (*tāttvika-bheda*) between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) now? For that is a different topic altogether.

However, it is established that the probandum is proven by the fact that those properties which exist in a state of contradiction, while residing in a single substratum (*dharmin*), cannot be avoided as long as they differentiate that substratum. Now, if it is merely pointed out that the opponent’s position is inconsistent—namely, that there is non-difference from the effect regarding the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) while simultaneously maintaining that they are the objects of the application of a distinct collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa-kalāpa*)—even so, since this does not undermine the point at hand, what is the use of it? Furthermore, because properties that possess differentiation act as differentiators, the appearance of inconsistency arises among those situated in different conceptual frameworks when they are considered in relation to one another in their countless variations.
It occurs in various locations; however, what that reality (*tattva*) is like will become clear through the examination of those respective locations.

[27,1] In this regard, if you intend that one should remain by elaborating upon whatever is irrelevant to the subject at hand, this is possible for anyone. Moreover, the discussion of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is not concluded by this much alone. Therefore, why this insistence on offering a reproach against one who is no more than an infant in the womb? Furthermore, if that were the case, his conclusion—that there is no difference in the substratum merely because of a difference in properties—would also be untenable.

It is said that the Buddhist does not assert a difference in the substrata (*dharmin*) merely on the basis of a difference in properties (*dharma*), but rather on the basis of contradiction. Otherwise, he would have to declare a difference in substrata even for such properties as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*). By this very point, the phrase "due to the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties" has been established by him himself. If one does not perceive any distinction between contradiction and mere difference, then it is appropriate that he has said what he did; what else remains to be said?

Furthermore, this very person has said: "How could that which has the nature of performing a subsequent effect perform that effect at the beginning? If it were to perform it, then it would not have the nature of performing a subsequent effect. For that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth. Nor is there a difference in the possessor of those natures due to the difference between the natures of producing the first and subsequent effects, because it has been stated that a difference in nature is subject to deviation."

That too is hollow. For if by the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) one intends the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then when there is a difference in that [nature], there is indeed a difference among things; where, then, is there any talk of deviation? Therefore, it is logical that the "difference in intrinsic nature" refers to the multiplicity of imagined properties (*kalpitadharma*). And the opponent does not establish a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) by that alone; rather, he does so through contradiction (*virodha*). Furthermore, even when there is such contradiction, there is no deviation regarding the difference in the substratum. For contradiction never deviates from difference, whereas difference may deviate from contradiction, as has already been stated.

If it is asked: "But if those phenomena (*dharmas*) are merely imagined (*kalpita*), where is the contradiction, or where is the distinction?"—here, there are two kinds of referents for the word "imagined. First, when there is a real entity excluded from this or that [other thing], there is a mere distinction appearing as a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); even that is imagined, like the blueness of a blue lotus and so forth. Second, that which resides in mere conceptual construction is imagined, like the horns of a donkey, the hair of a tortoise, or the three qualities (*triguṇa*) of primordial matter (*māyā*). In that regard, if the latter were the intended imagined object, it would not be correct to say "because of the cessation of distinction," for such things do not involve any actual distinction.

In the case of a past [moment], however, since it is the very nature of the entity itself that is determined with respect to the imagined object, the distinction or contradiction being established functions only by taking recourse to correspondence; thus, there is no fault.
As for this [objection]: "How could that which is the nature of this [entity] to perform a certain effect in a subsequent moment perform it in the first moment?"

Otherwise, it would follow that the production of a subsequent effect is not an inherent nature (svabhāva) [of the entity]. That too was spoken without due consideration. For if an entity possesses a stable nature, why should this effect occur only at a later time and not at an earlier time? And since that [earlier occurrence] is absent, how can the cause also have the nature of producing a subsequent effect? Indeed, words are beautiful when they conform to the facts; the state of affairs does not conform to the words, as is the case with kings.
If you say, "What can we do? Its birth occurs only subsequently," then let it be so.

If, however, it were stable, that [succession] would be impossible, and thus it must indicate instability. If you argue that even in the case of stability, this very nature belongs to it—namely, that it acts only in the subsequent moment—then all hope for valid cognition is destroyed, since one escapes the contradiction by resorting to "nature" even when it is subverted by valid cognition.

For even when it is stated, "There is fire here because of smoke," or "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," it is possible to assert: "This is simply its nature that now there is smoke here even though it is without fire. Therefore, the reliance on intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) occurs when it is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the reliance on intrinsic nature does not entail the abolition of the means of valid cognition. And the determination by means of valid cognition has indeed been established. To say that what has the nature of producing blue does not produce yellow and so forth is a statement made without due consideration.

For the negation concerns its being a material cause (*upādāna*), but not even its being a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); for it is impossible to refute that it may, in some way, serve as a cooperative factor even in that case. Nor is there a negation of one letter-sound being the material cause of another letter-sound; for we observe that turmeric, which is yellow, becomes the material cause of red when aided by the cooperation of a powder—thus, the illustrative example is inconsistent. Furthermore, if it is argued that just as blue does not produce yellow, so too a preceding [moment] does not produce the subsequent producer?

Therefore, enough with this persistence in such idle chatter. This is established: because of the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties, there is indeed a difference between that which has a generative nature and that which does not, just as there is a difference between distinct locations, so too between distinct times.

By this, that which the author of the *Nyāyamañjarī* also said is addressed: "Now, those whose proximity is required as the cause for the production of an effect are indeed those whose proximity is required; what do these auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) do for it? Nothing at all."

Those for whom only the effect conforms to their presence or absence, and who assemble with their proximity required by that very effect, are called "cooperators" (sahakārin) because they produce that intended effect together with the cause; however, they do not deserve to be called cooperators merely by being the agents of that [effect] with which they act.

(12b) Therefore, for that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), there is a twofold capacity (*sāmarthya*) in the production of its own effect: one is its innate capacity (*nija-sāmarthya*), and the second is an adventitious auxiliary cause (*āgantuka-sahakāry-antara*). For in the absence of these two, that effect does not arise; indeed, it is because the production of the effect is accepted as resulting from this twofold capacity that others—who, while grasping a single non-momentary entity, imagine the production of the effect from that alone—remain ignorant of the actual nature of causal capacities.

Because we admit that even for a non-momentary entity, its capacity to perform those various successive causal functions lies solely in its successive auxiliary causes; and thus, since the multiplicity of successive effects is established by the multiplicity of successive auxiliaries, it is impossible to prove that entities undergo change at every moment.

That too has been refuted. Even if the capacity imagined through another cause is unknown to us, nevertheless, that essential nature which has entered the sphere of conventional usage—namely, "that which produces"—must necessarily be admitted; for in our system, the capacity of an entity is reckoned as its so-called *svalakṣaṇa* (particular characteristic). Why, then, have you raised this objection by means of the conceptual alternatives: "Does it exist even before, or only afterwards?"?

In this regard, what has been stated by him has been explained. As for the qualification, "those whose presence is required solely by the effect," that too is useless. For if the effect itself were independent in its own production, then this would be appropriate; however, this being the case, the postulation of a capacity in the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) would be fruitless. Why [postulate] a capacity in the cause when, due to its very independence, the effect sometimes occurs and sometimes does not?

Through the obsession with establishing the efficacy of causes—whether that efficacy is considered a mere conventional designation or not—it follows that nothing whatsoever is capable anywhere. If you ask, "Let it be so; what is the fault? [we reply:

the intellect would be purified by the view that real causes are entirely incapable of anything, while the effect is non-existent and independent. But consider this: if the effect already exists in its own form at the time of production, for what purpose would it depend upon another thing?

Therefore, by the statement "the effect depends upon the totality," the meaning is simply that the totality alone is capable of producing the effect; nor is that [totality] distinct from the individual members of the totality. Consequently, the members themselves are the producers. Or, even if they were distinct, the completeness [of the causal complex] would be a cooperative factor just like any other external object, and thus there would be no difference [between our position and yours].

Therefore, since as many auxiliary factors as there are, each one is individually capable, how could there be a bypassing of the activity by those that already exist? For it is your established doctrine (*samaya*) that completeness alone is logically possible at a later time; yet even that [completeness] must have its origin derived from those very auxiliaries—if they were previously non-existent, how could there ever be a state devoid of existence as long as even one of them is absent?
If you argue: "This is merely the fault of the effect, in that it does not arise at times when these [causes] are incapable," then [we reply]:
if the effect does not come into being even when the cause remains identical in all its states, then what is the point of calling it a cause?
"Then the effect would be independent; that being so, it would not be an effect.
Do you not see this?

It might be argued: "It is not called its effect because it necessarily exists when that [cause] exists, but rather because it certainly does not exist when that is absent; thus, it is defined by the primacy of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)."
If there is no existence even when that [cause] exists, how can there be existence when it is absent?
Since its absence is necessitated by the absence of that [cause], how can that [existence] belong to it? (PVA II 411)

For if the cause were indeed producing the effect itself, then it could be said that its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that [effect]. But when the effect has not come into being despite the cause being ready to produce it—due to the cause's very independence—how can there be the cognition that "its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that [cause]"? Therefore, if there is a causal relationship, then it must necessarily be the case that just as the effect does not invariably arise in the absence of the cause, so too it would invariably arise in the presence of the cause.

And it does not tolerate being regarded as its own cause. Therefore, this connection of the arising and passing away characterized by the capacity and incapacity of causes—even through a succession of efforts—cannot be concealed among the four types of intellects, just like the offspring of an adulterer.

[30,9] As for what Śaṅkara also said: "Nor is the difference of a cause established merely because there is a difference in the effects due to a difference in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). For example, even though it is a single entity, a lamp produces various modifications of consciousness, wicks, and flames through a difference in auxiliaries, yet it does not itself differ, because its non-difference is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is a novel kind of sophistry on his part.

Regarding this objection—having raised the dilemma of whether this nature, which possesses the property of unimpeded activity and is denoted by the term "capacity" (*śakti*), existed previously as well, or only now—the proponent states that what is denoted by "capacity" is for him the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakārisākalya*). He then resolves the issue by asserting that there is a difference [between the two states] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized as capacity and incapacity, thereby establishing a difference in the cause based on the difference in the effect. But who indeed has set out to state a difference in the cause based on a difference in the effect, such that it would be necessary to speak in this manner?

The difference in effects resulting from a difference in auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) does not constitute a difference in the cause itself; rather, whatever has the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to produce something at a particular time, it necessarily produces that very thing. For instance, a lamp is not capable of producing its various effects, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), all at once, yet it generates them in rapid succession. Or, if it were like that, why would it not produce its homogeneous and heterogeneous effects simultaneously, even though they occur sequentially? Therefore, it is logical to conclude that for those [sequential effects], the lamp is indeed a distinct producer. This same principle applies elsewhere as well.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cognition of the persistence of crystal and the like is non-erroneous because no causes for their individual production or destruction are perceived—just as in the case of manifest objects such as lamps—that too is like shooting an arrow in the dark; for even in the case of a lamp, no cause for the production of one thing after another is perceived. Indeed, the wick, oil, and so forth are the causes of the lamp, and since these change from moment to moment or from lava to lava, how could there be any determination [of identity]?

Otherwise, even in the case of a crystal, why would one not accept that each preceding moment is distinct from each succeeding one, since they follow the pattern of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as cause and effect? Furthermore, although there is a perception of difference due to temporal change in the case of a lamp, such is not the case for its oil and wick; so how can it be said that the cause of the production of individual instances of lamps and the like is perceived, while it is not perceived for the crystal? As for the cause of their destruction, we shall consider it later.

Nor is it tenable to say that the destruction of its cause follows from the fragility of the lamp, because if there were no difference in the cause, it would follow that the effect—the lamp—would likewise not differ [from its cause].

[31,7] Now, if it is argued that the exhaustion of the wick and the oil is perceived because the lamp is deprived of its pervasion of the space being consumed, and that this very [deprivation] constitutes exhaustion: [we reply that] the oil was abundant before, but now it remains little; the wick is likewise. The lamp too, by relinquishing one portion of oil and wick after another, pervades successive other portions thereof. However, how can cessation be determined in every respect, given that recognition remains as it was?

If it is argued that at the time of the disintegration of the wick and so forth, an action arises in a part; from that, a disjunction arises; from that, the destruction of the conjunction; from that, the destruction of the substance composed of those parts; then again, an action [arises], and from conjunction, another substance arises—thus, the persistence of a single substance is not established.

Even if this [consciousness], while descending into the realm of experience, were to take heed of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), how could even a Buddhist—who likewise proclaims his own system—be prevented from doing so? (13b) From preceding homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), when another auxiliary object is obtained—such as wind, sunlight, or darkness—there arises from them another [effect] of equal magnitude, whether less or more, according to the convention of the power of the auxiliaries; thus, it is not the case for things such as the hundred-pointed crystal.

[The proof] is established by the successful application of identity. However, when he has instead put forward a formal argument (*sādhana*), then its establishment does not occur through his own procedure, nor is there sublation (*bādhā*) by your procedure.

[31,18] If it is argued: "Do wind and the other factors accumulate or diminish anything in the crystal and so forth, such that they are postulated as cooperative causes? For if being a cause were based merely on preceding existence, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [The reply is: No indeed; no gross accumulation or diminution whatsoever is produced in it by them. Precisely for this reason, there is the arising of something absolutely similar. However, as for the subtle [change], because it is impossible to perceive, it is just as unfit to be designated as "this" or "that," so too it is equally unfit to be negated.

Thus, when there is a confusion of many entities, it may happen that at some time a certain one might serve as an auxiliary to a particular entity; therefore, one should not conclude that because a single thing lacks all other auxiliaries, its capacity for production is impossible. This is the meaning of the argument. As for the proof of stability, if you are able to maintain your own system, you may do so; however, this present discussion concerns the investigation of the Buddhist proofs.

And in this matter at hand, where there are multiple effects, it must necessarily be manifold; by whom was it whispered into your ear that your employment of the lamp as an illustration would be appropriate? Thus it is said: "The disease is one thing, the medicine another."

As for what was also said—that the very same proof which establishes the non-difference of a lamp despite a difference in its effects due to a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), applies equally to that which is non-sequential (*akrama*) despite a difference in effects due to a difference in sequential auxiliary causes—that too is utterly incoherent. For it is precisely sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*) in the form of non-duality that expects the disappearance of difference in the case of the lamp; for a lamp, being possessed of resistance (*sapratigha*), cannot occupy a single location.

Furthermore, the perception of difference in an object located in a different place—even if it is extremely similar—is unavoidable, as in the case of a ball of clay. Therefore, sensory cognition, which has a single form, establishes the lamp as being one and the same. For it is observed that even when an object is different due to a difference in time, recognition arises toward it if it is extremely similar; and there is no means of proving oneness other than recognition.

How, then, does that very [cognition] not fail as a means of proof? Nor does recognition, despite its similarity, constitute a factor of doubt due to a difference in time, because deviation is observed and there is no difference in its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Even in a perception that manifests non-difference at once, there is no certainty; for it is not seen to be so in some cases. Indeed, even when two objects are perceived in succession by sensory cognition, they do not obstruct one another; what is perceived as having become one is indeed perceived as such. So how can there be a lack of confidence in all cases?

Therefore, the objection raised by means of the example of the lamp is useless. Even in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, having taken this very form as the example, he says [the following] while illuminating its underlying intention:

Furthermore, by whatever intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) form (*rūpa*) produces another form, it does not produce taste (*rasa*) and so forth by that same nature, because it would follow that taste and the rest would also possess the intrinsic nature of form. Consequently, every effect of form would be perceived by the eye; and this is not accepted [as true]. Therefore, just as form produces another form by its nature of producing another form, it produces consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone by its nature of producing consciousness, and not form and the like.

And by virtue of its nature of producing taste, it produces taste itself; likewise, by virtue of its natures of producing odor and touch, it produces those two alone. Similarly, even that which is non-momentary performs that very first effect by virtue of its nature of producing the first effect, and produces only the subsequent [effect] by virtue of its nature of producing the subsequent effect. It does not produce the first, nor the subsequent and subsequent. In this way, even regarding subsequent effects occurring over an infinite duration of time, specific natures are to be understood.

It is also incorrect to say that only the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are causes, while the possessor of the nature (*svabhāvin*) is not, for this would entail the consequence that form (*rūpa*) is not a cause, since it is only the intrinsic natures that function as causes. Now, if one does not admit a distinction of intrinsic natures in form, but rather maintains that there is only a single such nature by which it produces effects that have different aspects and occupy different locations—then how can one speak of a "distinction of intrinsic natures" on the grounds of that [single nature's] production of effects with distinct intrinsic natures?

But surely, in this way, another person also—by postulating the nature of an entity in accordance with the production of multiple effects of successive natures from a non-momentary entity that possesses a single, undifferentiated nature—does not deserve censure.

[33,3] This too is merely an attempt to confuse those whose minds are stained by envy. For instance, if you intend to say only this much—that even though its nature is undivided, like a lamp, it performs multiple functions such as destroying darkness—well then, who is there to forbid it? It is indeed possible that one thing performs many actions. Likewise, if a single entity were to perform multiple actions in both the preceding and succeeding moments while remaining of a single nature, there would be no dispute.

It is not tenable to claim that there is merely a delay in the effect in some cases and instantaneous action in others; for if multiple effects are produced simultaneously like a lamp, then the example of the lamp is redundant. If, however, you intend to say that multiple things capable of being produced exist as the effects of a single self, then it is valid. Indeed, even now, the lamp cannot be used as an illustration. Even when such an illustration is offered, this must be said in response.

Nor does this [argument] hold: that whatever is manifold must be produced by many [causes], like the effect of a lamp; for while it is true that manifold effects occur at different times, it cannot be established that what is being produced as manifold becomes the effect of only a single [cause]. Moreover, if a single agent were absent, there would simply be no production of the manifold. This is because we observe that manifold actions, such as burning and immersion, are performed by many distinct agents, such as water and fire. If it is argued that what is intended is a single entity undivided by differences in time, [we respond:]...

[33,13] You do not observe that which is manifold being produced by a single self that is separated by many intervals of time. However, you might say: "Whether it be one or many, whether at different times or at the same time, it arises from that which is eternal. But this is merely the presentation of a thesis; it neither establishes any desired point of your own nor does it refute a proof employed by another. So what is the use of this? Even so, there is nothing gained by the example of the lamp and its form.

Furthermore, even if one who asserts "is-ness" (*asti-tva*) were to differentiate an entity (*bhāva*) based on a difference in its effects, you should nevertheless remain composed after demonstrating the lack of logical necessity (*anaikāntika*) by means of this very point: "How can form (*rūpa*), which is itself undifferentiated, produce both color-form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), which are differentiated? Moreover, what is the use of further proving the oneness of form, since it is already established?

Furthermore, even regarding Śaṅkara, he appears to be thinking of nothing at all when he asserts that "it cannot be that by the very same nature which [the cause] is the cause of the modification of the wick, it is also the cause of the perception of the flame," for this would entail the consequence that those two possess that same nature; since there is no contradiction in a single thing performing multiple functions.

Now, just as the Buddhist has asserted: "If the very same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity persists even at another moment, then it would follow that it must produce [the effect] just as it does now; yet it does not produce it. Therefore, there is a difference in the intrinsic nature of the entity. For instance, if a lamp were to produce the modification of the wick by means of the very same form that produces cognition, then it would follow that the lamp is also identical [to the cognition]; yet such identity does not exist. Therefore, must the lamp also possess a distinct intrinsic nature?

Just as there is no difference in the cause despite the absence of identity among effects, so too it is intended that there is no difference in the cause even when effects exist at different times. Even then, the Buddhist, relying on the force of his own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), has superimposed a difference in the nature of the entity between its causal and non-causal states. If you find this untenable, then it is only right to state the refutation, such as the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*). If he is satisfied with that much alone, what is the use of this elaborate argument?

Now, even if that proof is indeed faulty, nevertheless, whatever is established by it is indeed established for the time being. Let there be a difference in the nature of the lamp, or let there not; regardless, what is the use of adducing it?

Furthermore, as for the argument called "the absence of identity among effects" which is intended to prove a difference in the nature of the lamp: if that [argument] possesses an established necessary connection with its own probandum, then if it were to establish a difference for anyone even simultaneously, what would be the use of this Buddhist proof? One should abandon the effort to establish one's own probandum through it, like a second foolish Karṇāṭaka who has set out toward Prayāga and Vaṭa-prayāta.

Otherwise, once difference has been established by this [argument], why would one even proceed to establish the difference of lamps? Or rather, no proof whatsoever would function to establish its probandum, having observed that proofs such as smoke establish their own respective probanda.

[34,14] Now, if this proof for the difference in the nature of the lamp is either sublated by perception (*adhyakṣa*) or devoid of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with its own probandum, then let that very proof perish; there is no harm to the Buddhist's argument at that point. Nevertheless, what is the purpose of its presentation? If, in competition with the Buddhist, this other comparison has been brought forward merely to render the investigation of that [lamp] insubstantial, then this position—that there is a difference in the nature of the lamp—is untenable.
If it is argued that, such being the case, there is only one specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) which is the producer of those [effects], then...

This [position], being devoid of scriptural authority and logical reasoning, does not please those of a disciplined nature—even if accepted out of mere rivalry—because, in the absence of a specific material cause (*upādāna*), their arising everywhere has never been observed, and so forth; likewise, if there were no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause, then the difference in the effect would result in its being accidental (*ākasmikatva*).

Furthermore, by stating that "otherwise, the non-production of the universe would result in its being of a universal nature" (*vaiśvarūpya*), how could he [the opponent] reinforce the very distinction of intrinsic natures (*svabhāvabheda*) through his own words? Nor is this logical. For instance, as for what was said: "If the lamp, by the very same intrinsic nature that is the cause of the transformation of the wick, were also [the cause] of the flame and so forth, then it would follow that the flame and so forth are also transformations of the wick; but this is not the case."

Therefore, the meaning of the opposite position is that a lamp functions with a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the modification of the wick, and with a distinct one in the flame and so forth. In that case, there is indeed a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because the lamp and such are perceived therein as being partless. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its appearing surrounded by an infinite variety of natures, like a cluster of *kadamba* flowers. Nor can it be asserted that these [parts] are unperceived, because if they possessed the nature of the lamp, their non-perception would be a contradiction.

Furthermore, if you maintain that even while possessing the nature of a lamp, its invisibility is contradictory, then why do you not conceive that it is also the cause of the wick’s transformation and the cause of the flame and so forth—since you are thus preoccupied with the fabrication of a mass of essential natures? Therefore, that which is not perceived cannot have the nature of a lamp. And if it were perceptible, there would be no avoiding the refutation of the objection regarding direct perception. To claim that some other entity, whether visible or invisible, distinct from the lamp itself, is the "nature of the lamp" is merely the language of the world of Nagas.

For the terms *svabhāva*, *svarūpa*, and *svalakṣaṇa* are well-established as denoting that which is non-different in nature. However, regarding a property (*dharma*) presented by conceptual construction—which, although appearing as if distinct [from the thing], is nevertheless applied the term "nature" (*svabhāva*) solely through the force of cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), just as it is said that "permanence is the nature of sound."

Therefore, if the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is applied in some cases—even to that which is distinct [from the entity]—just as the term "capacity" (*śakti*) is applied to an auxiliary (*sahakārin*), it nonetheless means that "it acts by means of another intrinsic nature," which is to say, "it acts by means of an auxiliary that is a distinct entity. Nor is the agency of the possessor of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvin*) intended to be precluded. Consequently, the word "intrinsic nature" refers to an external object. It follows, therefore, that by means of that very same non-distinct intrinsic nature, it produces distinct effects; the only difference is that it is surrounded by a multitude of auxiliaries.

And for whom would that [causal relation] not be accepted? Furthermore, auxiliary causes (sahakārin) are not to be postulated according to one's own whim; rather, they are only as many as there are operations of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehend positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). And since such an operation does not exist for anything distinct from the flame, oil, wick, and so forth, what is the point of postulating anything further? On the contrary, by postulating entities denoted by the term "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) and attempting to include them within the six categories (ṣaṭ-padārtha), why will you undergo this fruitless effort?

And when it has been thus established at the conclusion that the intrinsic nature (*nijam rūpam*), which is the denotation of the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), is a single entity that serves as the cause for multiple effects, then the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that "whatever is produced by a single nature must be a single thing"—is not proven.

That being the case, just as in the original consequence (*prasaṅga*), there is likewise no avoidance of the inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding the reverse (*viparyaya*) as well. Furthermore, their having a specific, restricted nature as their material cause does not stem from the lamp itself possessing a plurality of real natures; rather, it is through the method of abstraction (*apoddhāra*) within that causal complex (*sāmagrī*), by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that one [assigns] oil to one [factor], the wick to another, and the lamp to yet another. How then could the production of all these [factors] be observed everywhere?

As for the claim that there is a difference [in cognition] due to a difference in causes: in that case, one accepts that the diversity of the effect is caused by the heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) of the cause characterized as the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because this is precisely how it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It has been explained in the very treatise (*śāstra*) that the multiplicity of causes within the complex does not imply a manifold nature for a single [effect]. Therefore, enough of this insistence on conceptual constructions based merely on their own imagination, independent of valid cognition. Furthermore, it has already been stated that even if these distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*) were real, they would not result in any actual accomplishment of an object; thus, this [insistence on] existence is fruitless.

[36,3] In that case, let the intention of these two also be determined according to how Trilocana conducts himself. And so it is stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī*: "Even existence (*sattva*), though it is a unique [property], can be brought forward by means of the Mādhyamika method. For instance, even in the theory of momentariness, by whatever nature (*svabhāva*) a preceding form-moment produces the immediately succeeding moment, does it produce the taste-moment by that very same nature or by another nature? If it is by that very same [nature], then it follows that taste would also possess the nature of form."

For we do not observe a diversity of effects arising from a cause that possesses a single nature, as that would entail the consequence that the entire universe is without a cause. Suppose, then, that it produces [the effect] by means of a different nature. If this were so, it would follow that a single thing possesses two contradictory natures. For the nature that produces form is not non-deviant from the nature that produces taste. In that case, if there were a different nature, then existence and non-existence would both occur in that very same place. Existence and non-existence are directly contradictory and would thus divide the prior characteristic of form. Yet, such a divided [form] is not observed.

[36,12] This might be argued: "When the preceding moment of form (*rūpa*) is to produce taste (*rasa*), it is simply the preceding moment of taste itself that possesses a different nature; and there is no contradictory difference in nature. If this were so, then even for a non-momentary entity, when there are successive manifestations of effects, the successive auxiliary causes themselves would constitute a difference in nature. Thus, everything would be the same, except for your dogmatic attachment.

Therefore, for one who accepts [the reason] as being uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), existence (*sattva*)—which would otherwise deviate from momentary things because it would entail a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—does not exclude non-momentary things. For the very manner in which the difference in intrinsic nature is refuted applies equally to the case of non-momentariness; thus, existence does not exclude non-momentary things. Consequently, since the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is unestablished.

In this regard, first of all, this person—who possesses pride in his knowledge of the Buddhist tenets without having considered the finality of the Yogācāra system—speaks according to the logic of the Madhyamaka, claiming that both [schools] agree on the negation of cause and effect in reality. However, having refuted such a lower-level proof, it has already been demonstrated in the *Sākārasiddhi* that this [critique] holds only if the relation of cause and effect is not established. Furthermore, it was stated that our investigation into momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) proceeds on the basis that the relation of cause and effect is established; and that establishment occurs only when the reality of the subject-object relationship (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is apprehended.

And in that case, whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something else, let that alone be the effect and the cause, as in the case of the seed and the sprout. Just as one thing is observed to be the effect of another because it follows its positive and negative concomitance, so too, if multiple things are perceived to follow the positive and negative concomitance of a single thing, then must those many things also constitute a single effect? For if the perception of another's experience were denied, then not even a single thing would be the effect of another.

However, in the case of one who cannot be refuted (*anapalāpa*), even if there are many [causes], the effect of a single [cause] is not precluded. Therefore, by entering into the position of a proponent who denies the perception of another, nothing is gained. But when the existence of the apprehended and the apprehender is established, the principle that many things can have a single effect—just like a single thing—is the same. Thus, it follows that what is produced by a single essence must indeed be of a single form.

As for what was said—that we do not observe a diversity of effects arising from a cause that possesses a single intrinsic nature—that is sheer audacity. Or rather, does one not see a single lamp producing various transformations while simultaneously dispelling darkness? Or does one not see the sun causing both the destruction of darkness and the blossoming of lotuses? Or, being perpetually immersed in darkness, do you perhaps fail to see the thousand-rayed sun performing its thousands of functions?

The meaning is that because the cause has a single nature, there is no difference in the effects; thus, from a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is no heterogeneity among the effects. For this very reason, the universe is not without a cause. Therefore, the production of multiple effects from a single [cause] is not contradictory. However, by way of the effects, one speaks of two natures in combination, such as "form is the cause of form" and "form is the cause of taste. For this very reason, there is no talk of contradiction; for when a combination is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is not even a scent of contradiction, just as in the case of wind and sunlight in a single location of space.

As for what was stated—that the nature of producing form is indeed non-deviant from the nature of producing taste—even by that much, only a difference (*bheda*) is established, not a contradiction (*virodha*), as in the case of "produced" and "impermanent. For just as yellow, which is non-deviant from the absence of blue, cannot be blue, yet there is no contradiction merely by virtue of that; for it is impossible to assert that whatever differs from something else is necessarily contradictory with it without further qualification.

As for contradiction (*virodha*), although it is the rule that two impossibilities cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmī*), this occurs sometimes because the existence of one thing precludes the other, as in the case of fire and snow; and sometimes because, by their very nature, one property cannot exist where another is already established, as in the case of existence and non-existence, or blue and non-blue. In that regard, if the existence of one substance—whether blue or yellow—were to entail the preclusion of the other, then indeed there would be a contradiction known as "incompatibility through non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*).

But it is not by the mere fact of non-deviation from its absence; rather, there is merely a difference [between them] to that extent. Likewise, even between blueness and yellowness, there is merely a difference by the mere fact of non-deviation from their respective absences, but not contradiction (*virodha*). Contradiction, however, exists because when a substratum (*dharmin*) has accepted blueness, yellowness—which is itself a difference from non-blueness—is absent therein. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even producedness and impermanence, and so forth, would be contradictory merely by the fact of non-deviation from their absences.

[37,25] Now, how is there here the non-deviation from its absence? For there is no logical justification for the claim that "being produced" must necessarily be "impermanent. If this were so, what would be the justification for the claim that "that which is a producer of color must not be a producer of taste"? If you say it is because of being a producer of color itself, [38,1] we say no; for such a justification is exhausted by the qualification through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), since the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is unestablished. To explain: does "producer of color" mean that it is *only* a producer of color, or that it is the producer *of color alone*? It is the former.

In that regard, in the first position, there is merely the exclusion of the non-production of form, and not the exclusion or affirmation of the production of something else; for since there is a contradiction with that very [non-production] only when depending on another means of proof (*sādhana*), the exclusion itself remains unestablished. In the second position, however, the negation of the production of something else is established beyond doubt; it is simply that no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required therein.

For just as one [cause] has an invariable concomitance (*tan-nāntarīyakatva*) with that [effect], so too would there be no fault if the second [cause] were likewise; this is like the case of a lamp. However, the mere fact that something generates color does not constitute a refutation of its generating taste, because the property of generating color is already fulfilled even by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*); thus, there is no valid reasoning here either.

In the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpanā-buddhi*), the capacity to produce color appears as if it were a distinct real entity; likewise, the capacity to produce taste—which is invariably concomitant with the absence of that [color]—is determined to be entirely separate. For, since the operation of a distinct verbal authority (*śabda-pramāṇa*) is required, one concludes the contradiction by that much alone. This understanding is not determined by anyone even in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*); nor is there any utility in asserting a contradiction therein.

For contradiction (*virodha*) is established precisely for the purpose of excluding one from another within a single substratum (*dharmī*). Thus, if there were contact with a single substratum even in the case of contradiction, what would be the point of considering contradiction at all? However, in the case of blue and non-blue, etc., contradiction is employed as consisting in mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*).

[Objection: But surely, although there is no difference in their being invariably concomitant with mutual absence (*parasparābhāvāvyabhicāra*), how is it that for some properties there is a contradiction consisting in non-coexistence within a single substratum, while for others there is merely a distinction and not contradiction?

It has been stated here: when the affirmation of one thing occurs through the exclusion of another, or the exclusion of one thing occurs through the affirmation of another, they are necessarily contradictory by virtue of being contraries (*pratiyogin*). Where this condition does not apply, they are non-contradictory; so enough with further exertion. Thus, it is established that although the production of color and the production of taste do not deviate from each other's absence, there is merely a difference between them—like "producedness" and "impermanence"—which draws in a different means of valid cognition (*śabda-pramāṇa*), but there is no contradiction.

As for what was said—namely, "if there were another intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*) therein," and so forth—is that logical principle afraid of being produced (*kṛtaka*) and impermanent (*anityatva*)? If you say, "let the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) apply there as well," [we reply: surely a *prasaṅga* proceeds by means of the opponent's own admission; yet I have not admitted that contradiction—which is the cause for the impossibility of coexistence in a single locus—is established merely through the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of mutual exclusion. Is this your own admission, or is it the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*)? In either case, it is not my fault.

Furthermore, the contradiction between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*), and so forth, is much more clearly established; it is not the case [that they are identical]. Therefore, because their mutual non-deviation functions to negate identity (*tādātmya*), "being produced" itself is not "impermanence. If there were no negation, then upon the existence of the single entity "being produced," both its existence and its non-existence would follow. It is said that this would be like accepting both the existence and the non-existence of a thing—such as blue—when its non-blue exclusion is not distinguished. For "blue" is indeed its existence.

Furthermore, "non-blue" is an absence; the presence of "non-blue," which is pervaded by that absence, is not capable of remaining without drawing along its own absence, as it cannot exist without the pervader. Since the contradiction between existence and non-existence has already been established, there can be no coexistence within a single substratum (*ekadharmī*). Thus, whatever is blue is not non-blue, such as yellow and other objects; likewise, regarding a property (*dharma*), whatever is "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) is not "unproducedness," such as impermanence and so forth; and whatever is the production of color is not the production of non-color, such as the production of taste and so forth.

Otherwise, if the means of knowledge known as verbal testimony were to operate in one case regarding such things as being produced or having the nature of sound, it would follow that in another case regarding such things as impermanence or the production of flavor, there would be no need for any other means of knowledge.

Therefore, the fault would be that existence and non-existence would occur in one and the same place if there were identity (*tādātmya*); it is not so if they are its substrata (*tad-ādhāratva*). For if those two properties, which are mutually distinct, were to reside in one place, what kind of fault would there be? This is because the fault of existence and non-existence [occurring together] is already accounted for by the very proof of their difference. Indeed, even in the treatises, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is stated to be the definition of difference (*bheda*), not contradiction (*virodha*). The definition of contradiction, however, is well known to be something else entirely.

The negation of identity is also stated on the basis of the non-perception of an intrinsic nature that does not depend on qualifiers, and not from the perception of a contradiction. Thus, because of the association with contradictory properties characterized as existence and non-existence, the two properties themselves—which appear as attributes of that subject—become distinct; it is not the case that there is even talk of a difference between those two underlying subjects merely through their connection with various properties.

Furthermore, when two properties (*dharma*) are divided in such a way that they constitute the aforementioned mutual opposites, then there is also a division of their substratum (*dharmin*), just as in the case of the properties of being blue and not being blue, or existence and non-existence; and it is also like [the distinction between] producing and not producing a single effect. Therefore, existence and non-existence are directly contradictory; it is precisely the two properties of "being form" and "producing" which, appearing as the very nature of their own substrata, divide [it]. They do not, however, divide the substrate characterized by its prior heterogeneous nature, because there is no contradiction in those [properties] themselves.

For this very reason, it is not perceived as distinct; and since [the two states] possess the capacity or incapacity to produce the same effect, they indeed differentiate their own substratum by way of being mutual opposites. Furthermore, because the perception of non-difference is opposed by the determination of opposition, the operation of inference is thus entirely faultless.

[39, 22] But this [opponent] himself says, "Indeed, we do not see a difference in effects arising from a single nature, nor is that [effect] seen to be distinct. Speaking thus, he is simply unwell and not fit for serious debate. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that a plurality of effects arises from a totality (*sāmagrī*) that does not possess a single nature; however, this is not the case for that which is devoid of a succession of natures.

Thus, by dispelling the doubt regarding the nature [of things], what was stated—that existence (*sattva*), when excluded from momentary things, would result in a non-commonality of the material cause and an occurrence of a difference in its nature—is refuted.

The appearance of difference is merely conceptual; it is not a real difference. Furthermore, even if a real difference in intrinsic nature were to occur, one must simply accept that existence (*sattva*) is unique (*asādhāraṇa*). For existence does not become excluded from momentary things any more than it is excluded from eternal ones by exceeding their measure, such that it could be determined as unique. If it is argued that within the abundance of intrinsic natures, something might also be eternal, [we reply: ...

In that case, let it be suspected that the entity which follows [the reason] is common (*sādhāraṇa*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); and that must be considered, because there is the possibility of subverting [reasons] with their mouths wide open.

Now, if it is argued that since a succession of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is possible, one must state for what entity—apart from the [succession of] moments itself—momentariness exists, and thus it is excluded even from the momentary, that too is not the case. For by establishing the efficacy of action (*kriyā*), one protects the possessor of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāvī*) as being distinct from the intrinsic natures themselves. Furthermore, when a distinction between intrinsic natures is impossible, the destruction of the root is also not logical; for even if an infinite number of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) were to occur, the loss of that which possesses them is not admitted.

Even in our own system, if indeed there is the emergence of a mass of other entities, it is nonetheless clear what kind of destruction could possibly occur for the entity under discussion. One must consider whether that mass conforms to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not. Or, let us grant the denial of the root [cause]. As for those intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) which are perceived as real, because they are submerged within that [root] essence, let the single root not be momentary and exist separately;
however, since many [natures] are indeed momentary, there is only an accumulation of momentariness. How, then, could there be an exclusion of existence from momentariness?
