Thus, such incoherent ravings, which produce pride only in the minds of common folk, are fitting for them alone, but not for Buddhists whose intellects are sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass and refined by logic. As for the argument beginning with "this would be" (*etad ity-ādi*) intended to prove a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*), let that belong to these very people; for one who is sound-minded is unable to assert that "one is the intrinsic nature of the other. Furthermore, a difference in intrinsic nature has already been refuted due to the impossibility of providing a proof and because it is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Nor does your [position] suffer from the same fault as the original one; nor can the reasons that establish a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—which employ the "teeth-pulling" method by asserting that an auxiliary cause is itself a different intrinsic nature—be subverted. For a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), who observes the auxiliaries and presents a proof to establish a well-known difference in intrinsic nature, cannot be deceived in any way by such words.

Therefore, that [alleged] means is not a means at all; it is merely a "boon" (vara) because it has been declared to be a contradiction of the very accomplishment of what was desired. And regarding this, we have already stated: "Nor is this effort of the opponent directed solely toward establishing auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). For since the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the effect has been experienced, and the auxiliary causes are established by direct perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what remains here to be proven?"

Therefore, when the proof of the distinction between intrinsic natures (*svalakṣaṇabheda*) has been presented regarding the successive manifestations of effects produced by that which is held to be non-momentary, if one were to offer no refutation but merely prattle that "another auxiliary cause is itself the difference in intrinsic nature" simply because it satisfies one's own heart—let it be so! But this does not invalidate the point to be proven for others. Consequently, it is established that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by impermanence (*asthairya*).

Furthermore, as for what he has said: first, this proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin) should be asked this: when the preceding moment is to produce the subsequent moment within a single continuum, there is nothing else whatsoever that must be depended upon. Consequently, because it is independent with respect to the arising of another, the subsequent moment—being necessarily bound to that [preceding moment] alone—must exist while that [preceding moment] still exists. Or, if it were not to exist, it would not be bound to that [preceding moment] alone; rather, it would have to be understood as depending on some other cause.

However, in the case of the arising of something belonging to a different class (*asabhāga*), since there is no distinction in their being included within a single continuum—namely, that they previously existed within the same homogeneous continuum—they would be either capable or incapable [of producing an effect]. But this is not the case for the arising of a moment restricted to its own homogeneous class (*sabhāga*). If it were so, then because there would be no distinction in their being invariably connected merely to the existence of the preceding moment, each subsequent moment would arise simultaneously, abandoning the sequence of priority and posteriority. Consequently, the continuum of those moments occurring at the time of the effect—which depends upon such a succession—would be severed.

Furthermore, because the continuum of all things existing throughout the three worlds would be severed by this very process, it would follow that the entirety of the triple world would be mutually crushed.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no relationship of cause and effect between two moments—just as there is none between the left and right horns of a cow—because they arise simultaneously, then in this case, an effect would have to arise from a different entity in a preceding past moment, or it would not arise even when such a moment exists; this would be an unprecedented manner of following positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). By this reasoning as well, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) of momentary things remains untenable.

[41,21] All of that, too, is incoherent. For instance, regarding the claim that when the subsequent [moment] is to be produced, there is no dependence on anything else: in that case, all moments whatsoever must be intended by you as the "subsequent. Otherwise, the consequence of the simultaneity of all [moments] would be untenable. In that regard, if this is a refutation of your own position, then there is no opposing view at all.

Then the follower of the Sugata himself must be questioned: if [the cause] is independent in producing the subsequent moment immediately after the preceding one, it is not independent regarding the later moment. In that case, that very nature which produces it does not exist; therefore, since it depends on its own nature, how can it be independent? If that nature might at some time belong to it, then it is dependent upon it—what is the meaning of such a statement?

This is the meaning: when it is said that Devadatta is capable of this task in dependence upon Yajñadatta, two things are understood there—namely, that he is himself incapable and that he is capable together with Yajñadatta. Furthermore, not every conventional usage conforms to ultimate reality; rather, in some cases something is true. Thus, even here, the portion stating that he is himself incapable is difficult to deny, because it is agreed upon by both parties.

The dispute here, however, concerns the claim that "that very same [entity] is subsequently capable in relation to another. For this very reason, sublation (*bādhana*) enters into the proof (*sādhana*). Therefore, because that part is unestablished (*aṃśāsiddhi*), even the word "itself" (*svayam*)—which depends on that [part]—is removed. In some cases, the meaning is simply "dependent" (*sāpekṣa*) in the sense of being "incapable" (*asamartha*). Consequently, when a subsequent effect is to be produced but is impossible, what is the meaning of saying that [the cause] is "dependent" with respect to its nature of producing that? It means it is "capable" (*samartha*) regarding the production of each subsequent effect. Thus, let whatever refutation there may be in this regard be stated.

It might be argued as follows: each subsequent [moment] is not distinct from the nature of its predecessor; therefore, just as the former is capable in relation to the latter, so too is it capable in relation to the subsequent-to-the-latter. If it were incapable in relation to the subsequent-to-the-latter, how could it be capable in relation to the latter? For the two possess an identical intrinsic nature.

That too is inconsistent, because a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatva*) is not established. If it is argued that a single intrinsic nature is established in relation to a succession of similar moments (*sabhāgakṣaṇaparamparā*), we say no; for similarity is not established in every respect. For the meaning of "similar" (*sabhāga*) is the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*). And homogeneity is of three kinds: by way of form (*rūpa*), by way of capacity (*śakti*), and by way of both. In this regard, although there is homogeneity between each subsequent moment and the one following it based solely on form, nevertheless, there is no homogeneity based on capacity.

Consequently, a state of heterogeneity (*vijātīyatva*) has indeed been established. For this very reason, through a certain succession of transformations of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pariṇāma-paramparā*) of the seed and so forth, the production of the effect—the sprout—is accomplished. In that process, the final moment of the seed possesses the capacity for the sprout; furthermore, the penultimate [moment] possesses it for the final one, and the one preceding that for the penultimate, and so on back to the occurrence of the first seed. Likewise, it should be understood that the collection of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-sāmagrī*) there is also distinct at each successive stage.

For this very reason, although conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), which possess distinct powers at every moment due to their connection with successive conditions, may be perceived as similar on account of some degree of uniformity, nevertheless their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed different. Consequently, it is the logical principle that only a specific [cause] is the cause or effect of a specific [result]. (18a) Therefore, since they are entirely devoid of homogeneity (*sabhāgatva*), even if the preceding moment possesses the capacity to produce the subsequent moment, it does not produce each succeeding one, because there is a distinction based on a particular power (*śaktiviśeṣa*).

Likewise, for that [moment] as well, there may be an increase or decrease of power from another [cause]. In both cases, it is precisely a distinction that is being stated: "it is distinguished from another. Therefore, how can there be any room for the objection regarding the simultaneous occurrence of all moments intended to be "homogeneous" (sabhāga) within a single moment? Furthermore, the final point regarding the emergence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is merely a sophistry; for when the capacity to prove momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been refuted, the fact that one [moment] arises immediately after another is itself what constitutes positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Furthermore, since that cause was non-existent prior [to the effect], the non-existence of the effect at another time or place is itself the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); what can be done about this, even by one who does not wish it? For even for the proponent of eternalism, the birth of cause and effect does not occur simultaneously; rather, the birth of the effect follows immediately after the birth of the cause. And since the effect arises from the moment of the cause, if the cause were to exist either before or after that, what benefit would it provide to the effect?

Since the effect is accomplished by that much alone—namely, that its birth occurs immediately after [the cause]—there is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by that much alone, as well as negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), in that [the effect] is absent when that [cause] is absent. The only distinction for the proponent of eternalism (*nityavādin*) is this: that even after that moment, the existence of what is considered the cause can be excluded merely on the grounds of its lack of utility toward the effect, as established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that has already been examined. It is thus established that positive and negative concomitance consist of nothing more than what has been stated.

Furthermore, having asserted the uniqueness of the sentient being (*sattva*), and after deliberating on whether one arises from one, many arise from one, or one arises from many, Vācaspati adopted the position that many arise from many and said: "Are the preceding moments the producers of the subsequent moments while being entirely independent of one another, or rather, are they dependent?"

But has it not been stated that those [causes] reaching their final moment produce effects independently of one another? Why then this proliferation of unwarranted imputations? Is it then the case that even the seed-moment which produces a capable seed-moment is itself independent in producing that [capable moment]? We say: "Yes. Alas! If by this reasoning all seed-moments are independent in producing their effects, then there is no need for auxiliary causes (sahakārin).

But was it not said that these [seeds] are not discerning beings; rather, their presence is restricted by their own internal conditions, such that they cannot endure even for a moment the intervention of an obstacle? Well then, is even this farmer not discerning, who, having removed the seed from the granary, sows it in the ploughed earth, since the seed possesses the capacity to produce a sprout through a succession of excellence-generations arising from its coexistence with the soil and other factors? For if it were otherwise, one would not see that [seed] even after a hundred years while it remains in the granary; therefore, he sows it there. If this is your argument:

Now, why is this seed-moment not capable of arising solely from its own continuum? If that were the case, why would it not depend upon another continuum as a cooperative cause for the production of the effect?

[44,1] But surely it does depend [on something] for its own production, though not for its own effect. It is said that it is independent in that regard [the effect], but not with respect to its own production. Now, even regarding its own production, there exists its very own preceding moment, residing within its own continuum, which is independent. In this way, each preceding moment, falling within its own continuum, remains independent and active in producing [the next]. Consequently, the farmer would have achieved his purpose simply by placing the seed in the granary. Thus, this discerning person would have done away with the laborious work of farming, which is a source of suffering.

[44,11] If one should think that there are two kinds of effects here: first, that which has the nature of producing a succession of specific excellences (atiśaya-viśeṣa) imparted by auxiliary causes (sahakārin); and second, that which produces its effect independently of any excellence from auxiliaries. In this regard, the sprout is born in dependence upon a succession of specific excellences; whereas the initial excellence, however, arises without depending on a succession of excellences produced by auxiliaries. Yet neither of these two kinds of effects can possibly arise from the seed’s own continuum alone.

It is postulated that the seed, whether residing in its own continuum or in a different continuum such as that of the earth and so forth, produces an occasional effect only in dependence upon other continua; thus the work of agriculture is undertaken. As for those auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) within other continua that bring about the occasional production of the effect, they are precisely the causes that awaken the capacity of the seed—just as they are the auxiliaries for the arising of the sprout. Furthermore, whatever are the generative causes of those [auxiliaries] such as the earth and so forth, they themselves become the causes of the [seed's] capacity, just as follows:

The "approaching conditions" (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*) are the causes for awakening the capacity [of seeds and so forth] to produce an initial excellence. In no way does a seed that has not had an excellence imparted to it by other continua produce a specific effect that occurs only occasionally. And the causes for awakening this capacity are both the cooperative conditions (*sahakāripratyaya*) and the approaching conditions.

This is untenable. For instance, let it be that the effect is of two kinds; and let it be that, because it is occasional, it depends on other continua. But the meaning of this dependence must be stated. If you say it is the awakening of the cause's own capacity—

Is it not the case that since capacity and its awakening are not distinct from the very nature of the capable entity, it has been stated that the arising of the cognition of capability [is identical to the entity itself]? And thus, the very cause required for its own production—which is indeed a cooperative condition—is being urged as a fault in the form of an admission.

Now, is this moment capable of producing a sprout, or is it the first excellence, produced by a preceding moment that arises solely from its own continuum and is independent [of anything else], rather than by something arising solely from its own continuum? For even this [moment] arises from the very same prior complex [of causes].

[45,1] Now, among the series of seed-moments arising in a granary, which possess equal capacity, why does only a certain seed produce a seed-moment that is conducive to the successive production of a sprout, and not other seed-moments belonging to different series? Indeed, prior to the advent of the auxiliary condition (upasarpaṇapratyaya), there is no mutual distinction whatsoever among these seed-moments, whether they belong to the same or different series.

Prior to the condition of the approach [of the auxiliary cause], those moments existing in the series of the seed do not produce, even through a succession, a seed-moment conducive to the production of a sprout, because they produce merely seeds. For a certain seed-moment, however, there occurs the production of an initial excellence co-arising with the condition of approach. Alas! In that case, if that [excellence] were absent, it would indeed produce [the sprout] even if it had arisen.

Nor is there a rule of concomitance with the condition of approach for this [seed], because the seed-moments existing in the granary—which do not belong to that same continuum and share the same fate as it—lack concomitance with the condition of approach; and because there is no determination of cause and effect between one moment and another moment, since the positive and negative concomitances regarding production, which have universals as their object, are established only in that specific case.

And thus, since deviation is possible for individual factors alone, one must—even against one's will—accept that the very nature of seeds and so forth as producers of the first excellence or the sprout consists in their mutual dependence.

This too has been largely refuted by the ancient masters. For instance, even if it were established that the nature of being a producer belongs only to those things that are mutually dependent, what does this prove regarding the matter at hand? Or, if it is argued that mutual dependence is observed among things that exist simultaneously;

Thus, even for that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), since it provides no assistance to its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the possibility of its ever producing anything would be abandoned; the intention is that the exclusion of the "real" from the eternal is established because such effort would be in vain. If this is so, how is the thesis of "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) maintained? It would be more appropriate to state that the exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is merely doubtful.

[45,19] Now, it has been established that there is no dependence on auxiliary causes for that which is momentary, nor is such dependence logical; and this intention will be explained further below. Therefore, since causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) is pervaded by both dependence and non-dependence, and since that [efficacy] is absent from the impermanent, it is excluded from it; and since it is excluded from the permanent—according to your own view—due to the absence of both successive and simultaneous action, it is clearly a non-common [reason]. Furthermore, there is no dependence on auxiliaries for the momentary because there is no benefit [to be conferred], nor is there non-dependence, because without that [dependence], the cause itself would be absent. Thus, the absence of the pervader is established.

[45,24] That too is trivial. For, with reference to what kind of object is this stated? If, first of all, "it depends on auxiliary causes" means that it must be assisted by auxiliary causes, then, because those [auxiliaries] are absent, how can there be a dual exclusion for the momentary thing, given that it is indeed independent? As for the impossibility of its acting without a distinction of auxiliary causes, that follows simply from its own non-existence at another moment.

If it is argued that there is no distinction between "it being thus" and "it being otherwise," and therefore, even though such a nature is possible, its non-production [at other times] is not tenable for something independent of auxiliary causes;

This is incoherent, because that which is not an agent lacks such a nature. (42b) If the very same nature—which belongs to one situated in the midst of all auxiliary causes whose powers are unimpeded, and which produces an immediate effect—were present at another time and place, then alas, it would likewise possess the capacity for action. Furthermore, similarity cannot exist between other seeds merely on account of a likeness in color and shape.

For indeed, even when there is a similarity of form, entities are established as distinct through differences such as the presence or absence of their results; likewise, they may also differ by way of a difference in capacity (*śakti*), as in the case of the *harītakī* fruit during its ripening and maturation. To the question of how that difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises among them despite their commonality as seeds, the only recourse is the difference in the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). This has been demonstrated in the discussion beginning with "by various successive conditions" (*aparāpara-pratyaya*), even though some degree of similarity is perceived.

[46,12] Therefore, what was stated—namely, "But surely, in the case of those produced from the same husk," and so forth—is refuted. For it is the seed, whose differentiation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) has been brought about through the transformation of the totality of causes, both seen and unseen, which, with the assistance of the conditions for germination, serves as the basis for the state of cooperation; that [seed], through a succession of transformations, produces either the initial excellence (*atiśaya*) or the sprout. Other moments of the seed do not do so, because, lacking such a succession of causes, they lack that specific intrinsic nature.

Now, one might object: when all seeds have been brought together and cast into a granary after being harvested from a single field, they are perceived as having a common form; so from where does this specific quality arise that belongs only to a particular seed and not to the others? And since this is so—because the touch of the hand during the harvesting of the field is the very nature of that [specific seed], and because it is subsequently seen even when other [seeds] are being carried away—how can its possession of an identical nature be denied?

To this it is replied: Indeed, in all cases the cause is twofold—namely, the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). This is established for all those who maintain the existence of all things (*sarvāstika*). Among these, the unseen has the nature of karma; it is produced in another birth, is determined solely by its non-perception, and its diversity is inferred from the observation of the diversity of effects. The seen, moreover, is of two kinds: that which has the nature of this world (*aihikalaukika*), and that which is both perceptible and imperceptible.

And that [causal complex] is fourfold, being either inherent in a conscious entity or inherent in an unconscious entity. Thus, the entire causal totality is not perceptible in every respect to an ordinary person. And so Trilocana says: "Some auxiliary condition is perceptible, while another is imperceptible; therefore, the completeness of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions cannot be established through perception by one who is not omniscient."

Even when that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is partially perceived, an ordinary person (*pṛthag-jana*), due to their coarse vision, is incapable of enumerating its internal subtle distinctions. Consequently, there may indeed exist such a difference in nature among certain seeds—those whose functional capacity has been brought forth by the hands of a skilled smith—which, through a continuous succession, are powerful enough to produce the intended effect, whereas others are not, even though they occupy the same single granary; yet the world would not perceive this distinction.

Nor does its non-existence follow merely from a lack of ascertainment; rather, there would be doubt. And that doubt is not overcome by you through the effect, namely the touch of the hand. For instance, among the parts of a single body which arise from an undivided causal complex such as the union of mother and father, certain marks like *tilakas*, *citrakas*, or *ciṇṭikās* are observed to appear in specific locations—whether innate or acquired—and yet there is a commonality of skin, flesh, and so forth in other parts as well.

Therefore, how can these [marks] such as the *tilaka* and so forth—which, being distinct, manifest even though their differentiation through the transformation of the causal complex of seen and unseen factors is imperceptible—not be established? The same applies to external entities as well; for the learned accept that the entire collection of effects arises from both common and uncommon karma.

[47,11] Now, it might be argued: "In the case of the body, since moles and the like appearing on the right or left, or in hidden or exposed places, necessarily bring about pleasure, pain, and so forth, the restriction of their location is appropriate due to the sovereign influence (*adhipatya*) of karma conducive to such results. However, in the case of a granary, when seeds are sown upon ground prepared by that or another means, there is no distinction; therefore, because of this disparity, one should not postulate a power of karma. If this is the objection:

Well then, since we observe and do not observe direct utility, there is little point in postulating or not postulating the capacity of means such as ritual action (*karman*) and so forth. One must admit that some effect in the world is produced by ritual action, or else accomplished by a Lord (*īśvara*) and the like. For you do not perceive any purpose in the rounding of the dung of goats and other animals by excluding the common characteristics of children or cattle.

In the case of the unenjoyed and withered fruits, flowers, sprouts, and so forth of the forest trees, those same men who possess the *tilaka* mark and other signs are seen to be unfamiliar with their own task regarding those marks; or even if they are familiar with them, they are observed approaching death without having manifested any pain or mental distress—so what utility is there in that as well?

Furthermore, since there exist many extensive locations—whether on the left, the right, or other concealed parts—that are suitable for the occurrence of moles (*tilaka*) and the like, how can there be a fixed rule regarding the location of their emergence? Moreover, in the case of deer and other animals, where there is merely a change in color in a certain limb, it is sufficient even to suspect it might be due to mental distress; what need is there to describe such a "utility" (*upayoga*) for them? Or rather, how much more of this kind could possibly be demonstrated?

Or how much more must you yourself understand? Why then will you come here in vain? Even in the absence of a logical inference, the observation of differences in effects among entities—which are restricted by their specific place, time, and nature—is everywhere permeated by differences in capacities for means such as action, even when those differences are difficult to perceive.

Whether directly or indirectly, that [nature] establishes by way of general determination—through a necessity that even intermediate yogis cannot fully discern—that which is useful for visible and invisible, sentient and insentient objects and their functions; therefore, a seeker of logic must be made to accept this, even by force, by one who knows logic.

This being the case, the nature of a certain seed alone is rendered harsh through contact with the conditions for its germination (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), whereas that of others remains unrefined due to the absence of such specific differentiation. Thus, by virtue of these internal and intermediate distinctions, that very momentary seed (*bījakṣaṇa*) is conducive to the intended effect through a causal series, while other moments of the seed are not. Furthermore, this internal distinction—though inferred from the touch of a hand—is not capable of being refuted either by the failure to perceive specific capacities for causal factors such as action (*karman*), or by the failure to perceive specific functional utilities.

Just as a specific part of the body, such as that where a *tilaka* mark arises, or a specific part of a tree, results from some slight modification (*vikāraleśa*) occurring in one particular location; even there, having encountered a cause—whether visible or invisible—for that specific part which is the locus of the modification, this distinct nature (*svabhāvabheda*) comes into being through a succession of specific portions of the material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, even if the specific difference is not precisely determined, it is established in a general sense that there exists some distinguished cause or function that is otherwise impossible, and which is capable of accomplishing a purpose that cannot be achieved by other parts.

Because of its connection with a cause of transformation, there is the determination of a difference in the nature of the factor (*aṅga*). Likewise here too, in the case of the seed, due to contact with the hand prompted by human cognition, there exists a difference in its nature that partakes in a subtle distinction between the husk and the fruit; thus, a general determination [of this] is difficult to deny. Therefore, since such a difference in nature is possible, it is established that only that specific seed is utilized—through a succession [of moments]—for the production of a quality conducive to the arising of the sprout, and not other seed-moments.

As for what was said, beginning with "Indeed, there is no approaching," etc.—with respect to which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this operation being considered? It cannot be perception (*pratyakṣa*), because even when a gross unity of kind is ascertained through the similarity of form, the internal difference—which remains unperceived due to its subtlety—cannot be negated. Moreover, it is observed that in the case of substances such as the *puṣā* plant, which possess a bitter or non-bitter taste despite having a similar form and belonging to the same gross class, perception falters by producing a single determinative judgment.

Therefore, the establishment of reality does not follow from mere singularity alone, because an invalidating factor (*bādhaka*) has been shown regarding that aspect. However, in the case of that which is cultivated through extreme repetition and is consistent, the establishment of unity is not contradictory due to the absence of an invalidating factor; thus, the mutual exclusion of excellence is not perceived directly in the present context. Nor can it be established through inference.

If it were argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, that material cause (*upādāna*) is already the very nature of the seed as earth and so forth, then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of them. For if it were independent of them, the distinction between those [products] and the sprout would be untenable. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that things do not depend on what provides no assistance; nor is assistance possible for a momentary entity other than its production, because such a moment is indivisible.

And likewise, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by the dependence on or independence from unity and plurality—since there is no third possibility—and because the negation of one of these two is inseparable from the affirmation of the other; and since, in the case of a non-momentary entity, those two pervading modes of dependence and independence regarding unity and plurality are absent, existence (*sattva*) is excluded according to the stated sequence. Thus, [the reason] is not an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) one, but is rather non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

[49,6] Because no indicative mark (*liṅga*) is shown, and because it is impossible to show one, and because a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) indeed exists; therefore, nothing is achieved by merely shouting what is undesirable. [49,8] By this, it follows that "assistance" is not the meaning of "dependence"; thus, for a momentary entity, there is simply no dependence upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), nor is there an exclusion of both [dependence and non-dependence]. Now, if "acting together" is the meaning of "dependence," even then, if "dependence" is qualified as "belonging to what previously existed," then for a momentary entity there would be no such thing at all; thus, the lack of dependence remains unimpaired.

Now, if [the term] "of that which was previously situated" is not required, and the meaning of "dependence" is merely the state of being combined, then there is only dependence and no independence. Even so, there is still no exclusion of both [possibilities]. Alternatively, if dependence is established according to our own system, then we have already established that what is dependent is indeed incapable. Thus, the formal rule is: that which is incapable with respect to an effect is dependent, whereas that which is capable is independent.
And at that time, because the affirmation of one follows from the negation of the other, incapacity itself becomes capable, being devoid of [intrinsic] capacity. As it has been said:
"It is indeed capable," and thus there is no exclusion of both [capacity and incapacity] in the case of momentariness.

And as for what you said: "Furthermore, does the seed that has reached its final moment, producing the sprout while being independent of earth, wind, water, and fire, produce those others by the very same form through which it produces the sprout, or rather by a different form? It cannot be by the very same form, because that would entail that the earth and the other factors also possess the nature of the sprout. Indeed, when there is no difference in the cause, a differentiated effect cannot arise, for that would lead to the absurd consequence of the effect's differentiation being accidental."

As it has been said: "This indeed is the distinction, or the cause of distinction, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and the difference in causes (*kāraṇabheda*). Nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is a single unity; otherwise, there would be no necessity for their coexistence. In another form, that [complex] produces those others. For instance, when a seed produces a sprout, it acts as the material cause (*upādāna*), since the sprout arises from the transformation of that [seed].

If it is argued that, in the case of the other [causes], these [latter] serve as its auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), whereas for them, the preceding factors such as wind and so forth are their respective material causes (*upādāna*), because those arise through the transformation of the latter;

Now, are these two—the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) and the material cause (*upādāna*)—one reality or many? If they are one, how can it be a producer by means of a different form? If they are many, is there a difference or non-difference between these two and the seed? If there is a difference, how can the seed be the producer, since the sprout and so forth would be accounted for by those two alone? Or, if there is non-difference, why would the seed not be manifold, given its identity with what is distinct? Furthermore, why would these two not be one, given their identity with the one?

If it were argued that when earth and so forth are to be produced, that material cause (*upādāna*) is already the very form of the seed itself as earth and so forth—then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of them. For if it were independent of them, their distinction from the sprout would be untenable. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that things do not depend on what provides no assistance; nor is assistance possible for a momentary entity other than its production, because such a moment is indivisible.

And thus, because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by dependence on or independence from unity and plurality—since there is no third possibility, and because the negation of one of these two is inseparable from the affirmation of the other—existence (*sattva*) is excluded from the subject by the aforementioned sequence, due to the absence of the two modes of dependence and independence that pervade momentary things. Consequently, [the reason] is an uncommon inconclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) one, just like "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) and so forth.

[50,15] If it should be thought that even those which do not provide assistance are auxiliary causes and are to be depended upon, because their presence and absence follow the presence and absence of the effect, and because they perform the function of an auxiliary cause;

But surely, even in the case of a non-momentary entity, by this same sequence, it may depend upon successive auxiliary causes—even though they provide no assistance—since its positive and negative concomitance with the effect is replicated; and it will produce effects sequentially through the power of the conjunction with successive auxiliaries. Thus, since the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished, existence (*sattva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to a doubtful negative concomitance in the proof of momentariness.

That too has already been refuted previously. Furthermore, as for what he says additionally: "Nor is there a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because that too is a unity. To this we reply: just as there is no difference in the causal complex, so too there is no difference among the effects; how then could there not be a conformity to the non-difference of the cause?

[50,22] But surely, what kind of verbal artifice is this, that there is no difference between effects which possess distinct and manifold forms? If this were so, then indeed no entity distinct from the collection as a whole would ever be an object of perception. And this must be considered according to the Buddhist view: since the collection is non-different [from its parts], then how can it be a verbal artifice to say that the very members of the collection—the distinct and manifold entities—are themselves non-different?

And for one who suspects that the difference or non-difference of the effect follows from the difference or non-difference of the cause characterized as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this doctrine of an undifferentiated causal complex by Vācaspati is appropriate. Otherwise, it is understood by this much alone: how could a single seed produce a sprout, a lake, the earth, a dwelling, and so forth?

And this objection is not valid, because if the intended point were a denial of the production of multiple effects from a single cause in accordance with the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then direct perception (*adhyakṣa*)—which apprehends multiple effects such as the transformation of the wick arising even from a single lamp—would undermine confidence in all those [theories] that contradict it.

If it is asked, "How so?"—surely, when an investigation is conducted by placing valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) at the forefront, beginning with perception and then enumerating the remaining ones, once a matter has been established or refuted by that [first means], there is no further authority for another [means] to refute or establish it. As for those who transgress the path of valid cognition, the same response should be given to them; let this suffice for now.

Now, how can that which produces a sprout be the cause of the moment of the earth? For even in this case, it is not reasonable to assert a contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because the moment transcends the range of such perception. Furthermore, if there were a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "whatever is the producer of one thing cannot be the producer of another," then there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of a lamp itself.

Now, if [the opponent argues that] the producer of the sprout is not the cause of the earth, then there is an inconclusive reason due to lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇānekānta*). If it is asked, "How can that which is the cause of the sprout be the cause of something else?", [we reply: is it the cause of the sprout alone, or of the sprout as well, or does it first belong to the sprout while being uncertain regarding other things? In all three of these positions, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) are respectively difficult to avoid. Therefore, no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates here.

The formulation of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) also occurs by means of the opponent's own admission; however, it is not the admission of the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇavādin*) that "one [cause] does not produce many [effects]. Therefore, for one who is not a child, the reductio that the unity of the effect follows from the unity of the entity within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not valid. Furthermore, when dependence on a cause characterized as a causal complex is accepted, it is established that even distinct effects such as sprouts conform to the difference or non-difference of their causes. Thus, there is no consequence of the unity of sprouts and the like merely out of compliance with conformity to non-difference.

For just as sprouts and the like, though each is a distinct effect, possess natures that are both different and non-different, so too the seeds and other factors denoted by the term "assemblage" (sāmagrī), while each acting as a cause, are likewise both different and non-different; thus, it is established that difference [in the effect] arises from the difference [in the causes].

[51,20] Now, even if seeds and the like are distinct in nature, they are made the objects of a single conventional designation (*ekavyavahāra*) by virtue of some proximity; the same applies to sprouts and the like. Thus, when there is no difference in the cause, non-difference is also established. In that regard, the fact that the causes produce each respective effect is the ground for the single convention; as for the effects, it is their being produced by each respective cause—this is the same.

Why, then, must [the cause] become one with the sprout and so forth? For even when there is dependence upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that much alone is sufficient for the effect to conform to the diversity or non-diversity of its causes. Furthermore, this is stated—following the lead of common cognition—to show that even for the opponent who derives the term "cause" from the causal complex, there is indeed no derivation of [the concepts of] diversity and non-diversity;
however, in reality, just as the causal complex is intended by the term "cause," so too are diversity and non-diversity intended as heterogeneity and homogeneity, as has already been demonstrated.

[52,3] But surely, since even now there is no "assemblage" (*sāmagrī*) other than the assembled factors themselves, it follows that the similarity or dissimilarity of the effects depends on the similarity or dissimilarity of those very assembled factors. This is indeed so; however, this does not refer to a determination of mutual similarity and so forth among the members situated within that same aggregate. Rather, it refers to a determination of similarity or otherwise with respect to their own class in relation to those situated in another aggregate, just as one army is determined to be similar or otherwise to another army.

In this regard, however many and of whatever nature objects are considered causes when they fall within the scope of a single conceptual designation of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), if that same number and those same types of objects exist in another place or time, then that is a similar complex; and since its effect is also similar, by the term "effect" (*kārya*) too, only a collection (*puñja*) is meant. The meaning is that however many and of whatever nature effects have arisen in one instance, exactly that many and of that same nature arise elsewhere as well.

But when there is dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*)—which is differentiated by degrees of difference—the effect (*kārya*) is also differentiated by degrees of difference; thus, the meaning is that the dissimilarity belongs precisely to the aggregate of effects (*kāryapuñja*) itself by virtue of those degrees of difference. This same principle applies even when one intends to express mere difference: when there is a disagreement, a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces a distinct effect. It is precisely such conformity of the effect to the difference in its causes that accords with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And if that [rule] were transgressed, the consequence would follow that the entire universe is without a cause; for there is no transgression of the restriction that a single effect must have a single cause when such a restriction is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, this talk of the Naiyāyikas regarding the imitation of both difference and non-difference resembles the report of a cowherd’s mouth claiming that he has heard the Vedic injunction that milk-rice (*pāyasa*) is his desired food.

Therefore, a single seed produces many things such as the sprout and so forth; likewise, each factor such as the earth and so on does the same. Consequently, there is no exclusion of either the "one" or the "many," since this other non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is presented even in the case of momentariness for the purpose of making [the opponent's position] inconsistent with existence by subverting causal activity. As for the position that [the cause] produces [the effect] through a different form, we have already rejected it; thus, there is no need to exert effort in providing a series of refutations against that.

And this is stated with reference to reality (*tattva*). In the play of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-vilāsa*), however, that which is the production of a sprout is not the production of the earth; likewise, being a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) is not itself being a material cause (*upādānatva*). Thus, even though such a proliferation of categories may occur, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the entity characterized by the absence of activity, because everything is accounted for through its very real nature.

For this very reason, why should we state that when earth and so forth are to be produced, their material cause (*upādāna*) is simply a prior transformation of the form of the seed of earth and so forth, such that the subsequent argument would be sound? Furthermore, since it has already been established that [the cause] is independent even with respect to its auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), the conclusion of the treatise’s purpose by one of confused intellect is entirely incoherent.

Furthermore, those who inquire, "Is it by the very same form that the seed produces the sprout that it produces the moment of the earth? are themselves to be questioned: "What is intended here by the word 'form' (*rūpa*)? Do you mean those factors (*dharma*) that, like "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) or "impermanence" (*anityatva*), appear as if distinct while resting upon the bed of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and which—such as being the producer of the sprout or its opposite—are already established in common usage even by the term "intrinsic nature" (*svarūpa*)?

Now, regarding "form" (*rūpa*), its own nature (*svarūpa*), or its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*): since there is no other distinction of the entity (*vastu-bheda*) apart from that [nature], it is spoken of with reference to that; namely, if that which is the very nature of the entity at the beginning were the same later on, then, just as before, it would not produce [the effect] later either, and so forth.

Alternatively, it has been stated that "form" refers to the cooperative cause itself, designated by the word "own-nature" (*svarūpa*), just as the Naiyāyikas use the word "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) in common parlance for one who does not know the name of the husband. In that regard, first of all, in the case of the former position, there is no logical consistency in the objection.

For phenomena (dharma) constructed by conceptualization (kalpanā), although they appear as if existing in relation to one another and to their substrata (dharmin), cannot function as instruments in any activity whatsoever because they lack existence according to their appearance and thus cannot withstand valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For indeed, although the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone—which is the object of direct perception—is devoid of parts, and although the accomplishment of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nevertheless, due to the power of beginningless latent dispositions (*anādi-vāsanā*), there arises in the conceptualizing mind a mere conventional discourse. This discourse proceeds by means of isolating various properties (*dharma*)—which are based on the force of the determination (*vyavasāya*) of objects as excluded from this or that—and asserting: "In this or that activity, this or that property is useful. This occurs within those [conceptions] that possess correspondence (*saṃvāda*) regarding the determination of things as excluded from this or that.

However, these [qualities] do not possess the status of being instruments (*karaṇa*) in any respect, because they themselves lack existence; yet, that which is produced by intention (*vivakṣā*) is not denied. Just as in the case of a lamp whose nature is light and which is yellowish in character, it effects the destruction of darkness and the making of space golden-yellow by means of its very undivided form; in exactly the same way, when it is determined that this lamp is of the nature of light, it follows from that that it removes darkness like the moon. And because it is yellowish, it is the cause of making things golden-yellow, like turmeric and so forth—such is the conventional usage.

And in that case, the luminosity and the orange color are not distinct; however, in the conceptualizing mind, they appear as if distinct, and having extracted each one separately, they are intended as being established by virtue of performing different functions. [Or rather, they are not so established. Yet, it is not by mere intention that the lamp becomes a non-agent or that there is a real distinction between its properties.

Likewise, regarding a seed as well, its production of a sprout is attributed to a conceptualized form that generates the sprout, while its production of that same effect is also attributed to its earth-generating form. Thus, even in conventional discourse, in reality there is neither a negation of a single entity performing multiple actions, nor the establishment of a distinction between them, nor indeed a state of non-action. Therefore, with respect to forms mounted upon conceptual construction, the claim that "it performs multiple actions through multiple forms" is a mere convention and not a real thing; yet this investigation is based on what is real.

So what is the use of this conceptualization—whether it be by that form or another? Even if there is conceptualization, the response is made by means of many [forms] as a mere matter of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), and there is no fault whatsoever.

As for the second position, however, it is tenable only when there is the perception of multiple particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). And even the particular characteristics of seeds are not the object of a single simultaneous observation. For indeed, when the full extent [of a population] has not been perceived, the question does not arise: "Is this man to be employed in this task, or is that one?"

In the third alternative, however, this would be the meaning: "Is it by the very same form that it produces the sprout that it [produces] the soil? or "Is it by the very same auxiliary cause with which it generates the sprout that it [generates] the earth? And when would this be said? Only if, when the seed's production of the sprout is established, there were some fixed-natured, active, and finalized auxiliary cause for one production, while its activity toward another production remained doubtful. But such a thing cannot be demonstrated.

Now, this being the case, the meaning of the alternative is as follows: if earth, water, and so forth are the auxiliary causes for the seed’s production of a sprout, are they the same [causes] for its production of earth? There is no utility even in that [question], because it is well-established that all things everywhere stand in a mutual relationship of auxiliary cause; what, then, is the point of this inquiry? Furthermore, the subsequent argument is not appropriate here, for even then there is no coherent connection to the principle that "the difference or non-difference of the effect follows from the difference or non-difference of the cause."
Therefore, those who consider themselves experts in logic desire to agitate others with senseless ravings that are tormented by the thorn of envy; enough of this persistence on this matter.

Moreover, this manner of proclaiming an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*) is unprecedented. For it is logical that a real entity which has unascertained positive and negative concomitance with both the probandum and its opposite—such as "possessing odor" and so forth—is considered uncommon. Furthermore, by the force of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) under discussion, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) itself is entirely non-existent; how then could such a thing be an uncommon inconclusive reason? It would be more appropriate to state the refutation on the grounds of being unestablished (*asiddhi*), and that has already been stated therein.

Now, if it is argued that [the reason] “absence of the pervader” has been stated regarding momentariness, and therefore there is no existence at all, then in that case, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), while existing, is excluded from the momentary alone; consequently, it necessarily rests in the non-momentary and is thus pervaded by it—let there also be contradiction (*viruddhatā*).

If it is argued that there is doubt because there is no direct sublation (*bādhaka*) or proof (*sādhaka*) regarding the non-momentary nature [of the subject], [we reply]: if its existence is established, then its exclusion from momentary things alone constitutes the proof, which leaves no room for doubt. Furthermore, if there is doubt regarding its existence, then "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) is indeed the flaw.

Furthermore, since the non-perception of the pervader of the subject (*prakṛtavyāpakānupalambha*) possesses its efficacy equally with respect to the non-momentary as it does with respect to the momentary, how can there be the establishment of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*)? Thus, non-establishment (*asiddhi*) follows in every respect. For one could indeed say this regarding the eternal as well: "There is no production by that which depends on auxiliary causes, because there is no benefit [conferred]; nor is there production by that which is independent, because it produces even without them."

Furthermore, [the opponent may argue that] a stable seed produces the soil either by its very nature as a producer of the sprout or by a different nature, and so forth; thus, there is the objection regarding the production of dissimilar things such as the soil. Moreover, for you, even a lamp is non-momentary. In that case, it is the same [question]: are the transformation of the wick and the exhaustion of the oil produced by one and the same nature or by different natures?

As for the claim that "the distinction in the nature of a concentration (*samādhi*) consists merely in its distinct auxiliary factors," by asserting this, one must now abandon any hope of conveying specific, determined meanings through words such as "self" (*ātman*) and "other" (*para*), for then the self would be the other, and the other would be the self. Nor is it appropriate to say that Yajñadatta is the nature of Devadatta, or that blue is the nature of white, even when they are engaged in a single common action.
Thus, this argument—which is devoid of both scripture and logic—is stated out of mere rivalry and will certainly become an object of ridicule.

[55,9] Furthermore, having disregarded the auxiliary factors, it is evident that a stable entity (*sthiro bhāvaḥ*) does not produce an effect—whether by its own nature (*svarūpa*), by what is denoted by the word "nature," or by means of an auxiliary factor, nor by any other mode of being. Thus, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is necessarily admitted. For even in the case of another [entity], that very same nature is the producer, and not the entity itself; therefore, nothing whatsoever is a producer. Consequently, this principle, which establishes the negation of action, is common to both stable and unstable entities.

If that [reason] were established as permanent, there would be no action whatsoever; thus, it would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because even the fault characterized by the absence of both successive and simultaneous occurrence could not ultimately be avoided. Furthermore, the cessation of action must necessarily be admitted even in the case of a stable entity. Otherwise, how could the mere statement of the negation of action in the case of a momentary entity serve to remove the charge of being "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇatā*)? For uniqueness does not consist merely in exclusion from the probandum (*sādhya*). Otherwise, why would one not simply call "exclusion from the heterologous" (*vipakṣa*) itself uniqueness? What is the point of such great effort?

If it is argued that a reason must indeed be a valid probans because it is restricted to the probandum through its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), then by parity of reasoning, it would follow that it is a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it is restricted to the dissimilar class through its exclusion from the probandum. Therefore, with respect to causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), there is simply non-establishment even in the mere thesis. Alternatively, if by some other means one merely demonstrates the uncertainty of both [the presence and absence of the reason] regarding existence, then in that case, the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) is indeed logical.

That is incorrect. For the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) necessarily brings about the ascertainment of non-existence; how then could there be no ascertainment? In that regard, even if the strength of the non-perception of succession and so forth—which excludes existence from a permanent entity—is considered inconsistent, nevertheless, the intended firmness of the present [reasoning] which sublates permanence in the momentary is indeed accepted, since otherwise its presentation would be illogical. Therefore, the absolute exclusion of action from that which is subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgura*) is itself the exclusion that constitutes its uncommon [reason].

For it is not possible to determine that the property of possessing odor is excluded from anything with absolute certainty. Thus, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), while depending on a non-perception of the pervader even in the case of a stable entity, is not valid for proving uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatā*). Since it uproots action altogether, it is simply a case of unestablished evidence (*asiddhi*); there is no relationship between the probandum and the probans.

Therefore, regarding external sensation and that which is established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as an external cognizer, and relying upon causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as a real entity (*vastu-sat*), one who argues for its "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) must not, in the course of the debate, demonstrate either the coexistence of the probandum and the opposite in a single locus, nor their identity or exclusion; rather, there should be mere doubt regarding both. Furthermore, such [coexistence] is impossible when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is not perceived. Thus, it is established that the presentation of uniqueness is not sound.

[56,7] This might be the case: if there is a difference in the nature of the producer when producing effects at different times, then this same consequence would apply to the production of effects in different locations as well. Therefore, the spatial separation of effects must necessarily depend upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). And since an auxiliary cause does nothing for the producer, temporal separation too—being likewise something that does nothing—should also depend upon auxiliary causes. Now, one might argue that spatial separation arises from a difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), whereas such a claim cannot be made regarding temporal separation.

If it is argued that for things produced at different times, there is the possibility of obtaining their material cause (*apādāna*) even at that [later] time under the view of permanence, and therefore the difference in time of an effect is based solely on the difference in its causes and forms—this too is not the case, because the distinction between the material and auxiliary causes is neither real nor unreal. Even if it were real, there would follow the undesirable consequence that a lamp or similar object would possess multiple natures, due to the distinction between the states of being material and auxiliary causes caused by the difference between the material and auxiliary effects.

Therefore, how could this difference in the cause—consisting of an imputed nature (*āropitasvabhāva*) due to the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*)—be capable of producing a spatial difference in the effect? If even an imputed difference in the cause were indeed capable of producing a spatial difference in the effect, then an imputed difference in the cause alone would suffice for a temporal difference; thus, one should desist from the hope for a real (*tāttvika*) difference.

Nor should this be said: that while there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) such as "whatever is a producer at a particular time is not so at another time," there is no such subverting argument regarding spatial difference; for a subverting argument of this kind can be stated even in the case of spatial difference. For example: whatever is an effect is located in the same place as that which is intended to be its material cause (*upādāna*), and yet that effect is also another effect [located elsewhere]. Furthermore, regarding what is said—"even when all conditions are equal" (PVA I 396a)—it is possible to recite the following in that regard as well:

"Even though the cause is the same in all locations, if there is no effect," and so forth. (PVA II 396ab) Now, this fault would indeed arise if one were to admit that the cause possesses a pervasive nature (*vaibhāva*). But if that [pervasive nature] is absent, what is the point of its being the same in all locations? In that case, it would not produce an effect even in another location, because it does not itself operate there. However, if it produces the effect there by virtue of mere capacity (*yogyatā*) without depending on its presence in that specific place, then its location is the same; for it receives no assistance from any single direction.

Therefore, when one says "it produces it in that place," the status of the place as a substratum is not from its own perspective, but rather in relation to the effect; and its production occurs through the exclusion of non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda). Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence of producing an effect located in another place. If that is so, then in the case of "it produces it at that time," that time would necessarily be the substratum of the effect alone, whereas for the cause, it might be both existent and non-existent [at that time]. However, by means of the exclusion of non-connection, the production of an effect at a specific time does not contradict the production of an effect that exists at other times as well.

Therefore, it is logically consistent that even for a thing whose intrinsic nature remains identical across all states, such as being in a granary and so forth, there is the production of effects at those specific times and not at others, just as there is the production of multiple effects in different locations.

[57,12] This is not tenable, because there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*). As for that "being its effect" which was put forward to prove that it occurs in the same location, it is simply no proof at all, because there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts its opposite. Furthermore, the causal relation is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); and just as these two are observed when an effect arises in the same location, they are likewise observed when an effect arises in a different location.

Nor is it correct to say that even when the cause is thus stable, the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of its effect—whether occurring at the same time or at another time—are identical. For even at a different time, it is that very same cause which persists; there is no means of valid cognition other than recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) [to prove this], and that recognition has already been refuted. Therefore, how could there be a grasping of the concomitance of effects that occur at different times with a permanent [cause]? Thus, this logic is not the same [as your argument].

Therefore, if a reason that establishes difference based on spatial distinction is capable of proving its own thesis due to being free from the sublation of its opposite (*viparyayabādhaka*), what follows for the powerful reason that establishes difference based on temporal distinction? For it is not logical to say that because a bull is incapable of yielding milk, a cow must likewise be so.

Or, even if we grant that the reason establishing difference through spatial distinction possesses the strength of being free from the sublation of its opposite, one might ask: "What fault does this entail for the reason establishing difference through temporal distinction? Is it that its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) is thereby established?
If you ask this, is it merely the recitation of a mantra?

If it is argued that the exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is considered doubtful because one observes the non-production of something capable of producing at certain times, even so, what is the use of this labor? For its establishment is achieved simply by the fact that "it would be capable, yet it does not produce. If it is argued that the example of the place serves to strengthen the doubt:

[58,1] If the sublation by the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*) is its strength, then even when fully developed, it accomplishes nothing beyond not being surpassed by doubt. But if there is an absence of sublation by the contrary, then since the reason is overturned by mere doubt alone, what further purpose is served by its development? And if that [development] is intended here, then once this [reason] has been refuted by the sublater of the contrary, what is the point of restating it? Alternatively, if it is argued that because the same principle is observed everywhere in terms of time and place, they share a common fate (*ekayogakṣema*), and thus—just as with a difference in place—there is no difference in the reason even with a difference in time due to the effect; [we reply: ...

That too is incorrect. For instance, proponents of eternalism do not accept that the spatial pervasion of an atom is similar to its temporal pervasion; nor do they hold that the temporal pervasion of a flash of lightning is similar to its spatial pervasion, as is the case with a jar and other such things. How, then, can there be a uniform principle of reasoning (*samānanyāyatā*) in all cases? Furthermore, even if a uniform principle of reasoning is not observed elsewhere, it does not follow that such a state exists everywhere, because in the present case, there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the possibility of the opposite being true.

[58,11] Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the difference in location due to the difference in material causes—that the state of being a material cause and a cooperative condition is merely intermediate—that too is incorrect. Even though those two states of being a material cause and a cooperative condition, appearing in conceptual construction, are not real entities despite appearing as if they were distinct, nevertheless, because such and such exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) are possible for a real entity, there is no establishment of unreality; and because they are mutually dependent, there is no contradiction. Just as, for example, the status of being both father and son for a single person is not unreal in relation to another, nor is it contradictory.

Nor is there the production of two effects by means of two forms, such that—because the two forms appearing in conceptual construction are unreal—there would be no production of the two. Just as a single form produces two [effects], so too it produces its own effect in its own location and the effect of another in the location of another; thus, although a difference in location is established through a difference in the material causes (*upādāna*), the difference in the location of the effect does not arise merely from an imputed difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather from those very [causes] which, while generating their own effects in their own respective locations, necessarily produce [the other effect] in a different location.

The principle is that [an entity] must perform its function through cooperation. Therefore, it is not merely due to a difference in its conceptualized nature (*vikalpita-svabhāva-bheda*) that a single, non-differentiated entity produces effects at different times; for such a difference is established by the force of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For this very reason, the cause does not occupy the same location as everything.

Indeed, its status as a cooperative factor (*sahakāritā*) consists in its acting upon what is produced by its own cooperators, and since that effect can only occur in the very location of its own material cause (*upādāna*), its capacity for cooperative action exists only there and not in another location. Thus, how could its location be identical with all things, especially given the absence of any assistance from them?

[58,24] Furthermore, as for what was said—that time is necessarily the substratum of the effect alone, whereas for the cause it is both that [time] and non-existent—that too is refuted by the same reasoning applied to space. For just as a cause situated in one location produces effects located in different locations, so too does it produce effects at different times while being at only one time; thus, it acts upon the time of the effect without reaching it, just as it does with respect to space.

And thus, even if [the cause] has perished after having arisen at some time, it might produce all effects characterized by [all] times by depending on auxiliary factors; therefore, it is appropriate that there be the fulfillment of the promise to perform a single purpose by coming together.

If it is argued that since the effect is produced only upon reaching the location, the example of location is not established, we reply: no, because for knowledge—which exists within the person and the earth—there is no reaching of a location. Even when there is contact with a lamp, which is the locus of knowledge, the light does not enter inside the body at the place where knowledge, pleasure, and so forth occur; thus, this [objection] is a mere grasping at straws.

Furthermore, this reason—namely, "being an effect of that" (*tatkāryatva*)—which was put forward to prove its existence in that location, is not independent, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Even if such a connection were to exist, we have already stated that it does not establish our position. Nor can it constitute a *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*), because the fact of being its effect is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and thus lacks the status of being a mere concession by the opponent, and because it is devoid of a conclusive reversal (*viparyayaparyavasāyitā*).

For in that case, since it would not be located in that place, it would also lack the status of being its effect; yet this is not possible. Even if it were possible, it would not undermine our fundamental arguments (*mūlaprasaṅga*). Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable, because the capacity for production exists at other times merely by way of its manifestation, and not through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And in the case of the opposite, there is the absence of non-arising; the establishment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) excludes the capacity for that effect in another moment. Thus, by negating both positions—that the cloud performs that action or performs another action—it proves momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga). Therefore, because the reason "existence" (sattva) is present in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is not contradictory.
The second chapter, titled "The Section on Positive Concomitance" (*anvayādhikāra*). [The third chapter: "The Section on Negative Concomitance" (*vyatirekādhikāra*)].

[60,3] Nor is there any suspicion of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), because pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established as encompassing all cases. But surely, the establishment of pervasion occurs through the force of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary; yet there is no mention of such a proof being adduced. How, then, can it be said that pervasion has been established? This is merely the play of a mind that is excessively wavering and unsteady. For it has already been stated: "That action does not belong to an agent at any other time; rather, it would be either the action of another or non-action altogether."

Therefore, in both modes, the momentary destruction of existence is necessarily consistent; that is to say, it is invariably concomitant with that alone, and this has already been established. Consequently, that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is indeed pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*). If it is asked: "In that case, let there be mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*); however, how can the absolute exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)—that is, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—be obtained? [The answer is: Precisely because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established. If it is further asked: "How is the establishment of pervasion itself achieved in the case of negative concomitance?"

No; for pervasion (*vyāpti*) is of two kinds: that which is positive (*anvaya-rūpā*), being a property of the agent (*kartṛ-dharma*), which is the necessary presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*dharmin*) possessing the probans (*sādhana*); and that which is negative (*vyatireka-rūpā*), being a property of the object (*karmadharma*), which is the necessary absence of the probans where the probandum is absent. This is according to the principle that pervasion consists either in the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) wherever [the pervaded is], or in the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only where [the pervader is]. And the establishment of one of these two necessarily entails the cognition of the second; otherwise, not even one of them would be established.

It is simply that in one case the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is direct, whereas in the other it is through necessary implication; by this much alone, there is a single designation [of "perception"]. And this being so, although doubt regarding the other object may arise before the operation of the means of valid cognition regarding the first, it is subsequently dispelled by that [cognition].

Just as for those who maintain that there is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates the contrary, the positive concomitance (anvaya), even if doubted, results in the removal of doubt through the force of its absolute exclusion from the heterologous (vipakṣa)—namely, "this existence, which is in every way impossible in a non-momentary entity, is necessarily restricted to momentary destruction"—so too, because existence brings about a distinct nature determined at every moment, the moment of doubt regarding existence, though previously active even in the absence of that [determination], dissolves of its own accord.

[60,20] If that which possesses activity must necessarily be momentary, then existence is necessarily absent in the absence of momentariness. However, if it were to exist even in the absence of that [momentariness], then how could there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) such that momentariness is invariably present when that [existence] is present? Therefore, whether it be the absolute exclusion (*ekāntiko vyatirekaḥ*) of the probans in the absence of the probandum, or the necessary presence (*avaśyam anvayaḥ*) of the probandum when the probans exists, there is no difference in meaning.

The operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, is twofold in its conventional usage: primarily and by implication. For this very reason, wherever there is a search for a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*), it should be understood that when the proof exists, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum; thus, the search for the proving proof (*sādhakapramāṇa*) is also indicated by that [subversion]. Furthermore, by the term "subverting the opposite" (*viparyayabādhaka*), both [the primary and implied operations] are indeed included.

For in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-rūpa-vyāpti*), there is a sublation of the probans when the probandum is absent; however, in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya-rūpa-vyāpti*), there is a sublation of the absence of the probandum when the probans is present.
