Thus, the meaning is that in the absence of both [concomitances], the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the probans with the probandum is untenable.

Otherwise, even if the means of valid cognition that ascertains the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not directly obtained, if one were to demonstrate the means of valid cognition that establishes the rule of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between the probans and the probandum, what obstacle would there be to the establishment of the probandum? For the negative concomitance implies the capacity for positive concomitance by its very force. Otherwise, the formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya-prayoga*) would be entirely dispensable, since the negative concomitance would not be directly demonstrated.

Therefore, even if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not explicitly grasped through its own form but is instead understood through implication, nevertheless, by the mere fact that "wherever there is the probans (*sādhana*), there is the probandum (*sādhya*)," one who possesses the probans achieves their goal and fulfills their purpose, being motivated by the expectation of the probandum. For even though the probans might be absent when the probandum is absent, if the probandum necessarily occurs whenever the probans is present, then the acceptance of the probans has borne fruit.

Therefore, both must be sought through conceptual analysis by the proponent of the proof; furthermore, the proponent must demonstrate at least one mode established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It should be understood that in the arguments of others, just as with negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*) characterized by necessity is likewise extremely difficult to find.

In our own proof under discussion, however, we have already demonstrated through the two preceding [arguments] a positive concomitance (anvaya) that possesses a necessary restriction, by means of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its contrapositive (viparyaya). Although these two operate with respect to the cloud, which has been taken as the similar instance (sapakṣa), they nevertheless function as follows: "Whatever has the nature of producing something necessarily produces it; whatever does not produce something does not have the nature of producing it" (msĀ p. 15|8). Thus operating, they demonstrate that everything endowed with causal capacity is necessarily restricted to momentariness.

The universal application [of the reason] is the seed for implying its exclusion [from the dissimilar instance], just like smoke and other such reasons. For example, just as one who perceives the pervasion of smoke by fire does not apprehend the existence of fire in the kitchen through a non-application [of the reason], so too the aforementioned inference, while apprehending momentariness in a rain-cloud, establishes the pervasion of momentariness with respect to whatever possesses activity in general, by virtue of the common logical principle.

[61,24] As for what was stated previously—that there is no inference other than from existence, because otherwise there would be an infinite regress—that has been refuted, since the contrapositives of the aforementioned reductios also establish that very point.

If it is argued that the presentation of the reason "existence" (sattva) is thus useless, we reply: Is another means of proof (sādhana) redundant merely because of the existence of another reason? Or is it because that [other reason] must also be presented regarding the subject under consideration (pakṣa)? Or is it because it is possible to present it? Or is it because it must necessarily be presented? Or is it because, once the pervasion (vyāpti)—that "whatever performs a purposeful action is necessarily momentary"—is established, the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) for mountains and the like, which also perform purposeful actions, follows by way of the example of the cloud? These are the possible positions.

In this regard, first of all, [the objection that the reason is] not tenable is incorrect; for even when multiple means of proof are possible, only that which is brought forward by the speaker's intention is useful to the opponent. For this very reason, the fact that [the reason] can be presented is not a cause for its pointlessness, since such a [reason] is indeed presented, having previously been unobtainable. Furthermore, the presentation [of the reason] in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is distinct from its presentation in the mere instance (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), provided it has not yet been established.

Precisely for this reason, the requirement of necessarily presenting [the reason] in the *pakṣa* is also unestablished; because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through the force of that [presentation], the probandum is established by this much alone: "this is a restless chowrie."

The final defect, however, provides an opening for doubt whenever the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which must include all instances—is unestablished; nor is there any distinction in that case regarding the subverting evidence against the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka*). For even if the pervasion of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*) in that which possesses activity is established in a general sense, one who seeks to act toward a particular instance must necessarily present the argument "this is it. What is the point of being so insistent on this matter?

Now, even so, one must necessarily resort to that inference regarding the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) in order to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*); and that very same proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgasādhana*) applies to its own subject. This being the case, one might as well achieve the goal by presenting it with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) itself; what is the point of this much effort to introduce those inferences separately? For, having understood existence (*sattva*) as being pervaded by that [momentariness], one would then conclude momentary destruction in the [actual] locus (*pakṣa*) simply because of existence.

[62,19] If this is so, then the same objection applies even to one who asserts a means of valid cognition that sublates the contrary, because such a person also requires the establishment of pervasion for the formal argument—"whatever has the nature of producing something at a certain time," and so forth—and because the efficacy of that [argument] remains unimpaired with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

Therefore, a distinction must be made here based on the difference in the practitioner’s engagement: for one who, introducing such [arguments] as "whatever is capable of producing a particular effect in relation to each object," is capable of investigating momentariness, the proof of the destruction of moments (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) follows from that very [investigation]; what need is there for another reason? Likewise, even in the case of instructing others, for one who establishes [the point] in exactly that way regarding each individual object, the presentation of another reason is superfluous.

However, one whose intellect is awakened by comparison with that [awakened person] understands—through the application of the logical means for establishing it—that this very same process applies to everything possessing activity. Thus, without needing to exert effort to apply that logic to each individual case, and without failing to ascertain its pervasion by momentariness, he establishes as impermanent every object he perceives to be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). This is the utility of the reason "existence" (*sattva*); and it is the same when demonstrating it to another.

There is no fault, for it is existence (*sattva*) alone that operates by means of a pervasion established through logic (*nyāya*). However, in this case, the effort required to apply that logic to every individual object is simply unbearable; nevertheless, a first-time cognizer, having no other recourse, must rely upon it.

The second [type of opponent], however, by means of the same logic applied to a single instance through the presence of cognition, immediately ascertains that mere action is dependent upon instability, and thus establishes the other [subject] as being existent (*sattva*). Yet, this does not constitute an obstruction to the capacity of that logic to prove momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in any instance possessing action, nor does it mean the proof of existence and so forth is rendered barren; for the logic has simply not been applied to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). Enough of this prolixity.

[63,10] Thus, pervasion (vyāpti) consists in the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) wherever the pervaded (vyāpya) exists. Since the proof of momentary destruction from the reason of existence is unimpeded by the very capacity produced through the pervasion in the form of positive concomitance (anvaya) as a property of the agent, what need is there here for the presentation of a subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) regarding the contrapositive? For this very reason, the impossibility of such a presentation does not cause any distress, because the probandum is established by the subverting proof of the contrapositive itself.

In the treatise as well, in the first rule, pervasion in the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been established in detail under the pretext of avoiding inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), like [the example of] seeds and so forth. However, because it is not clearly understood, people merely superimpose this as a preparatory framework for pervasion characterized by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

[63,16] Here too, there is a curiosity regarding the boldness of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) statements concerning pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its exclusive form (*vyatireka-rūpā*). Even then, it is not merely one kind; rather, it might be something produced by another (*parakṛt*), whether that which is considered stable occurs at another time—either before or after—as this indicates a temporal sequence. Or else, it would not be an action at all, since the restriction "not at another time" implies it does not exist even previously.

Nor is there an action after [the sequence]; thus, there is a teaching on the absence of sequence (*akrama*). However, if the action were to occur either before or after at some time, then there would indeed be sequence; in this way, the definitions of these two are explained as being unmixed. And although simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is in reference to an action occurring at the same time for a single entity, while sequence is in reference to different times, nevertheless, due to the difference in what is being referred to, there is no confusion between them, just as in the case of father and son.

And by the mention of "non-action" (*akriyā*), there may be, according to different views, either the total absence of a real entity in every respect, or its essential nature (*svarūpa*) remaining as devoid of action; there is no insistence on this point. Furthermore, in that context, the term "genus" (*jāti*) is used—not because one intends to express the identity between the preceding and succeeding [moments]—for the action may be either prior or posterior, and it may be either single or manifold. At any given time, both [the prior and posterior states], when considered in relation to the action, do not transcend being denotable by the term "successionless" (*akrama*).

Even there, only multiple actions are real, because the production of a new aggregate from an aggregate is what constitutes reality. The mention of "a single action" occurs merely as a hypothetical possibility or as a logical impossibility. For this very reason, since it is also implied by the term "simultaneity," the meaning subsumed under non-sequential order should be understood even in the word "simultaneity" within the treatise.

And since this twofold mode pertaining to the effect is compatible only with a creator who is subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), the exclusion from what is eternal is stated by means of a function that determines absolute non-existence. However, the word "primarily" (*pradhānyena*)—in the phrase "primarily compatible with momentary destruction"—is capable of indicating that such exclusion applies not only from the eternal, but also from the momentary. Alternatively, it may be for the purpose of following the rule that the pervaded exists only there [where the pervader exists].

By this, it is stated that because for a permanent entity there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—their existence, which is defined by that [efficiency], is lost; therefore, existence comes to rest in momentariness alone and is pervaded by it. Thus, through the non-perception of the pervader characterized by succession and simultaneity, and because of the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposite case, the pervasion of existence—defined as the capacity for causal efficiency—by momentariness is established.

[64,15] In this context, when the property of the agent (*kartṛ-dharma*) is causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then the conventional expression "causal efficiency" or "capacity" (*śakti*) has the same referent. One might raise the objection: "If the property of the object (*karma-dharma*) is pervaded by succession and simultaneity, how can there be a conventional usage of pervasion regarding the property of the agent? To this we reply: even in that case, the causal capacity, being pervaded by way of having successive and non-successive effects as its objects, is said to be "pervaded by succession and non-succession" for the sake of brevity in conventional usage.

By this, the objection of Trilocana—that this sequence [of moments] can be refuted by relying on a sequence characterized by the instrument (karaṇa)—is rejected as a worthless argument. Furthermore, in the phrase "due to the contradiction with causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-virodhāt*), causal efficiency should be understood as a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*) alone, because of the statement that "existence is defined by that [causal efficiency]."

Alternatively, if "characteristic" (*lak�șaṇa*) means a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then let it be a property of the action as well. In that case, the meaning is that for an eternal entity, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) as indicated by succession and simultaneity is contradictory. In the first position, however, the meaning is that for an eternal entity, the capacity to perform an action as indicated by succession and non-succession is contradictory. As for the phrase "by succession and simultaneity," there is no suspicion of permitting other [modes] because of the qualification, since it is employed for the purpose of establishing the reason (*hetu*).

Since causal efficiency occurs only through succession or non-succession, it is therefore contradictory to the notion of permanence, because permanence entails the transcendence of both succession and non-succession; this is the meaning.

What, then, is the contradiction here? First of all, it is not "non-coexistence," because both would attain the status of being real entities, and thus the eternal would always exist. Nor is the second [type of contradiction] applicable. For if it is argued that the eternal must be contradicted by its opposite, the non-eternal—

By the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is indeed a contradiction because it is proven that [the capacity for causal efficiency] is absolutely negated in what is eternal, or because of the statement that [it is a contradiction] due to sublation by another means of valid cognition. In reality, however, the conclusion will rest upon mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*) alone. If one asks: "What, then, is the valid cognition that negates causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in a non-momentary entity? [The answer is: Whatever is not applicable to causal efficiency characterized by either succession or simultaneity is incapable of causal efficiency, just as, for example, the lotus of Hari’s foot. And an entity considered to be eternal is not applicable to an action possessing the properties of succession or non-succession; this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

Indeed, there is no other mode apart from succession and simultaneity by which the possibility of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) might not be pervaded by those two. Therefore, because it is invariably concomitant with causal efficiency alone, and because [causal efficiency] is absent when either of those two modes is absent, its pervasion by them is established. Thus, since the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency is established when those two are absent in the subject under consideration, there is at least no inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*).

In this regard, what Śaṅkara said—when negating causal efficiency through both successive and non-successive modes while suggesting another possibility—namely, "Nor is the non-existence of a third alternative established, because the negation of a specific case has as its object the permission of the remainder," is refuted.

By the statement regarding the meaning of being a cause, it is argued that if [the object] has a nature that is perceptible, its absolute non-existence cannot be established precisely because of that very perceptibility, as in the case of a cloth and so forth; however, if it has a nature that is imperceptible, there is no certainty of its non-existence regarding remote things. Thus, how can there be a certainty of the absence of other modes [of existence], since the grounds for such [certainty] are lacking? So they object.

In that case, if there is such insistence, alas, it destroys the distinction between the paths to heaven and liberation—which is based on the determination of reality through the delimitation of the number of categories. For when a third category is suspected beyond two, a fourth beyond three, and a fifth and so forth beyond four, then, since there would be an infinite number of categories in every instance, how could there be a fixed determination of reality based on restrictions such as "only two" or "only three," as in the cases of "the four means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) or "the six categories" (*padārtha*)?

And when even hundreds of other types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are conceivable, then that which is not established by the four [means] might be established by another, and that which is established by the four might be sublated by another; how, then, could there be a definitive establishment of reality (*tattva-vyavasthiti*) on that basis?

Thus, when a thousand [other] objects are established as distinct from substance and so forth, what need is there for the pursuit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), since the final determination of reality has been subverted? Furthermore, how could he have himself pacified [the dispute] by refuting the two positions regarding whether the impermanent [cognition] performs or does not perform the act of knowing, given that it is impossible to refute even a hundred such modes in this manner?

Furthermore, even animals do not act immediately upon seeing what is improper; how then could this rash deed have been committed by him? Having restricted the two modes [of causality] through non-perception and the requirement of a specific visible object, the refutation of duality by means of succession and simultaneity is indeed impossible for proponents of duality, because it is impossible to demonstrate any other mode, even regarding succession and simultaneity.

Therefore, let this one exert himself for the nourishment of the great ocean of chatter; for when one negation implies the affirmation of another, there is the possibility of a third alternative, which is what is meant by the expression "uncertainty.

Furthermore, if another action occurs immediately after an action performed at a single time, there is the conventional usage of "succession" (*krama*); if it does not occur, there is "non-succession" (*akrama*). Thus, even regarding existence and non-existence, there is the suspicion of a third alternative—this is truly great logician-hood! Enough of this insistence. It remains established that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) is indeed pervaded by succession and non-succession.

Furthermore, Trilocana [argues] that some auxiliary conditions are perceptible, while others are imperceptible. Consequently, the totality of perceptible and imperceptible auxiliary conditions cannot be apprehended through direct perception by one who is not omniscient.

And this being the case, since succession and simultaneity are entirely beyond the reach of perception for that which possesses a complete collection of similar auxiliary conditions, existence—which is pervaded by them—is likewise beyond the reach of perception; how then can the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) be established through perception? To this he replies: "That too is useless. For it has been demonstrated that succession and non-succession are properties of the effect. Therefore, even in the absence of certainty regarding the completeness or incompleteness of the causal complex, the restriction of effects to either succession or simultaneity remains within the scope of direct perception.

How could it be that the production of an effect occurs at one time and not at another, if this were beyond the scope of perception? For even then, the effect must be either single or manifold; and it must be perceived by direct perception as such. Even if multiple [causes] are possible, let it be that only one is perceived; in any case, it is established that the accomplishment of an effect is pervaded exclusively by succession and simultaneity.

[66,21] But surely, on the view of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), there is neither the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) nor the cognition of succession or simultaneity; how, then, can pervasion (*vyāpti*) be established? Thus says Śaṅkara: "If things were momentary, because all cognitions would be restricted by their own nature, the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of cause and effect could not be established. Consequently, it would be impossible to ascertain the existence of that [cause] in every case. For the existence of the cause is not perceived through the cognition of the effect, since at that time the cause has already passed away."

Nor can the existence of an effect be determined by the cognition of its cause when that [effect] is absent, precisely because it is then non-existent; furthermore, there is no establishment of the past and future by means of the present, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Nor can the cognition of the cause’s nature be established by the cognition of the effect alone; for otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that one could determine that smoke is produced by fire even without having observed its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). By this, the cognition of the effect through the mere cognition of the cause is also refuted. Furthermore, for a proponent of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittivādin*), the absence of the effect upon the absence of the cause is beyond even the reach of their imagination, because they lack any means to apprehend the non-existence of the effect when the cause is absent.

For it is not logical to claim that "that [cause] does not exist, yet there is a cognition [of its effect] by means of it. Thus, one who perceives the presence of the effect when the cause is present and its absence when the cause is absent, thereby establishes a stable cognizer who links [the two states].

And thus, if a permanent agent were established, then the fundamental reason of "existence" (*sattva*) would be simply inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to its being common to both sides; what, then, would be the use of adducing a proof that sublates the opposite (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*) in this case? However, if that [permanent agent] is not accepted, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, and thus both [reasons] possess a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*). Just as it is impossible to perceive successive causes and effects, so too it is impossible to perceive them simultaneously; thus there is neither perception of succession nor of simultaneity.

As he himself has said: "Nor can there be simultaneity [of cognitions], because it is impossible to establish the simultaneity of determinate forms through a cognition that possesses a different form. Simultaneity cannot be apprehended by those very cognitions themselves, because if they are not mutually cognizable, their simultaneous existence remains unproven, just as in the case of distinct mental continua (*santāna*). Nor can a single [cognition] possess multiple forms, because if there is a difference in the forms that constitute its very nature, a difference [in the cognition itself] must necessarily follow.

Furthermore, if there were a difference [between the cognition and its forms], it would entail that the cognition is something other than its forms; in that case, the fact that the object possesses those forms would not be established."

To this it is replied: because the cognitions intended to be the objects of reconnection cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of being either different or non-different [from the self]. For if there were non-difference, it would have to be either that very self or the cognitions themselves. In the first case, since there is no action; and in the alternative case, since there is no agent, what would be the purpose of reconnection? Even if there were difference, what would be the purpose of reconnection for that which is insentient and distinct from the cognitions? If it is argued that its status as a reconnecting agent is like that of a seer due to its conjunction with cognition—[we reply: ...

In that case, since it is necessarily accepted that cognition alone is the seer and the unifier, what is the use of this borrowed ornament—the claim that another [entity] possesses those qualities through its connection with that [cognition]? If you argue that this is because cognitions lack agency, then it follows that the conventional designation of that self as a "seer" and so forth is untenable even by way of those cognitions.

For if the intellect (*buddhi*) were the seer of either the cause or the effect, and if it were the synthesizer and the conceptualizer of the specific rule of immediate succession, then—by virtue of that connection—it might indeed be said to possess the status of a seer and a synthesizer. However, as long as the intellect has not acquired distinction with respect to each particular object, even its connection [to those objects] is not capable of bringing about a distinction in practical discourse, such as: "now it is the cognizer of the relation," "now of the effect," or "now the synthesizer."

If, however, one accepts such a specific quality residing in the cognition itself, what else remains to be done? For practical discourse is fully accomplished by that alone. If it is argued that, without a permanent self, that very cognition would not exist;

[68,5] By whom have you been so deceived? Oh, the power of delusion, that it brings even such as these under its control! For instance, the statement that "this does not exist without that" is indeed appropriate only when the causal capacity has been determined through perception and non-perception elsewhere, as in the case of fire with respect to smoke; or, as in the case of the eye and other [senses], when the collection of visible causes is present but the effect is not seen, and is subsequently seen, one concludes in a general sense that something else must be required.

The first position is clearly untenable. Nor is the second possible. For when the cognition of an effect arises immediately after the cognition of a cause, there is no previously unobserved synthesis for one who proceeds with certainty, such as "this was seen by me immediately after that," on account of which one might postulate the causal capacity of something else. Likewise, memory also [arises] from experience either through some indirect transformation of potency, or through the force of its maturation.
If that is so, why is it that upon the experience of one thing, another does not remember it?
Since "of another" does not establish a [logical] connection, why such an objection?

In the course of a dispute concerning the establishment of a related entity distinct from experience and so forth, to raise an objection by relying on that very [entity] which has already been established is irrelevant. For once that is established, the dispute comes to an end; what further dependence could there be? Therefore, having removed "of another" because it is the subject of dispute, the remaining question—"How is there no memory in experience?"—is not useful for the present context. However, the following is the appropriate meaning of the objection:

If an experience is connected to a particular body, why does no recollection of it arise in another body? By asserting this, you are effectively saying: why does a seed belonging to one field not produce a sprout in another field? And from where does such a principle derive?

[68,21] Is it not the case that there is no other proximity between experience and recollection than the mere relation of cause and effect? Nor is there this restriction regarding the causal relation, namely, that the effect must have the same locus as its cause, since we observe the effect of cognition even when it occurs at a place extremely remote from its object. If that were so, then for the sprout as well, there would be no proximity other than the mere fact of being an effect; thus, like the cognition, the seed would produce the sprout even when situated at a distance.

[Objection: But surely, how can certain atoms that initiate a seed be established as the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of a sprout, while being unable to produce a sprout in another field? For you, such a proximity is lacking. Furthermore, since this [sprout] shares the property of being an effect with consciousness and so forth, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its production even at a great distance remains unavoidable. If this is argued:

Why, then, do the atoms of the seed function as the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) specifically for the effect that is the sprout, and not for cognition and so forth? Because all things are of one and the same nature insofar as they are effects. Consequently, like the sprout, cognition would have to exist in that very same location; or else, like cognition and the rest, the sprout would also be produced at a distance. This is because there is no distinction between them in their status as effects, and because the seed functions as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the sprout in exactly the same way as it does for those other things.

[69,6] But surely, that very sprout in which the seed-atoms attain the status of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the sprout itself; so how can it be urged that their status as inherent causes pertains elsewhere than in the sprout? If this is the case, then since the status of inherent cause cannot be avoided due to its single flavor as an effect, it follows by necessity that all [the atoms] possess the same form as the sprout and occupy the same location. Thus, your hope for a solution has borne fruit in the most appropriate place!

Furthermore, if all effects are indistinguishable by virtue of being effects, then all causes would likewise be indistinguishable by virtue of being causes; thus, the diversity of the universe would be left without a basis for explanation. Therefore, even though they share the status of being effects, it is not the case that there is only one single mode for all of them.

Just as, according to your own view, due to natural distinctions, something in one case functions as an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), in another as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and in yet another as an instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), so too for us: some effect produces its cause in the very same location, while some does so in a separated location; furthermore, some effect is by necessity characterized by arising in the very place of its cause, while others are otherwise.

Likewise, the possibility of recognition occurs with respect to a single effect and not elsewhere, despite the lack of distinction in their being effects—just as in the case of different lamps or [different] cognitions. Furthermore, regarding such an effect, where you establish the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), for us that is the conventional usage of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) with respect to the self and so forth, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, within such a succession of causes and effects, in one case there is the establishment of a single continuum (*santāna*), while in another there is merely a state of cooperation (*sahakāritva*); thus, despite this difference in process, the duality of effects remains established by nature in that manner, and even you cannot transcend this fact—this is settled. Moreover, given the occurrence of such a distinction, how could that which possesses the property of arising in the very locus where the action is performed arise elsewhere?

Or rather, how could a cause that produces its effect only within its own locus produce that effect elsewhere? Therefore, even in the case of experience, how could memory—which is produced in the very locus of the experience—be generated elsewhere, like a sprout from a seed? Or else, since memory arises necessarily in the same locus as the experience, just like a sprout, how could it arise elsewhere, such that the objection regarding the contingency of memory in another body would find any ground?

But in the theory of a self (*ātmavāda*), this is difficult to avoid, because that [self], being all-pervading, would exist in another body as well by virtue of its very nature of producing memory. Furthermore, the reliance upon the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) belongs only to something eternal. If it is asked: "How is it to be understood that the principle governing experience and memory is like that of the seed and the sprout, and not like other things?

[The answer is: That same principle is determined even for the seed and the sprout precisely because they are observed to be so; and such a rule of necessity exists for experience and memory as well, for when one person possesses experience in one body, another form [another person] does not possess the memory thereof.

[70,3] But how can the body possess experience? There is no flaw, for there is an intended relation [between the body and experience] by virtue of its being the locus of that [experience], its being the cause of that, or its having the same cause as that. Furthermore, how does the self possess experience? If it is argued that this is by the force of inherence (*samavāya*), [then...]

But surely, even inherence (*samavāya*), when accepted as the cause for the cognition "it is here," is merely a conceptual construction serving as the basis for the cognition "it is here. And since there is the cognition "here" with respect to the body, why is inherence not likewise postulated? If it is argued that this is because there is no inseparable connection (*ayutasiddhatva*) between the body and the cognition, since they are perceived as entirely distinct; [we reply: ...

[Objection: Is it not the case that the rule of the cognition "this is here" applies only to two things perceived as distinct? For when two entities are observed in an upper-lower relationship, the use of the locative and nominative cases is appropriate because they do not overlap. But when there is no perception of distinctness at all, how can one who designates them with the distinction "this is here" not lose their status as a discerning person? [If you say: "Because in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), no distinction is ever observed anywhere."

For this very reason, having produced by one's own will the cognition "it is here"—which is merely a conceptual construction (vikalpamātra) and capable of being brought about at will—one postulates what is called "inherence" (samavāya). The establishment of inherence depends upon the cognition "it is here," yet that cognition "it is here" would only occur if two things were perceived. Since no such perception of a pair ever occurs regarding its object, [the notion of inherence] is therefore merely one's own fabrication; thus, it is not a valid means of proof.

Thus, to apply the designation "possessing intelligence" to a self that does not exist at all imitates the story of joining the horns of a barren cow's son with a donkey's head. For when something is postulated for a certain purpose, its non-existence is established precisely by the fact that that same purpose is accomplished by something else; and since the purpose of the self—such as memory and so forth—is already established by something else, there is no need for it. Therefore, an experience residing in one body is not capable of producing memory in another body.

[70,19] If it is objected: "Since memory arises only in another body if [the self] were momentary, how can this be resolved? Or, if one accepts rebirth in another life, why would the same consequence not apply even to a body intended to be a different continuum, given that their distinctness (*anyatva*) is no different? [Response: Such production of memory in another body is difficult to avoid for the self as well; therefore, the consequence applies elsewhere too because distinctness is no different—this is the same [for both positions].

Even if the momentariness of the body is not accepted, its perishability is certainly accepted by them; therefore, the fault is the same, from which fear you accept the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*). Now, if it is argued that in the doctrine of a self there is no fault because memory is produced in the very body conditioned by the karma of that self, then in the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), whose is that karma? For apart from the body, only a momentary consciousness (*buddhi*) is possible.

For this very reason, the pleasure, pain, and so forth resulting from that action cannot belong to the momentary agent, because that [agent] lacks the experience thereof. And since the momentary state that experiences is not the agent, there would be the additional fault of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Furthermore, for you, there is no establishment of any karma whatsoever from which these inherent faults could be avoided. Moreover, even the "continuum" (*santāna*), though spoken of, is nothing distinct [from the moments]. Nor does karma exist as something distinct for you; thus, it is like a painting without a wall.

To this it is replied: First of all, the momentary state of the agent does not admit of denial even in the absence of that action or the experience of its fruit; for a man is not thereby deprived of fire simply because he possesses it without performing acts such as burning. Even the final moment is connected [to the result] by way of being an auxiliary to that action through a causal series, precisely because it participates in the experience [of the fruit]. Furthermore, simultaneity is impossible even between cause and effect, yet it is possible between Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.

Therefore, the connection expressed as "this belongs to that" regarding a distinct entity occurs solely by way of benefit (*upakāra*). And such a benefit exists in great measure for the final [moment], being produced by that [action]; and for the intermediate moments belonging to that same continuum, there exists the capacity to produce a similar final moment, either directly or through a succession. Since this arises from that very action, the relation of even those [intermediate moments] to it is likewise established solely by way of benefit.

And thus, when the established relationship between all [beings] and their karma is fixed, it is only in a body brought forth by the sovereign power (*adhipatya*) of that karma that there arises the emergence of moments of consciousness and body produced by that karma; not elsewhere, because of the absence of such proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, while karma is certainly not distinct [from its effects], the description as if it were separate is merely for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

As for that moment which is said to be connected with prior karma, it has arisen as characterized by such a specific quality, from which there arises—in the end—a continuum capable of producing the moment that experiences its fruit, as well as the arising of a succession of bodies corresponding to that [fruit].

In that process, from the first distinguished [moment], two moments of intellect and body arise which possess the slightest degree of excellence; these, acting together, produce two subsequent moments possessing a lesser degree of excellence, and those in turn produce two further moments with still less excellence. By this method, the intensity of the excellence characterized by capacity accumulates through degrees of "more" and "most," until finally there arises that which is capable of producing the ultimate result; hence it is called the "final."

Since the intellect and the body are mutually bound by their dependence on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and are thus distinguished from any other series, there is no room for the suspicion of duality apart from their non-separation. Even when taking up another birth, once the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that life-span are exhausted, another body corresponding to it is produced by a moment of mind (*manaḥ-kṣaṇa*) acting as a concomitant cause alongside the final moment of the perishing form; this body, as before, provides assistance to the mind. Thus, there is no room for concern regarding memory or the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) in another body.

And herein, there is nothing distinct by way of what is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*), because the continuum is established without obstruction precisely through the establishment of the connection between moments and their actions, since it is not separate from them. Nor is the presentation of the system primarily by way of the continuum, but rather by way of the moments; thus, everything is clarified through the purification of the root. As it has been said:
"In whichever very continuum the impression of an action (*karmavāsanā*) is deposited, therein alone it bears fruit, just as [the dye] is fixed in cotton."
Thus, that [is said] regarding the establishment of the definition of one's own intended continuum.

As for what the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, while refuting this, says: "No, because proof and refutation are impossible; there is no proof because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. For a positive concomitance such as 'memory [arises] from the causal relation, like the redness [of a flower] in cotton' is not possible. Nor is there a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) such that 'wherever there is no memory, there is no causal relation. And because one does not point out [the fallacies of] unestablishedness and so forth, there is no refutation."

For subsequent cognitions cannot arise with respect to an object already experienced by a preceding cognition, because they are distinct from it—just like the cognitions of another continuum. Thus, no fault whatsoever is established against this reason by the example "like the redness in cotton" (29b).

[72,12] That is an unconsidered statement, due to a failure to understand the meaning of the proof (*sādhana*). For in this verse, it is not perceived that the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is presented as the reason for memory. What then? It is the latent impression of action (*karmavāsanā*). For a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the formative influence (*abhisaṃskāra*) produced by action; indeed, that which is infused (*vasita*) is called "formatively influenced" (*abhisaṃskṛta*). The bond of results such as experience occurs only in that very continuum (*santāna*) where the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) produced by the action has arisen, and not elsewhere.

Having asserted the proposition that "there is no such distinction [in this case]," for one who says "just as [dye] on a cotton cloth," either the difference in the continuum of formations (*saṃskāra-santāna-bheda*) is intended as the reason, and the probandum here is the negation of results such as experience; yet, the suitability for those results within that very continuum is perceived. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Whatever latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is deposited within a particular continuum is capable of yielding its fruit only therein and not elsewhere. For example, in the continuum of a cotton plant, that which is produced by the application of a dyeing substance during the seed stage is capable of manifesting the fruit of redness at the stage of the flower or the fruit, but not in another continuum. And this latent impression is a continuum of consciousness (*cittasantāna*) generated by actions such as giving.

Thus, it is precisely a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) with respect to the composite probandum. For the capacity to yield a fruit within that continuum is invariably concomitant with the impression (*saṃskāra*), whereas in another continuum there is an absolute incapacity for it; this is because no other cause is required. However, when each [element] is taken as the probandum individually, the first is a *svabhāvahetu*.

In the second case, however, there is the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). This is because the nature of being a mental impression (*saṃskāratva*)—which is pervaded by the giving of a fruit within its own substratum alone, as this is contradictory to the giving of a fruit in a different continuum from its own substratum—is perceived. In that regard, if, even when a mental impression exists, the capacity to give a fruit in that continuum were to depend upon another cause, then the production of the mental impression through effort would be purposeless. Furthermore, if the capacity to give a fruit existed even in a different continuum, then a second effort [to produce it] would be futile.

Nor is it the case that because one *āmalaka* fruit becomes sweet when sprinkled with milk, all *āmalaka* fruits become sweet; therefore, the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is pervaded by the yielding of its fruit only within its own continuum, and thus there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*). Furthermore, having accepted—as established by scripture—that the refinement is a specific quality of the mind produced by karma, the resolution is equal to the objection; thus, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction, nor is there a failure of pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*).

Alternatively, whatever continuum there may be, it is capable of yielding its fruit only when the respective conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) has been rendered sweet; just as in the case of a cotton continuum, this too is a mental continuum, as explained previously.

[73,9] This same principle applies even with respect to the results such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth. If this [establishment of causality] were determined by way of a continuum (*saṃtāna*), then it would follow that it would apply even to a continuum well-known for its connection through knowledge or blood (*vidyā-yoni-sambandha*). Consequently, there would be memory and so forth in a disciple regarding what was experienced by the teacher, and likewise in a son regarding the experience and so forth of the father. Such a continuum is not intended here; rather, it is one consisting of a succession of cause and effect in the form of a relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). What, then, is the definition of material cause and its product?

The restriction to a single substratum applies when there is no cause for investigation; even when there is investigation, the restriction to its fitness [for that relationship] remains. Indeed, a diverse succession of causes and effects has already been established previously, and it has also been indicated therein that such a series characterized by these features is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*). Furthermore, this is not the case between the minds of teacher and student, or between the minds of father and son; thus, the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) alleged by the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* does not apply. Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding the determination of the continuum and the determination of the material cause (*upādāna*), because it has been demonstrated that the determination of the material cause does not depend upon that [determination of the continuum].

Alternatively, the two—nature (*prakṛti*) and transformation (*vikṛti*)—are characterized as cause and effect, respectively as the material cause (*upādāna*) and the product (*upādeya*), based on a single, non-erroneous, and agreed-upon determination. Within the continuum of cause and effect, this should be understood as being characterized by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which identifies: "this is the material cause" and "this is the product. However, in the case of the arising of something heterogeneous, the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself constitutes the characteristic of the material cause as nature and the product as transformation.

Alternatively, the definition is "the state of being both material cause and modification" (*prakṛtivikṛtitva*); this is an expression emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*), as in the cases of wood and a sacrificial post (*kāṣṭhayūpa*) or wood and charcoal (*kāṣṭhāṅgāra*). Even when many [parts] arise, it is only the distinct parts that constitute the material cause (*upādāna*), just as heat and so forth are the causes of smoke, or as embers are the cause of [hot] ash. Furthermore, even in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), there is a single conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) and a single determination (*avasāya*) regarding a person. Indeed, for one who discerns the coloring by objects and reflects upon pure consciousness alone, there arises within a continuum accepted as a single person the determination: "This is that very same cognition."

Furthermore, because they do not replicate the entire nature [of the cause] here, or even if replication were possible, the single-determination [of the effect] would be an error—just as in the case of different trees—there is no established relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth between father and son and the like. Thus, if one establishes the relationship of material cause and so forth in such a continuum while disregarding the definition of material cause and so forth, then when the question arises as to what kind of continuum the latencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*) are deposited in, there is no fault in stating that it is "wherein the relationship of material cause and so forth exists."

Furthermore, he says this: No, because in the absence of a specific relation, the distinction between material cause (*upādāna*) and other causes cannot be established based merely on a difference in the nature of the cause. Just as for us, even though there is no difference in their status as producers (*janakatva*), there is a distinction between inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*) causes due to a specific relation; we do not see such a distinction between material and other causes in your system.

This too has already been refuted, because even in the case of causal universality (*kāraṇatvasāmānya*), a distinction based on the effect has been demonstrated. For if cause and effect were not dependent upon each other's specific differences, the difficulty of establishing their relationship—even by way of a connection—would have been incurred. Furthermore, it was indicated at least in part that *samavāya* (inherence) is not capable [of serving as such a connection]. Therefore, there is no refutation whatsoever of either the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) or the continuum (*santāna*).

[74,11] Even though the term *karmavāsanā* (karmic impression) is employed here in this verse, its meaning does not follow that of cotton; nevertheless, since the sense of *vāsanā* as "formative activity" (*abhisaṃskāra*) does indeed follow, it is that very [activity] which should be understood as the indicated reason. Alternatively, by the word *karman* (action), "activity" (*kriyā*) is also meant; the meaning is that whatever formative activity has been produced by any kind of activity within a continuum. By this, the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is shown; however, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is to be understood from the context.

Therefore, having taken up that which was stated—namely, that memory establishes the causal relationship directly—all of that is undermined; however, the view that memory conforms to the specific particulars that serve as the basis for the causal relationship is beyond reproach.

Furthermore, regarding the argument that there can be no memory of an object experienced by a preceding cognition in subsequent cognitions because they are distinct, like the cognitions of a different mental continuum—here, is it being denied that the subsequent cognitions, which are the subjects (*dharmin*), possess a connection with a cognition in the form of memory? Or is it that their very nature as memory is being excluded? Or is it being established that they do not result in memory as their fruit? First of all, the first position is untenable.
For we do not maintain that there is a separate memory which possesses memory as its attribute such that it would need to be negated; rather, that cognition is of the very nature of memory itself.

If it is argued that at the time of looking for a cow while remembering a horse, that perception becomes possessed of memory, then is it intended to negate memory only in that specific state? If memory occurs independently [of such association], let it be so. If this is not the case, then what is the point of this reference to concomitance regarding subsequent cognitions?

If it is argued that the mention of the subject (*dharmin*) is solely for the sake of inference (*anumāna*), we say no; for the complete establishment of what is intended in the context is achieved, since at all times subsequent to that, the negation of memory is accepted, which results in the non-establishment of a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhi*) for the proof.

Alternatively, if it is held that the negation is not intended at the time of mere memory during the demonstration of incapacity, then what fault has the concomitance with another cognition committed, such that memory should be negated only at that time when memory occurs subsequently without a self? Furthermore, there is no subverting evidence whatsoever regarding the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In the second case, however, regarding the denial of the status of memory for subsequent cognitions, does this mean that experience itself is denied the status of memory, or rather that previous cognitions are? If it is a denial in all cases, then what is the point of specifying a particular distinction, as was argued previously?

Regarding the third alternative, the futility of specifying such a distinction must be established in exactly the same way. Now, if it is intended that—because the specification of a distinction is merely illustrative—all cognition other than experience is neither of the nature of memory nor does it produce memory; [we reply: the fact that experience possesses such a nature has not been refuted. Consequently, it follows that experience is both of the nature of memory and produces memory, which is undesirable for both parties.

Otherwise, the qualification "as other than experience" would be purposeless. Let it be purposeless; even so, if "being other than experience" were the reason for all cognitions, it would be unestablished in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*), because experience itself is not something other than itself.

Furthermore, the mention of "subsequent" (*uttara*) is intended as a subject of dispute (*vivādapada*), and not for the purpose of excluding others; for even the Buddhist does not accept that other cognitions possess the nature of memory. Nevertheless, this is not a valid response under the third alternative, because experience (*anubhava*) itself is also a subject of dispute. For, according to the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyapakṣa*), it is precisely what you do not accept that experience directly produces memory; whereas for the Buddhist, this is accepted. Thus, this [proponent] is unable to admit that experience generates memory because it is undesirable, yet he cannot reject it either, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhi*).

[75,16] Let it be so; nevertheless, pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established even for both positions. For instance, if one maintains that a subsequent cognition possesses the nature of memory or the capacity to produce memory, and if—upon obtaining those two—it were possible to demonstrate its non-difference from the experience (*anubhava*), then pervasion would not be established by the negation of those two in relation to its difference from them. And this is not possible.

If its distinctness from experience were abandoned, it would simply be experience itself; and how could that be called "remembrance"? Furthermore, if it is said to be the producer of remembrance, then that [status] does not rest without presupposing that experience is the cause of remembrance. For a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is applicable only when an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) has been established. Likewise, [objections] such as its occurring at a later time and so forth should not even be raised, for they can be countered in exactly the same way. However, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, if you are intent on raising objections, you should speak thus:

If it is argued that remembrance, experience, and so forth are produced solely from experience or solely from karma, then it would follow that they could arise even in a different continuum (*santāna*), which is not accepted even by the opponent. Whatever possesses or lacks a specific capacity in relation to something else must likewise possess or lack a specific result in relation to that same thing; for example, the two sets of causal conditions consisting of seed, earth, water, fire, wind, and so on. Furthermore, the two continua possess or lack the specific capacity [for remembrance] derived from experience; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

And the proof for this has already been shown by the passage beginning with "in that very [moment]," since the specific nature of the impression (*saṃskāra*) was clearly stated—like that of cotton—in the passage beginning with "the latent tendency of karma" (31a), as we have previously explained. Likewise, the principle is the same for the claim that memory arises from experience.

Alternatively, this is an inquiry regarding the reason stated previously: "Is it because this principle—that there is no production due to difference—applies only to experience, memory, and so forth, which are considered cause and effect in a continuous series, and not to other things? Or, if it applies to others as well, then if this principle is obtained as a specific case of the subject under discussion, some reasoning should be provided by which this particularity might be understood here, overriding the sequence established for general cases. If it is argued that [the principle does not apply] because it is not observed in the case of a different continuum (*santānāntara*), [we reply:]...

If production occurs through a succession of specific qualities when there is difference [of cause], then in the absence of that [succession], that [production] would not be observed, just as redness is not observed in cotton whose seeds were not red. However, it cannot be claimed on that basis alone that there is no production whatsoever in all cases.

In the second case, however, this is merely the pointing out of a lack of proof (*asiddhi*). For when a seed is red, one observes that the flower or fruit produced in its continuum is also colored by that same hue. As for the argument that memory is possible through a causal relationship because there is no deception regarding their distinctness (*nānātva*), here too the poor wretch of shame has been cast aside by that very statement; if the effect were excluded from the cultivated cotton, everything would be well. Thus, this is a general logical principle established by common consensus.

Even if they are distinct, the fact that a result occurs in one continuum and not in another—depending on other specific conditions—is impossible to preclude even in the present case. Let us leave aside for now whether this verse establishes a proof or a refutation. Thus it is established: even in the absence of a single, persisting entity, recollection occurs through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced in the continuum by experience. Furthermore, it is never observed through perception that experience and recollection share a single substratum.

[76,19] Furthermore, as for what was said here: "No, because it is observed. For instance, one determines that the experience and the recollection have a single substratum—thinking, "I now remember that very object which I previously experienced; I who was the experiencer am the same I who am the rememberer"—without depending on the recollection of a connection between a mark (*liṅga*) and its object, nor upon the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*). Nor is this a delusion, because there is no contradiction with reality. One who denies the perceptibility of pleasure and the like should not be instructed by means of sensory perception.

Likewise, the fact that even the desire for synthesis, aversion, and so forth have a single cause is apprehended through direct perception: "I see that which I saw before"; "having seen it, I desire it or I hate it"; "desiring or hating it, I exert myself"; and "exerting myself, having attained that object, I have become happy or miserable."

Thus, since the object that exists in this cognition "I" is the substratum for memory, synthesis, desire, and so forth, which appear through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the self (*ātman*) is apprehended by direct perception. For the cognition "I" is neither doubtful nor erroneous; nor is it inferential or verbal. That [objection] too is merely a false satisfaction. For instance, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) first arises: "I alone am the seer and the rememberer."
Furthermore, not every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an object of valid cognition (*āśvāsaviṣaya*). Thus, it has been shown by Trilocana that this [conceptual construction] is of four kinds.

Among these, it cannot first of all be one that arises subsequent to perception (*pratyakṣapṛṣṭhabhāvī*), because you yourself do not admit the existence of another perception that could grasp it, such that this [conceptual construction] might be described as its subsequent [cognition]. Its status as being based on inference (*lauṅgikatva*) has also been refuted by yourself. Therefore, if you accept as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) something that is either devoid of a real object (*avastuka*) or whose object is doubtful (*sandigdhavastuka*), what limit is there to your concessions?

Now, if this fifth [type of] perception is asserted as distinct from these, then this same logic would easily apply to everything that one’s own mind intends as an object, even when it lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there would be no obstruction to the establishment [of such objects] anywhere.
If it is argued that [perception] is distinguished by self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), [we reply:]...

Furthermore, it has already been largely established that this "corroboration" (saṃvāda) must consist either in the attainment of purposeful action (arthakriyā-prāpti) or in the operation of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara-vṛtti). If another means of valid cognition exists, let that alone suffice; what is the use of this [corroboration]? Moreover, no purposeful action is determined as something to be accomplished by a persisting entity, since all such action is established through the intellect and the body. Nor does the notion of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya) have as its object anything distinct from those two.

For just as in the case of the cognition "this is that Caitra," where one recognizes the same person as a unity across earlier and later times by disregarding the distinctions created by limiting conditions (*upādhi*) within Caitra’s body, so too is it with the cognition "I myself am the seer and the rememberer. This is merely a conventional designation based on the intellect (*buddhi*), such as when one says, "I who was a fool am now this [person] in bodily form."

Furthermore, some designation occurs by way of the body, as in "I am fair" or "I am fat," because it is well known that a designation for a whole is made through a part. Yet another [type of designation] occurs by way of both, such as "the kingdom was ruled by me" or "my misfortune," and so forth; these should be inferred accordingly.

Even those designations based on pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*) are indeed designations of the intellect (*buddhi*), because there is no distinction between them and the intellect, as in [the expressions] "I am happy" up to "I am righteous. Even the designation of difference, such as "the face belongs to him" or "the body belongs to him," is intended to express a distinction between a whole and one of its parts, just as in the case of "the branch of a tree. For this very reason, the expression "I am the face" does not occur.

[77,22] How then can there be "my intellect" or "my body"? It is just as with "the body of a stone-son" (*śilā-putraka*). In that case, one might also say "intellect-body," yet is it not also seen [in common usage] to say "Rāhu’s head"? And just as in that very instance there is the conventional expression "my self" despite the absence of a second self, so too is it the same regarding the absence of a first self in the expression "my intellect and body. And just as one says "I am not the self," so too one says "I am not the intellect or the body."

If it is argued that because the meaning has already been stated by the expression "I am the self," it is not fit for further application, then the same applies to the expressions "I am the intellect" and "I am the body," as their meaning has likewise already been stated. Furthermore, wise men do not insist upon words that depend solely upon mere convention; so let this matter rest for now.

Therefore, this word "I" (aham) of mine is intent upon the negation of another speaker; it does not, however, refer to any other entity apart from the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*vigraha*). And because of the identification (*ekādhyavasāya*) of those two—the intellect and the body—even when they belong to the past or the future—with the present [self], one employs such expressions as "seen by me alone," "touched by me alone," and "remembered by me alone. Consequently, just as in the case of "This is that Caitra," this is merely a superimposition of unity upon the two aggregates across earlier and later times; it is not a reference to a distinct entity. If it is argued that even Caitra is recognized as being the very self (*ātman*):

No, because there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of what has not been seen; for it is only the intellect (*buddhi*) and the body (*vigraha*) that are perceived. And although the intellect of another is inferable, nevertheless, due to extreme habituation, we observe that in this case one acts as if it were directly perceived (*adhyakṣavat*); thus there is no fault. For it is observed that from the mere sight of a friend or an enemy, one carries out the corresponding action. Moreover, in that case, there is no delay caused by following the process of seeking a logical mark (*liṅga*), its form, and so forth.

Nor does such practice occur merely upon the apprehension of the body, for that would lead to the absurd consequence [of it occurring] even in a dead corpse. Furthermore, because birth is the motivator of all bodily activity, the very perception of the self by the intellect from birth onwards remains constantly present as the seed for the habituation to its concomitance with the other [self]. However, the perception of the self is not likewise the seed for habituation, since all activity is exhausted by the body and consciousness alone.

Therefore, it is precisely the mind and body, which are the objects of the word "Caitra," that are recognized as "this is that very same one. Likewise, regarding those two which are the objects of the word, there is merely this recognition: "This was seen by me; this was remembered by me"; and even [the thoughts] "It was done by me" and "It will be experienced by me" are merely the conceptual determination of identity belonging to those two alone.

Therefore, in this view, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which follows immediately upon perception has as its object [the notion of] "assurance. If it refers to the mere existence and unity of preceding and succeeding moments, it is devoid of a real entity (*avastuka*). But if it has an object distinct from that, then—even though the object appears—because of the confusion between the suspicion of its being unreal and its being real, it is of a doubtful nature; how then could it establish for itself the status of being established by perception?

Furthermore, that which he proclaims as an inference—namely, that those who possess distinct desires and so forth must have a single related entity because they are the objects of the unifying cognition "mine," just as spectators are the objects of the unifying cognition of a single dancer—that too merely reveals his extreme lack of heart (insensitivity). For there is no such thing as a dancer who is a single, unitary entity in reality, since she is nothing more than a collection of atoms presided over by consciousness.

Since unity is established by conventional usage, and since the example is established on that basis, who can prevent its establishment by conventional usage in the case of the subject as well? And if it is argued that the example does not apply in every respect:

This is true. However, by whose power could a real identity (*tāttvikam ekatvam*) be established, given that its concomitance is not observed in the example and, consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not proven? For pervasion, which relies on the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is established even when it is observed in an example; but regarding what is not observed, there is not even the suspicion of its establishment. Therefore, even in the view that an example is not common in every respect, it must at least be made common by means of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).

Indeed, there is no purpose for an example other than the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*); nor does the demonstration of pervasion with the probandum (*sādhya*) become effective if the example is not shown. Furthermore, the removal of the charge of being devoid of the probandum is not achieved by establishing a single composite whole (*avayavin*), because a dancer lacks the status of a composite whole when considered as a collection of body, intellect, and so forth. On the contrary, from the perspective of the body, the refutation of the composite whole remains fully operative.

However, with respect to a self, that [self] remains unestablished even today; and because there is no sublation of the contrary, there is no peace from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). For the recognition "this is mine" is possible—even like a case of recognition—due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); how then could it be accepted as being dependent on a single underlying relation?

Thus, just as for the proponent of momentariness, the entire complex of memory, the connection between action and its fruit, and so forth, does not fail even in the absence of a persisting entity, so too is the cognition of the relation of cause and effect; therefore, there is no stain of doubt regarding the fallacy of the inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) based on commonality.

Śaṅkara, however, due to his loquacity, performs some sort of dramatic gesture; for instance, sometimes the cognition of smoke preceded by the perception [of fire] produces the certainty that "this object, grey like the neck of a pigeon, is an effect of fire"; sometimes it is a non-perception preceded by the perception of both [fire and smoke]. Furthermore, since non-perception has the nature of perceiving the counter-positive entity, it is essentially of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); moreover, since positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established when non-perception reaches its culmination, it should be determined as residing in that very [non-perception].

The method of perception and non-perception that grasps positive and negative concomitance has also been demonstrated in the investigation of the "threefold" and "fivefold" [criteria]; let that suffice for now.

We shall, however, speak to the matter at hand. In both cases, regarding cognitions that arise sequentially, the final cognition—due to the depositing of a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by each preceding one—is capable of producing the thought, "This is the effect of that," just as before; thus, there is no need to postulate a persisting entity as the connector.

As for what was further stated—that exclusion (*vyatireka*) is not even within the scope of mental construction—that is an extreme absurdity. For it is not said that the very same perception which apprehends a real entity also apprehends the exclusion of two entities upon the cessation of those two; rather, it is simply another perception whose nature is the apprehension of a distinct counter-entity (*pratiyogi*). Therefore, where does the argument—"that [exclusion] does not exist, and yet there is a cognition of it"—serve? It is not logical.

And in this way, there is no consistency with the doctrine of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) regarding perception. If it is argued that there is awareness of the preceding and succeeding moments, that from those two arises a latent impression (*vāsanā*), and from that [impression] arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines cause and effect—[this is not so].

[80,1] Now, do you follow this rule that whatever might be suspected must be stated? For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would have to be either a synthesis of what has been perceived or a superimposition of a form that is not that [of the object]. It cannot be the former position, because for a person who has not observed positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there can be no grasping of the relation between cause and effect; consequently, a specific latent impression (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*), which is the cause of the cognition of synthesis, is impossible. Furthermore, if there were a synthesis of what has not been grasped, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

This [objection] has not been correctly considered; for, since the preceding and succeeding moments existing as cause and effect are directly perceived through sequential experience, their status as cause and effect is indeed grasped. It is simply that, because the effect is absent at the time of the cause, even though the capacity directed toward it is grasped, the determination regarding it does not yet proceed due to the non-perception of the effect; [only] upon seeing the effect does it proceed.

Likewise, even when observing the effect, its status as an effect is apprehended and subsequently connected by conceptual thought; thus, this conceptual thought consists precisely in the recollection of what has already been apprehended. Furthermore, the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*); therefore, this [objection] is trivial. By this, that which was said is also refuted: namely, that for one who has not perceived positive and negative concomitance, the causal relationship between a latent impression (*vāsanā*) and the cause of that impression is not established; and since the same objection applies there as well, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

[80,13] Indeed, the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) regarding the subject at hand has already been established. The proof of the positive and negative concomitance between latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) follows from the final instance of perceptual non-apprehension (*adhyakṣānupalambha*), because activity does not occur based on a solitary perception or non-apprehension; for since a latent impression is of the nature of a potentiality (*śakti*), its establishment is untenable without an effect.

Furthermore, for that [cognition] established in such a manner, the proof of its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with its own cause, even through experience, occurs solely by way of the positive and negative concomitance of the effect. Nor is there the first objection: as long as there is no conceptual construction of synthesis (*anusandhāna-vikalpa*), so long is there no proof of positive and negative concomitance regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*) or the cause of the latent impression; and as long as there is no proof of positive and negative concomitance regarding the latent impression or its cause, so long is there no conceptual construction of synthesis.
