For a synthetic conceptual construction (*anusandhāna-vikalpa*) does not depend upon a determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-niścaya*) regarding the latent impression (*vāsanā*) or the cause of the latent impression; rather, it depends merely on the existence within one's own continuum of those two latent impressions which possess positive and negative concomitance. However, the determination of that positive and negative concomitance does indeed depend upon the synthetic conceptual construction. In this regard, just as smoke—which is dependent upon fire and fuel—is not itself dependent upon the determination of the positive and negative concomitance between fire and fuel (lest there be a circular dependency), so it is in the present case as well. Enough with excessive talk.

As for the position that superimposes a nature not belonging to it, that has already been set aside by disregarding it as irrelevant, since it leads to undesirable logical consequences (*dūṣaṇaprasaṅga*). Therefore, it is established that the cognition of the causal relation is unconfused and that [the object] is impermanent.

Furthermore, when those two are established, the perception of sequence is unavoidable, because the cognition that "this being present, this arises from that" is inseparable from the determination of sequence. Otherwise, the application of distinct grammatical case endings to denote the proven cause and the probandum would be untenable due to a lack of restriction regarding their respective objects. For there is no difference in terms of dependence on sequence, whether one perceives the sequence between cause and effect, or between two effects.

There is not even a suspicion of simultaneity, because immediately after the perception of several [objects] at one time, the conceptual construction "these have arisen all at once" arises, just as a sprout emerges from a seed. Indeed, there is no fault or contradiction regarding momentariness caused by the apprehension of the arising of those multiple effects. For while in the case of sequential perception there might be an initial impression of synthesis based on a stable [entity], in the case of simultaneous perception, what need is there for a stable entity?

It might be argued that even in the case of simultaneous perception, it would follow that there must be a separate cognizer for each subsequent memory; however, that has already been refuted previously. Or rather, let that very point be stated directly—why this belabored vomiting of objections regarding the "cognition with form" (*sākāra*), which is like scratching where there is no wound, since it is irrelevant to the present topic? If you maintain that there is indeed simultaneous apprehension, then it will occur through either a cognition with form or one without form (*nirākāra*); why then insist now on the application of the finality of all principles?

If, however, it is intended that there is simply no simultaneous apprehension of multiple [objects], then let it be the same as the refutation of the theory of forms (*sākāra*); for even in the case of the formless (*nirākāra*), the same applies. Otherwise, one would suspect that apprehension occurs by means of that very [single object]. Furthermore, how is the absence of the apprehension of multiple [objects] simultaneously maintained? Is it because multiple [objects] cannot exist at once, or because the mode of apprehension is impossible?

[81,15] First, in the case of the initial eon (*kalpa*), how is it that the lamp’s transformation of the wick, the destruction of darkness, and so forth, are produced by itself? For us, however, this being the case, there is only a simplification of effort and no harm; for the probandum is established precisely by the refutation of succession regarding what is eternal.

But in the second case, on what basis is the conventional usage of "many" established? Let it be established by inference. If, when asked "What is that inference?", you provide an explanation, then let simultaneity itself—accompanied by succession and pervading causal efficiency—be established by inference; how then can there be the fault of lacking an inherent nature (*prakṛti*)? If, however, you do not provide an explanation, you are defeated by that alone. Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous grasping or non-grasping of many [objects], it would be better to maintain simply that the internal organ, the mind (*manas*), cannot function toward multiple objects simultaneously; what is the use of this [other argument]?

[81,23] Now, if it is thought that a single synthesizer of multiple forms and multiple cognitions must be sought, then what of it? For our current position, which maintains a stable [self], is indeed undermined by the admission of succession; otherwise, this would merely be an entry into another doctrine. If it is argued that, in the same way, a synthesizer is established even in the case of succession—

Even that [cognition] would be established only if it were proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that its apprehension is invariably concomitant with a form; otherwise, since mere assertion is easily made, the opponent could simply maintain his position by accepting that [cognition] is formless. Furthermore, there is no effort to prove the existence of a form [within cognition]; rather, it would be the object itself whose possession of that form has been established. Therefore, how could one speak of a syllable that is independent of that [form]?

Moreover, even if one accepts a synthesizer (*pratisandhātṛ*) here that is not incompatible with instability, there is no necessity to accept [its] succession (*krama*), just as one who desires that a single nature produce effects in different locations does not thereby desire them to occur at different times. Therefore, for the sake of accepting a synthesizer in a successive manner, some entirely different mode must be resorted to; so what is the use of this? Thus, he has followed this procedure simply because "somehow a swelling of the boil must be produced. This is not being refuted now, on the grounds that it is not the occasion for a rebuttal of the critique regarding its form.
Now, even so,
if cognition possesses a form, there is no mutual perception of distinct objects; therefore,
this manifestation is one alone, and thus no contradiction arises here.

Therefore, the objection that [the universal] is "denotable" even if it is both capable and incapable [of being perceived], as well as the fault regarding the whole (avayavin) or the lack of a form (sākṛti), are refuted.

Indeed, for this very reason it was said: "This is not the occasion for a refutation of that. For neither the non-establishment of that [whole] nor the establishment of the composite whole is a subverter of our position. Furthermore, the Sautrāntika doctrine, which maintains that qualities such as permanence follow the three [times], is also not subverted in its essential part.
If not, then by refuting the person (pudgala), one has committed an offense precisely by contradicting the established tenets of the Buddhists.
Therefore,
if this doctrine of mine— that cognition possesses a form—
were faulty, how indeed could it be that its refutation is established by means of valid cognition?

If that [external object] is established by valid cognition, let it be so; however, this convention belongs only to the intellect—that there is a single state even within a variegated external [object]—and thus the external is indeed abolished.

For among objects, a difference in form is invariably concomitant with a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). In that case, if there were no difference in causal efficiency despite a difference in form, then—alas!—since nothing more than a difference in mere appearance would exist, the consequence would be the total denial of external objects. Therefore, this [proponent] must necessarily accept that for an external thing, a difference in form entails a difference [in the object itself], whether or not the cognition differs; for cognitions, even if they were of equal status, are not capable of apprehending [the object].

Otherwise, if self-awareness and the illumination of another were to follow even for an external object, it would utterly subvert the very relationship of grasped and grasper. Therefore, if the unity of cognition—even when possessing variegated forms—is established by valid means of knowledge, let that unity belong to that very cognition; however, the external object, having distinct forms, must indeed be distinct.

If it is asked how even the external world, which appears in diverse forms, can be [considered] non-different, we reply: let the three worlds be but a single entity; what is lost to us? However, in the absence of distinct objects, purposes, and functions, it cannot exceed the status of being a mere appearance, like a city of Gandharvas; this has already been stated. Furthermore, there is no occasion here for the distinction that "there is unity in some cases and difference in others."

[83,10] Now, if even the unity of cognition were merely a matter of convention (*samaya*) and not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then let that very convention—which is contradicted by sublation—be faulty. But how can this present distinction between entities, brought forth by valid means of knowledge, be abandoned simply because they are mutually contradictory? [83,13] Furthermore, if the reason (*hetu*) is defeated for the speaker by relying on convention, then [it is defeated] within that convention.
Let this [distinction] be for you as superior; however, the consideration of "convention" (samaya) belongs to the proponent.

Indeed, it is not the convention of the speaker that his statement is authoritative simply by virtue of being established in a treatise (*śāstra*); rather, when an inference is formulated through its formal characteristics (*rūpa*) for the sake of establishing valid cognition, scripture (*āgama*) possesses no such quality.

Moreover, for us, difference is not merely contradiction, but rather [difference] by way of capacity and incapacity. And this must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, since the engagement with and the expansion of refutation and proof would be rendered impossible, the debate would come to an end—what then would be the use of anything else? Therefore, difference by way of capacity and incapacity is difficult to avoid.

Consequently, even if mere contradiction were to deviate from difference, there is no deviation for the specific feature under discussion, just as smoke, though it may deviate from fire in the case of a mere entity, does not deviate from the entity characterized as smoke.

If it is argued that there is indeed a distinction based on being capable or incapable [of producing an effect], and that this distinction arises precisely from contradiction (*virodha*), and furthermore that such [contradiction] is fallible (*vyabhicārī*); [we reply: smoke too is a probans (*hetu*) and an indicator (*gamaka*) precisely because of its being a real entity (*vastutva*), and yet "being a real entity" is fallible—this is the same [in both cases]. Therefore, the meaning is that smoke is an indicator of fire precisely because of its being a real entity, and not by setting aside its being a real entity. It does not mean that everything that is a real entity is an indicator. Likewise, the meaning is that the distinction between being capable and incapable is established by contradiction alone, and thus it is not by setting aside contradiction.

However, it is not the case that as long as there is contradiction, so long does it prove difference. And it has been said: "If contradiction deviates from difference, then this specific [contradiction] intended for the cognition of difference prevails by virtue of being capable versus the other [which is incapable].

If [the reason] were powerless in the case of a universal, it would likewise be weak in the case of a particular; yet the inference of fire from smoke does not deviate, since that entity possesses the crest of flame."
If the strength or weakness [of a property] is established by contradiction alone, then even smoke would be strong when it is not distinct from fire, since it does not abandon its substantiality;
or rather, let smoke deviate from the substance fire, but its distinction [from it] is what is strong.
This same principle applies even to the subject at hand: that which is established by valid cognition is admitted.

[84,13] For if there were no difference between that which possesses power and that which lacks it, the entire three worlds would be thrown into total confusion, stuck in a state where neither engagement nor withdrawal is possible; therefore, the contradiction between the powerful and its opposite must necessarily be accepted as proving their difference, whether this occurs through a difference in form or not. But surely, even a difference in form is inseparable from a difference in power—so what constitutes the distinction? True; this is exactly so in the case of external things, such as water and fire, since they are perceived in precisely that way.

Otherwise, there would be no such thing as the "external," since nothing remains but mere appearance. As for the forms (*ākāra*) of cognition, they are not useful in acts such as burning or immersing, because those functions pertain to external objects. Furthermore, regarding the effects such as determination (*avasāya*), these too are subject to disputes concerning difference or non-difference from other forms; how, then, can a single operation be demonstrated in one and the same [cognition]?

Or, let there be even a single effect; even in that case, it must be considered whether the postulation of a single uniform operation occurs through the process of abstraction (*apoddhāra*), or rather, despite the difference [of the causes]. Furthermore, we have no insistence on proving that the variegated cognition (*citrabuddhi*) is either one or many; our desire concerns only its having a form (*sākāratā*). As for the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), we have no regard even for that. And when an object that is not invariably concomitant (*anāntarīyaka*) is sublated, what harm is done to the other? (PV 4.47cd)

According to this principle, therefore, the determination of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) regarding the capacity of an object and its sequential or non-sequential nature is not established by mere non-perception.

Furthermore, as it is said: "If it is pervaded sequentially, then how could it be pervaded non-sequentially? Or if it is pervaded non-sequentially, then it is not pervaded sequentially. By one who asserts that it is pervaded by both sequence and non-sequence, the very absence of pervasion is demonstrated. For pervasion consists in this form: the existence of the pervaded only where the pervader exists, and the existence of the pervader only where the pervaded exists; thus, [the claim] abandons the essential nature of both as pervaders. Indeed, fire is not said to be pervaded by both smoke and the absence of smoke.

Why should one speak thus to the speaker? For, by this method, a final libation has been offered to the mass of objections—variously formulated and refuted—by those who abide on the path of all logicians, as well as by myself.

One might argue that by refuting these types [of reasons], their non-existence is established, and thus the object of knowledge (*prameya*) would become non-existent; having thus conceptualized it, one perceives the refutations. However, if the object of knowledge to be refuted is not pervaded by those types, then even in the absence of those [refutations], there is no rule of its non-existence. Therefore, even when the refutations are stated, there remains doubt just as before; so enough with this presentation. Alternatively, if the rule of non-existence holds only when those types are absent, then that very [rule] constitutes the meaning of pervasion (*vyāpti*); in that case, what is being negated?

And thus, one who does not accept the substantiality (*vastutva*) of the continuum (*santāna*) initiates a refutation by means of the alternatives of whether it is different or non-different; and since he would find satisfaction only upon demonstrating the absence of both, he cannot succeed without accepting that reality is pervaded by both difference and non-difference. This remains the case even for the alternatives of three and so forth. Therefore, the logical principle is this: there is no pervasion by each individual [alternative], but there is indeed pervasion by their collective totality. Just as, for example, if someone is none of Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, he is not a Pāṇḍava at all.

For when one [instance] is excluded, reality exists by relying on another mode; but when there is an absence of all modes, where could it be? Therefore, a restricted exclusion is indeed pervasion (*vyāpti*).

As for what was also said—that fire is not pervaded by smoke and the absence of smoke—that too is most wretched. For the proponent of the pervasion of the arising of an effect by succession and non-succession has introduced a pervasion by those two properties which excludes any other category; so what is the use of this [objection]? Indeed, just as succession and non-succession are properties of effects, smoke and the absence of smoke are not properties of fire. Rather, it is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the subject (*dharmin*) that is here intended by the term "property" (*dharma*).

If, by the phrase "by means of smoke and the absence of smoke," what is intended is "by means of possessing smoke and not possessing smoke," then what is the connection for the cognition of that connection? For fire is never observed anywhere to be devoid of those two states.

Now, if it is argued that just as the aforementioned property [of fire] is invariably concomitant with smoke, so too is the absence of fire certain in regard to smoke that has become something else—namely, that which is denoted by the term "absence of smoke"—then how could there not be pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this [fire] by those two as well? For the definition of a universal (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) remains unimpaired; indeed, wherever there is the absence of both smoke and the absence of smoke, there is also the absence of fire, and wherever there is fire, there is the occurrence of at least one of those two, just as when smoke exists, there is the occurrence of at least one of the various types of fire. If this is your position:

[86,3] If this is your insistence, what fault is there in that? For mere undesirability (*aniṣṭi*) is not a constituent part [of a valid proof]. Indeed, pervasion (*vyāpti*)—sought for the purpose of the necessary exclusion of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) by means of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), so that when the pervaded is present, one of the various types of the pervader must also be present—is only vitiated when there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the operation of those two. And that [deviation] does not exist here; why then do you resort to mere undesirability?

Because it lacks a specific defining characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of fire by smoke and its absence is not stated directly. For instance, since there is a difference between fire and smoke, they do not possess identity (*tādātmya*); and since fire does not arise from the presence or absence of smoke and so forth, they do not possess the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Therefore, the pervasion of the locus (*āśrayabhuj*) is established directly only through the two properties residing within [the subject] itself: namely, "possessing smoke" and its opposite.

However, when expressed by means of smoke and its absence through the gateway of the apprehension of the object (*artha*), it does not entail any fault. Therefore, if such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not accepted by you, or if the reverse is accepted, let it be so;

for our part, this very sequence of pervasion is what we intend to express, and it alone is relevant to the present context. This is because the discussion on the pervasion of the causal capacity of objects proceeds by way of the total exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) through both succession and simultaneity, and that [exclusion] is established precisely in this manner. Thus, enough with insisting on such a minor slip.

Thus, when the pervasion of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by succession and simultaneity has been established, the pervasion of the absence of succession and simultaneity by the absence of causal efficiency is likewise established; for there is no other means to establish the pervasion of the absence of the pervader by the absence of the pervaded apart from establishing that very relationship between the pervaded and the pervader. Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Furthermore, there is not even a scent of contradiction in the establishment of the pervasion of the non-perception of the pervader under discussion, since it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is there a lack of proof, because the contradiction regarding the absence of succession and simultaneity in a permanent subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is established. On this point, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says: "If it is intended to prove the non-existence of non-momentary things, then what here possesses the status of the subject (*dharmin*)? If that very thing is the subject, it is illogical to prove its own non-existence. For when the subject does not exist, the reason cannot have the property of being a *pakṣadharma* (a property of the subject). And when there is no *pakṣadharma*, there is no capacity for proof."

Therefore, the proposition that non-momentary things are non-existent is untenable. Alternatively, if the meaning of the proposition is that existent things are not non-momentary, even so, how can [the reason] "because of the contradiction with succession and simultaneity" possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? Furthermore, the contradiction of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) with a permanent entity is understood precisely through the non-perception of its pervader; but how [can this be said] regarding succession and simultaneity, which are themselves the pervaders?

Moreover, in this way, it would follow that existence itself belongs to the eternal. And thus, every effort [to prove otherwise] would be fruitless. As Śaṅkara said: "One who pursues the establishment of a contradiction must also apprehend the contradictory [term], because the establishment of a contradiction is inseparable from the apprehension of that [contradictory]. This is as in the case of fire and snow, or of dependent and independent existents. And how can a non-momentary entity, being perceived as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), abandon its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) due to the obstruction of a subverting proof, since it possesses causal efficiency in the form of being an object of cognition?"

If it were not produced by that [cause], how could it be cognized? For that which is not a producer is not an object of cognition (*aprameya*). This has been written according to the essential points within these statements.

And likewise, Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says: "Because contradiction cannot be apprehended when that which is contradictory is not apprehended. For indeed, there is no apprehension of contradiction between fire and snow if either one is not apprehended. If the non-momentary is apprehended because of its contradiction with both succession and simultaneity, then how can it be non-existent? Because it possesses causal efficiency in the form of being an object of cognition. And if it did not possess that efficiency, how could it be cognized? For you do not accept that something which is a distinct entity and lacks generative power can be an object of cognition."

Now, if that which is non-momentary is not perceived at all, how can its contradiction with both succession and simultaneity be understood? Thus, since a permanent entity is non-existent in every respect and is therefore not an object of cognition, there is a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Likewise, there is also a lack of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

As Śaṅkara said: "Now, if the non-existence of non-momentary things is established because of the impossibility of successive or simultaneous action, and momentariness follows from existence (*sattā*), then, since that [existence] produces cognition, the inconclusiveness remains as it was; for even in the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), [existence] still persists."

For when the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is established, the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) must be understood as something distinct; for example, in the absence of fire, the absence of smoke—such as water and so forth—and in the absence of a tree, the absence of a *śiṃśapā*—such as a location devoid of it. Likewise, in the absence of succession and simultaneity, the absence of causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) must be understood as something distinct, because it is impossible to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a reason whose negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not certain.

However, in the case of actual practice (*pratipatti*), the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) consists in the cognition of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader; thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is unavoidable. For this very reason, it is also impossible to state that this [reason] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), because there is no cognition of the absence of succession and simultaneity in a sky-lotus, nor of the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency. If such a cognition were to exist, all things would be included within the categories of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar class (*sapakṣa*), resulting in the subsumption of everything under the fundamental reason.

As for what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says: "If it is argued that this [reason] possesses the power of proof solely through the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), we say no, because even a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is absent. If it is argued that a rabbit's horn and the like serve as the instance, we say no, because that is not an object of cognition. For that which is not cognized even in its own nature cannot be understood as being devoid of the properties of the probandum and the probans. Nor is it logical for that which is not cognized to function as an instance. Thus he says.
Furthermore, this proof for the absence of causal efficacy in a permanent entity is a proof of its non-existence. And like a proof of existence, it does not escape the threefold class of fallacies.
For, according to the sequence already stated:
"A property of an existent does not exist when [the subject] is unestablished; that which depends on both is inconclusive."
"How can that existence, which is a property (*dharma*) incompatible with non-existence, be established?
Thus do Śaṅkara and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa demonstrate.

Trilocana also, refining that very same set of objects of cognition (*prameya*), says: "Does the subverting proof (*bādhaka*)—the state of being devoid of succession and simultaneity—[1] establish the non-existence of non-momentary things, [2] or rather their exclusion (*vyatireka*), [3] or else their necessary connection (*pratibandha*)?"

[1] First of all, the former alternative is not tenable; for since the nature (*rūpa*) of space, time, direction, self, mind, and atoms is unestablished, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Furthermore, that non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) does not transcend the three types of logical defects. In this regard, it has already been stated that the property of absence (*abhāvadharma*), namely the state of being devoid of succession and simultaneity, is not established because its locus is unestablished. Indeed, no discerning person would accept that the state of being devoid of succession and simultaneity is a property of a rabbit’s horn.

Furthermore, as long as their non-existence is not apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their status as a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) is not established. Otherwise, there would be an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the establishment of their non-existence would depend on the establishment of their being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and the establishment of their being a property of non-existence would depend on the establishment of their non-existence. Moreover, if this were a property of existence (*bhāvadharmatva*), it would be contradictory; if it were a property of both, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This same logical consequence applies equally to non-existence as it does to existence.

Nor is the second alternative tenable. For even in that case, the meaning of the term "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) accompanied by the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*). Since this absence must necessarily be apprehended as a constituent part of the means of cognition, if it were apprehended through direct experience (*anubhava*), it would have that experience as its cause; and because that which lacks a cause cannot be perceived, the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is because, if negative concomitance were of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*) due to being produced by experience, it would be included within the category of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Because positive and negative concomitance are absent, an uncommon reason is non-probative. Therefore, negative concomitance must necessarily be accepted and necessarily known. Regarding its necessity to be known, the consequence that such knowledge [of the reason] would follow has already been shown.

It might be argued as follows: "Exclusion (*vyatireka*) is not intended to be grasped by a direct (*sākṣātkārin*) cognition, because [if it were], it would have to be the producer of that direct cognition; rather, it must be conceptualized (*vikalpya*). And it is not tenable for an object being conceptualized to be the cause of a conceptualization whose production depends upon its own immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). So why is it said that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?"

That too is untenable, because every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not transcend these four possibilities. To explain: one is a conceptual construction of blue and so forth that follows upon direct experience; another is a conceptual construction of a doubtful object, such as a *piśāca* and so forth; yet another is a conceptual construction of a non-existent object, such as a hare’s horn and so forth; and finally, there is a conceptual construction here that arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*).

In this context, by stating that all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—beginning with that which arises from a logical mark (*liṅga*)—is "a manifestation of what is not a real entity," it is described as a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābha*). For perception is the manifestation of a real entity (*vastu*), since in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no manifestation of it. Conceptual construction is not like this, because its manifestation does not conform to the real entity. Therefore, conceptual construction is a semblance of perception. However, that which arises from a logical mark is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it brings about the attainment of the object exactly as it is determined.

Furthermore, when a distinction (*vyatireka*) is being conceptualized, it cannot be conceptualized by a conceptualization born of a logical mark (*liṅga*), because of the absence of such a mark. Moreover, even though a conceptualization preceded by experience arises from a real entity through a traditional succession, it does not possess validity regarding that real entity, because only the direct experience itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since experience—which is the basis for the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*)—has just now been refuted, it follows by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whether its object is non-existent or its referent is doubtful, is what brings about certainty; thus, existence (*sattva*) that lacks a demonstrable exclusion or possesses a doubtful exclusion is not sufficient to prove momentariness.

Nor is the third alternative possible, because the exclusion of succession and simultaneity from a non-momentary entity—based upon its existence—establishes a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by settling upon momentariness along with its own pervader; thus, the establishment of the connection is understood to be preceded by the establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). And that negative concomitance has already been refuted by the previously mentioned sequence.
Therefore, in this way, a permanent entity does not exist, nor is it an object of cognition; consequently, the reason suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
Because of this, there is a loss of both the reason and one's own experience; therefore, even the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is rejected.

Furthermore, [the object] is established as empty by both [reasons], or rather, non-existence itself is not established—just as existence is not [established] by the permanent. Thus, it is impossible to establish a contradiction with a non-existent thing, such as through succession and so forth.
Ā4 Thus is the summary of the refutation.
In that regard, these [opponents] are questioned as follows:
"Is the establishment of some property (dharma) in a non-entity (avastu) by means of cognition (māna) [accepted]?"
Is there here any conventional usage regarding negation and affirmation, or not?
If it exists somewhere, why are there not so many fallacies?
If it does not exist at all, then there is the establishment of self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*).

Indeed, for no phenomenon whatsoever is the linguistic practice of affirmation and negation restricted solely to real entities (*vastu*); rather, it applies even to non-entities (*avastu*). If you hold the view that such practice does not exist at all regarding non-entities, then when questioned as to how this is so, if you should resort to the royal decree that "one must remain silent" and offer some reason for it, how could you avoid the fallacy of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddhi*)?

On the other hand, one who remains mute and lacks the capacity to sit [in debate] is no match for someone who speaks whatever comes to mind; nor is anything communicated to the opponent by such means.

Furthermore, by asserting that there can be no linguistic practice of affirmation or negation regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), you yourself have accepted the linguistic practice of negation regarding a non-entity; thus, you have mutually deceived yourselves. For there is no possibility of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) apart from negation. And if that negation is not established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could it be respected, or what would be the purpose of its verbal expression?

Furthermore, if one accepts the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception (*adhyakṣa*) cannot be the means of proving either a non-existent thing or its negation, because perception contradicts such an object and depends upon the causal efficiency (*arthasāmarthya*) of a real entity. If, however, one relies on inference (*anumāna*), the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is impossible to avoid. Consequently, in the context of discussing a non-entity, one would simply have to remain silent. Nor is there even room for a mere thesis (*pratijñā*); nor can this be possible unless the discussion of non-entities is prevented by royal decree.

In this context, however, a statement concerning what is possible for an existent entity must necessarily follow, because there is the possibility of an objection. Furthermore, speech has no function other than affirmation or negation. Therefore, one enters into a great and difficult dilemma: neither speech nor non-speech.

And thus, at this very moment, since there is an absence of both succession and simultaneity—just like an intermediate lotus in the case of a permanent entity—there is no causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*). Consequently, in the context of a non-entity, you, even though a learned person, cannot remain silent regarding the affirmation or negation of any property; rather, a negation has indeed been established, because for that which is not real, as accepted by the Buddhists, causal efficacy is precluded due to the absence of succession and simultaneity.
"But the absence of cessation is a positive injunction, which exists even though its object is non-existent;
yet the absence of that [injunction] is said to be 'it does not exist'—behold the manifestation of childishness!
This is an intermediate verse (antaraśloka). [PV 4.223; PVin 2.15]

Now, if it is argued that because an eternal entity is a real thing (*vastu*) by virtue of its internal purity (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*), there is no contradiction with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the negation of any property belonging to it—then does this mean that even the sky-lotus (*gagananalinam*) is a real thing by virtue of its internal purity? Or, if it were a real thing, what conceptual distinction could possibly be imagined?

[91,1] Therefore, regarding a non-entity such as a sky-lotus, let there be an absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) due to the lack of succession and simultaneity, or let there not; in either case, there is no fulfillment of this proposition that "there is neither affirmation nor negation in a non-entity. And when one seeks the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to understand how this is so, every inference (*anumāna*) relied upon in the absence of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is seized by the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Furthermore, a mere statement lacking a means of valid cognition is not required by a discerning respondent.

Nor can the absence of both be asserted, because affirmation and negation have the natures of existence and non-existence respectively, such that the negation of one entails the affirmation of the other; for affirmation is indeed negation, and negation is affirmation—so what else could it be? Furthermore, even if there were a thesis asserting the negation of both, there would be no avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) regarding the reason being adduced.

As for what was said—"Since the thing itself is eternal due to the purity of its locus (koṣṭhaśuddhi), what follows from that?"—it is not the case that the subject (*dharmin*) is [established] merely by virtue of being that thing, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence that the fault of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) would have no scope. If it is argued, "This is stated with reference to the opponent's own admission," then the meaning is that the reason in the *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) is unestablished on account of its locus being non-existent, since it is a non-entity; thus, the absence of succession and so forth is not a valid reason.

This being the case, it must be stated that in the absence of a real entity (*avastu*), the reason (*hetu*) is pervaded by the fault of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*); for no reason exists without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). While a reductio (*prasaṅga*) may be stated based merely on the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in reliance upon the opponent's own admission, such admission does not apply even to the pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is argued that this might sometimes be the case, even so, the opponent has not admitted that the reason is pervaded by the fault of an unestablished locus in the case of a non-entity, since they employ reasons only with respect to entities that are eternal (*nitya*).

Furthermore, precisely where the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) of a reason is brought forward because of its being a property of a non-entity (*avastu*), it is there that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is defeated by the principle that "there is neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity.

If you maintain that even the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is intended solely on the basis of what is accepted by the opponent—arguing that in the case of a non-entity, because it is a non-entity, the reason is not "governed by the property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*)—then this is not something you yourself accept; nevertheless, the claim that "there is neither affirmation nor negation regarding a non-entity" remains contradictory, because a negation is being accepted by you yourself, and since there is no meaning for the negative particle (*nañ*) other than [the negation of] another thing.

Furthermore, according to the logical principle that every reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) must culminate in its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), if a non-entity (*avastu*) were eternal, then there would be a lack of a locus for the reason (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Yet, there is no such lack of a locus; therefore, what is intended by the claim that "a non-entity is not eternal"? Even so, since the fault of *āśrayāsiddhi* was previously raised, and the property of being an entity (*vastutva*) is established for the eternal subject (*dharmin*), how is it not contradicted to say that "a non-entity is not eternal"?

Therefore, since this [subject] is itself independent and non-existent, the "unestablishedness of the locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) pertains to the reason when it is applied to a non-entity; thus, for one engaged in refuting the reason, this is the primary issue. Furthermore, the claim that "affirmation and negation do not apply to a non-entity" has been set aside. Moreover, this non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is employed here as a *svabhāva* [reason], based on the assumption that the state of being a locus is pervaded by existence. And that assumption arises from a failure to understand the contradiction with one's own words.

Indeed, for one who considers it a contradiction of their own words to claim that the status of being a locus (*dharmitva*)—which is to say, the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*)—cannot belong to a non-entity, the conceit of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not touch the mind; rather, it serves only to belittle oneself. This is the general rule. Furthermore, what kind of logic is this, wherein these [opponents] themselves extend the conventional practice of affirmation and negation regarding a non-entity, yet reject the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) as a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) while attempting to refute another?

For the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, by stating that "in the absence of a subject (*dharmin*), there is no property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) for the reason (*hetu*)," has clearly expressed a denial of the property-of-the-subject status of a reason when its locus is a non-entity. When investigating the logic of how this is so, he intends the reason "because of the non-existence of the subject. Otherwise, what regard would there be for mere words?

Furthermore, one who asserts that what is non-momentary is not perceived at all clearly states that there is no comprehension of contradiction because it is not an object of cognition. And that property, which is common to other non-entities (*avastu*), is also attributed to the eternal, which is likewise regarded as a non-entity; otherwise, if this principle did not apply elsewhere to non-entities, how could it be asserted even in the case of the eternal?
Śaṅkara also clarifies this very point: since a non-entity is not an object of cognition, there is no proof of contradiction; otherwise, the entire treatise would be purposeless.

If it is argued that there is no fault because—given the absence of a genitive or locative indication for this [non-existent]—there is no contradiction between the existent and the non-existent, according to the intended meaning; even so, since the non-existent is not perceived even now, the reason [stated] by oneself must still be required. Thus, how can there be a dismissal of the non-existent as the subject (*dharmin*) and of the two types of non-perception (*anupalambha*) which pervade its state? For, when the contradiction with it is not established, the reason is simply its lack of being an object of cognition.

And if you accept that the exclusion of the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is achieved by means of the third case ending (the instrumental), then there is no harm in [our argument] that because succession and simultaneity lack connection with the eternal, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) also lacks connection with the eternal. In this way, we shall explain the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) of the reason: its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*), its presence only in similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and its absolute absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). Let there be peace regarding the blow of the unestablished locus.
Therefore, since there is only a difference in intended expression and not a difference in reality, what is the use of this ascetic bodily exertion?

Furthermore, let it be granted that for the time being there is indeed a contradiction and sublation between an existent and an existent; however, if one accepts the question—“When, on the other hand, there is a contradiction between an existent and an existent itself, does it exist or not?”—then the Buddhist tenet is established, and the presentation [of the argument] is futile.

If, on the other hand, one accepts “no,” then one must rely upon that very reason, namely “because it is not perceived”; thus, the negation of contradiction regarding a non-entity occurs through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), and once again the Buddhist tenet is proven. Likewise, [the text continues]:
Regarding the statement, "A property of an existent does not exist in what is unestablished" (PV 1.191a), this very same principle is the refuge here as well.

And thus Trilocana clarifies with his own words: "The fact of being devoid of succession and simultaneity, which is a property of non-existence, is not established because its locus is not perceived. For in this case, it is clear that non-existence is the subject (*dharmin*), and its property—being devoid of succession and so forth—is being negated, on the grounds of the reason "because its locus is not perceived."

Thus, one who asserts that a non-existent thing possesses the status of a subject (dharmin), and immediately thereafter claims that discerning people understand it to have the nature of a rabbit’s horn—which is devoid of both sequential and simultaneous occurrence—is a great reckless person who does not laugh at himself by his own hand. For it is precisely because of its non-existence that the subject-status of a rabbit’s horn must be denied; yet, since the subject-status of even a non-existent thing has been accepted, what contradiction could there be regarding a horse’s horn and the like?

Now, if the status of being a subject (*dharmitā*) is accepted for non-existence by means of negating its lack of succession and so forth, why not accept it precisely as that very lack of succession? Oh, the power of the intellect! One considers the hare’s horn, which is non-existent, to have the status of a subject by negating its lack of succession and so forth, rather than by [affirming] its lack of succession and so forth.

Since the conventional practice of affirmation and negation is accepted in both cases regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), the Buddhist tenet is difficult to refute; therefore, it would be better if the status of being a subject (*dharmitva*) were established in both instances simply by virtue of being devoid of succession and so forth. Why, then, resort to the story of abandoning the horse for that price alone after having entered the Northern Road (*uttarā-patha*)?

Alternatively, what can be done here if the extremely subtle intellect does not perceive such a gross and incongruous distinction? Nevertheless, close your eyes and consider for a moment: does the horn of a hare possess a sequence and so forth, or not? If you say that it does, then what more is there for us to say? The members of the assembly and others are the authority in this matter.

Now, if the position is "no," then since that [entity] is devoid of sequence and so forth, how can you establish it as the subject (*dharmin*) by means of negating its lack of sequence and so forth? Having thus interrogated the reason in both ways, I shall certainly state, "Because it is a non-entity (*avastutva*). Enough with this elaboration.

[93,17] Even in such a context as "Is the son of a barren woman a speaker or not?", one cannot remain without asserting a negation; nor can one do so without presenting a proof such as "because of insentience" or "because of being a non-entity. If you ask, "Why does no one entertain such a doubt?"—and if you reply, "Because its status as a non-entity is well-established"—then why? If you say, "Because that status as a non-entity is established," then...

Once again, that very same point returns: the negation of the possibility of doubt regarding the speakerhood of the son of Bandhula, who possesses the property [of being a speaker], is based on the reason "because he is well-known. However, even when something is well-known, there is no absolute absence of doubt; for the power of delusion is boundless. Indeed, even among the authors of treatises, an error has been observed in the form of a misconception that denies the non-existence of the hare's horn, such as by asserting "it exists" or the like.

Therefore, just as one who conceives of impermanence in sound on the grounds of its visibility is not refuted by [the charge of] the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*), so too here there may be both doubt and its refutation; there is no contradiction. Consequently, even regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), the conventional practice of affirming or negating some property is unavoidable, since even those authors of treatises who are fundamentally opposed [to our view] accept this very point through their own negating statements.

In this regard, how can things that are non-entities—extending even to the son of a barren woman—possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*)? In the absence of any cognition, how can there be linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*)? If they do produce a cognition, how is it that they are not entities? Nor should mere words be accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, whatever reason (*hetu*) is adduced, how could it all not be "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*)? Consequently, this follows: "And that fault which is equal for both," and so forth.

And if these faults do not apply even to things whose existence is certain to be non-existent, then why would they not apply to an eternal entity whose existence is beyond doubt prior to the proof? What, then, is the ultimate truth here? For it is impossible for a person who relies on valid means of knowledge to avoid the conventional practice of affirming or negating any property whatsoever with respect to a non-entity.

If it is argued that these faults do not follow as consequences, it is replied: first of all, there is no absence of the status of being a subject (*dharmin*) for a non-entity. For wherever there is a reflective awareness (*prāmārśa*) in the form "this is thus," that very thing is the subject by way of this mode of presentation; "thus" indicates its connection with a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*). Just as in the case of "the jar is blue," the blueness of the jar is perceived as a property, so too in the case of "the son of a barren woman does not speak," the capacity for speech is perceived as a property of the son of a barren woman. Thus, there is no absence of the status of being a subject even in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Only some properties belong to a real entity (*vastu*), such as blueness and so forth; some belong to a non-entity (*avastu*), such as the absence of all designations and so forth; and some are common to both, being merely non-apprehension (*anupalambhamātra*). In this regard, it is logical to negate the status of being a property of a non-entity in that which has a real entity as its locus (*dharmin*). However, it does not apply to properties in general, because self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*) acts as a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, the claim that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) occurs despite the absence of cognition is also untenable.

Furthermore, it is not the case that a cognition of an identical nature for both [real and unreal objects] is a factor for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). For a cognition arises from the intrinsic capacity of a real entity (*vastu*), whereas conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is an indirect effect of perception and inference. However, in the case of a non-entity (*avastu*) or of something whose status as a real entity is doubtful, there is merely conceptual construction. Indeed, if—due to the absence of capacity—the cognition of those two were not established even as mere conceptual construction, then [the object] would never be conventionally expressible at all.

And since conventional usage is accepted, cognition in that case consists merely of conceptual construction (*vikalpana*); and the nature of those two [the object and its cognition] is precisely what is presented by that construction, and nothing else. Just as the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) is only that which is brought forward by perception and inference, so too the essence of an unreal entity (*avastu*) or of an entity whose status as real is doubtful is only that which is presented by conceptual construction, and nothing else. Therefore, those who are wise ought not to be considered "saintly" (*santa*) if they draw in a causal factor based on mere convention. As it is said: "Those who know the logic [of causality] understand that the very state of being a cause is what constitutes the state of being an object of apprehension" (PV III 247).

Thus it has been stated; that was said with reference to the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) as being distinct from the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) in the context of mental direct perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). For it is established that this same principle does not apply even to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

And thus the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* itself says (msĀ p.19|3): "For you do not accept that a non-producer (*ajanaka*) which is a different entity (*arthāntara*) is an object of cognition. Nor is a non-entity (*avastu*) a different entity; for it is only an entity (*artha*) that, in relation to another entity, is called a 'different entity,' but not a non-entity. That [non-entity] is merely the negation of its existence. Therefore, because there is no state of being a different entity, there is no dependence on a cognition produced by itself for a non-entity. Consequently, mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is the only recourse here."

Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that its nature is delineated by that very form and nothing else; otherwise, the non-utterance of words such as "hare's horn" would follow as a logical consequence, and how then could linguistic usage proceed? For instance, having referred to an object denoted by a word such as "donkey's horn," something must necessarily be predicated of it—either its being devoid of sequence and so forth, which is a property of a hare's horn, or its being possessed of such [properties], or else that there is no cognition of contradiction with anything on the part of a non-existent thing, or that it does not possess the properties of a real entity.

In that regard, if by words such as "the non-existent entity of a hare's horn" the intended object is not communicated, and instead an object entirely other than the intended one is the content of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by the sound, then for what would the enjoined negation of succession, non-succession, and so forth be perceived? And in the absence of such perception, the utterance of the word would result in being purposeless. Yet, there is indeed the linguistic usage of terms such as "tortoise-hair"; therefore, that [usage] itself is its meaning, and that alone is the determination of its referent.

Even when there is perception (*dṛṣṭa*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone constitutes the ascertainment (*niścaya*). If that is so, then let conceptual construction alone be relied upon in all cases; what is the use of perception? It is not so. For when an object has been excluded by perception, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required—either to establish its reality or to refute it—because in the mind of conceptual construction, there is merely the flashing forth of a mental image (*ākāra*). However, when an object has been made the focus of perception, the conceptual construction is an ascertainment to the same extent as the form [of the object] within that [perception], provided there is no deception due to similarity.

Therefore, even regarding a real entity (*vastu*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is not the final resort; however, regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), that alone is the resort. For in that case, it is precisely the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external form [as being internal] that is required, depending upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and that is established by conceptual construction itself. But in the operation of a [direct] means of valid cognition, there is no dependence on another means of valid cognition.

Therefore, when wise persons, through the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of that intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) delineated by that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), establish [the presence of] properties such as the negation of being devoid of succession and non-succession because it possesses those qualities, what kind of fault could there be in establishing a state of contradiction with a form that is the opposite of that nature?

Just as the negation of beauty and so forth in the case of the son of a barren woman is appropriate, so too, what contradiction could there be in the contradiction of reality? Furthermore, if the obstruction of contradiction occurs due to the absence of experience, then let the negation of beauty also not occur for that very same reason. Consequently, if no property whatsoever were to be predicated, the consequence would remain unavoidable that those words which express non-existence would never be uttered; and it has already been pointed out that this is impossible.

[96,1] Now, since the son of a barren woman and the like lack any other form distinct from the form that is the object of conceptualization, and since they are made objects of conceptualization as mere suchness, there is no harm to the corresponding conventional usage. This being the case, what harm could there be to the corresponding conventional usage of contradiction? Just as the son of a barren woman is contradictory by virtue of being a real entity (*vastu*), so too, how could there not be contradiction with whatever property can be established as an antithesis even to the eternal?

In that case, how could the mere absence of experience be a valid means of proof for subverting [the opponent's position] through contradiction, if it were not explicitly stated? For if, even in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there were neither an object corresponding to that [perceived thing] nor a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a form contrary to it, then one would have to intend to establish "contradiction" as the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). Only then would the establishment of contradiction be possible; for the determination of non-coexistence is established because when one thing exists, the other is absent.

And since existence is within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could it be possible for one thing to have another as its cause? Furthermore, the definition of "mutual exclusion" (*parasparaparihārasthiti*) is established merely by the conceptual apprehension of opposing forms; even when made an object by mere conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it is not necessarily dependent on a real entity (*vastu*) as the basis for its established arrangement. Otherwise, how could there be a contradiction between existence and non-existence characterized by mutual exclusion?

And regarding that contradiction, those same two [examples] serve as the primary illustrations. Even if one accepts that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*), there is no "existence" of existence within the entity designated as "non-existence," nor is there an "existence" of non-existence within what is called "non-existence. Thus, it is impossible to maintain a succession of real entities consisting of non-existences. If one maintains that a non-entity has as its sole nature the mere cessation of itself and is to be designated as such, how can that which is contradictory to it be established?

Furthermore, if there were no established distinction between contradiction and non-contradiction, then in that case a single entity—namely, its own self and its own exclusion—would both exist and not exist by its very nature; yet this is not the case as a rule. This is precisely what constitutes the meaning of contradiction, just as in the case of the momentary and the non-momentary: for just as one thing is not non-momentary, so too another thing is not momentary. Therefore, it is established that there is no sublation of the contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between an entity and a non-entity.

[96,19] But surely, if contradiction (*virodha*) is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) by means of it would also be unreal. For a contradiction cannot be ultimately real if its substratum is not ultimately real. As Śaṅkara said: "In that case, even the subverting argument based on the conceptualization of contradiction, because it consists of a conceptualized contradiction, does not establish a real exclusion (*vyatireka*); and since existence (*sattā*) thus possesses an unreal exclusion, momentariness—which depends upon it—is likewise unreal" (msĀ p. 19|4).

Nyāyabhūṣaṇa also, refining that very point, says: "If it is argued that the proof of contradiction is established by means of a non-momentary entity that is conventionally established (*saṃvṛtisiddha*), then even that which is conventionally established must be either real (*vāstava*) or conceptual (*kālpnika*). If it is real, how can it be non-existent? Or how could there be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For that which performs causal efficiency is called real. If, on the other hand, it is conceptual, then is the contradiction with it real or conceptual?"

First of all, [the contradiction] is not real, because it is a contradiction between two imagined things, like the contradiction between the son of a barren woman and something else. Now, if the contradiction itself is merely imaginary, then there is no ultimate contradiction between a non-momentary entity and causal efficiency—whether by way of succession or simultaneity. Consequently, the establishment of the exclusion of existence from the non-momentary is also not ultimately real. Since existence thus possesses an unreal exclusion, momentariness—which depends upon that existence—is likewise unreal.

[97,6] This is mere incoherent prattle. For we do not accept that "contradiction" (*virodha*) is some distinct entity that stands as a foot upon both sides and is designated as a relation; nor is such a thing logically tenable, by virtue of which it would become non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*) in the absence of reality in one of the two related terms. Rather, according to how it is accepted, it is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*). The meaning of contradiction between two things considered to be contradictory is simply their mutual exclusion of each other's essential nature (*svarūpa*).

And that [contradiction] between existence and non-existence is indeed ultimate (*pāramārthika*). For existence does not enter into the form of non-existence, nor does non-existence enter into the form of existence; this very rule of their non-confusion is what constitutes contradiction. And that rule establishes even its own self-contradiction within the sphere of the ultimate.

Thus, the restriction that the eternal does not enter into the form of succession or simultaneity, nor do succession and simultaneity enter into the form of the eternal—this very restriction constitutes their contradiction. Since it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that there is never anything else [besides these two], this alone is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatā*). How, then, can it be said that because contradiction is not ultimately real, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason "existence" is also unreal?

[97,14] Furthermore, since everything has been established precisely by accepting that the permanent lacks ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*), there is no fault whatsoever. As for what was said—that the contradiction with an imagined opposite is unreal because it is a contradiction with an imagined opposite, like the contradiction involving the son of a barren woman—let us for now set aside exposing how this poor fellow failed to perceive even the most obvious fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth.

[97,19] And this is considered: is it the very state of being opposed to that which is opposed to the imagined (*kalpita*) which is contradicted by reality (*vāstavatva*), or not? If, first of all, it is not contradicted, then there would also be opposition to that which is not opposed to the imagined, and reality would also follow; thus, how could the presentation of that [opposition] be exclusively effective for its refutation? For from the affirmation of something that is not contradictory, the establishment of a negation does not follow.

Now, if it is contradictory, is that contradiction real (*vāstava*) or unreal (*avāstava*)? In that regard, an unreal contradiction is ineffective because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of mutual non-existence. On the view that it is real, even a contradiction with an imagined contradictory is itself accepted as real; and yet you claim it does not express the negation of its own contradictory for us—behold the manifestation of such audacity!

For just as there is a contradiction between permanence and succession or simultaneity—which is a contradiction of an imagined opposite because the permanent is imagined—so too, in the case of a contradiction between the real and the imagined, there exists a "contradiction of contradictions," which is a contradiction of an imagined contradiction. This is because it is a contradiction of an imagined opposite; or rather, it is the opposite of that [imagined thing], since it is an imagined opposite. For we observe that what you yourself are attempting to prove is this: that even the contradiction of an imagined opposite is itself merely imagined and not real.

Therefore, the contradiction between that imagined contradiction and its real counterpart—namely, the contradiction of the contradictory—is itself established as imagined. If that [contradiction] were real, there would be a contradiction with one's own words; if it were unreal, the refutation has already been stated.

Moreover, what is called "contradiction" (virodha) is sought for the purpose of prohibiting the coexistence of two things in one place; however, the establishment of the reality of both is not the result of contradiction. But where there is the establishment of the reality of both, there—by the force of circumstances—one thing excludes another thing in a certain location, as in the case of "incompatible coexistence" (sahānavasthāna), as previously stated. The contradiction under discussion here, however, has as its result the prohibition of the presence of two properties (dharmas) in a single locus (dharmin).

In this regard, just as two properties that both exist are negated when it is said, "Where there is blueness, there is no non-blueness; therefore, blue and non-blue are not one," so too, even two contradictory properties in the form of existence and non-existence, when superimposed upon a single substratum (*dharmin*), are indeed negated. For it is not the case that the state of being the son of a barren woman, though superimposed upon the son of a mother, need not be negated because it is factually non-existent.

Or, in the case of the son of a barren woman—who is merely an object of conceptual construction—the attribution of being "the son of a mother" is not to be negated. For the son of a mother and the son of a barren woman are not one and the same entity; by that much alone, the function of contradiction is exhausted. What is the use of another so-called "contradiction," which does not achieve its own existence without depending on the actual properties of things? Thus, where there is permanence, there is no possession of succession or simultaneity; where there is possession of succession or simultaneity, there is no permanence; therefore, [the universal] is not permanent.

In ultimate reality, [existence] is not endowed with either succession or simultaneity; consequently, even that which is associated with existence is not necessarily so in ultimate reality. Therefore, existence must find its rest in momentariness alone, such that existence itself is dependent upon momentariness. Thus, there is no contradiction in the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) from the fact of existence.

And if, even so, you wish to enter the hollow of a mountain cave and proclaim—having grasped [the argument] through the sequence of "mother" and "sweetmeat" by means of recollecting the contradiction and the exclusion—then do proclaim it! But you will not be of any use whatsoever in obstructing the success of our undertaking. Therefore, enough of this obsession; it is simply better to accept that these contradictions and so forth are indeed real.

If it is argued that there is no such thing as contradiction other than the two contradictory properties of permanence and being characterized by succession or simultaneity, and therefore one must ask which of these possesses reality—this too is trivial. For we do not claim that contradiction is ultimately real merely because another property is possible; rather, if two things are contradictory, they remain contradictory even when another property is possible, and if they were not contradictory [in that case], then the contradiction would not be ultimately real.

If those two are contradictory, then by that much alone there is the conventional usage of "real contradiction"; what is the use of another property? As for what was said regarding the contradiction like that of a barren woman’s son, is this contradiction exemplified as having a single locus, or as depending on a second term? Even in the case of a second term, is it of the nature of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) or merely something else? First of all, the first position is untenable, for no one asserts a contradiction that has a single locus.

Therefore, if the contradiction between the son of a barren woman and [his opposite]—which share a non-different substratum—is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then it follows that there can be no ultimately real contradiction even for two things that possess distinct substrata; what logic is this? Likewise, there is no contradiction based on mere otherness, as in the case of "produced" and "impermanent. However, in that case too, contradiction with the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is indeed accepted. For the son of a barren woman does indeed have a contradiction with the son of a non-barren woman; and the negation of both within a single essence is precisely what is intended.

[99,9] Is it not the case that when two properties (dharma) are contradictory, the negation of the identity of their substrates (dharmin) is logical? For instance, the contradiction between "the son of a barren woman" and "the son of a non-barren woman" exists between the property and its substrate. This is not a fault. Substrates themselves are indeed designated only by means of their properties; likewise, the designation of two substrates may sometimes be made with the emphasis on the state (bhāva) itself.

Furthermore, the presentation of fire and snow as an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is also incorrect, because what is intended to be expressed is their mutual exclusion. As for the two states—dependence and necessary existence—which were mentioned as being the objects of that [distinction], in that case too, occasional occurrence due to dependence was stated to be impermanence (*anityatva*). If "necessary existence" (*dhruvabhāva*) means the necessity of its occurrence, then that is simply permanence (*nityatva*).

Therefore, how does this presentation of the state of contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal—not being based on experience—not provoke laughter? For the very point at issue is precisely how there can be a cognition of contradiction with that which is eternal. Furthermore, if the existence of what is yet to be (the future) is necessarily constant, then since that too is not an object of anyone's experience, the same fault applies as in the case of the eternal.

[99,18] It might be argued: "This is said with reference to that which has been necessarily perceived at some time. In that case, there is no contradiction at all, for that [object] is both dependent and permanent. Alternatively, if it is argued that at that [time of perception] there is no dependence because it is already established, then at other times there is even less; for it is precisely because it is not established [then] that [dependence would not exist]. If it is claimed that dependence belongs only to an unestablished property (*asiddhadharma*), then there can be no determination of contradiction regarding what has never been experienced; thus, the same fault remains.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with that which has been experienced only in relation to the time of its establishment (*siddhi-kāla*), then it is correct to say that if one accepts such dependence on the time of establishment, there is no contradiction at all. By this, when the non-establishment of the arrangement of contradiction due to the absence of experience is to be proven, the intended example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the property to be proven (*sādhya-avyatirekin*); whereas in the case of attributing contradiction to what is non-existent, it lacks the probans (*sādhana-avyatirekin*). Furthermore, if the meaning of "inevitable existence" (*dhruva-bhāva*) is taken to be permanence (*nityatā*), then it is simply included within the category of the property to be proven itself.

Let it be that difference, non-difference, and so forth serve as examples of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Nevertheless, there is no rule that contradiction between two things must necessarily exist only between two real entities (*vastu*), for this has been established even in other cases. As for the claim that "a property of an existent does not exist when [the subject] is unestablished" (PV I 191a;

PVin III 63a), that too is refuted because the objection regarding the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been cast far away. Since even a non-existent thing can be established as a subject (*dharmin*), and since the establishment of conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) and conventional determination (*pratīti-vyavasthā*) regarding non-entities is proven, the objection that space (*vyoman*) and the like cannot be cognized in their own nature is also avoided.

It might be argued: "If the avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) by relying on a cognition whose nature is conceptual construction is the same even when proving existence (*sattā*), then why is it said that 'there is no property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) in what is unestablished,' and so forth? And how is the proof of the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the self—namely, the quality of being perceived everywhere—cited as an example of the unestablished locus? [Response: Because of the requirements of the proof (*sādhana*), in both cases only a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) is employed as the reason (*hetu*), and only such a property is suspected [to be the reason]. Thus, although the avoidance of the unestablished locus is achieved through conceptual cognition, the logical fault remains insofar as the reason is restricted to properties of real entities. Therefore, the aforementioned restriction is stated. As for the example of the self's omnipresence, it is cited because it is a case where a property of an entity is adduced as a reason while the locus itself is unestablished. Consequently, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the property of being perceived everywhere is indeed a property of an entity, it is not the case that a property of an entity does not exist in what is unestablished; rather, it is the case that a property of an entity cannot serve as a reason for something that is unestablished. This is because, in the absence of a real substratum, a property of an entity cannot be established. Thus, the restriction is stated to exclude such cases. It is not intended to deny that a property of an entity exists in an unestablished subject. Otherwise, one would have to conclude that the reason in the argument for the self's omnipresence is not a property of an entity, which is absurd. Therefore, the restriction is stated precisely to exclude the possibility of employing a property of an entity as a reason for an unestablished subject. It is not meant to imply that a property of an entity does not exist in an unestablished subject. For if that were the case, one would have to admit that the reason in the argument for the self's omnipresence is not a property of an entity, which would contradict the fact that it is indeed a property of an entity. Furthermore, a property of an existent cannot have a non-existent thing as its locus (*dharmin*). For smoke, *śiṃśapā*-ness, and the like do not reside in a non-existent thing.
