Therefore, wherever a property of an existent serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*), there the locus must necessarily be an existent thing itself. Nor can there be confidence in the reality of that which is merely the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), since mere conceptual construction does not cease even with respect to non-existent things. Consequently, one who treats an existent thing as the locus must state that its establishment occurs through the forms of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

If, however, that [subject] is not explicitly stated, then an object that has become the domain of mere conceptual construction—whether its existence is doubtful or its existence is denied—and which is being made the subject (*dharmin*), how could it be established as certain by way of its reality? And this being the case, whatever property of a real entity serves as a reason (*hetu*) will all suffer from the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), because in one case there is doubt and in the other there is error.

Therefore, it is correct [to say] that in the proof of existence (*sattā-sādhana*), a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) cannot be a logical reason (*hetu*) because it suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*), since [the locus] is not established by either perception or inference, which have real entities as their objects. However, in the proof of non-existence (*asattā-sādhana*), a property of a non-entity (*avastudharma*)—which is established merely through conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) regarding a non-entity—cannot be refuted by the fallacy of an unestablished locus. For such a [property] does not depend on a real entity as its locus, precisely because it is a property of a non-entity; nor does its substratum depend on perception or inference, precisely because it is a non-entity.

However, when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is an existent entity (*bhāvadharma*), the real thing (*vastu*) itself is the locus (*āśraya*), because it is a property of a real thing (*vastudharma*). Furthermore, the ascertainment of the real thing occurs only through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*); therefore, in their absence, there is necessarily a failure of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, how can there be an identical fault for proofs of existence and non-existence?

As for what Trilocana stated—that in establishing the non-existence of eternal things, the fact that the absence of succession and so forth is a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharman*) is not established—that is an assertion difficult to maintain even for a child. For here, the eternal things are the subject (*dharmin*); non-existence is the property to be proven (*sādhya*); and the absence of succession and so forth is the reason (*hetu*). Its being a "property of non-existence" is said to mean its invariable concomitance with its own probandum, on the grounds that it is a property of non-existent things such as a hare's horn and the like, and not of existent things.

By this statement, it is effectively said that as long as the probandum is not established in the subject by some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is not established. Furthermore, we do not know where [the opponent] has perceived that [pervasion] in relation to which reason.

Just as elsewhere the invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatā*) with the probandum—established at another time by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and recalled by means of an example—is employed for the sake of establishing the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*), yet does not depend on any other establishment of the probandum; so too, in the absence of succession and simultaneity, the property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatā*), which is the very nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*), is established at another time through the presence of succession and simultaneity [in the case of existence].

At the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the example of a sky-lotus—established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that functions at that time—is employed as a reminder and is useful for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*); it does not depend on the establishment of the probandum from any other source. Otherwise, all inference would be useless. For, when the pervasion of existence (*sattva*) is established through [the exclusion of] succession and simultaneity, the absence of the pervader (succession and simultaneity) is established as being pervaded by the absence of the pervaded (existence); thus, the subject matter of succession and simultaneity possesses the nature of non-existence (*abhāvadharman*). (mSĀ p.19.6)

Just as the nature of pervasion was already determined previously, so too the property of being absent where the probandum is absent is not established in the subject by means of another proof through the establishment of the probandum; likewise, our position is that the probandum is established and settled even by the absence of both succession and simultaneity, because it has already been settled previously. Therefore, how can there be the fallacy of mutual dependence?

Furthermore, a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is likewise applicable here: the establishment of the absence of succession and so forth as a property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatva*) results in the establishment of their non-existence; and the establishment of their non-existence results in the establishment of their being a property of non-existence. However, by one with a biased view, it was not stated that there is no causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*) because the property of non-existence is unestablished, but rather because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is unestablished. What kind of circularity, then, is this?

Nor is the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) itself the property of non-existence (*abhāvadharmatā*), because the property of non-existence consists in its being inseparable from the probandum (*sādhyāvinābhāva*). Now, if the property of non-existence were to belong to the absence of succession and so forth, then it would be a property of those eternal things that have been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*); it is with this intention that the non-operation of that [property] was shown by way of the operation of the property of the subject. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to state a circular argument (*cakraka*). That too has already been discussed in the ancient deliberations.

Furthermore, if the nature of being an absence (abhāvadharmatva) constitutes the form of pervasion (vyāpti), then it would follow that this is the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva); however, this is not a logical principle common to other reasons. Nor does this reason possess such a character; for whether the nature of being an absence constitutes pervasion or not, by what means is the absence of succession and so forth denied of eternal things?

Nor are these [reasons] subjects (*dharmin*) by way of being non-existent; rather, they are so by virtue of possessing doubt regarding existence and non-existence. Therefore, this objection—that the property of being an existent (*bhāvadharma*) or the property of being both is not intended for this reason of "absence of succession" and so forth—is of no consequence; thus, there is no fault in the first alternative.

Nor is it the case in the second [alternative], because it has been established that even though exclusion (*vyatireka*) is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), it is nonetheless cognized through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For there is no cognition of things that are non-entities other than through conceptual construction, nor is there a lack of cognition; for in either case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of losing the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding non-existence. Therefore, since there is no dependence on direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no room for fault in the consequence of its [conceptual construction’s] production. However, a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) is indeed appropriate to be addressed.

That [perception] too has been set aside as being produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*), because the non-perception of the pervader—characterized by the absence of both succession and simultaneity—is possible. For indeed, this very investigation was undertaken for the purpose of purifying the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) of a valid mark; and once that is established, why is it forgotten? It is on this basis that it is said, "because of the absence of a logical mark. Therefore, how can there be a lack of confidence regarding the conceptualization of the exclusion of existence—which is pervaded by succession and so forth? For the object of a lack of confidence is precisely the suspicion that there is no such exclusion (*avyatireka*).

And since this [objection] has no standing regarding the ascertainment of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, existence—which is invariably excluded from permanent things—is established as being pervaded by momentariness; thus, there is no fault.

Regarding 89,12: Since even in the third alternative the certainty of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been firmly established, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), while establishing the absence of succession and so forth in its own substratum which is eternal, necessarily establishes the exclusion of existence from that [eternal thing] and establishes its connection with momentariness; thus it possesses three functions, yet these are subsumed within a single function and are not tainted by even a trace of fault.

And if the threefold nature [of the object] were a characteristic of existence (*sattā*) belonging to the power of the object itself, then, since it would merely establish the exclusion [of others], it would serve to establish non-existence; thus, it remains established that there is indeed a duality of functions.

[102,14] But surely, since the absence of a pervader is of the nature of a non-entity (abhāva), even if the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is avoided by its being a property of a real thing (*vastudharma*), how can that non-entity be a cognition of anything, or a cause for the cognition of anything? Or, how is the cognition of that [non-entity] itself not observed? Furthermore, it has been stated that the conceptual judgment of exclusion (*vyatireka-vikalpa*), which arises from that logical mark (*liṅga*), does not harbor any suspicion of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) at this very moment.

Furthermore, one who seeks to establish the cognition of a probandum (*sādhya*) must necessarily accept the conventional usage of existence (*bhāva-vyavahāra*) by means of the proof (*sādhana*); otherwise, everything would be contradicted if that proof were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*). Even regarding the "non-perception of the pervader" (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), if it is merely a non-perception, that same fault remains; nor can the non-perception of something else be called the "non-perception of the pervader," for that would also apply to the non-perception of any other thing whatsoever.

That too is of little consequence, because non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is established elsewhere precisely through the apprehension of the locus (*dharmin*). For instance, in the case of "There is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," there is the apprehension of the bare location as the locus with respect to the tree; this is the non-apprehension of the tree. And with respect to the *śiṃśapā*, the mere cognition [of the bare location] is itself the cognition of the absence of the *śiṃśapā*. Thus, the operation of the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) culminates in the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*).

Likewise, for an eternal substratum appearing in conceptual cognition, its mere appearance—considered in relation to succession and so forth—is itself the non-perception of succession and the like; and its mere apprehension, considered in relation to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), is itself the apprehension of its dissociation from causal efficiency. This is the distinction.

Furthermore, with respect to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), just as there is the expression of non-existence using the ablative case of a reason, as in "there is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees," so too is there the conventional usage that "existence is the means of proof" (*sādhana*). However, it is not the case that non-existence is ever exclusively the means of proof. And that conventional usage cannot be avoided, because it is non-contradictory with respect to the object as it has been determined.

Indeed, whatever is devoid of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is necessarily also devoid of the pervaded (*vyāpya*); since this very point is established by that [non-perception] in a manner consistent with the fact, what difference is there between this principle when the subject (*dharmin*) is real and when it is unreal? [Objection: But surely this is a great difference! For when the subject is real, the pervader is in a state of "cognitive co-inherence" (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*) with that very subject; thus, let its perception be the non-perception of the pervader. However, when the subject is unreal, it is not in a state of cognitive co-inherence with anything at all. If you say this:

By that very property connected to itself which is considered to be the pervader (*vyāpaka*); for in this case, "single cognition" refers precisely to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Since that conceptual construction grasps [the object] as permanent, it might—by way of possibility—represent even the form of succession and so forth for the permanent entity, just as it represents other forms; thus, the connection with a single cognition is unavoidable for both.

If [the eternal] were not perceived as being in the domain of cognition together with another property—such as the state of being incapable of having anything added to it—then simultaneity or non-simultaneity would not be an objective feature of the real substrate; this might indeed be the case. But it is not so. Furthermore, without the possibility of the object to be negated, the co-occurrence in a single cognition could never be attained at that time.

In this regard, just as a horn was perceived by him in connection with a single cognition on the head of a deer, and thus its connection [with permanence] is denied even in the case of Hari’s body through the very possibility of that [connection], so too, in the case of blue and other things whose status as permanent or impermanent is not yet established, succession and simultaneity are seen to be connected with a single cognition along with their own substratum; therefore, even in the case of the permanent, since they would be grasped by the cognition apprehending the permanent together with its impermanent substratum, they enter into the negation solely by way of being connected with a single cognition, based on such a possibility.

[103,18] But how is it that succession and the like do not manifest in eternal cognition? For one might argue: "We indeed conceptualize the eternal as being encompassed by both succession and non-succession. To this we reply: for this very reason, the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) enters; because without introducing a contrary form, that [argument] would be futile. While this superimposition of succession and non-succession upon the nature of the eternal may indeed necessitate the presentation of a subverting argument against it, it is not capable of including succession and non-succession within the eternal, due to their contradiction.

For permanence (*nityatva*) consists in having a single form throughout different times, whereas succession (*krama*) and simultaneity (*akrama*) consist in having distinct forms even across two moments. Consequently, since permanence and the capacity for successive or simultaneous causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) possess mutually contradictory natures, their opposition is unavoidable; how, then, could succession and so forth be included within the permanent? And because they are not included therein, how could there be any mention of succession or simultaneity by means of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of pure permanence that has eliminated all superimposition (*samāropa*), given that everything [in this context] is merely the domain of conceptual construction?

The establishment of contradictory properties—whether determinate or indeterminate—is made in dependence upon forms as they appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍha*). For example, in the case of the three qualities (*triguṇya*), oneness is a contradictory property; [furthermore], clarity, distress, and dejection are determinate functions, while their association with selflessness or its opposite is indeterminate. Likewise here, if [the agent] is a non-agent due to having a single nature across prior and subsequent times, then it is eternally a non-agent; and if it is an agent at all times, then it is eternally an agent. However, succession and simultaneity are sometimes the very nature of the power of action; for if there were simultaneity, [the result] would be manifest immediately.

“Functioning at one time alone” means having occasional activity; even in the case of succession, because there is functioning of what has already been produced and what is yet to be produced, the activity is indeed occasional, since dependence on auxiliary factors has already been refuted. Therefore, a contradiction is established between “having occasional activity” and “not having occasional activity,” as they are defined by mutual exclusion.

This being the case, when a permanent counter-positive is being considered, since it meets the criterion of being associated with a single cognition, the non-perception of its opposite—which is characterized by succession and simultaneity—is simply the perception of that [opposite]. Or rather, this itself is the non-perception of the pervader of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*). Therefore, because it is the perception of a property that pervades the subject (*dharmin*), it does not differ from other types of non-perception of a pervader.

If, even regarding that which possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*), the distinction between the real and the unreal remains poorly established in the mind of you, an unfortunate person, even now; then who can prevent those seeking distinctions from finding them even within a single real subject—for instance, the division where one part is hard and solid while another is liquid water, and so forth? Therefore, what use is the consideration of a distinction based on the real and the unreal?

[104,14] But surely its utility is great! For, with respect to a real entity (*vastu*) as the locus (*dharmin*), inference characterized by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), which is indirectly connected to it, becomes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because the establishment of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vyavasthā*) has the real entity as its basis. And this is not possible with respect to a non-entity (*avastu*). If [this is argued], then:

[104,16] First of all, if "being based on a real entity" (vastvadhiṣṭhānatva) means simply that [the property] has originated from a real entity even through a succession [of causes], then its dependence upon a real entity—which is the object of the apprehension of the pervasion between sequential and non-sequential [causality] and causal efficiency—is not lost; nor is its dependence upon a real entity that is the object of the conceptualization of the locus (dharmin) lost.

Now, is the state of being based on a real entity (*vastv-adhiṣṭhānatva*) the fact that something serves as a cause for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding an object in some form? Even that is established as a means for proving the momentary destruction of entities; or rather, since that very conceptualization of a subject (*dharmivikalpa*) serves as the cause for the linguistic convention that the object is not based on a real entity, what is the point of [asserting] that the basis in a real entity belongs to the real entity itself as the subject? And if this [conceptualization] were indeed perception (*grahaṇa*), then would validity belong only to inference as having its basis in a real entity? No.

In the case of perception, it is indeed the reliance upon linguistic expression (*loka*) that allows for the consideration of a subject (*dharmin*). However, perception that does not rely on such [expression], having arisen from a real entity (*vastu*), is a basis for the real entity itself through its engagement with the object; thus, let it be understood that inference likewise has the real entity as its basis in exactly the same way. For even in the case of perception, while its very birth is direct by way of a lineage, its practical application (*vyavahāra*) occurs only through the mediation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, for inference as well, both [the object and its cognition] are mediated through a succession; even the practical application (*vyavahāra*) is mediated by memory, desire, and so forth. Thus, the fact that inference has a real entity as its basis is indeed a defect due to this mediation. To claim that this [requirement] regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is superior to the mediation found elsewhere in inference with respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is merely a delusion of the intellect. Moreover, this characteristic is not common to all other types of inference.

For in the cases of the non-perception of the effect, the cause, and the pervader, the capacity to indicate [the probandum] exists through the pervasion of the contrapositive, having set aside the direct connection with its own probandum.

Similarly, if the fact that a real entity (*vastu*) serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were to occur in a particular object through the aforementioned mediation, what kind of fault would there be? For there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*). However, with respect to the conceptualization of the subject (*dharmī*), even such a degree of mediation is not possible; moreover, there is an uncommon proximity because the subject is unified with the form of the conceptualization. This is because, even in the view that [cognition] is devoid of forms (*nirākārapakṣa*), the subject—which possesses an unreal, eternal form—has its manifestation dependent upon conceptualization.

Therefore, the investigation into the substratum of the entity (*vastu*) as the locus of the subject (*dharmin*) fulfills its purpose by serving as the basis for a specific proximity, even through the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus, there is no fault whatsoever. This very principle is to be applied in such cases as: "The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because he lacks consciousness," and "A donkey's horn is not a substance because it is devoid of substantiality. It is also the refuge in such passages as: "There is no contradiction regarding a non-entity, because it is not an object of cognition" (p. 19.8).

If "not being an object of cognition" is meant in reference to mere conventional cognition (*pratīti*), then there is the fault of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*); if it is meant in reference to direct experience (*anubhava*), then there is the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Such is the capacity to avoid these types of refutations; however, there is no counting of any multitude of faults such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) and so forth.

By this, the claim that "in the case of the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi), the absence of the pervaded (vyāpyābhāva) must be understood as something distinct" is easily set aside; for it has been established that the subject itself (*dharmin*), being a distinct object of cognition, serves as the locus of the proof—just as, in the case of a *gaṇḍaśila* rock, the absence of the state of being a *śiṃśapā* tree follows from the absence of the state of being a tree (*vṛkṣatva*). Thus, there is no lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*) regarding the non-perception of the pervader under discussion, because the contradiction between permanence and [the alternatives of] succession or simultaneity has been demonstrated.

As for what was said—that there is a contradiction between succession and simultaneity—that is stated once again by way of its pervader: because of the contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Nor is there a lack of establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), since it has been demonstrated that even a non-entity can function as a subject (*dharmin*), and because its cognition is demonstrated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason, in the treatise, its establishment and ascertainment within the subject occurs either through perception or through inference.

Thus, it should be understood that this is clearly stated: while the general rule (*utsarga*) is that things such as nails, which possess a nature never previously produced by others, are not causes for sound and so forth at all times—thereby establishing the probandum and the probans regarding non-entities (*avastu*)—this constitutes an exception (*apavāda*).

[106] In this way, the objection regarding the non-establishment of the subject of the example is also avoided. Furthermore, the absence of the pervaded and the pervader is indeed established, because, as in the case of "eternal," there is no disagreement regarding that point. Consequently, the denial of the reason's presence in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is also destroyed. Now, if it is argued that a fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) has been committed, [we reply]: by this very [argument], through the necessary connection with the established probandum, the acceptance of momentary destruction for the subjects of the probandum is established by the reason of existence (*sattva*).
The third quarter, titled "The Section on Negation" (Vyatirekādhikāra).
[The Fourth Chapter:

Section on the Causeless Destruction] By means of perception that discerns positive and negative concomitance, it is established— just as in the case of smoke and fire— that there is a relationship of cause and effect between the factors of destruction, produced by the observation and non-observation of the visible.

Prior to the presence of its cause, the effect is non-existent; therefore, the claim that destruction extends over that period during which the effect remains is also false, for destruction is simply the non-perception of the thing's own nature.

For the nature of destruction is not perceived within the range of apprehension such that—through the determination of positive and negative concomitance—it could establish the stability of an entity for as long as the effect called "destruction" did not exist prior to the presence of the hammer or other factors considered its cause; rather, since the nature of the destructible object is unperceived, this [notion of a cause] is merely a false conceptualization. Thus, how can stability be established through the non-perception of a cause?

If it is argued: "But jars, hammers, and so forth are indeed seen; therefore, there is certainly something among them called 'destruction,' and thus the non-perception of the nature of destruction is unestablished (asiddha)," [the response follows:]

This jar has been seen, and its falling here has likewise been seen; the collection of shards has been seen, but no further non-existence has been seen. Therefore, where is this designation "non-existence" applied? What indeed is its cause here? This mere succession of potsherds, belonging to the obstacle [the jar], is simply perceived as it stands under its own power.

First, this jar is seen; here its falling is likewise seen; the collection of shards is seen; but no other "non-existence" is seen beyond that. Therefore, where has the expression "non-existence" been deposited? Furthermore, what is the cause for it here? Only this row of potsherds is seen, belonging solely to the jar [or, in the case of a door-bolt, to the bolt].

Even though we examine most skillfully with our physical eyes, we do not perceive any other entity here that could be made the object of the term "non-existence. And because we do not perceive such a thing, how can we determine its cause—that non-existent entity by whose absence it would be said that each preceding moment perishes? Furthermore, regarding the staff that is postulated as its cause, we observe only a series of potsherds that conform to its presence and absence, and nothing else whatsoever.

This has been presented again as an example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Just as this [pot], by manifesting positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) through perception and non-perception, is established as the effect of the stick because it is visible, so too, if the entity called "destruction" were also visible, its status as the effect of that same stick would be unavoidable once it was distinguished from the nature of non-self; but it is not so. Therefore, this is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
It might be argued as follows:
"Let the row of shards remain; this destruction of the jar did not exist previously.
Therefore, let stability also be established by that [destruction]; what is the use of a separate destruction? To this, the reply is:
If that very [destruction] is called "destruction," then how is it that when another jar is placed there, the term "non-existence" is used? Therefore, even in our view, non-existence is established.

This is the meaning: just as it is possible for you to demonstrate that there is no destruction of the jar prior to the blow of a swift hammer because the series of potsherds—which constitute its very nature—is not perceived, so too it is possible to say that there is no acquaintance with a succession of absences either. For even in the case of absence, it is not the series of potsherds itself that is being referred to, such that the non-perception of the nature [of the jar] would be the basis in that same manner.

Now, if it is argued that even non-existence (*abhāva*) is nothing other than a series of potsherds (*kapāla-paṅkti*), then how could there be the conventional usage of "non-existence" when one jar has been removed from a certain place and another jar is placed in its stead, given that the series of potsherds is absent there? Furthermore, for someone who perceives some kind of difference, the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs even in that case—where one person, deceived by the similarity of the new object, still maintains the conviction that the previous state persists. Therefore, how can the series of potsherds alone be non-existence? If, for one who applies the term "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) to this [series], [it were so]...

It may indeed be asserted that prior destruction does not exist because of the absence of the state of shards; however, it cannot be said that non-existence does not exist, for it is difficult to perceive due to the possibility of the emergence of another similar [object]. Therefore, since the prior non-existence of the jar is possible even before the blow, our desired point is established. This is merely the failure to apply the non-perception of the perceptible; hence, there is no utility in applying the designation "destruction" to the shards.

Furthermore, nothing else is observed that follows the positive and negative concomitance of the mallet; thus, destruction is merely a matter of conventional usage and does not exist as a real entity.

If destruction is not determined by its own cause, why is there a restriction in experience that "the jar has been destroyed" at a particular place and time? Therefore, it must be an effect. Nor indeed is there any other cause, for otherwise [the jar would be destroyed] even before a swift-moving staff [is applied].
Who can prevent the bold cognition of a destroyed jar that arises from its destruction?

In that case, then, the boastful talk of those with their cheeks puffed out—claiming that destruction follows the positive and negative concomitance of its cause just like other effects—is refuted, because, unlike other effects, it lacks any such experience.

[109,2] Having established destruction through reasoning alone, you now seek to prove its dependence on a causal basis for its non-existence; yet that reasoning is exhausted, since we see a succession of potsherds produced by a hammer and so forth when the water-bearing cloud [the jar] has been seen [to have perished].
First of all, the cognition of a destroyed jar is produced through the following of conventional designations.

In this context, there is no factor whatsoever named "destruction" within the causal complex; nor would such a thing exist even in this [complex], nor was it ever absent previously, for this collection has always been present in its entirety.

By the first half [of the verse], the causal complex for the arising of the cognition of a "destroyed jar" has been shown; by the second half, it is demonstrated that there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for this additional entity called "destruction," whereas both are observed for the causal complex of the discrimination of that [jar]. In this regard, positive concomitance is refuted because there is no such thing as "destruction" present here within the causal complex; furthermore, the reliance on negative concomitance—that the cognition would not arise even when this causal complex is present—is discarded.

In that case, why was this cognition not [produced] previously? [The answer is: by means of the remainder, there is the removal of the notion of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). If this causal complex (*sāmagrī*) had existed previously, then this cognition, necessarily arising, would have indicated a dependence upon another object. Yet this causal complex did not exist previously either, because it was absent due to the deficiency in the series of potsherds and the absence of causes such as the striking of a club. Therefore, how can there even be a question of negative concomitance?

However, regarding the aforementioned causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) expressed by the two negations: "this [cognition] would not exist even in this [complex], nor at any time. Furthermore, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is made explicit by the remainder [of the statement]. Since it is established that the causal complex itself is absent at the time when that cognition is absent, the meaning is that the absence of the causal complex is pervaded by the absence of the cognition.

However, for one of distorted vision who maintains that every causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed imperceptible because it consists of the totality of both perceptual and non-perceptual auxiliary factors, and who consequently claims that because of its imperceptibility there can be no determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding it—alas, even the connection between smoke and the causal complex of fire, fuel, and so forth would vanish, leading to the absurd consequence that the world would be devoid of purposeful activity and cessation. Therefore, since the acceptance of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) does not obstruct the observed capacity of the means [of accomplishment], enough with this elaboration.
Thus, it is established that for one who has the mental apprehension (*amarśa*) of a jar, the very experience of the potsherds is the means for determining that the jar has perished.
Therefore, this *arthāpatti* (presumption) is exhausted; it is not capable of establishing destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

If it is argued that "there can be no cognition of a qualified object without a qualifier," we say: no, because since destruction occurs at a different time from the [jar's] existence, its status as a qualifier is unestablished.
That by which something is colored through one's own cognition is its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Due to the difference in time, since there is no existence of destruction at the prior and subsequent times, what could qualify what? [Destruction] is sometimes made an object of cognition. Furthermore, destruction is not a property of persistence (*sthitidharma*) residing in an entity, but rather it resides in a location (*pradeśa*). And that which resides elsewhere cannot be a qualifier of another, just like a staff [qualifying a person]. If it is argued that this might still be the case because of their distinctness (*bheda*):

Now, a qualifier, appearing precisely through its distinction from all other forms, would cause the qualified object to become the object of a cognition colored by itself; it could not do so if it did not appear in its own form, just as in the case of a staff. If it is argued that this is inconclusive because the cognition of a "staff-bearer" arises even when the staff is established only through inference, we say no; for our intention is that [the rule applies] to that which in every respect lacks the manifestation of its own form.

Furthermore, although the staff does not appear at the time of inference, it certainly has a manifestation of its own nature at the time when its relation with the mark (liṅga)—which is intended to be determinative—is grasped. Therefore, through the recollection of that [relation], the staff may also impart a cognition colored by its own form at the time of inference. However, for one who has never before seen the staff, the staff itself was neither previously perceived as an object of inference nor as a cause for a cognition colored by its own nature.

In this way, how could the meaning of "destruction" also be such [as you claim], since it is in every respect unobservable? Furthermore, the cognition of "the man with a staff" (daṇḍin) is not distinct from the inference of the staff; for there is no difference in meaning between "the staff is here," "he has a staff," and "this is the one possessing a staff."

Furthermore, this [non-apprehension] cannot be an inference by virtue of being a mere thesis if it does not exist upon the abandonment of its logical mark (*liṅga*). For how could that which lacks the cognition of destruction be designated as a means of proof in itself, while still requiring a certainty that establishes the object named "destruction"? Nor is there any other logical mark, because since [the subject] is entirely invisible, no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) can be established for anyone with respect to it. It is precisely for this reason that all cognition is relied upon as a refuge for establishing it.

Therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding what is established by inference (*anumāna*), because the cognition of the qualifier of an inference is inseparable from and immediately follows the manifestation of the specific nature of that inference; for that which does not have a manifestation of its own nature cannot be the cause of a cognition colored by itself, just as an elephant’s mane [is not the cause of such a cognition]. And since there is no manifestation of a specific nature in destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

The state of being the cause for a cognition that is concordant with itself is pervaded by the very fact of appearing, since its occurrence when the manifestation ceases is sublated by the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is this unestablished (*asiddhi*); for there is no conventional usage of "appearing" for an external object that cannot be shown as "this," and there is no dispute regarding that which can be designated as "this. Indeed, even a staff is not something to be established by the cognition of the "staff-bearer," because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Even when establishing a convention for a deluded person, there is no designation as "this" specifically regarding what is within the range of the eyes.

[110,24] Now, if every entity appears by its own nature (*svarūpa*) and not by the nature of another (*pararūpa*), just as existence itself does not appear in the form of non-existence, so too non-existence, even while not appearing in the form of existence, certainly appears by its own nature. If it is argued that appearing as "this-ness" (*idantayā*) belongs only to an existent entity that is an object of the eye, and therefore, even in the absence of appearance as "this-ness," there is no total non-appearance at all; [we reply:]

An appearance in the form of another is not sought at all, since its non-existence is already established. Furthermore, when we examine what its own nature (*svarūpa*) is that appears, we find nothing; yet, even regarding entities, the designation "this-ness" (*idantā*) is not a royal decree.

If one were to say that even among entities, this designation applies only to certain things presented before the eyes and not to all, then what could be said in this case? For even the tips of fingernails and the like, though appearing again and again, can ultimately not be designated as "this."

Therefore, the logical principle is this: as long as an object moves within the range of the eye, it appears as a description through its "this-ness" (*idantā*); however, that which is devoid of such "this-ness" and thus lacks description cannot at all appear as something graspable by the eyes.

[111,9] Now, if it is argued that the appearance itself must also be established by means of a cognition of a particularity (*viśeṣabuddhi*)—just as the cognition of a man with a staff does not occur without the cognition of the staff, nor without the appearance of the staff; and likewise, because it is a cognition of a particularity, the cognition of destruction cannot occur without destruction or the appearance of destruction; therefore, how can there be a claim of non-appearance? [We reply: There is indeed a transformation, but it is not of such a kind.

If you argue that the appearance residing within one's own continuum must also be understood by us through inference, then the same would now apply to the appearance of jars and so forth. Consequently, even for one who is like a non-reliable person, the inference "Do I see something? would have to be accepted even on the basis of the word of a reliable person; thus, a physician would achieve his purpose even without applying a remedy. Ultimately, one would even resort to cessation [of treatment] based on an oath.

For these various modes find their scope only regarding an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), not regarding cognition itself. Furthermore, when one who does not see [an object] is made to grasp it by being told, "You are indeed seeing yourself," this is clearly a magician’s trick that deceives even one who is actually seeing. And he who, though not seeing, grasps "I see" because of such a statement, is truly a beast among beasts. For even in the doctrine that cognition is imperceptible, that which does not appear is established by the appearance of something else;
it is not established by logical arguments that "this is its appearance" or "this is not its appearance."

Therefore, the claim that even the appearance (pratibhāsa) is the probandum is irrelevant. However, if destruction (*nāśa*) is being proven while it remains unmanifested, let it be proven; but it is not proven by means of the cognition of a destroyed jar—this is established.
Or rather, let there be destruction, but it is not the producer of the cognition, just as [destruction] is not the cause of the cognition of a destroyed jar in the case of the jar itself.

Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say: let there be such a thing as "destruction," yet it cannot necessarily be maintained that the hammer or other such instruments are its perceived cause. Just as the experience of the shards is not accepted as the cause for the cognition of a destroyed jar, so too, even for destruction, there might be some other unperceived cause entirely, distinct from the hammer and so forth; therefore, the prior non-perception of a cause is not established.

Just as an unseen entity called "destruction" (nāśa), established by its own acceptance, is the basis for the cognition of "destroyed," so too there must be some unseen cause of destruction itself, and not the mallet or other such instruments. How then could the cessation of destruction be necessarily contingent upon their absence? However, this is the distinction: just as the efficacy of the mallet with respect to the potsherd, and the efficacy of the experience of the potsherd with respect to the cognition of "destroyed," are established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is not so for the mallet with respect to destruction, nor for the object to be destroyed with respect to the cognition of "destroyed. This point must be accepted only out of deference to you.

If it is argued that from the experience of the potsherds there would only be the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of the potsherds, and not the cognition of a destroyed jar—this is like pulling out the fangs of a living tiger. For one who has the perception of the jar, the arising of the cognition of a destroyed jar is directly experienced upon seeing the circle of potsherds; yet you deny this. If that were so, it would follow that one must deny every object established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, when a person’s cognition of a jar is void due to a lack of interest and so forth, then from the observation of the potsherds, only the conceptualization of the potsherds arises, because the difference in causal conditions (sāmagrī) is what differentiates the result. Even if, following your own position, they were to conform to your view, such would not necessarily happen; yet, even then, if you maintain that the cognition of destruction must arise solely from the experience of the potsherds, then it would indeed be so—thus, destruction itself is not the efficient cause (prayojaka).

Therefore, enough with this reliance on mere personal conjecture; the perception of the potsherd alone is the basis for that cognition [of destruction]. However, when it requires the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the jar, it likewise requires the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); thus, there is no over-extension of the principle. Furthermore, the convention cannot be established by demonstrating the destruction itself, precisely because that [destruction] is not perceptible; rather, it is by demonstrating a modification in the form of the production of a dissimilar state that one speaks of "destruction" in such a condition.
By this, those who imagine that the very perception of absence constitutes the non-apprehension of an entity are refuted.

[112,18] Precisely because one does not perceive a form consisting of non-existence, there is therefore no such thing as "destruction" that occurs subsequently. Furthermore, if this world is established as having another nature at every moment, then by the force of this robust reasoning, its death would either be delayed or not; what of it?
It might be argued:
"If that [otherness] were not without destruction, it would exist together with existence;
if it were both existent and non-existent, what could be the fixed nature of a thing? Therefore, this [otherness] is a subsequent state of being."

Because of its existence, [the effect] lacks a distinct cause; since that [distinct] cause is impossible, even the "otherness" produced by it vanishes—so how could there be destruction at every moment?

[113,3] It was stated that "if there were similarity with existence" (bhāvena sādharmyaṃ sa cet), this refers to the description of the arising of non-existence from the presence of an existent cause. In this regard, what is the meaning of "other than destruction" (dhvaṃsād anyatā)? Does one and the same entity get broken into pieces by it? Or is it merely the production of another entity from this [destruction]? Or is it both the cessation of the previous [entity] and the production of another entity? Or finally, is it merely the cessation of the previous [entity]?

In this regard, destruction does not cause a single entity to become manifold, because of the contradiction between oneness and multiplicity. If it is argued that even a single thing becomes manifold through a difference in time and thus no fault arises, [we reply: what does time avail if there is an absence of internal differentiation within the entity itself? For if a difference in time were to produce a difference in the entity, then this might be so. However, since the entity remains in its very same state (*tādavasthya*), such a resort to the straw of *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass is appropriate only for those [who hold such views]; thus, the first position is refuted.

If it is argued that [the jar] is broken, then there is no shattering of it; this is the second fault. For if a different entity is produced, the previous [jar] is not shattered; consequently, one would face the absurdity of perceiving the jar even when its shards and so forth have been removed. If it is asked: "What is the use of shattering it with something distinct? If the perception of that jar is admitted to occur through a different entity such as the shards, then that [shattering] serves no purpose. If you say its purpose is the production of that very different entity called 'destruction' (nāśa)," [we reply:]...
But since you undergo different births, why do you not [undergo them] for the sake of destruction?

Since the destruction of the hammer and so forth occurs from that very same cause, let the birth of the potsherd arise from that very same cause; why then posit destruction as something to be accomplished? By this, the portion concerning the production of another [entity] in the third alternative is also refuted; thus, only the fourth remains: "its cessation is brought about by destruction. Even in that case: If it is held that destruction produces destruction, then if another destruction were produced by that [first] destruction, there would be a succession of destructions, and that entity would never be perceived.
If it is argued that there is no cessation other than destruction, then how can there be mutual annihilation? [We reply:
It is not so, because destruction is perceived as the observation of the object itself; for destruction is manifested through such observation.

For destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) cannot possibly transcend the status of being a real entity (*vastutā*) or the status of being an existent (*bhāvatā*), because it possesses the capacity to produce a cognition and because its existence is established through other means. How, then, can one thing be called the "destruction" of another? As for the reply that "it is so because the object is no longer perceived when this [destruction] exists," that is not correct; since it has been demonstrated that there is no perception of destruction, how then can it be asserted that "when this is non-existent [the object is perceived]? Furthermore, if you claim that the cessation of the entity called "destruction" occurs because the object is not perceived when that [destruction] exists, then—

Let destruction (nāśa) be the mallet itself, or perhaps the shards; for in either case, the intended meaning—that "it exists when that [cause] is present"—is established because the mallet exists prior [to the destruction], while the shards exist simultaneously with it. This is like saying "the sprout exists when the seed is present," or "he has gone while the cows are being milked. "Destruction" means cessation (*nivṛtti*), specifically that which is called annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*). Let even this annihilation be the mallet or the like. Enough with the separate conceptualization of annihilation; for by that much alone, it is proven that the entity was stable previously due to its absence [of destruction]. To this, it is replied:
That pair [of existence and non-existence], being existent, does not obstruct existence;
for existence itself cannot be the opponent of existence. And if there is no opposition, how could there be the cessation or non-perception of the other? To this, the reply is:
for you, the very nature of existence is the difference from existence.

In this matter, there is no inherent capacity belonging to entities; rather, it is your own word, *bhāratī*, that possesses the state of being (*bhāvatā*) or non-being (*abhāvatā*). For instance, "it becomes" (*bhavati*) is the meaning of *bhāva*; thus, its "becoming," which is to say its arising, is indeed accepted. Even when [the term] "being" (*bhāva*) means "it exists" (*asti*), the meaning of *bhāva* is still existence (*vidyamānatā*). That too is accepted as being characterized by the reality of its own nature (*svarūpasattva*), adorned with permanence for as long as it lasts. And as for that which does not exist—that is, which does not "be"—how could it be connected with the act of arising? It would be like the son of a barren woman or like a sprout [from a barren seed].

Now, if it is argued that even capacity (*śakti*) is admitted to be existence because the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs only in the absence of any description of functional capacity, then that capacity is indeed already accepted as producing its own cognition; moreover, such effects as walking without hesitation are precisely its function. There is, however, no inherence in existence (*sattvasamavāya*) or inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇasamavāya*) as you yourself have asserted.

Furthermore, it is not the case that every existent property must be present in every existent thing, nor is it the case that because of the absence of every existent property, another existent thing would fail to exist. If this were so, it would follow that universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) would also be non-existent. That destruction arises even beyond these [categories] is indeed its own fault. Moreover, since a real entity (*vastu*) necessarily possesses destruction—meaning that purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) resides within it—it cannot be called a "non-existent" (*abhāva*). Alas, what a miserable obsession with a flawed philosophical tenet!
Therefore, you have autonomy in this matter: if you say that even destruction is an entity, then the mallet and so forth would also be the non-existence of the jar.

If it is argued that no one indeed employs the conventional designation "non-existence" for an entity such as a hammer and so forth, then surely, if even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) were perceived by someone as arising in some form—specifically, as something persisting eternally—who would employ the conventional designation "non-existence" for it? For we observe that things such as subtle smoke and the like, whose forms are unperceived due to obstruction, lack of attention, or other causes, come to be designated as "existent" when they are perceived once again.

Therefore, the cessation of the conventional usage of "existence" is personally experienced through non-perception alone, because its very nature consists in the perception of a counter-correlative. And that non-perception, if it is admitted to be an experience, is itself an existence; whereas if it were unperceivable, then to speak of its "arising" and so forth would be like painting a picture in space. Since the conventional usage of "existence" necessarily follows from the perception of both the thing's own nature and its arising, how could even this [non-perception] be contradictory to it?

Nor is it the case that the term "non-existence" (*abhāva*) does not apply even to the hammer and so forth, for its establishment occurs through the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of other positive entities (*bhāva*). Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). For by whatever relation the very entity called destruction is said to be the cessation of the jar, that same relation is not obstructed by the potsherds or the iron bar. Furthermore, their mutual opposition (*virodhitva*) is most appropriate, since they excel one another even in the slightest degree, namely, in being perceived.

Because the statement "the conventional usage of the absence of a jar occurs when those two exist" would entail an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the grounds for such a refutation are strengthened. Furthermore, it is not the case that one positive entity (*bhāva*) does not at all contradict another positive entity; otherwise, how could "cowness" contradict "non-cowness," or fire contradict cold?

Furthermore, contradiction is also known to be of two kinds. In that regard, if contradiction were coexistence, then it would belong only to two positive entities (*bhāva*), like fire and snow. For the determination of non-coexistence occurs when one thing exists while its cause is unimpaired, yet another thing is absent. And it is evident that this [kind of] relationship is not possible between existence and non-existence.
This is because, in the case of characteristics established through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*), the negation of one does not imply the affirmation of the other.

Indeed, it is not the case that contradiction defined by characteristics (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*) has the function of subverting an existent entity; rather, this function belongs only to contradiction defined as non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). For the latter, which is defined by characteristics, there is only the establishment of two properties (*dharma*). Once an entity is established—whether by another entity or by a non-entity—the negation of the confusion or intermixture of their intrinsic natures (*svarūpa-saṃkara-vyatikara*) follows. Thus, just as blue is not non-blue because the two possess mutually exclusive intrinsic natures, so too would it be for a jar and its destruction.
Yet, even by that much, the desired conclusion is not proven, because the jar’s state remains unchanged [at the moment of impact], just as it does upon the mere proximity of a hammer.

[116,7] But surely, since it is only the two properties that are contradictory in the case of a jar and a thunderbolt and so forth, there is merely a difference between the two things occupied by them; however, the destruction of the jar and the jar itself are inherently contradictory, being of the nature of existence and non-existence—so how could they coexist?

No; for it is only between two properties (*dharma*), such as existence and non-existence, which consist respectively of being and non-being, that there is mutual exclusion. This is because there is no non-existence for that which is superposed by existence, nor existence for that which is established in non-existence; or else, because a jar, space, water, and a lotus do not possess oneness [in this sense]. However, mere contradiction is not denied, provided that one existing thing overcomes another existing thing. And to that extent, there is the operation of "non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthāna*). Therefore, mutual exclusion belongs only to two properties.

If it is asked, "How can there be [a contradiction] between blue and non-blue?"—the meaning is simply that because blue and non-blue involve mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*), there is no identity (*ekatva*) between them. Thus, even by this method, it is precisely the contradiction of properties (*dharmavirodha*) that is revealed. Otherwise, just as with snow and fire, there would follow the consequence of instability even for one wearing blue and non-blue garments when they are joined together. Furthermore, identity (*tādātmya*) does not exist at all in that case either.

If it is argued that the location (*deśa*) of the blue and the non-blue is indeed distinct, let it be distinct; however, there is no contradiction between the two entities (*vastu*) merely by virtue of that difference in location. Otherwise, it would follow that even water and fire could exist in a continuous state when combined in that same way, since contradiction is effective only through the exclusion of subtle points of space (*sūkṣmadeśa*). For this very reason, in the perception of a contradiction, the subject (*dharmin*) is the gross location itself, conceived as a single entity.
Thus, the statement "blue is contradicted by non-blue" also means simply that "the blue does not become non-blue."

If, however, there were a direct contradiction even between the subject (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*), then wherever non-blue-ness exists in a subject, blue-ness would not exist there. Yet, as in the case of another jewel, such as gold (*tapanīya*), this is not so; for although destruction is merely a property consisting of non-existence, the property of existence—namely, the pot—is not non-existent, and the property of non-existence is not existent. This is the meaning; therefore:

By means of the established property of non-existence (*abhāva*), it is only a non-existent jar that is conventionally designated as "non-existent," but an existent jar is not thereby negated. However, existence (*sattā*) is negated everywhere; this is the function of their mutual non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). But how can the non-existence of a jar be a property (*dharma*)? To what, then, could this belong as a property? If you argue that because it is accepted as a property, it necessarily implies a substratum (*dharmin*), and therefore let it belong to the surface of the ground (*bhūtala*) itself—then does it follow that the non-existence intended is that of the ground itself?

[117,5] If it is argued: "Surely, the absence (abhāva) of a jar, which is connected to the jar through the relation of the sublated and the sublator, is said to be merely a property (dharmamātra) of the ground, and not the sublator of the ground itself," then let it be so—that it is neither the sublator of the ground nor its property alone. Just as the presence of a blue object is not contradicted on a ground that possesses non-blue-ness (which is the opposite of blue), so too there would be no contradiction in the presence of a jar on a ground possessed by an absence that is considered the opposite of the jar. Therefore, their status as the sublated and the sublator is established merely through conceptual presumption (abhimāna).

Therefore, it is logical that the conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*), which manifests the absence of a jar on the ground by way of its relation to the jar—the substratum of the ground—causes that absence to be treated as a property (*dharma*) of that [ground]. However, with respect to what is determined (*adhyavasita*), there is either correspondence or otherwise. Thus, a property that is mutually exclusive (*parasparaparihāraviruddha*) causes the non-existence of its own opposite—which is indeed non-existent—to be treated as a property within its own substrate (*ātmadharmi*). But it does not exclude [the opposite]; rather, it is precisely the cause for the treatment of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) regarding the substrate.

And likewise, in the case of water, fire, and so forth, the quality of touch being either hot or its opposite becomes the object of the conventional usage of "contradiction" through the mere examination of their own natures—even at a distance—by virtue of possessing mutually opposing forms, without depending on their mutual removal. However, non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is established only by observing the exclusion of one thing's existence by means of another. Therefore, if contradiction is intended to mean non-coexistence, then let it be established that there is the cessation of both the existence and the perception of an entity;
however, this applies only to two entities, not to an entity and a non-entity.

[117,17] If it is argued: "Is not contradiction intended as co-inexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), defined merely by the fact that when one exists, the other ceases? And since this is obtainable even for a positive entity (*bhāva*) with respect to a non-entity (*abhāva*), the restriction that it applies only to two positive entities is not logical."

It has been stated here that the condition "only when this exists" is difficult to establish in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, what is the use of establishing such a nature of non-existence, since the contradiction between two positive entities (*bhāva*) is not thereby excluded? Moreover, since the contradiction [of destruction] is established by the mallet and so forth alone, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is of no further utility. If, on the other hand, a "definitional" contradiction is intended, then its purpose is fulfilled simply by the non-confusion of their respective natures; thus, the persistence of the positive entity remains unavoidable.

Furthermore, according to the position that contradiction is characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), an opposing factor cannot obstruct another unless it has already arisen; for example, as in the case of cold and fire. First there is arising, then activity, and depending on the degree of proficiency in that activity, the obstruction of the other occurs after some number of moments. Thus, during that interval prior to the obstruction, the factor would have to coexist with its own prior non-existence.

Now, even if the operation occurs at the very moment of arising, such that the entity, by means of destruction as a simultaneous auxiliary while it is in the process of arising, would produce its own effect, namely bondage, and from that [bondage] there would be cessation—then coexistence is unavoidable. Even if one disregards the production of a moment of bondage, since destruction occurs immediately after the subsequent moment of its own continuum, coexistence for even a single moment is established. And how can this be tolerated by one possessing consciousness: that in one and the same moment an entity both exists and does not exist?

Moreover, since you accept non-coexistence, just as cold is destroyed by fire by producing another destruction, so too must the substratum (nipādin) be removed by that destruction by producing yet another destruction; and by that [second] destruction, the counter-positive (pratiyogin) must be struck down by producing yet another destruction. Due to this infinite regress, even in a hundred human lifetimes, the conventional usage of "non-existence" would not apply to anything.

Now, as for the second contradiction: where there is existence, there is no room at all for non-existence. For this is the very nature of contradiction according to its definition (*lākṣaṇika-virodha*), namely, that when two contradictory properties reside in a different substratum (*dharmin*), there is no room for the other; thus, destruction simply does not arise.

Now, if it is argued that because of the efficacy of a cause, how could it remain without having come into being? Therefore, destruction must necessarily occur—[we reply: no, for it is impossible to postulate the efficacy of a cause regarding a matter sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Indeed, as long as the breath of an entity moves, there is not even a scent of non-existence. Otherwise, if two properties considered contradictory were possible in a single substratum (*dharmin*) for even a single moment, where would the contradiction consisting in mutual exclusion reside?

For indeed, even if existence [of the cause] occurs by the power of its cause, the coexistence of presence and absence in a single locus is difficult to avoid in reality. That entity (bhāva) was previously established; it does not cease because it is exhausted by the effort of coming into being. Furthermore, the function of the hammer and so forth consists solely in destruction. Even if they were to function in both ways, what need would there be for destruction? Nor can it be made to cease by destruction alone, since destruction has no operation prior to its own arising.
Therefore, the persistence of the entity and the arising of non-existence are established as coexistent, like a mountain and the lion produced upon it.

[118.20] If you then argue that [the existence of the entity] will be refuted later by the destruction of the fuel, just like the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), then one who—fearing the refutation consisting in the undesirable consequence of the coexistence of existence and non-existence—is accustomed to such fallacious reasoning, merely prattles on with a reply. Whether or not the entity is subsequently refuted by destruction, the fact remains that the coexistence of existence and non-existence follows as a consequence; thus, the position is already ruined. What is the use of further searching?

If an established entity were to be destroyed by that destruction, then it would be evident that this is an operation of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*); thus, there would be a loss of the subject matter at hand. For it was the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra-virodha*) that was initially undertaken for investigation. Therefore, if one who still considers this to be the contradiction of mutual exclusion now deviates from the context due to forgetting the subject, then the operation of removing an established state should not be touched upon; thus, there is a very long period of non-coexistence.

[119,2] Now, since existence and non-existence—respectively supported by their own causes—are brought together and maintained for a long time within a single substratum (*dharmin*), the discussion of contradiction is concluded.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the entity (*bhāva*) is constrained by its own destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and ceases to exist even before its own arising, while destruction subsequently proceeds; and if it is further claimed that this is not an operation of simultaneous non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*); we reply:
this cannot be so. For [this would require] the entity to be already established...
Even though it occurs later, destruction is merely its servant;
for while that [destruction] has not yet occurred, the entity itself remains more powerful.

It has already been explained that this operation [of the hammer] applies not only to non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) but also to mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*). Nor does a future entity possess any inherent capacity [to exclude itself]. If that were so, let it simply cease by itself; if this is the case, what is the use here of another destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) produced by a hammer? Furthermore, if its presence is required, the meaning of the word "by itself" (*svayam*) becomes empty. Just as when one says, "the sprout arises by itself depending on the seed," this does not exempt it from being caused by that [seed].

If, on the other hand, there is indeed a refutation, then one should not say "in dependence upon that. And if the probandum is established by that much alone, what is to be done here with this [argument]? Since an entity ceases by itself without depending on a cause of destruction such as a hammer, its cessation would be established even prior [to the stroke]. Furthermore, since destruction is invariably concomitant with the mere thing and independent of any other cause, [it follows: "If for you the contradiction between two things consists in their not coexisting, then how could cold and fire, which are incompatible, coexist even for a single moment? [119,16]

If one destruction, while bringing about another destruction, were to become its opposite at that very moment, then that too would lead to yet another decay; thus, destruction could never occur in any way whatsoever.

[119,20] Now, if an object exists by virtue of having mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), then there is simply no destruction; or let it coexist through the power of causes.
By this destruction, there is an impairment of its intrinsic nature, yet it does not arise [again].
If the object itself is already more powerful, what need is there here for another [agent] to cause its diminution?
Thus are the two summary verses.

By this, it has been shown that the statement made by Śaṅkara— namely, "If it is asked how there can be a negation of an entity through the production of its non-existence, [the answer is] because the very production of non-existence consists in the negation of the entity due to its opposition to coexistence"— is flawed, being devoid of an understanding of that contradiction and so forth.

Therefore, one who asserts that "the claim that the production of non-existence leads to the consequence of the persistence of the entity in its very same state is the talk of a fool" is clearly this poor fellow who, like a moth driven by a contrary wind, cuts himself with his own body; he should be understood by the great ones as an object of compassion due to being submerged in great delusion. If, for you as well, non-existence is conventionally designated, is it an intrinsic nature? If it is not a real thing (*vastu*), then there is no contradiction whatsoever with its being real in relation to the entity.

Or how is the establishment of the two types of contradiction [to be understood]? What is the cause of this? If an entity is occasional, and if it were not occasional, why would its existence not be designated as eternal? Or, why is there no production of a succession of moments even later, just as there was before? And if there is such production, why is there no contradiction consisting in the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*)?

If it is argued that even the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāra*) between existence and non-existence would be non-real because non-existence is not a real entity—then this very position of the opponent is incapable of withstanding critical examination.

Therefore, it follows that mere cessation is the object of conventional usage; however, the repeated naming [of that cessation] as an entity is contradicted by its actual nature, whereas its arising is not [contradicted]. What need is there for a cause?
Precisely because of obstruction, there is no conventional usage of that [cessation]; yet upon the exhaustion of the cause, its arising occurs, for obstruction is itself real.
This is because the destruction of the mutual intrinsic nature of two realities would otherwise be established.

The definition of its essential nature is that it is merely the cessation of an entity, designated as a non-affirming negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). In this context, since they maintain that in negation there is only negation and no real entity, it is described as "merely the cessation. To the doubt as to what this so-called "cessation" might be—a third negation of the entity—it is stated that it is called "non-affirming"; furthermore, that is an object of mere conventional usage and not an object of direct experience, for otherwise it would be a real entity itself.

Furthermore, not everything that is conventionally expressed by a conceptualizing mind (*vikalpabuddhi*) constitutes a real entity (*vastu*), for otherwise even things such as a donkey’s horn would follow as being real entities; moreover, it is impossible to establish a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that lacks a real basis (*nirvastuka*). And since that [non-existence] is indeed contradicted by existence (*bhūti*) as its property (*dharma*), this answers the second question. Existence (*bhūti*) means either the capacity for the purpose of being (*sattārtha-sāmarthya*) or abiding in one's own nature (*svarūpeṇāvasthāna*).

In both cases, because they are mutually antagonistic in form, they are contradicted by mere departure [from each other]; thus, the definition of contradiction as "existing through mutual exclusion" (*parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇa*) has been stated.

[121,1] Is it not the case that mere cessation (*pracyutimātra*) is nothing at all, and how could that be contradicted by anything? Precisely because mere cessation is nothing, while a positive entity (*bhāva*), being the opposite of the meaning of the negative particle, is therefore contradicted by it. Furthermore, this contradiction is not a mutual obstruction (*anyonyapratighāta*), as in the case of existence and non-existence; rather, it is merely the non-penetration of their respective forms. And since this [non-penetration] exists even between a conceptualized [object] and a perceived one, there is no fault. As for the question "What is the purpose of a cause?"—since mere cessation is never a positive entity—the answer is given in the fourth [chapter].

For a creator could only be postulated if [the effect] were to emerge in some form; yet that which is not occasional must either always exist or never exist. Since the position that it always exists has been rejected, it must therefore never exist at all. However, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is occasional, because that [usage] does not occur at the time when the entity exists. How so? Precisely because of contradiction. For non-existence (*abhāva*) is the opposite of existence (*bhāva*); having the nature of disappearance and existing as a conceptual reversal, how could it be conventionally designated at the time when the entity exists?

For an existent entity (*bhāva*) would indeed exist even at the time of its manifestation—whether it be causeless, produced by the cause of its own manifestation, or created by some other cause—and it would thereby acquire a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) that follows from its existence. However, when there is no existence of this entity, then there can be no linguistic convention following from its existence. As for the contradiction following from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how could it proceed for one who possesses certainty upon seeing the actual object, given the absence of the awakening of latent impressions?

For this very reason, as long as there is the determination that the very nature of the thing exists, there is simply no occasion for the conventional usage of its non-existence, even though momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) actually occurs in reality. However, when one determines through the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the intrinsic nature of an entity is indeed a property that lasts for only a single moment, then at the second moment—simultaneously with the moment that is the effect derived from that thing—one conventionally designates its non-existence.

But when that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not obtained, the linguistic usage of non-existence occurs only by depending on the observation of transformations such as potsherds; this is the resolution in the fifth [chapter]. In the sixth [chapter] as well, it is stated that there is no arising from the exhaustion of causes, but rather a continuity of homogeneous moments.
