This has been stated: in the case of things that are naturally perishable, because of the dissimilarity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in each preceding moment due to the cooperation of a hammer, a "barren" moment is produced; thus, the material cause (*upādāna*) is exhausted, and there is no further production. Furthermore, that entity which, by its presence, causes the imposition of a barren moment and thereby prevents the connection with another moment of the same kind, is established as the "opponent" (*virodhin*) of that entity; this constitutes the formal definition of the contradiction of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-virodha*).

By that very same fourth quarter of the seventh [verse], even if there is indeed a contradiction between the real and the unreal consisting in their mutual exclusion, nevertheless there is no loss of their ultimate reality (*tāttvikatva*). For there is never any commingling of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); this alone is the meaning of the contradiction between properties (*dharma-virodha*). Therefore, the mention of "stability" (*sthiti*) is intended to indicate a restrictive rule (*niyama*). By this, the third alternative (*vikalpa*) is also refuted.

Consequently, it is established that what is called "destruction" is neither of the nature of a negation (*prasajya-ātman*) nor of the nature of something to be produced (*kartavya-rūpa*), such that it would depend upon a cause; nor do these many faults apply. Thus it stands.

Furthermore, regarding whether an object is perishable or otherwise, what is the use of causes for its destruction? If it has a perishable nature, then causes for its destruction are redundant; if it has a non-perishable nature, then causes for its destruction lack efficacy. Likewise, regarding whether an object is destined to arise or otherwise, what is the use of causes for its birth?
For one could say that if the object is destined to arise, the causes of its birth are redundant; if it is not destined to arise, they are ineffective.

And thus says the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*: "That is not so, because it would follow that the discourse on causes is abolished, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is possible in every case. For instance, regarding a cause: does the thing come into being with the nature of existence, or rather with the nature of non-existence? If the first position is held, then it exists by itself, because it has that very nature; thus, the cause is redundant."

In the second case, however, [the cause] is ineffective; for it is impossible for anything to produce something such as a rabbit's horn, which has the nature of a non-entity (*abhāvasvabhāva*). Likewise, causes such as cutting or burning are also untenable—due to both futility and incapacity—under the two positions of whether [the object] possesses that nature or does not possess that nature. Thus, since the rejection of all causes is possible in this way, any effort toward liberation and the like, or toward the study of the scriptures and so forth, would be in vain.

[122,13] Here, this objection is raised: "What is the use of this approach that is like striking an axe at the root? It is said that in no case whatsoever, when something is presented as a reason, should a fault characterized by incapacity or futility be stated. This is first of all untenable; for indeed, the futility of an axe is observed in the case of what can be cut by a fingernail, and the incapacity of a fingernail is observed in the case of what can be cut by an axe.

Likewise, regarding that which is to be accomplished by Devadatta alone, Yajñadatta’s activity—though he be accompanied by Devadatta—is useless; yet, when deprived of him, [Devadatta] lacks the capacity. When the collection of fire and fuel is present, the donkey is useless with respect to the smoke; when it is absent, it lacks the capacity. Or, where there is the bolstering of what is already established, there is uselessness; and where any one of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), or the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) exists, there is a lack of capacity.

As for those who maintain that even the "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) is included among these [fallacies], their effort yields no fruit; for the fault of futility (*vaiyarthya*) can never be denied as a defect of the reason, and because even a probative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*) acts as a causal factor (*kāraka*) toward cognition. Moreover, if futility were not a defect of the reason—since there would be no other defect—the proof of everything would follow from anything whatsoever.

Now, if it is argued that the refutation based on the alternatives of "having that nature" or "not having that nature" is invalid, that too is incorrect. For whatever reason is adduced regarding a lamp—whether for its producing illumination or for its causing darkness—is it not defeated by either futility or incapacity?

Furthermore, he says this: even the analogy of light and so forth is untenable. For, in our view, it is not established that the lamp and its light are one, nor that they have a single cause. Our settled doctrine is that after the substance has arisen, qualities such as light arise from a different collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*).

That too is irrelevant. For even if the quality of luminosity (*prakāśa*) arises after the substance has arisen, nevertheless, that very substance which has arisen does not depend on any other cause for the accomplishment of its own nature; nor does the subsequent quality of luminosity depend on anything else for its being of the nature of the quality of luminosity. Thus, there is no deficiency in the example. Now, if it is argued that even the form of the substance, prior to the universal "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and its inherence (*samavāya*), is neither a substance nor a non-substance.

In that case, the position is that the substance-form is either known from the generality of "substanceness" (*dravyatva-sāmānya*), or it becomes the object of the conceptual thought and the verbal expression "substance. Regarding the first alternative, there is no fault; for it is the very subject under discussion that a substance may arise from any [cause] whatsoever through whatever nature it takes on, and once so arisen, it does not require any further cause for its existence as such.

Even in the second case, there is certainly no fault; for the entity in its substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*) has indeed arisen even prior [to the cognition], since the production of the cognition and the verbal designation of the substance occurs precisely because of the universal (*sāmānya*). And it does not follow from this that another cause is required for its existence. For it is not the case that the capacity of a cause toward its own object—which is exercised by means of the effect—is unestablished prior [to the effect]; nor is that capacity the cause for the existence of the effect, such that the effect itself would have to depend on another cause.

Furthermore, even if the quality of illumination were to arise later as something distinct, once the lamp has already become possessed of that quality of illumination, why would it require any other cause for its existence such that the illustrative example would be undermined? Therefore, there is no protection for the elaborated theory for one who relies on what lacks authoritative means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, in accordance with experience, the example may be exactly as one intends.

For there is no perception of a distinction between the first and second moments based on the presence or absence of connection with a universal (*sāmānya*). Nor is there an experience of a difference between the substance and the universal; thus, since the subject at hand is established otherwise, there is no insistence on this point. Therefore, manifestation is not produced by its own cause as having the nature of manifestation such that it would depend on another cause for its existence, because that would be redundant. It is also established that it lacks the capacity even for causing darkness.

[124,1] Now, it is observed that white cloth (*śuklam ambaraṃ*) is being colored through contact with a dyeing substance; in that case, why is the objection regarding the uselessness and incapacity of the cloth—whether its nature is red or not red—not likewise directed at the dyeing substance? If this is asked:

Indeed, it is not intended that this conceptual alternative (vikalpa) applies in all cases; rather, the point is that there exists, for the time being, a refutation of the reason by way of the two alternatives of its having that nature or not having that nature. Thus, a negation of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) has been introduced. Consequently, wherever this refutation can be established, it enters into the state of being a refutation. What is the use of considering other possibilities if there is a difference in reasoning? For instance, what is called "perishability" (*vinaśvaratva*) is either momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) or existence for a shorter duration of time.

Imperishability, moreover, consists in persisting for a very long time or eternally. In every respect, if an entity that arose from its own cause with a certain duration of existence were destroyed by something within that interval, then it would not have arisen with that specific duration at all. For it is not tenable for this [entity] to possess two mutually contradictory natures: namely, that it should both endure for a year and perish in a single day.

[124,10] But surely, there is no contradiction in this: that which remains for a year exists without a cause of destruction, whereas that which perishes sooner does so upon the encounter with an intermediate cause of destruction.

For if the certainty [of the nature of a thing] pertains only to its contradiction [with another], and not to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then it would be like this: if smoke were possible upon the falling of a leaf here, it would necessarily be embers; otherwise, however, it would be a cluster of *guñjā* seeds—yet there is no difference in their intrinsic nature. Similarly, if something perishes during the day, let it be produced by a cause limited to that very time; but if it perishes at the end of a year, let it be limited to that duration. However, there can be no conjunction of two mutually contradictory natures in a single place.

For on that day, it is not possible for that which is perishing to simultaneously endure for a year, or for both [endurance and perishing] to exist by means of partial portions. Alternation, however, belongs to knowledge itself as its nature of doubt; it is not a property of the thing-in-itself. Therefore, a thing possesses only a single nature and cannot be associated with another contradictory nature. And this endurance for a day and so forth must be determined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as to whether it is true or not.

However, having accepted this [position], it is considered as follows: because it is difficult to rely on the efficacy of a cause when that [efficacy] is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, even if there were non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatā*), it remains established that for as long as the duration of its persistence lasts, another cause is incapable [of acting] within that interval, and beyond that, it is futile.

Even in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), it is evident that nothing can be done by a cause of destruction at that very moment; yet since it ceases of its own accord in the subsequent moment, there is no purpose in a cause of destruction. As for the eternally existing [entity], this [cause] is simply incapable.

Therefore, when destruction is to be produced, no cause whatsoever escapes the refutations of incapacity and futility. However, when it produces a different entity such as a potsherd, that very hammer is not tainted by those two refutations; for the potsherd acquires its birth immediately after the operation of that [hammer]. Likewise, in the case of a dyed cloth, even though the substance of the dye undergoes that operation, there is neither incapacity nor futility regarding the red color that arises subsequently.

Furthermore, when a pale *caṇḍātaka* garment is being transformed, who is it that transforms it? Even when there is only a single material substance for the garment throughout both states, even then there is simply no transcendence of its defects; for it cannot be maintained that even in the state of being dyed, it remains purely white. Therefore, if at that time too that substance were purely white, there would be no room for the dye; thus the coloring agent would be ineffective. But if it were previously dyed, then with respect to that very same dyeing, [the agent] would be redundant.

Therefore, because a defect arises only with respect to stability, such a transgression concerns the convention (*samaya*) alone and not the entity itself. For when the previous [state] is naturally obstructed, by depending upon its material cause, the removal of that defect is established—just as when a previously white cloth is produced dyed with a coloring substance.

If it is argued that the state of things (*vastu-sthiti*) is not thus, then surely it is precisely this that must be considered: what kind of state of things is it? Why should the opponent be made to drink from the vessel of oath (*kośapāna*) here? Why, then, is it stated so abruptly that "the state of things is thus," given that the reliance on the validity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been refuted? But how can it be called a violation of convention (*samayāparādha*)? For one accepts the concealment and manifestation of two qualities within a substrate (*dharmin*) that remains established.

If this is so, then even though the operation of the dyeing substance would result in the removal of the previous quality and the consequent occurrence of incapacity and futility, its purpose is fulfilled simply by the production of a previously non-existent red quality; thus, how could it be touched by the aforementioned objections? For the consideration of futility and incapacity was undertaken with reference to the form already established, not with reference to something previously non-existent.

For even in the case of something previously non-existent that is to be produced, there is no room for a definitive conclusion that "if it has arisen from its own causes in such a form, then [a cause of destruction] is redundant," or "if it has arisen in this way, then [the cause of destruction] lacks efficacy. Furthermore, every entity that is to be destroyed is already established as existent. And since that entity, whether perishable or otherwise, cannot transcend the nature of one or the other—since there is no third possibility—it is impossible for an imagined cause of destruction to remain either efficacious or purposeful.

Nor is it logical that this would entail the annihilation of the doctrine of causes. For the recourse to a cause occurs when the effect is unestablished, whereas this [present] inquiry takes place when it is established. And if, at that very time, the cause were already produced in such a form, then the debate would proceed precisely by prioritizing the cause. Yet it has been stated that this is not possible when the effect is unestablished. Therefore, how could our aforementioned alternative apply in all cases?
Even if mere conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is possible everywhere regarding what is agreed upon as cause and effect, this does not constitute an admission of fault in our reasoning.

If, however, it were possible to demonstrate that even when the object is established and the two pervading natures are present, [the reason] still requires another reason despite the occurrence of incapacity and futility, then there would be a fault. But this is not the case. Therefore, since the fault lies merely in the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no fault in the [reason] accompanied by its qualification; thus, the presentation of that [mere reason] alone is useless, just as in the case of non-perception (*anupalambha*).

(50b) Now, if the fault lies solely in the fact that mere non-perception lacks the capacity to establish its own probandum, whereas mere conceptual construction—though crowned by the depiction of incapacity and futility—is not devoid of the power to refute the doctrine of causality, then this is an unequal comparison. Oh, what human effort is displayed by one whose ornament is ashes! For, by thus denying cause and effect in every respect, you have effectively established that destruction possesses a cause; clearly, you are mocking yourself by your own hand.

Therefore, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities and so forth—though its power is established through mental imagination (*saṃkalpa*)—must be abandoned with respect to the object by one who maintains the determination of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); otherwise, there would be a destruction of the very root from which the discourse proceeds. However, a conceptual construction based on an already established condition (*siddhopādhi*) devours only the destroyer, not the cause itself. It is indeed appropriate that you, fearing the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), do not pay heed to this; therefore, this effort to destroy cause and effect is fruitless once they have been established in their general form.
Reality is, in some sense, nothing but reflective awareness (vimarśa) conceived as the very beginning of an object.

"Prārambha," "upakrama," and "prastāva" mean commencement; he is "honored" (sambhāvita) or respected by that [commencement]. Having established the general existence of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), this inquiry of ours—whether or not the existence of a cause might possibly occur in some specific instance such as destruction—is appropriate to the present context. However, an effort to uproot the very notion of cause and effect is fruitless, because the treatise proceeds precisely after having established it in a general sense.

Furthermore, this conceptual distinction is not capable of subverting the relationship between cause and effect—that is, the claim that "that which has the nature of coming into being" or "that which has the nature of not coming into being" arises from a cause. For instance, first, regarding that which has the property of non-existence, such as the birth of a barren woman's son, and that which has the nature of coming into being: according to your own view, since non-existence (such as that of space and so forth) never occurs at any time, the operation of a cause toward these two is either rendered ineffective or is simply futile.

Speak of an occasional entity as being either subject to existence or subject to non-existence; however, this [entity] cannot be merely occasional without depending on something else. That object upon which it depends for the restriction of time, place, and nature is itself the cause. Now, if by "having the nature of coming into being" you intend not a property of existence (*sattā-dharma*) but rather a property of origination (*utpatti-dharma*), even then, what we call "origination"—the acquisition of self-nature by that which was non-existent—is nothing other than its occasional occurrence; thus, the answer remains the same. Furthermore, the denial of the occasional nature of destruction has already been stated.

[126,21] Now, regarding the alternative that it exists from a cause, the question is whether that which exists is something other than itself or not; this is the purpose of the conceptual analysis. In that case, the argument comes to rest in the very first alternative. For it exists from a cause, and not previously; thus there is no futility. It exists from a cause and does not exist from anything else—how could there be any lack of capacity? And any insistence on this point is barren; therefore, only a mere direction is stated here, since both positions are established and because the relationship of cause and effect has not been introduced as a subject for dispute.

Since this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which possesses an established qualification (*siddhopādhika*), subverts only the cause of the destruction of an existent (*san*) and not the production of a non-existent (*asat*), because the logic is not the same as previously stated; therefore, causes such as cutting and burning are indeed possible—just like the cause of a red silk garment—and so too is the cause for the specific state called liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, effort directed toward that [liberation] is fruitful. Consequently, there is no cause whatsoever for the destruction of an existent; rather, its manifestation as time, just like its spatial form, occurs solely from its own cause.
Furthermore,
whether it be destruction by the force of an affirmation, like a barrier, or whether that entity is like a pebble— since it remains in that very same state, those [factors] do nothing at all to it.
Therefore, there is no cessation of its activity; having bestowed [its result] in three moments, how could its time—like its place and form—not be determined by its cause, since it is held to be so?

For just as it is considered that a hammer or a heap of pebbles might [cause destruction], it has been stated that there is no arising of destruction because a cause for destruction is untenable. Or, let there be a distinct entity called "destruction" produced by the power of a cause; like a staff, even upon the destruction of pebbles or redness, let it remain presiding over another internal locus. Let things remain in that very state, for nothing whatsoever can act upon that [destruction].

For just as a hammer or a heap of sugar-candy is incapable of affecting that [entity], because otherwise it would follow that the very admission of its destruction would be purposeless; likewise, how could even destruction—which arises from its own causes when the entity is already established—be incapable of doing anything to it? For just as its total destruction is impossible for that which exists by the power of its cause, due to the aforementioned [absurdities of] incapacity and futility, so too is destruction impossible with respect to its corresponding parts.

In that case as well, since there is no way to prevent the introduction of the conceptual alternatives of "perishable" and "non-perishable"—just as before—regarding a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is stated merely in accordance with conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), even though the entity is partless (*niraṃśa*). In reality (*tattvataḥ*), however, even if there were a destruction of parts, it would be a total destruction; and since that is impossible, the production of something unprecedented (*apūrva-nirvartana*) has been established. But in fact, it is what is being prevented.

Therefore, whether it be some unprecedented thing, hidden within another treasury like the previous one, that remains for a kalpa, or yet another distinct entity called "destruction" produced by that [thing], let it be so; however, the consequence that nothing at all happens to the entity itself—namely, the impossibility of avoiding its continued engagement in activities such as producing its own cognition or maintaining its support—is unavoidable.

By this, that which Vācaspati said is addressed: "Now, even when this [non-existence] has arisen with a distinct form, what has happened to the entity? Nothing at all has happened; let this venerable entity remain. Since its non-existence—which depends on its own causes, is characterized by the absence of its own nature, possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and brings about practical activity corresponding to the object—has dispelled all causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), what is lost to us?"

That [objection] is rejected, because when it remains in that very same state, it is impossible to accomplish the negation of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). If you argue that "the refutation of its remaining in that state occurs precisely through the absence of that [causal efficiency]," we reply:

if [the negation] exists, then while it remains in that state, the non-existence (negation) must arise from the power of its own causes; then, having emerged from that, it must perform the refutation of it. Thus, the aforementioned consequence of simultaneity is difficult to avoid. And this being the case, the claim that [negation] is "characterized by the absence of its own nature" is untenable; for if it consists in the absence of that [nature], its occurrence at that time is indeed impossible.

Therefore, if the name "absence" were applied to something common to other objects such as a mallet and so forth, it would not establish the manifestation of that which possesses the intended specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); for only if the initiation of a corresponding linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) were asserted would it be appropriate. Furthermore, by that [name], the integrity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) would remain unimpaired; thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence of mutual contradiction and the production of yet another destruction.

If it is argued that because its nature is self-cessation, there is no room for another destruction, we say no; for the claim that cessation constitutes its very nature has already been refuted by the fact that they could not exist simultaneously. Like any other distinct entity (*padārthāntara*), only a form excluded by negation remains. And by means of that destruction, there would necessarily be the production of a separate entity called "destruction," just as with a mallet. For what difference is there between this [supposed destruction] and a mallet, given that its nature is merely the exclusion of that [entity]? Therefore, this [destruction] would destroy [the object] while itself remaining independent of anything else.

But for the mallet, which does not depend on that [destruction], it would be "destruction" [itself]. However, there would be the acquisition of the designation "destruction. Without that [designation], even for the mallet, there would be no distinction [from the object], since a mere difference in form exists even in the case of gems and the like. [128,19] If perception and non-perception were restricted to a single [object] as the proof of causal capacity, then a distinction might exist; but that is not the case, as has been demonstrated. Therefore, in the position of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), there is no simultaneity; nor, in the position of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), is there the avoidance of the destruction of another.
If something else were to exist elsewhere while that [first thing] still exists, it would necessarily follow that it occurs simultaneously, owing to its conformity with the nature of another moment.
This is the summary.
[129,9] If it does not arise even when the cause persists at one time, what is the purpose [of that persistence], since momentary destruction is possible?
What fruit could there be for that which persists in space, such that its destruction by a fruit would even be observed?
This is an intermediate verse.

However, if the effect called "destruction" is not what brings about the cessation of that [entity], but rather something else such as a staff or the like, then it would follow that existence ceases and non-existence begins; thus there would be a difference in time. But this serves no purpose, nor is it the case that all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has been excluded by its absence. Furthermore, the issues of incapacity and futility have already been raised. Therefore, this verbal formulation is empty.

Furthermore, regarding what was conjectured here—that as it has been stated, an entity arises from its own cause either perishable or imperishable—it is said in reply: we do not recognize [entities] as being either perishable or imperishable; rather, existent things arise from their own causes and perish due to other causes whose presence is dependent upon their own conditions. Moreover, destruction is distinct from that which is being destroyed, both because of the difference in causes and because of the difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). To this, it is further replied:

If you have spoken thus while being ignorant of the nature of that which is perishable and that which is imperishable, then where indeed is the entity called "destruction"? Or from what exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) could it be established as something distinct from the perishing thing, as was just now asserted? Since it is being established through an ignorance of the nature of the perishable and the imperishable, why is it not likewise established in the case of space and other such things?

If it is argued that "destruction is not observed in them," well, is it not the case that destruction is indeed observed elsewhere? This is something that must be admitted even under oath. Therefore, you have been forced to reveal that there exists a nature other than that which is perishable; what need is there for an oath in this matter? Furthermore, since the production of such-and-such a form occurs from its own cause alone with a necessary occurrence, we too do not understand how you can still assert another cause, even while seeing the refutation consisting in the futility and ineffectiveness [of such a cause].

Now, this is the underlying intention: how can the production from something and the destruction from something else—which are perceived directly through the speech of Vaidarbhi’s daughter—be set aside by the conceptual alternatives of "perishable" or "non-perishable"? For that which is established by direct perception cannot be sublated even by a hundred conceptual arguments, since the operation of all means of valid cognition finds its final rest in direct perception alone.

In that case as well, if "destruction" is said to be a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*) established by its own technical convention—that entity which, born from a hammer or similar cause, renders objects such as a jar useless—it has already been demonstrated that it is a great audacity to claim that its birth and its activity fall within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, how could there not be room for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?

Now, if what is intended by "destruction" is that which appears as if distinct when one’s own form is perishing—due to the exclusion of other differences while there is a desire to know that alone—then the statement "they perish from other causes" was made without even considering the following: if that were so, then according to the established tenet that "jars and the like perish due to sticks and such, not of their own accord," destruction would be nothing more than a fancy conceived in sleep, since it would entail the cessation of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Therefore, we do not know what Vācaspati intends by this. If that is so, then how can there be a denial even of that much which falls within the scope of perception? And to what extent does this scope of perception extend? It is established that when an entity is arising from one cause and another entity is ceasing from [another] cause, the cause of its production is distinct from the cause of its destruction.

Nor is there any such thing as "destruction" that is distinct [from the entity itself], from which it would follow that there is scope for the objection regarding its being an object of perception. Shame on this! If destruction were non-different from the entity, then the cause of destruction would simply be the cause of the entity; and if it is the cause of the entity, it cannot be the cause of the entity's production. Therefore, how could there be a cause of destruction other than the cause of production? Furthermore, how could there be a cause for something already produced at a later time? Moreover, this relation of priority and posteriority is indeed established by direct perception.

[130,17] Furthermore, is the entity that is arising and ceasing one or many? First of all, its being one is untenable because of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). If it is argued, "What can we do? It is established as such by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," [we reply: if two properties residing in a single substratum are perceived at once by a single direct perception, then their non-contradiction is valid, as in the case of blue and squareness. However, when two distinct perceptions occurring at different times each grasp a single form, then it is merely recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that conflates them.

And that has been stated to be invalid. Therefore, due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, there is indeed a difference [between moments]. However, because there is no division within a single moment, there is no contradiction, since they exist in one place through a mere distinction of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). For instance, that very same moment of existence is called "arising" when it comes into being from prior non-existence, and it is called "ceasing" when it exists subsequently.

No, for contradiction is established precisely by way of pervasion (*vyāpaka*). Even at the first moment, an entity that is arising is pervaded by its non-existence in subsequent moments; it does not touch its prior state for even a single moment. And when it is ceasing in the final moment, it is pervaded by its non-existence in prior moments; it does not touch its future state for even a single moment. Thus, there is indeed a contradiction.

Furthermore, since this distinction occurs within a single moment, it is merely a difference of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and not a contradiction. Therefore, even if two moments are intended to persist, there can be no identity because of the contradiction between the properties of arising and perishing. And in the case of multiplicity, the preceding entity—ceasing even in the absence of any enumerated causes of destruction such as a hammer—is merely manifesting the capacity of its own cause to grant a duration fixed for a specific time; thus, there is no such thing as a "cause of destruction."

Now, if the causes of destruction are indeed incalculable, then what is improper in this: that some cause, difficult to perceive and remaining unrecognized, might bring about its own basis, namely destruction? If that were so, then since the possibility of destruction would never recede even for a single moment, the formal establishment of a "cause of destruction" would be useless.

For, lest the determination of destruction fail—due to the certainty of prior non-existence regarding a cause whose characteristic is well-established and yet subsequently perishes—it was begun to prove that destruction has a cause. However, if one accepts a cause that is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety, effort becomes futile; therefore, enough with this false conceptualization.

Therefore, since it has been demonstrated that everything is ineffective with respect to an entity that possesses stability, this is the meaning of the position: "Entities arise from their own causes and perish due to other causes. How then could this magical illusion of jewels, mantras, and herbs have been learned by an entity, such that this very thing—remaining in that same state where the causal conditions for its perception are unimpaired—is sometimes perceived and sometimes imperceptible?

[131,17] But surely this fault has been stated and is appropriate only within the doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇika-nīti). As Śaṅkara said: "For there is no loss of the intrinsic nature (svarūpa-hāni) of an entity after its cessation, as there was before, such that it would only then become an object of non-perception and not previously; or, if there were a loss [previously], then the very production of its cessation would occur later.
This is incorrect, for in the position of momentariness, to claim that there is no loss of intrinsic nature even after [the moment of existence], just as there was before, is sheer audacity.
If you argue that the loss of intrinsic nature—even if admitted—is incoherent without the production of a cessation, [we reply:]...

[131,21] Whether or not there arises another distinct entity called "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) and so forth, precisely because this object is restricted to abiding for only a single moment, it is said that "it does not exist in the subsequent moment" since it does not extend into that other moment. It is by means of this very expression that it is stated: "destruction has occurred for that same object in the subsequent moment. No production of a previously non-existent thing is being enjoined; for the application of words follows one's intention, whereas the actual object must be investigated.

In this regard, if the determination of the existence of a thing in another moment is established by its dependence on a single moment, then the doctrine of destruction is fulfilled by that alone; what is the use here of searching for the production of anything? For it is not the logical principle that because Devadatta exists in his house, one must understand the cessation of every other entity everywhere else.
If it is argued that even there, there is a positive affirmation of non-existence in other locations:

Let it be so, for it is precisely for that purpose that particles which serve as restrictive adjuncts (*niyamanibandhana*) are employed. It is simply that some entity, whether existent or in the process of arising, does not enter the path of cognition, because only a negation is perceived. And by that much alone, one who is pursuing Devadatta attains proficiency in both engagement and withdrawal.

For even when the cognition of another object has been established, as long as one does not—by means of a restrictive rule—settle upon the negation of Devadatta's presence elsewhere than in the house by way of implication (*prasajya*), [the argument] is not well-founded. Therefore, a mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*) whose nature is untouched by the form of a positive entity must necessarily be demonstrated.

Nor does the cognition "it is not elsewhere" establish some positive entity-form (*vastu-rūpa*) and then convey that "only this exists, not Devadatta," such that it would be a sequential experience as in the case of "it is only in the house, not elsewhere. Let it be so; nevertheless, the final rest (*viśrāma*) occurs only through the subsequent cognition of mere non-existence. Otherwise, the entire span of a person's life would be consumed merely by the apprehension of another positive entity-form, and the accomplishment of the intended understanding of negation would not occur.

Therefore, just as in this case the mere negation of Devadatta’s presence elsewhere than in the house is conventionally expressed, and that alone is the object of cognition—the absence of Devadatta elsewhere—and such is also the meaning of the conventional usage, so too, existence occurs in one very moment and does not exist in another moment; the absence of that [existence] in another moment is cognized, and thus only a negation is made known regarding the other moment, without any contact with the actual nature of a real entity.

Nor is it for the sake of establishing a negation dependent upon that [destruction]. Thus, even the claim that "there is a loss of its own nature" (*svarūpahāni*) is merely a conventional expression of negation. And since nothing there serves any purpose through arising or existence, how can it be said that "the loss of nature occurs without the arising of cessation"? For this very reason, the notion that "upon its loss, that itself is the arising of its cessation" is a fallacy that must be avoided like a sin, as it leads to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, the claim that "there is a loss of its own nature" later is also merely a subsequent conventional usage of negation; it is not the arising of any real entity. And that conventional usage of negation is inconsistent in its correspondence [to reality], because it is restricted by the necessity of Devadatta's existence elsewhere at some other time.

By this, one may also address what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa said: "Who indeed would believe that an entity exists only in its present state and is non-existent later, yet does not perish later? To that, we ask: who says that it does not perish later? If it perishes later, then you have admitted the arising of destruction later. If you alone are the master over the meanings of words!

This might be so: the establishment of an object is twofold—following valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and following convention (*samaya*). In the first case, the meaning is established as follows: "it perishes later" means that it is designated as "non-existent later. Therefore, how could one who relies on valid cognition be able to assert both "it is non-existent later" and "it does not perish later"? However, in the second case, there is no contradiction.

For one who maintains that "it perishes later"—that is, who accepts the arising of destruction at a later time—[the entity] is non-existent later; it cannot be treated as existent, nor does it perish later, nor does there arise for it a thing called "later destruction. How, then, can this not be a subject of disbelief?

[133,6] Alas! It is a pity that you harbor the desire to sustain your own philosophical system merely through the delusion of words concerning a reality that is never fully established—a mere thing that pleases the minds of common folk. Therefore, an entity arises with a duration fixed to a single moment from its own cause; it does not exist at any other time. But if you think, "Is such a capacity of the cause even within the scope of possibility?"—even then, if there is a capacity for production, it must necessarily produce an effect in some form.

What could form (*rūpa*) not produce, even by abiding for only a single moment? But for whom would it be a matter of faith that a cause could produce its effect without touching the entire form? Therefore, just as this entity arises from its own cause with a restricted location and a specific form such as the shape of a particular object, so too is it restricted in time; what is inconceivable in this regard? Nor should it be said that the restriction of place and so forth effects the very non-existence of the entity by contracting its own nature.

For non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot either contract a produced entity, nor can it produce something already contracted by coming together with the cause. In this regard, if even non-existence—which is devoid of independent human agency and included within the causal totality (*kāraṇasāmagrī*)—could somehow be established as a producer of an entity, what would be lost for us? Whether the causal totality be of such a kind or that kind, it will simply produce its effect.

We ask: if it is capable of producing [an effect] with a restricted place and form, what power could possibly obstruct it from doing so at a restricted time as well, such that the production of another [cause] would later be required for that purpose? Even regarding the first position, we must consider these alternatives: is that entity produced in its universal form (*viśvarūpa*) by its own cause and then restricted by non-existence; or is it produced in no form at all; or is it indeed produced in some form, but not yet in terms of place, form, and time?

[133,22] First of all, the final [position] is untenable. For that very form in which [an entity] is produced is its own aspect (*ākāra*), and that [form] does not exist anywhere without an entity; nor is there ever an entity that has not existed [previously]. Thus, how can there be a rejection of aspects and so forth? Let it not be so; however, for one who is capable of producing [an effect] in some form through its own cause, what is this laziness or envy toward anything else, since the restriction of capacity in one place is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? As for the middle position, on what basis is the status of being a cause established, or is it merely the favor of a king?

Even in the first case, when the mere cessation of existence for a subsequent moment—which is subtler than the simultaneous destruction of the entire form of the three worlds—is the effect to be accounted for, there is no need for further deliberation. Therefore, since the restriction of time is already established by that previously proven entity called "non-existence" which effects the contraction of space and so forth, what reason is there to seek another enduring cause existing at a different time that depends on other causes? This has essentially been stated already.

If it is argued that there is a distinction for each respective object regarding non-existence, this is a mere act of audacity, since its nature is entirely unperceivable. Therefore, why is it not accepted that space and so forth are excluded from everything, just as all phenomena are excluded? Furthermore, experience does not tolerate such a prior state of being devoid of activity.

Therefore, since an entity is produced from its own causes as restricted by space and so forth, it is likewise restricted by time; thus, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the object] being seen again does not apply to the position of momentariness as it does to the position of stability, because the entity itself no longer exists. On the other hand, in the position of stability, since that same state persists, the undesirable consequence is not averted even when another distinct thing arises, because that [newly arisen thing] has no effect upon the former. Furthermore, this is an irrelevant statement, for while the cessation of the entity is the topic at hand, you are avoiding the emergence of a different thing.

[134,12] But surely, while the cessation of an entity is the subject at hand, it is the arising of that cessation which is being taught; what, then, is irrelevant here? Indeed, as long as there is no teaching of its arising, cessation must be understood as having a non-affirming (prasajya) nature. However, once there is an arising, because another thing excluded by it is being enjoined, there is a subsequent drawing-in of the cessation through presumptive implication (arthāpatti); yet that is not the cessation itself, precisely because it would then be a positive entity (vastu), otherwise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

As for what Śaṅkara says: "If it is asked, 'Since there is no difference in being a distinct entity from one thing to another, how can that very thing be the cessation of itself?'"—to this, the answer must be given by the inherent natures (*svabhāva*) of things: those [things] arise from their own causes with the very property of existing in contradiction to coexistence. For it is not a logical rule (*nyāya*) that because two things are distinct entities and lack contradiction in coexistence, the non-existence of one must follow upon the existence of the other; rather, the contradiction between the coexistence of those two is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is not the case that something is a non-cause of other things simply because it is a different entity; otherwise, let this [non-production] also not be a cause of its own effect. This very point has also been refuted by Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, on the grounds that both types of contradiction are applicable there. Furthermore, it has been shown that if the absence of a different entity were to occur due to contradiction, it would be better for the absence to belong to the mallet itself. Moreover, neither perception nor inference is operative regarding such an absence; and since a contradiction established by valid cognition must necessarily be stated, this is quite elegant.

In the case of fire, smoke, and so forth, however, the relationship of cause and effect is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, even when describing the arising of a different entity, there is no appearance of the cessation of that [cause]. Therefore: "If a different entity were produced from fire, the wood would still be seen;
nothing at all would happen to it—it would simply not exist."
Thus, this principle is difficult to circumvent.

As for what Nyāyabhūṣaṇa says—that if nothing happens to it, then even its negation does not happen to it, and therefore, since its un-negated nature remains as it was, it would be perceived just as before—this has already been refuted previously.

For if the meaning is that even a negation does not occur for it—that is, if even the category of reality called "negation" is not produced—then this is true; however, the object's nature is not thereby un-negated, because its state of being negated in a subsequent moment is established by its own causes alone. Alternatively, if a verbal negation is intended, then who can set that aside?

In this view, the claim that it would be perceived just as before is incoherent; for that which does not exist at a certain time cannot be perceived at that time. Otherwise, one residing in Kānyakubja would be seen in Pāṭaliputra, or even Māndhātṛ would be perceived today.

[135,15] But surely, since Māndhātṛ does not exist today, he is not perceived by him. Who indeed has said otherwise? Even though a distinction is apprehended due to the use of the genitive case alone, no entity distinct from that [non-existence] is being predicated. To the extent that the meaning is "Māndhātṛ does not exist today," to that same extent is the meaning "the non-existence of Māndhātṛ today," because his existence is restricted to that specific time. But surely this is also the same: to the extent that the meaning is "the non-existence of Māndhātṛ today," to that same extent is the meaning "Māndhātṛ does not exist today."

As for what is also said—that [the thing] exists as restricted to that specific time—even there, by stating "it exists at that very time," its non-existence at other times is precisely what is being established; so what more has been stated here? This has already been explained. Nevertheless, it is further said: regarding the two designations of difference and non-difference, the object is in reality one and the same. If, however, the establishment of distinct entities were to rely on the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then even for the sentence "the first does not exist," the meaning would be simply this: "the non-existence of the first exists."

Now, if the sublation of a distinct entity is itself dependent upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then let it be granted for now that its absence exists. Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence "the absence has arisen today" should be understood simply as "it does not exist today. And when searching for a means of valid cognition, it has been stated that the non-perception of that which was accepted as being perceptible is indeed the sublater; thus, it is said that there is neither any prover nor any sublater whatsoever.

It has been established that even if there is no present perception, [the non-existence of] something existing at that time is proven merely by its absence at another time, provided that this absence does not touch upon the nature of some other entity. Nor can one hope for its status as a real thing based on the mere mention of the "instrumental power" (*karaṇa-śakti*) in the phrase "merely by its absence," because the linguistic usage of action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-vyavahāra*) is dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). For example:
"This son of a barren woman goes from a city of the Gandharvas to offer a handful of water to his father after bathing in the waters of a mirage."
[Objection: "If it is argued that this [dream object] is entirely false because it lacks substantiality despite possessing all the causal capacities [of a waking object], [Response:
This is not so, because it was cited as an example merely by virtue of its dependence upon the speaker's intention."

If it is asked, "Who could speak such a thing as being correct? [the answer is: let no one speak it, for there is no contradiction to the point at hand (*prakṛta*) being established. Nor is it impossible for even a correct person to utter this; for if someone who has heard that [statement] asks, "In every respect, why would a correct person not speak that?", the mere recitation of that [statement] does not cause any loss of correctness. Furthermore, must even the fact that the hairs of a tortoise are false be stated by something incorrect? Nor is this entirely false.

Likewise, in the case of "Māndhātā does not exist" or "one does not dwell here today as Māndhātā," the clearly expressed capacity of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) does not revive its status as a real entity (*vastutā*).

If it is argued that there is merely a negation of it, then for that very reason, the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is independent and free from doubt. Therefore, the hope of establishing the reality of a thing through the designation of causal capacities (*kāraka-śakti*) resembles the desire to cross water by means of a mass of foam.

Thus, since this [designation] is not dependent upon the name but rather follows the reality of the object itself, the specific designation "now its non-existence has arisen" should be established in the sense of a mere *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation)—expressing "this does not exist now"—as if one were apprehending the arising of a distinct entity; it should not be taken in the opposite sense, because this distinction lacks any basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, to state that there is an absence at another time by means of a restriction to that specific time is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For it is only the arising of another entity at another time that is being negated, and not merely the conventional usage of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). Thus, even when demonstrating this refutation, no other ultimately real category (*paramārthasat*) is established.
Therefore, having set aside the verse from the *Vārttika*, the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* has composed this verse:
"If non-existence does not exist later, what is desired for that existence?"
Nor can this [negation] be accepted as a negation of non-existence. What then is it intended to be?

Thus, that is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because we merely accept the subsequent application of the conventional usage of "non-existence" based on the certainty of sublation (*bādhā-niścaya*), since it is precisely the arising of a real entity that is being negated. But what kind of verbal artifice is this—to claim that only the conventional usage of non-existence is accepted later, yet there is no actual non-existence? For if this were so, it would entail the consequence of the conventional usage of non-existence being deceptive; and if non-existence is false, then the very thing to be negated would be a real existence. And what other kind of negation could there be than the affirmation [of the opposite]? (PV IV 221cd)

This is because this principle is asserted by [the author] himself. Furthermore, since that non-existence occurs only subsequently, its being occasional clearly implies that it possesses a cause and is a real entity (*vastu*). And thus he says: "The very non-existence of a thing that occurs after [its existence] is called destruction (*nāśa*). How is it that no destruction other than the thing itself is perceived? If it is said that destruction belongs to the thing, yet it is not stated that "it comes into being" (*bhavati*), what fault is there in expressing it as "it comes into being"?

If it is argued that [the non-existent] must indeed become an existent, then does the nature of the object undergo a transformation simply through its being denoted? And if such a transformation were to occur, then one should say that it "is born. If it is asked how there can be the birth of a non-existent, the answer is: because it is occasional (*kādācitkatvāt*). For if it were not occasional, then the non-existent would have to exist even in the present state.

To this it is replied: First of all, for us, the term "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) refers to both ascertainment (*niścaya*) and speech (*vacas*). And speech has precisely the same object as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, the object of conceptual construction is twofold, distinguished by the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). Among these, that which appears to the conceptual cognition as it arises is called the apprehended. However, that upon which activity and cessation depend is the determined, such as the arising of a different entity (*arthāntarotpatti*) in the case of the very conceptualization: "the non-existence of an entity has subsequently arisen."

That which appears directly is the apprehended object (*grāhya*); it is that upon which one who seeks the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of its presence relies for their withdrawal [from other things]. Furthermore, it is the object determined (*adhyavaseya*) as having a nature distinct from that [apprehended object] at that particular time and place. This is because, when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of that [determined object] arises, one who is averse to the mental engagement with the production of the entity called "destruction" and who seeks the causal efficiency of the absence of the object to be negated, does not act toward the entity existing at that place and time, but rather withdraws from it. Therefore, it is said to be determined as having the nature of that place, time, and entity.

In that regard, what is called "mere conventional usage" is said with reference to another object appearing [in consciousness], because even with a thousand eyes and through diligent investigation, no other entity is perceived apart from it. Therefore, even when there is a discrepancy regarding that [appearance], as long as a conceptual construction (vikalpa) completes its function through engagement or withdrawal, there is neither discrepancy nor correspondence with respect to the determined object (*adhyavaseya*). And the consideration of whether there is correspondence or otherwise applies to the determined object, not to the appearing object (*pratibhāsī*).

Therefore, even though this is a general principle, in the present case we shall establish consistency solely through correspondence with the object to be known (*avaseya*). As for the appearance [of the object], it is only when its lack of correspondence is proven that the probandum is established—if the deities are pleased, what is the use of your indignation in this matter? (55a)

Therefore, even though the effect-form appearing as a conceptual construction of non-existence is false, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "non-existence" is not deceptive, because the reality of the object as it is determined (*adhyavasita*) exists. And although that constructed form is false, there is no consequence of the existence of a real entity upon the negation of a thing, because the mere absence (*pracyuti*)—which is the opposite of existence and whose sole nature is to be conventionally designated—is not itself false. Nor is that [mere absence] negated in its nature as mere absence; rather, it is negated in its imagined nature as a real entity.

[138,9] But is it not the case that "the thing does not exist" is itself a negation? And so, regarding the question "does that passing away exist or not?"—if it exists, how can it not be a thing? If it does not exist, how can there be no negation? It is replied: the negation is merely the attribution of "thing-ness" to the mere absence of a thing; it is not a negation of "thing-ness" itself. That is the negation of it.

Therefore, the statement "there is a falling away" means that there is no falling away from the very nature of falling away; this is the intended sense. However, there is no positive injunction (vidhi) regarding even a conceptualized entity—such as its being composed of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*)—merely by virtue of its being formulated. Just as it is correct to say "the jar does not exist as permanent or as momentary" only insofar as one does not expect a form distinct from the excluded forms of the jar, so too it is correct to say "there is no falling away" only insofar as one does not expect it to exist as a real entity (*vastu*).

However, there is indeed a "falling away" (pracyuti) that is free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*); thus, it does not entail a fault in the non-falling away from its own nature (*svarūpa*). As long as the absence of the object to be negated does not exist, so long does falling away persist; for these two are essentially of the nature of mutual absence (*parasparābhāva*). Precisely for this reason: "If there is no cessation [of the reason] in that [subject], why is the presence of the reason not desired? [PV 1.25]
"Nor is this a negation; what is it that is being excluded by [the term] 'cessation'?

(PV IV 224 = PVin III 15). This principle is difficult to bypass. Thus, having raised the doubt regarding the subsequent absence—by means of the phrase "if there is no [existence] later"—one asks: "What is intended by that [phrase] as the existence of that [absence]?"

If it is stated thus, then there is no fault. For when the opposite of "that which exists for someone at a certain time"—namely, "it does not exist," which is a mere absence, a non-entity in form, and a conceptual inversion—is negated, then that [existence] necessarily attains a presence within the internal dimension in the form of "it certainly exists."

But when, subsequently, without rejecting mere absence, there occurs the negation of a conceptualized entity-form based on the power of the transformation of conceptualization— expressed as "it becomes" or "it arises"— then how could there be the consequence of existence arising from the rejection of mere absence,
such that existence would be desired for it?

Thus it is said: for a jar does not undergo a fall from its own nature (*svarūpa*) when its imagined form is negated, because that would entail the absurdity of its being devoid of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as holding water. Nor does the mention of a "fall" from its nature fulfill the expectation of its being a real entity (*vastu*), just as in the case of [the statement] "the son of a barren woman has the nature of non-existence," since even if one were to posit the persistence of a nature, that [fall] remains impossible; or else, it is like [the argument] "the reason is unestablished" (*asiddha-hetu*).

Therefore, the claim that "destruction occurs later, arising from such things as a hammer" is merely a conventional expression of the ignorant that is being denied. We say, however, that what is expressed by that [convention]—the nature of the thing characterized by its occasional occurrence and so forth—does not exist.

Nor can it be maintained that everything as far as it is presented by conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is the reality (*vastu-tattva*) of things, for that would entail the absurdity of rendering the composition of treatises (*śāstra*) purposeless. Furthermore, if one were to demonstrate conventional usage as being false, it would not be possible to easily distinguish between what is to be adopted and what is to be rejected based on the strength or weakness of its foundation (*mūla*). And it has been shown that the foundation is the object of determinate cognition (*adhyavaseya*). Therefore, in the investigation of reality (*tattva-cintā*), it is said that "existence does not exist," and likewise, "non-existence also does not exist" (PV I 278cd).
Either non-existence occurs after existence, or existence itself is imperishable.

And thus, it is stated that an entity does not exist subsequently because it is restricted to its own time alone; therefore, there is no production of a different object. Consequently, under the theory of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), perception and so forth are impossible due to the persistence of the same state; rather, it is established that they occur only under the theory of stability (*sthirapakṣa*).

First of all, an object does not cease by itself, because a cause for destruction is not purposelessly obtained; nor is it destroyed by a blow from a staff, since that [staff] is described as being occupied with its own activity;
nor is it destroyed by annihilation, because that would entail the consequence of a separate destruction, like a [striking] bar.
Why does it not throb? What is this that has occurred at the time of the sparrow?
This is an intermediate verse. But if there is momentariness,
then just as an entity arises from its own cause with a form distinct from other forms,
why does an entity that exists in a distinct and different moment not likewise arise from its own cause?
Thus it has been said.
Regarding the sublation [of existence] by non-existence as a distinct entity, another non-existence must also be observed there.
In this regard, he says: "Some maintain that there is no such state, just as with heat and light. To this, it is replied:
The view that the lamp serves as an illustration is not acceptable, because it lacks the demonstration of its own intrinsic nature.

For a lamp, being observed to possess the power to illuminate other things, how could it be denied? On the other hand, for non-existence (*abhāva*), even the cognition of its own nature is difficult to find, even in a dream. In that case, who would be so audacious as to act like a painter in the sky, saying: "This is its distinction when there is existence; this is not there when it is non-existent; and while it is differentiated by this form itself, it does not depend on anything else"? How, then, can it be comparable to a lamp? Furthermore:
"If, like a lamp, this non-existence also differentiates an entity and is itself differentiated," [then it follows that it is an entity].
That very entity, having arisen from its own cause, differentiates both the entity itself and that which is to be differentiated.

For a face does not become crooked by being described in such a manner; this is because the absence of another person's agency is not perceived. Nor is the probandum established by a mere example; for what reason could there be that, when employed to prove its existence, is not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*)?

Furthermore, as for what was said: "But we do see that an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is not accepted in a case where some perceived fact would be contradicted by that infinite regress; and here no perceived fact is contradicted. To the extent that there is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of a jar from things such as cloth, by that very [exclusion] the jar is established as excluded from [other things] such as cloth. In that regard, there is no disruption whatsoever by an infinite regress of further exclusions."

If it is argued that the object is not established as excluded because its capacity is exhausted by the grasping of a succession of exclusions and further exclusions, we say: no, for it is admitted that even those [objects] inverted by qualifiers are grasped. To this also it is replied:
let that admission stand; however, in this case, the entity is reached through a succession [of cognitions] via that succession of its grasping.
If it is claimed that the cognition of a qualifier-of-a-qualifier is not desired, then the logic is the same, and thus there is no distinction between the two cases.

It is said that even an unperceived eye causes the perception of form; thus, for one who thinks that a qualifier, though itself unperceived, causes its own qualifier to be perceived, it would follow that even the first qualifier would cause the qualified object to be perceived while remaining unperceived itself—rendering the perception of that [first qualifier] unnecessary. Moreover, this is not the actual sequence of qualifiers.

Therefore, just as at the very first moment the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is incapable of being characterized without depending on the apprehension of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), so it is with the second and subsequent moments as well; how then can this division be considered tenable? For just as there is a fear of apprehending a confused [object] without the apprehension of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of non-existence, so too, if that adjunct itself is not apprehended as distinct, how can it be called a differentiator of another, being like a supportless substance? Thus, if there is mutual dependence, the disappearance of the excluded object (*vyāvṛttavastu*)—due to its failure to be apprehended even after many eons—is unavoidable.

If, moreover, non-existence (*abhāva*) were the qualifier, then since distinct existence is possible from its own causes alone, and since the perception and conceptualization of distinction are established through presumptive proof (*arthāpatti*), what is the use of non-existence? For a distinct thing is not to be experienced as non-distinct by a non-erroneous cognition, nor is a distinct thing experienced as being contradictory to the conceptualization of distinction. If, however, there is neither the distinct nor the non-distinct without non-existence, then where would the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) apply? Thus, non-existence itself becomes accepted as a causal factor.
Nevertheless, since everything is uncontradicted when things arise as distinct solely from their own causes, the theory of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not a subject of consensus.
And as for what he said: "Alternatively, even the infinity of exclusions and the excluded is grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*),"—regarding that too, he says:
"That which this shameless one asserts to appear within the heart during non-conceptual [cognition] does not even abandon the covering of a mouse."
Where even a single thing is unperceivable and manifests under the name of non-existence as all-pervasive, there [arises] the succession.
If false speech has begun, what is the point of concealment here? This is entirely appropriate for Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, who writes as follows:

"Is the cognition [of an object] by its own nature excluded [from others] or non-excluded? If it is excluded, then exclusion is purposeless. If it is not excluded, there follows the undesirable consequence of a confusion of entities. What is the meaning of 'by its own nature'? Does it mean without exclusion, or by a nature distinct from exclusion? It is not tenable to say 'without exclusion,' because exclusion is an eternal property [of the entity]."

For a substrate (dharmin) is designated even in the absence of a property (dharma) that only occasionally exists; for example, a man is "without earrings" when he lacks earrings, or as something is "undesirable" prior to its destruction. However, a thing is never devoid of exclusion from other things, just as there is no cow devoid of cowness, nor fire devoid of heat.

Now, if it is intended that [an entity] is "excluded" by way of a form that is distinct from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then that is precisely what we accept, because difference (*bheda*) is admitted. Nor is exclusion thus rendered purposeless. If a person is wealthy by virtue of wealth that is distinct [from him], does wealth thereby become useless? Therefore, even mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is indeed a separate entity (*arthāntara*) from existence (*bhāva*).

That too has been refuted. For this is not an objection based on the acceptance of a real entity (*vastusat*) distinct from the exclusion; rather, the meaning of the objection is that since it is useless and ineffective with respect to the cognition of the excluded, the exclusion is not established by means of that [real entity]. Among those, futility was stated regarding the first position, while inefficacy is intended regarding the second.

[142,19] Now, this is the meaning: if an entity possesses an excluded nature (*vyāvṛtta-svabhāva*) and arises from its own cause, then it must be cognized as being indeed excluded by that cognition which arises in dependence upon it. For there is no such obsession on the part of the object—or rather, nothing determined by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—to the effect that "even when all other conditions are present, I must not produce my own cognition in the absence of that [exclusion]."

Nor can there be a grasping of that cognition produced by it as being devoid of that [exclusion] without [the exclusion itself]; thus, this exclusion is purposeless, and since a cognition of exclusion is possible through other means, it should not be postulated.

[143,1] Now, if an entity has not arisen as excluded from its own cause, and yet has arisen, then how could the exclusion of that which has arisen with a mixed nature—which is itself non-existent—produce a cognition of exclusion? Thus, it is incapable. And while proceeding with this objection, having established exclusion as already proven, what is the use of [discussing] whether exclusion is an eternal property and so forth? For by this, the point regarding the avoidance of the futility mentioned in the first position is not addressed.

For instance, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is postulated by virtue of the power of the cognition of exclusion; yet, since that cognition of exclusion is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), what is the point of this postulation? To this objection, the respondent replies: "Exclusion is an eternal property (*nityo dharmaḥ*); therefore, without it, [the cognition] is not possible. But how is this reply relevant?

For as long as one maintains that the cognition of exclusion is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*) except through exclusion itself, there is no occasion for such an argument. What is the use here of discarding that and merely stating a formal tenet (*siddhāntamātra*)?

Nor is it appropriate to cite as an example that "prior to destruction, it has not been destroyed," because a difference in destruction itself is not established. Furthermore, regarding the claim that "an entity is not devoid of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), if there is no real difference (*tāttvikabheda*) from exclusion, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is because a difference is not established; for even in the case of the example, it is impossible to demonstrate through the difference between a cow and fire that "cowness" and "hotness"—which consist of the exclusion of what is other—possess such a difference.

Furthermore, regarding the second alternative within this very position—namely, whether [exclusion] is by means of a distinct operation (*vyatiriktena vyāpāreṇa*) as expressed by the phrase "or what is exclusion?"—that is already refuted simply by its non-acceptance, because what is intended to be expressed is the meaning: "it is cognized as excluded by its own nature," that is, "it is cognized as having a form excluded from everything. Nor has the avoidance of the first [point’s] futility been addressed; thus it was said.

Nor is the establishment of distinct exclusions achieved by the example of "wealth," because there is no restricting cause; for if it were independent of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), then other qualifiers such as "staff-in-hand" or "white-complexioned" would also have to be treated as related [to the person]. Therefore, there is no such thing as "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*), since things arise from their own causes as mutually excluded. This applies equally to what is excluded by another time. Thus, nothing at all is produced by a cause of destruction. As it is said: "If something were to exist as an effect, then another [cause] might depend upon it. (PV I 279ab)
Thus the principle is established. What is the point of this grinding of flour?
"Destruction has arisen today"—this does not mean that existence (bhāva) is the referent of another word; rather, existence is restricted to its own time and does not exist at any other time.

For one who holds that even the statement "it does not exist at another time" refers only to the arising of something else, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) regarding the cessation of the object of negation.

Furthermore, as for the distinction he established—by means of the objects of the linguistic conventions of "non-existence" and "existence"—in order to prove the difference between the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) and the *paryudāsa* (relative negation), that was already refuted within the context of your own statement: "the otherness of existence is merely a verbal convention. For it is not right to subvert what is established by logic through mere convention. To explain:
those who perceive something being produced and acting purposefully, and who employ the linguistic convention of "existence" for it, they alone are the wise (*santaḥ*).
This [distinction] does not follow from convention; if it were subject to destruction [by convention], this would result in the instability of existence, and it would not be a *paryudāsa*.

For when someone, by the power of their own whim, might assert the existence or non-existence of something among various modes—such as being material or immaterial, resistant or non-resistant, invisible or visible, distant or near, gross or subtle—and might even assert the existence or non-existence of things like the Vindhya mountains or the son of a barren woman, then there would result an instability regarding the nature of entities. Yet such a consequence does not occur, because the use of distinct designations is possible in accordance with one's own conventional system (*svasamaya*).

[57b] What, then, is this entity that is being excluded (*paryudasta*) which should now be designated? Therefore, even if the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) does not apply due to conventional usage, one must state that another entity of the same kind is what is being excluded—whether it be something whose occurrence depends on causes or something that is perceptible.

How, then, can there be an exclusion of the *paryudāsa* (relative negation) by means of the mere linguistic convention of the word "non-existence"? If, on the other hand, it is argued that even the possibility of perception regarding that which is intended as non-existent depends solely upon convention (*samayamātra*), then this is indeed a real *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) and not a *paryudāsa*; thus, there is no fault. However, this person who fancies himself a knower of logic, having transgressed that very mode established by reason, must accept that the capacities for possibility, perception, and causal efficiency belong to non-existence as its actual reality.
And as for the distinction between exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and its opposite, absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), what further calamity is there than this endless [debate]?
