Furthermore, regarding what he said: "For origination is not the defining characteristic of an entity such that cessation, being an occurrence, would be an entity; for even things like space, which lack origination, exist. To that also [we reply]: According to Pāṇini, the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers are not "rivers" when they are dry land.
Even when it does not exist, it is not an entity for him; even when it exists, it is not an entity for him.
A person who has attained independence does whatever he desires;
this principle applies equally in both cases, according to the opinion of those who know the law.
Even when the notion of a "river" is negated, there is no sublation of the act of plunging;
even when the notion of "existence" is negated, the exclusion (paryudāsa) is not sublated.
For everything that has the capacity for the object of apprehension and whose arising depends upon causes is excluded [from being ultimately real], since it exists only in relation to another entity.
In the absence of the notion of non-existence, the establishment of relative negation (paryudāsa) would not be possible anywhere, because the notion [of existence] is easily found everywhere.

Furthermore, regarding this claim that the arising of destruction is held to be characterized by the cessation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), and not characterized by the connection with existence of what was previously non-existent, nor characterized by inherence in a cause— even there,
it is simply the cessation of the nature itself that is called "arising" in all cases. By introducing the concept of inherence (*samavāya*), however, the deluded have lost sight of even that.

Since *samavāya* (inherence) itself does not exist, where could there be a connection with *sattā* (existence) and so forth? Or, let it be granted that even such a thing exists; nevertheless, "origination" (*utpatti*) is simply the acquisition of a previously non-existent nature. As for other factors such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), their presence or absence are neither establishing nor subverting proofs [for origination]. Furthermore, even in the case of an effect that is a non-entity (*abhāva*), there can be no connection with *sattā* for that which was previously non-existent—what is the meaning of this? Does it mean that what was previously non-existent simply does not come into being? Or does it mean that it lacks existence even afterwards? In either case, how can it have the status of an "effect," like a sky-flower? Let there be the existence of what was previously non-existent, but not a connection with *sattā* afterwards.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that *sattva* (existence) and *sattā* (being) are not different in meaning, and that *yoga* is a relation? In that case, what is this peculiar logic that there is a connection with *sattva* but no connection with *sattā*? Therefore, *sattā* is called the 'Great Universal' (*mahāsāmānya*), and even in its absence, a thing is later said to 'exist' by virtue of its mere existence as its own nature (*svarūpasattvamātra*)? If this is argued:

In that case, if that existence by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*) were real, then by that alone would there be "being an effect"; what further function would need to be performed for any other thing to be an effect? Or, if it is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), then how could even destruction possess the status of being an effect? For indeed, even if the subsequent existence of the son of a barren woman is figuratively attributed, his being an effect is certainly not real.

As for the claim that "cessation (*nivṛtti*) also has a beginning," even then there is nothing additional [to our position]. We do not accept that this cessation possesses a beginning by way of being a non-entity (*abhāva*), because it has been demonstrated that it shares the same nature as other effects. This mere assertion is fitting only for kings. The argument that "it is because its form is not perceived at the time when the entity is perceived" also gains favor only later, upon the perception of the form [of the absence].
Yet that [form] does not exist; rather, it has been shown that it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) regarding the impossibility of a jar, following conventional usage (*saṅketa*).
When a person seeking the functional efficacy of a jar does not perceive it, they do not act; thus, there exists [a cognition] other than the perception of the counter-correlate.
Therefore, enough of examining this mere heap of rubble consisting of formal analysis, for its faults can be inferred by oneself.

As for what was said—that there is no consequence of [non-existence] being an entity merely because it is a cause of causal efficiency, since the definition of an entity as stated by you is not accepted—there too it has been stated that this does not transcend the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*). Consequently, non-existence is not something other than existence.

Furthermore, as for what you said—that you have also stated a distinction in the characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) of existence and non-existence—how then can there be identity? It is precisely because of the difference in the characteristics of all things that their distinction is established; if, on account of that [identity], no distinction were established, then the distinction of anything from anything else would not be proven, which would lead to the consequence of non-duality (*advaitaprasaṅga*).

That too is the result of a lack of careful consideration. For when one says "destruction destroys," the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the frequent application [of Pāṇini’s rule], or it is designated by that term through the conceptualization of it as having that property (*taddharmatā*). We maintain that this destruction is the very nature of the entity;
and depending on that very [nature], because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent (PV I 269ab).

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, this very point was raised by him [the opponent]: "Destruction is simply an entity characterized by the property of momentary duration. To this we reply that we maintain its non-difference [from the entity]. The term *nāśa* (destruction) must be explained in two ways according to its etymological derivation (*prasajya-ātmā*): first, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), because it lacks the nature of a functional entity (*vastutva*), this destruction is not an entity at all, being devoid of both identity and difference; thus, it is merely a locus for the negation of existence, like the horn of a donkey.

However, just as in conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) it appears to be occasional when conceptualized according to the difference in time, so too, because its nature is the absence of all designations (*sarvopākhyāviraha*), it appears as if distinct from an entity; thus, there is no contradiction in describing a difference in characteristics even though it is not a real thing. This being the case, since a difference between existence and non-existence is accepted through conventional difference in characteristics, and since—given the absence of identity of characteristics in terms of ultimate reality (*tattva*)—the oneness of an entity with that [non-existence] is denied, how can the charge of the consequence of monism (*advaitaprasaṅga*) be leveled?

As for the claim that "destruction" (*nāśa*) means perishing, how could that which has a perishable nature avoid being of the same essence as the entity itself? Furthermore, that [destruction] must have a cause, and its cause is precisely the cause of the entity; there can be no other cause for it, because [that other cause] would itself have the nature of an entity. Thus:
"For this conceptual distinction regarding an entity would exist only through the affirmation [of existence], since it conforms to a real thing. (PV I 278ab)

To this he says: that too is untenable because it contradicts your own words. For you have asserted the identity (*tādātmya*) of existence and non-existence; yet that is contradicted if one does not accept their essential nature (*tattva*). Even if one accepts their essential nature, the distinction between their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is contradicted. For how can that which is said to be distinct by way of a difference in defining characteristics be described as being either identical or non-identical in its essential nature?

Nourished by that pleasure, because of its playful nature, it causes whatever has been done to be done again and again. Indeed, we do not assert that there is identity between an entity and a non-entity whose nature is the cessation of that entity. As for the non-entity which "does not exist" in relation to a subsequent moment, what contradiction to identity could there be with it? This has already been resolved through the investigation of destruction (*nāśa*). In this same way, it should be understood that other [objections] as well have been set aside without further elaboration.

As for what he also said: "But surely, since non-existence has the characteristic of being the separation from all phenomena, its arising is not logical; for that [arising] belongs only to the nature of existence"—this is not so, because even in the absence of the nature of existence such as knowability and so forth, [non-existence] still exists—and so on; that too is without substance.

For it is not the case that merely by virtue of possessing a common property there is room for properties that are mutually exclusive; otherwise, it would follow that even fire possesses coldness, or that non-existence itself exists everywhere, since even properties such as "knowability" would be negated. Furthermore, it has already been established that origination, being of the nature of coming into being after having not existed, is indeed a property of an existent entity.

As for the statement that "it does not exist by itself," what is its meaning? Does it mean that this non-existence is itself self-existent? Or does it mean that it brings about its own non-existence? Or that it does not bring about existence? Or that it does nothing at all? Or that it is itself nothing? Having raised these alternatives, you have begun your refutation; yet even that is little more than a piteous cry born from the cutting of one's vital organs.

For in that case, the meaning is indeed made manifest: "by itself" means that it was produced by its own cause with a duration fixed for a single moment without depending on any other cause; therefore, nothing [further] exists in the subsequent moment. Consequently, how could this thing, which does not possess that nature [of momentary existence], arise later?

For that thing, by virtue of its own cause, has arisen with a nature that is excluded from having a different nature. How could it later possess that other nature? For a stone excluded from having the nature of lightness can never become light. That [thing] indeed floats; for just as it has arisen excluded from staying in another place, so too, being excluded from staying in another moment, how could there be room for it to stay in another moment? This has already been explained.

Now, it is not the case that the very same entity is designated by the term "non-existent," because [the latter] is the object of a positive injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, you do not accept that there is anything else denoted by the word "absence" (*abhāva*) that has entered the range of cognition; therefore, a negation that lacks an object would be non-veridical, and thus the entity would remain unrefuted.

This is not so; since even "disappearance" (*pracyuti*) is what is being established, how could there be a lack of an object? Nor is there any contradiction, for a contradiction would occur only if the negation were applied while the entity still exists. But that is not the case, because disappearance has already been established. Furthermore, it has already been stated that it is not impossible for a non-entity to be an object of conceptual construction. As for the objection: "Even if the negation has another thing as its object, how can it negate the entity? [the answer follows].

It was asked how that which expresses the absence of something could not be a negation; that too has already been effectively answered. For that absence is not of a non-implicative (prasajya) nature, since another entity is admitted [by you]; and if it were merely an exclusion (paryudāsa), the cessation of one thing does not necessarily entail the manifestation of the existence of another thing. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no contradiction [between them]. Even if a contradiction did exist, why resort to the mediation of a contradictory term? Let the absence itself be established directly.

It might be argued: "When the non-existence of something is established by means of speech, there remains room for doubt; however, certainty arises through the door of the contradictory. This is incorrect. For even the presentation of the contradictory occurs solely by means of speech. Just as, regarding fire which is to be understood by mere speech, it is correct to say "there is no cold here," but not "there is no cold here because of fire"—so too is this case.
Now, another point is considered:

[the opponent argues that] the apprehension of one thing is not capable of effecting a negation; if it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), how could the apprehension of another thing be a negator of the other?
Or how does the form of your conceptual construction, "that jar is destroyed," effect the negation of the jar?
To this, the reply is:
for one who is intent on the conceptual construction that "this does not exist here," there is no negation-rule distinct from that [construction], nor is it for any other cognition.
Even for the cognition that conceptualizes non-existence, its status as a negator is not set aside when there is no lack of certainty regarding its being an auxiliary factor.
It has been stated that the destruction of an existent thing is not tenable;
for there is no power to produce what is non-existent, since a thing is already existent.

Therefore, the experience of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) may produce a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the absence of other counter-correlates; thus, there is no inconsistency here. Nor does the operation of negation by that experience consist of anything other than that [construction]. Even for a conceptual construction such as "the jar is destroyed," which serves as the cause for moving about without hesitation or for the state of withdrawing from activity due to the presence of its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it does not have the capacity to negate anything else.
In the same way, it should be understood that even the function of a verbal statement as a means of negation occurs solely through the production of such a conceptual construction.

By this, the removal of such objections as "In that case, non-apprehension is simply the cognition that 'it does not exist'; how then could even that, being a real entity, be the object for the negation of another entity? is established.

For us, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is not the cognition "it does not exist"; rather, it is simply the non-conceptual apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). The cognition "it does not exist," however, is merely a mental linguistic convention (*mano-vyavahāra-rūpa*), which is itself the result [of that apprehension]. Furthermore, such insistence is useless for investigating the nature of reality (*vastu-cintā*). As for the attempt to define the object of the cognition "it does not exist," that too is already accounted for by defining it as "the unreal" (*asad*).

As for the objection raised regarding the possibility that the ground and so forth, as distinct from the jar, might be the object [of the cognition], it was stated: "No, because the ground and so forth are a different entity; and when one entity is established or cognized, another entity such as the jar—which was previously non-existent—is not thereby established or cognized.
For in this way, the refutation that was stated against the view that "destruction is indeed a different entity" would be avoided by that very [argument].

That too is incoherent: since its object is merely the bare ground (*kevala-bhūtala*), how is it that there is no cognition of the non-existence of a jar or other objects? For that very state of isolation (*kaivalyāvasthā*) of the location relative to the jar and so forth is itself the absence of the jar. Likewise, when a mere location is communicated even by speech and the like, why should it not be a communication of the absence of the jar and so forth under consideration?

Thus, if there were a perception of mere destruction—just as one perceives a potsherd and so forth—then let it be that the cognition of the negation of the jar occurs; however, by what means was the negation of the jar itself produced? For the pre-existing absence of the jar must be apprehended through that [perception of the locus]; indeed, the absence of the jar is not produced by the location, but rather the already existing absence of the jar is to be ascertained through it. For if the jar were also non-existent, there would be no cognition restricted to the single form of the location alone.

[150,1] Thus, just as if a jar were to exist even now, there would be no cognition restricted to the single form of the potsherd, so too there would be no cognition restricted to the single form of destruction; let the ascertainment of the jar's absence follow by force of this. However, if the jar's absence had existed previously, that is not the case. Even if it did exist, what would be the use of destruction? For its meaning is already conveyed by the counter-positive, the potsherd itself.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no cognition of destruction either; therefore, since the refutation of the existence of a real entity (*sat*) upon its destruction was stated in terms of its being either existent or non-existent in nature, how could there be a determination of whether it is existent or non-existent in nature? Thus, the rebuttal is not equivalent. As for what he said—that "if there is no cognition of the distinction (*viveka*), there can be no apprehension of that which is distinguished," and that "this distinction is not merely the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the ground and so forth, because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)," that is outside the bounds of logic. Even the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists only in a form mounted upon conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*). And that—

It perceives differentiated existence as non-differentiated; clearly, it conquers the world—which is partless yet appears with parts—through its own portions, like the vast display of a *kadamba* tree in bloom.
Moreover, it is capable of burning away the delusion regarding objects through its mere own form.
Volition is like a supreme magician, having shaken off the stability of all beings.

For just as [a cognition] arises by unifying a divided entity, so too is there the sense that it perceives an undivided entity as divided—such as "the body of a stone statue," "hands and feet in the body," or "Devadatta with long ears. Therefore, since the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is dependent upon conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), how can this conventional usage—which, even regarding an undivided entity, depends on the intention to express division—extend itself into the nature of a fixed distinction?

If it is argued that this is merely a figurative designation (nirdeśa), such as "this is the head of Rāhu" despite his movement being faltering—if this were true, then it would be solely because the distinct [entity] is not directly perceived. Furthermore, this mode of expression exists even with reference to another category of entity called the "exclusion of the jar" (ghaṭaviveka); nevertheless, the drinking from the vessel (koṣapāna) is the proof [that this is not the case]. Therefore, this is simply the location of the absence of the jar; it is "other" insofar as it is devoid of the jar, but it is not qualified by a distinct exclusion of the jar.

Therefore, although some qualifiers, such as a horse and so forth, are indeed seen to be distinct, there is no such rule; for the opposite is also observed, and because there is a possibility [of non-distinction] and no subverting evidence is seen. Furthermore, dependence upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is the seed for the possibility of such an example. Thus, it should not be said that [the qualifier and the qualified] are different entities because they are distinct from each other, like a horse and so forth. Moreover, if difference were pervaded by the state of being qualifier and qualified, then in the absence of difference, that state would necessarily be absent.
Just as there is no such thing as a "distinguished place," so too this [world] exists; it appears as both existent and non-existent due to the difference between the views of the seer and the seen.

Nor is there a sublation [of the non-apprehension] by means of a valid cognition consisting in the non-apprehension of the perceptible—on the grounds that "this is other than the jar" merely through a specific conventional usage directed toward an object; rather, it is simply "so for this [non-apprehension] as well.

And as for what was said—that even in the case of non-difference there is no proof whatsoever—that is appropriate only for one whose eyes are not yet opened, because otherwise it would be impossible to prevent the arising of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if the object of both this cognition and its verbal expression, "the jar does not exist," is the ground itself and not a separate absence of the jar, then the object of the cognition "the jar exists here" would likewise have to be the ground itself. One need not postulate a jar as something distinct from that; rather, let it be the case that in both instances, it is simply the ground characterized by the presence or absence of the jar.

And this is not tenable; for just as there is a jar’s existence, so too in the case of a jar’s non-existence, something other than the elements appears. For in this way, the employment of affirmation and negation would indeed be meaningful. It would be better to be blind from birth than to have an intellect scorched by such fallacious reasoning. We must ask: if, like non-existence, the jar itself is merely an object of conceptual construction and not within the range of the eyes, what can we say to this?

If one were to say that "the ground has arisen together with the jar" (59b), this would entail simultaneous production; yet there is no confusion of their forms, because the perception of their difference and their assignment of distinct causal functions cannot be denied. Likewise, it has already been considered that non-existence (*abhāva*) does not appear as something distinct from the ground, the potsherds, and so forth.
Furthermore, let people—who, having forgotten the conventional agreement, turn their backs on critical inquiry—declare whether the destruction of the jar is perceived here or not.

Furthermore, as for which objects you perceive here in this world— if the Supreme Lord alone directs [the senses] toward the earth and other elements, then you yourself are the one who knows, and not we.

Consequently, what inconsistency could there be even in the application of affirmation and negation, since both states are established? Likewise, how can the absence of light that has entered through a lattice window—which is itself manifest—be denied? It is merely that, being distinct and possessing a vivid blue luster, it remains in that particular location; yet, because its object is determined to be different [from the light], it is designated by another name, "non-existence" (*abhāva*). Just as with light, so too regarding the absence of other things, when the nature of the self is made manifest, is it a jar or is it the perception of a distinction from sunlight? This is a great marvel!

For even when one examines minutely, the subtle distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) in the mass of entities—which are extremely diverse—is not within the range of perception, like darkness, unless one employs a figurative designation of difference based on the differences among their related objects. Therefore, it is better that even the discernment of light be considered as non-perception, just like the discernment of all other things; rather, accept that darkness is indeed a real entity (*vastu*). Why, then, do you involve yourself in this painful dilemma and distress your own mind?

[Objection: "But surely, even for one with eyes closed, such an appearance of blue is possible, yet it does not present the object 'blue' [as an external thing]. [Reply: That is incorrect, because it would follow that all other things of black color would likewise be non-existent.
[Objection: "This other black is of a different kind, even by a fraction, from the appearance for one with eyes closed."

In that case, darkness (*andhakāra*) as well is experienced as having a limited extent and various shapes when it appears; moreover, its form is clearly distinct from the appearance perceived with eyes closed, which is of a single uniform nature. Furthermore, while the appearance with eyes closed is always of one taste, darkness is sometimes thin in form at times when there is a mixture of a multitude of light-ray atoms, and at other times it is dense or even denser. Thus, how can there be any similarity? Only the mere quality of blackness is common to both.
If, on the other hand, it is argued that in any object of blue color there must necessarily be the concomitance of another tactile quality;

No, because that [touch] is absent in a lattice of sapphire and other jewels or in an elephant's trunk. The hypothesis that the touch there is imperceptible does not fear the darkness. Therefore, let both [color and touch] be merely form (*rūpa*). For indeed, nothing that is perceived can be called "impossible. Moreover, if a substratum must necessarily be sought, there certainly exist things such as jewels and walls. Furthermore, in the determination of reality, no wise person is pleased by the assertion of error based on a confusion of appearances, while relying on the appearance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Otherwise, because things such as a flaming pillar are perceived due to disturbances of wind, bile, and so forth, even a real flaming pillar would be unreal. However, just as there is an absence of that appearance when one returns to one's natural state, so too is there an absence of the delusion regarding the non-existence of blue at the time of opening the eyes. As for the non-perception of darkness, it depends precisely on the healthy state [of the senses], according to the specific distinction already described. Furthermore, the cessation of that appearance upon the disruption of the causal complex capable of producing perception is indeed a merit, not a fault, since the nature of perception is intended to be such.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that it is impossible to perceive black color without light—is it not the case that yellow, white, and so forth are also not perceived independently of light? If so, then lamps, the moon, sunlight, and the like would also require another illuminator. However, the diverse intrinsic natures (*prakṛti*) of entities, as established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), do not admit of such questioning.
Moreover, Śaṅkara and Nyāyabhūṣaṇa maintain that just as with light, the eye is independent of any further light even when perceiving its absence.

That too is nothing; for visual consciousness, which is determinative, is not a grasper of non-existence because it is not a real entity, and it is already established that it does not depend on another light.

Nor should this be said: "Whatever entity is apprehended by a certain causal complex, its absence is also apprehended by that same [complex]; therefore, darkness, being apprehended by the causal complex for the apprehension of light, is simply the absence of that [light]. This is because it would lead to the over-extension (anaikāntikatva) that light itself—when apprehended by the causal complex for the apprehension of darkness—would be the absence of that [darkness]. Furthermore, it would entail the consequence that a jar and a cloth, having an identical causal complex for their apprehension, would stand in a relationship of mutual absence.

Therefore, darkness—which appears in perception as distinct from other objects by way of its specific form—is indeed a real entity that is opposed to light. As for the objection that, if it were truly opposed, darkness might at some time overcome even light, this is not a valid critique; for the theory of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) still stands, just as in the case of cotton and fire.

By this, it is established that the perception of darkness itself—the very thing that serves as the counter-entity—is capable of immediately bringing about the conventional usage of "absence," even when there is a cessation of light within that darkness. Thus, the hope held by Śaṅkara and others—that just as there is the perception of the absence of light here, so it is everywhere else—should be understood as refuted. Furthermore, it has been shown that when non-apprehension is the basis, the establishment of absence occurs even when the counter-entity exists in the form of a cognition; and thus, no fault whatsoever arises. Let this suffice for now. Therefore, it remains settled that there is no such thing as "absence" (abhāva) wherein the operation of a cause could take place.

By this, Trilocana is also refuted, who said: "For those who do not accept a cessation distinct from the entity itself, it is impossible to establish the cessation of its own nature (*svarūpa*). For if that very state of the entity which was previously observed by you to be capable of performing a causal function were to persist even at a later time, then how could the entity be established as having ceased in its own nature?
At that point, this entity would be destroyed; it is not the case that some state, distinct from the nature obtained from its own causes, should suddenly arise for it."

At the time of its arising, that very thing has another self born within it; thus, there is a change of state (*atādavasthya*). We call this very change of state "destruction. If there were no change of state, there would be identity; we do not know the true meaning of the expression "the entity has ceased in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa nivṛtto bhāvaḥ*). For this cessation of its own nature, when occurring, must be either the entity itself or something other than the entity.

In reality, for that which has been produced from its own causes and does not arise otherwise, the consequence of permanence follows for sentient beings starting from the moment of its production; and if there is alteration, then that very thing is different from its cessation—thus the beloved has merely performed what was pleasing [to the opponent]. Therefore, abandoning this delusion, one must accept that destruction itself is the state of having perished. Why, then, is it said that "there is no perception of the destroyed" and "nothing happens to it"? The non-perception of the destroyed is simply the perception of its non-existence.

We accept that the destruction of the self is indeed the arising of non-existence; thus, everything is faultless. [Thesis: Existing things are non-momentary, because they possess causes. [Reason: Whatever possesses a cause is non-momentary, as in the case of the destruction of an entity. [Example: And these existing things possess causes. [Conclusion: Therefore, they are non-momentary.

[154,10] However, since this [non-existence] possesses a cause, the suspicion that it might occur in the opposite of the probandum (the non-momentary) excludes precisely the state of having a cause for destruction. Thus, because its lack of a cause is established through a well-known pervasion (*vyāpti*), momentariness is proven; for it has been demonstrated that the cessation of the entity's own nature (*svarūpa*) occurs even without the cessation of something distinct from it. Consequently, how could the previous state of capacity persist after the moment? And even if something distinct were produced, how could the entity be said to have "perished"?

The statement that "non-existence in that state" (*atādavasthyam*) and "non-identity with that" (*atādātmyam*) have arisen is, in its very literal sense, said to mean that this [entity] has arisen from its own cause as something devoid of any change in state or nature. Consequently, the subsequent conventional usage of terms such as "non-existence in that state" is based solely on that [fact]; it is not a separate entity appearing as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference. Therefore, casting aside delusion, let the conventional usage of "perished" stand; however, nothing other than that [entity itself] arises.
And since non-perception is precisely the perception of non-existence, this has just now been refuted; thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Therefore, there is no cause whatsoever for non-existence (*abhāva*) in the sense of a mere negation (*prasajya*), which is termed "destruction. However, in the case of a perishable nature (*vinaśvara-svabhāva*), since its capacity is established by its own causes alone—having set aside the power of any other cause—it perishes immediately upon being produced and does not persist into another moment; this is proven. Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of having a cause by non-momentariness is unestablished, and thus [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Moreover, if one accepts that produced things necessarily undergo destruction even at the end, there is a contradiction.

It is established that if that which is within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the thesis is sublated by inference; if it is not within its scope, there is non-establishment of both the locus and the essential nature of the subject. Furthermore, regarding this momentariness established by perception—which the venerable commentator himself has established through direct perception—this [opponent], failing to comprehend it, indulges in the negligence of misrepresentation while desiring to offer an elaborate refutation based merely on highlighting the absence of a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, this should be understood as merely the manifestation of the lack of self-knowledge, which is easily accessible to the fickle nature of a novice. For instance, although momentariness is established by perception, it is not conventionally expressed through perception because a corresponding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise; rather, it is grasped by perception because its conventional usage is established through inference.

And if that inference, having established [the object] for itself from some mark (*liṅga*), were to effect the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of grasping momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) through perception by implication, then there would be no distinction [between it and other inferences] such as that based on existence (*sattva*). For in that case, the grasping of momentary destruction being established by perception only through the force of the matter (*artha*), and lacking any touch of its own personal agency, does not nourish the established proof of the realization of momentary destruction as a result of perception.

However, when inference—which relies on the apprehension of momentary duration by perception as established by other means of knowledge—arises to establish mere conventional usage, illuminating only that human agency which is no different from a subsequent conceptual construction (*pṛṣṭhaja-vikalpa*), then it is said that the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is primary through perception. This is the meaning: momentariness does not fall within the range of perceptual cognition; rather, this [momentariness] is established only as a conventional usage by means of the proof of the apprehension of what is present before one.
If momentary destruction were not established by other means, its apprehension would have to rest upon perception;
yet, because it is apprehended through perception, its momentary destruction is established.
For indeed,
whatever appears in whatever manner, all that is exactly so— just as the water of the Gaṅgā is white;
otherwise, if it were not so, there would be no restriction of power for each individual object in the state of their intermingling.

If conditioned phenomena appear to the senses and the intellect as persisting for a single moment, that would be due to their being perceived in a single moment; otherwise, what is seen would be a fragmented [object] belonging to the three times.

This application of the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is interspersed with the occurrence of the form of the logical mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no fault of contradiction. By the second quarter [of the verse], the exclusion of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) is established.

To explain: "manifestation" (*pratibhāna*) is said to be the appearance in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, if an entity were to abide in its own nature while bypassing that specific restriction by which it attains manifestation in direct perception, then its nature would be entirely intermingled; consequently, there would follow the absurdity of everything being useful for everything everywhere.

Therefore, when there is a requirement for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to determine the essential nature [of an object], for one who desires engagement or withdrawal, whatever appears in perception in a certain way exists exactly in that way and not otherwise.

By this, it is shown that the appearance in perception is pervaded by non-falsity; for if the object were situated otherwise—in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—the pervader would be absent, and thus [the appearance] being absent would be pervaded by its being situated in that very way.

The application of the property to the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) is [established] by the third quarter [of the verse], and the refutation of its non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is by the fourth. For if there were identity between earlier and later times, then because an entity lacks any other form than the form perceived, the form—even when residing in another location—would necessarily manifest as being permeated by all moments of time; thus, there would be no occasion for seeking another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its state in another place or time.

Furthermore, there is an inquiry as to how that object exists in another place or at another time, [thinking], "Has it perhaps been sprinkled with the essence of passion that does not currently manifest? This is because such deliberation occurs when there is the possibility of its manifestation. However, such a possibility does not exist for that which has already been made an object of perception. Nor can it be said that there is no determination even when something is seen; for in the case of a desired form such as redness, there is no lack of habituation, just as there is none regarding momentariness. Otherwise, even upon seeing it later, no determinate cognition would arise. Therefore, the absence of such a determination is due solely to its non-appearance [at that time].

[156,11] But surely, even if there is an appearance of an entity as pervading the three times, the non-appearance of its specific related particulars—namely, other times, places, and conditions—is not a sublation; for this is the same as the case where, even when a moment is apprehended, there is a non-appearance of other entities related to it, such as causes, effects, or conjoined things. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to seek another means of valid cognition with respect to those other related factors, if one should so argue.

This is not so, because since place, time, action, qualities, and so forth exist, difference is not established [between the moments]. However, let there be no appearance of a distinct related entity when that [entity] itself appears. Therefore, having excluded all other states of subsequent moments, it is established that every object appears with a form that encompasses the moment alone. Thus, for as long as a dissimilar state such as redness or the like is not present, let there be a perception of them as unified over that duration of time.

That too does not exist; for immediately after the characteristic of perception, when there is a sudden movement of the eye, even among objects that are similar, a suspicion of error arises regarding the subsequent moments in reality, whereas such a suspicion is impossible in the case of things directly perceived.

If it is argued: "In that case, the movement of the eye and its seeing [of the object] would not be momentary; for an ordinary person, to establish a connection [between the two], one must eliminate the suspicion of a mistaken judgment. Indeed, the seeing of that [object] must necessarily persist for at least two or three moments to be effective for that purpose. Therefore, how could there be a lapse in the manifestation of a form that endures for two or three moments during the first moment, such that a distinction between the second and subsequent moments could be established? [Response: ... (The text continues with the refutation).

For one in whom the conceptualization of an object arises immediately after the very moment of perceiving the first instant, there is an unavoidable opportunity for reflection upon the contradiction of all moments being non-distinct.
If it is argued that this is not possible for anyone, what is the refutation here? And if it is asked, "What is the proof here? [the answer follows].

It is said: if the search for a probans (*sādhaka*) occurs immediately after the moment of perception (*īkṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) when the determinative cognition (*avasāya*) arises, then there are two kinds of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following perception: the conceptual construction of the mere seen (*dṛṣṭamātra-vikalpa*), and the conceptual construction of the specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa-vikalpa*), such as "this cloth is seen" or "this is a genuine or artificial gem, a pearl, and so forth. In that regard, the error of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) of dull intellect, which is removable by similarity regarding its object, is dispelled by [the conceptual construction] arising from the excellence of practice established through generalization (*utsarga*).

Therefore, since the limit of the degree of lightness of time is reached through the gradation of excellence in its arising, this [cognition] attains its emergence even immediately after the moment of perception; thus, its negation is impossible to conceive. However, in the case of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has just been perceived, its birth immediately following perception—which would otherwise be established as a festival—is precluded by the difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

For indeed, since conceptual constructions have by nature become habitual through the beginningless continuum of saṃsāra, all beings—whose engagement and withdrawal depend upon conceptualization even regarding an object directly perceived, and who especially seek to obtain pleasure and avoid pain—have their mental continua perfumed by the repeated practice of investigating the means to those ends. How could they, when the efficient cause for experiencing that object has presented itself, be capable of experiencing a delay in the occurrence of conceptualization? They do so only occasionally when [the conditions] are conjoined.

Since there is no practice of withdrawing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and because at times there may be attachment to something else, or at other times its manifestation due to extreme delusion—it is through such a collection of conditions that conceptual constructions arise with a delayed succession. In the absence of those [conditions], however, the arising of conceptual construction immediately after the moment of perception is indeed established.

Consequently, when all object-moments are deprived of that perception, why would there be no room for the mind to swing on the swing of doubt regarding their redness and so forth—even in the second moment when they are made the objects of reflection, just as in the case of a remote series of moments? Nor does this occur even in the manifestation of direct perception; therefore, the mass of objects enters into the manifestation of direct perception as if already encompassed by the moment.

It might be argued as follows: This [argument] would be tenable if perception were momentary; however, since perception extends over multiple moments, there is room for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) when that which extends over multiple moments appears. Therefore, how can the establishment of the apprehension of a single moment be proven?

It is said in reply: First of all, does perception pervade multiple moments because it is employed for the production of its own nature, or because that which is produced in a single moment persists? Regarding these, the first alternative is impossible; for since cognition lacks the nature of a composite whole, its production in parts is untenable. And if those distinct moments constituting the parts of perception were by nature determinative [of their object], then there would be as many perceptions as there are moments, and thus the same difficulty arises in relation to the first perception.

However, if the nature [of the object] is undivided (*aparicchitti*), then even when [the parts] have come together, it is not perceptible. "Undivided discernment" means that by means of the collection [of parts], there is a complete discernment of the entity as a whole. Even then, the entity as a whole is merely a fragment delimited by the first moment, because that which has not entered into it is distinct from it. Otherwise, the entire universe perceived in succession would be a single entity, and the entirety of what is perceived would be a single perception.

Even in the second position, is it that which has already completed its operation, or is it that which has completed its operation by pervading another moment? In the first case, since its very operation consists in the apprehension of the object, there is room for the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by that much alone; what does it matter whether it itself persists into another moment or not? If that were so, then while the eye or the object moves, the perception (*adhyakṣa*) would remain inclined toward the apprehension of that same object—this is an unprecedented method!

However, even if there is non-apprehension during the momentary state [of perception], liberation does not occur merely by that much, because there remains the opportunity for the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Nor can it be believed that there is a state of stability for that which previously apprehended when it subsequently fails to apprehend; for even one who does not apprehend when the sensory object is present would have stability [if such were the case]. Likewise, it is difficult to believe that there is a state of an unaccomplished operation (*vyāpāra*), for knowledge has no operation distinct from its arising, unlike other effects.

And let it be so; nevertheless, the well-spoken verse remains as before: "Perception, having arisen upon the proximity of the sense organ and its object, cognizes—as if it were 'existing'—an object not previously apprehended at the time when both [the object and the cognition] are being examined.

Therefore, enough with these excessively stubborn false conceptualizations! For, whether before or after, when a variegated form such as red and so forth manifests at that very moment, there is a reversal of the operation of other means of valid cognition, as indicated by the fourth quarter:
"Whatever form is capable of being determined while something is manifesting anywhere..."
A means of knowledge that has ceased does not long for [to appear] there, nor is it capable of manifesting therein—

just as taste is not [manifested] in the appearance of form. Likewise, while that [object] is appearing at that moment, another means of knowledge is required in the form of a dependence upon the determination of its prior state.

Thus, by the perception of the pervasion of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), it is established that the manifestation of direct perception reveals the very nature of an entity as persisting for only a single moment. Furthermore, it has already been largely demonstrated in the section establishing pervasion (*vyāptisamarthana*) that its nature does not exist outside of that manifestation. Therefore, it is proven that fragility (*bhaṅguratva*) is established by direct perception; it is conventionally expressed by inference; and its establishment is accomplished through other means of knowledge. This is because the direction of the reasoning regarding the determination of momentariness by direct perception has been indicated.
For the wise, there is no need for an extensive treatise when the practical application [of the system] is already established by implication;
nevertheless, the eminent teacher Ravi composed this work because, due to a lack of understanding of the truth, those of small intellect are by nature loquacious and utter falsehoods.
[159] Nor do we depend upon the path of the teacher Ravi for the apprehension of momentariness, since our sequence follows from this;
and as for the consistency with the statements in the Bhāṣya, it has not been sung here for fear of excessive prolixity.

Therefore, enough with this insistence on tangential discussion. It is established that what is called "destruction" is not some distinct entity, produced by a mallet or similar instrument, other than the iron bar and so forth [that cause it], which—by its non-occurrence at the time when those causes have not yet fallen upon it—could fulfill one’s desire for the permanence of an existing thing.

[Thus ends the section] playfully uprooting the very firm pillars of the sacrificial altar of the wicked system [of the Naiyāyikas], namely those known as Śaṅkara, Nyāyālaṅkāra, Trilocana, and Vācaspati.
By whatever merit I have acquired through uprooting this momentary flux [of existence],
may this person become one who has reached the further shore of the glory of knowledge throughout the three worlds.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Section on Destruction Without Cause," is completed.
And this chapter on Momentary Destruction is completed.

**The Examination of Pervasion (Vyāpticarcā)** Homage to the Blessed One, who is free from passion! In this context, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and so forth by fire and so forth is established as being characterized by perception (*pratyakṣa*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), proof (*sādhana*), and origination from that (*tadutpatti*).

For those who preceded us have indeed postulated that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekitva*) consists simply in the observation of smoke where there is fire and its non-observation where it is absent. In that regard, since such observation and non-observation might occur even by chance once, they require repeated occurrence. But surely, even with repeated observation and non-observation, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has been perceived in cases such as the jar and the unfaithful wife.
If it is asked: "Is it on this basis that you say there must also be inference in that case? Or rather, that it should not be so in the case of smoke and the like either?

First, the initial position is rejected precisely because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The second is also rejected precisely because of non-deviation. For when another thing deviates, it does nothing to smoke. Indeed, just because poisoned food is undesirable does not mean that other types of food should also be abandoned.

And since all cessation is obtained by that much alone, what is the use of seeking the production [of the effect]? Or rather, it is by means of perception and non-perception which serve to ascertain that [relation].

If its production were also apprehended solely through seeing and not seeing, what fault would there be? Let inference itself proceed by way of distinction; thus is that [distinction] sought. And that distinction occurs by way of deviation and non-deviation.

[This is] established. And when there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the capacity to indicate [the probandum] exists by that alone; the production [of the effect from the cause] (*tadutpatti*) is useless. Furthermore, in the case of deviation, even a hundred instances of such production are not efficacious. Therefore, the search for proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) is fulfilled by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) alone.
For this very reason, smoke is said to be the "conjoined" (*saṃyogin*) reason for fire, and not its "effect" (*kārya*).

Trilocana, however, says: Since perception and non-perception have particulars as their objects, how can there be a cognition of a relation between two universals by means of them? If it is argued that the relation is indeed cognized as that which is excluded from non-fire with that which is excluded from non-smoke—well then, of what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is even that the object? It cannot be that of perception, because perception has only particular characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object.

Nor can it be established by inference, because that too is preceded by perception. Furthermore, there is no connection whatsoever between two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Now, if it is argued that a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising subsequent to perception determines non-difference in what has been perceived as different—that itself is the universal (*sāmānya*)—even so, the object of conceptual constructions is not the real thing itself, but rather the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*). And that is not a real thing; for them, the real thing remains entirely beyond the reach of perception (*parokṣa*).

[161,23] How, then, is the apprehension of the relation established by that [single observation]? For us, however, the relation among things of that same class is apprehended by the mind aided by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Therefore, smoke does not deviate from fire. If it were to deviate from it, smoke would transcend a relation that is free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*); thus, the proof that removes the suspicion of a counter-example for the reason (*hetu*) is the absence of a limiting condition that meets the criteria for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
The reason is precisely perception known as non-apprehension; from that, the natural connection is established.

Vācaspati, however, offers this elaboration: for instance, the relation between smoke and so forth and fire and so forth is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), but the relation of fire and so forth with smoke and so forth is not. This is because those [fires] are perceived even without smoke and the like; rather, it is when they experience a connection with wet fuel and so forth that they become connected with smoke and the like. Therefore, [the relation] of fire and so forth is produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of wet fuel and the like.

The connection, however, is not intrinsic; therefore, it is not necessary. But the connection of smoke and the like with fire and the like is intrinsic, because no limiting condition (*upādhi*) for it is perceived, and because no deviation is observed anywhere. Furthermore, it is illogical to postulate a condition that is not perceived, even if it were invisible due to its being beyond the range of perception.

It is logical that an *upādhi*, which is suspected due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that either establishes or refutes it, obstructs the inherent nature of the relationship. For those who do not perceive a restrictive factor, doubt must necessarily arise.
And thus, having been granted this opportunity, the demoness of doubt, by transgressing the boundaries of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), gains a foothold;
she would not fail to exist anywhere, for there would be no one who would act anywhere, since there is always some kind of misfortune that serves as a ground for suspicion.
And because the suspicion of misfortune is a factor in the desistance of prudent people, even when consuming pleasant food and drink, there is the fear of death at the very end.

Because it is seen from experience. Therefore, one who maintains the worldly course according to authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) should entertain doubt only in accordance with what has been observed, and not even regarding that which has never been seen before. For doubt depends upon the recollection of specific features; it does not arise in the absence of such recollection. And recollection cannot occur with respect to something never previously experienced. As it was said by the author of the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika*:
"An apprehension that lacks a basis in valid cognition is not [justified].
Likewise, by that same author, in the *Bṛhaṭṭīkā*:
"For he who, out of delusion, might imagine a subverting factor even where none exists..."
"He would perish, being full of doubt in all worldly transactions.
Therefore, searching diligently for an *upādhi* and not perceiving one, we understand that it does not exist and conclude that the relation is inherent (*svābhāvika*).

[162,24] This might be the case if one thing were related to another without a cause; then the relation would be inherent (*svābhāvika*). Consequently, everything would be inherently related to everything, and everything would be understood from everything. Or, if one thing is the effect of another, why does everything not arise from everything? Because there is no distinction in their being "other" (*anyatva*). And thus, that same over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains. If it should be argued:

The intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities are not to be questioned. Therefore, even though there is no distinction in their being "other," only some things are causes and only some things are effects. But surely this lack of questioning regarding intrinsic nature applies equally even to those things that do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, provided there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*). Consequently, this [objection] is also trivial.

By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), moreover, is this essential relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) apprehended? In the case of relations perceived through direct perception (*pratyak�sa*), it is by means of direct perception. For instance, when one first perceives the relation between fire and smoke—both being accompanied by moist fuel—at that time, is the relation of both essentially inherent, or is it adventitious (*aupādhika*)? Or is it that the relation of smoke is adventitious, while that of fire is not?
[163,8] It is intrinsic; yet it is impossible to determine that fire is extrinsic while smoke is intrinsic.

[163,9] In this regard, since fire without wet fuel is observed in things such as glowing iron balls even in the absence of smoke, it is certain that its connection with smoke is conditioned by the adventitious factor (upādhi) of wet fuel, and not intrinsic. [163,10] However, because a specific kind of smoke is never perceived without fire, and because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for postulating an unperceived distinction in the adventitious factors, [the relation of smoke is determined to be intrinsic], depending upon the recollection of its specific nature.

Because doubt does not arise regarding that which has never been perceived before, or because if it were to arise there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) resulting in the cessation of activity for discerning persons, an intrinsic relation (svābhāvika-sambandha) is determined. This determination is not mental; for if the mind operated externally without dependence [on the senses], there would be no such thing as the blind or the deaf.

[This follows] from the consequence (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, if its operation were dependent upon repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), it would result in the occurrence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). For it is not the case that something is "mental" (*mānasa*) merely because the mind (*manas*) is its cause. If that were so, nothing at all would fail to be mental, since every cognition (*pratyaya*) has the mind as its cause.
If, however, the designation of a specific means of valid cognition is made in dependence upon its respective uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), then here too, repeated observation [is the cause].

Since there exists a unique cause, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has arisen; therefore, it is logical that the sense faculty itself— assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation— grasps the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) between smoke and so forth with fire and so forth, just like the discernment of the true nature of various noble gems.

Thus, in cases where the relation is known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those very same means of valid cognition—assisted by repeated observation according to their respective natures—are to be inferred as the instruments for grasping the essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*). And since reasons (*hetu*) are essentially bound to their own probanda (*sādhya*), if they were to exist without the probandum, they would necessarily deviate from their very nature. Thus, assisted by reasoning (*tarka*), the probandum is excluded.

Wherever instances of doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are observed, those [reasons] certainly establish their own probandum (*svasādhya*). Furthermore, there is no possibility of a natural necessary connection (*svābhāvikapratibandha*) between "being the son of Maitra" and such qualities as "darkness" and so forth. Since the specific transformation of food and drink exists as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for the connection between darkness and being the son of Maitra, "being the son of Maitra" is not a prover (*agamaka*). By this same reasoning, [the following is explained: his [fruits] are ripe...

The fruits situated at the top of a tree [are known as such] because they originate from that very tree; likewise, relations based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhikasambandha*), such as "having tasted the fruit," have also been explained. Therefore, that whose relation is natural (*svābhāvika*) and necessary is a constituent of inference (*anumānāṅga*), such as smoke, being produced, and so forth. However, that whose relation is adventitious does not become a constituent of inference, such as "being his son" and the like.
Thus it stands.

To this, it is said: what is called "pervasion" (vyāpti) is either the necessary presence of the pervader (vyāpaka) there, or the presence of the pervaded (vyāpya) only there; thus, by way of being attributes of the agent and the object respectively, it is intended as two-fold through the forms of positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka), according to the requirements of inference.

Otherwise, inference would be useless. For if it were established in a general sense that "when the proof exists, the probandum necessarily exists," or that "in the absence of the probandum, the proof necessarily does not exist," then there would be hope for the probandum in a locus possessing the proof, because of the absence of the latter when the former is absent. However, when the aforementioned necessity does not hold, then—

If there is the apprehension that "there is a means of proof (sādhana) but no object to be proven (sādhya)," how can there be any scope for inference? Therefore, one who desires inference must necessarily rely upon the aforementioned pervasion (vyāpti). Nor is that [pervasion] established by mere repeated observation;
for just as the possibility of a single instance of correspondence may occur by chance, so too might it happen by mere chance even on several occasions.

There is no negation of correspondence. Just as, when a concomitance is observed only once, a deviation may be found, and thus there arises the suspicion that there is no rule of necessary concomitance at all times and in all places; likewise, even when there is repeated observation, because a deviation is still observed, such a suspicion arises and cannot be negated.

As for the claim that inference is invalid because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that is not tenable. For instance, whose observation of deviation here serves as the cause for obstructing inference? Is it that of the cognizer alone, or that of the author of the treatise, or of just anyone at all? In the case of the last alternative, what has happened to the cognizer such that he would not perform an inference?

Otherwise, if another person has already accomplished their purpose by directly perceiving that very object, why would one necessarily seek out inference? Furthermore, it is unworldly to claim that one might infer fire from smoke even without having observed the relationship between them simply by asking the author of a treatise.

For a cognizer, however, even if a deviation exists, it does not necessarily come within the range of perception; for it is not the case that wherever there is a deviation, one is immediately aware of it.

During that time and in that place, it necessarily enters into one's cognition; and as long as it is not being cognized, it cannot be determined that it simply does not exist. This is because it may be seen even after an absolute lapse of time, and because its destruction remains unestablished for those who have not yet developed a subverting cognition. Consequently, even if there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is possible that the cognizer has failed to perceive it. It occurs thus.

If one remembers what was taught—that inference occurs when there is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and not otherwise—would this person proceed to infer based on the certainty of that non-deviation, or would they refrain? Since certainty cannot be reached through mere non-observation, non-deviation is unestablished; thus, the reason is unestablished due to doubt. In the first case, one might even perform an inference from a camel. But in the second case, one would not even do so from smoke. For it is not the case that...

At a time when no deviation—whether existing or non-existing—is observed, there is no distinction whatsoever. Therefore, if one suspects that even the frequent simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*) of a camel and a donkey is merely accidental, why not suspect the same for smoke and fire?
This is the same. Now, I observe that even when a camel and a donkey are in close proximity, they are perceived as independent of one another.

[165,1] First, one who acts with the desire to know whether "when one thing is being removed, does another follow it like a calf follows a cow" does not perceive it in that way. However, when fire is removed, one perceives only the disappearance of smoke; or, when fire is present, one perceives the occurrence of smoke.

If it is argued that, therefore, deviation is possible for the camel at other times but not for smoke, then it follows that only a specific kind of observation and non-observation regarding smoke is the grasper of its production, whereas such is not the case for the camel. For instance, when in the absence of fire—

One perceives the absence of smoke. At that time, preceded by simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), the non-perception of smoke in the mere absence of fire is employed for the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Otherwise, in the absence of simultaneous observation—where there is merely the removal of glowing embers and the like, while smoke exists, yet there is no donkey because of the presence of a camel—how could there be an understanding of a relationship? Even if there were simultaneous observation, if it were another object...

[165,9] When there is the removal of fire together with its absence, at that time it is not certain whether its prior existence was negated by the existence of the fire or by the existence of some other entity. However, if there is merely the absence of fire, it is easily understood that its prior existence was indeed conditioned by that [fire]. Even when there is the existence of smoke in the mere proximity of fire, at that time there is first the non-perception of both, followed by the perception upon the presentation of the fire alone.

[165,12] Regarding the smoke, it has already been employed [in the argument]. Otherwise, if only fire were brought forward while smoke certainly exists, how could the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) be proven? It would be like the case of a camel. [165,13] Even if fire accompanied by other things were brought forward, there would be no certainty as to whose absence is what causes the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the smoke.
[165,14] But when only fire is brought forward, it is logical that its absence is what causes it.

Thus, in this way, the non-perception of one thing preceded by the perception of another is called "distinct" (viśiṣṭa) with respect to that prior perception; and that prior perception is also distinct with respect to the two aforementioned types of non-perception occurring at a later time. In the same manner, a distinction should be inferred even in a perception that is preceded by non-perception—that absence of which causes a lack of confidence regarding [the presence of] a camel and so forth. And it is precisely that distinction between perception and non-perception [which must be understood].

Relying upon the operation of perception and non-perception, there is the conventional usage [of these terms]. And that which is their object—the nature of two entities—is called the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Furthermore, that which is dependent on another, being independent of anything else, is also said to be "constrained" therein by way of arising from that. For indeed, it is produced by that alone.

Since even the second concomitance is negated when one is removed, it is evident that the latter depends upon the former. This should be understood to apply equally when only that [the first] is removed; otherwise, there would be a requirement for the removal of the second as well. How, then, is there the removal of only that? It is by the very production of that [effect] that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated through the means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), and not merely by seeing and not seeing while devoid of those specific characteristics.

And when there is a requirement for that specific [certainty], since cessation is attained through a single occurrence, there is no further need for repeated activity. For just as one does not require another means of cognition beyond the mere perception of concomitance—established through once-and-for-all observation and non-observation—which fails to provide confidence; likewise, once the relationship between the two distinct types of causes and effects has been established through direct perception and non-perception occurring a single time, nothing further remains to be cognized by subsequent means of cognition.

Thus, cessation occurs by that much alone. If there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*) by a person of another class through similarity and so forth, then the cognizer must be one who is discerning. However, when there is mere co-occurrence (*sahacāra*), there is doubt regarding that very same class. Furthermore, the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) elsewhere in cases of mere co-occurrence is a potent seed for this [doubt]. Moreover, the example of poisoned food does not lead to peace [of mind] in this case.

This is because the other food is of a different genus (*bhinnajātīyatva*) from poisoned food. However, in this case, since the predominant portion that acts as the cause is characterized by constant concomitance (*sahacāralakṣaṇa*), smoke possesses precisely the same genus [as fire]. It is not the case that being smeared with poison is a common property (*sādhāraṇa*) of curd-rice and the like;

thus there is a disparity. Furthermore, since there is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) at all without such origination from that [cause], there is simply no non-deviation when there is a difference [in kind].

Because it has the nature of being produced from that (*tadutpatti*). With regard to the implication of non-deviation, the exclusion of production from that is indeed improper. Therefore, smoke is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) for fire, because it implies non-deviation through production from that. It is not a reason based on conjunction (*saṃyogin*), since that merely refers to the observation of co-occurrence.

How then is the example of the camel and the donkey [given], given that there is no conjunction? Let there be satisfaction with the frequent observation of the conjunction between a maidservant and a water-jar.

Nor is it the case that there is a restriction regarding the coexistence of a camel and a donkey, or of water and a crane, at that same time and place, because such a thing is observed; therefore, this argument is of no consequence. Consequently, it is established that when another entity is to be understood, it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), and the proof of its existence is based on perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

Regarding the objection raised by Trilocana, we reply: "Perception has particulars as its object. Does this mean that particulars are also its objects, or that it has particulars alone? In the case of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), there is no obstruction to its having universals as its objects; so how could there be no room for perception and non-perception regarding two universals? Furthermore, why is the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) stated by resorting to our own established tenets?

Or from the perspective of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*): for us, both [types of cognition] are indeed valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to both objects, by way of the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). For that which appears in a cognition is the apprehended; whereas that toward which it proceeds is the determined.

In this regard, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the apprehended object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while the universal (*sāmānya*) is its determined object. For inference (*anumāna*), however, the reverse is the case. In that context:

[166,17] The direct perception that serves as the means of proof (*sādhana-pratyakṣa*) has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object even when one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyārthin*) perceives a single moment, because it depends upon the continuum (*saṃtāna*).

[166,18] Furthermore, in the context of grasping pervasion (*vyāptigrahaṇa*), even when a single individual instance (*ekavyakti*) is seen, it has a universal as its object because its domain consists of all individual instances of the same class. [166,19] [The cognition] "I have determined through direct perception that smoke is born from fire" refers to an individual instance excluded from everything other than that [fire].

[166,20] This is because, by including what has arisen within itself, there is the experience of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) produced by its power. Just as, through the perception of mere color-form (*rūpa*), there is a conceptual determination regarding a jar—which consists of a specific collection of color-form, taste, smell, and touch—and thus perception has that [jar] as its object.

[166,21–22] Furthermore, "universal" (*sāmānya*) is not something entirely other; rather, it is simply the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves whose mutual distinctions have not been discerned.

[166,23] These are called "universals. However, when distinguishing between particulars (*bheda*), each is designated by its own term as a "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, [166,24] even if all particular characteristics that are distinct from others do not constitute objects by way of being apprehended (*grāhya*) because they do not appear [to cognition], nevertheless, they cannot be avoided as being objects by way of being determined (*adhyavaseya*). Thus, how can there be an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)? Furthermore, it is also said that the object of conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*).

This is stated precisely because of a lack of understanding regarding the final position of others. This is because both synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and inference (*anumāna*), insofar as they depend upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects.

As for the rest, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Now, suppose the position is that this occurs "by way of the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛttyā*). That too is untenable, because it is impossible to bypass the twofold nature of the object of all cognitions, namely the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). For the very validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is what remains superior.

The duality of objects, however, is established everywhere. In that regard, first of all, in inference (*anumāna*), because the real thing (*vastu*) does not appear [directly], it is only the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavaseya*); the apprehended object (*grāhya*), however, is its own internal form (*svākāra*). We have already examined such a case in the *Apoha-prakaraṇa*, so it shall not be introduced here. Furthermore, even if the form of cognition is not accepted [as being external], nevertheless, since it has arisen through the force of the real thing (*vastubala*), how could it be excluded?

For there can be no such thing as cognition without an appearance. And since it is established that what appears in inference is not the external object itself, it must necessarily be its own internal form (*svākāra*).
