If you argue that this form is false (*alīka*), even so, when that form appears, the apprehended and the determinable are the external; thus, once the duality of objects is established, why persist in this insistence? In the same way, even in perception, only certain individuals appear and are apprehended, while all others—

[At the time of cognizing the necessary connection, there is a determination of what is of the same class. For if there were no manifestation [of it], then even the determination would not occur; indeed, even the slightest scent of the establishment of the cognition of the connection through perception would be dispelled.

As for that which was stated—that there is apprehension by means of the mind, or by the sense organ aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by repeated observation—in that regard, this is [the response]:

[167,10] This is investigated: First of all, there is the repeated sensory perception of individual instances of fire and smoke. There is also the reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*) arising from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [perception]. This [fire] is perceived only in conjunction with this [smoke]. Therefore, is this concomitance between these two eternal? Or is it merely like the association of two friends who part when their time is spent? Even for one whose power of reflection is weak, there is the cognition of the necessary connection (*antaryaka*) with the cause.

[167,13] It occurs; and there is a corresponding performance [of the action]. However, no further manifestation of cognition (*jñāna-vivarta*) is perceived here. In that regard, [167,14] frequent observation (*bhūyodarśana*) merely serves as an auxiliary by way of generating a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); it cannot be said to be the primary subject under discussion.
[167,15] To claim that this [cognition] has as its object all individuals of a single class without exception is mere wishful thinking, because those individuals do not appear [in the cognition].

Doubt, occurring immediately after that, is likewise not determinative of the relationship precisely because it is doubt. And as for the final [cognition], even though it has the form of a certainty, it is devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Therefore, what confidence can there be in the object of knowledge (*prameya*) presented even by that which is called "perception"? For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is not born of a logical mark (*aliṅgaja*) conforms only to the operation of a prior perception that has already occurred; thus, the object is exactly as it was [previously perceived].

The arising of an entity does not occur through independence, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, prior perceptions are witnesses merely to concomitance (*sahacāramātra*), like the concomitance of wind and sunlight; they do not penetrate any specific distinction. How, then, can they be capable of establishing the truthfulness of this [subsequent cognition]? Even if it were so, those [prior cognitions] alone would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein. But this [subsequent cognition] is a memory (*smaraṇa*); it is not a means of valid cognition.

[167,22] It is well said that it is being demonstrated. One should not say that there is a distinction [between smoke and the wind] because their co-occurrence is subsequently disrupted by the wind and heat; for the intended meaning is non-difference with respect to the period during which no deviation is observed. Furthermore, as has already been stated, even in this case, a certainty regarding the absence of disruption is untenable. For as long as the non-arising of smoke prior to the operation of fire remains present in the mind, so long indeed—

The discernment of a distinction arises from another instance of concomitance. And for that very reason, it is logical that if there were deviation from that [concomitance], smoke would transcend its relationship with fire as being free from any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Otherwise, when only mere concomitance was previously perceived—just as when fire is seen in the absence of smoke, one postulates a limiting condition for the relationship of fire with smoke—it would likewise apply generally to smoke in the absence of fire.

[167,28] If one assumes the existence of an entity, there will be the postulation of another limiting condition (*upādhi*); therefore, for what could there be a relation—whether adventitious (*aupādhika*) or intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)—with what? For it is not the case that when two friends are perceived, even in the absence of one, there is no possibility of perceiving the other; rather, because the existence of Maitra is not contradicted even in the absence of Caitra, as in the case of a mountain cleft—

Even for that which has entered [into the mind], its fitness for perception does not vanish. However, in the case of smoke, there is certainly no arising at all without fire; thus, there is no possibility [of mistaking it].

And by that much, the very fact of "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*) is taken as the refuge. Furthermore, it has already been stated that this [certainty] does not arise from repeated observation and non-observation.
For this very reason, it is impossible to assert that the relation between a cow and "cowness" is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).

This is because, in the absence of the cognition of their being produced from one another (*tadutpatti*), there is no distinction from other concomitant factors (*sahacārin*). Furthermore, even the observation of concomitance does not exist, since neither part is apprehended by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, what is the point here in casting aside the theories of the intrinsic and the conditional (*aupādhika*)?

By way of distinction: the capacity to indicate [the object] belongs to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) because of its causality; since a single cause produces [the effect] only in dependence upon others, there is no fixed rule regarding the effect [as to which specific cause alone is productive].
However, the effect is restricted by each individual member through its necessity to the causal complex. Thus, it is established that this [effect] is the logical mark (*liṅga*), not the cause.
Now, since smoke is observed when fuel is present alongside fire, fuel is established as a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*) specifically with reference to that particular [fire]. As for smoke—

Furthermore, when there is a connection with fire, that which exists as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) would necessarily be perceptible; yet that which is not perceived is said to be non-existent. Now, is fuel itself the ultimate limiting adjunct by virtue of which the necessity of perceptibility is intended in the case of the connection? For the limiting adjunct must be designated as either another object to be depended upon or a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*). And another object is not necessarily perceptible. Consequently, [the following applies]:

Even in the case of smoke’s connection with fire, there might be an *upādhi* (limiting condition), yet it is not perceived; how then can it be said that it does not exist simply because it is not seen, such that the establishment of an intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) would follow? Furthermore, if there were another factor to be depended upon, how could there be the rule that the existence of fire is determined by smoke alone?
[168,18] If you say this, then surely this very point is being considered: whether fire necessarily occurs when smoke is present, or not.
[168,19] Since at times smoke might exist even without fire due to some other factor—an *upādhi*—what is the cause for certainty in this matter?
[168,20] Therefore, how could smoke—which is established as arising in dependence upon fire—be accepted as existing in the absence of that [fire]? This is precisely the point.

Excellent! This non-perception of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is unestablished. For just as fire is not connected with smoke without fuel, so too smoke is not connected with that [smoke] without fire; thus, the status of being a limiting condition is equal for fuel in both cases. Now, if it is argued that the establishment of the limiting condition is based on the fact that the occurrence of smoke depends on its concomitance with fuel once fire is established—

If it is argued that, because smoke—which is not yet established—obtains its own nature through that [fire] as its cause, it is non-deviant from it, and thus an "essential" (svābhāvika) relation is established; even so, it follows that this very [relation] is "origination from that" (tadutpatti), and that alone is the essential connection. Furthermore, such a relation is not graspable by the aforementioned mental perception (*mānasa*) and other means of cognition. Nor can a limiting condition (*upādhi*) be refuted by the non-perception of the perceptible; therefore, when there is a suspicion of an adventitious condition (*aupādhika*), there is no exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Thus it is established that [the inference] is "of smoke."

In the treatise of Vācaspati, however, it is stated that in the case of the connection between fire and smoke, fuel is indeed observed as the limiting condition (*upādhi*). But in the case of the connection between smoke and fire, there is an inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*), and the sublation [of a condition] occurs through the mere non-perception of a limiting condition. And in that regard, the reason is "because no deviation is observed anywhere. On this point, the following is considered: does this reason establish the non-perception of a limiting condition?

[169,4] Now, even if that very [non-perception] were his proof, it would be a sublater of the [probans] due to the suspicion of its lack of firmness, because of the non-perception of its intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*) as a condition (*upādhi*). [169,5] In the first case, it is useless; for the existence and non-existence of cognition are not to be established by another cause, since they have the nature of being cognitions that are self-aware (*svasaṃvedya*).
[169,6] And since there is no perception of a condition, non-perception is indeed established. Thus, even when no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed...

Or rather, it must be stated that there is no application of the reason (*hetu*). If it is argued that "application" means the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), we say no, because there would then be no point of contention (*vimati*);

for the mere non-cognition would already be established. Nor is the third alternative tenable: if the first [non-cognition], being devoid of the qualification of being perceptible (*dṛśya-viśeṣaṇa*), lacks the power to establish a negation, what kind of power could the second possess? It is intended that the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurs only in the case of the perceptible.

If [you argue that it is so], then it would not be the case everywhere or at all times; and consequently, since there would be no deviation anywhere, it is illogical for the relation to be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). Furthermore, the mere fact that no deviation has been observed in some cases would lead to the unwarranted conclusion (*prasajyeta*) that fire is also intrinsically related to smoke, or that Caitra and Maitra are intrinsically related to one another. And if this were so, even if a relation were intrinsic, it would result in a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*).

Therefore, non-deviation must be sought in every case. Consequently, even regarding the object of inference, as long as one does not establish the probandum through perception, one cannot cognize non-deviation; thus, what is the use of inference? Furthermore, the doctrine of essential nature (*svābhāvikavāda*) was resorted to in order to avoid the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) regarding smoke—on account of its being produced from that [fire] and so forth—since inconclusiveness arises from the suspicion of deviation.

[169,16] Therefore, because it is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) anywhere; and because there is no deviation anywhere, it is intrinsic—thus, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). However, for one who holds that the cognition of the production of one kind from another kind occurring even once is itself the cognition of non-deviation everywhere, this undesirable consequence does not apply; for it is logically established that the application of that [non-deviation] depends precisely upon repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*).

For just as in one instance of perception there is dependence on another when doubt arises, so too in other instances there is dependence on doubt. Everywhere, the requirement for perception is indeed mutually induced. However, if even in that case one were to demonstrate a restriction regarding the number of repetitions—as we do: "Having previously not seen it, by seeing it in succession, one knows the established relation between cause and effect."
Or, if one does not perceive [the object] sequentially during the observation, there would otherwise be no finality.

Thus, there is a rule of three repetitions for perception and non-perception regarding the individual parts, but only one repetition for the whole. At that time, it would be well-established by just that much. However, as for "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), since the number is not fixed, to what extent could one who follows the target reach satisfaction?

And if that were impossible, this person would never perform an inference; thus, the treatise on definitions (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*) would be useless. However, in the case of memory, some degree of observation will proceed for the purpose of instilling clarity in the mind. Therein, nothing is lost without a restriction regarding the measure (*parimāṇa*).
It is like the restriction regarding the measure of time for a seed to produce a sprout. So it is in the case of the manifestation of the true nature of a noble gem.

Nor is there a restriction on the number of perceptions, because what is intended is merely the manifestation of subtle distinctions in form—like one who has entered from a bright space into a dark chamber, or like twins. In the case of smoke and the like, however, it is not a distinction of form that is intended, but rather a distinction of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
For instance, even if there are hundreds of perceptions of blue and other forms, they do not [differ] prior to [the perception of] the more intense one.

[The senses] are capable of determining distinctions. Thus, prior to observing deviation (*vyabhicāra*), when two things—one deviant and one non-deviant—are presented as distinct objects, there is no determination of any difference in their form. In the case of smoke, however, it has been stated that the mind does not even perceive a distinction in its form; rather, it perceives it as having its existence dependent upon fire. For this very reason, the establishment [of the relationship] occurs through perception and non-perception operating only once.

[170,6] However, with respect to form (*rūpa*), even in the case of smoke, whatever the initial perception is like, even the final [perception] at the limit is exactly like that; it does not possess any distinction, unlike a gem.
[170,7] If the cognizer is free from doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in such a perception, then there is no need for a second perception.
[170,8] But one who harbors such doubt has no conviction even through a hundred perceptions; thus, the word "repeatedly" (*bhūyas*) in your mantra—
[170,9] What is the destiny of the reciter? Therefore, even one who has previously observed a hundredfold non-deviation remains in a state of doubt.
[170,10] As for the claim that "the conceptualization of something unperceived is impossible," this is merely the lamentation of a sleeping person.
[170,11] That is improper even for a child; for it is precisely of that which is unperceived that conceptualization occurs, as in the case of Primordial Matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), and so forth.

[170,12] However, the distinction is that some imagined [objects] conform to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while others do not. For a pot that is actually being perceived is not called "imagined.

Therefore, the conventional usage of imagination applies only to things that are not being perceived. In certain cases, however, there is a firm determination of existence due to the absence of sublation through such means as the word of a reliable authority (*āptavacana*). But for one who investigates, it remains merely tentative. Therefore, if even smoke...

[170,15] Deviation has indeed been observed; what doubt can there be in that regard? But when it has not been observed, then let there be no determination of its existence as a single part, since we are concerned with what is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). However, how can the mention of its existence as a possibility (*pākṣika*) be prevented? Now, if the intention is this:
non-perception is not intended here in that specific case alone, but rather, even elsewhere, that which is not perceived cannot be suspected—if this is your view, then consider fire... [170,17]

[170,18] Furthermore, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is indeed observed in the case of gold and other such things; let there be satisfaction with this. Now, if you say it is not observed in the case of smoke—well then, has "manhood" (*puruṣatva*) ever been observed in a post (*sthāṇu*), such that one would suspect it in a post? If you say it is observed in something characterized by verticality (*ūrdhvatā*), then here too, it is simply observed in another thing that frequently co-occurs (*sahacārin*). For this very reason, the statement beginning with "even though not being seen" (*na cādṛśyamāno ’pi*) and so forth is refuted. But in whatever case...

[170,21] Regarding that which is doubted, its observation is required in that very instance; thus, it is extraordinary (*alaukika*). Therefore, even if deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is not observed within the class of smoke, it cannot be negated by means of observation. This doubt, whose nature consists of a doubt regarding intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikatva*), necessarily obstructs the ascertainment of intrinsic connection for the time being. [Regarding] an intrinsic relation—

And how can smoke be a prover by virtue of its power (*bala*) if that [power] is not ascertained? For a reason (*hetu*) is not a prover merely by its existence in the subject (*dharmī*); it must be capable of being a prover even when there is doubt regarding its existence. And whatever proceeds despite doubt regarding something X necessarily proceeds even when X is absent. This applies to smoke as well as anything else, even apart from an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*).

[170,27] There would follow the consequence that anything could be a prover. Therefore, the connection with certainty is in fact nothing other than a connection based on essential nature (*svābhāvikatva*). This is because, without certainty, the factor that serves as a prover is itself incapable of effecting anything. Therefore: "For those who do not perceive a restrictive factor, there must necessarily be doubt regarding smoke even in the absence of fire" (PV III 324).

Thus, this is difficult to transcend so long as one does not rely upon that [absence of a sublating cognition] as the basis for its production. Nor is there, in this way, the reproach of overstepping the boundaries of the world of authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*). For no one asserts uncertainty regarding the domain of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor certainty in the absence of a means of valid cognition—just as you yourself assert certainty regarding non-existence even in the absence of a sublating means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*) due to the lack of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). Precisely for this reason, there is no room anywhere for the demon of doubt; [this applies] in the case of the absence of a means of valid cognition.

Because it has already been accepted as such. If you say that something can also be stated regarding the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then if there is a face, let it be said that it exists. However, if one speaks while accepting the characteristics of a means of valid cognition, then the answer is easy to give. But if it is otherwise, then that must be stated by the other party alone; we have no occasion for it, because for one who accepts a means of valid cognition, [the statement] must result in certainty.

The acceptance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance of certainty regarding its object, which is not subject to dispute. Otherwise, how could the demoness of doubt find an opportunity everywhere? You may simply say that the definition formulated by you is not a valid means of cognition; and that very point remains to be examined. Furthermore, if it is argued that even an unperceived limiting condition (*upādhi*) might be suspected in the case of smoke, then one must be a proponent of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

If it is argued that this constitutes a transgression of worldly practice (*lokyātrā*), we say no; for those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) have already prohibited the authority to refute through non-perception of the unperceivable (*ayogyānupalabdhi*). Otherwise, one would be offering a funeral libation to the means of achieving lordship, heaven, and so forth, since these too would be undermined. If it is argued that this fault does not apply because they are established by the valid means of inference and scripture (*anumāna-āgama*), we say no; for it has been proven in the demonstration of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) that once something has been refuted previously by non-perception, inferential and other such proofs cannot function as establishers.

Therefore, this mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi-mātra*), which results from the discernment (*viveka*) through the consideration of what precedes and what follows, is the means for establishing certainty.

Consequently, since there is no room for doubt regarding the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is incoherent to claim that one would never act toward anything. Nor is it the case that action does not occur simply because of suspicion; for action is unavoidable when there is doubt regarding the purpose, just as in the case of pleasant food and drink. However, this [objection] is raised by one who cites an example based on doubt concerning something useless.

Even the object of doubt regarding what is beneficial or harmful remains unknown; what more could be said than this? Moreover, this is not the subject at hand, for the subject under discussion is whether or not there can be doubt regarding the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And that has already been stated. Now, if this is the underlying intention: because smoke is observed never to deviate from fire, one might suspect that at some time smoke could exist even in its absence—this is the suspicion of harm (*anartha-śaṅkā*).

And since that [certainty of non-deviation] is a factor for cessation, the meaning is that one should set that aside and instead establish the cognition of an essential relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) alone;

just as, for example, one proceeds toward food and drink only after dispelling the suspicion of death. If this is so, then it is logical that even doubt regarding the object is a factor for engagement. For, through repeated observation of coexistence, non-deviation itself is indeed common, just as [the coexistence of] food and drink with life. Now, such...
If you say, "We speak only of that which is certain to be useless," then that [cognition] is indeed a motivator. Therefore, how can it be said that this [person] would not act at all?

Or else, how is even a doubt regarding uselessness a factor for desisting? And this [point] remains the same even if there is occasional deviation, just as in the case of begging for alms from one who gives only occasionally. Thus, the intrinsic connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) of smoke is well-established.

[171,28] Proof [is established]. Furthermore, the suspicion regarding what has been observed was already demonstrated previously. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "viśeṣa" (the particular) is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
[172,1] As for the statement beginning with "tad uktam" (so it has been said), this refers to taking a sick person and entering the fire.
For indeed, [172,2] as long as a cognition of sublation (*bādhājñāna*) has not arisen, there can be no groundless suspicion.

[172,4] If a subverting cognition (*bādhajñāna*) has arisen regarding the object being delineated, or if there is a validating means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then what room is there for doubt? For that [doubt] consists in uncertainty, whereas a validating or subverting cognition establishes a definitive conclusion. [172,6] Now, if it is intended that no subverting cognition—such as one caused by cataracts (*timira*)—arises with respect to the sense faculties, that is irrelevant; for [the issue at hand is] not the nature of smoke and so forth...
[172,7] Is it not rather the lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is suspected, and not non-establishment (*asiddhi*)?

[172,8] And what is the meaning of "lacking a means of valid cognition" (*niṣpramāṇikā*)? If you mean the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*), then what is the point of the suspicion? [172,9] Or does it refer to the object being delineated by the suspicion? Does that [object] exist in that very place, or elsewhere? Even if elsewhere, would it be in something of the same class (*sajātīya*)?

Or [is it] in another thing in general? First of all, the first position is not consistent with the context. Or let it be so; nevertheless, regarding the cognition of that other thing, the means of proof—whether it be mental perception (*mānasa*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—is not exhausted by this [absence]. It has been stated that the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhakapramāṇa*) in the case under discussion merely proves the suspicion itself. As for the means of knowledge regarding something else of the same class...

[172,13] But this is the meaning of the term *bhāva*: that which is suspected to be the independence of smoke from fire is understood by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to belong to that same class (*tajjātīya*). [172,14] In that regard, "belonging to that same class" may be considered either with respect to individual instances (*vyakti*) or with respect to the universal (*jāti*). [172,15] First, with respect to individual instances, another instance of smoke itself belongs to that same class. And if its non-dependence on fire is cognized, then, because there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*), [the inference holds].

In this way, smoke becomes a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) because it is excluded from pervasion. What, then, is the point here in introducing a doubt regarding the exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*)? If it is argued: "Even when fire is not known, since there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*), why should there be a doubt? [The answer is: Because the absence of deviation is not established by mere non-perception; rather, absence is established only through the non-apprehension of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).

Because the context concerns proof (*sādhana*), there is room for doubt that, due to frequent co-occurrence alone, a thing might be neither definitely non-deviant nor definitely deviant. However, with respect to genus (*jāti*), the genus of smoke is indeed distinct from other genera; yet, by some proximity such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, it is considered homogeneous (*sajātīya*). Therefore, it has already been stated that when the intended subject (*pakṣa*)—such as water and the like—is encountered, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed. And this [latter case] alone is logical.

[172,22] This is the position. In the investigation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding smoke, because the determination proceeds by unifying smoke that is spatially and temporally remote, the observation of what is suspected is appropriate only within the same class (*jātyantara*). Even with that much, there is no loss of the fact that memory is preceded by direct experience (*anubhava*).
[172,24] Otherwise, this syllable would be non-expressive apart from the first position and would be useless therein; thus, this [objection] is trivial.

[172,25] For one who perceives no subverting factor (*bādhaka*), even the state of being characterized by doubt is merely the prattle of a child. Indeed, it has been stated that the perception of a subverting factor is opposed to doubt because it consists of certainty (*niścaya*). Nor is a subverting factor something that results in non-certainty. Therefore, where there is an absence of such a factor, for us there is no doubt; so how could there be the nature of doubt in all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*)? Or if—

What is intended here is not that one "imagines" (*utprekṣate*) a sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding smoke’s dependence on *uṣarbudha* (fire); rather, it should be understood as follows: the very doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding its lack of necessary connection (*apratibaddhatva*) with fire is stated to be the sublation, because it contradicts the ascertainment of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Even so, the phrase "one might imagine" (*utprekṣeta*) is contradictory;

for the meaning of "imagination" (*utprekṣā*) is conceptual construction (*vikalpana*), and it is not the case that the conceptualization of doubt itself—which is already of the nature of conceptual construction—is what is under discussion.

[173,4] However, production is logical. Even then, the qualification "unborn" is purposeless, because it is incoherent to speak of the production of that which has already been born. Alternatively, [173,5] if one were to suspect that even what is unborn, non-existent, and unreal could be a cognizable object (*prameya*)—such as dependence on fire and so forth—and might imagine it to subvert its own opposite, [173,6] meaning one might bring it forward by mere imagination; even then, if one were to establish that unreality by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and proceed in this manner...

One might say: everything would be commendable; yet there is no means of proof for this reckless person other than verbal abuse (*ākrośa*). Furthermore, if one becomes a fit object for abuse simply by conjecturing something beyond what is commonly established, then why would it not be the truth for one who conjectures a "natural connection" (*svābhāvikasambandha*) and so forth, in order to dispel the suspicion of the reason occurring in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣavṛttiśaṅkā*) within a discourse on pervasion (*vyāpti*) that is established merely through observation and non-observation?

Furthermore, for one who asserts that this very relation is perceptible by the senses—which contradicts its being graspable by the mind—or who asserts that the proofs against an omniscient being, such as "being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth, are valid; or for one who asserts that the meaning of words like *ūrva* and *asi*, which are well-established, is actually a cooking vessel and so on—which contradicts their conventional meaning; or rather, for this very person who has devised such an unprecedented weapon of abuse, intended to strike down the assembly of Buddhist doubts—[it is as follows].
[173,13] It is appropriate that the first [step] be the attainment of cessation (*kṣayagamana*).

[173,14] If it is argued that this is desired for one who gives rise to doubt, [we reply: surely he has already failed, because he gives rise to a doubt that had not arisen previously. [173,15] Furthermore, why would he not be at fault for giving rise to a certainty—brought about by either a proving or a subverting factor—which likewise had not arisen previously? [173,16] Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)...

If you argue that certainty is difficult to overcome because of the [reliability of] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then in their absence, doubt would likewise be difficult to overcome; enough, then, with this overly prolix discussion. Therefore, how could anyone who is not insane—having reflected on what precedes and follows—propound doubt regarding something other than the object of a *pramāṇa* out of delusion? For if certainty, which is bound to a *pramāṇa*, were to occur even in the absence of that [means], for what purpose would one exert effort?

The investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) belongs to the discerning person; or rather, the exertion of the authors of treatises is for the purpose of refuting misconceptions regarding them. Therefore, since doubt necessarily arises when the means of valid cognition are absent, how can it be refuted by mere denial? Even if this is so, nevertheless, because there is no other alternative and because one generally observes concomitance in worldly practice, yet fails to observe it even once—

[173,22] Regarding deviation: having rendered what is delineated by conceptual construction—namely, an unfulfilled doubt—as if it were non-existent, one must proceed with certainty alone, not with doubt.
[173,23–24] To this it is replied: Does the causal relationship exist as established by valid cognition in reality, or not? If it does exist, it is restricted—

[173,25] Or else, the object is otherwise. If one takes the position that it is not so, then everything collapses without effort, because there would be no scope for either proof or refutation; this has been analyzed in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅga*. Furthermore, even if it were existent, if its object were indefinite, then it would be as if non-existent; this is explained at length in the treatise. Nor can it be said that those seeking heaven and the like must necessarily follow the Veda, God, and so forth, because it would follow that even the killing of a Brahmin and similar acts would result in obtaining that [heaven].
Therefore, since that [invariable concomitance] exists, has a restricted object, and is established by the aforementioned means of perception and non-perception, it must necessarily be accepted.

Since certainty is thereby established, the absence of any other alternative is proven. Without that [concomitance], there would be no basis for establishing an essential connection (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). As for the argument beginning with "though one searches with effort," even in that case, there is the search for deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
In this way, we understand the search for a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it is impossible to establish a limiting condition without deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Therefore, as long as smoke is observed, the process of investigation is not concluded because it is undermined by the suspicion of deviation; this has already been stated. Otherwise, what would be the meaning of the phrase "being sought with effort"? It refers to non-deviation occurring on a few occasions—
[174,6] For if [the object] were made a domain of experience, what kind of cessation would there be in the other [world]?

[174,7] Even that which has been prattled about, beginning with "it might be thus" and so forth, is likewise devoid of substance. For when a form is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is an apprehension of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

[174,8] However, the determination of the nature of a thing does not occur solely through the force of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*). Therefore, if [there were] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding a restricted object—

If the causal relationship is established by the means of valid cognition consisting in the perception of the apprehender and the non-perception [of the non-apprehender], then what has come of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) regarding an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*)? In that case, having mentally cast aside the totality of conditions for the cognition of "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), when there is a cognition based on the lack of distinction between two things that coexist elsewhere, the very means of such cognition becomes most remote. And if one depends upon that totality of conditions, it is simply "origination from that."

What is the point of this boastful assertion involving the invention of another name? In this regard, the process up to the final apprehension by means of the sense faculty assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced from repeated observation has already been refuted by the previous critique.
Furthermore, as for this [argument] that doubt depends upon the perception of specific features...

"From the perception of common characteristics, from the non-perception of specific characteristics, and from the recollection of specific characteristics, doubt arises" (VSū 2.2.19). By not accepting this definition of doubt, he [the opponent] evades it. In that case, is it because of the fear of violating the definition that one maintains that there can never be a cognition with two aspects regarding what is not an object of valid cognition? Or rather, is it intended that even if there were two aspects, it would not be doubt?

[174,19] Now, whether there be doubt from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) or not, we nevertheless employ the convention of "doubt" because our own defining characteristics have ceased; such are the positions. First of all, the first [position] is impossible. For when there is an absence of both a definitive proof and a refutation regarding a form delineated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—such as the thought, "Is this true or not? like news of a beloved's arrival tomorrow—a conceptual construction that delineates both sides [of the doubt]...

[174,22] Because even by the command of a king one is unable to prevent birth; for bodily and verbal activities can indeed be forcibly altered into something else through fear and the like, even when the mind is otherwise directed. But the manifestation of the mind (*cittavivarta*), which arises through the gateway of valid or invalid cognition, cannot be so altered. This, however, may be the case: because a single part is perceived more frequently, that limb appears as if fully developed; but another [part] is [perceived] due to absolute incapacity.

[174,25] The portion is as if exhausted. However, in the absence of such a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), both [aspects] are common to both cases. Just as in that house, the state of having two aspects—namely, "Is there a crow or is there not?"—does not disappear anywhere. That very thing is the object of doubt;
thus, the second [position] is also untenable. Otherwise, being distinguished from error and correct cognition by way of the forms of non-ascertainment and ascertainment, [it would be distinct].

If there is no doubt, then why is this a fourth category? Therefore, let this fault belong to the definition itself for failing to grasp it; the object of definition (*lakṣya*) cannot be altered. For this very reason, even the last [category] is not useful. If it is established that cognition which relies on both parts depends upon a one-sided operation, then what is the point of your Honor’s [effort], since the natural relation (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is not established by that much alone?

[175,4] With respect to the conventional usage of "doubt," enough with this talk like that of a child. [175,5] As for the refutation of mental [cognition], let it be a case of proving what is already established; what is the use of further exertion here? [175,6] Regarding the capacity to indicate [the probandum] through an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), it is indeed a case of proving what is already established. And it has been established that this [connection] is characterized solely by origination from that (*tadutpatti*). And thus:

[175,7] Because the efficacy of repeated observation is undermined, other means of knowledge that rely upon it should be understood as sterile for establishing an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) with the object of perception. Rather, one must infer the inferential mark (*anumāna*) that serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary case;

for in its absence, it is impossible to negate the presence [of the reason] in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), just as [the reason] "being his son" cannot prove "darkness of complexion. Furthermore, regarding what was said here concerning food—

[175,10] The response that there is an absence of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) because of the existence of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting in the difference in the digestion of drink is not tenable.

[175,11] This is because there is no certainty regarding the status of the difference in the digestion of food as a limiting condition. For just as smoke does not arise from mere fire in the absence of fuel, fuel is said to be the limiting condition for the connection between smoke and fire; likewise, if for some [person] born of Maitra...

[175,13] Because of the absence of the intended transformation of the food, blackness will be apprehended. If that limiting condition (*upādhi*) were to be excluded, then what would be the use of speaking of a limiting condition? For it would suffice merely to say that "being Maitra’s son" is not a prover because of its deviation (*vyabhicāra*). But this cannot be established. [175,14] Therefore, how is this limiting condition certain? Could it be that, due to Maitra’s own aspirations in another birth, even seven or eight... [175,15] (sons were born)?

[175,16] Since sons with dark bodies are being seen, what proof is there that they were not born [from such causes]? In that case, one might suspect the mother’s or even the sons’ own *praṇidhāna* (vow/intention). Furthermore, if their merit (*puṇya*) and *praṇidhāna* are not firm, the efficacy of a difference in diet is also conceivable. Therefore, the very doubt as to what is the cause of their darkness constitutes an inference based on the suspicion of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). [175,18] It is invalid.

[175,19] He explains: What is the point of this certainty? Now, with this final proof for dark complexion, the matter is concluded. How is it that you are not afraid of raising the demon of doubt by squeezing your belly to render the reason "being his son" a non-reason—a reason that has been excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), rests upon the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), possesses an uncontradicted object, and is an unopposed reason? Therefore, regarding the dark complexion resulting from being his son—

Since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), and since non-existence cannot be established by mere non-perception in the case of "non-blackness," the reason is simply invalid; this alone is correct. What is the use of this useless赘疣 (*antargaḍu*) talk of "limiting conditions" (*upādhi*)?
Furthermore, one must admit that the defect of a reason consisting in its doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is indeed a real one. It is not...

Otherwise, it would be impossible to remove the status of this [reason] as being "beautiful in all its parts" (*sarvāṅgasundara*). Furthermore, if you do not accept this, then when you seek to prove that a diamond (*vajra*) can be scratched by iron by means of the reason "being composed of earth" (*pārthivatva*), what *upādhi* (limiting condition) are you observing that leads you to reject the inference?
If you say that the immersion of an iron point is observed in things like wood, whose parts are loose, whereas a diamond is firm, then...

If it is argued that this is due to a limiting condition (*upādhi*), it is not so. Indeed, we do not perceive any difference between a hundred-edged diamond (*sphaṭika*) and a crystal (*ghana*) by virtue of their having dense parts, such that iron which is not obstructed by the sun-gem (*taraṇimaṇi*) would be obstructed by it.
It might be said: "Iron is indeed observed to be obstructed when applied to a diamond (*vajra*). But for whom...?

[176,2] A proof that functions either by subverting the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) or by establishing the probandum itself has not been undertaken against such a person; for whom, however, [176,3] there exists merely the act of making the "hundred peaks" the subject (*pakṣa*), how could inference be avoided by him even when the determination of an essential connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) has occurred, due to his lack of awareness of the condition (*upādhi*)? This has already been stated. Now, even if no other condition is perceived in the case of being produced from clay (*pārthivatva*), there is one inherent to itself... [176,4]

If it is argued that there will be some specific quality (*viśeṣa*) or limiting condition (*upādhi*) because of which there is no property of being scratchable by iron, then the demoness of doubt, having found her opportunity, will pursue even smoke. She will say: "There will also be some specific quality inherent in smoke by which it could exist without fire. But surely, even when we search with great effort, we do not perceive such a thing in smoke?

[176,8] One understands that the limiting condition (*upādhi*) possesses a specific characteristic inherent to itself; for instance, in the case of a diamond (*vajra*), which is a type of earth-element, we understand this from its ability to cut through iron.

[176,9] Now, is that cutting of iron performed when the inference has already proceeded for the sake of a purpose? Or is it by chance? Or perhaps [176,10] out of a desire to know? In the first case, since a great accomplishment of purpose results from the inference, another such inference would likewise be required.

[176,11] According to you, there is no such exertion as that required for a definitive determination through writing; or rather, let it be that this [writing] is not an inference, but how could another [inference] be so? For the desire to know [the nature of things] would have no scope at all. For instance, among the earthy substances—clay, wood, stone, and iron—even when one observes millions of instances of iron being submerged in millions of [other] iron objects, no deviation is seen; therefore, [the property] is inherent (*svābhāvika*).

[176,14] For one who has dispelled doubt regarding deviation by means of an inference that delineates the determination of the connection, what room is there for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) that is preceded by such [perception]?

[176,15] Otherwise, even upon perceiving smoke wafting from a mountain slope from the top of a palace, one who possesses the cognition of an intrinsic connection through repeated observation would have only the desire to know in that case as well, rather than inference. Therefore, in every respect, inference—

[176,17] It is simply a matter of exclusion. When a correspondence has occurred on a few occasions, because the natural connection (*svābhāvikasambandha*) has been ascertained, inference from smoke follows at a later time. It is not the case that one must wait for correspondence throughout one's entire life, as is the case with "earthiness" (*pārthivatva*) and so forth; such a person is one whose wisdom is truly praiseworthy.
[176,19] Now, even regarding earthiness, since a gradation of hardness is observed, it is possible that in some cases the capacity to be scratched (*lekhyatā*) might also be absent.

[176,20] Thus, even with further agreement, there is no inference of "earthiness" and so forth. If it is argued that in the case of smoke, however, no gradation of independence from fire is observed, [176,21] we reply: surely "independence from fire" must be stated as nothing other than the cessation of fire. And it is not the case that where an absolute cessation is about to occur, there must necessarily have been a prior observation of a gradation of cessation, as in the case of a man in shackles; for this occurs only at the very end, in a few moments. [176,22]
[176,23] This will also apply to smoke. It is not merely a conjunction of smoke and fire as two things established separately, like a man and his shackles.

[176,24] Rather, since smoke is born from fire alone, there is no suspicion of its cessation even at the end. However, if one does not touch upon such specific characteristics, [176,25] there is indeed suspicion. Therefore, the nature of smoke—which is distinct from fire—or the quality of being scratchable by iron in earthy [substances], is not observed directly.

Furthermore, since the perception of perversion (*viparyaya*) is common to both cases, there is no establishment of an essential (*svābhāvika*) connection fixed to one side alone. And if there is no determination of adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), then inference is the same as non-inference.

However, when it is the very fact of being produced from that (*tadutpatti*) which establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the case of smoke, then because there is no difference [in this case], it does not apply to what is earthen (*pārthiva*).

Nor is there identity [between the two], because it is unestablished that "this very thing has 'scratchability by iron' as its essence," since it is impossible to demonstrate an inference that sublates the contrary. This is just like the case of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*).
Furthermore, perception functions only with respect to specific types (*jāti*); therefore, scratchability by iron is found only in those earth-substances where it has been observed.

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) does not occur elsewhere; therefore, smoke, being a product (*kṛtakatva*), and the like, are valid reasons (*hetu*). However, being made of earth (*pārthivatva*) or being someone’s son (*tatputratva*) and the like are fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), because their exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. The same applies to such cases as "originating from that branch" and so forth. This is because, depending on factors such as contact with wind and sun intensified by the first sprouting, there is the possibility of doubt regarding the absence of ripening even in something originating from a single branch. Thus, for some things, there is no pervasion with another object.

If repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) in the positive instance (*sapakṣa*) were the means [of establishing pervasion], then exclusion from the counter-instance (*vipakṣa*) would not be established merely by its non-observation; furthermore, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed in such cases, smoke and other such reasons would not be conclusive (*ekāntika*) for proving the probandum due to their doubtful exclusion from the counter-instance.
As for the doctrine of "intrinsic nature" (*svābhāvika*) and so forth, it should be avoided like filth smeared on the heart, being based merely on the superficial passion of the *ḍiṇḍika* [fools].
It has been established that no additional meaning beyond the mere fact of appropriation by another is being conveyed.

Therefore, when there is difference, the cognition of causal origination (*tadutpatti*) itself is the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that [cognition] occurs precisely through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
[Objection: Let it be that the cognition of pervasion is the cognition of causal origination when there is difference; however, it does not occur through perception and non-perception.

Because perception is restricted to the apprehension of the present moment, and because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) has that same nature; and as for what was stated regarding the sense-cognition’s possession of all specific features of its own class by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), even there, what is called "determination" is nothing other than the immediately preceding conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the claim that perception becomes omniscient through the power of that [determination] is merely a borrowed ornament. It would be better [to say] "smoke [is the mark] of fire."

Thus, let it be accepted that conceptual construction alone—having as its object the two types of universals characterized by all individual instances of both [classes]—is the grasper of their existence, whether it be considered a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or another form of perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that this is because it apprehends what was not previously apprehended, and because it occurs at the time of the operation of perception, that too is insubstantial. For even in conceptual construction, the state of having all things as its object is merely a matter of cognitive determination (*adhyavasāya*), since there is no manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Because it manifests only its own form by merely imitating the shadow of a single exclusion (*ekavyāvṛtti*), what kind of distinction does this have from perception (*pratyakṣa*)? It is simply that, in relation to the subsequent continuum beginning with the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) corresponding to itself, the determination of the object (*viṣayādhyavasāya*) is established in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*). In perception, however, there is a difference in that it takes even that conceptualization into account. [This applies to] all things—

But contact (*sparśa*) does not exist even in a single instance; nor is there any other mode of apprehension (*grāhaka-prakāra*), as has already been discussed. Therefore, within the realm of conventional discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*), it is established that the determination of an object (*viṣaya-vyavasthāna*) by means of conceptual ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) is unavoidable, and this is common to both direct experience (*anubhava*) and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, regarding the causal relationship (*hetu-phala-bhāva*) made an object of perception, mental discourse (*mānasa-vyavahāra*)— [The text continues: ...is established. Furthermore, since the nature of the object is determined through conceptual ascertainment, and because the capacity for action (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) is the defining characteristic of reality, the establishment of the object is necessarily linked to the ascertainment of its causal efficacy. Consequently, even when an object is directly perceived, its status as an object is finalized only through subsequent conceptualization. This is why, in the context of sensory perception, the mental activity that follows the initial sensation is indispensable for the practical application of the term "object. Thus, the distinction between the object and the subject is maintained through the mediation of conceptual determination, which bridges the gap between the raw sensory datum and its meaningful identification. This process ensures that our linguistic and practical conventions remain grounded in the objective world, despite the fact that the immediate experience itself is devoid of such conceptual elaborations. Therefore, the validity of perceptual objects depends upon this inextricable connection between the non-conceptual apprehension and the subsequent conceptual judgment. In this way, the framework of conventional truth is preserved, allowing for the coherent functioning of human cognition and communication based on the objects presented to the senses. This concludes the discussion on how the object is established through the synthesis of experience and conceptualization. Now, let us consider the specific role of mental discourse in this process. As previously noted, the causal relationship between the sense faculty and its object is first grasped through direct perception. However, the full realization of this relationship—and the subsequent engagement with the world—requires the intervention of mental discourse. Without this mental activity, the mere presence of an object would remain unapprehended in a meaningful sense, as the mind would lack the capacity to categorize and interpret the sensory data. Thus, mental discourse serves as the necessary medium through which the causal structure of the external world is internalized and integrated into our cognitive life. By means of this mental operation, the raw material of perception is transformed into a determinate object of knowledge, thereby enabling the continuity of human experience and action. This demonstrates that the establishment of objects in conventional reality is not merely a function of the senses, but is fundamentally dependent upon the conceptual and linguistic activities of the mind. Through this interplay, the Buddhist epistemological system accounts for the emergence of a structured world from the flux of immediate sensations. This analysis underscores the central role of conceptual ascertainment in bridging the gap between the ineffable nature of ultimate reality and the requirements of conventional truth. In sum, the determination of objects through conceptual ascertainment is an indispensable feature of our cognitive engagement with the world, ensuring that our perceptions are not merely passive reflections but active constructions that guide our practical conduct. This concludes the examination of how mental discourse operates within the context of perceptual objects and their causal foundations. Now, we shall turn our attention to the specific characteristics of conceptual construction and its relationship to direct experience. As we have seen, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is distinct from the non-conceptual apprehension of direct perception. Nevertheless, it is through this conceptualization that the objects of perception acquire their definitive status. This raises an important question: if conceptual construction is inherently distinct from direct experience, how can it be said to be "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) to both? To address this, we must examine the nature of the conceptual process and its capacity to reflect the content of sensory experience. While conceptual construction involves the synthesis of mental images and linguistic categories, it is nonetheless constrained by the data provided by direct perception. In this sense, conceptual construction is "common" to both experience and thought insofar as it is rooted in the sensory input. This shared basis allows for the seamless transition from the immediate givenness of an object to its conceptual identification. Furthermore, the causal relationship between the sense faculty and its object, which is initially grasped through perception, is further refined and stabilized by conceptual construction. This stabilization is essential for the practical utility of our cognitions. Without it, our experiences would remain fragmented and disjointed, lacking the coherence required for effective action. Thus, while conceptual construction may distort or simplify the raw data of perception, it is nevertheless indispensable for the formation of a stable and meaningful world. This dual nature of conceptual construction—both derivative of perception and capable of shaping it—highlights the complex interplay between the two modes of cognition. It is precisely this interplay that allows for the dynamic and evolving nature of human understanding. By recognizing the limitations of conceptual construction while acknowledging its necessity, we gain a deeper appreciation of the Buddhist epistemological project. This project seeks to navigate the tension between the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), using conceptual tools to point toward the ineffable reality beyond them. In doing so, it provides a sophisticated account of how we come to know the world, emphasizing the role of conceptual ascertainment in mediating between the two truths. This concludes the exploration of the relationship between direct experience and conceptual construction. We now turn to the implications of this analysis for the theory of inference (*anumāna*) and the role of mental discourse in logical reasoning. As we have established, the establishment of objects relies heavily on conceptual ascertainment. This reliance extends to the domain of inference, where the relationship between the reason (*hetu*) and the consequence (*phala*) is determined through conceptual processes. Mental discourse is thus central to the formulation of logical arguments and the validation of inferential knowledge. By examining the role of mental discourse in inference, we can further elucidate the mechanisms by which conceptual construction contributes to our cognitive life. This will involve a detailed analysis of the criteria for valid reasons and the nature of the logical connection between them. Through this investigation, we will gain a clearer understanding of how conceptual thought functions as a bridge between perception and reasoning, ensuring the integrity of our cognitive processes. This concludes the section on the role of mental discourse in the establishment of objects and the causal relationship between sense faculties and their objects. We shall now proceed to the next topic. Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and memory are not valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Even by way of a single part, perception (*adhyakṣa*) is established as grasping the entire class of similar things through contact with the whole; this is not the case for conceptual construction, which by its very nature lacks external objects.
Therefore, it is established that the proof of the essential pervasion (*svabhāvavyāpti*) of the relation between cause and effect is possible only through perception and non-perception.
The treatise titled *Vyāpticarcā* is completed.
This work is the composition of the great scholar, the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra.
Examination of Difference and Non-Difference [179,3] (1b) || Homage to the Buddha ||
[179,4] Desiring to avoid falling into either of the two individual positions, the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), which is resorted to by some, is now examined.

[179,5] In this regard, does this have the nature of a conjunction of both, or is it of the nature of the absence of those two? If it is an absence, is it a mere negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or is it another entity through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? Is that too a third form opposed to the two under discussion, or—

[179,7] Is it something entirely irrelevant? [179,8] Regarding that, in the first position, if those very same distinctions and non-distinctions—which were previously swallowed by the net of various faults—are now asserted to reside in a single entity, or if they are asserted to be different from it: if they are identical to it, then because its refutation necessarily follows, the admission is futile.

Even if they were distinct, just as that defect applies, there would likewise be no persistence of the quality. Perhaps you think: "I shall avoid the defect of the consequence of separate cognition—which arises on the side of the position of difference—by accepting non-difference. Thus, you accept non-difference even while there is difference. And if that very same non-difference, which sublates the perception of separateness, has now been brought forward, then such an avoidance of the defect might indeed occur; however, it is merely a case of sharing the same fate (*ekayogakṣema*).

[179,13] Because of their identity (*samāveśa*), it would also entail the non-occurrence of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Therefore, if one were not to entail this by way of its being something else, then for that very reason, one could not even establish the negation of separate perception. [179,14] Now, if the result of identity is merely the sublation of separate perception, and not the inherent nature of the exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāvṛtti*), even so, the admission of duality is fruitless. The same should be said regarding the position of difference (*bheda*) as well.

Now, if it is argued that the sublation by separate apprehension (*pṛthagupalabdhibādha*) alone is the result for non-difference (*abheda*), whereas the occurrence and cessation of other words is the result for difference (*bheda*)— for even that [difference], being possible, must indeed produce its own effect— then likewise, for difference as well, dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) alone is the result, while the sublation by separate apprehension is the result for non-difference.

It is said: both are observed to be the effect of both. For difference (*bheda*), there is the fault of the undesirable consequence that it would have to appear separately, whereas its dependence on other words is an advantage. For non-difference (*abheda*), there is the fault of the undesirable consequence that it would depend on other words, whereas its non-separate manifestation is an advantage. Therefore, in this case, one must remain with the mere occurrence of other words through difference; but as for the second effect—

One must consider the counter-strike of the opponent. Even when producing an appearance together with that which is non-different, what is the basis for the distinction between a counter-strike in one effect and [the original action]? It is due to the fact that entities conform to your own intention;
or because attraction and aversion toward qualities and defects arise spontaneously; or because of the possibility of a temporal difference between the two natures and their effects.

In that case as well, is the sequence of qualities and defects fixed or unfixed? Regarding the first alternative, either the position of difference or non-difference, by imparting only its own specific quality, will remain untouched by refutation; nor will any refutation be brought against it.
So why has this adherence to dualism been undertaken by one ignorant of the means of self-cognition? Furthermore, because entities are devoid of consciousness, they possess no intention.
[180,3] Conformity.

[180,4] For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable. Granted that there may be affection and so forth toward inequality; however, that would apply to one who either benefits or harms oneself, but nothing is harmed by these [words] through the relationship of signifier and signified, nor is anything benefited by the difference in their appearance.

[180,5] It is by means of the other. However, the employment of the terms "quality" (*guṇa*) and "defect" (*doṣa*) is made out of deference to you. Therefore, even if that which is devoid of following after them were to exist in such a state, it would not matter at all; or, if it does not follow after them, consciousness has already been explained [as being impossible].
[180,7] This might be the case: that the conformity to intention occurs by its very nature, just like the operation of the collection of instruments that are the causes for the arising of sound.
Nevertheless, the acceptance of duality is indeed a non-apprehension. It has already been stated that why not simply assume such an operation for a single nature?
Nor is the proposal of a third alternative tenable; for if there is a difference in time between two natures, then when there is no difference—

[180,11] Then there would be non-difference; and at the time of non-difference, there is no difference. Thus, there would never be a refutation of the opponent's fault. In that regard, just as in the case of an object—whether distinct or non-distinct—the effects such as synonymy, which necessarily arise from absolute difference or non-difference, are not obstructed, [180,13] so too [these effects] do not obtain when there is a difference in time between two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), because of the absence of their respective opposites. Nor [is it the case] by means of what is yet to be.

[180,14] Negation is not a real entity (*avastu*). Therefore, there is a distinction between its own time and the time of its effect; this must be accepted as a refuge. In that regard, as soon as a distinction, having established itself through the operation of another word, begins to establish a difference in appearance, it is simultaneously obstructed by being subsumed under non-difference.
Who, then, being so confounded by logic, would dare to propose such a thing—a mere product of his own hand—to you, who are the sole ground of audacity?
[180,17] Without an interval? For there is indeed a difference in time between two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

And for what entity would that [difference] be difficult to find? Indeed, it is not logical for that which arises later to belong to that very same [entity], because even in that case, each [moment] possesses a difference in time due to being devoid of any consideration of a cause. It is not...

For this would indeed be logical if there were a dependence on a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*); even in that case, the sequence of performing desired effects and avoiding defects would remain fixed. However, since there would otherwise be the consequence of falling into a precipice due to a lack of restriction, it is clear that one whose heart is carried away by mere desire does not perceive anything at all and thus deserves to be disregarded. Indeed, we do not observe any cause here other than his own will. Moreover, when—

If the admission of difference occurs after the difference [has already been established], then who can prevent the second effect of non-difference, which subverts the perception of distinctness? If you say "by difference," no; for if that difference is another factor arising at a later time, then yet another must be sought to eliminate its own defects, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is by the prior [difference], then if such is its power...

[180,25] How could that which is subsequently presented without distinction, appearing as non-separate, not produce a binding [cognition]? If, in relation to the former, the latter possesses the quality of sublation (*apavādakatva*), one must consider why this is not the case in relation to what precedes even further. Therefore, since each [instance] performs both functions, the claim that there is either an exclusive exclusion or an exclusive acceptance of difference and non-difference is groundless. Consequently, [the object remains] separate.

It would follow that for a single entity, appearance and non-appearance, simultaneous arising and non-arising, and the occurrence or non-occurrence of other words and so forth, would all apply at one and the same time.

Furthermore, there is not even a trace of experience of the adjunct as distinct from the possessor of the adjunct; nor do others admit that even a fraction of the individual instance remains when the individual is destroyed, in the case of a universal.

If it is argued that it is indeed intended [to exist] in the form of a manifestation (*vyakti*), surely "in the form of a manifestation" is intended to mean "not in its own form" (*nijena rūpeṇa*); otherwise, the qualification would be purposeless. Since this dilemma arises when considering the difference or non-difference of the very form itself, what has been resolved by this? Furthermore, if no other form whatsoever is possible for it, then of what [is the difference or non-difference being considered]?

The investigation into difference and non-difference establishes that phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of limiting conditions (*nirupādhi*). Now, one might object: "Even if non-difference were possible for that which is different, we recognize the futility of other words; what can be done about this? If so, then even for one who says, "Even though a limiting condition is different, its manifestation (*prakāśa*) is not different—what can be done about this?", there is no fault even in the doctrine of non-duality (*ekāntavāda*). Nevertheless, the recourse to the theory of duality (*dvaitavāda*) is ultimately futile.
Because the "stretching out of the feet" (i.e., the evasion) has not been avoided; rather, only excessive exhaustion or mere bravado is being displayed.

Furthermore, it might be argued that when opponents charge one who accepts identity with faults such as the non-exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāvṛtti*), then the possibility of difference (*bheda*) serves as the rebuttal. And when there is difference, the introduction of non-difference (*abheda*) occurs upon the production of a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*).

Thus, it is not possible in the case of an extremist position (*ekāntavāda*), nor is it a case of "stretching out one's legs" (i.e., a lazy or unexamined approach), nor does the consequence of both faults follow. For when difference (*bheda*) was previously introduced, and once the fault attached to that has been uprooted, non-difference (*abheda*) is then introduced.
If it is argued that there is no harm even if there is no finality due to this succession of repeated cycles?
In that case, it follows that the subverting or proving property being presented by you does not function through its own inherent capacity alone.

Furthermore, if the application (*upanaya*) were not expressed within the verbal formulation itself, then even fire (*uṣarbudha*) would not be a subverter for you. By this, the argument "because it is not accepted by me" for the sake of a reductio (*prasaṅga*) is also refuted; for it cannot be said that poison being consumed for the sake of survival does not kill.
Therefore, for those of dull intellect who desire to avoid both extremes, this grasping at both sides is like a pair of wooden bolts.
The formal argument is as follows: whatever has a specific cause necessarily occurs when that cause is present, just as, for example, visual perception and so forth.

The arising of cognition has as its cause merely the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), and the aforementioned collection of faults depends merely upon difference and non-difference; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Being caused by that alone is pervaded by independence from anything else; and even when that [causal complex] is present, if the effect were absent, there would be dependence on something else, which is the opposite of that [independence].

Therefore, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), the property of being caused by that alone—being excluded from the contrary—is established in that [subject].

When the entity exists, it is necessarily restricted; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established. Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because this depends solely upon that [entity]. For no cause for simultaneous arising is logically possible other than non-difference (*abheda*). Or, if distinct manifestation were visible, nothing other than mere difference (*bheda*) would suffice.
Even in the case of an iron ball and fire, or milk and water, where there is difference, the non-arising of a distinction in manifestation is established as being dependent on something else.

If you ask why, it is not so, because non-erroneous sensory cognition (*abhrāntendriyajñāna*) is the subject under discussion. In that case, how can a cognition that presents two distinct things as one be called non-erroneous? By this, the appearance of two moons is also explained. Now, suppose that single object were produced by both causes.
The notion that "it has arisen" exists; therefore, since there is no deviation whatsoever, it is established that [the effect] depends solely on that [cause]. It might be argued:

"Even for that which depends solely on that [cause], its occurrence is necessarily tied to the existence of that [cause], just as bile and phlegm arise from substances that are pungent and sweet respectively. This is incorrect, because substances can produce effects other than those [typically associated with them] even when considering their potency (*vīrya*) and post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*).
[182,7] Because bile and so forth transgress by depending on the mere presence of taste.
The Examination of Difference and Non-difference is completed.
In this *Anupalabdhirahasyam*,

a clear compendium is provided here of that very nature of non-apprehension which, according to our established doctrine, is scattered throughout various works and resides within the definition [of negation].

When negation is the probandum, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the third logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, if that [non-apprehension] were merely the absence of apprehension, how could there be the cognition of anything, or how could it be the cause of cognition? Furthermore, how could there even be a cognition of it? Therefore, like [the term] "non-eatable" and so forth, non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of something else through the function of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

In that case as well, if it were the negation of anything other [than the perceived object], then upon the perception of any single thing, there would follow the negation of everything. If it is argued, "The negation of identity with everything is indeed intended," then the negation of its location is also unavoidable. This, therefore, is the distinction.

For when there is a cognition regarding an object of knowledge that necessarily [occurs] or does not occur, the wise accept that as non-perception; it is the basis for the establishment of the knowledge of the absence of anything else.

When something is being cognized, the thought "it might exist" serves as the negation of those things remote in space, time, or nature. By the word "necessarily," the absence of any deficiency in other causes of perception is indicated. By this, it is shown that the establishment of the cognition of non-existence applies only to that which has attained the status of being a "perceptible object" (*dṛśyaviśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence of negating everything.

And when something is being perceived, whatever cognition necessarily arises regarding it—that alone is accepted as the "cognition" [of that object], because it is capable of inducing a continuous determination of the non-existence of a second, other thing. By this, it is not mere absence [that is meant]; rather, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), it is stated to be a cognition of another particular. And here, the phrase "of that very one alone" is implied by the force of the context; otherwise, since the perception of the other would be unprohibited, its non-existence could not be established.

For example: "There is no jar here, because it is not perceived," as in the case of something being absent in a certain place.
