In this context, the phrase "of that which is perceptible" (dṛśyasya) should be understood as referring to a specific nature [of the object] and the completeness of all other conditions for perception. The phrase "because of non-perception" (anupalabdheḥ) means "because of the perception of the counter-positive" (pratiyogin).

And that [locus], having attained the status of a substratum because it is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the non-existence, is either the ground (*bhūtala*) itself or something else that is in contact with a single sense-faculty cognition; or it is something other than that, because of the general statement that "when that which is being cognized is perceived, the object to be negated is necessarily apprehended. In this regard, if the production of a jar is to be proven on a portion of the earth that is indeed perceptible, then that very [ground] is the counter-correlate—what need is there for anything else? But when [the locus] is in the sky, even then it is that very thing known as light; or else it is another thing, such as a jar, whose presence is not restricted [to that spot]. However, in the case of the negation of a tangible object, it is precisely this [light] that serves as the locus.
By this, the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) that is associated with a single cognition has been explained; however, in some cases, it is otherwise as well.

Now, one might argue that a lamp is not swallowed here [by the mouth], because its taste is not perceived despite being visible; thus, touch alone is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). For when those two [taste and touch] exist together, their cognition is restricted to a single form, as in the case of a beverage (*pānaka*). [Response: In that case, why is there no negation of taste even when a form is seen from a distance? Because for those things situated at a remote location, there is an absence of the capacity for perception, since the nose, tongue, and body-sense function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). And it has been said: "When X is being experienced, Y is necessarily experienced."

Nor is there a negation of form (*rūpa*) upon the experience of taste (*rasa*), because even then, the definition [of that object] is not applicable. Likewise, the perception of sound (*śabda*) does not constitute a negation of form; for in darkness, the cognition of sound does not invariably accompany the cognition of form, even though form exists. However, in light, there is no negation of that which is actually being seen. As for the negation of an unperceived but suitable [object], there is no fault, because its defining characteristics have not been abandoned.

By this it is shown that when a temple or similar structure is perceived, the non-existence of its local drum or other sounds is established without necessarily depending on the perception of another sound occurring simultaneously with it; thus, there is no rule that those two must be perceived together. (3a6) This is not the case for a portion of ground and a jar either. However, the absence of a rule regarding the simultaneous perception of both things when they are present is the same for perception in that case as well. There is no distinction whether [the object] is part of a single cognition invariably connected with the apprehension of another, or part of a different cognition invariably connected with the apprehension of another.
The same applies whether it is produced by a single sense-faculty or otherwise.

Even in a completely dark room, if there were an absence of light, it would follow—according to the opponent's own system—that this is known through another cognition devoid of that [light’s] form, even if ultimately through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). However, in reality, darkness itself exists as a real entity (*vastusan*) and can coexist with a single cognition of the lamp; so what need is there for anything else?

But surely, even when there is a specific nature [of the object], the proximity of other conditions constitutes its fitness for perception; and although that [fitness] serves as the cause for a cognition by a different sense organ, it is not utilized for the ascertainment of the conditions for a cognition by a different sense organ. Consequently, when a negation is made regarding the doubt of another's proximity to other conditions, how could that negation—made ultimately even on the basis of a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) of a determinate form—be established for something perceptible?

It is said: Indeed, it is not only a cognition by means of the same sense-faculty (*samānendriyajñāna*) that is dependent upon the establishment of the presence of other conditions; rather, there is also the perception of a particular state of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) characterized by the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). This is so when no further illuminator is required beyond the specific nature of the sense-faculty and its object, as in the case of sound, a lamp, and so forth.

For in those cases, how can anyone prevent the establishment of the non-existence [of an object] for one who has previously heard or seen it, who knows the application of the sense-faculties to that state, and who possesses a cognition devoid of the respective forms [of the object], regardless of where that cognition arises?

What, then, is the utility of apprehending another cognition? For the non-existence of that [first cognition] is established simply by the non-arising of a cognition of its state. Or how could there be a negation of something else based on a sensory cognition whose object is different?
It has been stated in this regard that non-existence has no causal capacity whatsoever.

And so forth. Therefore, another cognition is not relied upon for the sake of ascertaining the excellence of the sense faculty; rather, it is for the purpose of generating a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding the absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). In this regard, just as a cognition associated with the same sense faculty is capable of ascertaining the absence of another thing, so too is any other [cognition]. There is no distinction whatsoever, because even when existence is present, there is an absence of the form of a cognition of some other object that is invariably concomitant with it.
If one asks, "How so?"

In this case, desire and non-desire have no causal efficacy. Rather, for whatever follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something else, there is the acceptance of a cause-and-effect relationship between those two. For example, because the cognition of a bare patch of ground is restricted to that single form, its positive and negative concomitance is replicated by the conceptual exclusion (*vikalpa*) of other things; likewise, when one thrusts a lamp into the mouth, because the cognition is restricted to the form of touch alone, that cognition [of touch] is replicated by the cognition of the absence of taste. Indeed, there is no distinction between mediation and non-mediation regarding the arising of these two.

Likewise, for one whose nose is applied to pure water and who neither touches nor sees it, even though there is no direct experience of another odor, there arises a conceptual construction through the cognition of the absence of odor; this [cognition] is devoid of that [odor's] form.
If it is argued that "this is inferential," [the response follows].

No; because for one in a state of repeated practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), there is no intervention (*vyavadhāna*). For when the ascertainment of X occurs at the very moment of the cognition of Y, that [ascertainment] is neither inferential nor established by perception, as in the case of "blue is not yellow. And indeed, when water is present, for one who possesses a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the mere form of applying the nose [to it], there is the ascertainment that "there is no odor. In that case, if the experience of a conceptual construction with a restricted form were not the cause for establishing the mere absence of the cognition of odor, then let the experience of blue also not be the cause for the cognition of the absence of yellow.

Or rather, for one who maintains that there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the human agent here, it would be difficult to avoid [the same conclusion] in other cases as well. And that very same perception is called "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) with respect to the object to be negated, as has already been stated.

Furthermore, this [non-apprehension] is a logical mark (*liṅga*) which, directed toward a deluded cognizer, determines the absence of a property in a particular locus according to a prior convention. For one who is not deluded, however, this determination—which is free from any subsequent doubt—is indeed stable; thus, it is said to be "set in motion by perception."

But is it not the case that no linguistic usage regarding non-existence is produced by perception? Nor has perception been said to be fruitful by way of ascertaining the absence of an object; rather, it is only by way of ascertaining the absence of cognition. However, because it includes the ascertainment of the object's absence through that very [ascertainment of the absence of cognition], it is said to be "produced by perception."

And although that [cognition] arises through the power of that [perception], it is subsequently overridden by doubt; thus, for a deluded person, it is inferential. For there is no restriction on an object to having the nature of illumination as there is for cognition, since its existence is not contradicted even when unperceived. Non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is the refuge [for the non-deluded]; however, for one who is not deluded, it is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the existence of the perceptible is pervaded by being an object of perception. Some, however, maintain that the former is "deluded" due to an inability to distinguish between these two.

That is incorrect. For just as cognition might be non-luminous and unstable, so too might an external object be invisible; thus, like that [cognition], the practical usage of its absence could not be precluded by perception alone. Only by its very nature is cognition visible, whereas an external object is visible only in some cases, in some ways, and at some time.

In this regard, for a cognizer possessing a specific degree of practice, the immediate establishment of a negation regarding a specific external object—just as with the generality of another cognition—is experienced repeatedly through perception alone; how can such an experience be denied?

If it is argued that inference is possible in reality (*tattvataḥ*), then even the determination of the intended capacity (*yogyatā*) would not be produced by perception; thus, this [objection] is trivial. Furthermore, the aforementioned doubt does not exist solely with respect to external objects. For otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of being unable to state such things as: "This [perception], whose nature is seeing, is either a non-conceptualized [state] or the seeing of a conceptualization whose nature is the visible; therefore, it precludes the conceptual construction (*vikalpaka-kalpanā*) within sensory cognition. Consequently, even regarding a cognition, there may at times be a reflective investigation (*vimarśa*) of another cognition.

Even regarding an object, certainty is a state in which no internal doubt has arisen; thus, the capacity of perception—whether it be of the other [inference] or not—is established through a division of stages (*daśā*), but not through a division of genus (*jāti*).
Now, [one might ask]: "Is this not because of the experience of perceiving a single [object]?"
If it is argued that by such statements the capacity for the negation of other cognitions is expressed, and that experience is likewise [of this nature], we say no.

For just as "this is not perceived" is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too for one who is practiced, "this does not exist" occurs instantaneously. However, for one who is unpracticed, there is first the ascertainment of the absence of cognition; through that, however, there is the [ascertainment of] the absence of the object. It is with reference to this that it is stated thus in the treatise (*śāstra*). The same should be said regarding effort and so forth, which are associated with a single cognition. For this very reason, those of great intelligence determine all aspects from a mere glance.

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, effort is required at various points specifically for those of dull intellect. Therefore, for one of sharp intelligence, just as in the case of distinguishing between a gem and silver, even the linguistic convention of negating that [object] is difficult to prevent based on perception alone. Moreover, non-existence (*abhāva*) does not possess a physical form such that it must be directly perceived through a nature distinct from other things; rather, it is something to be engaged with through linguistic convention. And because it is restricted to a single form, it is indeed possible for one of sharp intellect to engage with it through direct perception.

Furthermore, one who is dull-witted and thus doubts even when there has arisen an ascertainment of non-existence regarding the object at first glance proceeds to employ that conventional usage by relying merely on the non-perception of the perceptible. However, one who is even more dull-witted than that, doubting even regarding the non-perception of the perceptible, proceeds by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). But for one who is not deluded, there is no proceeding by this [latter method]; for it is precisely when there is dullness of perception that inference is sought. And that proficiency [of perception] is established by the generation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and its state of greater acuity arises from the absence of hesitation (*vimarśa*) therein.

However, regarding the Cārvāka who maintains that non-existence is a distinct [entity], it has been shown that perception has no function in negating it, because of the statement concerning the dependence on the causal capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthya*) and so forth. Furthermore, unlike inference, the determination of apprehension for perception does not depend on conceptual ascertainment (*niścaya*), but rather on appearance (*pratibhāsa*). And its very possession of a determinate form (*niyatākāratā*) is the manifestation of the absence of anything other than that [object].

Therefore, the possibility of the capacity for the conventional usage of non-existence regarding perception is difficult to avoid. As for the statement that "negation occurs everywhere due to non-apprehension," this is not a rejection of perception, but rather [a rejection] of another logical mark (*liṅga*). Just as it is said that there are only two means of establishing a positive entity, so too this negation of odor in water is produced by perception itself because there is no intervention; it is not inferential.

Furthermore, what here is the logical mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with the absence of odor? If it is argued that it is the non-perception of the effect, namely cognition, then this would be appropriate when the cognition apprehending [the object] itself serves as the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*). However, when that [odor] is indeed perceptible, then the absence of that which is fit for perception—if it is not the non-perception of the perceptible—would mean that even a jar would not exist [as a non-existent]. Thus, this is merely the fruit of deceiving oneself regarding the nature of the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

If this proponent says this without having ascertained the excellence of the sense faculties, it follows that even an existing odor or other object would not be perceived. On the other hand, if he has ascertained it, then it should be understood that the non-perception of the effect is sufficient [to establish the absence of the cause].

Furthermore, he laboriously applies the non-perception of the effect to causes and so forth that are merely suspected to exist beyond perception; yet now, out of fear of even a trace of error, he entertains doubt even regarding what is suspected through direct perception—this is incoherent.

Therefore, this is established: when one thing is being perceived, that which is necessarily perceived—whether it be something else that is apprehended by the same sense faculty or something else that is not apprehended by a sense faculty—is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). And this [non-perception] establishes only conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), because otherwise there would be establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that reason, it was stated that it is the basis for the stability of the cognition of absence; however, it is not the basis for the certainty of absence.

Just as for two things that are necessarily perceived together, one cognition serves to negate the other, so too it is for those that are necessarily not perceived together; thus he says, "or not. For the meaning is: where, regarding an object of cognition (*vedya*), the cognition of [its opposite] would necessarily not occur. This is, for example, like [the cognition]: "This blue is not non-blue. Here too, it is precisely conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is to be proven. By this, the contradiction characterized by the state of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitilakṣaṇa*) has been explained.

[Objection: But surely this has already been covered by the statement: "When X is being perceived, it is possible that the cognition of Y will necessarily arise. For even an invisible object, when being negated through identity, is negated only after having been conceived as visible; otherwise, one would be admitting a distinction between the visible and the invisible by oneself. So what is the point of this separate statement? [Reply: In that case, then, this absence characterized as destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-lakṣaṇa*) is explained by the phrase "or else it would not exist" (*na vā syāt*).

The meaning is that even though the cognition has arisen, it necessarily ceases when a certain object of knowledge is present. And this necessity is logically appropriate only as the non-existence [of the other] upon the sublation of its existence; for example, "there is no cold here because of fire. By this, the opposition characterized by the impossibility of coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is explained. If it is argued that since there is necessarily no perception in darkness, one need not necessarily assume an opposition, we reply: this definition does not depend on a single perceiver, but rather applies generally.

Furthermore, there is indeed the perception of form even for those lacking light; or else, it may be possible [to perceive it] through specific ointments and the like. However, regarding the destruction of existence (*sattoccheda*), there is a strict necessity (*niyama*); thus, there is no fault. [Objection: But even in this case, if cold were present, there would be no certain cognition of fire as having a single nature. How, then, is this different from the previous case? [Response: It is not so, because the negation is intended only with respect to what is accessible through touch. In that case, although the cognition of cold has arisen, it is impossible to ascertain that it has necessarily ceased once the fire is perceived, because such a cognition occurs at other times.

[188] Because it is intended [to be so]. In that case, since its operation is mediated by the recollection of a contradiction previously grasped, there would be no ascertainment of non-existence from the activity of perception. Let it be so; however, even with this mediation, it is precisely the cognition of the contradictory that is the factor for the ascertainment of non-existence, and not the mere [recollection] of anything else. Thus, there is no damage to the basis for the establishment of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

And it is not accepted here that the mere establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is the goal; thus he says: "But since the subsequent [cognition] is dependent upon memory, here even non-existence (*abhāva*) is to be proven. And once that is established, there is also the conventional usage characterized by the stability of its ascertainment, but not merely that alone—this is the meaning.

Likewise, in the case of the denial of a cause (*hetu*) or a pervader (*vyāpaka*), it follows that "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is also the probandum (*sādhya*). For example: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire"; or "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees. For in these cases, the mere perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—namely, fire and the tree—does not produce the ascertainment of the non-existence of smoke and the *śiṃśapā* without depending on the recollection of the previously established cognition of the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). Therefore, in this case as well, the conventional application of the proof of non-existence is established.

These are now the reasons for negation: non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Likewise, there are two for establishing an affirmation (*vidhisādhana*); thus, five reasons would result.
No, because they are one, since they rely upon the commonality of non-perception (*anupalabdhisāmānya*).

Moreover: non-apprehension is of two kinds—of itself and of another. The non-apprehension of the cause and the pervader is simply the non-apprehension of their own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*). For another [kind], namely the non-apprehension of the effect or the pervaded, there is what is called the non-apprehension of the cause and the non-apprehension of the pervader. For just as the perception of one thing is itself the non-apprehension of another, so too the non-apprehension of the nature of something is itself called the non-apprehension of the cause or the pervader in relation to the effect or the pervaded; thus, there is no difference in the underlying reality (*vastubheda*) despite the difference in designation.
Therefore, since the negation of everything arises solely from the non-perception of its own-nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), there are only three types of logical mark (*liṅga*).

By this, the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*)—which pertains to a cause capable [of producing it]—should be understood as being characterized by the very non-perception of the effect's own-nature; or rather, because the word "cause" (*hetu*) is explained as having the meaning of a "logical mark. For example: "There are no causes for smoke here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the absence of smoke."

How, then, is the statement "there is no touch of frost here because of fire" included within the category of "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader"? In this case as well, there is indeed the non-perception of the nature [of cold]—which consists in the perception of fire, the opposite of the pervader, cold—and this is called the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) of the pervaded, namely the touch of frost; thus, there is no fault.

And although that [non-apprehension] could also be described as the non-apprehension of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), it is nevertheless designated as such for the purpose of demonstrating its nature as the cognition of a contradictory counter-correlate (*viruddhapratiyogipratīti*). In this same way, the apprehension of a cause-contradictory (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) and so forth are to be explained. In all cases, non-existence itself is the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is not established by direct perception; rather, conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established by means of that [non-existence]. Now, one might ask: how can there be the conventional usage of "non-apprehension" in cases such as the apprehension of a contradictory?

It has been stated in this regard that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is simply the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and that counter-correlate is of two kinds. Among these, when the counter-correlate is a contradictory one (*viruddha*), the employment of the word "contradictory" implies that the word "apprehension" itself must be employed. But when the other type of counter-correlate is understood, the use of either the word "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) or the word "visible" (*dṛśya*) designates it by the term "non-apprehension" in relation to the object to be negated. Thus, in one case "apprehensibility" is understood, while in the other "non-apprehensibility" is understood; however, since their reality (*tattva*) is one and the same, there is no fault.

And when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is contradictory [to the object], and the negation of a second [object] that is itself imperceptible (*parokṣa*), then for that [negation] as well, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not necessarily only perceptual; rather, it may also be inferential (*anumāna*). For a counter-positive is considered such because, by its own existence, it removes the existence of another. And who can prevent that from occurring even when [the counter-positive] is imperceptible? However, when the counter-positive is necessarily perceived together [with the object], the negation applies only to that which is capable of being perceived; thus, in that case, there is necessarily a requirement for perception.

For if a jar were present in the location being inferred, it would necessarily be perceived; yet, since perception is not applicable [there] and there is no rule for the commencement of inference, how can there be a negation?
If it is argued that, in this way, there is no negation because it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), [we reply:]...

Even in that case, it is not said that when the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) is being experienced, one would also experience an external object in the intended location provided the capacity of the sense faculty is unimpaired. However, it cannot be maintained that when an external object is being conceptually constructed, a second [object] would also be experienced. For even when an external object is being conceptually constructed, why should it not be the case that another object in that same location is indeed perceived? Indeed, the cognition of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogijñāna*) is not the basis for the visibility of another thing;

rather, it is the cause for the arising of the ascertainment of non-existence, because it is a real entity (*sattvavastu*). And since this is true of conceptual construction as well, what is the distinction?

Now, suppose it is argued that one must conform to the cognizer; and thus, even conformity with that which is associated in a single cognition is correct. This is not so, because we observe the conventional usage of non-existence regarding smell in water, taste in fire, form in wind, or when only a remnant is perceived. In those cases, according to the theory that non-perception is the effect of cognition, the same principle applies elsewhere as well; so what is the use of association in a single cognition?
If it is argued that through the non-perception of an effect, only a capable entity is negated—[we reply: no.

In that case, even though odors and the like exist in water and other such substances, they are not perceived due to a defect in the sense organs; thus, the fruit of one's great exertion in the study of the treatises is indeed significant. For while he may doubt—postulating that there is an obscuration by stronger [objects] despite the non-perception of a cause for the defect—he does not likewise doubt when, even with keen senses, he postulates a failure to perceive what is actually present on the ground caused by those same factors. Therefore, during the stage of practice, worldly transaction proceeds precisely through the persistence of that very state.

But for the Lord of Logic (*nyāyanātha*), there is neither a challenge nor a relinquishment following conventional usage; rather, it is by virtue of his boldness (*prauḍhi*) to demonstrate that even with such an interpretation, there is no impairment of our own definition—just as, for instance, even when the determination of all minds and all cognitions is not established, he alone is the Omniscient One.

Furthermore, in common practice, it is observed that when one perceives something associated with a single cognition, one determines the absence of another object—the counter-correlate—even though such a determination is common and non-contradictory; thus, the apprehension of what is associated with a single cognition is not a necessary condition. Moreover, in the state of relying upon conceptual construction, it is logical that the mere awareness of its own form is the means for establishing the negation of the other, precisely through such habitual practice.

[190] Because the capacity of direct perception is observed, in this way, even the perception of something contradictory that is beyond the senses—being of the nature of inference—establishes the non-existence of its opposite. For example, "There is no cold here because of smoke"; in this manner, the perception of the effect of something contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-kāryopalabdhi*) is to be understood. As in: "There is no frost here because of smoke. This is the explanation to be given at the time of formal application (*prayoga*), having synthesized these points. In reality, however, there is a single formulation: "There is no cold here because of fire. But for the sake of avoiding the charge of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*), [the expanded form is used].

There is another [inference]: "Fire exists here because of smoke. Likewise, there is no frost from fire; for that which is contradictory to the pervader is indeed contradictory. And [the inference] "fire because of smoke" [is established]. The remainder should also be inferred in this way.

If the non-perception of the nature of the cause and so forth is the non-perception of another's cause and so forth in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), then how is it [applied] to things that lack any designation (*nirupākhya*)? For example: "The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because of the absence of consciousness."

In that case as well, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) consists in the cognition of the mental image (*buddhipratibhāsa*) itself as being devoid of consciousness (*caitanya*). Furthermore, the cognition [of the subject] is qualified by the exclusion of speakerhood (*vaktṛtva*); this is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*).
Since all non-perceptions ultimately resolve into the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), there is no fault in their separate enumeration based on the determination of the proof of negation.

If it is asked: "Even so, since negation is directly the non-perception of essential nature according to the sequence already stated, why did the venerable Teacher describe it as figurative (*aupacārika*) because it is expressed through a succession? [The answer follows:]...

If the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is intended by the negator as referring only to that which is to be negated, then it is figurative (*aupacārika*). But if it applies to others as well, then it is primary (*mukhya*); what contradiction is there? One might ask: "What is the purpose of speaking of it as merely figurative? In that case too, the negation is possible only for the perceptible, and not for others such as the Omniscient One, the Passionless One, or Primordial Matter (*pradhāna-puruṣa*); thus, they are included therein by way of their effects. In reality, however, it is the non-perception of that [object] or of anything else as described that serves as the proof.
The Secret of Non-apprehension is completed.

[191.3] DISCUSSION ON THE ABSENCE OF ALL WORDS: Here, some provide the non-perception of the effect of cognition (*jñānakāryānupalabdhi*) as the means of proof for establishing the absence of all words. They claim that because there is an absence of association with a single cognition, there is indeed no occasion here for the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

For indeed, three things must necessarily be stated in this context: the qualification by way of the negation of the existence of a jar or the like, the essential nature (*svabhāva*), and the result (*phala*). Among these, by virtue of the qualification regarding the object of perception, there is no negation of things such as *piśācas*. And because it has the nature of being perceived through association with a single cognition, there is no negation of taste by means of the cognition of form. Nor does the fault belonging to the position of non-existence (*abhāva*) follow; for the establishment of perception is presented as having conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) as its result.

And that [non-perception] is possible when there is a basis for the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). That very basis, by virtue of being inseparable from the non-existence of other counter-positives, possesses the capacity to generate the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of their absence; therefore, it serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*). Consequently, it is logical that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which consists of that [basis], is the means of establishing the conventional usage of absence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) for one who is deluded.

Furthermore, when the non-existence of all sounds is to be proven, not a single thing is found that is associated with a single cognition; thus, there is no scope for that [inference]. However, since that mass of sounds existing in the intended location is at that time incapable of initiating the effect of cognition, even by the negation of the effect, existence itself is negated without distinction—this is the sense.

On this point, it is considered as follows: It is not the case that sound alone is what produces hearing, for if it were, it would follow that even a deaf person could hear. Therefore, it is only sound when assisted by the efficacy of the sense organ (*indriya-pāṭava*) that generates the cognition of hearing. Furthermore, that auditory efficacy is difficult to ascertain in the absence of a connection with a single [perceptual] cognition. For this very reason, the negation of a jar depends upon the perception of its location. Thus, while taking account of the excellence of the sense organ, one determines through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) that the fault lies solely with the jar.

Nor is the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of the sense faculty established in the same way as that of mental attention (*manaskāra*), because the sense faculty is insentient (*jaḍa*). Nor can it be apprehended by another sense faculty, because it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Its effect, moreover, is simply its perception (*upalabdhi*). And if that [perception] is not established, then the non-perception of the effect is itself unestablished. If it is unestablished, then the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason is proven; for even when an object exists, a non-perception that is possible due to a defect in the sense faculty cannot be said to be necessarily determined by its absence. If it is argued: "We do not say that the sound is absolutely non-existent, but rather that there is no [sound] capable of producing the cognition of it."

This has become the practice of a quack physician: first, having accepted with boldness the undertaking of a desired remedy, one proposes what is not a means under the guise of being a means; then, when the opponent demonstrates the truth of the matter, one subsequently proclaims that it is incurable. For this non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is said to be a proof only when the absolute non-existence of the object is what is sought to be known, and not when there is an inquiry into the absence of the capacity to produce cognition. Therefore, if the failure of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is somehow acknowledged, why on earth is the failure of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) not also admitted?

It would be better to seek another means of valid cognition altogether; why, then, is its very non-establishment being proclaimed? For it is not possible for one who is deaf and does not hear to deny the absence of nearby sounds such as the beating of a drum, since that would entail the consequence of there being no distinction between the deaf and the non-deaf.

If it is argued that there is a distinction made by hearing—namely, that [the sound] exists before and after [the act of hearing]—it is not so. For if this [sound] were indistinguishable from its prior state in terms of its capacity for being heard, how could there be no hearing when the word is present? Otherwise, there would have been no hearing even before. If, on the other hand, it is possible that the sound is in a dissimilar state [even while present], then one should not place trust in the hearing itself, because such a distortion is possible. In that case, there is no difference between non-hearing and the hearing of what does not exist.

If it is asked, "From where does the reversal of capacity arise at the beginning?", [we reply that] the objection is the same: "From where is its absence in the middle? Therefore, this is not even a valid position; for although the word exists at that time, it is not heard. When considering what the proof might be in this case, it has already been stated that the non-perception of the effect is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the proficiency of hearing is difficult to ascertain.

[192,11] But how can this be so difficult to ascertain for one who is engaged in listening and possesses the strength of keen sight, hearing, and memory? For even if there were momentariness, in the absence of other dissimilar auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), it is impossible for a dissimilar state to arise. Indeed, those conditions that cause a modification of the sense faculties—such as disturbances of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) or physical blows—whose powers are well-established, are clearly perceived as the causes for the agitation of the continuum within one's own stream of being (*svasantāna*).

But how can those who have not perceived [the cause] tolerate the suspicion that there is a difference arising from its own source? For one who suspects that even for a powerful being there is a subtle cause for modifications such as supernatural empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), what confidence can there be even in hearing [his words]? Therefore, even when a sensory illusion characterized by disorientation of direction is produced by an unperceived cause, the instability of the senses cannot be established merely because a well-known cause is not perceived; otherwise, it would follow that all cognitions other than those [sensory ones] would be erroneous. Why is this not taken into account even now, so that there may be no total collapse of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)?

However, the reliance upon the presence of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) is the same in both cases. For we do not say that there is a certainty of non-existence for a deaf person who has ascended to the power of hearing through medicinal treatment, even though he does not hear; this is because there is simply an absence of certainty regarding his capacity. The same applies to another whose capacity has not been ascertained. Indeed, when those who have slept through the entire night and then awakened—even though they do not perceive that state—exhibit unerring practical behavior (*vyavahāra*), what occasion is there for one who is awake to suspect that their own self is otherwise?

Therefore, the negation of that which is not in its original state, or of the persistence of that state, occurs either due to the absence of the well-known causes or the absence of the indicators thereof.

If, with respect to the stage of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), one maintains that the basis for perceptuality in seeing, hearing, and so forth is the persistence of the state (*tādavasthya*)—and if, regarding what is established by conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), one resorts to the persistence of the sense faculty, or the persistence of the cognition awakened by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or even self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself with respect to a common capacity—then since that very [capacity] exists even during the stage of non-hearing, how can there be any inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) regarding the absence of sound?
If it is argued that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) occurs only within the nature of cognition itself, we say no.
[193] When there are objects of a single resolve that are conducive to a single effect,
a single cognition is established as having all those objects, existing without division.

Even regarding the five aggregates, there is a single conviction of "I. There is utility in a single referent for speaking and so forth, as well as in mutual dependence. This principle is well-established in the case of color, taste, and so on, which are designated as "pots" and the like; otherwise, conventional usage would be impossible.

[193,5] Is it not the case that the direct perception of the body does not follow upon the cognition? This is indeed so with respect to their specific individual forms (*prātisvikarūpa*), just like color, taste, and so forth. However, by grasping them through their commonality (*sāmānya*), they are said to be the objects of a single cognition, provided there is no insistence on their analytical distinction (*vivecanā*). But when there is such analysis, a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated. Therefore, the two propositions—that Caitra is perceived and yet the cognition is not directly perceived—are not contradictory.
For this very reason, even the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "I am in such a state" follows from experience and has everything as its object.

If it is argued that this is an error, we say no; because there is no subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), the status of being an error is unestablished. Therefore, since it is possible to determine that the auditory faculty remains in its previous state as it was previously perceived, the non-hearing of the sound is due solely to the fault of the sound itself. Thus, even through the absence of cognition, the non-existence of the object is established with certainty; hence, there is no contradiction with the subject at hand. If this alone constitutes the complete set of conditions for the definition of "non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), what is the purpose of applying the designation "non-perception of the effect" (*kāryānupalabdhi*)?

For it is only by means of non-perception that a sound which has attained its specific nature and the completeness of other conditions can be negated. Nevertheless, if another name [is used], even when a jar is negated, who is the negator? It is simply said that, like a jar, the negation of sound is also established through the non-perception of what is perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*). If it is argued that negation by that [means] is appropriate because of the possibility of association with a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*), [we reply:]...

In that very context, first of all, with respect to what is there a need for [the object] to be associated with a single cognition? For in the perception of color, taste is not excluded [from being perceived] precisely because it has reached the condition of non-apprehension due to its location in a remote place; this is because the nose, tongue, and body-sense function by reaching their objects. Furthermore, since the stability of the sense-faculties is established by the aforementioned sequence, what is the use of requiring association with a single cognition? It is not so, because light—which is distinct from the sense-faculty—is required in that case.

For that [object], whose nature is subject to arising and ceasing dependent upon external causes easily available, is not something to be established by its own state of being; therefore, the requirement for co-occurrence within a single cognition, which is sought for that purpose, will also serve as an auxiliary factor even in the cognition of the excellence of the sense organ.

Thus, it is established that where the capacity for apprehension is independent of illumination, there is no requirement for association with a single cognition. Furthermore, that [association] is required in some cases of proof only when, in its absence, one of the defects—namely, contradiction (*virodha*), non-establishment (*asiddhi*), or doubt (*saṃdeha*)—would necessarily occur. Now, this [requirement] does not exist when something that has attained the fitness for being perceived in two ways (*dvividhopalabdhiyogyatāpanna*) is negated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), such that an associated entity would necessarily have to be expected. Even in those cases where this [association] is expected:

In that case as well, it is solely for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) when negating an object whose apprehension depends upon light. However, this does not mean that such dependence is required in all instances. For instance, while independence with respect to destruction is the means of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is not required in every proof of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), even in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, if this [object] were necessarily dependent, what need would there be for the qualification "visible" (*dṛśya*)? For visibility is never absent in anything that is associated with the same cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsargin*). Indeed, a *piśāca* (demon) has no association with any [perceptible] thing within a single cognition.

If it is argued that "the object is one and the same in both cases, so there is no need to discuss a separate application [of the reason]," we say no; for the distinction remains unmanifest due to the relationship between the general and the particular. Indeed, a relation (*saṃsarga*) does not deviate from the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), whereas the mere qualifier certainly deviates from it. For this very reason, a relation is brought forward to establish the qualifier, but the qualifier is not capable of attracting the relation—otherwise, it would follow that the same applies to the word itself. And if that were so, the thesis (*pakṣa*) would collapse; what, then, would be the point of such exertion?

Therefore, what is called "conjunction within a single cognition" is proclaimed only with reference to the specific example under discussion; it is not to be required in every case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Indeed, regarding the present negation of the jar, let that same direction be adopted for the sake of establishing the qualification. For the definition of one's own non-apprehension is simply this: "that which is apprehensible is not apprehended. Thus, both in the definition and in its formal application, there is the mere presentation of the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions of apprehensibility. Furthermore, in the treatise, when demonstrating the sublation of the contrary, it is explained that non-apprehension is impossible in the case of an entity possessing a specific nature when other causal conditions are present.

Otherwise, one would have to show that the factor which serves as the logical reason (*prayojaka*) is everywhere merely a relation (*saṃsarga*), just like a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). However, since identity (*tādātmya*) is negated only after having accepted its perceptibility (*dṛśyatva*), this is merely a case of not mentioning the qualifier; it does not imply a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*), unlike the case of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) for a learned person. Or rather, when there is a specific statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is [the implication] of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, even for the Lord of Nyāya, there is no necessary intention to rely on a relation with a single cognition in the case of the non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Moreover, one might claim that all [types of non-perception] are subsumed under the non-perception of the effect alone, since the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is but a part of it; and one might establish the inclusion of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*), with the exception of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).

Therefore, just as there is no establishment of an inference from effect regarding the object of sensory perception, so too why should there be an establishment of the non-perception of an effect for that which is not apprehended by it? For just as there is a fear of the collapse of the system of direct perception in one case, so it is in the other case regarding the non-perception of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*). Or, just as the effect is a logical mark (*liṅga*) when [the cause] is not perceived, so too is its non-perception [a mark] only when [the object] is not capable of being perceived; thus they are equal.

Or, for example, this very Blessed One employs the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) to establish, even within knowledge, the absence of another [simultaneous] knowledge. As he said:
"When there is the perception of a conceptualization whose nature is perceptible, the non-perception [of it] prevents the construction of conceptualization in sensory cognition."

In that case, what is the correlate within a single cognition? Furthermore, if this is accepted, then even the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) would be unestablished; thus, there is indeed an abandonment of the original position. For the absence of the effect of cognition cannot be known through the non-perception of that very effect, because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), being restricted to a single form, can only imply the certainty of the non-existence of anything else; thus, regarding that which is doubted, if there were another cognition, it would necessarily be experienced. Therefore, in practical discourse, the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) alone is the refuge, just as in the case of external objects. However, there might be a failure to state the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*); there is no other way. And since that [qualification] is also absent when dependence on association (*saṃsarga*) is required, the reason (*hetu*) is "unproven due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
Therefore, it is impossible for non-perception to function without violating the rule of dependence on association within a single cognition.

If it is argued that there is a restriction based on the external, we say no; for even in that case, there is no underlying cause. For if that capacity which exists internally can be obtained externally even upon its transgression, why should the situation not be the same? Indeed, the nature of objects is diverse. In that regard, with respect to the manifestation of its own self, an object requires nothing more than mere suitability (*yogyatā*).

Sound, odor, taste, touch, darkness, and light, however, require a sense faculty distinct from mental attention (*manaskāra*); whereas the specific forms (*rūpa*) residing in arrangements such as jars generally require illumination as well. Likewise, why should the non-apprehension of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in a negation not depend on a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), just as the apprehension of these [other objects] does in their affirmation?

In that regard, just as in the first case there is no utility in depending on the stability of the sense faculty, so too in the middle cases there is no utility in [depending on] what is associated with a single cognition. While it might be appropriate for one who requires something additional to depend on it, it is likewise possible to argue: "If the cognition were present, it would certainly be perceived; why then wait for the stability of the sense faculty? Just as this is the logical implication, so too it can be said: "If taste and so forth were present, they would certainly be perceived by me through the stable sense faculty; why then wait for what is associated with a single cognition?"
Therefore, the possibility of a restriction even regarding external objects is extremely remote; or, if it were admitted, one would have to expect such a restriction regarding cognition as well.

If it is argued that even in that case there exists a connection with a single cognition based on the expectation of a single perception consisting of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), [we reply: surely there is no such thing as a single perception called "self-awareness," because that which is merely a property (*dharma*) is distinct in each individual instance. If you are satisfied by applying the designation "single cognition" by relying on a universal (*sāmānya*), then the same consequence would apply even to objects apprehended by different sense faculties, or even to the objects of self-awareness and sensory cognition. If it is argued that this rule applies only to those two things whose existence is invariably concomitant with one another's perception, [we reply:]...

This rule does not apply even to two forms (*rūpa*), since a *piśāca* is not perceived in a location. It certainly exists in the case of specific instances (*viśeṣa*). If it is argued that "the fault of the universal (*sāmānya*) does not infect the particular," even so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) regarding sound and space, or sound and mental attention (*manaskāra*). For the perception of space or the perception of the experience of mental attention does not deviate from the perception of sound when sound exists. If, however, there were such deviation, then because the effect would not be perceived, there would be the consequence of [the reason] being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, the requirement of being apprehended by a single cognition is not all-pervasive, and it is easily available for other things as well; so enough with this dispute.

Furthermore, this conjunction of two minds within a single cognition is something entirely unprecedented, because a primary [conjunction] is impossible and a secondary one is absent due to the lack of inclusion within a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*). If it is argued that "inclusion within a single sense-base" is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), then why is "conjunction within a single cognition" itself not declared to be the illustration? However, both of these were stated with reference to the example of the jar under discussion; thus, there should be no dogmatic attachment.

For just as the non-deviation of mutual perception is observed through their inclusion within a single sense-base (*āyatana*), so too it is logical that through association within a single cognition there is likewise a dependence solely upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

And what is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of what? It is that pair for which perception, restricted to a single form, is capable of establishing the ascertainment of the absence of the other. And of which two is there such non-perception? It is of those two for whom the perception of one is non-deviant from the non-perception of the other; for if both were present, a cognition restricted to a single form would be impossible. Therefore, it is on the basis of specific time, place, state, and continuum that two things are established as being mutual counter-correlates.

That [object] is visible because their non-union (ayoga) is characterized by the attainment of consciousness; for this very reason, the cognition of those two as restricted to a single form is able to establish a conceptual exclusion (pratiṣedha-vikalpa) of anything else. Thus, the absence of such [other things] is said to be established by direct perception (pratyakṣa-siddha).

For that very same certainty regarding the deluded person, non-perception—which is of the nature of the perception of a counter-correlate—being possible for those who are simultaneously in contact with what is perceptible, establishes both the verbal expression and its absence; since the establishment of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the result (*phala*) is thus fully accomplished by this alone through the rejection of other views, what is the use of including the requirement of being apprehended by a single sense-faculty?

Indeed, this counter-argument—whether by means of a single or multiple sense-faculties—is equally applicable to two objects, two cognitions, or a cognition and its object, and it remains unassailable in establishing non-existence; so why should one conform to that?

For just as the perception of a single form regarding both the ground and a jar, or regarding two cognitions, is sufficient to produce the ascertainment of their absence because it is not contradicted by other perceptions, so too, for one who has perceived both [the taste and the touch] during the act of drinking a beverage and perceives them to remain in that same state, the perception of touch alone when swallowing a lamp-flame produces the ascertainment of the absence of taste.

Alternatively, the mere awareness of the form of one's own conceptual construction is indeed capable of establishing the determination of the absence of a proximate tangible object. For that awareness of the conceptual construction does not deviate from the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a tangible object that exists at that time. Nor is there any other capacity for producing a certainty regarding the absence of a second [object] elsewhere than through the non-deviation of mutual perceptions. Furthermore, the so-called "direct perception of absence" is not something distinct from the capacity for producing a certainty of absence;
for absence is not a substantial entity (*vigrahavān*) by which it could be directly perceived.

And when, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), the counter-positive itself is the absence, then its establishment through perception is indeed primary; thus it is logical that in all cases the result is practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, this counter-positive does not exist for anyone with respect to things remote by nature and so forth, such that someone’s perception could be capable of manifesting their absence. Nor, in this way, is non-apprehension said to be a mere cessation.

The Bhaṭṭa, however, even under the view of *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation), maintains that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by apprehending anything other than the specific counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) as previously described; thus, in his system, the exclusion of [the existence of] things such as *piśācas* is logical. But for one who perceives color, taste is indeed spatially remote from that location. It does not bring about the aforementioned counter-correlate. However, that which is in contact with the tip of the tongue does not deviate from the non-existence [of the object] in the case of non-apprehension.

[197] Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. For this very reason, it is stated that the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) and so forth, which are incapable of functioning directly, are included within the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) by way of a mediated sequence, because their respective counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are of such a nature.

Therefore, the definition of the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) is simply the non-perception of that which has attained the state of being capable of being perceived. And since this [non-perception] exists as the conventional absence (*abhāva*) established by way of the perception of its counterpart as previously described, there is no contradiction with either the Nyāya or the Śāstra. As for the mention of "perceptible by a single sense-faculty," it should be understood as referring specifically to examples such as a jar; thus the point is settled.

In that regard, when one perceives the absence of a drum or similar object in a place such as a temple—which is perceived as a region of space characterized by darkness and light—then either that very [space] or the cognition that has become the object of a cognition colored by the form of that [absence] is the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which is the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the perceptual arising that would necessarily occur, or of the cognition that would be the object of negation. However, for one whose eyes are not engaged, there is the exclusion of the object of knowledge, such as taste or the like, or the cognition thereof, or ultimately even the mental attention (*manaskāra*) itself;
and the awareness of that [exclusion] is also an exclusion.

For even that [perception] is not possible for one with acute hearing without the arising of auditory perception of sound. However, there is no authority to deny non-conceptual perception. Simply put, as long as the direct perception of the sound connected to a particular location does not deviate from the perception of taste and so forth, or from the experience of the form of conceptualization, the exclusion must be stated in relation to the sound occupying that specific location; for it is impossible to state a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) in reference to something else characterized by a lack of deviation from the mutual perception of each other.

Consequently, as before, the non-existence [of an object] is established through perception; and it is proven that the practical consequence (*vyavahāra*) is the result of the very non-perception of the perceptible, even in the case of a word. For, even in the absence of a single cognition [of both the object and its absence], the operation of this [non-perception] is not obstructed, because the undesirable is not drawn in by virtue of its dependence upon the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Thus: In the case of sounds, lamps, and so forth, it has been indicated that for the attainment of their complete manifestation—such as light and the like—they depend on additional manifesting conditions, namely birth and so on; thus there is a single cognition of them. However, for those whose minds have previously heard or seen such things, there is a perception of them as they appear; whereas in other cases, one's own non-perception is indeed a cognition of another object that is devoid of the form of one's own [perceived] flavor.

If the persistence of the sense organ is established, then there is no capacity for the non-perception of the effect; if the persistence of the sense organ is established, then there is no result from the non-perception of the effect.
[198] If even the non-perception of intrinsic nature necessarily requires dependence [on other factors],
how can the establishment of conjunction be achieved for you, even though you perceive it as an effect of cognition?
If this restriction applies only to external objects, then what causes it even there? For the status of objects is manifold, due to their fitness for occupying specific locations.
Just as the cognition of what is not illuminated does not constitute a sublation merely because it is not stated to be distinct [from it],
so too, in some cases, there is sublation even while disregarding the related object.

However, there is no fear for Bhaṭṭa that the form of that [non-existence] could be the cognition of a real entity as its counter-correlate; for even that state of being a counter-correlate is nothing other than a mutual non-deviation from direct perception.

Therefore, a single cognition itself produces the conceptual construction of the absence of other things; it is not the case that absence is cognized by perception, since [perception] does not go beyond the certainty produced by that [cognition].
Only when there is the state of being a counter-correlate as previously described is sense-perception capable of determining its absence; such is the nature of things.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) alone is what is associated with the same cognition, since direct association with a single cognition is intended and because the primary form is accepted? Therefore, by implication, the word "one" (*eka*) remains as a mere indicator of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). And its application as "one" is solely in reference to the single genus (*jāti*) of perception. Nor is this a mere matter of terminology, for such usage is seen through conventional usage (*rūḍha*), just as in the expression: "One grain of rice, when harvested, brings about an abundance of food."

Therefore, even where it is said that "it is seen as associated with a single cognition," the meaning is precisely this: that they are mutually non-deviating from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, the state of being in a single sense-field (*ekāyatanabhāva*) should be explained as a mere indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), due to its relevance to the context, just as [in the definition of non-perception] a location and the cognition thereof are mentioned.

And thus, in the case of the non-apprehension of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), since it is said that the locus is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it amounts to saying that the locus is precisely the co-occurrence within a single cognition (*ekajñānasaṃsarga*). So how could "co-occurrence in a single cognition" not be a pervading [condition]? True, this is so. If it appears to you that the counter-correlate must reside in the same cognition as the white [object], what is the harm? Let the negation of sound itself be the non-perception of it when all its constituent parts have been withdrawn.

[199] Since the non-deviation of mutual perception is possible even in the case of sound by anyone, whereas its counter-positive (pratiyogin) is impossible [there], for one who considers the association with a single cognition to be delimited by the counter-positive, what further dependence on another could there be regarding the negation of the subject at hand—namely, one's own non-perception? Therefore, in establishing the absence of sound in a specific suitable location, the non-perception of the effect of cognition (*jñānakāryānupalambha*) need not be resorted to, because the proof is established by the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) alone.

However, since it is easy for darkness and light—which exist by mutually excluding each other's locations—to come into contact within a single cognition produced by the same sense faculty, the consideration of other means of proof [for their non-existence] pertains only to those situated at a distance, under the heading of proving their absence through the non-perception of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*).
The investigation into the non-existence of all sounds is complete.
APOHAPRAKARAṆAM [201,3] It is established that exclusion (apoha) is manifested by means of words and logical marks;
[201,4] this is proven for the purpose of establishing that all phenomena are inexpressible.

"Stability" (*sthiti*) means "establishment" (*vyavasthā*). By the phrase ending with "is manifested after having been established," exclusion (*apoha*) is stated here as the subject to be expressed (*abhidheya*); by the remainder, its fruit—that is, the result of that establishment—is indicated. Alternatively, the meaning is: "This is for the purpose of establishing the position (*vyavasthā*) maintained by the Teachers (*ācāryas*) that exclusion is manifested by words and so forth. In either case, the formulation of exclusion (*apohavyavasthāpana*) has as its ultimate aim the demonstration that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible.
This is what has been stated.

But is it not the case that this claim—that exclusion (*apoha*) is revealed by words and logical marks—is contradicted by experience? For instance, here in the region of a mountain, the cognition arising from a word or a logical mark that "fire exists" is observed to represent only a positive form (*vidhirūpa*).

The statement "it is not that it is not fire" merely presents a negation (*nivṛtti*). Furthermore, regarding that which is sublated by direct experience (*anubhava*), there is no consideration for other means of proof (*sādhana*), because the efficacy of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) comes to rest right there; for they arise from that [experience], and that [experience] is their fruit. Indeed, the emergence of another means of valid cognition does not occur independently of the assistance provided by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is one's purpose fulfilled merely by the emergence of another means of valid cognition.

As long as there is no experience of the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) brought about by that [first] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), another means of valid cognition—being devoid of capacity and seized by futility due to its independence from it—is in itself nothing at all. Therefore, it finds no scope for operation whether [the object] is established or sublated by it. So how can it be said that exclusion (*apoha*) is the domain of words and the like?

[201,17] Now, even if there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form "I cognize a cessation," nevertheless, the very mention of the referent "cessation" is itself the mention of cessation. For a cognition that does not include the qualification is not a cognition of the qualified. Therefore, just as in the case of a universal (*sāmānya*), even in the absence of a conceptual construction such as "I cognize a universal," because of the manifestation of a common form, the conceptualizing cognition is [of the universal].

[Objection: "The cognition of others is likewise; the cognition of exclusion (*nivṛtti-buddhi*), projected by the cognition of cessation, extends the conventional usage of the apprehension of exclusion (*apoha*). [Response:

But if the establishment of the cognition of a universal is based on the manifestation of a common form in the manner of a positive entity (*vidhi-rūpa*), then what has been gained for the establishment of the cognition of cessation in a mind where the form of non-existence does not manifest? Therefore, I [say] "cessation."

If there were a non-manifestation of the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*) even in the absence of such a mental mode as "I understand," who indeed would deny the established status of the cognition of cessation? Otherwise, if the conventional usage of "cognition" applied to that which merely appears as such, then let there be the "cognition of a horse" even when the mind has the form of a cow. Now, if it is argued that the cognition of cessation is included as a qualifier, even so—

If the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has such a form as "that which is excluded from non-cows," then let there be its inclusion [in the cognition] by way of being a qualifier; however, the actual cognition is "cow. And in that case, since the specific characteristic defined as exclusion (*nivṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), though existing, is not brought forth (*anutkalanāt*) therein, how can there be an establishment of that cognition?

This follows: how can this be the rule—that even though a positive entity (*vidhi*) manifests, it does not have objective status, whereas exclusion (*apoha*), though not manifesting, does? Furthermore, how can that form which is not determined by determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) be their object? Nor is there such a thing as "determination" of something that does not manifest within conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). As for that positive form which manifests within the internal domain, even for that, there is the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*).

That is called "cognition. Even there, it is merely a relation of exclusion (*apoha*); however, since the positive entity (*vidhi*) appears directly, there is no escape from the aforementioned defects. Moreover, in this way, it is unavoidable that even direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) has exclusion as its object, especially for a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) which, while delineating the exclusion of one thing, perceives everything else as excluded. Therefore, like a direct perception that grasps a positive form, [it would follow that conceptual cognition likewise grasps a positive form].

Even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has only affirmation (*vidhi*) as its object, not the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object. Furthermore, that which is excluded from another, or in which another is excluded—that is, the external object itself as distinguished from things of a different class—is what is called the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) when it appears as a mental form (*buddhyākāra*). Therefore, there is no utility whatsoever in [positing] affirmation alone under the name of "exclusion."

Because it is intended to be expressed, and because changing the name of a thing does not entail a transformation of its essential nature, therefore, in accordance with experience, let the external object itself—possessing a positive form—be what is apprehended by words and the like. Furthermore, regarding this, the treatise states: "Of these, two are reasons that establish a positive entity, and one is a reason for negation."
By this [type of negation], a negation whose object is not admitted as a real entity is established;
however, regarding a real entity, through the two preceding [types of negation], there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) by way of affirmation.
And if, as in the case of the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*), there were a cognition of mere non-existence even from another reason (*hetu*), then...

[202,21] Since there is no distinction based on non-perception, the entire system of formal determination—preceded by the differentiation of logical marks (*liṅga*)—has fallen into difficulty; how, then, can there be exclusion (*apoha*)?
Because it is said that [exclusion] is manifested by words and logical marks, he says: "It is a fixed state. This is merely a conventional arrangement.
The meaning is that it is not the actual reality (*vastutattva*) that exclusion is the primary object of words and so forth. What, then, is the actual reality here?
If one asks why: first, the primary meaning is expressed by words;
therein, exclusion (apoha) is understood as a secondary quality (guṇa) of that [meaning].
The object appears as one through superimposition, while another is established as the expressible;
in reality, however, there is nothing at all that is truly expressible.
Thus is the summary of the meaning of this section.

Indeed, a treatise cannot exist by disregarding direct experience; therefore, since it is impossible to deny that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises precisely upon manifesting the form of certainty (*visadhirūpa*), such is the meaning of the first quarter-verse. Because there is no dispute regarding the application of the negative particle (*nañ*), it is not addressed therein.

[203,8] Objection: The phrase "by means of words" (*śabdaiḥ*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should also be understood that [an object] is "established by logical marks" (*liṅgaiḥ*) and "made an object of conceptual constructions" (*vikalpaiḥ*). This being the case, let alone the fact that exclusion (*apoha*) is the denotable meaning (*vācyatā*), even its mere establishment is lost. For that establishment is twofold: through proximity (*saṃnikarṣāt*) and through an efficient cause (*prayojakāt*). In this regard, although all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible—

It has been stated that the means of presentation (*pratipādana*) is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*), but not some form of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that case, there is exclusion (*apoha*). For when a positive entity (*vidhi*) is primarily presented, exclusion is indeed understood as a subordinate element by virtue of being its qualification.
In that context, the phrase "by way of being its attribute" refers to a connection with the object (*arthasannikarṣa*). Consequently, it is both connected to the object and cognized.

Exclusion (*apoha*), although it is a positive entity (*vidhi*) that is primarily perceived, is said to be the principal denotation (*abhidheya*) because of the stated purpose; or rather, it is understood only as a subordinate quality (*tadguṇatva*) and not as the primary object—thus those who maintain the direct theory of exclusion (*apohavādin*) are refuted.

Furthermore, even though it was stated that there is no mention of words such as "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*), nevertheless, there is certainly no lack of cognition of exclusion when it functions as a qualifier.

Because the word "cow" and so forth are applied precisely to that which is excluded from non-cows and so forth. For the treatise states: "And the application [of a term] is such that one excludes that from which [the object] differs," and so on.
Just as, when the word *indīvara* (blue lotus) is applied to a blue lotus, its cognition necessarily involves the manifestation of "blue."

Likewise, even from the word "cow" (*go*), when it is applied to that which is excluded from non-cows (*agavāpoha*), the manifestation of the exclusion of non-cows (*ago'poha*) is unavoidable upon the cognition of a cow.

As for those who point out the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*)—which they describe as a confusion of the simple-minded—in the formulation of the convention (*saṅketa*) of the word "cow" upon the exclusion of non-cows:
how can they, who advocate for a convention based on a universal (*sāmānya*) or that which possesses a universal (*sāmānyavat*), escape from this fault?

Do they perceive the self? For indeed, by "universal" (*sāmānya*), one does not mean a mere universal, because that would entail the absurd consequence of applying the word "cow" even to a horse; rather, what is intended is the universal of cowness (*gotvasāmānya*). And if the convention of the word "cow" is established with respect to that universal of cowness, or with respect to the possessor of that universal, then when the object is the ultimate referent, that same fault remains: if the cow is not cognized, the universal of cowness—[is not cognized].
