Because of [the necessity of] full comprehension; for if there is no full comprehension of the universal "cowness" (*gotva-sāmānya*), there is no full comprehension of that which is denoted by the word "cow. Now, if the convention were established through such syllables as "the word 'cow' applies to cowness" or "to that which possesses it," then there would be faults. But when, having pointed out a single individual object standing before one, [the convention is made] regarding that which abides in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a form common to all individuals scattered across different places and times, based on the context and so forth—

If one determines the user [of the convention] and establishes the convention "this is a cow," then, since that person perceives only that common form (*sādhāraṇa-rūpa*) therein, he employs that very thing with the word "cow. Thus, how can there be the fault of mutual dependence? And if it is argued: "This is merely a restatement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the commentators—that the convention pertains either to the universal *gotva* or to the possessor of that universal (*tadvat*)—but such was not the sequence of instruction from those who originally established the convention"?

If, in that case, the formulation of the convention takes the form "the word 'cow' applies to what is excluded from non-cows," then this fault arises. However, when the convention "this is a cow" is established for a listener who—through the context—has ascertained that it refers to those specific individuals intended to be expressed, which are characterized by a single conceptual reflection (*ekākārapratyavamarśa*), then where is there any room for fault? For he [the listener], while reclining on the bed of his own conceptual construction, perceives all...

[204,11] Without depending on individual instances such as the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*), one who understands by himself those instances which are excluded from all heterogeneous instances and are denotable by the word "cow" (*gośabdavācya*)— and who, in whatever [instance] he understands that exclusion of the heterogeneous, employs precisely those [instances] with the word "cow"—

[204,12-13] thereby merely restates the established tenet (*siddhānta*) that the word "cow" refers to the exclusion of non-cows; it is not a description of the manner of linguistic convention (*saṅketākāra*), as intended.

[204,14] Because when the word "cow" (go) functions, the remainder can be expressed by the word "non-cow" (ago). That common form excluded from heterogeneous classes—which appears as the manifestation of a universal (*sāmānya*) in conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), or as the very self-nature of the individual—is what will be determined later.

[204,16] Furthermore, it is established that there is no circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). And it is established that, just as upon hearing the word "puṇḍarīka," one understands a white lotus, so too...

Even upon hearing the word "cow," when there is a cognition of the exclusion of non-cows (*agavāpoha*), even the proponent of the universal (*jāti*) must necessarily admit that the positive entity (*vidhi*) is inseparable from the mental apprehension of the qualifier, which is the exclusion (*apoha*). Furthermore, the distinction is not merely that the two are perceived directly as being related, nor is it simply a matter of one being primary and the other subordinate; rather, the term "quality" (*guṇa*) here denotes a property (*dharma*), namely, the positive form (*vidhirūpa*) which has the exclusion of others as its property (*anyāpohadharman*).
Because it is perceived.
Regarding this, Vācaspati, while refuting the similarity based on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) between two superimposed external objects belonging to the third form, said:
"And you do not admit that exclusion is a property of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That [objection] is indeed flawed. Now, [if it is argued that] it is real...

If it is argued that this is what was intended there, even so it is of no use, because it is precisely the relationship between subject (*dharmin*) and attribute (*dharma*) as established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that is accepted.

Only this remains to be addressed: why is there not a designation by way of positive affirmation alone, or else why does the consequence not follow that even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object?

To this we reply: In this context, certain established conventions (*vyavasthā*) are formulated otherwise for a specific purpose, based on a mere fraction of reality (*tattvaleśa*), even though they exist otherwise. For example, the case of "self" (*ātman*) and "its arising" (*tad-utpāda*). For arising is indeed a property (*dharma*) of an existent entity characterized by prior non-existence; nevertheless, based on that mere fraction of reality characterized as prior non-existence, it is conventionally established as "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*).

[205.2] This is for the purpose of warding off the contraction caused by the suspicion that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*). Or, just as— relying on the designation of a single continuum (*eka-santāna*)— one might be deceived by the fallacies of the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) or the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), thinking, "Who else will experience the karma performed by this very person?", so too, even now, the statement regarding the scope of the injunction (*vidhi*) is intended to dispel the suspicion that, in reality, a thing itself accepts a denotability imposed upon it by another.

Even the cognition of an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyaka*) is established as having exclusion (*apoha*) alone as its conceptual object; therefore, linguistic usage does not proceed by way of affirmation (*vidhi*) alone.
However, when exclusion itself is superimposed as the primary meaning of a word, then affirmation is also brought forward.
As it has been said:
[205,8] First of all, it is by means of words that an object is primarily expressed.

[205,9] However, since there is no dispute regarding direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not correct to establish a rule in that manner. It has already been stated that in that case, there is no excellence consisting of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*). For the treatise says:
"It delimits that [object], and thereby excludes what is other than it," and so forth.

However, with respect to that which is to be negated, the operation of negation is indeed placed foremost there by the term "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*). Or, as in the case of a positive function (*vidhivṛtti*), "non-apprehension" in the context of the non-implicative negation (*prasajyapakṣa*) is simply the capacity to produce a conceptual construction of absence, based on the experience of a determinate form.

Likewise, in the case of positive conceptualizations (*vidhi-vikalpa*) as well, the capacity for performing the corresponding action as prescribed in the tantra is itself the apprehension of the negation; and there is also the capacity for generating the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), such as "Fire has been cognized by me. Furthermore, in the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa-pakṣa*), the very perception of a restricted nature constitutes the negation in both cases.

[205,16] The inclusion. Both of these are intended by the author of the treatise; in some instances, according to the context, they function as a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), as in passages such as "there is nothing whatsoever in that form," and so forth.

In some cases, however, there are statements such as "because it establishes merely the thing itself as excluded from what does not have that nature," which rely upon *paryudāsa* (exclusion by affirmation).

Yet, there is no single fixed rule. Therefore, what the author of the *Ṭīkā*, who was eager to introduce that meaning for the sake of establishing his own *apoha*, and Trilocana said—that "the Master is inferred to be one who favors *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation)"—is refuted. Moreover, this is not so because of a lack of distinction.

There is no loss of the linguistic convention of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-vyavahāra-hāni*), because that which is produced by intention—such as "Rāhu’s head" or "cowness is a universal"—is not subject to removal. Furthermore, even you yourself certainly employ the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) in cases such as "the absence of a pot in a location" or "the absence of a *piśāca* in a pillar. Therefore, how can we [be accused of this], given that we maintain that negation is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-abhāva-vādin*)?

If this is argued, then the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*) is not being defined here, but rather its cognition (*pratīti*). And that [cognition] cannot be denied. Even in the case of the view of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), the negation of the other is simply the affirmation of that [remaining thing]; thus there is no loss of cognitive validity.
Nor is there a problem regarding the status of the qualifier, since by this very statement the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of affirmation and negation is demonstrated.

For this very reason, even the objection regarding contradiction is not to be faulted; for there is a contradiction with existence by way of its own nature (*svābhāva*), but not with the absence of another, since they coexist.
Therefore, it is rightly said:
"In that case, exclusion (*apoha*) is understood as a subordinate quality (*tadguṇatva*) of that [existence]."

Alternatively, this very exclusion of others (*anyaniṣedhana*) is the merit of that expression of meaning; therefore, it should be understood that "it is understood by means of that. As for the treatise, its application of words is such that it proceeds by way of excluding what is other; otherwise, its employment would be purposeless. By this, the fact that exclusion (*apoha*) is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) has been demonstrated, as well as the avoidance of the charge of being non-pervasive (*avyāpitva*). This is the path.

In the case of "he approaches Śrughna," this same principle applies with respect to the path under discussion; however, with respect to the destination that is the counter-correlate (*prati-anīka*) of Śrughna, it refers to Śrughna itself. Because there is no interruption—as in the case of a forest path—he indeed approaches it. By excluding [other possibilities] such as a caravan or a messenger, the restriction that "it is the path" is easily established. If it is argued that the meaning "it is the path" is already understood from the pointing gesture of the index finger, [we reply: it is the exclusion of others (*paravyavaccheda*).

[206,10] For that long, it is indeed accepted as existing. Moreover, in common usage, the employment of a term is observed even when its meaning is already understood, as in "two Brahmins are arriving" (*abhyāgacchati*) and so forth. Just as there might be a question—such as "Which path leads to Śrughna?"—intended to exclude other possibilities like those of caravan companions or other persons, so too is the answer "This is the path," for in every case, an injunction applies only to that which is marked by doubt regarding what is to be established.

Regarding the two negations: if exclusion of others (*parāpoha*) is not apprehended at the time of hearing the word, how could there be activity by way of avoiding other things? Consequently, one commanded "Tie up the cow" might even tie up horses and the like.

As for the claim that, upon the cognition of the cow, its own nature is not the nature of others, and thus exclusion of others is determined subsequently through implication (*sāmarthya*), [this is incorrect].

That view is untenable, because even for the first-time listener, no sequence of cognition is observed. For one who has mastered the linguistic convention at that time, when told "Bring the cow," does not resort to presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) regarding the exclusion of others. Nor is it logical that there should be a certainty regarding the cow if the cognition from the word "cow" were mixed with other things. Or, if such a cognition did occur, how could presumptive reasoning arise even subsequently?

For a cow is apprehended as being accompanied by the exclusion of other forms; how then could it be capable of establishing its own non-mixture with those others? Therefore, the cognition of a cow is said to be the apprehension of the cow as excluded from non-cows. Consequently, the very time of the cognition of its own object is the time of the cognition of the exclusion of other objects, just as at the time of the cognition of the moon when the word "moon" is employed, there is also the cognition of its whiteness. And just as when whiteness is cognized, what kind of moon—

The same applies to cognition: even when there is a cognition mixed with the form of another, what kind of cognition of a cow could there be? Nor is it possible to apprehend an object as being either unmixed or not unmixed, because its capacity [to function] remains impossible even subsequently. Therefore, it is not better to rely on the objective capacity of things for the sake of understanding negation.

As for what Vācaspati said—that individuals possessing a genus (*jāti*) are the objective domain of conceptual cognitions and words, and that the form of those individuals, being excluded from what does not belong to that genus, is understood through its meaning; thus, one who is commanded, "Bind the cow," does not bind horses and the like—this too is refuted by this very [argument]. For even if a genus is added as something additional, [the nature] of the individuals...

If form (*rūpa*) is indeed excluded from what is not of that same class (*atajjātīya*), then since it appears as its own form to both sound and conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), how can the apprehension of its exclusion from others (*atadvyāvṛtti*) be avoided? On the other hand, if the individual form (*vyaktirūpa*) is not excluded from dissimilar classes, nor is it perceived as such, then this is merely the grace of the universal (*jāti*); thus, it has already been stated that there is no comprehension of it even through the object itself.
If it is argued that [the exclusion] is excluded from others solely by the power of its birth, then it must have existed even previously; thus, it was not capable [of producing cognition] before.
If that were so, how could it produce it later either? For the requirement of the cooperation of the recollection of convention pertains only to the application of names (*nāmayojanā*);
however, the conceptualization of what is of a different class and its opposite depends on mere perception, as in the case of infants and the like—thus, this [objection] is trivial.

Alternatively, "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to that which is multiplied or practiced—that is, the property to be adopted (*upādeya-dharma*). By this, prominence (*prādhānya*) is to be characterized here.

Consequently, that very quality—namely, exclusion (*apoha*) itself—is the primary element in those words; thus, through its being, it is exclusion alone that is said to be the object of comprehension in words denoting positive entities (*bhāvavācin*), and not a positive injunction (*vidhi*), even though it may manifest, as if it were non-primary. For it is so because it depends upon the non-perception [of the word] in all heterogeneous instances (*vijātīya*).
In some cases, however, the treatise states that exclusion (*apoha*) is connected to the heard word (*śruti*) which belongs to the same class as the perceived object.

Furthermore, even when both [the positive and negative aspects] appear, because there is no object of cognition corresponding to the appearance, and because the exclusion of others is necessarily a positive entity, exclusion alone is primary. As the treatise says:
[207,13] There would be contact with the form of a real entity when a sound effects a separation; for that [contact] exists there in reality.
(PV III 132) [207,16] But in the case of words expressing non-existence, it is precisely because the entity does not exist. As the treatise states:

"Because non-existents lack form, words that denote form cannot even be suspected [to apply to them]; they are established as such, being the indicators of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). (PV I 185). Or rather, when that exclusion (*apoha*)—or the form excluded by it—is the object of expression, the "quality" (*guṇa*) consisting in the negation of faults remains established.
Regarding those words for which the denotable object is expressed as being already excluded by that very nature, as it has been said:
"Because cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature, there is no postulation of another locus; and since the cognition of a universal is an error, it is therefore not a fault. (PV I 169)

Thus, while these reasons for establishing exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object are being stated in the treatise, one should understand that in words expressing positive entities (*bhāva*), there is a contradiction with the primary manifestation of exclusion. Furthermore, it has been stated that in the section concerning words denoting non-existence (*abhāva*), this alone is the primary distinction (*viveka*). This indicates that in words expressing positive entities, the distinction is secondary and thus not primary. Specifically...

This indeed must be understood: in words denoting non-existence (*abhāva*), the exclusion (*apoha*) is the very object itself; in words denoting existence (*bhāva*), however, there is the exclusion of the object from others, and likewise the exclusion of others from the object. Between these two, the difference is merely one of expression. If the status of exclusion as the denotable meaning is established based on such a foundation, yet the object itself is declared to be primary, then alas, the ineffability of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirabhilapyatā*) [is undermined].

It has been indicated that "this time has arrived," and "the undertaking was for that purpose. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the system of denotation is established primarily through *apoha* in order to negate the imposition of the denotability of real entities (*vastu*), there too one might suspect: "One accepts the denotability of the object itself, yet teaches it otherwise to another; this is a great lack of discernment. Anticipating this, he says:
"The object is one," and so forth.

This is the meaning: for an object (*artha*) is of two kinds—external and internal—since no other exists. Of these, first, the external is established as the denotable (*vācya*) solely through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and not through the vivid manifestation of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If one asks how this is so, it is because of experience itself. For instance, in the case of perceptual consciousness, objects are restricted by place, time, and state, and possess vivid forms.

[208,14] Particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) appear and are experienced; however, it is not so at the time of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For at the time of conceptual construction, some form—distinct from those of a different class, as if intermingled with the forms of others, and as if indistinct—is what appears and becomes the object of experience, namely a perception that is not another's mind. As the treatise states:
"Because an object does not appear in the cognition of one whose eyes are not engaged by sound, just as it does not appear when the object is being seen.

If it is argued that there is a difference in appearance for the very same object due to a difference in means— since in one case the sense organ is the basis for cognition, while in the other case it is sound and so forth?
Regarding this, it has also been said:
"The basis for the various cognitions of that object is indeed produced one after another;
how can the form of a single thing appear as having diverse aspects? (PV III 235)

For two forms, one clear and one unclear, which are mutually contradictory, cannot belong to a single entity, such that one would appear to sensory cognition and the other to conceptual construction; for if that were the case, there would be a perception of a difference in the entity itself. Indeed, there is no difference in the entity other than a difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*), nor is there any difference in its own nature other than a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Otherwise, the three worlds would constitute a single entity.

[209,2] But surely, even though there is a difference in appearance—clear or unclear—with respect to a single tree for those situated at distant and near locations, there is no difference in the tree itself, because there is no difference in its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Thus, it is only an appearance assisted by a difference in causal efficiency that serves as a differentiator. [209,3–4] And since there is no difference in causal efficiency here, how can an object such as a cow, which is the object of a cognition produced by both a sense faculty and a word, be differentiated?

If it is argued that there is a partial correspondence (*bhāga*), we do not say that a difference in appearance is necessarily restricted to distinct objects; rather, it is necessarily restricted by the absence of having a single object. For instance, whatever appearance is contrary to the perceptual appearance regarding a certain object, that appearance does not have the same object as the former; just as the appearance of a cloth is not the same object as the apprehension of a jar, or as [the appearance of blue] is not the same object as the apprehension of a conch shell.
[209,8] It has a yellow appearance. Thus, at the time of conceptualization, there is an appearance contrary to the appearance of direct perception regarding the cow;

this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For having a single object is pervaded by the non-difference of appearance, as is seen in the case of what is perceived by the left and right eyes. However, if it were not so pervaded, then even another direct perception might have a contrary appearance, and the thing—

And it would be of two forms; yet since that duality does not exist, there is indeed a pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, when cognition—which arises from a difference in its substratum—is made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), its opposite is established. Therefore, wherever there is a difference in appearance accompanied by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, there is a difference in the real entity (*vastu*), as in the case of a jar and a cloth. However, when that auxiliary factor is abandoned, [cognition] proceeds necessarily toward a single object.
[209,14] To say that it "removes" [the error] is simply to say that here there is only a single erroneous appearance, like the appearance of yellow in a conch shell.

[209,15] If you argue that even in that case, the object is indeed the conch shell itself, [we reply: to claim that a cognition which does not touch upon its whiteness has the conch shell as its object is a most ill-spoken thing. [209,16] If you say that it cognizes the conch shell alone, no; for nothing other than that [yellow appearance] flashes forth as the "conch shell alone. When asked—

If it is argued that the mind flashes forth as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding what is to be, it is nonetheless established that the yellow appearance has the conch as its object, not the conceptualization. Likewise, even the perception of a globular form from a distance regarding a mountain peak does not have the tree as its object in the absence of specific features such as leaves, which are capable of determining distinctions like *pippala* and so forth; thus, this case is equal to the one under discussion. Furthermore, this is so because there is an absence of differences in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and the like.

[209,20] If it is argued that the object is not distinct because its erroneous nature is attributed to the single [cognition], then we say: if the manifestation in perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not erroneous, then the manifestation of something else is precisely what constitutes error. This same logic applies equally to the appearance of yellow and to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a cow. [Objection:
Surely, in some cases, the superimposition (*āropa*) of something upon another occurs due to some similarity; and this is not like the manifestation of a conceptual construction.

[209,23] "If it is argued that some mixed form has been perceived even in another birth, then from what, for whom, and where does this superimposition arise such that this is an error? This is merely another fault of yours, in that you maintain that the object of conceptualization is accessible only through direct perception and not through any other means; thus, even if it lacks a real object, it cannot be called an error."

For us, however, the proof of the matter at hand is established simply by the fact that its object does not extend beyond that. If it is argued that "that very thing appears otherwise" and thus remains within its own domain: since there is no entity existing apart from the form presented directly by perception, what is there to be made to appear otherwise? But that [object] does not appear at all; so enough of this prolixity. Therefore, it is not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—
The principle is that there is a manifestation within conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, what Vācaspati said—that there is no difference in cognition between verbal and perceptual cognitions when they have a real entity as their object, because the distinction between mediacy (*pārokṣya*) and immediacy (*apārokṣya*) is established by the difference in their causes—is not tenable. For a mediate cognition [does not apprehend] the real entity...

Because it cannot be established as an object (*gocara*). However, the distinction in causes based on being beyond the senses (*parokṣatā*) is fulfilled simply by the absence of grasping an object within the range of the sense faculties. If it is argued: "But surely you yourself have stated that if [cognition] has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object, there would be the consequence of non-difference between cognitions; therefore, by the very avoidance of that [consequence], it is established that [cognition] has a real entity as its object, and since no other entity exists, it follows that it has that [entity] as its object," we say: not so. For, [regarding] appearance—(12a)

[210,8] Since the proof of pervasion is established by showing that difference in kind (*vaijātya*) does not have that [single object] as its domain, this reductio (*prasaṅga*) is ours. For us too, this effort is precisely for the sake of dismantling the pervasion. When a difference in appearance is possible due to a difference in the causes, how could there be a pervasion [of the effect] by having that [single object] as its domain? When would even this be tenable? Or [how could it be tenable] by the mere fact of having that as its domain with respect to the cause?

A difference that is pervading can be demonstrated; however, that is not the case here, because the distinction of causes fulfills its purpose precisely by not being perceived in the object. Now, if it is argued that this manifestation of difference is possible even from a difference in causes, despite the two appearances having the same object, then let it be granted that the cognitions of the Gandhāra note and the sweet [note] also have a single object.

Since a difference in causes is possible even there, there is confidence regarding the identity of the object because both the non-conceptual and the conceptual cognitions have the mere nature of fire as their content. But if it is argued that in those cases, neither the quality of being a *gāndhāra* nor the quality of sweetness is reflected in the two respective cognitions—alas, this is a great degree of established certainty! For this is the result of an absolute difference in causes; namely, the state of having a single object.

Furthermore, reassurance will arise from the apprehension of the object at the end; in the case of doubt regarding a difference in the nature of the cause, there is the apprehension of an intermediate property such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*).
But in the case of absolute [non-apprehension], it is of a property common to all [things]; therefore, it is not on that account alone that [the inference] lacks that as its object.
Moreover, the persistence of the unreal property of sweetness (*mādhurya*) is also found in *gāndhāra*.

If it is argued that its sweetness is of a different kind, then even firehood as projected by conceptual construction would be something else entirely. Furthermore, even when a single form is being delineated, there is no identity of object between two appearances of distinct attributes, just as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver;
for the appearance of mother-of-pearl does not have silver as its object, nor does the appearance of silver have mother-of-pearl as its object, even though there is a common delineation of whiteness.

Therefore, just as in the conceptualization of fire, even though the thing itself appears, because the subordinate property of "donkey-ness" does not appear, it is not a cognition having a donkey as its object; likewise, even though the subordinate property of "fire-ness" appears, because the specific form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear, there is no appearance of another substance—this is the logical principle, since the particular characteristic alone constitutes the substance of fire. Consequently, there is a difference in the causes of cognition.
[210,26] Let there be a distinction between the two appearances; however, it is established that neither of these two appearances has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object.

[210,27] Therefore, it is proven that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not the object of words and the like. [211,1] Furthermore, if this were so, because affirmation and negation would both be of the nature of exclusion (*apoha*), their very utterance would be impossible; for those two [refer] to the substratum (*dharmin*).
Or it might concern phenomena (*dharma*), such as whether a tree exists or does not exist, or whether a tree is blue or not blue.

Regarding these, first of all, the first position is untenable. For a tree, which is determined by its existence or non-existence, is denoted by the word "tree. Thus, in the case of a position that restricts it to existence, the statement "it exists" is redundant, while "it does not exist" is contradictory because of the opposition. In the case of defining it through non-existence, however, the opposite holds true.
Furthermore, since there is an expectation of affirmation and negation upon hearing the word "tree," this appearance of a tree from the word "tree" is common to both existence and non-existence;
it is a tree [in appearance], but not an external tree—this is the logical conclusion (*nyāya*).
As for that which was introduced by the author of the *Tātparyaṭīkā* on the *Nyāyadarśana*, using his own words, as the denotation of the individual possessing the universal (*jāti*):

Immediately following this, it is not the case that the commonality of existence and non-existence for the universal (*jāti*)—which is the referent of the word—is untenable. For although it is eternal by its own nature, it becomes common to both existence and non-existence by virtue of depending on multiple individuals scattered across space and time; thus, it is fit for connection with "is" and "is not. Indeed, the existence of a universal consists in its relation to a present individual, while its non-existence consists in its relation to past and future individuals.

And as for the claim that "it does not exist," the lamentation— that because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), common to both existence and non-existence,
or else established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*)— does not, for its part, undermine the present argument. This is because, by placing the burden on the universal (*jāti*),
one has oneself accepted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible.

Furthermore, when a universal (*jāti*) is denoted by a word prior to the employment of terms such as "exists" (*asti*), it must be denoted as being either connected with a present individual, or connected with past and future individuals, or connected with both, or unconnected; these are the possible positions. Not even one among them can withstand the clever objections raised previously. For in the first position, there would necessarily be existence.

In the second case, however, there is a restriction to non-existence. As for the third case, if one’s desire is to apply the conventional usage of existence and non-existence to this [universal] based on its connection with the manifestation of the existent and the non-existent, then the word must likewise denote those very substrata through which its connection with a present manifestation is conventionally expressed, as well as those through which its connection with past and future manifestations is expressed. For otherwise, it could not be connected to both types of manifestation.
[211,20] It would thus be established. And that being the case, it follows as an undesirable consequence that those very words such as "exists" (asti) and so forth would not be employed.

Now, suppose this view is held: that form which is related to both individual instances is indeed denoted by the word for them, yet there is no cognition of those two related individuals. For it is not necessarily the case that the cognition of one related member entails the cognition of the other related member, just as in the case of the cognition of a son and so forth. If this is argued, then, in the absence of the cognition of the related members, there can be no cognition of the relation.
[211,24] Furthermore, there is cognition [of a relation]. For:
[211,25] The perception of a relation residing in two [terms] does not arise from the cognition of a single form;
[211,26] rather, the cognition of a relation occurs when there is the grasping of the essential natures of both. (PVA II 3)

[212,1] Therefore, just as in reality a person who is someone's son, when his connection to a father is not determined, is perceived as a mere man and is independent like a jar, so too an entity designated as a "universal," being perceived as independent, does not result in a cognition in the form of a universal. This is the refutation of the fourth position. Furthermore, because it does not imply its relata, there is no employment of words such as "exists" (*asti*) and so forth.

[212,4] It is established that when that [subject] is being determined independently, the application of words such as "exists" must pertain to its very existence or non-existence, and not to anything else. For even when a relation is ascertained, the application of words such as "exists" to one relatum does not follow from the existence or non-existence of the other relatum. Indeed, Maitra—who is ascertained as Caitra’s son—does not exist or not exist based on Caitra’s existence or non-existence.

The word "or" (*vā*) is capable of establishing a connection; but what kind of universal (*sāmānya*) could there be that lacks such a connection? If it is argued that the connection in that case is of a different nature, then regardless of its specific form, if it has not entered into common cognition (*pratīti*), it is merely a conceptual fiction (*asatkalpa*). Therefore, the application of words such as "exists" (*asti*) does not logically follow for that which is perceived as being like an iron pin—remaining indifferent to the existence or non-existence of other things—because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since its own nature (*svarūpa*) has already been established as existing, the term "exists" (*asti*) is redundant, and the contradiction with the term "does not exist" (*nāsti*) remains as before.

Therefore, the fact that the appearance in conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratibhāsa*) is common to both existence and non-existence is neither established otherwise nor is it conclusive for proving that it has an external object (*bāhyaviṣayatva*). For the determination of objects is invariably pervaded by the possession of a cause (*nimittavattā*).

And no other ground for [the cognition’s] occurrence is possible than the establishment of the existence or non-existence of the object, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, in the absence of that [object], since there is an absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), the state of possessing an object—which is restricted precisely to the establishment of existence or non-existence—is necessarily pervaded by that [establishment].
How, then, could it remain in something contrary to that? For a cognition whose appearance is common to both the presence and absence of a thing does not [establish] that thing by means of itself.

[212,16] Having an object, (13a) as in the case of the cognition of a cow [having as its object] a horse; and the conceptual cognition of a tree has a manifestation that is common to both existence and non-existence regarding external things—this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For "commonality" (*sādhāraṇya*), which consists in not establishing that [external thing], is incompatible with "the establishment of existence or non-existence," which is the pervader of "having that as its object. Thus, there is likewise a fault even in the statement that [a word] denotes an individual possessing a genus (*jātimat*).

If it is argued that [the universal is perceived] through the individual (*vyakti*), then the cognition is established; whether the universal (*jāti*) is additionally perceived or not, there is no liberation from those defects.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the followers of Kumārila—that because the thing itself possesses parts, there is no defect of commonality, for "treeness" is understood from the word without its existence or non-existence being determined, and it is then connected with one of those two as understood from another word—in that case too:

If "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is intended as a universal (*jāti*), then its refutation is accomplished by that very same [refutation of universals]. Alternatively, if "treeness" is that which is not apprehended as either distinct or non-distinct [from its instances], then it is necessarily restricted to either existence or non-existence, and since it is expressed by the word in exactly that way, what further purpose is served by words such as "exists" (*asti*) and so forth?
It might be argued: "Even though it is restricted to that, the word expresses only the factor of treeness (*vṛkṣatvāṅga*), not the factors of existence or non-existence."

If this is argued, then is the difference between those two parts conceptual or real? If it is conceptual, how can it be established that this verbal cognition—which appears as if directed toward two distinct entities—is actually object-directed toward a single reality? If it is real, there would be no possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression "the tree exists," just as in the case of a pot and a cloth; for according to the principle, two properties must be restricted to a single entity.

The rejection of the view that [words] possess a distinct [cognitive] faculty will be stated later. Furthermore, the position of their being either different or non-different has already been refuted elsewhere.

As for the claim that "the manner in which words convey meaning is not like that of perception, such that there would be no need for words like 'exists' (*asti*) as there is for what is perceived; for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess diverse capacities"—this too has been refuted by the critique of the appearance of difference when [words] have a single referent. Therefore, if...

The presentation of an object through perception would appear in the same way as it does when expressed by a word; and if it did not so appear, it would be incapable of making that object known. Therefore, this diversity of capacity among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is caused solely by the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) resulting from the experience of the actual nature of things, and not by a difference in the object itself, even though the object is one. This is because, if there were a difference in the object despite its being a single entity, such a state would be contradicted by the means of valid cognition. Consequently, this remains established: it is not [the case that...].

If the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were expressed, affirmation and negation would be impossible for the subject (*dharmī*); thus, the employment of further words would be redundant. Nor could they apply to the properties (*dharma*), because by the word "tree," the subject is presented in its entirety—just as in perception—leaving no room for affirmation or negation of blueness and so forth by another word, nor for any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is true even in the case of perception.

If it is argued that there is observed dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let that be so; however, this applies only to a case where the nature of the object has not been familiarized, because even that [other means] is non-ascertaining in nature.

But conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is itself of an ascertaining nature; therefore, regarding that which it grasps, what need is there for another? And yet, there is indeed dependence on other words or signs.
Consequently, there is no grasping of the actual nature of the thing, but rather only the experience of the arising of a conceptual construction that mimics the shadow of a single property.

[213,15] It is established. It is not established, for the properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are distinct from one another as well as from the substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, even when the tree is cognized by way of a single property such as genus, there is no cognition of its possession of other properties; why then should the apprehension of other properties—such as being blue, moving, or very high—not depend upon distinct designations?

That is incorrect; for if, despite the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) through its distinction [from other things], there were no cognition of its properties (*dharma*) by means of words or logical marks (*liṅga*), then let it not be so by means of the sense organs either. Now, if it is argued that by the force of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), the properties—which possess the contact of inherence and so forth—also become objects of cognition when the substratum is in proximity to the sense organ, then this same [principle] applies to the logical mark as well.

The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is indeed not deficient even by a fraction. Now, although for a word there is neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) with its denotatum, a proximity characterized as that of the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakalakṣaṇā*) is certainly accepted; for in the absence of that, the consequence would be the non-existence of the cognition of the denotatum itself.

Or, if there is such cognition, what need is there for conjunction and the like? And this [is true] even for those who rely on a natural relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*), such as in the case of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

[213,24] It is the same regarding the cognition of the object-entity (*vastu*). Nor is there any suspicion of an intervention that would obstruct the cause for engagement (*pravṛttinimitta*) when the cognition occurs by way of the word.

[213,25] For according to you, the individual (*vyakti*) possessing the universal (*jāti*) is determined from the word all at once. But if there were a sequential understanding of each one individually, there would never be a cognition of an individual possessing the universal. Furthermore, no sequence of certain cognitions is perceived. Therefore, let the universal be understood as something additional.

As for the name, the individual (vyakti), however, being perceived as the substratum (dharmin), could not attain its own stability without conveying the qualities, actions, and so forth inherent within it.
Otherwise, even in the case of perception, the cognition of other limiting adjuncts (upādhi) would be without a basis.
If it is argued that, this being the case, let there simply be the cognition of the individual by means of words—what is the point of accepting the accompaniment of limiting adjuncts?

[214,2] Now, must entities abandon their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) simply because your own position is rendered futile? Whether this other fault of yours remains or not, one cannot remain—like the sense organs—without first establishing the cognition of those things related to it through the means of knowledge regarding their object-domain. [214,4] If you argue that such a thing is observed only in the case of the sense organs and thus there is no such consequence for anything else?

If that were the case, then since a grass fire is observed to be capable of producing smoke that is inseparable from the process of transforming the fuel, a *khadira* fire would not be so. However, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists in both cases by way of generality; thus, there is no distinction. Therefore, if there is an absence of transformation in the *khadira* fire, then that is not smoke at all, but rather a mass of dust stirred up by the wind; nor is there a fire (*dhūmadhvaja*) there.

However, if this mass of rays from a heap of radiant ruby gems is elevated, and if that were smoke, and if that were fire (the bearer of smoke), then there would necessarily be a modification in the *khadira* wood; likewise, if that were the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) and the word were its means of proof, then there would certainly be the fault of cognizing a property (*dharma*) that resides in that [subject]. If, on the other hand, there is no cognition of a property residing in that [subject], then it is neither a cognition of the subject nor—

[214,11] A word is that which makes known the possessor of properties (dharmin). Whatever is a means of cognition for something is necessarily restricted to being a means of cognizing its properties, just like a sense-organ. And so, the logical reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is this: "The mark (*liṅga*) and the word are pervaded by being means of cognizing that which is intended to be beyond perception (*parokṣa*). [214,12–13] But this is not the case, because they depend upon other words and marks. That which is not a means of cognizing the properties inherent in something is not [a means of cognizing that thing].

That [word] generates knowledge of its own form; for example, the word "cow" does not cause the cognition of a horse, nor does a horse [cause the cognition] of a donkey, and smoke from cow-dung does not [cause the cognition] of a fire. Thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) in the case of the contrary [position]: that [the word] is not another property inherent in the object intended as its own referent. Since there is no possibility of perceiving a real entity devoid of genus, quality, action, and so forth even in a dream, the perception of a real entity [occurs] through the knowledge of another property which arises merely from the existence of that [entity].

"It is pervaded" means that even though both appear as if distinct within the conceptualizing mind (*kalpanābuddhi*), this [statement] is intended to show their non-separate manifestation. Therefore, it is better that there be no difference at all among the properties (*dharma*). For if one accepts the cognition of a real entity (*vastu*) in every respect, the objection regarding the cognition of its properties is difficult to avoid; what is the point of accepting a distinction that has fallen away from experience? The properties are simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity.
[214,20] Birth and so forth.

[214,21] As for that which is the ornamentation of the statement, it is not the case that what is related to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the intrinsic nature; if that were so, there would be a lack of relation.
For that very thing cannot be established by that very same thing. That is incorrect. In the phrase "related to the intrinsic nature," it is precisely the intrinsic nature [that is meant].

[214,23] It is intended as the nature of some particular entity, yet there is no difference between the two; for if there were a difference, it would possess its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatva*), which is contrary to worldly experience. [214,24] How, then, can it be resolved that "that very thing is connected with itself"? Otherwise, the use of the genitive case in the expression "its intrinsic nature" (*asya svabhāvaḥ*) would be untenable. [214,25] Alternatively, if by "intrinsic nature" one means simply a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, then there is no fault at all, provided that the universal and the like [are what is meant].
[214,26] It is the discernment of the nature of the mere thing (*vastumātra*). For it cannot be said that this is not the nature of the thing in its isolation.

[214,27] And it is precisely this that is intended here by the phrase "that which is related to the nature," because by the word "related" (*sambandhin*), the universal (*jāti*) and so forth are intended.
[215,1] Therefore, when something, though non-different from another, is shown as if different through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the conventional usage is that "it is related to that."
It is difficult to avoid.

And as for what Vācaspati says: "When this [substance] qualified by one limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is perceived, there is no perception of it as qualified by another limiting adjunct; for while the limiting adjunct qualifies the nature (*svabhāva*) of the substance, neither the limiting adjuncts nor its state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) constitute its nature"—that too is indeed unstable. For it has not been argued that the perception of another limiting adjunct follows from non-difference; even in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*), [it is stated that] the beneficiary—

For, by prioritizing the distinction based on the door of assistance (*upakāra*), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasañjana*) of grasping all aspects [of the object]. However, it has been stated that there is no difference between the powers (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). This [objection] has not even touched upon that point.

Furthermore, as for the refutation offered there by Bhūṣaṇa—namely, the consequence that when the sun and so forth are perceived, there would follow the perception of the entire mass of things assisted by them—that too is irrelevant.

It has been stated that the result of not fathoming his intention is as follows: this is the underlying motive. Having firmly established the refutation of *samavāya* (inherence) which you yourself will state later, you, the preeminent Naiyāyika, must accept that at the time of perception, when there is a connection with the sense organ (*akṣa*), the cognition of properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—which are admitted to be distinct from the substratum (*dharmin*) that experiences that connection—must be sought through their very capacity to assist, since they are assisted [by the substratum].
For there can be no dependence of one thing upon another that is devoid of assistance; thus, by means of establishing the non-difference of capacities, he says:
"If those capacities for the assistance of properties were different from it, what would they be to it?
If there is no assistance, then they would not belong to it, and thus there would be an infinite regress. (PV I 54)

Thus [it is said]. As for the claim that "capacity" (*śakti*)—whether innate (*sahajā*), generic (*jāti*), or adventitious (*aupādhikī*)—is distinct from the completeness of auxiliary causes (*sahakārisākalya*) and is therefore the objective basis (*ālambana*), this has been refuted and established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya* that capacity is simply the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) engaged in the performance of an action. Furthermore, it has also been shown in that same work that assistance (*upakāra*), which consists in the nature of producing a common effect, is possible even for that which is not itself an effect.

[215,19] Destroyed. Even between the effect (*kārya*) and that which assists the effect (*upakārin*), there is in reality no distinction at all; however, in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), when something new arises, it is called "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) because of the exclusion (*apoha*) of what was not previously there. But regarding the object of the conceit (*abhimāna*) that it was previously established, it is called "that which is assisted" (*upakārya*) due to the experience of a particularity (*viśeṣa*). Yet, in reality, for something to be both previously established and now qualified by a particularity is a contradiction. Therefore, in this case, it is by way of prioritizing the genus (*jāti*) conceived as stable...

In the case of reflection (*cintā*), the conventional usage of "being benefited" culminates in the state of being an effect; whether this occurs through actual identity of essence or through having a single object, there is no fault.
Thus, since proximity characterized as "benefit" must necessarily be accepted, the deviation from experience regarding those things benefited by the sun and so forth follows as a consequence;
therefore, this point is indeed common to both of us.
As for what Vācaspati says—that the natural relation between an individual and its universal does not depend on any further assistance—that is not the case.

There is no such thing as a "natural" relation that is something entirely different from those already well-known; rather, it is within the very existence of relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth that there is a distinction in their mode of occurrence based on whether they are deviant or non-deviant with respect to the relata. Thus, there are both adventitious (*aupādhika*) and natural (*svābhāvika*) relations.
The so-called "relation" is merely a conventional designation. An investigation into this matter should be sought in the discussion on pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Just as the relation between an individual and its genus is innate because the former is never found apart from the latter, so too is the relation of the genus with the individual innate, precisely because it is never found apart from the latter.

[216,7] According to the principle that "there can be no universal without a particular, like a hare's horn," [216,8] since there is no other proximity between those two, and because inherence (*samavāya*) is merely a conceptual construction,
[216,9] even if the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary does not exist reciprocally— like the earth and a seed— there is nonetheless a rule of non-deviation (*avyabhicāraniyama*).

[216,10] For those who are addicted to the admission of difference, [the relation] is untenable due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For when there is assistance, either the essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) thereof is invariably concomitant (*tannāntarīyaka*); thus, the meaning of non-deviation applies only here and not elsewhere, so there is no over-extension. [216,11–12] But in the absence of that [assistance], its avoidance is twofold: by resorting to the theory of essential nature (*svabhāvavāda*) or the power of inherence (*samavāya*). Not the first.

[216,13] This is a fallacious position (*pakṣa*), because it would entail the absurd consequence of overturning the observed capacity of anything whatsoever. Furthermore, a perceived benefit (*upakāra*)—as in the case of fire, a craftsman, water, and so forth, being the non-deviant cause for smoke, a jar, and a crane—is indeed observed. The only distinction is that it depends upon time, place, and other such factors. Therefore, by asserting that there is non-deviance solely through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) despite the difference [in entities], and not through a perceived benefit, one has necessarily excluded causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*). Second—
[216,16] Furthermore, the position [of the opponent] is untenable, because inherence itself does not exist. For inherence is accepted as being established by the cognition "this is here";

[216,17] yet that cognition is not to be accepted by those whose vision is obscured by the mass of cataracts consisting of the grasping of conventional designations, because it would follow that everything would be established for everyone. [216,18] This is because conceptual constructions arise under the sole control of mere desire, as is the case for other people in the world.

In every case regarding the point of dispute, that cognition does not exist at all, because its cause is absent. For the cause of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which differentiates between the meanings of the locative and nominative cases as "this is here"—is the appearance of two objects whose forms are unmixed with one another. This cause is absent even when there is water in a jar, for one who perceives only the jar lacks the entire collection of other causal factors;
and such a state exists later when there is merely the perception of the second [object]. Furthermore, that appearance of duality [does not exist].

In some cases, even regarding the object of inherence (*samavāya*), the conceptualization of "it exists" is merely an object of the conceptual construction of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Where there is no perception of both [entities] by way of excluding their non-self-nature, there can be no cognition of "this is here" for one who is not insane, as in the case of a vessel and a jujube fruit when one of them is not perceived. Furthermore, there is no experience of the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) through a distinction in the appearance of the forms of self and what belongs to the self; thus, there is a non-perception of the cause.

Because the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the two intended [terms] is established—just like smoke and fire—there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, those who imagine a different meaning by means of the term "self-made" (*svayaṃkṛta*) fall into the same error as one who attempts to weigh a horse on a balance scale; this very point he will state:
"And these words such as 'the cloth is here in the threads' are themselves self-made" (PV II 149).

[217,3] Thus [it is said]. But surely it has been stated that even a dual-natured entity is apprehended by non-conceptual cognition; so how is it that there is no manifestation of two intrinsic natures? In that case, the non-perception of the cause would be unestablished. This is quite wretched. For when an object is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), an instruction from another is not authoritative. If you argue that the manifestation is likewise [non-dual], then this follows: [217,5] ...For when an object is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), an instruction from another is not authoritative. If you argue that the manifestation is likewise [non-dual], then this follows:
When these five fingers are clearly manifest in direct perception,
he who perceives a sixth finger common to them all is like one who sees a horn upon his own head.

Thus, we who possess only the physical eye, even though we open our eyes as far as possible and examine [the matter] a hundred times, do not perceive anything else; yet for you, despite such an appearance through the grace of an unseen deity, there is no proof of the cognition of another in that manner.
Therefore, one who asserts that perception itself must be seen—that which is single and common to many observers—[is speaking thus].

Trilocana, too, appears to have been wounded by another’s gaze; for he says that although a universal (*jāti*) is perceived, because it does not exist in a separate location from the individual (*vyakti*), it is not seen as distinct from the individual, just like one individual is not seen as distinct from another. In this regard, by saying that the universal is seen but not as something distinct, he has effectively stated that, by necessity, it is the object of perception as non-distinct. And just as it is grasped by perception...

[217,14] For you alone, the object is entirely [particular]; indeed, there is no application therein of either a sublater or a prover. Consequently, the description of a logical justification—that the universal will differentiate itself from the individual through the recurrence of a cognition—is without foundation. Furthermore, it is also not tenable to say that a tactile cognition differentiates touch from odor and so forth; for there is no [cognition] that perceives even the non-difference between odor and touch.
[217,17] It is perception. [217,18] In that case, let it be explained that "it is not seen as distinct" means "it is not determined as distinct.

Even then, [217,19] regarding the statement "the universal (jāti) is being perceived," is it intended to mean "as distinct" or "as non-distinct"? If it is "as non-distinct," then there is determination.

[217,20] Let it be either through difference or non-difference; what is the use of considering this, since non-difference is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Or is it intended that they are seen as different? That, moreover, is impossible, because the absence of a difference in appearance has already been stated. If you say that a difference in appearance is established by reasoning (*yukti*), then this is a cause for shame. For:
"That which is non-manifest is established by means of the manifestation of something else;

it is not, however, within the scope of logical reasoning to say that this [other thing] lacks manifestation. This has been analyzed by us in the section on "The Absence of Causeless Entities" (*Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, p. 111).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that even when there is an appearance of a single form, another appearance can be established through reasoning, then the statement "fire is not hot" would not be sublated by perception; for an appearance of non-heat could also occur therein, just as there is an appearance of a universal (jāti) within an individual (vyakti).

If it is argued that there is no parity because there is no proof for the appearance of non-heat in fire (*citrabhānu*), even so, let there be doubt; how then can perception be a sublater (*bādhaka*) of non-heat, and how can there be an absence of proof, given that the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) exists? If it is argued that the logical reason (*hetu*) is non-deviant (*avyabhicārī*), then deviation also occurs either directly or indirectly.

Or [it may be established] from perception itself. And it has been stated that in that case, a contrary appearance cannot be negated. Furthermore, if non-establishment of non-heat follows from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the property of being cognizable (*prameyatva*), then the observation "fire is not hot" is not a fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), because the non-heat is not contradicted by that [observation]. Nor is the proof [of heat] perceptual; for fire is indeed hot.

Furthermore, it is not both hot and not-hot. Therefore, even one who is unwilling must admit that the experience of a determinate appearance necessarily sublates the appearance of anything else; otherwise, there would result a confusion of practical activity (*pravṛtti*). And thus: "For this person, while seeing fire... and so forth.

[218,14] Therefore, that which is proclaimed by those fallen into the flood— that when a convention is established regarding individuals possessing a genus (*jāti*), wherever the genus is perceived, there the cognition of being denotable by that word occurs— this merely mocks the empty sky, for that which is distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not perceived even in a dream. For this very reason, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which joins the qualifier and the qualified as they are grasped in their mere own-form (*svarūpa* alone)...

That validity which was asserted has been refuted, because previously the very perception of duality was shown to be non-existent. Therefore, there is no lack of proof for the non-perception of the cause.

Furthermore, since this [cognition] is unestablished here, where is there any talk of inherence (*samavāya*)? And how could it be tenable that there is an innate connection between the manifestation and the universal? Consequently, even if the doctrine of the difference between the attribute and its possessor were difficult to avoid, then—

Even if proximity is characterized by assistance (*upakāra*), since the capacity of that which apprehends a real entity (*vastu*) is restricted to grasping only what occupies the same location, the avoidance of the deviation regarding subtle assisted entities remains the same. Therefore, if the nature of the entity is cognized even through the medium of a single property, then because the cognition of its entire essence has occurred, where is there room for affirmation or negation by means of another word? What, then, is the use of the word "tree" alone even now? Consequently, where is there scope for the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of a universal?
[218.23] What is the establishment of the relationship between qualifier and qualified? But when, [218.24] in the separation of the connection of a single object, one sound [or] gender operates,
[218.25] there is no referent at all that is divided for you.
Because of the denotation of which, through the power of the thing itself, there is a comprehensive understanding;
therefore, a single word, having a single substratum, may have various results according to its different modes of differentiation.

(PV I 129–30) For when a thing is the object of expression, it is impossible to apply affirmation or negation with respect to its entire nature. However, when—due to beginningless false conceptualization—...

[219,5] By the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from the habitual practice of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), cognition itself arises from the awakening of certain latent impressions, culminating in the form of the exclusion of a single [object].
At that time, what room is there for the aforementioned faults, which would arise if there were the capacity to grasp a real entity (*vastu*)?

For instance, when "tree" is said, by virtue of the appearance of a form common to *dhava*, *khadira*, and so forth, the universal (*sāmānya*) has as its ultimate reality the exclusion (*apoha*) of non-trees.

It is established that this form (*rūpa*)—being non-rejected, appropriated, and characterized by distinctions such as existence (*sattā*), substance (*dravya*), and so forth—is dependent upon the employment of other words.

Thus, within a single substratum (*dharmin*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words such as "existent," "blue," or "moving," which are based on other attributes (*dharma*). Furthermore, when there is a requirement for the indication of a specific distinction in accordance with the intellect, there is the designation of a distinction, such as "the existence of the tree."

The relationship between qualifier and qualified is established in both ways. This being so, just as in the case of a tree, increase and decrease are observed due to contact with water and fire, and through the superimposition of identity there arises the cognition, "This very same tree has become like this," and that [tree] is determined to be as if endowed with those [qualities] even when the properties suitable for such connection have not arisen; likewise, it is so in the case of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as well.

Even when other properties do not appear, that which has the form of a tree is determined to be "capable of that" (i.e., capable of being a tree); and in such applications as "the blue one is not fruit-bearing," it appears as if it partakes of increase and decrease, and is likewise apprehended as being that very same thing. However, an external object—unlike water and so forth—is not subject to increase and decrease even at the time of the utterance of the word. And this [phenomenon] would not be tenable if the object were external, because it occurs exactly as it appears.

Because it is not the reality, and because it does not appear according to its true nature. For this very reason, even with respect to distinct qualifiers, there is no occasion for the employment of another word, such as "Caitra’s cow is possessed by Maitra, but not by the horse," because the appearance of increase or decrease produced by those [qualifiers] does not exist externally. Therefore, this is merely a play of the intellect; and where this delusion occurs, it is indirectly inseparable from the entity that is excluded from others (*anyāpoha*).

In that regard, people whose purpose is fulfilled by the performance of a desired causal function do not exert effort to infer such a specific distinction, nor are they capable of doing so; thus, their conventional practice remains undetermined. Even when there is a discrepancy, they do not establish that "this is false. Furthermore, it is not the case that at other times there is no objective referent (*bāhya-viṣayatva*), for even for the authors of the treatises, such an inference is possible; what then to say of others? Therefore, it is not [the case].
It is established that the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is not within the domain of words and the like.

Having apprehended a single substratum as the locus of various excluded properties, this primary cognition— which appears to involve the presence or absence of each individual property therein— deludes people just as they themselves are deluded.
Having attained fulfillment through a portion of reality, one no longer considers it to be an affliction.
Thus is the summary verse.

Nor does it belong to the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). For instance, in the sentence "Cows are grazing on the northern bank of the river," from the word "cow" (*go*) and so forth, there appears an image consisting primarily of a synthesis—such as the dewlap, horns, and tail-hair—which is surrounded by the forms of the syllables; yet this is not the universal itself, because it does not involve a reflection upon the distinctions between members of the same class.
Indeed, "cowness" (*gotva*) is said to be empty of color, shape, syllables, and form;

nor does anything else appear [therein], like space. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no distinction between the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of "cowness" and "horseness. For that very thing—the mere form of blazing light—is, despite being absolutely distinct from every individual (*vyakti*), [perceived] through its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

That which is being unified is called the "universal" (*sāmānya*). However, that universal is not identical to those [individuals], because it follows after them as the form of a cognition. For the treatise states:
"And how could that which is non-different from cognition become a separate object? (PV I 71cd)

Furthermore, in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as "this is that," "this is like that," or "this is a cow"— which is intended to be produced by the sense organ and the object immediately following sensory perception—
there is no appearance of an external object. However, just as it joins a superimposed,

non-worldly form appearing within itself to a physical object appearing before one, so too, because that external object does not exist, this is nothing but an illusion, like [the perception of] hair-tufts.

[220,16] Like light. [220,17] If it is argued that this is so because of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), [we reply: Is there not a contradiction regarding a mass of hair, since there is an absence of resistance when the hand is intentionally directed toward it? But in the case at hand, if there were a subverting proof, would that very experience of the manifestation and the manifested not itself be the subverting proof?

[220,19] As for the other [position], it has already been stated that people lack the capacity for discernment. Or how is it that even now the absence of resistance (*pratighāta*) and so forth does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*)? For those very things, such as horns and the like, though situated in their respective places with indistinct forms, appear even today as if they were being conflated—possessing infinite manifestations due to differences in place, time, and so on, and lacking a fixed state of location—despite their resistance and other properties. [220,21] Of these, resistance and so forth...
Since it is fixed, what kind of distinction could there be from hair and the like, such that one might say there is no sublation here?
Therefore, let this be a transformation (*vivarta*) of cognition itself into that form by the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); or let that form appear as something non-existent;
or let the individuals themselves appear otherwise through the exclusion of distinctions among their own kind, due to the intervention of experience.
Or let it be called a lapse of memory; in any case, this report of a "universal" (sāmānya) with respect to the external world is nothing but an error.

Furthermore, it is logical that it should arise from the experience of the object present before one as "this very thing. Now, the causes of error—such as cataracts, rapid spinning, and so forth—which produce a distortion of the sense faculties, have indeed been enumerated; yet not even one of these is present here.

How can this error be accidental? Or do you think that those [factors] are the causes of non-conceptual error alone, while this is a mental error? Even that [mental error] is based solely on the perception of similarity between the superimposed object and the locus of superimposition;
since such a distinction does not exist, how can there be even mental error? Furthermore, all error is based solely on similarity.

Indeed, it is not possible for there to be a perception of similarity even in another birth without having seen something similar [in this life]. Furthermore, since nothing with a mixed form has ever been seen even in another birth, how could there be a superimposition of that? Oh, what great human effort! For if, as stated in the sequence above, the lack of an object cannot be avoided, then whether one engages in the conventional usage of "error" or not, it makes no difference.
[221,10] Since the point at issue is already established, what is the point of this insistence?
[221,11] Furthermore, that which was stated regarding its being accidental is incorrect, because you too must necessarily admit a difference in the causal complex (*janakasāmagrī*).
[221,12] Otherwise, how could the sense organ and the object, which are observed to be restricted to producing non-conceptual cognition, produce a conceptual construction?

[221,13] Does it produce [the conceptualization]? Therefore, this causal complex (*sāmagrī*), possessing a capacity that exceeds [its constituent parts] through the cooperation of the recollection of the previous perception of the object-mass (*piṇḍa*), produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The meaning is that it indeed produces a cognition devoid of an external object (*nirviṣaya*), because the nature of conceptualization (*vikalpatā*) is established in its lack of an object, even with respect to that [perceived] portion. Thus, it is better to regard [this conceptualization] as distinct from the experience (*anubhava*) which has a vivid appearance, just like a conceptualization of a different class.
It is better to say that there is also a conceptual construction of a similar kind; therefore, the establishment of a universal (jāti) does not result from perception.

Nor does it result from inference, because the relation of cause and effect—such as that between fire and smoke—cannot be grasped by anything other than the very sphere of perception. However, regarding the production of cognition in a general sense, there is another cause besides those causes already observed.

That which is to be depended upon might perhaps be established as being like a sense faculty, if it could demonstrate the absence of the intended effect—namely, cognition—at some time even when all other causes are present. But this is not possible in the case at hand. For if one were to show the absence of the cognition of a cow either in another individual body of a cow or in the interval between them, then the absence of the cognition of a cow would be logically accounted for by the very absence of the individual body of a cow.

How could it imply dependence on something else, such that there might be the expectation that "this very thing is cowness"? Is it not the case that a "cow-body" is so called precisely because of the universal *gotva* (cowness); otherwise, even a horse-body would be a cow-body? If this is so, then the universal *gotva* must also [be derived] from the cow-body itself; otherwise, even horseness (*turagatva*) would be cowness. This is the same [in both cases]. It is not [the case that one is dependent and the other is not].

Furthermore, it is impossible to determine the existence or non-existence of such a universal anywhere, just as one cannot do so for an individual object (*piṇḍa*); therefore, this argument amounts to nothing.

Now, it might be argued: "If, due to the absence of a Bāhuleya individual, there is no cognition of 'cow' in a horse, then let there likewise be none in a Śābaleya [cow], since the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not persist anywhere. It is true that the particular characteristic does not persist; however, just as [the universal] belongs to its own class—

In a cognizer who possesses the recollection of having seen another individual cow, there is the capacity to produce a reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*) of that form in both a *bāhuleya* (a dark-spotted cow) and likewise in a *śābaleya* (a white-spotted cow). Therefore, it is not just a single individual cow, but rather all such individuals that ascend into conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
