Consequently, there is no cognition of "cow" with respect to a horse.

[222,3] But surely, since capacity (*sāmarthya*) is power (*śakti*), it is simply a universal (*jāti*) that is being spoken of. For is that power distinct or non-distinct [from the individual]? If it were non-distinct, then—like a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—it would not be pervasive, and thus no other [individual] would be capable. If, on the other hand, it were distinct and common to others, then this is nothing but a universal; the dispute is merely over the name. To this it is replied: it is indeed non-distinct.

Regarding each individual thing: just as one entity possesses a nature capable [of producing an effect], what kind of fault does another entity bring about by being likewise? For just as in your view, even a single universal (*jāti*) is the cause for the production of a uniform cognition and verbal designation, and another [universal] is also so by its very own nature because it lacks any other universal; so too, in our view, an individual (*vyakti*), though distinct, is the cause by its very own nature independently [of anything else]. Therefore...
However, the nature of manifestation is bound by a succession of causes.

As for what Trilocana says— that the inherence (*samavāya*) of universals and particulars, such as "horseness" and "cowness," in their own substrata is the cause of the designation and cognition of a "universal"— that is refuted by the very rejection of inherence.

Alternatively, it may be that inherence (*samavāya*) itself, by its very nature, is the cause; thus, there is no damage to the illustrative example. Nor is there a mutual causal capacity between the universal (*jāti*) and inherence through the postulation of their acting together; for in that case, since even a single entity would possess generative power by its own nature, one would be offering a libation of water to the notion of a "universal" and its cognition. Indeed, it is only those things such as seeds that are generative by their own nature which require auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

[222,15] Since "completeness" is a capacity conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikī śakti*), the fact that production occurs by way of intrinsic nature (*svarūpeṇa*) must necessarily be asserted; thus, reliance upon *samavāya* (inherence) is a mere mockery. [222,16] Furthermore, in the absence of its operation (*vyāpāra*), the arising of a cognition bearing its form cannot result from other causes alone; otherwise, one might as well ask why the universal (*jāti*) is not produced by the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves when a cognition with a recurring form arises. [222,17] Such is the consideration regarding the universal.

[It would be] like scraping away everything down to the roots. Even if [the universal] were accidental (*ākasmika*), that same fault remains; thus, by placing a foot upon the neck of one who accepts a universal, [we ask]:

since the universal must be made to accept its own operation through its very own nature within the recurring cognition—out of fear of infinite regress—and since it must be made to accept other universals that have not themselves been superimposed, how can inherence (*samavāya*) serve as a solution? Furthermore, that [inherence] would require an additional auxiliary cause.
Whether it be so or not, the universal (*jāti*), however, being independent of the individuals and possessing its own inherent capacity by its very nature, produces the recurring cognition;

for since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be questioned, one cannot state—without the command of kings—that it is the individual that does so. By this, it is explained how this recurring cognition, which follows an underlying recurring entity, occurs with respect to individuals that are absolutely distinct.

It has also been rejected that this [inference] proceeds by way of reasoning (*ūha*), on the grounds that it ought to apply to those things which follow the state of being objects of excluded cognitions;
for there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of universals (*jāti*), which, though manifested as mutually excluded, are nevertheless apprehended by a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*).

If it is argued that "since universals are not perceived, where could there be a recurring cognition such that a deviation would occur?", we say no, because that would contradict your own accepted position.

Because it is established by this sequence: for indeed, the recurrence of conditions is adduced to prove the existence of a recurring entity; and if that [recurrence of conditions] is invariably concomitant with the absence of a recurring entity, who—other than one possessed of dullness—is able to withstand this contradiction? Furthermore, even regarding imagined universals (*jāti*), the fallacy of deviation remains exactly as it was; what more is there to say here?

[223,4] By means of perception? [223,5] Or is a restriction stated regarding objects currently being perceived? No; for even in that case, because there is no sublation by a contrary [cognition], a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established. Furthermore, since deviation is observed in general, there is a seed of doubt regarding other cases as well. And if...

The exclusion of deviation regarding the universal (*sāmānya*) is made with respect to a specific visible object (*dṛśyaviśeṣa*). In that case, one should not say: "That recurrence of designation and cognition among distinct things is caused by a recurring entity, just as the recurrence of designation and cognition as 'thread' occurs among flowers, so too does the recurrence of designation and cognition as 'cow' occur among distinct cows. For the designation [occurs] precisely when there is a visible cause.

Because there is a pervasion due to the fact that the recurrence of the cognition follows from the recurrence of the object as its cause, and because there is a rule regarding the cessation [of that cognition], this is logical. Indeed, even according to the Sūtra, there is no recurrence of the cognition of a Sūtra with respect to things not made objects of vision. For conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—which possesses a real basis (*savastuka*)—is established as having the perception of a real thing as its effect, even without inference. Therefore, by the non-perception of the cause through the opposite [of the effect], the recurring [conceptualization] is turned back.
The pervasion of the recurrence of designations and cognitions by an entity comes to rest only in the state of having a perceptible cause, provided that there is an objective reality as their domain.
However, when there is a dispute regarding the existence of such an objective reality, this rule does not hold.
Furthermore, as for the subverting argument against the contrary position stated by him—that the recurrence of designations and cognitions must cease from something—[it is refuted as follows].

[223,15] "It occurs only in certain instances and possesses a cause; nor is there any other cause," and so forth. That is not correct. For it has already been established that even without a recurring [universal], there must necessarily be an acceptance of a specific nature that is excluded from what is not of that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta-svarūpa-viśeṣa*), because of the recurrence of both designation and cognition. Therefore, just as one excludes the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and [perceives] only in "cowness" and "horseness" etc., [there is] the universal, the universal.
Thus, the recurrence of verbal designation and cognition occurs due to some form of proximity; let it be the same in the case of individuals as well.

By this, when the recurrence of verbal designation and cognition is to be proven regarding a recurring entity, both [the reason and the example] should be understood as inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) serves as the subverter of the contrary in the case of its pervasion. Furthermore, there is no other such "proximity."

Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is distinct [from the universal]. For just as "cowness" is excluded from the generality of horses, so too are "horseness," "substantiality," and so forth; likewise, just as one individual cow is excluded from cowness, so too is another. Regarding the difficulty of analyzing whether this [exclusion] is identical to or different [from the individuals], the answer is the same as in the case of causal capacity (*śakti*). Consequently, those objects which, by virtue of being excluded from what is not themselves, are mutually proximate, produce a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) upon the perception of one [of them] followed by the perception of another, and no others. And that very thing is causal capacity; it is not...
[The entity] has birth as its nature. Otherwise, since that [nature] would exist even in a single instance, auxiliary causes would be useless.
(PV I 164cd) This should be understood from the discussion on momentary destruction and auxiliary causes; and that proximity is a causal succession.

It was just stated immediately prior that [the universal] has arrived. Furthermore, one must necessarily postulate a specific proximity produced by causes, on account of which only certain individuals become the substratum or receptacle for a genus, while others do not. Otherwise, if it were otherwise, the statement that "an effect possessing a restricted genus arises due to the restriction of the causal complex" would be a mere triviality for the *Bhūṣaṇa*.
And this being so:

"Since the difference [between individuals] is equal, let that very same proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by which a universal (*jāti*) extends to some [individuals] and not others be the basis for words and cognitions. (PV I 162)
What is the use of "birth" (*jāti*) here?

Furthermore, regarding what was said by him as another faulty objection: it is not the case that there is no such proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by which a staff, a thread, and so forth, extend in some places and not elsewhere; for that very same proximity exists in the case of a person, a crystal, and so on, [accounting for their being] "one with a staff" or "one with a thread," and so forth.

[224,12] Let there be a basis for conventional usage; what is the need for a staff, a string, and so forth? When would this be appropriate? Only if some capacity established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were denied in some instance. For instance, proximity based on causes such as the perception of approaching—which is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—is the cause for the movement toward a man or a crystal of the staff and the string respectively. This is the experience of the person and the crystal in contact with them.

And just as the basis for the cognition of a "man with a staff" is established for a cognizer who possesses the memory of convention (*samaya*), so too this cognition of a "cow" is not observed to follow the presence or absence of the entity "cowness. Rather, in the dark, there is merely a groping with the hands; someone must state that such a thing is to be designated by some basis for the cognition of a cow. In that case, if it is by means of another alternative that must necessarily be accepted...

If that [inference] is established, there is no sublation; so why is it said that this involves a more cumbersome conceptualization? Otherwise, having postulated even that, one could not prevent the postulation of hundreds of useless things. However, if—in the case of a person and so forth—it is observed that the proximity of a staff and such follows the presence or absence of conditions such as the act of approaching, and if the experience of the proximity of a staff and such in a person and so forth is observed—

The cognition of "one who possesses a staff" and the like conforms to the presence or absence of the object; likewise, the function of the causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*) consists solely in the restriction of the genus (*jāti*), and not in the unifying synthesis (*ekāmarśa*). Furthermore, if there were such a synthesis, it would be experienced that this very genus itself is currently active;
thus, the fault would belong to one who denies it. However, this is merely a conventional designation (*samayamātra*), since it has been established that the genus transcends direct experience.

Thus, how could there be a charge of futility regarding that [reason], since it would also take objects such as a staff and so forth as its domain? In this manner, sublation (*bādhana*) should be inferred in other similar counter-arguments as well.

Now, the inference is as follows: whatever is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇagrahaṇa*), just like the cognition of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍijñāna*).

And this cognition, "this is a cow," is a qualified cognition; thus, by implication, it is a reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*). For in the example, [the cognition] is seen to be the effect of the experience of the qualifier.

[225,3] "The cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) is established"—herein lies the inquiry: is it to be proven that the cognition of a qualified object is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of a distinct qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), or is it to be proven that it is necessarily preceded by the mere experience of the qualifier? In the first case, the thesis is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), which leaves no room for the application of the proof; for in perception, which grasps the actual entity (*vastu*), there is no appearance of both [qualifier and qualified as separate]. [This is because] the state of being a qualified cognition...

Furthermore, the universal (*sāmānya*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*), because it is observed even without the apprehension of distinct qualifiers, as in the cases "the pot possesses its own nature" (*svarūpavān ghaṭaḥ*) or "cowness is a universal. However, in the second case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the relationship between qualifier and qualified is accepted by assuming an imagined distinction, as in "the individual possesses the universal cowness" (*gotvajātimān piṇḍaḥ*), based on the experience of the exclusion of non-cows.

[225,9] Because of its cultivation, there is the conventional usage "this is white. Thus, in verbal and other types of cognition, there is no appearance of either an external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) or a universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the universal is not established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) should be considered in the same manner.

[225,12] If this is so, how then is it that the treatise is consistent with the statement: [225,13] "First, the primary meaning is expressed by words"? [225,14] For that [primary meaning] is not established by that [word], nor does the manifestation of that [meaning] occur upon the cognition of it.
Some say that there is a connection [between the two], namely, "it is superimposed.

The conventional usage of objects is twofold: by way of appearance (*pratibhāsa*) and by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, in this case, even though there is an absence of appearance, [the object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) excluded from others].

Objectivity has been stated to consist in mere determination (*adhyavasāya*). And thus, because one proceeds toward the very thing-in-itself (*vastu*) by means of that determination even from that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), [it is so called]. Now, what is this so-called "determination" that is distinct from conceptual construction, given that there is no difference in meaning between "that which is conceptually constructed" and "that which is determined"?

How, then, can there be a designation of a distinction as "by means of determination from conceptual construction"? Furthermore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not [excluded from others].

When conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) manifests, it is determined as "conceptually constructed" (*vikalpita*). What logic is there here by which, depending upon that determination, even that [external object] is established as the object of conceptual construction? Furthermore, the external world would be both the non-object of conceptual construction and yet its apprehension through association with words—this is difficult to reconcile. Moreover, since that [association] does not exist within itself, that which is called "conceptual construction" would simply not exist at all.

[225,24] For what purpose, then, would there be an investigation of the object? If activity were to proceed from a word when the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has not been apprehended, it would follow without distinction in all cases, because there would be no distinction since everything remains unapprehended. Consequently, even the attainment of the intended object would not occur with certainty; thus, there is a failure of inference as well.

To this it is replied: It is true that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) have the same object; however, the term "conceptualization" is based on the association with words and so forth, whereas determination is based on the capacity for engagement even with respect to what has not been grasped. And although the entire world is ungrasped, nevertheless, activity is restricted to specific objects because conceptualization possesses a restricted form. This restriction—

For entities are capacities whose intrinsic natures are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); they do not admit of the objection regarding the confusion of capacities, just like the arising of what was previously non-existent.

For even though everything is non-existent therein, only a sprout arises from a seed, because its capacity for that [specific result] has been determined by valid cognition. Likewise, here too, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) having the form of fire for one who seeks the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) of the object "fire," [only that specific effect arises].

[226,7] For one who possesses the memory of that [object], how can the capacity for activity directed toward fire—which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—be subject to the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
[226,8] And by considering proximity, even though the actual fire has a blazing and radiant form, so too does the representation (*ullekha*) of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

[226,9] To that extent, the power of the conceptualization of fire to prompt activity resides only in that [fire] and not in water or other things; nor does it prompt activity through the superimposition (*āropa*) of similarity.

We reply: there is no room for the critique that consists in superimposing an external form upon the external, nor upon the form itself. What then? That cognition, arising solely through the maturation of its own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), projects an engagement with the external even while not perceiving the external;
thus, it is indeed erroneous (*vipluta*).
As for the treatise:
"And the delusion regarding place does not exist in cognition, because it arises simultaneously with the intellect;
for such a [delusion] is not admitted in any other case, since the intellect is not present there. (PV III 13)

Thus, it is not the case that [the cognition] proceeds by way of superimposition (āropa), as is the case with silver and the like; rather, it is due to the restriction of the power [of the cause] bound to the production of such a form. This is just as a rice seed is the material cause (upādāna) for the rice sprout—the effect (upādeya)—even though the latter arises without a persisting substrate (niranvaya), because the stability of the status of "rice-ness" and so forth has been refuted by the critique of permanence. Furthermore, this does not imply that the investigator, while determining [the object], fails to perceive the thing-in-itself.

The consequence of non-occurrence is consistent; for even in the case of perception, activity is accompanied by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), and the attainment of purposeful action depends on the necessity of the existence of the real object (*vastusattā*). And just as that necessity is established through perception by way of a connection with the real object, so too is it established indirectly through a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpaviśeṣa*); thus, inference is not without foundation. However, in the case of verbal cognition, because there may be doubt regarding the object, even the attainment [of the object] is uncertain.

In this regard, there is no fixed rule. Therefore, "determined" (*adhyavasita*) means that even though it does not appear [in consciousness], it has been made the object of engagement. Consequently, even though it does not appear in conceptual cognition, the fact that it is determined is not sublated by the external [object]. This very point is the meaning of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized, and of the teaching on the realization of non-difference. And therefore, that [external object] is not cognized by that [conceptual cognition].

It has been shown that the objection—that there is no appearance of non-difference—is untenable, because the demonstration of its meaning has already been established. Just as the determinate cognition "and this fire is here" gives rise to physical activity, so too does it give rise to verbal activity in the form "fire has been perceived by me. It also produces mental activity in the form of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) having that very aspect. This being the case, just as by means of conceptual construction...

The determination that "this object has been grasped," as well as the thought "it has been conjoined with a word," occurs because the form of the word flashes forth just like a slight portion of the form of the object. Therefore, as long as a person possesses the conceit of grasping an object, they likewise possess the conceit of grasping it as conjoined with a designation;
thus, the establishment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is based solely on the adherence to such a judgment, and not in reality.
And it is said:
"Nowhere, whether externally or within the mind, does a connection with words manifest; rather, there flashes forth a mere fragment of the form of an object, permeated by the shapes of syllables."
Although both "selves" are merely the determinations of the intellect itself, nevertheless, because conceptual construction is established therein, it places them externally and in words.

For this very reason, with respect to the conventional person whose mind is withered by pride regarding that [direct perception], the qualification "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) is employed in the definition of direct perception. Even according to the Sūtra, there is a distinction made between conceptualization and determination (*adhyavasāya*). In that context as well, this term "determination" is not used as a designation for the subject—the conceptual construction itself—but rather for the act of determination residing therein.

[227,13] Regarding the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon (*dharma*): this is the meaning. Even when [the object] is not seen, there is a certain phenomenon called "fitness for engagement" (*pravartanayogyatā*); through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), activity (*pravṛtti*) occurs by means of that. If the object is known and established through determination (*adhyavasāya*) by way of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), then the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object is also obtained; thus, it is logical that "object-ness" (*viṣayatva*) consists in mere determination.
Therefore it has been said:
"The object is one, yet it is expressed through superimposition.
As the author of the Bhāṣya stated:
[227,19] How is it that it has that as its object? Because it functions toward it.

(PVA***) As for the "lion's roar" which, having raised the doubt of how one can act toward what is unperceived, asserts that action occurs everywhere precisely toward the unperceived, we have not elaborated upon it here for fear of making the text too voluminous.

Thus, regarding the statement "because one acts through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object within one's own appearance," here too, while there is an object that is one's own appearance, the determination is as previously described. However, an "object" (*artha*) has been defined as something external capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). By its exclusion, an "non-object" (*anartha*) is the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*).
In this way, it should be regarded as both a "real entity" (*vastu*) and "non-existent" (*asan*). And this has been made clear by the words of the *Vārttika* itself:

In the *Sākārasiddhi*: "The activity of inference is by means of the determination of an object" (*arthādhyavasāyena pravṛttir anumānasya*)—this indeed means that inference is the determination of an object (*arthādhyavasāyānumāna*).
However, as for the commentary provided here by the author of the *Ṭīkā*, it should be rejected in favor of his own proof of *Apoha*; we have not raised it here for fear of prolixity.

If, then, the denotability [of the object] is by means of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the external, how is it so for the form of the cognition (*buddhyākāra*)? Regarding this, the treatise states: “The referent of a word (*śabdārtha*), established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), is a threefold property-bearer (*dharmī*) based on existence, non-existence, or both. (PV III 204–5)
And so forth.
It is bound to the reflections of conceptual construction which are grounded in those [particulars];
therefore, because it is grounded in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to perform the exclusion of others.

"That reflection of the object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from it], even that is not the essence of the object; it is an error arising from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). (PV II 164–165) For it is impossible to maintain that there is a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) even regarding the form within cognition, since such determination is established only with respect to the object of practical activity (*pravṛtti-viṣaya*).
And since that which seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is indeed external, he says:
"Another object appears as the denotable.
The meaning is that the mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*) is other than the external; for in the cognition produced by words and so forth, only the mental aspect appears. Therefore...

[228,17] Thus, it is said that this is the object (*viṣaya*), just as form (*rūpa*) is the object of the eye; the point is that it is not [an object] by way of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). And it has been stated:
[228,18] "This meaning of the word is described according to how it is perceived, even though it does not exist" (PV III 83).

[228,20] The phrase "it does not exist," however, is because it does not exist externally in accordance with its appearance, and because the investigation is conducted from the perspective of the external world.

[228,21] By way of context: this very point is that, because it is not the reality, it is according to conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), and because it is not determined, it is according to reality.

[228,22] Since "conceptual determination" is a synonym for "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), the meaning is that it is according to the manifestation of conceptual construction, because it culminates in the object. [228,23] Even regarding the manifestation of non-existent objects and so forth, the meaning is simply their external non-existence according to how they are perceived. Even "error" (*bhrāntitva*) is only in relation to the external; thus, everything [is established].

[229,1] It is unconfused. However, it is not correct to assert the non-existence of that which is the object of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), on the grounds that it is an object by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, like the appearance of hair and so forth. For this very reason, even though it is expressible, [229,3] there is no establishment of the reality of either the form (*ākāra*) or the external [object] through affirmation (*vidhi*).
[229,4] Even conventionally, it is only external; however, it is not so for that which lacks a form (*akṛti*).

[229,6] For there can be no application of affirmation or negation by means of words and the like toward a form that is free from doubt, self-cognized, and [therefore] lacks an objective referent, because such an effort would be futile and incapable [of effecting anything]. Nor [can there be such application] toward an external object that does not appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because if the object is not apprehended, for what [could affirmation or negation apply]?

Would it be an affirmation or a negation? Therefore, just as an external tree is established as the denotable object of the word "tree" through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), so too, through that very conceptual determination, an affirmation or negation of the external is expressed in conventional discourse. Even when an investigation is conducted by taking up some mental form (*buddhyākāra*) from a particular context by means of another conceptualization, even then, [the operation proceeds] from that conceptualization.

Affirmation and negation pertain only to the external world; for it is said in the treatise: "For one who discriminates that [external object], he falls [into error] regarding the referent" (PV II 220). Therefore, in reality, there is neither affirmation nor negation for either [of the two]; for according to conventional truth, they pertain only to the external.
And these two [affirmation and negation] are difficult to avoid, for otherwise there would be the consequence of the collapse of conventional discourse.

By this, the statement made by the commentator—that affirmation and negation have as their objects an external reality that is superimposed—is shown to be unworldly, lacking scriptural authority, and unphilosophical; for [conventional discourse] cannot exist without relying upon the two truths, the conventional and the ultimate.

[229,18] There is a certain established distinction. In this regard, it is first of all not conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), because that [conventional reality] consists in the conceit of the world (*lokābhimāna*).

And for the world, the meaning of an external object is established or negated; thus, there is a pervasive conceit that serves as the basis for engagement and withdrawal without differentiation. The world does not touch upon such things as the externality of a superimposed [object]. Nor is this ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), for that which is inexpressible...
Affirmation and negation do not apply to anything in reality; such is the scriptural tradition (*āgama*). Nor is there any other direction for reasoning (*tarka*).

Furthermore, affirmation and negation do not apply to that which is not an object of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*), and it is proclaimed by you yourself that there is no determinate cognition from a word regarding anything other than the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, what follows from this regarding the affirmation and negation of an imputed externality? [It follows only] from appearance and determinate cognition—

And by means of these doors, the entire systematic arrangement fails to touch reality (*tattva*). In that regard, neither that which is superimposed (*āropita*) nor that which possesses a superimposed externality is the object of appearance (*pratibhāsa*), nor is it the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). To begin with, that which is superimposed does not even touch appearance, as he himself has stated: "Superimposition occurs at the same time as the experience of a mental image (*ullekha*); being of a non-apparent nature, it is a non-entity (*avastu*) whose object is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)."

[230,2] Thus, for this very reason, its externality (*bāhyatva*) does not appear either, because that is a property of it (*taddharmatvāt*). As for the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), since it is restricted solely to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), it does not belong to these two; so enough of raising this point.
[230,3–4] Even what is called "superimposed" (*āropita*) is said to be merely imagined (*kalpita*); and the function of imagining consists in both the appearance and the conceptual determination.

[230,5] There are two [factors]. Whence, then, does this other so-called "superimposed" heap arise? Therefore, reflection upon the conventional and the ultimate is appropriate only by taking the external object as the basis for the form of cognition. Furthermore, when there is a desire to express such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), what is the use of resorting to a circuitous and difficult path?

Enough of this excessive persistence. This is established: that the external object exists through conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), whereas the form of cognition exists through its manifestation (*pratibhāsa*).

"It is said that 'being expressible by words' is stated. Now, if you explain it in this way, you have accepted the expressibility of the entire collection of both types of objects; how then is this introduced for the purpose of establishing that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible? To this he says:
"It is established."

This is merely a formal convention established with a specific purpose: that "denotability" consists in mere conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) or mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*). Thus, for one who apprehends the external object as a mere establishment of its reality, the object is said to be "excluded from others" (*anyāpoḍha*); this is intended solely to exclude the collection of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In this way, the form excluded from others—

The statement that "the object of conceptual construction is its own self" is intended as the ultimate negation of all external objects; it does not, however, imply that the status of being an object finds its final rest within itself.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Why is this so? Because even though the status of being an object is established in various instances, it is not intended that this constitutes the final resting point.
[230,17] However, he states that the intent is the exclusion of other [possibilities]:

[230,18] "In reality, there is no object whatsoever to be expressed" [230,19]. For a manifestation accompanied by conceptual determination (adhyavasāya) is, from the perspective of conventional practice (sāṃvyavahārika), the cognition of an object of knowledge in its true nature (tattvataḥ).

It brings [the object] into the state of being an objective domain (*viṣayatā*), just like perception (*pratyakṣa*). For a mere appearance (*pratibhāsa*) that is devoid of determination (*avasāya*), or whose function is overridden by another determination, is not capable of establishing an object for one who desires to act, just like the touch of grass to one walking, or like the superimposition of water upon a mirage. Nor is mere determination, devoid of appearance, capable of it, just like the superimposition of water itself. Therefore, regarding purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*)—

The determination of objects is pervaded by capacity; the absence of both, being overcome by the absence of the pervader, is necessarily tied to the occurrence of both. When one is accepted as being excluded from the other, it is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). That which does not appear in a cognition, or that which is not determined by it, is not its object—just as a horse is not the object of the cognition of a cow. And [the object] does not appear in verbal cognition.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not determined by this mental form; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Even though it is observed that activity and the status of being an object occur through mere appearance even in the case of extreme habituation, nevertheless, that very habituation does not exist without determination (*avasāya*); therefore, the agency for that belongs to determination alone. Consequently, whatever is not determined by something [cannot be its object].
[231,2] The qualification "when there is practice" must be required.

[231,3] But surely, even in the case of perception, there is no determination of the apprehended moment, but rather of the continuum (*santati*); and since this [continuum] does not appear [in perception], by what means could it have an object? For [the object] exists neither in the moment nor in the continuum. In inference, however, there is indeed examination (*parīkṣā*).
[231,5] It proceeds. And there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for which some object exists by way of the occurrence of both; thus, this is impossible.
[231,6] Therefore, if it were established that each one individually is the object of application, then everything—whether external or internal—would have to be expressible as having a fixed object.

[231,7] To this it is replied: he states the determination of reality (*tattvavyavasthā*): the status of being an object occurs precisely through the occurrence of both, but it is merely conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*).

In relation to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), that which is lower conventionality is designated as "truth" (*tattva*) in dependence upon it; for when one enters into the distinction of moments, conventional discourse is not abolished, since from the perspective of worldly convention there is no absence of momentary destruction. In ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*), however, there is no possibility of both [existence and non-existence] being perceived simultaneously; thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is certain that for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is a grasping of the non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized.

If it is argued that the fire is thus determined as having indeed appeared, we say no; for the delusion regarding that appearance has been dispelled by the recollection of another appearance. Furthermore, just as it is possible to demonstrate that the appearance of a real object in conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is entirely distinct from its [conceptual] appearance, so too there is no appearance of a real object other than the appearance in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since the appearance of the real object finds its rest in that very [perceptual] appearance.
It would be better to exclude the appearance of an entity that is of a different class from it. Therefore, it was rightly said:
"In reality, nothing at all can be established as expressible.
(20b) Alternatively, even if it is not expressible as another entity, exclusion (*apoha*) is understood there as its qualifier.
The status of exclusion (*apoha*) as the denotable object is indeed accepted. Nevertheless, one might ask: how can there be the ineffability of all phenomena?
To this he says: "In reality, no object whatsoever is denotable.

This is the intended meaning: first, according to the position of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), its status as a denotable object—just like the form of a real entity—is produced merely by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

[231.20] It is not so because of its appearance, as in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, in the case of the negative alternative (*prasajya-pakṣa*), there is no distinction even at other times for that which is merely the exclusion of another;

nevertheless, since this [exclusion] is not the object itself, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Or rather, that which is stated in the treatise—therefore, it is established that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have as their object the non-differentiation of all words—this is the summary. He demonstrates its establishment in the object (*arthaniṣṭhā*) by means of that very summary.
"In reality, no object whatsoever is expressible.
This is stated because, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), expressibility is shown to exist merely through appearance and conceptual determination;
therefore, he specifies "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*).
This is the meaning: that which was concluded in the treatise as "only exclusion (viveka) is to be expressed" does not have anything at all as its expressed object.

Just as the statement "non-existence comes to be" has the meaning "existence does not come to be," so too, the expression "exclusion is the expressed object" has the meaning "the expressed-ness itself is the exclusion. And this has been established as having been made clear by the treatise itself through such means as the analysis of the three reasons.

Thus, when the question is asked, "In what way is exclusion (*apoha*) the denotable object of words? the answer is: "By virtue of its being a quality of that [exclusion], according to the meaning as previously stated. Now, if the question is asked, "Why are the mental image (*buddhyākāra*), the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), or the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) not the denotable objects? the responses are given in order: "Because of the absence of the determination (*adhyavasāya*), the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), or both. However, when the inquiry is: "What, then, is denoted by words? [the following applies].

In that case, because there is an appearance [of an object] and a determination of an object, or else by conceptualizing "in reality," it is stated that these responses— namely, that the form excluded from others (*anyāpoḍhākāra*) resides in the conceptual construction,

and that the particular characteristic excluded from others (*anyāpoḍhasvalakṣaṇa*) is nothing at all— are given precisely in sequence. Therefore, the establishment of the fact that words and logical marks have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object is intended primarily to demonstrate that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are inexpressible.
[232,11] Summary of the meaning of the first verse.
[232,12] Let there be this proliferation of arguments regarding apoha for the clever; however, the failure of the essential nature of the real entity to manifest is the vital point.
[232,13-14] If that [essential nature] is not firm, everything falls apart without effort.
But when it is firm, there is indeed well-being by that much alone.
[232,16] This illumination of the direction has been provided by us in a non-extensive manner. [232,17] But its full elaboration is to be sought in the source itself. [232,18]
[232,19] By those who scatter it like blown cotton.
The Chapter on Apoha is completed.

"He who proclaimed that the world, which possesses a diversity produced by karma, is without a Lord..."
I bow with reverence to him whose teaching is unimpeded.

Here is the counter-argument of others: "The mountains and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, have an intelligent creator, because they are effects. Whatever is an effect has an intelligent creator, just like a pot. And these mountains and so forth are effects; therefore, they are preceded by an intelligent being. Nor is this [reason] unestablished (*asiddha*), for even a Buddhist does not dispute that the Vindhya, Gandhamādana, and other such mountains are effects. Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is impossible to demonstrate that in any effect whatsoever there is no deviation from being presided over by an intelligent agent. Nor is it "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because it is not contradicted by perception or scripture. Nor is it "neutralized by a counter-reason" (*prakaraṇasama*), because there is no opposing reason. Therefore, what is established by this [argument] should be accepted by the wise, as it is established by a means of proof other than [the opponent's].

Nor should it be asserted that because the probans is not obtained through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) everywhere, the effect is not a proof for an intelligent agent, since both [concomitances] are unestablished; for while this [probans] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is absolutely excluded from the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), such as space and the like.

For there are three classes of entities: those with an intelligent agent, such as jars and the like; those without an agent, such as space and the like; and those whose agent is doubtful, such as mountains and the like. Among these, "being an effect" (kāryatva)—which exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa) such as jars, and is absent in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) such as space—possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). This property, being present in the remaining cases, necessarily establishes the probandum (sādhya).

And although for the Digambaras and others non-existent things do not exist, and in their view atoms are indeed effects, nevertheless, the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) of even the non-existent is certainly accepted. Thus:

"If there is an exclusion [of the reason] from that [subject], why is its presence [therein] desired? (PV 4.224)—thus says the treatise. Nor is there any impairment of the status of being a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), since the definition of a counter-example is that which does not possess the locus of the probandum (*sādhya*). So what is the point of this effort to prove their existence? Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) with respect to an agent as described. The same should be applied to [the reasons] such as "having an origin," "having a non-conscious material cause," "abiding," and "activity."

(234) Here, Śaṅkara, raising the Buddhist objection, says: "The establishment of the fact that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent agent is not achieved by mere production; rather, it would be so if the earth and other things were exactly like palaces and the like, which are observed [to be produced by agents], such that even one who does not observe the actual act of making would conceive the idea that they were made upon seeing them. It is not [established] merely through the commonality of the term 'being an effect,' for in that case, deviation is also possible. For [an inference] does not [follow] from a different object merely because of a non-distinct similarity of words" (PV II 12).

If it is argued that inferring fire from its paleness is logical, and that likewise one may infer a creator for the earth and so forth because they have insentient material causes—just as a jar and the like do—then it follows by the same logic that since jars and other products of clay are preceded by a potter, an anthill must also be inferred to be preceded by one.
As it has been said: "Whatever kind [of thing] is established... (PV II 11).

The three *vārtikas*: This [objection] has been stated by one who has not ascertained the opponent’s intention. For it is thus: the presence [of the effect] when there is the existence of an intelligent cause is observed in the case of a jar and so forth; and its absence when there is the absence of production and so forth is observed in the case of space and so forth. And that [cause], whose invariable concomitance is well-established, generates in those who know it the cognition of an agent capable of producing it—such as the earth and so forth—precisely where it is perceived.

But the case is not the same for paleness and the like, because those qualities, which inhere in a different class of entities, are observed to deviate from fire. Likewise, it has never been observed that instruments and actions possess independence in their activities when they are not presided over by an agent possessing effort; for in all cases, the production of structures such as palaces is observed only when they are presided over by an intelligent being.

Vācaspati, however, having introduced the concept of an inherent relation (*svābhāvikasambandha*), says: "In this case as well, the effect-ness (*kāryatva*) indeed possesses an inherent relation with an agent who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth, because no deviation is established due to the non-perception of any limiting condition (*upādhi*). Furthermore, it has already been stated that grass and the like are included within the subject (*pakṣa*). Moreover, it has also been demonstrated that one must not merely indulge in mere conjecture (*utprekṣaṇamātra*)."

Therefore, if that which is naturally connected with its own probandum were to exist in the absence of that probandum, it would necessarily deviate from its very nature; thus, when supported by such reasoning (*tarka*)—which eliminates doubt regarding the occurrence of the probandum's absence—is it not possible for [the reason] observed in mountains and the like to establish its own probandum? Of what use are personal prejudices?

However, as for those [marks] such as whiteness, being a product of clay, or being a cow, they are not valid reasons because their deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since they inhere in other classes of things (*jātyantara*). This is because whiteness found in snow and the like—which belongs to a different class—deviates from fire; likewise, a product of clay deviates from a potter, as it may be preceded by a master builder (*sthapati*) or others. The same should be understood in other cases as well. Therefore, the distinction there is as follows: only that which is a specific form of white substance or smoke [is a valid reason].

(235) That alone is the cause of fire, because its non-deviation from it is observed there. On the other hand, that which is merely a pale substance produced from a cause distinct in character from fire—which is actually different but not so perceived due to a similarity in name—cannot lead to the inference of fire, because its deviation from fire is observed therein. This same principle should be applied to the products of clay and so forth. Furthermore, the existence of the general property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), characterized by coming into being after having not existed, on mountains and such things is indeed accepted by others.

However, they say that [the reason] is inconclusive because the necessary connection (pratibandha) is not established; and since that connection has been demonstrated just as it is for smoke and so forth, it is logical that the inference from it is valid.

Vittoka, however, says: "This might be the case—it is not through the mere observation and non-observation of the similar and dissimilar classes that there is a certainty of non-deviation, because a rule of non-deviation is impossible for that which does not have the same nature or does not arise from the same cause. Therefore, this property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not a proof, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful. To this it is replied: There is no doubt regarding the exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), because the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*)—established by perception and non-perception—is proven for the cognition of the effect and the intellect, just as it is for smoke and fire.

If it is argued that the establishment of the production of that [effect] pertains only to a specific effect and not to the generality of effects—just as there is no certainty regarding the being-produced-by-fire in the case of "thing-ness" (vastutva) and so forth residing in smoke and the like—we say no, because there is no specific reason [to distinguish them]. Since perception and non-perception are accepted as the means of proving the production of that [effect], and since there is no distinction between the generality of the probandum and the probans, the dependence of the mere effect upon the substratum of its manifestation is established just as much for the specific effect as for the general effect.

Nor, however, does the property of being a real entity (*vastutva*) possess the quality of being an effect of fire, since it is perceived thousands of times even in the absence of fire. Therefore, just as an effect such as cloth is seen to possess a material cause (*upādāna*), another effect is likewise established [as having a material cause]. Similarly, since that very effect such as cloth is seen to have an intelligent agent (*buddhimaddhetuka*) as its cause, even an effect whose agent is not perceived is established as being preceded by an agent; for the agent, just like the material cause, exhibits a positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the effect.

Just as it is impossible to suspect that something could be both an effect and without a material cause, so too one should not suspect that something could be both an effect and without an agent; for there is no distinction, since the production of any mere effect is established through a mere agent, just as it is through a material cause.

As for what is said—that only a specific kind of effect is pervaded by an intelligent agent, such that from the sight of it, even one who has not observed its production forms the cognition that it was made—and that this [pervasion] is unestablished in the case of oceans, mountains, and so forth: well then, what is this "cognition that it was made"? Is it a cognition of the means (*sādhana*), or a cognition of the goal (*sādhya*)? As for the cognition of the goal, it is already established for you, since you accept that "the variety of the world is born of karma."

Now, as for the opposing position: by that, the following meaning is established—this "product-ness" (*kāryatva*) perceived in earth and so forth is not capable of proving the probandum through inference; rather, it is only some other [kind of product-ness] that is so, because it does not generate the cognition of the probandum. But this is not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference. For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could just as well say: "This smoke is not capable of inferring fire, but rather some other [smoke], because it does not generate the cognition of the probandum in those who perceive the probandum."

And thus, the means of proof is not established as long as the cognition of the probandum is not established; nor is the cognition of the probandum established as long as the means of proof is not established. Therefore, the circularity of mutual dependence is quite evident.

Śaṅkara also said: "Nor does the reason become unestablished (*asiddhi*) for someone due to delusion when there is an absence of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), because that would entail [the same problem] for all inferences. (cf. J 298,25f)

The author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*, however, says: "If it is perceived as being produced (*kṛtaka*), why is there no cognition that it was made? Even in the case of all [ancient] palaces and such, the cognition that they were made does not arise; rather, just as for those who know the pervasion (*vyāpti*) there arises the cognition that long-standing palaces and such were made, while for those confused about the pervasion there is only the cognition that they were not made, so it is with the earth and so forth—there is no difference. If it is argued that the cognition that they were made by a person does not arise in the case of the earth and so forth, as it does in the case of palaces and such..."

Is this [cognition] regarding those for whom the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well-established, or regarding those for whom it is not? Even among those for whom it is well-established, is it for those who lack the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or for others? First, for those whose memory has not failed, the cognition that [the object] was made by a person certainly occurs; even in the world, there exists the common understanding that "this diverse universe was created by some Creator. However, for those who are confused regarding the apprehension and recollection of pervasion, the cognition that [things] were made by a person does not arise even in the case of certain structures such as palaces. Yet, it does not follow from this alone that these [palaces] are not man-made.

Furthermore, since the Mīmāṃsakas do not even entertain the notion that the Vedas were composed by a person, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (vākyatva) adduced there to prove human authorship would be unestablished (asiddha). Moreover, the reason "being produced" (kṛtakatva), which was stated for the sake of proving impermanence, would also be unestablished; for the kind of "producedness" observed in jars and the like—which is perceptible to the ear—is not present in sound.
Therefore, this discrepancy between the example and the subject (dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika-vaidharmya) is common to all inferences and does not constitute a refutation of the inference for God alone.

In the *Mañjarī*, Trilocana further states: "How do you establish that birth, which is pervaded by being preceded by an intelligent agent, exists only in things such as jars? If you say it is because they are the cause of the notion of having been produced (*kṛtabuddhi*), then you must specify that particularity of jars and the like by virtue of which, through a distinction not found in the great elements (*mahābhūta*), only jars and so forth produce the notion of having been produced, and not the great elements themselves. It cannot be a distinction consisting in the perception of an agent and an action, for you admit that even one who has not witnessed the action is the cause of the notion of having been produced."

If it is argued that the specific distinction [of a jar] is its dimension of magnitude (*mahattva-parimāṇa*), that too cannot be the case, because such a distinction is observed even in the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) due to the plurality of their causes, their own magnitude, and their accumulation. Nor should it be said that the specific distinction is simply "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), for the manifestation of what was previously non-existent—characterized as inherence in its causes—is no different in the case of earth and the other elements. Furthermore, no distinction other than these can be identified even by Śakra himself, by virtue of whose existence jars and the like alone become the cause of the cognition "produced," while earth and the like do not.

Vācaspati, however, says: "In this matter, may you examine more precisely: is the distinction the fact that [the production of things] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an intelligent agent, or rather the observation thereof, which is said to be absent in the case of mountains and the like? If it is the former alternative, that is certainly accepted by those who maintain that the body, the world, and so forth have an intelligent cause; for [they do not deny] the cause."

(237) No one who is not shameless would claim that another thing possesses the presence or absence of the effect [of an action]. Now, if it is argued that "it is the perception [of the causal relation]," this is the final resort. In that case, for one who does not perceive the action itself, the cognition that something has been "produced" cannot arise. If it is argued: "Only that very jar which was seen by him to follow the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of an intelligent agent is its product, and not one found in the marketplace; because we see that whatever belongs to that class follows the positive and negative concomitance of that [agent], therefore even those things whose positive and negative concomitance were not seen belong to that class and are produced in that way. [Response: This is not so. For if the cognition of being produced arises from the mere observation of the positive and negative concomitance of the class, then why does such a cognition not arise regarding a jar found in the marketplace? If you say it is because of the lack of memory, then why is there no such cognition regarding a jar seen at a later time? Furthermore, if the cognition of being produced arises from the observation of the class, then why does it not arise regarding a jar made by a different potter? If you say it is due to the difference in the maker, then why does it not arise regarding a jar made by the same potter at a different time? If you say it is because of the difference in time, then why does it not arise regarding a jar made by the same potter at the same time? Thus, since the cognition of being produced arises from the observation of the positive and negative concomitance of the individual object, it must be admitted that the action is directly perceived. Otherwise, the cognition of being produced would never occur. Therefore, the perception of the action is established. Moreover, the action is not something other than the conjunction and disjunction [of the parts]; rather, it is the conjunction and disjunction themselves, as they are observed to be the cause of the production of the jar. If it is argued that the action is inferred from the conjunction and disjunction, then the cognition of being produced would arise from the mere observation of the conjunction and disjunction, and not from the perception of the action. Consequently, the action is indeed perceived. And since the action is perceived, it is not eternal. Therefore, the means of knowledge for the existence of God is refuted. Since things such as jars, which possess an origin, follow the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, other things as well—such as bodies and the world—being likewise characterized, cannot be set aside by a mere stick [of an objection]. If you say that 'whatever belongs to the class of jars, being possessed of an origin, is preceded by an intelligent cause,' then surely palaces and the like would not have that [intelligent agent] as their cause, because they do not belong to the class of jars. Alternatively, whatever class of thing is observed to follow the positive and negative concomitance of an intelligent agent, that very same class—even when its positive and negative concomitance is not observed—must have an intelligent agent as its cause."

In that case, why is it that things such as palaces, which belong to the same class as effects, are not seen to have an intelligent cause, such that the body, the world, and so forth—which possess the quality of being produced—would not likewise [have one]? Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever based on belonging to that same class.

Furthermore, O Vittoṭa, let there be some unspecified particularity; however, what is intended by this proponent of a particularity? Is it that the generality of being an effect (*kāryatva-sāmānya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), or that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "mere effect" from an intelligent agent (*buddhimat-kartṛ*), or merely a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? And what follows from this?

If it is argued that the reason is unestablished for the effect in general, then that is not so; for in the case of the earth and so forth, as well as in the case of jars and the like, both [the existence of the effect and its production through the operation of a cause] are established for both parties. If, on the other hand, it is claimed that the reason is unestablished for the specific effect residing in jars and such within the subject (*pakṣa*), then there is no harm here, because the specific [effect] has not been adduced as the logical reason (*hetu*).

If, however, it is intended to demonstrate that the general property of being an effect deviates from its agent, that is impossible because such deviation is not observed in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), and because grass and the like have been included within the subject (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, if it is argued that a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*) between the probandum and the example is being highlighted, that is not the case, for such a difference is easily found everywhere.

Thus far, it has been established that the essential connection (*svābhāvika-pratibandha*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—just like smoke and the like—is demonstrated. Now, however, for the sake of pleasing the followers of the Sugata (*saugata*), even subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) that are not [accepted as] valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) are being stated. Indeed, we do not suffer from a poverty of subverting proofs; rather, we say it is a matter of logic (*nyāya*). In this regard, the very subverting proof is this: namely, the fact that [the cognition] does not arise from a person even once.

Just as for the Buddhists, in the inference regarding fire (*citrabhānu*), if smoke were to arise in another place or at another time from a cause other than fire, then even in those observed places and times, it would never obtain its own existence through fire; because it is not logical that there be a restriction of something being its effect when it occurs in the absence of that [cause], as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And consequently, since everything of that nature would not have that as its cause, it would not arise from it even once.

And because that is the case, the connection [between cause and effect] is established through the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary position, namely: "that which is not produced by something cannot be of such a nature.

(238) Likewise, for us as well, if some effect were to arise from another source even without the superintendence of an intelligent agent, then alas, it would never be produced from an intelligent agent such as a potter. But since it does arise [from them], the fact that it is produced by them constitutes one subverting proof.

Or, even for the followers of the Sugata, it should not be suspected that smoke arises from something else, because if it had an indefinite cause, it would follow that it is causeless. And for that which is causeless, there must be either eternal existence or eternal non-existence, since a causeless thing does not depend on anything else.
For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible. (PV I 35; PV II 180ab)
"Likewise for us as well"—this is the second subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

This being the case, just as this rule is established for you: that smoke is a specific entity which follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of fire, and that fire is that which produces it; so that if that suspected smoke is indeed the effect of fire, then likewise for us, that which is preceded by an intelligent agent is its effect, and that person is the one who performs it.

Likewise, if the activity and cessation of insentient things were to occur in any effect without a conscious supervisor, then there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-cessation of the production of effects. For instance, if insentient things were to act by their own inherent nature, then, because their operation would be devoid of intention, they would always be active; for it is not logical that their activity should cease without cause. Consequently, there would be no cessation of the effect.

If, on the other hand, [the atoms] were indifferent, then there would never be any activity at all, because there would be no distinction [between states]. However, we consider it logical that they are set in motion at times by a presiding agent who possesses effort, and not by something insentient; for in the case of the latter, activity and cessation dependent upon will are impossible. This is the third subverting proof.

In this context, the state of being an effect (kāryatva) is indeed pervaded by the presence of occasional causes; and the presence of occasional causes is, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), dependent upon the operation of an agent, as is the case with the presence of the shuttle, the loom, and so forth. In the contrary case (vipakṣa), there is no existence of the presence of occasional causes; for an insentient entity cannot bring about the proximity of causes, or if it could, it would follow that the operation of an agent would be unnecessary even in the case of a jar and similar objects.

And thus, since the property of being an effect (kāryatva), by the non-perception of its pervader, is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) and is thereby pervaded by having an intelligent agent as its antecedent (buddhimatpūrvakatva), the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established; this is the fourth subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa).

Likewise, the consequence of there being no restriction regarding place and so forth would be a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For instance, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is pervaded by the restriction of place, time, and material cause (*prakṛti*); if it were to come into existence without an intelligent agent (*prayatnavant*), it would not occur with such restriction of place and so forth. Indeed, by the will of a creator, it arises in a certain place and excludes other places and so on. In the absence of that [will], it would have to exist everywhere, in all places and so forth.

(239) The establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*)—that the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*), when excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by the non-perception of its pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), is pervaded by the necessity of being concomitant with an intelligent agent (*prayatnavat*)—is the fifth subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

As for what Śaṅkara [says], that there would be no spatial and other restrictions on all effects if they arose from operations devoid of intention; nor is there any distinction between the causes of the earth and so forth and the causes of palaces and the like, by virtue of which these [latter], while being devoid of intentional operation, could—being dependent on effort—possess such [operations] through an operation that is specifically restricted. (cf. J 299,1-3)

Vācaspati, however, raising the argument for God (*īśvara*) in his *Kaṇikā*, says: "If, on the other hand, insentient things were to produce an effect without being presided over by a sentient being, then they would produce it wherever they might happen to be; thus, an effect characterized by a specific restriction of place and time would not be observed. If it is argued that the effect is not produced by each individual cause because its birth depends upon the conjunction of causes—this is true—but from what does this very conjunction of the causes arise?"

If it is argued that [the production of effects occurs] due to a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) whose maturation is occasional, [we reply: But how could this too, being insentient, bring about the causes in their proper order? Indeed, it is not observed that staffs and other tools situated anywhere at random produce an effect through mutual interaction solely by the power of a specific *adṛṣṭa* without the effort of a potter; for since such production would otherwise be impossible in the absence of a preceding intelligent agent, the exclusion of the cause from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) by the negation of the pervader (*vyāpakavṛtti*) entails that the production of the effect is pervaded by having an intelligent agent as its antecedent. Thus, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established.
If this is so, let it be that the existence of a mere agent is established; however, how can he possess omniscience, given that such a quality is absent in the illustrative example? If you ask this:

On this point, Trilocana says: "This is not so; for it is not a creator characterized by specific attributes that we wish to prove, but rather the general property of being a creator (*sādhyasāmānya*). And when that general property is to be ascertained, its real connection with whatever specific attribute exists—namely, the specific attribute consisting of the direct perception of the material cause and so forth—must necessarily be ascertained as well, because if that were abandoned, there would follow the abandonment of the general property to be proven."

Nor can it be abandoned, because the generality of the probandum (*sādhyasāmānya*) pervades the substrata such as earth and the rest. Furthermore, the material cause (*upādāna*) of earth and the rest consists of the four types of atoms; the actions whose nature is established as inhering in all *kṣetrajñas* [are the efficient cause]; space and time are the instruments (*upakaraṇa*); that which is characterized by all *kṣetrajñas* is the recipient (*sampradāna*); and that which is characterized by the experience of the *kṣetrajñas* is the purpose (*prayojana*).

The agent who perceives all this through direct perception is omniscient, having directly perceived every division of the universe. Furthermore, no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) preceded by a formal presentation [of the reason] is demonstrated in an example for him, such that there would be the occurrence of a host of faults like "lack of concomitance" (*ananvaya*).

(240) This might be the case: since no specific sequence of dyads and so forth is perceived in the production of a jar—just as there is none in the arising of the great elements or the sequence of dyads and so forth—the potter who makes this jar must also be making a dyad. Yet the potter does not perceive its material cause (*upādāna*) or its instrumental cause (*upakaraṇa*) through direct perception. Therefore, this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): namely, that whoever is the maker of something knows its material cause and so forth.

To this it is replied: there would be inconclusiveness [of the reason] only if the potter were the maker of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). For the potter does not produce every component up until the completion of the ultimate atoms (*antyāvayava*), because the definition of an agent consists in being the employer of causes whose causal capacity has been observed. Therefore, even the dyad—like the great elements—is itself a probandum (*sādhya*) because its having an agent is doubtful.

Thus, that general property of the inferable (*anumeya-sāmānya*) which the proponent desires to establish cannot be obstructed by the opponent. However, that particularity (*viśeṣa*) which the opponent desires to obstruct is not what the proponent of the general property to be proven intends to establish. What then? When the general property to be proven is to be ascertained, the proponent does not disregard the establishment of a particularity possessing a real connection (*vāstava-pratibandha*), which occurs by force of necessity.

The Master, considering that the attainment of a specific [property] depends upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), raised this objection: "To whatever extent the means of proof pervades the range of an object, to that same extent does the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) also. If this specific property has not been made an object of the means of proof, how can it be established from that? Or, if it is being established, how can it not be its object? If it is its object, how could it fail to touch the range of defects residing in itself? This [objection] is refuted.

For this would be the case if the proponent of the proof were to accept the establishment of a specific property as dependent upon that very proof. However, the Naiyāyika does not rely on the establishment of a specific property as being contingent upon the proof. What then? He relies on the establishment of a specific property drawn forth by the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the general property to be proven (*sādhya*). For example, when the Buddhist establishes momentariness, he relies on the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*) because of the real connection between them;
for if the self were eternal and all-pervading, one would not be able to infer momentariness regarding all things.

Even the Mīmāṃsaka, while determining the whole (avayavin) through both seeing and touching, relies upon these many points: the plurality of the sense organs, their restriction to specific objects, the fact that the sense organs have the apprehension of their own respective objects as their inferential mark, the status of the knower as the possessor of the means of knowledge, the substratum of qualities as distinct from qualities such as odor, and the conscious agent as one whose objects are not restricted.
Likewise, even the specific proof is relied upon by the Naiyāyikas; thus, everything is the same except for their dogmatic adherence. Therefore, omniscience is established.

Vācaspati, however, concludes: "Thus, it is established that from the very fact of being an effect, aided by its presence as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there is the proof of an Īśvara of such a nature."

Or, let it be that from this [inference] there is established merely a creator who is omniscient regarding the material cause and so forth. However, the specific nature of that creator—known by the second name "the Excluded" (vyatirekin)—is established through the inference of elimination (*pāriśeṣyānumāna*). For instance: the creator of bodies, worlds, and so forth is not one whose intellect is non-eternal or limited in scope; and this [creator] is one who is omniscient regarding their material causes and so forth. Therefore, he is such [an omniscient being]. Indeed, no one other than such a Lord is capable of knowing the infinite distinctions between atoms and the distinct latencies of karma (*karmāśaya*) inherent in each individual soul (*kṣetrajña*).

Vittoka, however, argues that just as by the sight of smoke, through the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), a specific quality of fire—namely, its being located in a thicket—is understood even though it is not a pervading characteristic, so too is it with respect to the agent; thus there is no fault. Consequently, such a specific person as God (*īśvara*) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The opponent asks: How, then, can the Blessed One, who teaches that the world is not created by a Lord, possess an uncontradicted teaching established by valid cognition?
The summary of the prima facie position in the section on the doctrine of God is completed.
