In the section on the Refutation of the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravādādhikāre Saṅkṣepadūṣaṇam*): This is a brief account of the refutation of the doctrine of God, intended for those who fear extensive treatises that require a commentary on the *Vārtikasaptaślokī*.

In this case, although the agent possessing effort has demonstrated the mere concomitance of the effect for the most part, and has also shown its absence in some instances where that [effort] is absent, nevertheless—since a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established—the following doubt may arise: "The effect might exist, yet it would not be preceded by an intelligent agent. Thus, because there is an absence of sublation (*bādhaka*), the reason "being an effect" in the proof of "having an intelligent creator" is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) characterized by doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛtti*).

Nor can the mere observation and non-observation of the probans in similar and dissimilar instances constitute the proof of a pervasion—expressed by the term "necessary connection" (*pratibandha*)—in the form that "the probandum necessarily exists when the probans exists," or "the probans is absent when the probandum is absent. For such a pervasion is observed even in cases where a future deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is known to occur. For one who merely observes concomitance and possesses a reflective disposition, it is simply impossible to determine whether this current non-observation of deviation arises from its actual absence, or rather from the lack of the convergence of conditions for its observation.

For this very reason, Vācaspati’s proclamation of an "intrinsic relation" (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) is merely a verbal embellishment, as it does not support any meaning beyond that [already established]. For an intrinsic determination occurs when, through repeated observation, no deviation is perceived. And the non-perception of deviation is said to mean simply its non-observation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

As for the claim that the non-establishment of deviation (vyabhicāra) results from the non-perception of a limiting condition (upādhi), in that case there exists no such thing as a "limiting condition" that functions like a visible mark, whose non-perception could establish non-deviation in practice; rather, its postulation arises solely from the observation of deviation itself.

And because its non-perception [is not established], there is no intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*); thus, due to the absence of any distinction, nothing follows from the doctrine of intrinsic nature. This is because it is sufficient simply to state that a reason (*hetu*) which has been observed repeatedly together with the probandum (*sādhya*) is a reason, whereas one that is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not. Furthermore, all of this has been analyzed in detail during the discussion on pervasion (*vyāpti*), where it was established that in some cases the "connection" (*pratibandha*) of one thing with another occurs only through origination from it (*tadutpatti*), and that this [origination] is established solely by means of perception and non-apprehension (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). Therefore, that alone should be understood. By this, those who rely on the views of Śaṅkara and Vācaspati are refuted.

Let it be then that even for one possessing effort, there is a causal connection characterized by the production of the effect from that [effort], just as smoke has with fire. As Vīttoka has stated: "For instance, prior to the activity of the potter, although the lump of clay, the staff, the wheel, and so forth exist, the effect called 'pot'—which meets the conditions for perception—is not perceived; yet immediately after his activity, it is perceived. Thus, since the relationship of cause and effect is established, how can there be any doubt regarding its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? This is true in this case.

There is no doubt that [the reason] occurs only in the similar and dissimilar classes; for here, because the nature [of the subject] is accepted as being suitable for perception and non-perception, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of trees, *vīraṇa* grass, and so forth, whose operation by a perceiving person is unmanifest. If it is argued that "the grass and so forth are themselves made the subject (*pakṣa*), and there is no deviation by that which has been made the subject," we say no; for there is no logical principle in making that which has been refuted the subject. Otherwise, even in cases such as "fire is not hot, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), making [fire] the subject would be the only refuge. For instance:

"The reason is doubtful because of the statement of the reason; [an object] that is excluded is not a locus for the reason"—this is the logical principle (*nyāya*). Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is said to be the very perception (*adhyakṣa*) of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) with respect to another counter-correlate. Therefore, even that which is sublated by non-apprehension is indeed sublated by perception. However, with respect to the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), it is inference (*anumāna*). And there is no room for anything else even when something is sublated by inference.

In that case, [the inference] would only establish the absence of that which has attained the status of being a perceptible qualifier; however, since intelligence is common to both those whose bodies are perceptible and those whose bodies are imperceptible, the restriction of perceptibility is untenable. How, then, can there be a negation of an intelligent agent merely through non-perception regarding the production of grass and such? If it is argued that "it is logical to take this as the subject (pakṣa) because of doubt," then this is like trying to guard a cow after it has already been sold.

Because it is precisely by granting scope to perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the acceptance of [the cause] having a perceptible object (*dṛśyaviṣayatā*) is necessarily entailed. For neither perception, which establishes positive concomitance (*anvaya*), nor non-perception, which establishes negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), can function as a means of proof regarding that which is imperceptible (*adṛśya*). Thus, while determining the causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*)—characterized by positive and negative concomitance—between two distinct things through perception and non-perception, this [proponent] is not able to avoid the requirement that the probandum (*sādhya*) be perceptible. And since there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the necessity [of the effect] arising from grass and so forth [even when the cause is absent], the reason is an "inconclusive" one that is too common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).

Now, might one grasp the pervasion through the marvel of non-deviation by means of an intelligent agent who is beyond the scope of perception? Let him do so; however, this [agent] is not superior to the reliance upon perception and non-perception. Is it not the case that the grasping of pervasion occurs merely by an intelligent person, without depending on the qualification of "visible" or "invisible"? It is not so; for even with that much, there is simply no room for a pervasion established by perception.

For since that [universal] is necessarily restricted to having only the visible as its nature, how could it have both the visible and the invisible as its objects? Indeed, that which is visible and that which is invisible—though they may share common properties such as being cognized by a single cognition—are of entirely distinct categories due to the difference between their proximity and remoteness of nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*). Therefore, perception, operating by accepting only the visible category, remains ignorant of any report concerning the other; thus, even when presenting a universal property, it demonstrates it only as qualified by that [visible aspect].

Although that which is remote in space and time is not perceived, it nevertheless belongs to the same class by virtue of its capacity for perception; thus, the exclusion [of non-perception] applies only to that which is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*). For if all other [possible objects] were excluded, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would simply not exist—just as in the cases of smoke and fire, or trembling and wind—since there would be a reduction to the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone.

For instance, the pervasion established by perception—which functions by taking as its primary object the blazing, radiant form suitable for its own manifestation—is not restricted to the common form shared with the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) in the case of fire (*saptārcis*). Otherwise, one who suspects that the intended form might be like that of grass-blades and so forth would not proceed with a mind single-pointedly intent on obtaining the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it; nor would one proceed while reflecting that there might be a deficiency in the causal connection, as in the case of "not being digestive fire."

[245] There would be an occurrence [of this]. Just as the pervasion of wind, established through perception by means of the manifestation of sprouts, results in the apprehension of a form that is not tangible—since it excludes a form common to still air—otherwise, even today, one who infers the wind from the trembling of a new leaf would certainly act with movements and cessations corresponding to a tangible breeze; likewise, in the case of the Person (puruṣa) as well, the apprehension of pervasiveness produced by perception occurs only by excluding an invisible form.

Therefore, under the guise of perception, if at most only that which is desired [by the opponent] is being established—and not actual perception—then because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) even with respect to the generality of the visible and the invisible, the reason possesses a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva). The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: Whatever determination of causality is produced by perception does not terminate in the form of the visible and the invisible, just as [the determination of causality] regarding fire excludes the common form shared by the fire born in the stomach and the fire born from fuel. And this [determination of causality] regarding the intelligent agent is produced by perception; thus, there is the apprehension of a property incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi).

For being produced by perception is pervaded by having a visible object as its domain, since perception does not operate upon what is invisible; its opposite is having both visible and invisible objects as its domain, which is pervaded by the state of terminating in both visible and invisible forms.

Furthermore, if you intend to state the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of "mere intelligence" alone, setting aside the qualification of being visible or invisible, then when one demonstrates the absence of the potter's effect in the absence of an intelligent agent for the sake of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the absence of mere consciousness—devoid of the qualifications of being visible or invisible—established? For the non-perception of the visible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) has jurisdiction only over the negation of that which is visible; otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the presence of] grass and so forth.

Furthermore, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) restricted solely to the object of a perceptible person cannot serve as the means for establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of mere intelligent agency, because the absolute difference between their objects is evident. Otherwise, even in the case of the production of grass and such things, non-apprehension restricted solely to the object of a perceptible person would become the cause for confirming the deviation [of the reason]; for there is no principle that "entry occurs upon gain" and "exit occurs upon cutting."

Therefore, in the view that [the absence of the probans] is not firmly established by the qualification of the perceptible object (*dṛśyaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no means of apprehending the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) at the time of grasping the pervasion; thus, because the pervasion is not established, there remains once again doubt regarding the exclusion [of the probans] from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Nor is the observation of the absence of both [the probans and the probandum] in space (*nabhas*) a means for apprehending the negative concomitance, because it is impossible to ascertain that the absence of the effect is necessitated by the absence of the operation of an intelligent agent. For only when all other causes are present can the absence of the effect—occurring solely upon the absence of that [specific cause]—be understood as being necessitated by that absence.
As was considered in the *Tripañcakacintā*, in the case of two [factors], even if they are not related as cause and effect, mere cessation is easily found in some instances.

Furthermore, regarding the ether (*vihāyas*): is the absence of being an effect due to the absence of the operation of an intelligent cause, or rather due to the mere absence of any cause at all? What is the certainty here? If that were the case, every effort [of inference] would be fruitless. For even in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there remains a doubt as to whether it is grasped between an effect in general and a cause in general, or between an effect and a cause qualified by a specific person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*). Now, if this distinction is indeed perceived—as in the case of fire within smoke—how can it be set aside? If it is so, then [the cause must be] of a visible bodily form.

Even this distinction is indeed well-known; how can it be avoided, like the radiant form of the fire (citrabhānu)? If it is argued that "that distinction is then shown to be inconstant with respect to the effect," let it be inconstant. Let the positive concomitance (anvaya) regarding the effect also be restricted to the observed distinction, just as it is regarding the cause, because it is seen even in the case of a palace and so forth, just as it is in the case of a jar—what is certain about this? And this mere positive concomitance is stated while disregarding the refutation [of the opponent's view] by closing one's eyes like an elephant.

In reality, however, since neither perception nor non-perception can function with respect to even one [of the two terms], there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Furthermore, while the state of being an effect exists in things such as mountains, positive and negative concomitances do not touch upon a creator who transcends the range of perception. Since there is no third category between being produced by such an intelligent agent and being otherwise—just as in the case of odors and so forth—this is indeed an inconclusive reason due to its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Therefore, it is established that the pervasion of "mere effect" cannot be grasped through perception.

And thus, these [cognitions] proceed toward the apprehension of the causal relation precisely by delineating a specific class of effects that is distinguished by both perception and non-perception, and not merely by the delineation of "effect" in general. For, immediately following the operation of perception and non-perception, one proceeds by delineating a specific pair of classes—excluding all other types of cause and effect—in this manner: "From such a particular object characterized by a blazing and radiant nature, there arises such an object which produces a change in the throat and eyes as if smeared with whiteness. In this way, the conventional usage of the causal relation (*hetu-phala-bhāva*) functions by excluding every other possible class of cause and effect.

This very principle applies everywhere in the conventional usage of the relationship between cause and effect; however, we observe that this [usage] involves a transgression of established logic due to deference to the Lord (īśvara).

What, then, is the fault here, if perception were to apprehend the pervasion of the effect-in-general by an intelligent agent—even setting aside distinctions such as mountains and so forth—just as it apprehends the pervasion of smoke-in-general by fire even while setting aside distinctions such as grass-fire and so forth? For just as the apprehension of pervasion occurs through the inclusion of a mere subtle sub-genus within the smoke that is a specific class of effects produced by fire, and not through contact with something of a different genus, so too let it be the case for the intelligent agent in relation to fire and the like.

Or, just as you wish to grasp the pervasion of all that possesses existence by a conscious being—even by including within it classes of effects that are utterly dissimilar—so too you might grasp it by means of fire. For how could the operation of sensory perception itself adopt two different modes of functioning in these two cases? If you argue that this distinction is caused by the observation or non-observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then that observation and non-observation, failing to reach the level of a conceptual determination (*saṅkalpa*), would be as ineffective as the mere touching of grass; thus, one must necessarily engage in a corresponding reflection (*vimarśa*). And yet, such a reflection does not exist.

For no one, having experienced the conceptualization that "the entire class of effects arises from fire" during the operation of perception and non-perception which grasp the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) in the case of fire, smoke, and so forth, can subsequently determine through the observation of deviation—or because other effects are observed to be perceived even without fire—that "smoke alone is produced by this [fire]," but rather [one determines] immediately through another instance of perception and non-perception that "this [effect] arises from this fire."

The synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*), which brings about the conventional usage of the relationship between cause and effect regarding the two specific types of genus such as "smoke" and so forth, is experienced within the sphere of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[247] There is no difference between positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And when, for one who is situated in another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there arises the cognition grasping the relation of cause and effect—such as "pain from a thorn" occurring instantaneously—this cognition is established by perception preceded by non-perception (*anupalambha*); at that time, the absence of reflection upon the observation of deviation is manifested, because conceptual constructions cannot exist simultaneously. Therefore, in this case as well, the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) proceeds by setting aside intermediate subtle differences, such as "this effect, characterized by a broad base and belly, belongs to this artisan."
But when one observes even such things as cloth or carts being produced from a person, then the non-contradictory cognition arises: "This too, and that too, is produced by a person.

Furthermore, does so-called "deviation" (vyabhicāra) merely undermine inference once the pervasion (vyāpti) has been established, or does it establish that the pervasion itself is false? Even in this latter case, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that grasps the pervasion remains manifest through its own power.

Or rather, does it bring about the destruction of its own validity regarding all objects or only regarding a restricted one? If it is restricted, is it so by virtue of the [intended] purpose (*iṣṭi*), or because perception operates only there? First of all, the first position is not tenable due to contradiction; for it is not possible that a logical reason possesses a pervasion (*vyāpti*) characterized by inseparable connection with the probandum (*sādhya*), while at the same time there is an absence of inference caused by the possibility of the probandum's non-existence, especially since there would be a lack of confidence in the pervasion even in other cases.

Thus, when the means of valid cognition that apprehends pervasion maintains its status as a valid authority, it should be understood that even the attempt to demonstrate the falsity of that pervasion is incoherent. Furthermore, if the validity of the means of cognition apprehending pervasion were to fail in every case, then fire could not be inferred from smoke either, because there would be no other means of cognition to apprehend the pervasion.

What, then, will be the refuge for the inference of a Lord (*īśvara*)? If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established within a restricted domain by one's own whim, then the wretched means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) becomes indifferent; thus, in reality, there is neither a reason nor a non-reason, because it would follow that even in the case of smoke, the pervasion could be undermined by one's own whim.

But how can perception, even when its object is one of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), have a restricted scope? For just as that which grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*)—operating within a restricted genus—is held to be all-encompassing, so too should that which has deviation as its object be all-encompassing as well, since the capacity of both is neither deficient nor excessive. Therefore, if the apprehension of pervasion and the cognition of deviation pertain to the very same object, what now would be the means of proof (*sādhana*) and what the non-means of proof? Or, let it be granted, out of deference to you, that there is a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that makes the contradiction known.

[The opponent argues: "There is a restriction on the object [of the cognition]. Nevertheless, it is certainly not the case that those things which possess deviation are perceived as being sublated all at once; rather, it occurs sequentially. And at that time, there is no direct perception of deviation even among those things that do deviate. Therefore, because smoke lacks that specific qualification, it would again be a non-reason (*ahetu*), or else anything else would also be a reason."

Nor should it be said that there is no confidence in the pervasion (*vyāpti*) regarding smoke because of the observation of deviation in all other cases; for if this were so, then immediately after grasping the pervasion in smoke at a previous time, one would not be able to infer fire from smoke on a mountain slope rather than from a tiger, due to the requirement of waiting for the observation of deviation elsewhere. And this [waiting] is impossible when one intends to rely on observations of deviation in other places.

[248] Regarding the phrase "the resting place of pervasion" (*vyāptiviśrāma*): because even the objects of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are infinite, and because a human lifespan is shorter compared to the time required to perceive those things situated at a great distance in space and so forth, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*)—like the observation of deviation—is faultless only when restricted to a specific domain, since pure conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) proceeds through differentiation. For this very reason, only natural conceptualization (*svābhāvikavikalpa*) has the authority to grasp the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), not that which is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

For there exists a conceptual construction (vikalpa) common to children and animals that depends solely on the perceptual cognition (*ālocanājñāna*) produced by a pure object; it is called "pure" and "natural" (*svābhāvika*). By virtue of this [construction], even animals determine that the means for allaying hunger, thirst, and so forth, are effective only in that specific place, and consequently, through association with that [means], they proceed toward it or, through non-association, withdraw from it.

Furthermore, there exists a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) produced by a perceptual cognition accompanied by the recollection of linguistic convention; for example, when one observes soot from a lamp, there arises the conceptualization: "This is blue, useful for dyeing and so forth. This is said to be characterized by such adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), being cultivated by an experience aided by the recollection of the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of an object previously perceived. Yet no discerning person concludes that, merely because there is a conceptualization of blue at that time, all blue things arise from the lamp.

However, that very object which—preceded by a conceptual construction corresponding to the mere sight of collyrium—is fit for the linguistic convention of the word "collyrium" due to its connection with a universal (*jāti*) or its specific nature (*svarūpa*), is precisely what performs the function of a lamp; this has been stated regarding the basis of deviation (*vyabhicārālambana*).

Similarly, even in the case of smoke, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following the convention that "this white object is produced from fire" implies snow and the like only through an adventitious condition (*aupādhika*). However, in a pure conceptual construction, it is only the universal of smoke (*dhūmajāti*) that manifests; therefore, it should be understood that the exclusion of snow and the like from the pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on that [universal] alone is not a valid ground for deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Likewise, every conceptual construction of an effect (*kāryavikalpa*) is everywhere adventitious. For that which is blind regarding its own production depends upon the operation of another.

Since its production from sensory perception—assisted by the recollection of the convention that "this is the effect"—is not a constituent part of the conventional usage regarding the relationship between cause and effect, even though a conceptual construction such as "this is the effect of this" is as easily available as the construction "this is a jar" when one observes the arising of a jar from a person, nevertheless, because it lacks intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), there can be no determination of its being an effect based on that [conceptual] form. However, let it be so for that which is made the object of a natural conceptual construction.

But surely, even regarding an object that is the domain of pure determination (*śuddhādhyavasāya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is seen to be produced by the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketasmṛti*), as in the case of "this jar is man-made," because of the mention of a name. Therefore, it follows that this too is adventitious (*aupādhika*). No; for in the conceptualization of that [object] alone, recollection is not the operative cause, since its capacity lies solely in the mention of the expressive component (*vācakāṃśa*).

And although the arising of an indivisible conceptual construction (vikalpa), which is suffused with the forms of the signified and the signifier, occurs through the assistance of memory, nevertheless, its operation is said to pertain to that [object] alone by way of abstraction (apoddhāra), just as the potter’s operation pertains only to the fact of being made of clay. However, the postulation of properties such as the inherence in a different genus, the effect, and whiteness, cannot belong to a pure determinative cognition (śuddhādhyavasāya) without the recollection of previous operations, such as the grasping of the relationship between the convention and its object.

[249] Since the purpose is fulfilled by the mere delineation of that [object] alone, as in the case of infants and others, it follows that the pervasion (vyāpti) established by perception has only that [particular object] as its domain; thus, there is no fault. Therefore, it is established that the apprehension of pervasion produced by perception and the cognition of deviation have entirely different objects.

If it is argued that, in that case, the establishment of the "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) fallacy is untenable due to the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), we reply: this is indeed so, provided there is a uniformity of intellectual acuity among all people. However, one of dull intellect, even when perception has occurred regarding a specific class based on similarity and so forth, unifies it with another class and, through the conceit of having grasped a pervasion (*vyāpti*), maintains an inference. When such a person is shown a deviation by a more acute opponent, the difficulty of grasping the pervasion is brought home to them; thus, the status of the common inconclusive remains established.

Just as when smoke has appeared, even though perception is capable of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), one who recalls the pervasion by fire in the form of rising, thick smoke might infer fire from a mass of dust stirred up by the wind; yet, seeing the deviation caused by the emergence of steam—which lacks the characteristic of a well-known cloud of vapor—he is dissuaded. For that reason as well, it is established that the pervasion is grasped by perception only with respect to a specific class (*jāti*).

For if perception were to grasp the relation as being restricted to a single class of smoke, then it would be appropriate for there to be a superimposition of that form upon another object based on similarity, and its exclusion would be justified by the deviation from other similar things.

But when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs in every instance of the class of effects, then what is the need for dependence on similarity? If, then, the cognition of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) by perception is restricted solely to a specific class [of objects], how is it that jars, pots, walls, and so forth—though belonging to entirely different classes (*atyantavijātīya*)—lead one to infer the processing of substances such as turmeric, since they all share the common property of being dyed? Or how is it that the intellect (*buddhi*), though belonging to an entirely different class, leads one to infer [the existence of] an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of cutting, such as an axe, which is observed to have the function of performing that action?

If it is argued that even things such as Mount Kailāsa and the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*), though extremely heterogeneous, will lead to the inference of a Person (*puruṣa*) because they possess common properties such as being effects, we say: not so. This is because that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*) is the means of cognition; and it is only with respect to that [pervader] that one considers whether something is homogeneous or heterogeneous. Furthermore, the pervaded is of two kinds—relative to the agent: that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is to be modified (*vikārya*)—and it consists either of the substratum (*dharmī*) or of the property (*dharma*). Among these, pervasion of the substratum is stated when there is an entirely new production, as in the case of smoke and the like.

And in that case, another smoke is indeed the similar (*sajātīya*) instance, while any other object is the dissimilar (*vijātīya*). But when there is the determination that a different property (*dharmāntara*) has arisen in the very same previously existing substrate, then it is called "pervasion by a property" (*dharmavyāpti*), as in the case of heat and so forth in water; and in that case, another instance of heat itself is the similar property, such that at present there is no requirement for the class of the substrate (*dharmin*).

In the same way, even redness (*rāga*), disregarding the heterogeneity of substances such as jars or cloths, serves as an indicator of the refinement of a red substance only with respect to its own homogeneous effects. For this very reason, when there is a particularity in that [redness], the contact of saffron is inferred in some cases, while in others, that of turmeric or similar substances is inferred. And it is not the case that, in the instance of mountains, clouds, and so forth which already exist, an agent is intended merely as the producer of properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*); rather, he is intended precisely as the producer of something previously non-existent (*apūrva-utpādaka*), just like a jar.
And in that case, properties such as "being an effect" are [inferred] just as whiteness and other qualities are in smoke.

Even though properties (*dharma*) that inhere in different classes of entities (*jātyantara*) exist, they are incapable of performing any function because they lie outside the scope of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, the apprehension of the pervasion of the factual subject (*dharmivastu*) does not depend on the proximity of a mere property (*dharmamātra*), nor does it depend on the homogeneity (*sajātīyatā*) of the subject with respect to the pervasion of the property. Furthermore, the distinction between what is homogeneous and what is heterogeneous was stated only with reference to a pure, singular reflection (*śuddhaikavimarśa*). Consequently, even when there is heterogeneity (*vaijātya*) of the subject—as in the case of passion (*rāga*)—properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) do not possess the capacity to indicate [the probandum].
Otherwise, it would be difficult to avoid the undesirable consequence of inferring fire from white ash, since the rebuttal based on deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would be invalid.

However, such an inference applies to the sense faculty as follows: "That which occurs only occasionally despite the presence of other causes depends upon another cause; for example, a sprout [depends on a seed] despite the presence of earth and water. And cognition occurs only occasionally despite the presence of the object, mental attention, and light. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that if there were no dependence (the counter-example), occasional occurrence would be contradictory and thus non-existent.

The established position is that whatever else is required [to complete the causal complex] is the sense-faculty (*indriya*); therefore, there is no inference of the cause by way of the effect, nor does perception grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, perception must necessarily be held to apprehend a universal (*sāmānya*) only by way of presenting a distinction between types (*jātibheda*) brought forth by innate conceptual construction (*svābhāvikavikalpa*); otherwise, when a convention such as "this is a jar" is made after having pointed out a single pervasion by means of perception, would that convention apply to the entire universe characterized by properties such as being an effect?

Is it brought to a state of restricted scope by the observation of deviation? Or does the instructor himself, by negating [the term] in all other classes, establish its restriction to a specific object? Or is it that this convention does not have a general class as its object at all?

The same should be understood regarding the distinction between the classes of words that denote [an object]. However, a word denoting an action (*kārya-śabda*) is applied merely to the arising of something dependent on another, within the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) without depending on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, it does not function with reference to a specific [individual]. If, however, even that were applied as "this is the action" to that which exists in direct perception, then it too would possess other synonyms and would function only with reference to a specific [individual]. Therefore, the natural function of direct perception is precisely the apprehension of a specific class of actions.

And if perception, even when directed toward a difference in the genus of the effect, takes as its basis merely the effect in general, then why, when operating upon a cause, should it not determine merely the cause as the pervader? Why does it instead rely on [the cause] as qualified by the cognition of the material cause and so forth? Therefore, unless you comply with our position, this perception must be either a basis for a generality or a basis for a particularity in both cases; if it has a generality as its object, how could there be an inference of the cause from the effect?

[Otherwise,] how could there be the establishment of the Lord of News (*vārteśvara*)? Furthermore, if one relies upon a specific [instance], the pervasion by the mere effect would remain unestablished. Therefore, it is logical that perception, based on experience, demonstrates only a specific class of effects as being pervaded by a specific cause. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever perception grasps the relation of causal agency (*kārakāraṇabhāva*) has an operation restricted to a specific class [of objects], just as [the perception of] fire and smoke [is restricted to their specific classes]. And this [perception] which establishes the pervasion of the effect by an intelligent agent is likewise [restricted]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

There is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the suspicion of its functioning otherwise, because that is sublated by the non-perception of a cause. For a difference in causes is indeed the cause of a difference in effects; otherwise, it would follow that everything is without a cause. And there is no difference in its cause.

[251] It exists, because it arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by the object, the sense organ, light, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the suspicion that the example might be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya-śūnyatā*), [the response is]: whatever is perception (*pratyakṣa*) takes a universal as its object by virtue of a specific genus (*viśiṣṭa-jāti*) alone; for example, the perception that apprehends deviation, and the perception that apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*). This is simply its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This itself is the avoidance of the inconclusive (*anekānta*) fallacy. This same formulation applies even to the case of the subject (*dharmin*) that apprehends pervasion, which possesses the connection between an intelligent agent and an effect.

Alternatively, in both cases, whatever perception grasps a relation does so by means of a qualified universal (*viśiṣṭajāti*) alone, as in the case of the signified and the signifier; and the perception that grasps the relation between cause and effect is likewise, as before.

Therefore, even if this entire collection of effects is in reality invariably concomitant with an intelligent agent, nevertheless—because the classes of effects are infinitely diverse and because the apprehension of pervasion must be sought for each distinct class—it is rightly said that the inference of [an agent] is direct only for those effects whose nature as being preceded by a person has been determined;
thus, it is established that [the agent] is of such a kind [as previously described].

And so forth. Likewise, regarding the effects of fire—such as smoke, ash, embers, cooking, the expulsion of mercury, observation, injury, and so on—in whichever specific effect the perception that establishes the necessary connection has operated, from that very [perception] follows the inference of that [fire], and not from anything else.

Thus, even in the case of things such as temples, water-jars, palaces, chariots, and fine silk—which are in fact produced by human agency—we accept the inference of that [agency] from an effect belonging to the same class, provided that human activity has been observed in things of that very class. But regarding the class of clouds, mountains, and the like, since their operation cannot be discerned, what talk can there be of inference? For, due to the possibility of an absolute difference in class (*jātivaijātya*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped; and even if the pervasion were grasped, no such effect would be observed. As for the inference of knowledge in the case of pillars and the like, it is based on the observation of constructed objects such as pleasure-mountains and the like.
Nor is it the case that they do not possess iron-like [stability], since their gait falters; for that reason, their name alone is the same.
Furthermore, if lords created by many similar men could achieve success, what talk can there be of an awareness of equality in the fruit? From what cause would there be a state of distinction?

Thus runs an intermediate verse. Now, one might ask: what kind of class of effects (*kāryajāti*) is pervaded by an agent possessing effort? Anticipating this, it is stated for the sake of brevity—since that class of effects is also infinite—that upon seeing which, even one who observes only causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) forms the cognition that [the object] has been produced (*kṛtabuddhi*). In this context, "forming the cognition that it has been produced" does not mean the cognition of a means (*sādhana*), nor does it mean the cognition of the specific probandum under discussion, characterized by knowledge of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth; rather, it refers to the cognition of a producer whose nature is like that of a weaver (*kuvinda*) and the like.

And because of that absence, neither is the non-establishment of your reason (*hetu*) intended here, nor is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) under discussion; rather, this is intended to demonstrate absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*). And by means of that, the non-establishment or the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason is precisely what is intended.

For instance, when one observes a temple or similar structure in an empty city, the cognition of a craftsman—such as a potter or the like—arises; this does not occur in relation to things such as a garland or the ocean. The intention is that the presence or absence of this cognition of a craftsman cannot occur without an absolute difference in genus (*jāti*). If there were no apprehension of a distinction [from other causes], or if there were a lapse in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of memory, then this identical cognition of a craftsman would not arise even in the case of a temple and so forth.

Just as the cognition of fire arising from smoke excludes that of a donkey, thereby necessarily establishing a specific distinction in the genus of the donkey, so too does this [cognition] establish a distinction for Kailāsa, the thunderbolt, and so forth, from those entities whose human origin is firmly determined.

If it is asked, "How, then, is the very absence of inference to be understood? [The answer is: because even in a dream, one is free from the suspicion that the production of clouds, rainbows, and so forth could arise from a potter. Otherwise, the world would not suffer the hardship of drought caused by the trampling of weavers' feet, nor would one who fears invasion by a foreign army seek refuge in the gaps between mountains and oceans, finding relief therein.

If it is argued that another factor, standing in the place of the weaver, must indeed be expected there, we say no; for when the production of an effect is identical, it is illogical to search for a cause of a different genus, since the accomplishment of the goal is achieved by the weaver alone. Indeed, even in the case of another cloth, there is no requirement for anyone other than the weaver.

If it is argued that there is indeed a dependence on a specific artisan regarding a particular type of cloth, this is true only so long as there is a firm conceptual identification (*ekajātiparāmarśa*) with another piece of cloth; for this very reason, the artisan is conceived as being specifically the weaver (*kuvinda*). In the absence of such a conceptual identification, there is doubt regarding its being a human product (*pauruṣeyatā*) alone. However, mountains such as Meru and Mandara are not the objects of a single conceptual identification by any human agent.

Thus, one who out of deceit denies the extreme heterogeneity of these [effects]—which is established by direct perception—and instead accepts them as having a common artisan due to the absence of inference, is refuted. Once the difference in genus (*jātibheda*) is established, it is seen that while effects such as jars are proven to be dependent on a person, effects such as embryos and infants are not. Since this [latter] is not of the same nature as that [former], the pervasion by a person is not established; thus, both [the arguments for a creator] are unproven and lack pervasion (*avyāpti*). This being the case, the objections—which function by preventing the arising of the cognition of the probandum under discussion—are cast far aside.

For we do not assert that the reason—such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—is unestablished because of the absence of the cognition of the specific probandum under discussion. What then? We assert the non-establishment of the property of being an effect belonging to the same class as cloth and so forth, due to the absence of the artisan's cognition (the cognition of a weaver) in the case of Mount Mandara and the like. Consequently, there is no distinction [between our position and yours] regarding the deficiency of the cognition of the specific probandum. Furthermore, since it is accepted that there is simply a lapse in the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to what is produced by a weaver, there is no room for the alternative objections raised by the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

However, the mere cognition of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not what is intended [to be negated]. For those whose memory has not failed, the notion that the earth and so forth are "made by a person" certainly does arise; thus, [the objection] is far from relevant. Indeed, what is proposed to be stated here is the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the negation of the notion of being made, as formulated by the Buddhists. And that [negation] cannot be established, because by the term "notion of being made," the intention here is the notion of an artisan (*śilpin*). [This is] the demonstration of the existence of the notion that [things] are made by a person.

[253] Furthermore, this is irrelevant; for this consideration of refutation applies only when that [creation by a creator] is already accepted. Even there, the claim that "those whose memory has not failed" is inconsistent, because an absolute difference in kind (*atyantavaijātya*) is established, and because no pervasion (*vyāpti*) is perceived from the ocean and so forth to anything else, and because the failure of the latent impressions of memory (*smaraṇasaṃskāra*) cannot be avoided. For this very reason, what confidence can there be in the mere babble that "the world was created by someone"? And by the very fact of having refuted the objection regarding the non-establishment of the understanding of the probandum under discussion, the argument beginning with "in the case of the Vedas as well" and so forth is also rejected.

If, however, the Mīmāṃsaka were to demonstrate an absolute difference in genus (*vaijātya*) between the Veda and human utterances such as sentences, then why should he be defeated merely by a convention (*samaya*)? For there is no distinction between the two based on their essential nature (*svarūpa*) or their capacity (*śakti*). Thus, having recited both before someone who has not grasped the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), consider this: what kind of distinction could the listener describe for which one, or do you not see the removal of poison and so forth effected by mantras such as those of Garuḍa? This follows: one [the proponent], while conceiving a specific effect, [establishes] his own specific cause.
One person perceives that the mere effect is pervaded by this [cause], just as one perceives the mere effect of fire through its mark;
yet another does not understand that such an effect has that very thing as its cause.
Alas! This is a particular kind of darkness among the learned, even regarding an object of direct perception.
Therefore,
since that which follows the presence and absence of the person in speech participates in its existence,
there is no difference between ordinary speech and Vedic words, as both are capable of possessing a nature [of their own].
Furthermore, the Veda merely indicates things that are equally beyond the senses, and it provides no certain assurance regarding any single point;
therefore, it does not rest without reaching the status of being human-authored.

If that were so, what need is there to speak of the human origin of the cognition restricted to those specific classes—such as jars, oceans, and thunderbolts—which are absolutely distinct from one another and beyond the scope of investigation? Furthermore, that which was alleged as a proof for [the world's] impermanence is also outside the bounds of logic; for such an inquiry into whether something belongs to its own class or another occurs only when the apprehension of a necessary connection (pratibandha) is within the domain of perception.

Regarding impermanence, the establishment of the probans "being merely produced" occurs through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts the contrary, which is of the nature of inference; thus, there is no requirement for a specific genus (*jāti*) therein. However, it must be considered whether that *pramāṇa* is capable or incapable of establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to "merely being produced" when it is not delimited by a specific genus. If it is capable, there is no contact with a fault.

Therefore, it is not correct to claim that the pointing out of a difference there by means of the difference between the words "pot" and [the word for the substance] constitutes a statement of dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). This is because, since the two properties (*dharma*) are extracted from the nature of the property-possessor (*dharmin*) in order to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*), the property-substance itself is the property-possessor; thus, the meaning of stating a difference between them is simply a difference between the property-possessors alone.

[254] If it is argued that even here, in the case of effects as the subjects (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is "being produced by a person" (*pauruṣeyatva*) while the reason (*hetu*) is merely "being an effect" (*kāryatvamātra*), and thus there is no distinction at all—then it is replied: what is the meaning of this statement that "merely being an effect" is the reason? Is it said because, in a primary sense, the cause (such as saffron and the like) operates only upon the quality (*dharma*) of color? Or is it because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established for the effect in its entirety, just as "merely being smoke" is the reason, since all smoke [is pervaded by fire]? Just as every single bit of smoke...

[The opponent argues: "It is pervaded by the probandum; for there is the certain conviction that whatever is an effect is entirely produced by human activity. Both of these [arguments] are refuted. As for the statement that "the mere fact of being produced is pervaded by impermanence," this is merely a formulation intended to express totality (*kārtsnya*); its meaning is simply this: "whatever is produced, all that is impermanent."

In this matter, once the authority of the means of valid cognition has been joined and the produced nature of sound established, the question "How could sound be [eternal] when only a pot is seen to be produced and impermanent? leaves no room for doubt; thus, this very point is elucidated by the method of stating that "this is merely a difference in the substratum (dharmin)."

For just as, in the context of the discussion on the essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) are established as distinct with respect to their forms as they appear in conceptual construction (*vikalpārūḍharūpa*), so too is the locus (*dharmin*), such as sound and the like; for there exists no other locus possessing those properties. Nor is the impermanence of sound established by proving the impermanence of an object through the fact of being produced when the locus is something else. And one who, having raised an objection by introducing a difference in the locus itself—such as by treating the jar and the word "jar" as distinct—is defeated by means of that very distinction of the mere locus.

In the present case, however, because of the conceit that [the body] is the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the aggregate of effects—which stands in the place of smoke—is distinct from the person to be proven (*sādhya*), just as fire is [distinct] from smoke; yet it is not restricted to that same place and time as the fire.

However, [the agent] must be ascertained as being present at the time and place of production; for instance, by means of the ashes and the pot, the potter—who is present at that location and whose activity is inferred—is ascertained. Furthermore, the cause is the actual entity (*vastu*), not the property of being an effect (*kāryatva-dharma*). Thus, when the Person (*puruṣa*) is to be proven, it is the entity itself that is the reason, not the property of being an effect. This being so, one who asserts that effects such as mountains and the like are dissimilar to the effect [of a pot] which is pervaded by the Person, has pointed out a dissimilarity in the *sādhana* (the proof), not a dissimilarity in the *dharmin* (the subject).

For at that time, the subject (*dharmin*) is precisely the place and time of its own arising; nor has anyone undertaken to state a dissimilarity between the place and time of a jar or the like and the place and time of Kailāsa or the like, by which a demonstration of dissimilarity in the subject might occur.

Therefore, just as there is an inference of fire from the mere form of heat, this pointing out of a dissimilarity in the means of proof (*sādhana*) is intended to demonstrate either non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); thus, the claim that this refers to the subject (*dharmin*) is a misconception of others. This very point is taught by the following direction: "The kind of 'being an effect' (*kāryatva*) that is perceived in temples and the like as being pervaded by a person is not the same kind found in the Yugandhara mountains and so forth. The meaning is: "That class of things such as temples which is pervaded by a person is not the same class as the Yugandhara mountains and the like."

And because of their absolute heterogeneity, it is said that there is a similarity merely in terms of being "effect-words," but there is no deficiency whatsoever in the exclusion of being an effect. However, we maintain that [the property] is not included within the universal "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) when it comes to pervasion (*vyāpti*). For this very reason, similarity based on that alone is not useful, just as [similarity in] corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is not useful for inferring fire.

[255] However, Mañjarī’s objection is misplaced. For by stating that the universal (*jāti*) of jars and the like is indeed established as pervaded by persons, he intends here merely to express doubt. Furthermore, the cognition of something being "made" (*kṛtabuddhi*) refers to the cognition that it was made by a human such as a potter; and the absence of that [cognition] has been addressed regarding the difference in universals. Since that [absence] is established for both parties, it does not allow for a dismissal [of the argument]. And it has already been explained that this is not possible without an absolute difference in universals.

In this way, it should be understood that even for Vācaspati, the search for a distinction is prompted by a failure to understand the subject matter and the purpose, resulting from a deficiency in cultivated intellect (*kṛtabuddhi*). For if what is intended is that "cultivated intellect" means the absence of the cognition of the thesis under discussion, then one must consider: in this dispute regarding comprehension, on what basis does that [cognition] exist elsewhere—such as on a mountain—and why is it said not to exist there due to its absence?

But when one has formed the cognition that "it does not exist," the intended meaning is that "the cognition produced by a potter does not exist," and in that case there is no dispute. Furthermore, the purpose [of the argument] is to demonstrate the absolute heterogeneity (*atyantavaijātya*) of clouds and the like compared to jars and so forth; yet even that cannot be avoided. Therefore, how can there be a cognition of the subject under discussion (*prakṛtasādhyabuddhi*) from something entirely distinct from those things from which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped? This is what is intended [by the opponent]. At that point, everything of this kind simply collapses.

Furthermore, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been refuted in respect to mere "possessing origination" (*utpattimat*), alas, the reply beginning with "that which possesses origination" and so forth is indeed shattered by the "Staff of Time" (*kāladaṇḍa*). Therefore, for one who has perceived the pervasion in the case of a jar, only that which is of the same class as the jar is preceded by an intelligent agent. However, it has also been stated that when the apprehension of pervasion occurs even in the case of a palace and the like, then the fact of being preceded by that [intelligent agent] is established for that genus as well.

And as for the objection, "Of what kind [is that]?"—anticipating this, one might ask, "Of what kind of effect is it? and reply, "It is not seen to be so. But even that is rendered futile by establishing through perception the fitness for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a universal (*sāmānya*) that appears within an innate conceptual construction (*svābhāvikavikalpa*). Therefore, although the conventional usage of "belonging to that class" is difficult to avoid even with respect to a form appearing in a conceptual construction based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), there is a great distinction [between the two cases], since [the latter] has been rejected in the context of grasping pervasion.

For this very reason, even these various conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) amount to nothing. To explain: if the question concerns our intended position, then a specific class of effects characterized by temples, jars, and so forth, is indeed pervaded by an intelligent agent; for from the observation of such things, one infers a craftsman of a similar kind even when his activity is imperceptible. However, that [specific class] is not established in the case of oceans, mountains, and the like. As for mere "effect-ness" (*kāryatvamātra*), we ourselves loudly proclaim that it is not so pervaded. Therefore, reflect upon what is to be gained by these conceptual alternatives.

The claim that "that particularity (*viśeṣa*) by virtue of which a specific class of effects is distinguished—does that particularity itself have an unascertained nature? is even more wretched; for it is impossible to deny the mutual dissimilarity of classes of effects established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for whether pervasion (*vyāpti*) resides in a specific class of effects or in the category of effects in general, one may at most dispute this point superficially.

Otherwise, how could he himself have avoided the charge of inconsistency by relying on the non-production of the state of being a real entity (*vastutva*) as an effect of fire? For it has already been demonstrated that there is no dispute regarding the fact that cognitions of inconsistency have restricted universals (*niyata-jāti*) as their objects. Therefore, since one perceives the capacity for form and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) and so forth, it is better simply to disregard the claim that this person perceives a single, extraordinary form in a world of variegated forms solely through the grace of God.

As for that previous example of the material cause (*upādāna*) offered with the intention of establishing a pervasion over all effects, that too is not useful; for even there, the operation of perception cannot be established, because it is the object of natural conceptual construction and because the material cause possesses both visible and invisible natures.

Is it then that there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the class of effects by the material cause (*upādāna*) at all? Or is it that this [pervasion] must be cognizable through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Regarding both [alternatives], there is doubt; for even if a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) exists, it is possible that no subverting inference (*bādhakānumāna*) against its opposite has been stated, since at present there is no one-sided reason (*ekāntahetu*).

Therefore, this universal tenet established by all schools—that every origination possesses a material cause—is followed because it is free from contradiction; furthermore, as long as we observe an effect, there is also a consensus in practice that it necessarily possesses a material cause. Moreover, since the cognition of the full extent of an effect does not belong to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), doubt is difficult to ward off even regarding the slightest contrary portion.

Since it is certain that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Buddha, it is established that consciousness does not have consciousness as its material cause; thus, there is no contradiction. Therefore, even if one determines that pervasion (*vyāpti*) holds according to the established tenet (*siddhānta*), there is no harm whatsoever. However, let it be that this is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, the settled conclusion (*vyavasthā*) is that in this position, the reason "having a non-conscious material cause" might be suspected of being unestablished in part (*ekadeśāsiddha*).

And that [consequence] has already arrived; what can be done? However, upon obtaining a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates the contrary, even that [consequence] would not occur. This objection—that there is no example at all for the claim that perception pervades the entirety of its effects—is merely [a point made] while [the opponent] maintains that perception functions with a restriction to specific types [of objects]. Therefore, [the argument] beginning with "because of the absence of a specific reason" is also refuted by establishing that perception is restricted to its operation within specific classes [of objects].

Furthermore, regarding the human effort in presenting another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that subverts [the opponent's] misconception, even there, the first two [means of proof] are indeed subverting; for once the production [of smoke] from that [fire] is established—just as in the case of smoke—it is possible to establish the operation of the perception and non-perception that prove it by way of a specific genus, specifically with respect to effects such as a jar and so forth.

And thus, if [the world] were to arise even once without an intelligent being, it would not exist at all; or, if its causes were non-restricted, it would follow that it has no cause whatsoever—not merely with respect to some specific effect, because there is no proof for the production of that [effect] from a person. Consequently, the claim that "this effect is preceded by a person" is also rendered untenable.

Nor does the consequence of the non-cessation of effects follow, because even though there is no constant presence of that specific state of the cause—which depends on its own causes and has the transformation of *adṛṣṭa* as its auxiliary—the occasional nature of effects is established. It is in dependence upon this [specific state] that the Lord, despite possessing eternal power, does not always act (or exercise his agency). For if the cause were restricted to a single state, one would have to postulate a desire to bring about the activity or cessation of other causes;
but such a restriction does not exist, given the familiarity with a succession of transformations, such as the progressive swelling of a seed.

[257] Because it is impossible to deny them; or, even if there were a restriction to a single state for Īśvara, since his will (*icchā*) is also eternal, the non-cessation of effects would remain in that same state. But if it is impermanent, and its occasional occurrence depends upon something else, what fault would there be if the collection of effects were likewise dependent upon that? If one objects: "In the sequence of effects such as jars and so forth, what is the need for a person's will, since it can be said that whatever it depends upon for its own sequence, that very thing also serves as the basis for the sequence of the jar and so forth? That is incorrect.

Because it is impossible to exclude a cause whose causal efficacy has been observed through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas in the case at hand, due to the absence of such valid means, one merely relies on the fact that the effect is occasional; since this could be explained otherwise, how can there be a rule that the effect must originate from a person? If it is argued that the occasional occurrence of jars and the like is seen to be dependent upon a person, and therefore other effects are likewise so, then in that case, mere observation and non-observation alone have arrived as the proof for the pervasion (*vyāpti*). What is the use here of boasting about the presentation of a counter-proof (*viparyaya-bādhaka*)? Thus, the third [position] is also refuted.

As for what is said—that certainty depends on the presence of a cause and is subject to the intellect—there too, this very same point must be stated regarding the mere reliance on observation. Furthermore, no subverting argument against the contrary has been stated. And if one takes recourse to perception and non-perception, [the reason] is inconclusive because of factors such as wind-injury and so forth in the case of the *jambāla* seed and other causal complexes; thus, everything accompanied by the removal of dependence should be understood as being like an effect, up to the conclusion that only a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī-viśeṣa*) is fit for pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Therefore, the pervasion of the causal complex by the Person is not established; since non-existence [of the Person] in the counter-example follows from the non-perception of the pervader, the fourth [argument] is also refuted.
By this alone, even the hollow prattle of Vācaspati is cast aside. For it has already been stated that the seed of non-production for extended things is simply the absence of a particular state.

Even if it is observed that staffs, wheels, and so forth meet only with a person, and that the undertaking of an effect occurs when they are accompanied by his effort, nevertheless, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish a rule that this is always the case everywhere, the pervasion is unproven; since the conjunction of causes—which is the pervader of the production of an effect—is itself dependent upon an intelligent agent, the same fault remains.

And just as the occasional existence of effects depends solely upon specific states of other causes, so too does the specific nature [of the cause]; thus, the fifth [reason] is also subsumed within the five [previously mentioned ones].
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated in the treatise that this is a proof establishing the occurrence of the mere cause.

By this very [argument], even what was stated by Śaṅkara—that "there is no distinction whatsoever," and so forth—has been reduced to a mere literary composition, because the means of knowledge that establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) have been exhausted. And although there is no distinction between the causes of palaces and the like and the causes of mountains and the like insofar as their activity is devoid of intention, nevertheless, if there were a difference based on the dependence or non-dependence upon an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat*), what fault would there be? It is just as there is a distinction between being scratchable by iron and not being scratchable by iron, despite the lack of distinction in their being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*).
And this must necessarily be the case, given the lack of distinction in their being devoid of intention.

[258] Furthermore, a specific distinction must be sought here regarding power; otherwise, how could there be an absolute difference in the nature of effects? If that power were capable of disregarding even the absence of dependence on effort, what harm would there be? Moreover, it is not observed that a corporeal effect is accomplished by the mere volition of an agent without the operation of hands and other limbs; so what need is there to mention mountains and the like, which transcend such [human] volition?

If it is argued that hands and other organs are also set in motion by volition (*samīhā*), we reply: it has already been stated that even volition accomplishes nothing if it lacks the activity of lying down and so forth within that which possesses a specific configuration. Therefore, who would believe this: that by whatever power they dispense with dependence on the activity of hands and other organs, the causes of mountains and such are not obstructed in their causal function despite being devoid of intention, yet they do not likewise transcend volition? For indeed, at the time of the rising of smoke, there is no object manifesting a thick, surging form [without a cause].

Just as that which is conceived as being produced from fire and fuel, when its absence is ascertained, does not lead to a suspicion of its existence even when the other [cause] is absent—this case is exactly like that.

But if one accepts that [the Lord] possesses a body, then because he would be localized, non-eternal, manifold, and non-omniscient, the Lord has been effectively refuted by the wise. Or rather, by this very point, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth. For, based on the statement beginning with "not of those who are unguided," [the opponent] touches upon nothing other than mere observation and non-observation as a means to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) for this [reason], and that has already been answered.

If perception and non-perception alone are the refuge [of proof], then just as the performance of an action is observed in one who possesses effort, and thus—in the presence of an effect—an inference of one possessing effort is accepted; likewise, since corporeal action is observed only in one who possesses hands and so forth, why is it not determined that when the operation of hands and so forth is impossible, the person is simply inactive? Indeed, there is no difference whatsoever in the validity of the reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*) and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

If, however, there were another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) restricted to a single [object], established independently of mere perception and non-perception, then there might be a cognition of a single thing to be proven; but in its absence, there is merely a mutual contradiction between the two, not a sublation (*bādhā*), because they are of equal status—this is the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*) fallacy according to the opponent’s intention.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not possess the operation of its own parts is not seen to be capable of producing a material object, just as a potter is [incapable] in a state where the operations of his hands and so forth have ceased; and in the case of the person under discussion, there is no operation of his own parts. This is a non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

If it is argued that there is no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) by virtue of the logic established in the *Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya*, then in reality another refutation would be more appropriate; for if one asks, "What room is there for a counter-reason (*pratihetu*)," we say: No, because this [counter-reason] is presented for the purpose of demonstrating that repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is not a constituent factor in establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*). Since it has been stated, "If repeated observation were the means, then even this [fallacy] might occur," it is established that the [proposed] modes of grasping pervasion are untenable, and thus the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Or, let it be granted that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs somehow; even so, the hope for proving God is not fruitful, because there is no certainty regarding the restriction of the intelligent probandum (*sādhya*) to being one. For if its unity were established, then the proof of its being eternal, omnipresent, and omniscient would justify the conventional designation "God. But when the collection of effects, distributed across different places and times, is conceived as being produced by multiple agents exceeding the number of one, then neither omnipresence nor eternity is possible; and if only the knowledge of their own respective materials and instruments is established, where is the omniscience?

Now, if it is argued that when many [agents] act with distracted minds, there would be a failure to produce the effect, and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its destruction and so forth—[we reply: this suspicion might indeed apply to the activity of Lords (īśvara) who possess qualities such as omnipotence individually; however, it is stated here that not even one such [Lord] is established today. Moreover, we actually observe numerous beings of limited power who, having begun a single or multiple task, successfully bring it to completion.

If it is argued that even in the case of many [agents], there must be one who is predominant or more powerful—like a master builder or a general—and therefore he alone possesses agency because the others follow him, we say no; for even in those cases, there is no such rule, as we observe that some independent beings come together for the sake of a single purpose, such as the creation of a living being, according to their own respective interests.
Furthermore, there is no requirement that only one among them be the primary instigator, since the longing of the heart may arise in many, and even a lowly person can be an instigator.

Therefore, just as in the case of bees, honey-bees, or creatures in an anthill, when even such minute living beings are capable of constructing things like the *aināka* mountain one by one, what need is there to mention the creation of the entire universe by a single being? In that regard, the earth, the netherworld (*adhara*), and so forth, have their existence in previous births [established] merely by the inference of conscious agents whose purposes have been fulfilled by those very acts.

Furthermore, those small creatures would proceed—just like the insects in an anthill—only if they were aware of the extremely minute material substrate such as earth, the instruments, the recipient of pleasure and so forth (which is the self), and the purpose, which is the pleasure of their own maintenance and the like. Moreover, even if [the existence of a creator] were established, such supervisors would not necessarily be perceived, either because they depend on actions of diverse potencies or because of the remoteness of their nature from our perception. As for trees and the like, which are produced by visible causes and are of human origin, there is no need for such inquiry regarding them.

Furthermore, as for those entities located in the vicinity of the Vindhya, Yugandhara, and other mountains where no human activity is observed, they too must have agents—countless presiding spirits such as Piśācas and the like. Who, then, could be an omniscient knower? Moreover, since space and time are indeed distinct [from one another], how can they possess omnipresence and eternity? Nor is there any subverting inference (*bādhaka-anumāna*) proceeding from the force of reality that would counteract such a doubt.

But surely, even you yourself have not accepted this very point. And if you argue that among such extremely difficult conceptual constructions, the postulation of a Lord (Īśvara) alone is better due to its simplicity (*lāghava*), we reply: True, if this were merely a matter of setting aside one conceptual construction for another; in that case, we would indeed favor your proposal. However, as long as you do not abandon the guise of inference (*anumāna*), we must necessarily apply ourselves to a firm investigation.

Now, if it pains the mind that the Narmadā and other rivers were created by countless minor [deities], then it is all the more so if they were created by a single bodiless one. Therefore, valid cognition alone is everywhere more powerful; the status of an object is exactly as it establishes it. For this very reason, that [cognition] is firmly determined. And there is no consideration whatsoever for those who are minor.

[260] Let the arrangement of the world be created by hosts—whether small or large, visible or invisible, of equal or superior power, independent, or accompanied by individual beings regarded as primary—consisting of immeasurable groups that know only the material causes and so forth for their own respective effects, whether gross or subtle, single or multiple, and which are included within the six states of existence; however, let there not be a single creator of this universe.

Nor is it accepted by the Buddhists in that way; therefore, there is an exclusion of the reason (*hetu*), because it would follow that [the reason] is excluded even from one side. Furthermore, in an inference that functions by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta-anumāna*), there is no dependence on the acceptance of another. This is because there is no contradiction in abandoning mere acceptance. Thus, when "mere intelligent being" is the probandum (*sādhya*), the desired conclusion is not established with certainty—whether by proving the agent who directly knows the material cause and so forth through its necessary connection with the specific characteristic of knowing the material cause and so forth, or otherwise—because it is not established that all causal activity has a single agent.
