Furthermore, if one seeks to prove merely that [the subject] possesses superknowledge such as grasping [objects], it is futile, like the stories in the *Mahābhārata* and other such works. Consequently, since there is no other means of proof, the desired establishment of [the subject] as possessing qualities such as omniscience must be accepted from this very [reasoning]; therefore, it is established that the refutation must be stated in relation to that very point, characterized by the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*).

Therefore, the passage beginning with "to whatever extent the scope of the object" and so forth is difficult to refute. Even though the establishment of a particular is drawn forth by the connection with the generality of the probandum (*sādhya*), its proof remains dependent upon the means of proof (*sādhana*), because the means of proof is presented solely for that purpose and because there is no other means of proof. For even for a Buddhist, the establishment of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is indeed dependent upon the means of proof.

For if the proof of momentary destruction were to achieve its purpose even upon the abandonment of selflessness (*nairātmya*), then what would be the point of establishing selflessness through the proof of momentariness? According to your own position, however, having set aside the establishment of omniscience and so forth, you have instead established a specific distinction characterized by the direct knowledge of appropriation (*upādāna*) and so on. Therefore, it is irrelevant [to argue] that a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) preceded by the introduction of a self is not demonstrated in the example.

Even when there is direct observation of its presence in similar instances, the necessary concomitance of the general property to be proven must still be demonstrated; and that is impossible because, due to [the subject's] being a single entity, there is no pervasion of the locus of all possible actions.

By this very argument, Vācaspati’s display of proof for omniscience is also refuted. However, once an omniscient creator is established, our labor in determining the oneness of that creator is useless; therefore, we shall desist. As for the negative inference (*vyatireki-prayoga*) he has stated, that too is invalidated precisely because oneness is not certain, since it has been demonstrated that even if one possesses non-eternal cognition whose objects are not all-encompassing, it is still possible to have knowledge of the material cause and so forth.

But if [the exclusion of non-connection with the mountain were established] through the concentration of wealth, then by the same logic as the exclusion of non-connection with the mountain from smoke, there would follow the inference of fire’s possession of a mass of five-colored flames as well. If you say that this [latter] capacity is not present here, then in that case too, it is precisely the exclusion of non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavaccheda*) that follows by implication. Even if an effortful agent is established in relation to a mountain, since oneness is not certain, how can the establishment of omniscience be achieved?

But surely, since even a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is an effect, its agent must necessarily be one who perceives the atoms that serve as its material cause; and those with fleshly eyes cannot possibly be such. Otherwise, what offense have we committed that— [the opponent asks]—[this should be so]?

[261] "If it is asked, 'Do we not exist in that way?'—then one who perceives supersensuous objects must necessarily be accepted as the agent, and it is not logical for anyone other than Īśvara [to be so]. But that too is trivial. For even in the case of having a physical eye (*māṃsacakṣus*), the capacity of the sense organ is not common to all; this is because even among those far inferior to us, such as vultures and the like, an extraordinary excellence in the acuity of the senses is observed."

Furthermore, some among the most minute beings might even possess the vision of atoms due to a particular capacity for action, just as ants perceive odor-molecules that are beyond our own range. However, by observing what is subtle merely to that degree, can one perceive other subtler things remote in space and time, or indeed everything gross? Therefore, there is no hope of establishing the existence of God on that basis alone.

If that is so, let there be the possibility of perceiving the atom; but how could there be such a possibility regarding all the fields (kṣetrajña) and the specific dispositions of merit and demerit inherent in them? Not at all. For in the example of the potter, the performance of an action is not seen to be pervaded by a thorough knowledge of the nature of the field-knower and so forth; rather, its accomplishment is held to occur through the cognition of the recipient and the instruments. And that [cognition] is impossible, because it lacks the necessary capacity, since—even according to the sequence just stated—the mere cognition of those [atoms] would suffice for the purpose.

Because, since [the object] is intended by the agent as that which is desired for itself, it is unavoidable that it should possess the status of a *sampradāna* (recipient); as in the expression, "he builds a temple for himself. Otherwise, there would arise the contingency of a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the requirement of the cognition of a recipient.

If it is argued that another person, who knows the recipient (*sampradāna*), will be inferred there, we say no; for, since deviation is observed, the fact that the agent is invariably concomitant with knowledge of the recipient is not established, and thus there is an absence of any basis for inference. Nor does his status as a non-agent follow merely in relation to the one being inferred. For if that were so, it would follow that even the potter is a non-agent; and if he were an agent, then his own self would have to be accepted as the recipient.

Nor is he capable of knowing even that which is commonly recognized in worldly transaction as the recipient (*sampradāna*), setting aside its nature as a field (*kṣetra*), nor even those things comprised by the terms "distinctions of latent impressions" (*karmāśaya-bheda*), "objects," and "instruments. Therefore, just as a potter knows those [instruments] without having pierced them through the very perception of the staff, wheel, and so forth, so too will living beings, even while being inferred, ultimately come to know their own hands, mouths, and other organs.

Whence, then, comes this thorough knowledge of the nature of the *kṣetrajña* and the distinctions between his own merits (*dharma*) and demerits (*adharma*)? Furthermore, for one who is bodiless, how can there be any connection with the activity of his own limbs? And what kind of connection with supernatural powers (*siddhi*) could a bodiless being have? For if oneness were established, the embodied being would be localized and incapable of all actions; thus, the hope for the proof of a bodiless state arises from such incapacity, yet it has been stated that oneness itself is difficult to prove.

Furthermore, even in the state of bodilessness (*aśarīratva*), since instruments such as the staff, the wheel, and the mouth are impossible, it follows by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that the culmination of the knowledge of instruments occurs solely through the knowledge of the various latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*). This is for the sake of excellence; for even though space, time, inherence, and so forth are included among the instruments, one achieves the fulfillment of one's purpose merely through the knowledge of them. But what is this distinction, such that in that state the knowledge of instruments arises only through the knowledge of space and the like, and not through the knowledge of merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth? If it is argued that it must be through the knowledge of both, that too has already been addressed: for [the Lord] does not require every single instrument.

[262] It is observed that the agent must necessarily know [the instrument]; yet we do not maintain that the cognition of direction and so forth constitutes the knowledge of the instrument such that it would lead to a definitive conclusion, which would then invite a specific inquiry. Rather, it is said here that because other instruments are possible, there is no finality in the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).

Therefore, just as in the case of successive makers of jars and other objects, where a continuity of dependence on various external instruments such as the staff, the wheel, the shuttle, and the loom is observed even in the absence of others, why should it not be so here as well? Or rather, must it be by taking recourse to *dharma* and the like? This remains a mere doubt. If, however, there were no other instrument, then an explanation based on the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) would be appropriate.
Furthermore, while there is doubt regarding the paths to worldly prosperity and the supreme good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*), what could be accomplished by such a being called "God" who lacks wealth?

Therefore, even if bodilessness were established, there would be no attraction of knowledge regarding *dharma* and so forth; how much less so when that [bodilessness] itself is unproven? Let it be granted that one who experiences *dharma* and the like does not necessarily do so as an instrument; however, the claim that "the creator is the knower of the nature of his effects, and he is God" is likewise hollow. For those who perform acts such as giving and non-violence certainly experience them in their own right, yet they are not thereby God. Nor is anyone else proven to be a knower of them in their entirety.

However, the ascertainment of [an action] as being merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) does not necessarily follow even for one who performs it, just as in the case of a potter. Furthermore, because those who perform such actions lack ascertainment of its true nature, the claim that "ascertainment of the true nature would bring the agent—namely, God himself—into proximity" because it is an effect is also untenable. For even the ascertainment of merit and demerit remains one whose existence is merely doubtful, despite being correct.

How can there be hope from that [God]? For one whose nature consists of conceptual constructions (*saṅkalpa*) accompanied by doubts and errors that have not been dispelled, [the understanding of the connection between action and its fruit] occurs primarily through the gateway of the scriptures. Furthermore, because they accept [the existence of] those who remember their births as gods and so forth, even they possess a slight degree of awareness regarding the connection between correct actions and their fruits. Yet, this much alone does not suffice for sovereignty. Thus, since God is unestablished, the auspicious and inauspicious actions of all living beings are not merely instruments [of God], but are themselves the causes of the diversity of the world; such is the meaning of the first verse, which is to be accepted by the wise.
The refutation of God is complete.
In the section on the Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravādādhikāra*), the first section of the commentary on the *Vārttikasaptaślokī*:
He who proclaimed that the world, which possesses a diversity produced by karma, is without a Lord (*anīśa*).
I pay homage with full measure to him whose teaching is unimpeded.

Having established the refutation of eternal validity, the skillful author, demonstrating that invalidity resides in the impermanent state, says: "This path removes the portion of delusion regarding that very aspect."

Even if one has personally refuted the criticisms of others, if there is no satisfaction in merely mentioning the name of the Vārttikakāra when they are irrelevant, then it is better that one's prowess be directed toward the further description of those very [criticisms].

Whatever is an effect is preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimatpūrvaka*), just like a jar; and the earth, mountains, and so forth are effects. Alternatively, whatever is not preceded by an intelligent agent is not an effect, just like space; and trees, mountains, oceans, and so forth are effects. Thus, by implication, this is the reason based on the nature of being an effect (*kāryahetu*). In the same way, [the reasons] such as having non-conscious material causes (*acetanopādānatva*), performing purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), possessing a specific arrangement of constituent parts that initiate themselves (*svārambhakāvayavasanniveśaviśeṣavattva*), performing actions after having remained stationary (*sthitvā sthitvā kāryakarmāṇi*), and having the property of activity (*pravṛttidharmakatva*) should be employed. So how can it be said [that they are not valid]?
"Is it not the case that [the reason] is also non-authoritative regarding the impermanent?

And this proof is indeed common to both the permanent and the impermanent. However, when the discussion turns toward impermanence, the opponent would proceed to seek a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is merely for the purpose of introducing that [proof] that there is a restatement using the word 'impermanent. We do not, however, maintain that the Blessed One is impermanent. For instance: He is one, all-pervading, omniscient, the locus of a single consciousness, eternal, and is called the Lord (*īśvara*)."
The Creator of the world is accepted as the authoritative source; he is to be petitioned by those who seek heaven and liberation.

To this it is replied: Is the desire to establish the excellence of the Supreme Person—who is the abode of the multitude of qualities taught—accomplished by these very reasons alone, or by the force of other reasons? Regarding this, the first position is not tenable. For, a means of proof establishes only that extent of an object's nature which it pervades, and no further object. Indeed, the capacity of a means of valid cognition does not extend over as much of an object as one might wish for.

Rather, to whatever extent the capacity of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) extends, the establishment of its object occurs by means of that [capacity]. And even though being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth is pervaded by having been preceded by a conscious agent, it is not capable of producing a cognition restricted to [the agent's] oneness and other such qualities; for no pervasion is perceived with respect to those specific attributes, otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of determining even the opposite nature [of the object]. Indeed, having perceived smoke pervaded by fire in general, no one is able to infer a fire possessing a flickering mass of five-colored crests.

[Objection: Even so, one indeed infers the qualification by place and time through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); likewise, for one who has perceived that being an effect in the case of a mountain and so forth depends upon the superintendence of an intelligent agent, the desired conclusion will be established by the logic of a *siddhānta* based on the locus. [Reply: No, because the capacity [of the evidence] is untenable.

For just as in the inference from smoke and so forth, there is the capacity [of the argument] that what is produced by fire at a certain place and time does not possess that same place and time, we do not perceive such a necessity—that the placement of trees in a forest would be impossible—without [assuming] a conscious agent endowed with unity, omniscience, and so forth. Therefore, even if the capacity to produce those [trees] were established for a potter or similar agent through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), this would not suffice to establish the specific qualities [such as omniscience] that we intend to prove.

Now, if a perfected being (*siddha*) capable of creating mountains and such things is established, what else remains to be sought? Why then is there satisfaction with a mere expressive word whose expressed form is as yet unestablished? For in this way, the intended subject under discussion is not proven. Indeed, the operation of production is nothing more than the state of necessarily preceding that which is about to arise; and that [operation] is common to insentient things and is not established as being restricted by specific qualities such as intelligence or omnipresence. Therefore, with respect to the intended probandum, nothing is achieved by the establishment of a mere statement.

Who, moreover, asserts that mountains and so forth are preceded by an omniscient being? Rather, suspecting that they are caused by an intelligent agent, [the author] says, while inwardly mocking [the opponent], by means of a proof:
"In the case of [the arguments for] acting after having remained stationary, specific structures, purposeful activity, and so forth, what is desired is already established" (PV II 10ab’c).

Thus [it is said]: for the entire aggregate of things is held to be produced by both common and uncommon karma. Since karma is insentient by nature, the fact that oceans, mountains, and so forth—which are the causes of all-knowingness—fail to be established does not bring about anything undesirable for us; this is the sense. Furthermore, if one intends to prove [omniscience] as being achievable by those [elements] alone, there is no contradiction [with our position], and thus the presentation of the proof would result in futility. Therefore, what is to be proven by this [argument] must be qualified; and it has already been stated that the probans lacks the capacity to establish that [qualified object].

"Let it be, then, that such establishment occurs through another means of proof. Anticipating this second position, he states "or there is non-establishment," thereby pointing out the absence of certainty.

The meaning is that there exists neither another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor another logical reason (*hetu*) from which this certainty could arise. Alternatively, since direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) is impossible due to [the object's] being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), inference (*anumāna*) must be invoked; and for that purpose, he speaks with reference to every possible reason.
[267] Or, there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*).

For, although by means of the aforementioned inference a conscious being who is the creator of all things is established in common with the opponent, there is no specific property (*viśeṣadharma*) that could serve as a reason (*hetu*) without being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*), other than mere existence (*sattā*). This is because there is no occasion for an inference regarding a property that exceeds mere existence. However, since existence itself implies momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), he says "or non-establishment" with respect to the expectation of permanence and unity.

The meaning is that there is a "contradictory proof" (*viparītasiddhi*). For, just as in the case of *adharma* and so forth, even in the case of the eternal [the self], the refutation is intended to be like the opponent's own proof by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); the mention of "non-eternal" serves merely as an introductory pretext. Furthermore, he states that there is "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the nature of pervasion (*vyāptitva*), or else there is "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). What is meant is this: because pervasion does not exist in an ultimate sense, and because there is no observation of it in the example, the pervasion of any property (*dharma*) by it cannot be established. Even if all cognition exists, there is no perception of its being a pervader. Why? He says:

"Or else there is doubt regarding the example," because it is impossible for one of limited vision to ascertain [the subject] in its specific nature as a real entity. Therefore, for that whose qualities have been proclaimed, there is no establishment—either directly from the aforementioned proofs, nor by the logic of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*, nor from another proof. Thus, the absence of a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. However, since the desired [subject] is established even in the absence of its specific [qualifications], [the argument fails].

Alternatively, when reasons such as "being an effect" have been set forth, there may be a conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) regarding the relationship between the general property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) and its specific instance, such that one asks whether there is proof or non-proof. In that regard, since the proponent's position is already established by the fact that [the world] is well-known to be an object of action (*karmavāditā*), proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is evident. Thus, demonstrating the lack of concomitance (*anugamābhāva*) with respect to the specific instance—which is the basis for the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*)—he says:
"Or else, there is non-establishment in the example, or else doubt."

Thus, "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*) is the subject under discussion. In that regard, since the potter and others—who possess qualities contrary to omnipresence and so forth—are established without dispute, there is a lack of proof for the intended [probandum] in the example. Now, if the view is that the attributes of omnipresence and so forth belong to that portion [of the self] distinct from the body, which is by nature difficult to distinguish, even then let there be doubt; what is the point of such persistence here? This is the sense. As for the phrase "establishing what is already established in the general case" (*sāmānye siddhasādhyatā*):

Therefore, because the instance lacks the property to be proven (sādhya) or because it possesses a doubtful property to be proven, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" and so forth with the property to be proven in the instance; thus, since the specific feature (*viśeṣa*) remains unestablished, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Now, even when smoke follows [the fire], there is an absence of following in the particular (*viśeṣa*), while in the general (*sāmānya*), it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Thus the logic is the same: therefore, for these two, is their validity restricted or otherwise? If it is restricted, that is not a sound consideration. For it is established that inference does not attain its status as valid cognition without establishing a specific [object].

But that distinction—characterized as the mere exclusion of what is unfit to be the subject (*pakṣāyogyavyavacchedamātra*)—is possible as something distinct from that [subject], as for example in "there is fire here because of smoke," or is it of such a nature? In that regard, if the first [type of distinction] were denied, there would be a repudiation of inference itself, because the establishment of anything distinct is rooted in that [inference]. Nor can that [first type of distinction] be refuted without following upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

For a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) that is established as being necessarily connected [with the probandum] would, if it did not demonstrate the subject as inseparable from that [probandum], be separated from its own essential existence; this is so unless one goes beyond the requirement of time and so forth by virtue of the context of the reason to be proven. As for the second type of establishment, however, since it has only that [subject] as its object of proof, even though it does not occur without the apprehension of the specific quality produced by that [connection], it is not capable of invalidating inference; for its purpose is fulfilled even by the establishment of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) through a property devoid of those specific qualities.

However, there would be a denial of a specific type of inference (*anumānaviśeṣāpalāpa*). For instance, suppose someone intends to infer a peacock with five-colored crests by means of the proof "there is fire here because of smoke," and is challenged by another on the grounds of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and lack of concomitance (*ananugama*). If that person were then to say, "In that case, since smoke itself would be sublated, there could be no inference at all here," he might indeed appear brilliant [in his logic]. But it does not follow that inference as such is sublated, because at that very moment he is establishing the inference of the generality of fire (*dahanasāmānya*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the refutation is based solely on the distinction of excluding the non-connection with the subject (*pakṣāyogavyavaccheda*).
The refutation applies to those [entities] other than the desired goal, its accomplishment, and their connection.

These two [fallacies] are not restricted to being either defects or non-defects; rather, it is held that their status as one or the other depends on the difference in the subject matter (*viṣaya*). Similarly here, even while accepting the exclusion of the impossibility of an intelligent controller (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhāna*) in cases such as the ocean or mountains, those who raise these two [fallacies] with respect to some other intended specific detail are directly liable to the consequence of destroying the inference of the "variegated beauty" (*citrakāntiśikhā*), but not the destruction of inference in general.
Therefore, validity or invalidity is not restricted to a single case in relation to a specific type of inference, but rather it is appropriate to speak of them in a general sense.

[269] But surely, even now, a particular difference is established without depending on a commonality; so what is the obstacle to another difference? Indeed, there is no establishment whatsoever that is devoid of a commonality. For a commonality, in its very continuity, is incapable of remaining without drawing forth that particularity. Nor can it be claimed that it necessarily possesses this power with respect to other particulars as well, for as was described previously, otherwise the inference of the "five-colored crest" (*pañcavarṇaśikha*) and so forth would be unavoidable.

In this regard, the objection regarding impossibility and so forth applies equally even to a person possessing a single-mindedness (*ekacittatva*) and other such qualities. An inference of that kind arises there as well in the same manner. Therefore, one who wishes to assert a specific distinction must necessarily demonstrate a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); since that is absent, the reason is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, it is established that if one were to prove merely the existence of an intelligent agent (*buddhimat-mātra*), it would result in proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*).

It might be argued as follows: "Intelligent" does not mean merely possessing consciousness, but rather it is intended to mean one who knows the material cause and so forth, or one who possesses effort; and since a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with such a being is established in the case of effects like jars and the like, the fact that "being an effect" is perceived in the mountain and other such things also presents [as the cause] a maker of precisely that kind. Thus, neither of the two faults [previously mentioned] applies.

If it is argued that he is omniscient precisely because he knows their material causes and so forth, and because he is restricted by place and time—such that if there were no distinction [between his knowledge and theirs], he would not be capable of producing the collection of effects being produced—and thus properties such as eternity and omnipresence are also established for him; then this is like the hope for the enjoyment of fruit from a tree whose roots have been severed.

For if their oneness were established, then this perfection of these qualities would be established; otherwise, when it is possible for an effect existing in different places and times to be produced by many [causes], to whom would such powers as sovereignty belong? And since they perceive only the objects of their own respective functions, who could possess omniscience?

If unity were established, the entire probandum would be entailed; yet there is no basis for its ascertainment. Nor is the one capable of creating the earth and so forth established merely by the occurrence of the singular number, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). For if such a connection were established, how could an opponent who had realized that unity overlook it? However, this might occur in reference to a genus (*jāti*), as in the case of fire cognized through various successive instances of smoke; thus, there is no insistence [on a specific individual].

Nor can the oneness of a single creator be established on the basis of the persistence of specific qualities across diverse effects—just as the oneness of a single artist is established in a variegated painting due to the persistence of similar lines and so forth—because no such persisting entity is actually perceived. Furthermore, observed properties such as "being an effect" or "being an entity" cannot prove oneness, for they are just like the case of the painting itself [which does not prove a single creator].

For even when other qualities are possible, there remains doubt as to whether the agent is one or similar; how much more so, then, can there be certainty of oneness in their absence? This is certainly like painting a picture on a non-existent wall, that upon the lack of certainty regarding non-difference, omniscience and such qualities are determined.

The other, however, says: "Unity too must be understood precisely through the production of an effect. How so? Because if many individuals with conflicting minds were independent, there would be a lack of mutual coordination; due to their mutual opposition and their failure to understand each other's intentions, there would be a non-production of the effect simultaneously, or there would be the consequence of the destruction of what has already been produced."

[270] Here it is considered by many: regarding the principle that "there is no simultaneous production of effects," the intended meaning is the non-production of effects that are distinct in time and distinct in space; or else, the position is that it refers to the non-production of effects of a single great composite whole, such as a mountain and so forth. In this regard, we do not perceive any contradiction to production when multiple causes act upon a single locus. For just as there is activity on the part of one, so too may there be for others, as in the case of an anthill.

If it is asked, "With what purpose in mind do they act?", the answer is no; for because the activities of minds are diverse, it is impossible to determine the specific cause of their engagement. Otherwise, one would not be able to resolve the persistent inquiry as to what even the Lord himself has in mind. Or rather, such a determination might be possible for others who are adept at discerning the sublation of intended meanings and so forth, but not for the Lord, whose nature is gentle.

Nor can a rule of mutual coordination among many [agents] be established, since we observe ants (*valmīkaukas*) undertaking a single task. If it is argued that such coordination is possible among humans due to their competitive impulse (*ahamahamikā*), then even those who possess discernment (*sadvivekin*) may undertake a single task; and since it is possible for one massive object to be produced sequentially by many others of that same kind, why do we insist on restricting it to humans alone? Furthermore, no one has ever seen the simultaneous production of objects such as the Yugandhara mountains.

This is merely a possibility, since the capacity for such a thing is conceivable only for some single [agent]; nor can a rule of mutual exclusion among persons be established through a competitive struggle (*ahamahamikā*), because it is impossible for a person to possess two mutually contradictory [capacities] without their being in conflict with one another. Therefore, this deserves to be presented as a mere hypothesis, not as a path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); or rather, it is merely a recollection of a conventional tenet that "one [effect], such as Mount Maināka, is not produced by many [causes]."

If it is argued that even in a single undertaking there must be one predominant and powerful agent—like a master builder or a general—and therefore agency belongs to him alone because others merely follow his lead, we say no; for even in those cases there is no such rule, as we observe that some independent individuals, acting according to their own respective purposes, may together construct a single bridge or similar work.

Even in that case, there is no such thing as a single primary instigator, because there is no one to prevent the simultaneous surge of desire in many people, and because even a non-primary person can be an instigator. Merely by that much, one cannot claim primacy, for that would contradict common experience. Furthermore, when an immense undertaking is possible through numerous groups—each consisting of countless individuals acting as architects—what kind of failure could possibly occur? By this, the argument regarding the ants in the anthill is refuted.

Moreover, just as a specific arrangement of parts for comfortable furnishings is perceived in a palace being constructed by many people following a single mind, such a thing is not found even in the great mountain ranges, which are composed of masses of irregular, massive rocks; whereby it would follow that these too must have been preceded by a single primary person.

Therefore, since the operation of many [agents] cannot be subverted in the case of the construction of each individual Kailāsa and so forth, how can it be subverted in the case of entities located in various distant places and times?

If it is argued that the identity [of the person] is established through scripture (*āgama*), then this procedure for binding a protective amulet with mustard seeds against one afflicted by a planetary conjunction is indeed not a refutation for Buddhists whose minds are solely adept at investigating scripture.

For if there is an adherence to the scriptures of investigation (*parīkṣā-āgama*), then since this is precisely the time for investigation, why should one comply with them now? On the other hand, if it is independent of investigation, then let all desired objects be established from that [scripture] alone; what is the point of this addiction to adducing inference, which consists essentially of mere exertion? For the endeavor to purify logical reasons (*hetu*) is arduous for those whose intellects are devoid of subtle penetration, whereas the attainment of one's desired goal is easy through the study of a single portion of a scripture.

Furthermore, even this very proponent, while establishing the authority of the scriptures, recites the following five-membered syllogism: "The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are not unauthoritative, because they are the means for producing concordant knowledge for all those in the [four] stages of life (*āśrama*), just like perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for if they were unauthoritative, there could be no such thing as 'concordance' among all those in the stages of life, since, given their lack of authority, a lack of concordance might also be possible through someone's realization of their invalidity; and the rule of concordance is established only in the case of authoritative means of knowledge, such as perception. Thus he argues.

That too is applicable only within the assembly of disciples; for indeed, what is called "corroboration" must be either consistency with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), and neither of these two applies here, as in [the Vedic passages]:
"The Person has a thousand heads" (*Ṛgveda* X.10.1) and "He knows all this, yet there is no knower of him" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.19).

In the sense of such statements as "The one God, generating heaven and earth, has pervaded them" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3), or regarding the Agniṣṭoma and other rites that are means for attaining heaven, such a conviction may arise in someone; for just as one member of a religious order possesses the thought that "there exists a single, all-pervading, eternal Creator of the world," so too does another.

If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] consists in the performance corresponding to that [scripture], then this cognition of theirs must either originate from that very scripture, or originate from something else of a similar nature, or consist merely of accidental conceptual construction; it cannot, however, take the form of perception or inference, for that would entail the possibility of such cognition even for those who do not belong to an *āśrama*, since perception and the like are not subject to error by other persons. Furthermore, knowledge based on scripture would not exist for one who has neither heard nor respected it; rather, it is logical that it occurs only for another person through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from practice in a previous life.

In this regard, this [scripture] is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it arises from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) that is possible whether an object exists or does not exist. Thus, its connection with another means of valid cognition is said to be due to its originating from such [an independent source]; however, since that [source] itself lacks validity, the logical principle applies that "that which is established by what is unestablished is itself unestablished. Therefore:

[272] This is merely a recollection of such a convention, namely that "there exists someone who is like this. Furthermore, we understand that even the term "ascetic" (*āśrama*) is a mere designation; consequently, the qualification "of all ascetics" (*samastāśramiṇām*) is unestablished, because agreement with Buddhists, Digambaras, and others is not established. Moreover, since partial agreement exists even among those with contrary views, its presentation is not fruitful. For this very reason, the absolute cessation of disagreement—which would allow for the establishment of validity—is unproven.

As for the claim that this might be possible even for those in the [four] stages of life (*āśramin*) due to the power of a common delusion persisting from beginningless time, that is trivial. Therefore, even regarding a single object such as Mount Mandara, among those who possess effort and who know the portion of the material cause and so forth that is the object of the activity of countless persons, which one of them could be "all-knowing"? Furthermore, if such things were produced by individuals existing in different places and times, how could [the creator] possess attributes such as eternity and omnipresence? Nor is there any room for the knowledge of the unseen portion [of the material cause], since we observe that even a potter produces the object of his own activity without such knowledge.

Furthermore, since there is no logical connection between the fact that something has been produced by many and the inevitable consequence of its destruction, it follows that once their unity is lost, the subsequent disappearance of omniscience and other such qualities is unavoidable; thus, this [objection] which was stated is likewise entirely groundless.

Since they would be many and omniscient, and because they would possess the capacity to act as creators of all things, there would be no evidence for their simultaneous engagement in effects restricted by specific place and time; thus, the coexistence of omniscience and creative action in a single substratum is not established. For this very reason, the consequence that the rejection of a single [creator] entails the abandonment of many more is not a refutation. For if it were established that there are many who are both omniscient and all-creators, then the rejection of a single one would be useless, and one would instead be accepting a far greater exertion.

But when a multitude of beings, like the creatures in an anthill, are brought together such that each one is a producer of a single result, and they do not touch upon the qualities under discussion, then what loss is there? For in that case, those very beings would not be the ones sought after by those desiring heaven and liberation.

By this, the view of one who thinks that God must also be manifold—just like your own omniscient being—is also rendered untenable, because not even a single substratum for all actions has been established. For us, however, the establishment of all-knowingness does not arise from all actions, but rather from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).

And since that [omniscience] follows from a presumptive inference (*sambhavānumāna*)—because the conceptualization of all forms that are to be directly realized is possible—the establishment of such omniscience would apply to one person just as it would to another; or rather, it is accepted [as existing], so there is no fault.

If it is argued that, by means of practice alone, the creation of all things will likewise occur, we say no, because it is impossible. For instance, the generation of stationary beings or the transformation into a moving being is not the fruit of practice. Even in the case of imagining the construction of other remaining replicas, one might think, "It could be like this," but there is no certainty that "this very thing which is currently perceived, such as a forest and so forth, shall be so and not otherwise. This is because an inference based on possibility cannot function with respect to a specific objective.
Furthermore, even in that case, [the success] would be dependent on others and subject to the excellence of obtaining rare external implements.

[273] It is not the case that the cultivation of that [power] is as easy as the transformation of mind-only (*cittamātra-parāvṛtti*); such is the conviction. If it is argued that when one depends upon the assistance of an excellence of power (*prabhāvātiśaya*), what is the use of craftsmanship (*śilpa*)? That it has no capacity without it is unproven; for if you say this is because it is seen to be so elsewhere, we say no, because the creation of a body while still in the womb and so forth occurs according to a visible sequence. Therefore, there must necessarily be something other than power. Furthermore, there is no certainty regarding any specific path for the attainment of such power.

Or, let it be granted that there is the accomplishment of the art of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and that "practice" is included by the word "etc. (*ādi*); nevertheless, he says: regarding the reasons such as "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*), there is either the proof or the non-proof of the desired [property], namely, the absence of an agent (*akartṛtva*). It is indeed a non-proof, because it lacks utility.

For there is no utility whatsoever for hell and the like for one who practices with conscious awareness; even in the creation of mere instruments of pleasure, there is no purpose. Since one's own highest good (*svaśreyasa*) can be attained through effort, those [instruments] would otherwise be superfluous, or else the elements themselves would provide happiness. At most, for those ignorant of that path, the instruction of it alone constitutes a favor; therefore, for that purpose, the practice of directly realizing the path is superior. Thus, due to futility and lack of resolve, there is no such practice.

If that is so, one might ask: even if there is practice of knowledge with respect to every atom, how is it that there is no impairment, as in the case of performing all actions? To this he says: "In the case of the omniscient of all things, there is doubt regarding the example.

This is because the position of the "omniscient of what is useful" (*upayukta-sarvajña*) will be primarily discussed later. Alternatively, the meaning is that in that case there is doubt regarding futility and lack of determination, but not a certainty of non-existence. Furthermore, since "mention" (*uddeśa*) is defined elsewhere as pointing something out, there is no equality with the opponent's view. Therefore, even if those possessing effort are established by the aforementioned reasons, there is no impairment [to our position].

If it is argued: "Is it not indeed undesirable for you that mountains such as Gandhamādana were produced by a multitude of living beings possessed of effort? Therefore, since no other alternative exists, an intelligent agent who is excluded from multiple instances [of non-intelligent causes] must be established as the sole creator of all effects; and thus, being established, he also revives qualities such as omniscience"? This is not so, because a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the desire [to create] and the actual object is impossible; therefore, the exclusion from multiple instances caused by that desire cannot serve as a valid proof.
And if he should somehow not accept it, then the opponent must be propitiated by means of prostrating at his feet, remaining out of sight, and so forth, in order to make him accept it;
however, this is not a sound principle, for even a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is not applicable against one who is independent.
For when its unity is forcibly removed, its multiplicity is certainly not desired.
"Because its operation culminates in the opposite [of what is intended].

Now, even in both cases, it is certainly undesirable for the opponent; for the entire world of sentient beings is not held to be a cause by way of effort, but rather solely through the sovereignty of karma characterized by consciousness. Therefore, [the world] is invariably concomitant with effort.

[274] If it is argued that the property of being an effect—whether singular or manifold—is a means of proof that places an agent possessing effort in close proximity, yet this results only in what is undesired [by the proponent], then is this proof now presented merely to establish something undesired by the opponent, or rather to establish one's own thesis? In that case, whether the opponent’s desired point is established or not, there is no fruit whatsoever in presenting such a proof. Thus, he says:
"In the cases of persistence, non-activity, and so forth, there is either the establishment of what is desired or its non-establishment."

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that this [objection] is identical for both [parties], based on the statement of a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*) being purposeless (*anarthakya*). Nor is the proponent of the proof (*sādhanavādī*) alone [at fault], because it would not be fitting for him alone to have an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭa*) imposed upon him in two ways. For even though an undesired consequence has arisen in this context, he has begun to establish the very reality of the universe’s being eternally and unitarily omniscient, rather than just anything at all. If that is so, then even when the proof is presented, one must state what the basis for its lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) is.
As for what was further stated—that there is a lack of concomitance (*anugama*) with respect to a particular—[that too is addressed].

Thus, although there may be non-establishment (*asiddhi*) or doubt (*saṃśaya*) regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) due to [the opponent's denial of] the creator being omnipresent and omniscient, as the case may be, let these faults not arise by virtue of [the creator] being one. For when a single creator possessing unitary effort is established, the entire probandum is established. And since it is observed that a single potter is the maker of many jars, pots, and so forth, [the author], anticipating this objection, states the following while establishing the positive concomitance even in the case of unity, with respect to the example: [In the example...]

Thus [it is said]. The term "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) carries over. This is the intended meaning: it is not the case that because one particular effect, such as a jar or a pot, was produced by a single agent, all effects must likewise be so; for in those cases, the activity of multiple potters and others is clearly perceived. Therefore, how can there be a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with a single effortful agent regarding effects that are observed [to be otherwise]? Alternatively, what is this so-called "potter"? Is he some single entity consisting of a collection of the elements and their derivatives (*bhūta-bhautika*)—the object of the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) "potter"—or is he merely a collection of hands, feet, and so forth?
The meaning is: in reality, by which single instrument is the production of things such as a jar brought within the range of perception?

Now, what is the point of this insistence? Whatever kind of single agent is observed to be the object of worldly transaction, if such a single agent—possessing a composite nature—is established as the creator of everything, being cognizant of the material cause and so forth, he is established as omniscient.

Therefore, even if other qualities are set aside, its status as something to be accepted is established by that much alone, and its capacity to bring about both human goals (puruṣārtha) is logically consistent; thus, there is no flaw whatsoever. With this in mind—intending to show that even under this position, all these reasons such as "being an effect" (kāryatva) are fallacious—he states [the following], clearly indicating their inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).

[275] Thus; the word "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. For, although there is the state of being an effect due to being a mere aggregate—just like a potter—and the presence of such features as its specific arrangement (*saṃniveśa*), there is nonetheless an absence of being preceded by an agent possessing effort; or else, even in the absence of that [effortful agent], it [the state of being an effect] may still exist. Furthermore, if one were to desire another cause for that [agent], there would be an infinite regress, and thus no comprehension [of the ultimate cause].

But surely, that which is insentient by nature requires an effortful agent for its own production and for producing another; yet, since he himself is the substratum of such an intellect, what need is there for another? For there is no rule that because insentient objects like jars require illumination, another illuminator must in turn be required by that illumination. Therefore, what is this infinite regress?

If that is the case, then how could the collection [of factors] consisting of the intellect, the sense organs, and so forth—which possesses effort and is designated as a "potter"—require anything else? Therefore, one must admit that whether conscious or unconscious, a collection arises or produces by its own nature while depending on another consciousness; thus, there is indeed an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Alternatively, if the group of conscious entities is held to be independent of any other consciousness, then the properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing in things like pots would be established as invariably concomitant with an opposite—that is, with a controller who is not the desired agent—and they would consequently fail to maintain their status without succumbing to the refutation based on contradiction.

If, however, such a basis [of operation] were accepted, then even though there is non-perception due to the remoteness of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*), there remains the possibility of its activity; consequently, these [reasons] would not be invariably concomitant with the observation of the opposite. Thus, because of the absence of negative pervasion (*viparyaya-vyāpti*), there would be an absence of the contradictory convention. Even then, if someone skilled in considering the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for the sake of establishing the relation of cause and effect does not take up the objection, thinking, "This has not yet been commenced," then let it rest for now.

So what is the use of this persistence? For if one persists, there is the risk of introducing gross defects that contradict perception; furthermore, even if [the reason] were unestablished (*asiddhi*), the opposite would be proven. Thus, either disregarding him with a "blind-folded" air like an elephant full of internal pride, or—just as he has accepted God as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the production of all effects—one might entertain this [view] and, fearing an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if a conscious being were to depend on another conscious being, and relying instead on that very [God] because of His non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), state a doubt.

Now, if a potter, despite possessing effort, does not [act] upon his own body but rather upon the jar and so forth, why then would he not depend on something else for the sake of accomplishing his own body? In that case, why would even the one intended as God—who possesses effort directed toward the subject at hand—not depend on something else, since there is a contradiction in agency within oneself? Yet he does not depend on anything else. Therefore, the principle that "whatever produces an effect, such as a product, must be presided over by one possessing effort" is contradicted by that very [instance]; thus, doubt is established.

But surely, since he has no body at all, how can this [argument] be inconclusive? This is merely the result of forgetting the context. For, with the intent of demonstrating positive concomitance (*anvaya*), you yourself have accepted that the world is produced by a single person who is conventionally (*saṃvṛta*) one—just as you accepted the conventional oneness in the case of a potter; this is our point. However, if it were indeed real...

If oneness is maintained as being incompatible with coexistence in the body, then one must not introduce a conventional oneness as a pervading property in the example for the effect and so forth. Nor is it fruitful to hope for the establishment of such a state in reality based on that [oneness], which is merely a matter of names; for indeed, no one infers a real fire upon perceiving an effect such as a specific utterance associated with a boy to whom the term "fire" is metaphorically applied.

If it is argued that there is a single, unerring cognition of a person as a composite whole (*avayavin*), who here explicitly asserts that this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*)? It is said that the application of a term to what is not its actual referent is common to both [positions]. Since the existence of a composite whole is sublated by the fact of being a body, one must conclude that the determination of it as a single entity is an error. Furthermore, even if such a whole were to exist, whether it be the composite of the body and its parts—such as the hands and so forth—or the collection beginning with the elements (*bhūta*), it is established that the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) is not ultimately real; for it is merely this entire complex that is denoted by the word "one."

It might be argued: "In that case, it is the *puruṣa* alone who is the presiding agent or the creator, and he, being distinct from the body and other such factors, is one and only one. [To this we reply: Even when the production of an effect is brought about by a collection of visible causes, another invisible factor (*adṛṣṭa*) is postulated; yet even there, having set aside what is visible, that very same thing is [further] imagined. And that is not one, for it is manifold and limitless—this is a diverse and boundless delusion.

First of all, it has been stated that the very existence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is difficult to ascertain through inference here due to innate discrepancies. Furthermore, its status as a cause is to be established by perception accompanied by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible. And that [status] belongs to that [unseen force] alone by way of the exclusion of what is seen; otherwise, if activity were possible even for hands, feet, and so forth, then those too would entail the necessity of inference, and thus the same fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) would recur. Otherwise, the inference of a person (puruṣa) [as the creator] would likewise be without foundation.

By this, the conceptualization of the continuum of consciousness (*caitanyasantāna*) as a single person (*puruṣa*) is refuted; for even this [continuum] is perceived as possessing power only when conjoined with hands, feet, and so forth. Consequently, from the effect, there would necessarily follow an inference of its reality exactly as it is, just as from smoke one infers fire together with fuel.

If it is argued that pervasion is apprehended by pure consciousness alone and not by anything else, we say no; for, by the same logic, it would be impossible to effect a distinction [between them]. Therefore, this [consciousness] must be stated as the cause of the intellect and body precisely by excluding any other connection (*anyayogavyavacchedena*), since only in that way could one be able to infer it through a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and grasp the pervasion based on ultimate identity.

And this being the case, to abandon the collection of causal factors—the observed concomitance of presence and absence—and instead postulate some other cause altogether is another object of contempt. Furthermore, if that too were somehow manifold, all effort would be fruitless; thus, it must be postulated as a single entity. We perceive this entire endeavor to be like the clamor of bees attracted by the fragrance of a lotus in the sky.

Therefore, enough with this introduction of [an agent] distinct from the body and so forth. Consequently, the pervasion by the oneness of an effortful agent is not primary, because oneness in reality is untenable for potters and the like, who are denoted as agents. Furthermore, since such a [pervasion] would result in an inference based on a conventional (sāṃvṛta) locus, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) of the property of being an effect and so forth by that very [conventional agent]; thus it was stated that there is doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya).

But even so, if such a probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, by what means could there be deviation (*vyabhicāra*); and if it is established, what would deviation accomplish? If you argue that "because of deviation, it is simply unestablished," then, since deviation does not exist when [the subject] is established, on what basis is it determined whether there is non-establishment or establishment? Nor is there any objection to the fact that for a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*) such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), the locus (*dharmin*) must be a real entity itself; rather, this is stated in order to demonstrate, through this sequence, the contradiction with one's own accepted tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*).

Because it has been initiated in reality, this [reason] exists through the three-fold nature of the means for proving the probandum (*sādhya*), and through the probandum as intended by the three-fold means of proof. In that case, since there is an absence of exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) when the probandum is present, it is said to be a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason because it is established by one's own admission rather than being established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that context, the admission is a factor of the effect.

Because of this statement: it is indeed logical that the opponent’s own admission is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since [the argument] proceeds precisely for the purpose of subverting it. For this very reason, it does not serve as a basis (*āśraya*) for an independent reason (*svatantra-hetu*). Furthermore, the result of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is its contrapositive (*viparyaya*). However, if one’s own admission were not a valid means of knowledge, there would be no utterance of words at all; for speech is the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself, and it constitutes inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).

And since this [statement] does not effect the illumination of the three aspects as perceived by oneself in such a manner, it is appropriate that for the proponent of that [position], the statement of a non-essential member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). However, it remains established that for the opponent, it is merely the pointing out of a fault. Alternatively, having raised the objection that the instrument is presented by one [of the two] solely for the sake of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he says:
"Or else, there is doubt regarding the example" (PV II 12).

Thus [it is said]. First of all, there is simply a lack of proof regarding the instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of a single example. Or, even if it were proven, there would still be doubt as to what it is for the sake of which the example is adduced—namely, for the sake of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases. For it is not the case that the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is perceived for just any object merely because it has been seen in an example; for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Rather, it is through the establishment of an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) [that such a relationship is known].

And since there is no basis whatsoever for this [inference], agency and the like—even if established in the subject of the thesis—do not entail a self restricted to oneness, because there is an absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.

[278] Furthermore, although properties such as being an effect (*kāryatva*) are necessarily concomitant with an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat-kartṛ*), they are nonetheless reasons for doubt when proving a single creator, because their exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is uncertain. Thus, Śaṅkara himself stated: "There is no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) of the property of having a non-conscious material cause (*acetanopādānatva*) with respect to a single creator," and so forth. As for his further claim that "there is no deviation of the property of having a non-conscious material cause by the mere fact of being presided over by one possessing effort," this alone is of no use in the present context.
Because it was previously established that [the probandum] is dependent upon the establishment of the property that serves as the basis of the dispute.
|| First Section ||
Second Section [279]:

Having thus stated the refutation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to a specific probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*), he speaks, while considering how to state it even with respect to "mere effort" (*prayatnavanmātra*): "In the case of [the reasons] such as 'acting after having remained stationary,' 'specific configuration' (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), and 'purposeful action' (*arthakriyā*)."

"Either the desired [conclusion] is established, or it is unestablished; or else there is doubt regarding the example (dṛṣṭānta). (PV 2.10) The meaning of "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*)—derived from *dṛṣṭa* (seen) and *anta* (end)—is "that which is seen to the end," i.e., a settled conclusion (*siddhānta*). This is because pervasion is established by mere effortful action alone, and because a real entity cannot transcend the nature of being either one or many. When [reasons] such as "acting after having remained stationary" are put forward, the question is: regarding the thesis, does the proponent’s desired [conclusion] become established in the case of unity? Or is there merely non-establishment in the case of multiplicity? Or is there even no pervasion at all? Thus, the sense of the question is that there is indeed doubt regarding the settled conclusion in both cases.

And here, immediately following, in the section establishing non-difference, the answer has already been given through the argument that [the reason] has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*). Therefore, only the third position remains. For we do not perceive any subverting argument (*bādhaka*) when the production of an effect is possible even without the application of effort.

How, then, could there be a restriction regarding the effect and so forth in that case? If it is argued that the undesirable consequence of a lack of restriction regarding time, place, and so on serves as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), that is incorrect; for even when there is an absence of a particular state of the cause—which possesses restricted capacity, does not exist at all times, and whose presence depends upon its own causes—the absence of the effect is possible. Thus, it is not tenable to assume that [the effect] is invariably concomitant with effort. Only if there were a total independence from a cause would such a subverting argument be applicable to establish that the effect is pervaded by the cause in general; however, it cannot establish that it is pervaded by a specific cause, namely one characterized by effort.

Is it not the case that what is called a "cause" everywhere is merely an aggregate, and that this aggregate does not exist in a state of disjunction? Furthermore, if the conjunction of those [parts] were to occur without one possessing effort, it would necessarily be eternal. The same should be said regarding location as well.

And if it is argued that this leads to the very same contingency regarding the restriction of place and time—namely, that since the pervading property of being an effect of the *kalāpa* (the causal complex) is absent due to independence from consciousness, properties such as "being an effect" are impossible and are instead pervaded by dependence on an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat*)—then, in that case, if that possessor of effort were also momentary and localized, the entire collection of effects would exist only at that single moment and in that single location; therefore, he must be accepted as eternal and all-pervading.

Consequently, that very same lack of restriction regarding place and time remains applicable even today; what, then, is the point of accepting this [theory]? Or, if it produces [the effect] by depending on the unseen (adṛṣṭa), would it produce it necessarily? But for insentient things, the unseen is not a "seeing eye."

If it is argued: "In that case, even without conscious deliberation (*nirālocā*), the conditions, aided by the maturation of that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-paripāka*), will necessarily produce [the effect]; so what is the use of consciousness?"—for one who speaks thus, it would follow that the potter and others are also useless, for there too the unseen force does not exist as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*). But this is not the case; therefore, the opposite is true: whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) exists, it does not render human effort fruitless by depending on the unseen force, just like the thread, lump of clay, staff, wheel, and so forth. And such is the causal complex here.

[280] This is the perception of a pervasion contrary [to the probandum] regarding the locus consisting of mountains, oceans, and so forth. For the state of being independent of effort—namely, the rendering of effort fruitless—is established in the case of space and the like, and it is that which is to be negated. That which is contrary to this, namely dependence on effort, is pervaded by the state of being a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because such a complex is produced by effort. To this it is replied: If the causal complex were established as the effect of effort through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*), then this would be correct. But it is not so; for even in that case, there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) against the contrary.

For just as an effect—whose presence depends upon its own cause—is conceivable as not occurring at all times because it requires a specific state of that cause, why should the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) not be the same? Why, then, would the consequence of its being eternal be urged against it? Furthermore, if the causal complex were to be restricted to dependence on effort while the suspicion of its occurrence in the opposite case (i.e., eternally) remains unremoved, then what kind of fault has been committed by "being a direct effect" and so forth, such that when those [reasons] are presented, the causal complex is brought forward as a refuge for one who is still in doubt?

If it is argued that clay and other materials are seen to come together only from a person, why is it not said that an effect is also observed to be produced only by one who possesses effort? And just as, even though some effects are seen to arise from one possessing effort, there may still be the suspicion that another effect might exist [produced] by an intelligent being while setting this aside, so too, what purpose does the possibility of a causal complex (sāmagrī) serve? Therefore, this argument is equivalent to what has already been stated.

Therefore, even by inserting the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself into the middle, one must take the very observation of that complex in jars and the like as the proof. This being the case, it is correct to say that the effect itself is established as being invariably concomitant with effort through direct perception and non-perception.

What is the use here of resorting to the forceful presentation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) to establish pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Or rather, if—according to the sequence to be explained later—it were possible for perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) to apprehend only a specific class [of things], then it would not be established that "every effect" is pervaded by an intelligent agent. For that purpose, one resorts to the subversion of the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*). If that is so, then even in the case of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) being an effect of an intelligent agent, those same perceptions and non-perceptions are the refuge; thus, such a collection [of causes] is produced by an intelligent agent, and a universal conclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) is therefore valid. And so:
Arising never occurs from that which is distracted, nor can it come from that which is devoid of consciousness;
if this were so, would not this same fault apply even to an eternally existing entity?
If you say that its dependence on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) accounts for the restriction of time, then what is the use of the mind at that point?
Even in the case of a jar or similar objects, the artisan's effort is not fruitless; nor is this a reversal of that [principle].

If, in the case of a water-jar and so forth, there is pervasion (abhividhi) because of perception, why is there refutation when the order is reversed? Is it not considered that pervasion is established through perception and non-perception? If this were the case, then if their object is indeed a specific genus, such would it be.
If the array were due to consciousness, what certainty would there be in other cases?
Thus are the two summary verses.

Nor is it reasonable to argue that if another causal complex does not have that [prior entity] as its antecedent, then this [complex under discussion] should likewise not have it; for we observe that even all-pervading properties (*dharma*) exist only in certain locations, such as the quality of being scratchable by iron in the case of earth, or as the non-established fact of having a body as a prior cause in the case of an effect. If you say, "In those cases, there is no omnipresence because of subverting evidence," then what can remove the doubt regarding the manifestation of this [entity]?

For just as there is no requirement for dependence on an intelligent agent even in other collections of causes or in the production of other effects, so too for you, there is no proof that such dependence must necessarily exist in every class of things. And just as you observe a dependence on an intelligent agent in some cases, so too the opponent observes the pervasion of a property seen in one instance by a different class of things.

Therefore, for the opponent, the non-observation of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) regarding the case of iron-striking and bodily activity is indeed sufficient to establish doubt; otherwise, it would follow that doubt itself would be without a basis.

Nor is it the case that a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason has been introduced here to be discussed now, such that the non-exhibition of a subverting argument here would constitute a subversion for the respondent; rather, it is precisely the "uncertainty of exclusion from the counter-example" (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatva*) [that is at issue]. And this is established, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established by mere observation in the example, due to the absence of a subsequent cause [for such certainty].

By this, the following argument is also refuted: that because the causes of the earth and so forth are insentient, their activity being necessarily directed implies—like the causes of palaces and such—the establishment of their being presided over by an intelligent agent. For, just as in that case, there is no evidence to prove that the activity of even insentient things, such as time and so forth, which is likewise restricted, is invariably concomitant with an intelligent agent.

Nor does the consequence of the non-cessation of activity present a valid objection, because the possibility of a difference in intrinsic nature produced by the conjunction of successive conditions renders the persistence of a single power in entities remote. Therefore, having introduced doubt regarding the unity of the agent, he says—following the same logical principle—in order to satisfy his opponent by refuting the [probans] through common inconclusiveness (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*), thereby obstructing the [opponent's] intellect:

"In the cases of [the probans] such as 'acting after having remained stationary,' 'specific configuration,' and 'purposeful action,' etc., there is either the proof of what is already accepted or a lack of proof in the example" (PV 2.10abc).

Thus [ends the quote]. The word *vā* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). When these [conditions] are present, the establishment (*siddhi*) or non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the desired consciousness occurs respectively in a subject (*dharmin*) possessing the probans (*sādhana*)—such as a jar—as a positive example, and in a tree or the like, as a negative example. Therefore, the meaning is that these [reasons] clearly exhibit presence in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

By this, the following alternative is also refuted: that if, as in the case of "being produced" (*kṛtaka*) and so forth, it is impossible to state a sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhā*), then—just as with smoke and the like—the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) between effort and effects such as sound will occur through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). For it has been stated that even in the absence of that [effort], the effect arises; thus, there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) itself.

But surely, how is it to be understood that "intelligence"—a property common to things other than visible and invisible bodies—is not operative in the production of trees and the like, given that the absence of something is not established by mere non-perception? This is correct, provided that pervasion were intended with respect to intelligence in general, stripped of the limiting condition (upādhi) of a visible body. If you say, "Certainly so," then, in that case, he speaks with reference specifically to negative concomitance (vyatireka), as in the case of smoke, or else there is doubt.

Thus: when the absence of the jar prior to the potter’s activity is to be understood, then the absence [of the jar] caused by the absence of the probandum would not be understood, because of the doubt regarding the absence of the probandum. For it is not with a mind conditioned by such a physical body that the pervasion is sought to be known, whereby a negation could be established through a specific non-perception; rather, it is sought by means of mere effortful agency.

And just as at the time of the birth of a tree or other such things, it is impossible to negate the possibility [of its absence], so it remains even now; thus, even if that [tree] were possible, the absence of a jar that is merely being imagined cannot invalidate its own dependence upon the absence of that [tree]. Therefore, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful.

If it is argued that it is correct to say "the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful when there is doubt regarding the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*)," but that the absence of the jar prior to the potter's activity is not doubted, that too has been answered: the proponent of pervasion (*vyāpti*) must demonstrate that the absence of the probans is necessitated by the absence of the probandum; yet this is not demonstrated here because the absence of the probandum is itself merely suspected.

Alternatively, there is no distinction [between the two cases] because there is doubt regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) even in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*); for in both instances, that [subject] along with its qualification remains doubtful. For this very reason, it is stated that having a subject in which the probandum and the probans are doubtful is a defect of the two examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).

If, however, only the absence of the means (*sādhana*) were stated without regard for the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), then this would be correct; yet even so, there would be no apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Otherwise, having established pervasion through perception and non-perception, when a tremor brought about by a means of proof for the affliction of wind is made common to other types of tremors—such as those resulting from massage and the like—one would be unable to avoid it by excluding the presence of still air, since that cannot be denied on the grounds of its being unsuitable to touch. Thus, one would be left without a defense.

If it is argued that because a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) is being established, there is indeed a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), [we ask]: from what, then, is this specific qualification established by that [reason]?
