If it is argued that the word "destruction" (*upahati*) will have an object corresponding to it—just like the operation of an incorporeal agent—because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is described through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), then that too is the same for you. Just as, when avoiding deviation by treating it as invisible with respect to such mere wind, there is a failure to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) precisely because of its invisibility at the time of grasping the pervasion; so too [is it for you].

For you as well, consciousness exists even when the body is absent; therefore, just as one might falsely imagine that a pervasion is grasped merely by the absence of the effect despite a doubt regarding the absence of that [body], so too, even when there is a doubt regarding the absence of an untouchable wind, the absence of trembling is established, and thus there would be a pervasion.

[283] Now, suppose that no one establishes pervasion (vyāpti) by means of the body-possessor alone, nor even by means of one devoid of a body, but rather by mere consciousness (caitanya) alone; and since that [consciousness] exists even at a time when the body is absent—because a universal must necessarily exist whenever a particular is possible—the apprehension of pervasion, in relation to that [consciousness], remains restricted to the universal alone, just as in the case of fire, because it does not involve the entry of the specific nature of another fire. This same point applies equally to the inference of wind.

Furthermore, no conscious person infers the wind from mere trembling alone; for even when there is a determination that [the wind] is omnipresent, the capacity of the mere trembling to serve as a probans is not perceived. Indeed, the fact that "sovereignty" is desired does not, merely because it is uttered after naming it, validate one who speaks of its means; nor does the probans, "being produced," actually become a member of the proof for establishing impermanence simply by being presented as a pervader.

Therefore, satisfaction should not be found in the mere purity of the internal organ (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*) through the fact that the object of cognition exists as it is; rather, the excellence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaguṇa*) must be investigated. Furthermore, in establishing the pervasion of trembling by air alone, there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary. It must necessarily be accepted that perception and non-perception can include even that which is remote in terms of nature, place, or time—provided it is capable of becoming an object within their own respective domains—but they cannot include anything else.

Otherwise, just as the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is restricted to that [consciousness], deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would also necessarily result as being restricted to it alone. Therefore, just as positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), which have particulars as their objects, are established as having as their sole object consciousness—which is not within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge—why is deviation, which also has particulars as its object, not likewise established as having that alone as its object? For it is not the case that one enters upon gaining something only to exit when it is cut; such a thing is not obtainable.

It is logical that fire, although spatially and temporally remote, is as if present because it is of the same nature [as smoke], attaining entry [into the cognition] through its suitability for perception despite the remoteness of its own nature; for, due to the determination of identity with that [fire], everything being apprehended as the pervader of smoke is not faulty, whereas the gastric fire is not so determined due to its unsuitability for such [perceptual] apprehension. For this very reason, the activity of one who is free from doubt toward the intended fire upon seeing smoke is justified.

Otherwise, even when pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by the perceiver through a [fire] that is not perceptible, the pervasion of smoke would be established as having for its object only the generality of fire—whether perceptible or imperceptible. Consequently, one who is doubtful regarding the specific form, such as whether it is fire from grass (*tārṇa*) or otherwise, would not act with a mind focused solely on obtaining the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by it. Or else, action would occur even when there is a deficiency in the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as if one were considering "it is not abdominal heat" (*jāṭharatva*) while it is absent.
But this is not the case; therefore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not establish pervasion through a generality while being restricted to a specific individual essence (*svarūpa*).

However, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) by "impermanence" (*anityatva*) functions by way of mere coming-into-being and ceasing-to-be, without being delimited by any specific [instance]. Thus, it apprehends it only as a generality (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, no one who proceeds from the fact of being produced can possibly possess a focused cognition directed toward a single intended impermanent instance; therefore, it is established that even a means of valid cognition whose conclusion rests upon a generality does not grasp the pervasion through a particular.

And it has been stated by Śaṅkara, the follower of Nyāya: "Whatever means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) extends its scope to whatever extent of an object," and so forth. Whatever means of valid cognition functions in dependence upon a specific nature of its own, that very [means] does not establish the pervasion of anything by a nature other than that; for example, [the inference] which, while serving as a sublater of the contrary, depends solely upon existence.

[284] By means of a specific instance of impermanence, there is the [inference of] the state of being produced; or, for example, perception and non-perception (adhyakṣānupalambha) dependent upon a specific nature as intended [by the proponent] establish the pervasion of smoke by fire in its common form as that of the digestive heat (jāṭhara). Furthermore, since perception and non-perception function in dependence upon specific natures, there is the apprehension of pervasion between trembling and wind; this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi), because there is an absence of perceptual activity [of trembling] in the case of the lightness of air (mātariśva).

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). For the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily pervaded by the fact that it functions in dependence upon the specific nature (*svarūpa*) of the object intended [to be pervaded]; otherwise, the faults of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and confusion of function (*pravṛttisaṃkara*) would follow. Furthermore, a function that depends on a nature other than that [intended one] is contradictory to it. Therefore, the meaning of the valid cognition is this: perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), which depend on a specific nature, do not establish the pervasion of trembling by mere air—which is common to both still and moving states.
Consequently, there is no inference of wind from trembling in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

Furthermore, there is no conceptual construction for establishing your own tenets that does not follow this [same logic], nor is there any basis for its invalidity that is not brought forward against your own inference. Consequently, if, in order to establish the pervasion between "having an effortful agent" and "being an effect"—just as between fire and smoke—one resorts to perception and non-perception as the refuge, then, with respect to the nature of that which is capable of being perceived, there is an inevitable deviation of "having an effortful agent" from "mere effect," such as grass and the like.

Now, if it is maintained that there is a pervasion by an intelligent agent who is the locus of the wonder of deviation [from the rule], then, just as in the case of the birth of trees and the like, when the operation of an intelligent agent—which cannot be excluded even prior to [the existence of] the product—is present, one must determine for what absence the absence of the pot and so forth is caused, such that [the pot] could be established as being pervaded by that [agent]. Thus, because its exclusion from the heterologue (vipakṣa) is doubtful, the reason remains inconclusive (anaikāntika), especially since, as previously stated, there is no subverting proof (bādhaka) against the contrary when one disregards the distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible.

This was established by demonstrating it oneself; now, however, since the reason is not established as being absent [from the counter-example] even in view of the proponent's own accepted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a distinction. It has been stated that the subverting proof against the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhaka*) should lead to the comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the reason alone, and not through the cognition of its specific qualification, such as "possessing intelligence" (*buddhimat*).

But surely, since trees and the like have been made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*), how can there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of them? For the mass of existing things (*bhāvarāśi*) is threefold: those whose production is doubted, those with an intelligent agent (*buddhimatkartṛka*), and those without an agent. Among these, having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception and non-perception in the case of jars and the like—which possess an intelligent agent—and having applied the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) to mountains and the like, which are subjects of doubt, one proves the existence of an effortful agent. This [subject] cannot, however, be a locus of deviation.

As for what was said—that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*)—that is incorrect. For that which is the very object of deviation cannot possibly be the subject (*pakṣa*), because "the statement of the reason applies to what is doubtful; a reason excluded [from the subject] has no basis" (PV IV 91).

According to this principle, it is therefore appropriate to take only mountains and the like as the subject (*pakṣa*) whose agent is doubtful. However, one must then postulate a fourth category: trees and the like, which have non-conscious agents. [Objection: Since no agent is perceived in the production of things like trees—which are considered perceptible—how can they be made the subject? [Response: Let there be no total elimination of the inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*) that applies to all [cases].

If an imperceptible agent is postulated to prevent the reason of "being an effect" from occurring in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then how can pervasion (*vyāpti*) ever be established, given that it is devoid of proof through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)?
Obstruction, however, is restricted solely to that which possesses a stated cause; it does not pervade [the subject] by way of distinction.
Furthermore, non-dharma, which moves within the sphere of deviation, is not capable of being made the subject of the proposition.
Thus is the summary verse.

But even so, how can there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), given that space (*ākāśa*) is possible as a locus for the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? As it has been said: "The existence of production and so forth in things such as jars occurs when an intelligent cause exists, and their non-existence occurs when it is absent; and since that [concomitance] is well-established as being inseparable (*avinābhāva*), wherever it is perceived—in earth and so forth—it generates in those who know it the cognition of an agent capable of fashioning them. By "production and so forth," the meaning is "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and the like. To this, the following is replied:

The establishment of the probandum does not occur through a mere example, whether by way of similarity or dissimilarity, because such a possibility exists even for that which has arrived by chance. Therefore, what is called an "illustration" (nidarśana) is useful for the logical reason (*hetu*) only by way of recollecting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*), which had been grasped but forgotten; it is not so by its mere presence.

And that invariable concomitance (pratibandha) would either be remembered from having been apprehended through another means while one was in the air, or it would be established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) whose locus is oneself. Of these, the first alternative is already discarded, because even in the case of a jar, there is no means for apprehending the concomitance of "being an effect" and so forth with the mere intellect or with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of a visible body. And the latter is impossible.

For instance, even if the cessation of duality were perceived in the sky, nevertheless, because it is impossible to ascertain that this is necessitated by the absence of one [of the two], and because the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) is not present there in the absence of the other, what could have a cognition of a relationship with what? Furthermore, it would follow that one could grasp the causal relation even for a camel, a donkey, and so forth. If you argue that such a cognition occurs when aided by the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) elsewhere, then surely the meaning of "concomitance" is simply co-observation; and since such co-observation sometimes exists even for camels and the like, your established rule is flawed.

The meaning of concomitance (*anvaya*) is not simultaneous observation; rather, it is the presence of one thing conditioned by the possibility of another. If it is argued that this [conditioned presence] exists between "being an effect" and "having an intelligent agent," but not elsewhere, we say no; for the fact that the presence of one is conditioned by the other does not consist in its arising from the operation of that [other].

Since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is distinct from the attainment of existence by what was previously non-existent, and since this antecedent non-existence does not occur without the operation of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), once the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been ascertained through perception and non-perception, what kind of doubt could there be regarding the establishment of the causal relationship? Thus, it is merely the recollection of the connection between the cognition of those two that is enjoined "in the sky" (i.e., is utterly baseless); therefore, this belongs to the first position alone.

Furthermore, what is this? Is it merely your display of turning back or not turning back against the Lord, or is it a counter-objection (*pratibandī*)? The same logic applies even to the inference from smoke: having observed the possibility of both [fire and smoke] in one instance, one grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) because, upon observing the cessation of one activity in the sky, the cessation of the other is likewise observed.

If this is indeed the correct principle, then for those who desire that [conclusion], their current hostility is groundless; by merely lamenting in this way, they have lost even the inference of fire, let alone the proof of the matter at hand, because—even if it were a donkey—they would abandon their grasp on the fire according to the stated sequence. But when another possibility exists there that is compatible with the subject at hand, how can taking a prisoner be a refuge?

If you argue: "In that case, the operation of perception and non-perception is resorted to only for fear of such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), but it is not that very [operation] which constitutes the convention (*samaya*)," then, since this is so, you yourself must undergo the ordeal of drinking from the jar (*kośapāna*) to determine whether or not this burden has been placed upon you by the over-extension. For against one who, setting aside perception and non-perception, asserts pervasion (*vyāpti*) by taking the cessation of smoke to follow from the cessation of fire's operation in the sky—since even the mere entity itself would have its operation ceased there—he too [would be subject to the same consequence].

There would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) such that pervasion (*vyāpti*) could be established; for likewise, one who sets aside both perception and non-perception, and—by the absence of the activity of a specific person capable of such [perception]—demonstrates the exclusion of the state of being an effect like a jar from space, and thereby considers there to be a pervasion by that [absence], must also admit a pervasion by the mere absence of any person whatsoever, since even that is excluded there. Similarly, since the state of being another kind of effect is also excluded, there would be a pervasion by that too. Thus, we see that this is clearly nothing but an over-extension and is not a logical principle (*nyāya*).

It is correct to say that because one observes deviation [of smoke] from donkeys and the like, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) by the mere thing; however, since no deviation is observed in the case of a mere person, this objection will not be a mere frivolous cavil (atiprasaṅga). Not so; for the observation of a sublation in one instance among things governed by the same logic gives rise to doubt regarding the other as well.

For if the observation of the cessation of both [fire and smoke] in the sky were to establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then even in the case of real fire and smoke, that connection would not be sublated; however, since it is sublated there, how could it serve as a means for a definitive conclusion elsewhere? Nor can it be said that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding what has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), for making something the subject is not a magical incantation, but rather the firmness of the grasp of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

And if that [absence] in space were merely the non-existence of both [the probans and the probandum], then, because a sublation (*bādhaka*) is apprehended there, its firmness is lost; thus, even if [space] is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not cease.

If it is argued that space exists as the locus of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-bhūmi*), then why would that same [space] not also serve as the occasion for smoke’s production from fire, since that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?
[287] If this is so, why has the "other than over-extension" (nātiprasaṅga) not been established by you yourself?
Furthermore, the observation of sublation (*bādhā*) here also draws forth suspicion regarding that [other].
This is the summary.

Therefore, the pervasion is not established by the absence of the two [fire and smoke] in space; rather, the observation of their non-existence in that case would only serve as a cause for recollecting the pervasion already grasped. Furthermore, it has been stated that no means for grasping the pervasion is possible. Consequently, even if there were mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is absent, it remains established that [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In reality, however, even positive concomitance is as difficult to obtain for this [reason] as negative concomitance is.

For when it is impossible to ascertain that the absence of an effect is caused by the non-existence [of a cause] because that cause is beyond the scope of perception, its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is cast far away indeed; for such a thing must be graspable by perception. Indeed, perception determines pervasion (*vyāpti*) by including within its own operation even those things remote in space and time, provided they are capable of being perceived, but not those that are remote in their very nature (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*); this has already been stated at length.

Therefore, having disregarded mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the "elephant's eye" gesture (*gajanimīlita*), he stated the refutation based solely on the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In reality, however, there is neither positive nor negative concomitance; thus, he says, "Or rather, there is doubt," in order to show that when "merely possessing effort" is the probandum, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is indeed inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*).

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that, with respect to what is perceptible by the senses and so forth, it is a "common inconclusive" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*) reason; but with respect to mere consciousness (*caitanya*), it is an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. Now, one might object: if an effect produced by the intellect (*buddhi*)—which has the body as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—is established, then an effect produced by the intellect alone is necessarily established, just as being produced by a *śiṃśapā* tree implies being produced by a tree, since the general category is not excluded when the particular is present. If this is the case, then there would also be a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with respect to that [intellect]; what loss is there for us, given that the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) resides in the intelligent agent?

Is it because of the acceptance that [the reason] possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? To this it has been said: if one were to conceive of positive and negative concomitance in this manner, then even when fire is inferred from smoke by means of a form residing in a kitchen hearth or a painting, one would remain doubtful; consequently, one would not proceed with a mind focused on the intended object, and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not the case that by perception alone any form of an entity whatsoever is ascertained as being pervaded by its effect; rather, this occurs in dependence upon conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). And since such determination is indeed produced by a person, the [inference] proceeds only with respect to a specific object, namely "by an intelligent being," because the conventional usage of the word "person" (*puruṣa*) and so forth is established precisely in that sense.

But it is not by consciousness alone, independent of the activity of the hands and other organs; for although pure consciousness exists, it remains indifferent, because at the time of grasping the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*) proceeds only toward a specific [object]. Or, even though the term is general, it implies the specific context at hand, just as the word "fire" implies its pervasion [by smoke]. And that determination, following the operation of perception, would project only that form which is capable of being perceived externally, and not that which is incapable of it, such as the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) or the like, nor like grass-fuel and so forth. In this way, there is a pervasion of something by the person (*puruṣa*) as well.

[288] There would indeed be a rejection of pure consciousness (buddhi-mātra), which is devoid of the limiting adjuncts of the body and is incapable of that [cognition]; however, there is no rejection of the various distinctions such as the "stump" and so forth. This very principle applies everywhere in the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvaya) through perception.

If it is argued that for one who perceives smoke produced from a piece of *aguru* due to contact with charcoal, there would follow the consequence of its concomitance even with things other than fuel and so forth—because it is suitable for perception—is it then intended that perception, disregarding the restriction of the objects of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), should establish concomitance with whatever [object] it happens upon? If this were the case, the distinction between a valid reason and a fallacious one would be destroyed, and since everything would be established by everything, the search for a specific means of proof would be fruitless.

Now, if it is argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is apprehended by perception even by transcending what is suitable for it, that is unproven. For when perception, even regarding an object suitable for its own operation, apprehends a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) while setting aside the universal (*sāmānya*) with respect to internal distinctions, then what need is there to mention an object that is absolutely heterogeneous and unsuitable for its own operation? Nor is our position that pervasion is [apprehended] by everything suitable for perception; rather, our position is that pervasion is established by that which is indeed suitable for perception.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even donkeys and the like would possess a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with smoke-pots and such. What could be more absurd than this? But why is it that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) here depends precisely on internal distinctions and not merely on the suitability for perception? For conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which requires the presence of perception and so forth solely for the purpose of awakening latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), is incapable of introducing a specific, restricted particularity because its arising form is indeterminate.

True; for this very reason, there is an application of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as a means of establishing negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). In that regard, just as non-apprehension assists in the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between fire and smoke, or between a person and a jar—establishing a negative concomitance that is distinguished in three ways, namely: [the object's] prior existence, its production from another, or its arrival from elsewhere, since otherwise it would be useless—likewise, if it were to establish [concomitance] with donkeys or with mere cognition, it would indeed be [effective] by those two as well.

Pervasion [is established] in no other way; for it has been determined many times in the treatise that pervasion is not apprehended by perception alone, nor by non-apprehension alone, but rather by perception and non-apprehension acting together through positive and negative concomitance—as we have also stated somewhat in our investigation of the "trika" and "pañcaka."

Nor does non-perception provide any assistance to that [inference] regarding the lineage of donkeys and the like. By this, the absence of the operation of non-perception with respect to specific instances of smoke is explained; thus, there is no objection whatsoever against one who speaks in this manner. However, for one who describes the pervasion effected by that [non-perception] even in the case of what is within the range of perception, the absence of the apprehension of pervasion occurs precisely regarding that object; such a position is untenable. This is because, for one who asserts a pervasion effected by that [non-perception] even when it is perceptible, and who desires that pervasion despite the absence of the operation of non-perception—[the consequence would be absurd].

[289] Who would be the objector? For if he possessed a sense of shame, how could he describe that operation when it is indeed beyond the scope of perception? Or, if the donkey is excluded simply by seeing the cause—namely, the intelligent agent who knows the material causes and so forth and possesses effort—what is the use here of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)?

In that case, one describes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) solely through what is actually perceived, and not through that which has transcended the path of vision; nor is pure consciousness ever perceived anywhere apart from its adjunct of the body.

If, moreover, the establishment [of the causal relation] is based solely on observation—such that a body presided over by mere consciousness is seen to produce jars and the like—then there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding the donkey; so how can non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) be rejected as a means of proof? If you argue: "Only general properties residing in the pervader (*vyāpaka*) are the establishers of pervasion (*vyāpti*); because other [properties] are seen to deviate (*vyabhicāra*), there is no positive concomitance with the donkey due to the possibility of doubt regarding others," then we reply: But what is this "observation of deviation"? Is it not the case that even in the absence of that [deviation], [the relationship holds]?

The statement "the perception of existence" indicates that when the operation of non-perception is absent, its lack of probative force is brought forward; this illuminates the very operation of non-perception in determining the constituent parts of the proof.

Furthermore, if you, troubled by the suspicion of an operation in a particular instance, resort to a general property, then let [the opponent] likewise assert a pervasion based on mere sentience—which is common even to a donkey, excludes any particularity such as knowledge of the material cause and so forth, and is thus susceptible to proving what is already established—or even based on a more general category, namely, the mere cause. For if this were the case, every opportunity for doubt would be entirely eliminated.

However, by disregarding this much generality, one might maintain that [the pervasion] resides in a specific instance known through perception of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth; yet, even that is not disregarded, for it remains "just as it is observed. What power is there in this [position] other than stupidity? For one who maintains the doctrine of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), there is no doubt regarding that generality to which the operation of perception and non-perception extends, nor is there operation where there is room for doubt. Thus, he does not himself introduce or remove a pervasion by his own will at any point, because it is established solely by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, there is no fault.

But does he not also, when asserting that the entire collection of effects is produced by causes alone, perceive the operation of perception even with respect to what is perceptible? He certainly does perceive it, because his acceptance of that [operation] follows from scripture which sublates the contrary, as well as from perception and non-perception; however, he establishes that perception and non-perception as pertaining only to a mind associated with a specific body.

Even in the case of desire (*icchā*), when the activity of the hands and so forth ceases, the effect does not arise; therefore, it is precisely by means of that [activity] that the aggregate—which is the object of the designation "potter" and so on—is treated as being perceptible. However, this principle does not apply to the mind alone, even when accompanied by effort. In that case too, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) will be understood through inference. Nor is there any requirement for perception alone; rather, the determination of positive and negative concomitance must be made through apprehension and non-apprehension.
And whether that apprehension takes the form of perception or the form of inference—there is no insistence on this point.

Here it is considered: Is that very mind which possesses the body as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and is endowed with effort intended by the term "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), or is it something else? If it were the former, what would be the use of inference, since there would be no dispute regarding what is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Furthermore, by that [direct perception], positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established; and its deviation from the effect in general is evident. If it were the latter, there is the fault of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

[290] Since the effect, such as speech and the like, fulfills its purpose through an embodied being alone, and since pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not accepted even by means of that which is inferred—just as before—due to the lack of certainty regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it follows that even in the case of fire and smoke, the pervasion is not with fire restricted by place, time, or state, but rather with fire in general. And since that [fire] is distinct from what is actually perceived, the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth is common to both alternatives; therefore, pervasion must be stated in terms of a generality devoid of such specific qualifications.

If you argue that it is the same here as well, then even by means of a form residing in the stomach and so forth, there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of smoke being pervaded [by fire]. Therefore, it is not the case that only a universal (*sāmānya*) is employed in pervasion, nor is it the case that only a particular (*viśeṣa*) is rejected; for if the latter were true, the inference from smoke would be utterly destroyed, and there would be doubt regarding the application [of the reason] to the intended flame.

Therefore, if one's own whim alone were not sufficient to establish the delimitation [of objects], then in the process of determining [reality] by investigating the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), some universal must necessarily be accepted even by perception—which, though engaged in affirmation—excludes it as a matter of course, since perception does not apply to that which transcends its specific [object]. This is just as the perception grasping the pervasion of smoke excludes anything that transcends the form of a blazing, luminous [fire].
However, non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) excludes even that which has been accepted by perception through its inherent capacity, as in the case of a cooking pot and the like.

For that [inference], while establishing the absence of the effect in the absence of fire by demonstrating that its presence is necessitated by the presence of fire, proceeds to establish its status as an effect through the exclusion of what is incapable; yet it likewise establishes the causality of something else, in the absence of which it itself does not occur.

However, in the case of perception preceded by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), when the absence [of an object] is established through the non-apprehension that functions to subvert its prior existence and so forth—due to the absence of the existence of multiple things in the form of various objects—then whatever presence is perceived by direct perception in the vicinity of the nature of a single object, because its prior absence was already manifested as being necessitated by the absence of that [single object], it is precisely that which is rejected by perception when its capacity for non-activity is used to prove its status as a cause; thus, it is indeed rejected.

Consequently, there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with respect to the digestive fire and so forth, nor is there a negation of a nature differentiated by distinctions of time, place, or state (*kāla-deśa-daśā-bheda-bhinna-svabhāva-pratikṣepa*), because everything is accepted through perception as possessing the capacity for its own production. Nor can this be established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); for it is logical that non-apprehension, occurring in the absence of a nature not of that kind, negates the causality of something of a different class, but not that very [nature] itself; otherwise, its reliance would be purposeless.

Now, one might object: even if there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) differentiated by place and so forth, this smoke is still perceived; for it is unified—by means of a conceptual recognition (*pratyavamarśa*) of a single form—with that visible aspect which is observed, and not with any other aspect whose nature is unobservable. For this very reason, that which is denoted by the term "fire-in-general" is precisely that [visible aspect], because even when a distinction is drawn from the unobservable, there is still an appearance of non-difference from what is observable.

Is it not the case that even that which is remote in terms of space and so forth is simply incapable of being perceived? True; however, this applies only occasionally and in certain instances. But as for that which is remote by nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*), because it is absolutely heterogeneous, its existence does not contradict the distinct operation of acceptance or rejection. Therefore, just as a proponent of inference must follow after a universal (*sāmānya*) in order to avoid the possibility of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), so too—

[291] With respect to the specific objects of perception, even an additional universal must be excluded in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*). This being the case, just as it is logical that pervasion and the establishment of oneness occur by means of a subordinate universal that is perceptible, while excluding a fire-universal that is imperceptible, and not by mere "possessor-of-effort" (*prayatnavat*) alone—because such a claim is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—so too must it be here.

In that case, one who—out of delusion—seeks a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is questioned regarding [the effect's] identity with or difference from [the cause]. However, it has been stated that in the case of fire, the resolution comes precisely through that very position [of the opponent]. Therefore, when there is a desire to grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of perception and non-perception (*anupalambha*), and there is a requirement for a universal (*sāmānya*) suitable for that [pervasion], then regarding a jar or a tree as an example, the desired [concomitance] may be either established or unestablished; thus, the effect is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) due to being common [to both sides].

But since [consciousness] is unsuitable for that [pervasion] merely by its nature as consciousness, and because neither the positive nor the negative concomitance is certain even in one respect, it is rightly said that its positive and negative concomitances are "doubtful" (*sandigdha*).

"Or else, there is doubt. This refers to the context of "success or failure. By these two, existence and non-existence are expressed; as it has been said: "Perception itself is existence; non-perception is non-existence. Therefore, because there is a doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of that which is intended as the probandum (sādhya) in a subject (dharmin) possessing a proof such as "being an effect"—namely, whether it exists merely through the agency of an intelligent agent or not—and because all things are subsumed under those two [possibilities], the occurrence of neither presence nor absence (anvaya-vyatireka) in a single instance is established; thus, its status as an uncommon inconclusive reason (asādhāraṇānaikāntika) is logical.

But even so, let there be non-exclusivity (anekānta) as well; why is mere positive concomitance (anvaya-mātra) rejected, given that the operation of cognition alone is observed in the production of an effect? In that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of positive concomitance of smoke with the common nature of the digestive fire (jāṭhara), because the operation of burning is observed [in that case too]. Consequently, there would also be negative concomitance (vyatireka) relative to that, and thus the aforementioned fault remains. Furthermore, the rejection of perception is common [to both cases].

If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because smoke exists even in the absence of a digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), since there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), then why is the making of a pot not also cited as an example by one who lacks the skill for making Mount Kailāsa? Or, if you claim that here the concomitance is based on the general property of "being a means of production" (*karaṇakauśala-sāmānya*), then in that case too, it is based merely on "being a burner" (*dāhakamātra*); thus, there is nothing gained by introducing specific individuals.

If, however, [the concomitance] is considered with respect to the genus (*jāti*), then since it exists at other times as well, how could there be smoke even in the absence of that [fire]? If, on the other hand, deviation is asserted by postulating a genus distinct from the observed particularity—namely, mere combustibility—then, in relation to that [genus], how can there be positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? For the genus is apprehended through perception only as something specific; otherwise, if there were positive concomitance, deviation would be impossible.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised regarding the ascertainment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) through perception by means of a similar class (*sajātīya*), and the claim that "not everything of a similar class is inferred, because what is perceived is of a dissimilar class; and the collection of the eye and other organs is inferred from the manifestations of color and so forth, which are not themselves perceived; likewise, the far and near sides of the moon and the earth [are inferred]," that too is even more flawed. For indeed, inference is never devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and pervasion exists between a universal and a universal.

[292] How could a non-homogeneous [reason] support inference? Furthermore, that [inference] is of only two kinds: either from perception and non-perception, or from the sublation of the contrary. In both cases, the inference is only of that which is of the same class as what is observed in the example. Otherwise, it would be a great lack of discernment to assume a pervasion by means of a property of one class and then infer something of another class.

For even in the case of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), it is precisely that same commonality of motion which was perceived as the cause for reaching another location that is determined in another locus; so how can there be an inference of a dissimilar property? If it is argued that this is said with reference to a specific internal distinction established by capacity in view of the difference between substrata, then that is equivalent to stating the obvious (*anuktasama*). For no proponent of inference, desiring a particularity by that alone, is able to justify a fruitful inference.

If such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) were to exist even in the inference for God (*īśvara*), then the desired conclusion would be established by the proof of that specific property alone; who then would harbor any resentment toward it? Nor is it correct to say that one cannot infer a thing of the same class in all cases merely on account of that specific property, for such a statement is made even when there is an inference of a different class in some instances; moreover, that specific property exists in every inference.

In the case of that which is seen through particularity, even when it pertains to a generality, that very same [particular] is determined; therefore, with respect to that, one should not say that "that very same thing" is inferred everywhere, because the consideration of a common genus is based upon difference.

But that [point] is indeed irrelevant. For it is not the case that everything which is perceived is inferred. If you are speaking with reference to the means of knowledge for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as in the case of fire, then inference occurs everywhere based on perception alone, since no other means of knowledge operates elsewhere. If, however, you are referring to the sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*), then one should not say that there is no difference between the inference of God and the proof of fire; rather, it would be more appropriate to say "from the proof of impermanence."

If it is argued that this is stated merely on the basis of the nature of an effect as a reason (*kāryahetu*), then the causal relationship itself is established only through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*); thus, that very same fault remains. Furthermore, it has already been discussed that there is no subverting argument (*viparyayabādhaka*) [to prove the contrary]. Moreover, the consequence of the lack of restriction regarding place and so forth also establishes the reduction [of causality] to mere logical reason (*hetumātra*). Therefore, because it does not penetrate the actual object of knowledge under discussion, the claim that "not everything perceived is inferred" is undermined.

However, with respect to the time of inference, everything that is imperceptible is inferred, and there is no disagreement regarding this; thus, [your objection] is equivalent to stating the obvious. But the sense organ cannot be directly inferred from cognition, because the necessary invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is not apprehended. Rather, since the effect of cognition—being present when certain [other causes] are present and absent when they are absent—necessitates dependence upon a cause distinct from those, such is the [logical] proclamation of the sense organ.

In that regard, just as dependence—which is of a type observed in things such as sprouts—is established, so too are the upper and lower portions [of a jar] established in the case of effects such as jars. Since these are inferred based on what is generally observed (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) as being restricted to a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīpratibaddha*), the example is also devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnya*). Enough of this prolixity. Alternatively, the principle is this: the general nature of the effect is pervaded by the general nature of the cause, whereas the specific nature of the effect is pervaded by the specific nature of the cause.

Or rather, there is the common saying that a specific effect arises from a general cause merely through the force of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). In this regard, one who asserts that the general class of effects is pervaded by a specific cause—namely, an intelligent agent (*buddhimat*)—would indeed be overstepping established consensus on the basis of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that means of valid cognition which establishes the pervasion is of only two kinds: either perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), or the sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*), because these two consist in the nature of perception and inference, and because certainty cannot be attained through any other means. Now, first of all, regarding the general class of effects according to the sequence already stated:

Pervasion is not established through differentiation by means of the sublation of the contrary; nor is the pervasion of the whole [class] established through perception and non-perception for one who does not touch upon the distinction between that which belongs to that class and that which does not.

Since the cognition of birth follows—preceded by the negation of prior existence and so forth—just as in the case of smoke and the like, such that "from such a thing, such a thing arises," there are thus two types of universals.

"This [thing] has reached the conditions for perception and yet is not perceived; its perception would be perceived"—such is the sequence for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-perception (*anupalambha*). In this context, "this" refers to smoke and so forth, which, by virtue of belonging to a single genus, appear in a single conceptual determination (*ekapratyavamarśa*); "its" refers to fire and so forth, by way of excluding other genera of effects and excluding other genera of causes. This is the meaning.

Therefore, regarding cause and effect, there must be an activity preceded by a reflective awareness (*paramarśa*) of their mutual difference from things of the same and different classes; otherwise, such activity would be useless due to either incapacity or futility.

For instance, would this [cause] be determined as "conforming to the presence and absence of that [effect]" by way of excluding the mass of non-effects, or by way of excluding other effects? In the first case, the meaning "these entities are restricted to this" would be "this is not that entity," because a single uniform reflective awareness (*ekākārapratyavamarśa*) is impossible in the absence of a single uniform form (*ekākāra*).

If it is argued that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), because one is able to say "this is an effect" or "this is a configuration" by means of the general property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and so forth, we reply: here, the cognition that establishes existence or non-existence occurs in two ways—having either the substratum (*dharmin*) or the attribute (*dharma*) as its object—since an effect is twofold, distinguished as that which is produced (*nirvartya*) and that which is modified (*vikārya*).

Among these, the first [cognition] takes as its object that very subject (*dharmin*) which, based on the certainty of its arising in its entirety, encompasses a specific form; even though its nature is differentiated by distinctions of time, place, and so forth, it makes it its object by including it within a single internal reflective awareness (*antakapratyavamarśa*). Therefore, it is said to have that as its object. For it sets aside even those possible properties (*dharma*) that are opposed to the differentiation of that specific form, just as whiteness and the like are set aside in the case of smoke and such.

Furthermore, when another property arises in a subject (*dharmin*) that remains exactly as it was, then the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) belong to the property alone by means of reasons; thus, it is said to have the property as its object. Moreover, setting aside the specific form (*ākāra*), it takes the mere property as its locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), just as in the case of passion and so forth.

For cloth, woolen blankets, and the like, which experience a distinct difference in form, action, and so forth, and which possess a common redness, do not find satisfaction merely by inferring a connection with another coloring substance whose capacity has been previously apprehended. Rather, the first [cognition] takes the form as its sole refuge, because it arises in its entirety [as such]. For just as an object colored by a specific form arises from some cause, so too is it experienced by a sensory cognition produced through the power of that [object], and subsequently brought within the range of linguistic convention by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

[294] How is the exclusion of specific forms (*ākāraparihāra*) achieved? Precisely for this reason, when a person perceives a particular instance of smoke, a jar, or the like, whose origin was not previously perceived in one place, if its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established at that very moment through a logical distinction in another place, then the determination of its cause arises in that very instance, and not elsewhere—even while depending on the observation or non-observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Subsequently, however, one may set aside the specific form for one who perceives merely the emergence of a property (*dharma*) within a substrate (*dharmī*) that has already been established.

Furthermore, when a jar or similar object is already present, one does not observe the arising of the mere property of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), nor is such an arising admitted in the case of mountains and the like; for if that were so, one could—disregarding the form—infer a cause as being merely that [property], just as one infers passion from redness. If it is argued that the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) exists precisely within that substrate [of clay] by means of the potter, we say no; for even immediately after [the potter's work], no clay is perceived that is devoid of its specific arrangement.

If it is argued that such a thing did not exist previously—that which is the objective domain of the designation "jar"—then that very configuration must arise from the person [the potter]; thus, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) by that [property of being an effect] alone.
Nevertheless, if the action of a person were directed toward the generality of shape,
then even the application of turmeric substance would be a prescription for color alone.

But even so, does the mere fact that there is no perception of something already established not contradict the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) being grasped in another individual instance? For it was just established immediately prior that, by the force of that [concomitance], there is indeed inference in that case. And yet, on that basis alone, the proof that color alone arises from safflower is not valid; for the ground of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is weak. What, then, is the conclusion here?
Therefore, even in the case of a quality, just as with a substance, there is an inclusion of its own kind.
Thus, there is no inference of saffron from color, even when that [color] is previously established.

For if one does not grasp the specific qualities determined by that [color], how could saffron be inferred even from passion? It would be even more remote [from inference] based on color alone. Just as with color, the very diversity of genus (*vaijātya*) belonging to shape (*saṃsthāna*) is also an object of experience. Therefore, between these two, the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the restriction of a genus in a single instance—whether by way of necessity or non-necessity—is not fixed, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the individual instance.

Therefore, just like color, even though a universal (*sāmānya*) such as "being of many kinds" persists within shape (*saṃsthāna*), it remains entirely external to the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Likewise, it is impossible to claim that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) previously existed in a non-entity such as a person; for this would entail the consequence of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) characterized by a total absence of capacity, which would result in its being something newly produced (*apūrvotpatti*). Thus, it is established that causal efficiency, too, follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the specific person.

Therefore, even when the cognition of pervasion has a property (*dharma*) as its object, it does not pursue a universal (*sāmānya*). However, when it has a substratum (*dharmin*) as its object by virtue of the context of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), then—just as in the case of splitting [wood], where a perceptual cognition determines pervasiveness by relying on a commonality of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the form as it is observed, namely through a commonality of specific intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*)—so too in the case of an effect, the perceptual cognition determines pervadedness precisely by way of a commonality of specific forms; thus, there is no doubt.

Otherwise, why would an active cognition, even regarding the cause—just as it does regarding the effect—bring about the desired conclusion by excluding specific attributes such as intelligence? Therefore, just as with the cause, one ought to determine that the effect likewise possesses such specific characteristics.

In this regard, even if "being an effect" were asserted to exist in things such as the ground—which are external to that [cognition’s] form—it would be entirely useless; for, with respect to the operation of perception, which grasps the cause and effect within the domain of the property (*dharma*), a mere similarity in properties is of no consequence. Indeed, it is neither that very form consisting of objective efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth, nor is it the cause for the manifestation of that similarity. Therefore, this similarity serves no purpose whatsoever, except as a basis for the non-figurative application of the term "effect."

For he has established a convention regarding an object that exists solely within mental construction and requires the operation of another for its arising—setting aside [external] form and so forth; thus, there is no contradiction for him. As for a property perceived as being pervasive by means of another logical argument, it is in that very [property] that the operation of perception depends upon a similarity with the form and so forth manifesting at the time of its own arising, like [the property of] destruction. However, when there is a difference caused by location and so forth, there is a determination of dissimilarity; thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore, because there is no single [all-encompassing] form (*ekākāra*)—that is, no single cause—and because one must rely on individual perception and non-perception, the determination of pervasion must be made solely through this mode: "these things follow that cause. However, since even now it is not possible to apply this to the entirety of all instances, it remains restricted to each individual object among all types of effects. And that [individual application] is impossible, because [the cause] cannot function either successively or simultaneously.

For it is thus: first of all, their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) cannot occur simultaneously, because when all possible modes [of obstruction] are encountered, it would follow that the seer himself vanishes from view. Nor can their negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) be ascertained, because certain factors—such as the substratum, light, and the body—are impossible to exclude.

Furthermore, this observation of every mode is not possible within the span of a single human lifetime, due to the exhaustion of the object; for how could there be completeness when only a few [factors] are being considered?

Indeed, even for a larger portion of this [term], there is no cessation in the understanding of its inclusive application (*abhividhi*); for it cannot be asserted that "whatever is an effect, that alone is such," though it might be said that "it is just this much."

Furthermore, as for the claim that an investigation (*vicāra*) which has proceeded with respect to one [object] establishes all entities as being of such a nature, this refers to its operation through a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*), because it relies on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by excluding [specific qualities] such as "action" (*ākṛti*) and so forth. For it was stated that the very function of perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists in the restriction to the apprehension of a single genus. [Objection: But even in that case, since there is the possibility of numerous internal subdivisions, there is a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) because one is unable to state, "This is exactly thus."

If it is asked: "Or, in this case, by disregarding difference and relying on another universal such as 'smoke-ness' (*dhūmatva*), and by resorting to the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*) in conventional practice, what fault could there be even regarding other universals?"—we reply: we do not disregard some particular difference or promote some universal according to our own whim. Rather, we enter into the conventional practice of the relation between cause and effect exactly as the conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*), preceded by direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), presents objects, whether through difference or non-difference.

But if that [nature], having encountered a particularity of its own essence (*prakṛtiviśeṣa*), differentiates its function among the particulars through the presence or absence of the capacity for suppression—whether in a subtle or gross state—then what is there for anyone to do? (The word "some" appears in the *Mātṛkā*). However, its transformation (*vivarta*) must be considered. In this regard, just as smoke, despite possessing internal subdivisions, takes as its object a similarity that excludes other classes, so too should it be understood regarding the heart in relation to mere effects.

Regarding the presence or absence of conformity with a single shape and so forth, since these are to be personally experienced by each individual, no further basis for determination is required here; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion in designations, purposeful action, and functional application.

Therefore, it is impossible to establish a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—whether by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*)—between any single cause and all types of effects, either successively or simultaneously. What, then, is the use of these two [methods]? For this very reason, the claim that there is a pervasion of all effects by [the cause] through such a gateway is merely a disclosure of one's own intention, like the proclamation of a "post" while standing on the path. This being the case, since mere desire would be the proof, the pointlessness of these two [methods] is clear.

Therefore, the cognition "this [is] from those two" arises only by means of the exclusion of other effects; it does not attain correspondence by taking the mere effect as its object. Consequently, by setting aside the doubt that one might be a knower of the material cause and so forth, he says:
"Or rather, there is no doubt."
The establishment of what is desired by another does not [follow] from the refutation or the proof of another, when there is merely the cognition and the effort [of the opponent].

There is no positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) in the case of proving a specific desired [property]; however, a means of proof (*sādhana*) that tolerates doubt regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is indeed a valid proof.
If the probandum is perceptible, there is indeed deviation; if it is not perceptible, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is not established.

Nor is there pervasion (vyāpti) through positive concomitance (anvaya), just as in the case of negative concomitance, unless it is specified for the particular instance, in which case the other [the general] does not hold.
The Second Section.
Third Section [297]:
If this is so, one might ask: "Even if there were pervasion (*vyāpti*), it would be impossible to ascertain; what is the solution here? Look:

an effect is indeed manifold in its nature, yet a single, insentient producer is observed; and when there is knowledge of a restriction to one among many varieties, that [restriction] does not apply to other varieties.

Whatever belongs to a particular genus and is known to have a single cause, that very thing constitutes its constituent part; otherwise, there would be no production [of the effect], nor is this method accepted in the case of the example for the probandum (*sādhyopama*). For it is not the case that the production of various kinds of effects is restricted solely to that which possesses volitional effort (*prayatnavat*); for even fire and other such things, when situated within various collections of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), are seen to perform a variety of functions, such as producing smoke, ash, embers, heat, cooking, melting, drawing forth, burning, and inflicting injury.

[This is] because we observe various causal operations, such as producing smoke, ash, charcoal, heating, cooking, purifying mercury, observation, injury, and so forth. If there is dispute only regarding whether these occur through the superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of one who possesses effort, and if, once a rule has been established for one [effect], the knowledge of a rule for other effects is not thereby established—as was stated previously—then however many modes are determined to have a single cause, that many are appropriate as proofs for that cause, whether it be conscious or otherwise.

Otherwise, one might infer fire from ashes and the like—even though they are not known to have the nature of its effect—simply because smoke has been observed to be pervaded by fire in the case of damp fuel. But this is not so; therefore, the distinction between types [of fire] and the separate apprehension of the pervasion in each individual instance, when required, uproots inference based on the apprehension of [a mark] in any random place by means of any random [mark].

Who, moreover, says this—that one may infer by means of whatever [reason] in whichsoever [case] the pervasion has been grasped—given that in the absence of the recurrence of a single property, there is simply no reason (*hetu*) at all? For in that case, ash would not be a proof because of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*), nor would smoke be a proof because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*). If it is argued that even in the case of a pot, a bell, and so forth, the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) would serve as the reason when it occurs in an inference despite the non-recurrence of other properties, we say no; for the state of being an effect has also been proven in detail to lack pervasion prior [to the inference].

In this regard, just as a mountain peak possesses a fixed nature characterized by the absence of a potter's activity at the time of its formation, so too, even if "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) exists, there is no difference [in the case of cognition] from smoke arising from a donkey insofar as there is an absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through the occurrence of validity. Therefore, one who has apprehended the pervasion in a specific effect such as a jar cannot infer the pervader on the basis of "mere being an effect" in every instance.

However, since this does not transcend the fact that the locus of the apprehension of pervasion and the locus of the establishment of the proof are distinct, how can the objection regarding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) be avoided?

Therefore, mere conformity with a single property is not sufficient for [logical] utility. Or rather, by whom were the properties of being an effect (*kāryatva*), being a real entity (*vastutva*), and so forth—which are possible in smoke—reduced to ashes in the case of ash? If it is argued that even though these properties exist, they are deviant (*vyabhicārin*), we reply: surely a reason is deviant only because of a lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*), since even the scent of such a deviation is absent when pervasion exists. And that absence of pervasion is not avoided even by the property of being an effect; thus, deviation remains difficult to ward off even in that case. As for the non-observation [of the concomitance] in some instances, that may occur even due to remoteness.

[298] It does not follow from that alone that the probans is non-existent, because the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), which is its very root, remains as it was. If, however, there is deviation (*savyabhicāra*) even when there is pervasion, then it is all the more so when there is no pervasion; therefore, enough with this false obsession. Thus, even if you accept a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) as the probans while disregarding mere pervasion, why not likewise accept a property common to the mountain and other such things? If you do, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains exactly as it was.

Nor does this principle apply even to jars and the like, which are treated as being on the same footing as the probandum; for even in those cases, just as we perceive the activity of the potter in the case of the water-jars, arrows, bowls, and so forth, we—recognizing that "this too is produced by him" and "that too is produced by him"—ascertain his operation precisely through those types of objects whose production he has mastered before. Otherwise, one would not escape the aforementioned fault.

Therefore, even if from the perspective of ultimate reality this entire collection of effects is invariably concomitant with an agent possessing effort, nevertheless, from the standpoint of the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is established that whatever kind of arrangement and so forth follows the presence or absence of a controller— that is what is inferred from it. (PV II 13)

Thus: when one sees something such as the arrangement [of parts] in an empty city or a temple seen therein, even though one does not see an agent, the cognition that "it has been made" arises; if such a thing were seen in the case of mountains and other subjects (*dharmin*), then it would be logical for this [reasoning] to establish the desired object through its proof.

And that [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*); this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Indeed, for us, there is always the cognition of being produced (*pauruṣeya-buddhi*) in every case; that [cognition] is the cognition of having been made (*kṛta-buddhi*). And the rule is that inference is precisely the cognition of what is to be proven (*sādhya-buddhi*), because in some way, for someone, even in those cases [of mountains and so forth], there is no absence of it. Furthermore, what is meant by "the cognition of having been made"? Is it the cognition of anything merely as an effect, or the cognition of [an effect] as having been made by a person? If it is the cognition of anything merely as something made (*kṛta-mātra-buddhi*), that is established even for the Buddhist in the case of the oceans, mountains, and so forth. Moreover, since they possess parts, their very state of being originated from those [parts] constitutes their "being made" (*kṛtatva*).

Now, if the cognition of a human agent (*pauruṣeyabuddhi*) is the cognition that [the scripture] was composed (*kṛtabuddhi*), then that is nothing other than the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*), and it is precisely this that is called inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, how can it not be undermined to say that because that [cognition] is absent, there is no inference? As it has been said: "Nor does the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) arise for anyone simply due to delusion when the cognition of the probandum is absent, because that would entail the same consequence for all inferences. Furthermore, as for what is said: "The state of being such an effect (*tādṛkkāryatva*) and so forth is denied in the case of mountains and the like," [this too is problematic].

[299] Even in that case, we do not perceive any distinction between Mount Kailāsa, a water-jar, and so forth, on the grounds of their being effects (*kāryatva*) and the like. And it has been said: "Nor is there any distinction between the causes of the earth and such things and the causes of palaces and the like, by virtue of which these [latter], while being devoid of intention and independent of effort, would possess [the capacity for] activity through a restricted operation. For we have never observed independence in the performance of actions among instruments characterized by functional properties unless they are supervised by an intelligent agent; since everywhere, the production of palaces and the like is observed only when they are presided over by an intelligent being."

To this it is replied: this "produced cognition" (*kṛtabuddhi*) was not stated with reference to those whose intellects are permeated by an adherence to a specific philosophical tenet; rather, it is intended merely with respect to ordinary persons proficient in worldly convention. And for such a person—who possesses the recollection of a previously perceived invariable concomitance and lacks any aversion toward reflecting on the cause—such a cognition indeed arises in a temple and the like, but not in a place like a pond filled with fish and crocodiles. Therefore, the presence and absence of this cognition in these two cases cannot be established without positing a difference in genus (*jāti*), for otherwise, the same [cognition] would follow upon seeing even two different types of smoke.

Granted that this is indeed the very cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*), who then has stated that it is the basis for inference for one who possesses it, or why—due to its absence—is it absent in the case of mountains and the like? Rather, the presentation of its presence and absence is merely for the purpose of indicating a difference in kind (*jātibheda*); it is intended for the instruction of a certain person of dull intellect, with respect to those of similar standing.

For once such a difference in kind is established, one would not be able to say that perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) operating in one instance is capable of establishing a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) in another.

Therefore, the establishment of the probandum does not follow from a configuration (*sanniveśa*) and so forth that lacks a necessary connection (*apratibaddha*); and since that which is connected is unestablished (*asiddha*), how can there be inference? Thus, even when this is presented for the ultimate purpose of negating inference, what is being stated is that "the absence of that [inference] follows from the absence of that [connection] in one case alone. Now, if that is so, since there is no arising of inference for one thing, it must also not exist for another; how then could such a position be consistent? For it has been said: "And it is not due to delusion," and so forth. That, however, is incorrect.

Because when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the means is identical, it is impossible for the result to be restricted to only one [of two parties]. Whatever possesses a specific causal complex with another thing must necessarily have an identical result with that thing; for example, two locations possess mutually identical results from the collection of fuel, fire, and so forth, which serve as the common means for producing smoke. And the person engaged in worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahārika*) together with you possesses the same causal complex for grasping the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and other factors that constitute the means of inference. This is a *prasanga* based on a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For even for you, only perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*)—operating through the agency of temple architects and the like—is the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*). And this is common to the opponent as well. However, the uncommon means—the proof that sublates the opposite (*viparyayabādhakapramāṇa*)—would be difficult to find; and it has already been shown that even for you, such a proof does not exist.

Therefore, if attachment to one's own view does not obscure the mind of the observer, but rather that very [view] is a means of proof common to others, then for him too, the inference of human authorship regarding Mount Meru, Mandara, and so forth would be unavoidable—just as in the case of temples and other structures seen in an empty city. But this is not the case. Consequently, when the operation of the valid cognition that apprehends the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for a given [object] occurs...

For one who possesses correct recollection, that which arises from seeing something is not an inference when there is no established connection (*pratibandha*) between them; for example, when one who remembers the connection of smoke with fire infers fire upon seeing a donkey.

Furthermore, there is no inference of a person on Mount Malaya, the Himalayas, or elsewhere based on the memory of having visited a temple or similar place while conscious; this is the non-perception of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*). It establishes the deficiency of the subject being grasped by the means of knowledge that previously proved the connection, due to the possibility of other cognitions—such as the turning away from pursuing the cause of the memory—and because that [deficiency] exists even in something possessing internal distinctions, provided there is no excellence of difference in genus, just as smoke [does not prove a person] in the case of a donkey.

However, this desired proof [of the object] does not follow if there is a failure in either the apprehension or the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). For that purpose, there must be a correct apprehension. In that regard, if there is a failure in recollection, one would not infer even from another temple. Furthermore, a failure in apprehension is impossible with respect to perception, because it has been stated that the capacity for a single unifying reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*) simply does not exist [in such cases]. Otherwise, even those seeking water and the like would have to depend upon potters, architects, and so forth.

If it is argued that even in that case, another factor standing in the place of an architect is required—just as in some instances there is an architect standing in the place of a potter—we say no. For when there is no dissimilarity in the nature of the effect produced, it is illogical to require a dissimilarity in the causal capacity. Otherwise, one would not find satisfaction even with a mere potter in the production of other jars.

Or, just as a farmer might suffer the hardship of drought that cannot be averted by the efforts of a potter, such a distinction between classes (jāti-bheda) is indeed established; therefore, because the conceptual determination of a single form is untenable, the pervasion (vyāpti) established through perception—by virtue of its specific objectivity—does not incur the fault of being difficult to grasp. For, even in the absence of inference, since the excellence of the distinction between classes remains unestablished, there would be the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

And thus, since the apprehension [of the probans] is established exactly as it is, there is no inconclusiveness [in the reason], because where there is no inference, there is simply no apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is asked: "How, then, is it to be understood by people that in such a case there must be an abandonment of inference? It is because of what was already stated: otherwise, even one seeking water would have to trample upon the legs of a potter; or a person terrified by the invasion of a hostile army would desire the protection of great mountains and oceans. We do not perceive a pervasion based on mere sentience alone.

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply because [the pervasion] is restricted to the specific state of the potter and so forth, then what fault could there be in grasping the pervasion as being restricted to that very state? What is there to say about this? Furthermore, you need have no concern for someone like me whose intellect is stained by the blemish of sectarian bias; rather, your concern must be for the world at large.
