If it is then argued that even the world does not understand [the pervasion] through that [specific instance] due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then in that case, one would not be able to perform an inference from another jar either.

If it is argued, "What fault is there in this, since deviation is observed elsewhere?"—this [objection] is not tenable provided that there is no dissimilarity in the genus (*jāti*). Therefore, why not simply say this: perception, which grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*), operates only with respect to a specific genus; consequently, inference does not extend its operation to anything else? Why then introduce the charge of deviation here? Furthermore, one must necessarily accept that perception determines a specific genus; otherwise, even a perception whose object is free from deviation would not [be valid].

If it were of a fixed nature, it could enter another jar as well; and that being the case, the same fault would persist. If you argue that this is because the very cognition grasping the pervasion has already occupied the other jar—surely, when the mind wanders into error regarding an object already occupied by that [pervasion], how can it avoid that very [object]?

But if both [the perception and the inference] have restricted objects, this fault does not arise. Now, since perception has already accepted a qualified object, the presentation of an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is no longer fruitful. However, for the sake of one who is confused, the means of knowledge that grasp pervasion (*vyāpti*) are employed to instill a memory regarding the operation upon a qualified object. But pervasion, which extends everywhere, is not made restricted in its scope by a deviation once it has been grasped; nor is there a mere refutation of inference, precisely because of the reasoning already stated.

Therefore, it is established that pervasion (vyāpti) is apprehended by means of a potter and so forth as having a specific object, because perception functions only with respect to a single genus, depending on whether or not deviation is observed.

Thus, even when one desires to grasp a pervasion by means of mere consciousness alone, no deviation [of the rule] is observed; it is therefore established that whatever genus or object the activity of perception extends toward, that very thing is proven to be pervaded by it. Consequently, how can one who asserts a pervasion in a general sense not deserve censure merely for restating a conventional consensus (*samaya*)? However, if one who wishes to grasp a pervasion through a mere person relies upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) while rejecting direct perception (*adhyakṣa*), then this fault does not apply.

But that has already been examined: if, through the grace of God, this proponent’s perception were to arise everywhere with a single uniform form, abandoning the diverse forms of the world, then that [perception] would be unique and thus not a factor for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Between an embodied and a disembodied agent who both possess effort, there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the grasping of pervasion (*vyāpti*) through perception with respect to the properties of action; for, if one seeking a water-carrier were to fail to follow a potter and thus lack the inference based on his work, then even if an inference were possible by another means, the flaw of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would recur because there would be no obstruction [to the inference] other than the specific difference in genus (*jātibheda*).
Therefore, the absence of inference in that case—which is established as being caused by the difference in genus—demonstrates that inference is restricted to and bound by specific genera.

Alternatively, if the inference of human authorship restricted to specific classes of beings is not established, then one who out of deceit denies the distinction between classes—though it is established by experience—is forced to admit that distinction by means of a counter-inference: namely, that the absence of such activity (in the case of the world) is proven by the absence of an inference for its being created by a potter or similar agent, since the latter is invariably concomitant with the former. Otherwise, the emergence of a different inference would result, leading to the admission of the distinction between classes; just as it is said: "If there were such a thing as conjunction distinct from the post and the crow, the world would also perceive this third entity."

And likewise, if the kind of arrangement seen as preceded by an intelligent agent were to exist in the case of clouds and the like as well, then people would also have the cognition that they are made by a person, just as in the case of other jars.

And thus it is stated that this distinction is not made on the basis of a difference in genus (*tajjātibheda*), because there is no other cause for it. Consequently, when the question arises as to what kind of arrangement (*sanniveśa*) is established as being invariably concomitant with a supervisor (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), the phrase "even for one who does not observe the act" and so forth is stated. This is for the sake of avoiding the cumbersome burden of enumerating various types [of arrangements] conceptualized through synonyms. In that regard, both interpretations are consistent: either the inference of an agent possessing effort (*prayatnavat*), or the inference of the activity of a potter and the like, which is designated as "the cognition that it was made by a person."

[302] According to the sequence previously stated, the mere absence of an inference for a potter—due to the fact that the causal complex for proving a creator consists solely in the negation of one possessing effort—is itself the *liṅga* (probans), or rather, the absence of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as established by those who know that [pervasion]. This has been elaborated by following the wishes of others. However, ordinary people follow what they observe; whatever kind of thing they see to have been preceded by a person, they understand that very thing to have been made by a corporeal being. They do not even entertain a doubt regarding the cessation of a body; thus, their conviction that something was "made" culminates in an inference based on a similar human agent.

Even if, by the power of some supernatural accomplishment (*siddhi*), someone were to perceive a demonic illusion (*māyā*) and a certain mental impression (*ullekha*) should arise even toward an immovable object—thinking, "Could this have been made by someone or by something?"—even then, it appears as being utterly colored by hands, feet, and limbs. Certainty, however, remains far off. Moreover, that [impression] would not be possible if there were a single genus [of cause], just as smoke or a jar [cannot be produced] without fire or a potter. Furthermore, there is not even an impression of something devoid of the activity of hands, feet, and so forth.

Nor can the denial of inference by the proponents of momentariness and the like be established merely on that basis. However, we maintain that inference—which requires the grasping of pervasion preceded by perception and which functions with regard to specific universals—is not possible for either the common person or the investigator, because it is common to both.

And although the second [type of inference] is also indeed worldly (*laukika*), nevertheless, due to the unfamiliarity with a certain object, there may exist for a person of subtle intellect—even for one engaged in worldly convention—some object that requires more intense deliberation (*tīvratarābhyūha*). In that case, even though perception is incapable [of establishing it], an inference may be employed based on a pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped by means of another inference that sublates contrary positions (*vipakṣabādhaka*), relying solely upon worldly consensus; thus there is no fault, just as in cases where the world has a particular proclamation of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, it is entirely logical that the cognition of "produced" (*kṛtabuddhi*), which is of the nature of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhyabuddhi*), establishes a difference in genus through both existence and non-existence. Even when the cognition of "produced" is understood as the mere cognition of what has been made (*kṛtamātrabuddhi*), there is still no fault. Nevertheless, what is called "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) consists in having its own origination dependent upon the operation of another; and this is certainly not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*) in things such as mountains, in the same way that it is established in trees and the like. Furthermore, that which is established merely by the opponent's own admission is simply not a valid factor (*anaṅga*) in the context of an independent proof (*svatantrasādhana*).

Then, when relying on that which is established by inference, is it relied upon as being of the same class as what is observed, or in some other way? In the case of the position that there is no end [to the series], if "being an effect" were established as being restricted to a specific location merely by virtue of being a succession of moments characterized by a beginningless stream of causal capacities, then what hope could there be for the intervention of a Person (*puruṣa*) based on such a thing? Rather, it is appropriate that the factor of the same class as what is observed should be its constituent part.

Setting aside the distinction made by the basis of being conscious or unconscious, one might indeed draw in human agency, since the arising [of an effect] is obtained through the conjunction of a multitude of diverse causes, for that conjunction is determined to depend upon it. For even the mere fact of having an unconscious material cause is fulfilled by the previous sequence [of causes] and would not draw in the specific [agency] under discussion. This alone is what is known in the world as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). And since that is not established in the case of mountains and the like, how can there be an avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*)? It is simply not...
This is not a direct proof of non-establishment; rather, it is for the purpose of proving heterogeneity. Nor is it directed merely toward the state of being an effect, but toward everything.

This is the meaning: is it established by the presence or absence of a conforming arrangement and so forth that follows from the existence or non-existence of a presiding agent, such that even a person who perceives no activity develops the notion that something was "made" upon seeing it? Therefore, if you maintain that the notion of being "made" applies to things with parts, yet it does not apply for the world [to mountains and the like], then their belonging to different categories is established. Otherwise, the world would perceive that even a potter pervades mountains and the like; thus, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) as before would follow.

Therefore, it is established that due to the difference in their origins, that which is produced by a person is indeed something else entirely, as is understood through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*).

As for what was said—that there is no distinction whatsoever in being an effect—here, even though "being an effect" is a property common to all things, if you intend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) to be established by perception, then even if that [pervasion] exists, it is effectively irrelevant; this has already been stated. However, if you intend to express a pervasion of consciousness by the mere fact of coming into existence after not having existed, while disregarding any specific distinctions, then you should likewise disregard the operation of perception and take refuge in another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the absence of that [specific cause], nothing exists as an effect, even if it were present.

As for what was said—"nor is there any distinction among the causes such as earth," and so forth—that too serves merely to confuse the common folk; it cannot be a means for understanding the intended meaning. It is like someone who, while attempting to prove that diamonds are scratchable by other stones because they are composed of earth, says to one who is doubting: "There is no distinction between wood, stone, and the like on the one hand, and thunderbolts on the other, by virtue of which these [diamonds], though being composed of earth, would be devoid of scratchability by iron."

For earthiness has never been observed in things that cannot be scratched by iron; rather, earthiness is observed only in jars, trees, and so forth, which are admitted to be scratchable by iron. Similarly, the present case also appears to be a mere verbal construction. For just as all persons, being devoid of intentionality, are perceived to engage in the undertaking of actions dependent upon a [specific] person (*puruṣa*), so too are [things] characterized by the nature of being scratchable by iron due to their earthiness. And just as there is no other recourse here than to rely on extensive observation, so it is in this case as well.

Just as here, despite extensive observation, there arises the doubt whether this quality of being scratchable by iron is invariably concomitant with mere earthiness, or whether even within the category of earthiness it requires some further specific qualification; so too, it is the same [doubt]: does the fact that something is insentient require the presence of a sentient agent for its purposeful actions, or is it dependent solely upon the nature of the action itself?

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no distinction [between causes] because they are all equally fit for a single conceptual identification (*ekapratyavamarśa*), disregarding subtle internal differences as is the case with fire and the like, then it would follow that there is no distinction even regarding the effect; consequently, just as smoke might arise from anything, it would be impossible to prevent the absurdity that even a palace could be produced by a mountain. If God were accepted [as the cause], perhaps this might not happen; however, if the opposite were always true, it would follow that even a rice seed would be incapable of producing a rice sprout, or else the production of other palaces would be prohibited.
Or [is it] even when there is an absolute difference in genus, with respect merely to the property of being devoid of intentionality? That too is a delusion.

[304] This is so; for indeed, a common property is not difficult to find anywhere. Nor does that much imply that things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), because it would follow that poison and nectar would perform the same function. What undesirable consequence is there? Or rather, having disregarded the commonality of being unintentional—which is unavoidable even in the case of the construction of palaces and the like—there may still be a negation of the restriction regarding dependence on effort, provided that there exists a power based on a distinction of intrinsic nature which initiates an absolute difference in effect.
"What kind of fault?"—this is a phrase used for the meaning [of the objection], such as "there is no distinction whatsoever," and so forth.

Therefore, because there is no means of apprehending a pervasion characterized by various specific features, and because doubt remains unremoved, such a mere prattle—which lacks even the capacity for conviction within one's own heart—is nothing more than a defense of a mere possibility. Consequently, this remains established: with respect to the connection established through perception, that kind of structure and so forth which is proven to be pervaded by an intelligent agent is not found in mountains and the like; and that which *is* found there has not been proven to be so pervaded. Thus, [the reason] is either unestablished (*asiddhi*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

By this, [the author] addresses what Trilocana said: "Now, what is this 'intellect that has acted' (*kṛtabuddhi*)? Is it the intellect regarding the means of proof (*sādhana*), or the intellect regarding the probandum (*sādhya*)? First, the intellect regarding the means of proof is already established for you, since you accept that 'the variety of the world is born of karma. If, on the other hand, the latter position is held, then the meaning becomes this: the 'product-ness' (*kāryatva*) perceived in earth and so forth is not capable of serving as an inference for the probandum; rather, it is something entirely different, because it does not generate the intellect regarding the probandum."

And this is not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference (*sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅga*). For even in the case of smoke and the like, one could just as well say: "This smoke is not capable of producing an inference of fire; rather, it is something else entirely, since it does not produce the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) for one who perceives the probandum. In that case, the means of proof (*sādhana*) would not be established so long as the cognition of the probandum is not established, and the means of proof would not be established so long as the cognition of the probandum is not established; thus, there is a clear case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, that [objection] is refuted.

For this is not a direct statement of non-establishment (*asiddhi*); rather, since a person accustomed to worldly convention does not have the cognition of "produced" (*kṛta*) with respect to the Indus River and so forth—even though they remember the pervasion [of the term] with jars and the like—therefore, because there is no single genus (*jāti*), this would merely establish a difference in genus. Consequently, it is entirely logical that non-establishment or inconclusiveness (*anekānta*) follows by way of the pervasion of a specific genus. And in that case, the absence of the cognition of "produced" means either the absence of the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) or the absence of the cognition of the probans (*sādhana*); thus both [alternatives] are accounted for.

As for what the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* says: "If there is cognition [of earth and so forth] as being produced, why is there not the notion that they were made? For everyone, even regarding palaces and the like, the notion that they were made does not arise; rather, it is only for those who know the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the notion of being made arises in respect to ancient palaces and such, while for those confused about the pervasion, there is only the notion that they were not made. It is the same with respect to the earth and so forth; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever."

If it is argued that the cognition of being created by a person is not possible in the case of the earth and so forth, as it is in the case of palaces and the like—[we ask: is this [cognition] absent for those for whom an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is well-known, or for those for whom it is not? Even among those for whom it is well-known, is it absent for those who lack the recollection of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or for others? First, for those whose memory has not failed, the cognition of being created by a person certainly does occur; for even in the world, there is the common perception that "this diverse universe was fashioned by some Creator. This is the case for those who are deluded regarding the apprehension and recollection of pervasion.

Furthermore, even regarding the Vedas, the Mīmāṃsakas do not entertain the notion that they were composed by a person; therefore, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (vākyatva) and so forth, which were stated to prove their human authorship, would be unestablished (asiddha) in that case as well. Moreover, the proof of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) that was stated for the purpose of establishing impermanence would also be unestablished; for the kind of "being produced" and so forth observed in jars and the like—which consists in being perceptible to the ear—is not present in the case of sound.

Therefore, this dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the inference is common to all inferences and is not a sublation specific to the inference for God alone; thus, that [objection] is also refuted by this very [argument].

Furthermore, regarding what was conceptualized with reference to the cognition of the probandum—namely, "Is [the inference] of those for whom the existence of established inference is not present? and so forth—we reply as follows: Consider a person who, having once observed the production of a temple’s dome and other such things through the activity of a master builder and others, later infers human agency upon seeing a dome or similar object. How should such a person be described: as one who possesses the recollection of a well-known invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), or not? In the first case, why would that same person lack the cognition of human agency regarding a mountain and the like? For if he were to infer human agency there, it would follow by extension that he must also infer the agency of a potter in the case of a jar.

Thus it has been established. How then can there be a necessity for that state in those whose vision has not failed? For that very reason, even the notion that "the world is diverse" and so forth does not arise from the power of grasping and recollecting a pervasion; rather, it arises from the force of doctrines produced by other visions, because it is absent in those who have not heard them, just like a contrary doctrine.

However, [the argument] beginning with "for those who are confused about pervasion" (*vyāptivimūḍhānām*) and so forth is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, the example (*udāharaṇa*) is even more flawed, because it merely serves to demonstrate a difference in genus (*jātibheda*) regarding the absence of the notion of having been produced (*kṛtabuddhi*). Nor has it been stated that the consideration of the presence or absence of that [notion] depends upon the proponent and the opponent; for one may oneself, through dogmatic attachment, form a conceptualization otherwise as well. Rather, this consideration is made from the perspective of perception (*pratyakṣa*) by way of the domain of conventional practice (*vyāvahārika-adhikāra*).

Furthermore, consider this: for one who is ignorant of the conventions of the Vedas and so forth, yet hears a Vedic sentence and another work composed in imitation of it—even if he examines them with great skill—what kind of determination of their difference could there possibly be? This is because, like jars, thunderbolts, and other such things, all types of objects are seen by humans to have [human] causes. If one were to postulate perceptible differences in words—which are themselves of a perceptible nature—it would lead to the absurd consequence that such differences could also be postulated for smoke and the like. Therefore, whatever exists as a result of the presence or absence of a person remains subject to the presence or absence of that person.

There can be no difference between other speech and the words of the Veda, for both are capable of being uttered; they are equal in indicating supersensible objects, and there is certainly no greater reliability in one than the other.
Therefore, the Veda does not rest without reaching the status of being human in origin.

If that were so, what room is there for the existence of that [universal] in mountains and the like, which are perceptually distinct? This follows: one who conceives of a specific effect as the particularity of the cause mistakenly thinks that the mere effect—just as smoke is the effect of fire—is pervaded by this [universal], in vain.

Alas, it is a particular kind of darkness for the wise that another person does not understand that an effect of such a nature must have that very thing as its cause— even regarding an object of direct perception.

Furthermore, since a difference in nature (*vaijātya*) between worldly and Vedic sentences is possible, the Mīmāṃsaka should not be defeated by mere convention (*samaya*). Nor can "the state of being a sentence" (*vākyatva*), whose pervasion is established by perception, serve as a refuge in this matter. As for what was said regarding the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), that has already been examined and will be further considered immediately hereafter.

[Objection: But even so, since the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is observed elsewhere as well—even in that which is pervaded by [the Creator]—just as a jar and the like are invariably concomitant with an effortful agent, so too might the earth, mountains, and so forth be such. [Reply: Has this not already been stated? Although the property of being an effect exists there, it remains indifferent because its pervasion cannot be grasped. Therefore, even though other effects are not distinct from them, not even a touch of the effortful agent can be obtained; only the mere word "effect, effect" remains, undifferentiated.

If that very [reason] has been taken as a refuge by the Venerable One through another door because no direct refutation was heard there, then he says—showing that even this is for the most part like being eaten by crows:

"Inference is not valid for one who, due to the identity of the word, fails to distinguish between things that are established as distinct, just as [one might infer fire] from a white substance and the like. (PV II.14)

By this, that which was also said is rendered without foundation: "Nor can the probandum—the fact of having an insentient material cause—be established here through superimposition based on a mere similarity of words; for, just as in the case of 'producedness' [proving] 'impermanence' and so forth, the connection here too is real. Furthermore, a difference in genus does not everywhere destroy the real connection between two properties belonging to two subjects, for otherwise it would follow that there is no connection between 'producedness' and 'impermanence' due to the difference in genus between the word and the jar. This [objection] is likewise without merit.

For we do not claim that there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of insentience (*acetanatva*) and having a material cause (*sopādānatva*) upon mountains and the like; rather, those properties alone are as good as non-existent because they fall outside the scope of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is asked: "If one kind of insentient material causality is established as requiring a conscious agent (*cetana*), while another kind is observed in mountains and so forth, what is the basis for this distinction?"—the answer is: it is caused by limiting conditions (*upādhi*). If it is further asked: "Why should this not also apply to two properties belonging to two different substrata (*dharmin*)?"—we say no, because of the disparity between the cases.

The insentient material cause (*acetanopādāna*) stands in the place of smoke due to the misconception that it is an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); yet no one asserts a distinction for it based on a difference in the locus (*dharmin*). However, when the dependence upon a sentient being (*cetanāpekṣatva*) in mountains and the like is intended because of their having an insentient material cause, then the situation is of this nature: "by virtue of being smoke, smoke possesses fire. This being the case, a distinction between the two types of smoke and their two instances of "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*) would result; so how can there be parity? If you say, "Let it be exactly so," we say no; for a qualifying attribute (*upādhi*), when it is differentiated, differentiates the possessor of the attribute (*upādhimat*).

[307] It might indeed cause a division; however, this division—characterized by being excluded from a single unifying conceptual reflection (*ekapratyavamarśa*)—does not touch upon smoke as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), such that it would divide what belongs to its own nature, as in the case where a jar or a cloud is the material cause of insentience (*acetanatva*). Therefore, this objection is untenable.

If it is objected: "But surely, a difference in properties has not been observed through a difference in the substratum (dharmin)," [we reply: when a property is presented under a certain form (*rūpa*) by which the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) occurs, then even if the class of the substratum (*dharmijāti*) appears as distinct while being actually non-distinct, it does not constitute a sublation. However, the logical principle is this: when that [substratum] is distinct, another property residing within it, even if it is non-distinct, appears as if it were distinct and thus does not establish [the connection]. Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that one seeking a cloud would have to search for a potter.

If it is argued that [the relationship is not certain] because clouds are seen arising in the sky even when that [wind] has ceased, we say no; for why should the projection of that wind not be possible as being produced by that very [wind], just as a jar is produced by a potter? Furthermore, since the mere quality of holding water is observed in both cases, it is logical to establish that here too there is only a difference in terminology, just as in the other case.

For the ascertainment of an invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) occurs only when there is a restriction on the nature of the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatva*) consists in the lack of such a restriction, which is contrary to that [ascertainment].

For a certainty is bound to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); if it were to occur even when the essential nature of its object is transgressed, it would have to be established by both valid and non-valid cognition. But this is not the case; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). Nor is there an unestablished reason (*asiddhi*), because it follows the operation of direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). Thus, in this context, since a deviation of "whiteness" from fire has been observed, this is a refutation of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhya-śūnyatā*). For this very reason, it is not an inference; due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), this results in uncertainty in both cases.

However, there is no deficiency in the probans due to deviation in the case of fire and paleness, whose pervasion is established; for once pervasion is established, it is impossible to prove an exception to the inference, as deviation itself would be untenable. Indeed, pervasion encompasses all instances; if that were absent, how could "the existence of the effect when the cause exists" (tadbhāve tadbhāvaḥ) occur?

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as there is no inference of fire from whiteness because the latter lacks an invariable connection (*apratibandha*) with the former, and that [lack of connection] is manifested by way of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Otherwise, one would have remained at ease even while accepting an inference in that case as well. And that deviation demonstrates that every property common to both the nature of the object of valid cognition and its opposite is invariably unconnected; thus, it follows from the aforementioned "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatva*), which is drawn out by the lack of invariable connection.

In the same way, it is not possible to infer the superintendence of an intelligent agent from the mere fact of being an effect and so forth. Therefore, the observation of deviation (vyabhicāra) is indeed beneficial to the opponent. Consequently, it is established that, upon examining the actual nature of the object of valid cognition, the probans such as "being an effect" establishes intelligence only when accompanied by such a qualifying condition (upādhi). And since for such a case there is indeed a real difference in proximity (pratyāsatti), one is reduced to relying on a mere name.

Since it has thus been established that a difference in the genus (*jāti*) of the substratum (*dharmin*) is a differentiator of its properties (*dharma*), how can there be a denial of this in all cases? If, on the other hand, the meaning is that what constitutes a differentiator in every instance is here denied—even if it were a non-differentiator in some instances—then that is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For it has been stated that both [differentiation and non-differentiation] exist in relation to the nature of the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-viṣaya-svarūpa*). And such being the case, differentiation itself remains established.

[308] Furthermore, the touch of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth is employed as a non-refuting [reason]. For even in that case, pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established by the force of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, it is established through an inference that sublates the opposite (*viparyayabādhakānumāna*), because in its absence, an inference is not accepted.

If, in that case, the proof of the pervasion of a mere phenomenon characterized by "coming into being after not having been" by the phenomenon of "ceasing after having come into being"—which sets aside any difference in genus—were like the kitchen and so forth, which prove the pervasion of smoke by fire, then what would follow for the present case, where the method of grasping pervasion depends upon the operation of perception and is restricted precisely to a difference in genus? However, if even in the present case, it were the very properties such as "being an effect" residing in the actual entity that is the effect which must be understood as having their pervasion [grasped], [then there would be no problem].

Therefore, this is not a fault. It has merely been shown that because neither of the two types of means [for establishing pervasion] is applicable, the pervasion itself is indeed untenable. In that regard, the lack of possibility for those [means] consists in the absence of any acquaintance with a valid cognition that sublates the contrary (*viparyaya-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), since such an effort is observed only in certain "Buddha-fragrances" (i.e., Buddhists). And since it cannot be stated in the present case, one should discard reliance on that [pervasion]. Furthermore, in another passage, [it is said]: "Permanence would mean either constant existence or non-existence," and so forth (PV II 180).

It should be understood that the venerable author of the *Vārttika*, while establishing the cessation [of the opponent's view] by indicating—through the force of the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the contrary—that there is a necessary connection between the mere effect and the mere instrument by excluding specificities, observes that the opponent, who asserts pervasion based on mere observation and non-observation, relies upon the strength of perception and non-perception as a means for establishing that connection; he therefore brings forward an objection based on the distinction between types of logical fallacies (*jāti*) in order to refute that reliance directly.
Therefore, since the distinction between the universals (jāti) established by the operation of perception is extremely clear, it has been stated that even resorting to a mere name is of no avail.

Alternatively, let there be a difference in genus between mountains and the like on one hand and jars and the like on the other; for this reason, it is said [in the verse]: "Whatever is established as such... (PV II 13), and so forth. But since pleasure-mountains and the like are human-made and belong to that same genus, why should they not have the same cause as those [natural mountains]? Therefore, the meaning is this: whatever is a mountain, all of it is human-made, just as a pleasure-mountain is a mountain, and Mount Kailāsa is a mountain. Anticipating the objection that in this way, examples such as small streams, great lakes, rivers, and oceans should also be inferred [to be human-made], he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with "of that which is established in the distinction of objects," the meaning is as follows:

since even the cognition of mountains and the like, based on the observation of the construction of pleasure-mountains and such, possesses a faltering movement despite being supported by reasoning, it is equal to those things in being merely a name.
Furthermore, if these mountains were established as having been built by many common men, what would be the point of proving an Īśvara, and what would be achieved here? What would be completed? [309]

If a difference in genus (*jāti*) were established, one might fulfill such an expectation by following the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established as a corollary); however, if there is no difference, even that remains without a basis. For, neither from experience nor from admission do we find that the maker of something heterogeneous to a jar of the same genus is proven to exist in another jar of that same genus; thus, the genus of these two is indeed distinct and does not bring about a common cause, despite the mere similarity of their names. Anticipating the objection—"What is this restriction that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only in the two ways mentioned and not otherwise?"—he says: "Otherwise, [there would be] a potter for some product of clay..."
If [the existence of] a creator were established because of the production of jars and the like, then an anthill would also have to be established as their creation. (PV II 15)

Thus [it is said]. For even by one who pursues the matter very far, no method for establishing a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) can be found which—while avoiding the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the potter is pervaded by all earthen objects—would establish the pervasion of the potter by all effects; this is the sense. Indeed, what obstruction to power would there be for the potter, who is capable of establishing the pervasion of all effects, in establishing that particular instance of an effect, namely an earthen object? Or, let it be granted that the apprehension of pervasion occurs only through these two modes. As for what was stated:
"Not by way of distinction, due to the force of the subverting argument against the counter-example," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that "it might be otherwise," and considering the possibility of another way to state the consequence of searching for a potter when one seeks a cloud,
he says, "otherwise," and so forth.

For when one establishes pervasion (vyāpti) in a general sense—even while proceeding with the aim of sublation—how could one then infer a potter from an earthen object, since only a cause in general would be established? Even when, in dependence upon perception, there is a pervasion of a specific effect such as a jar by a specific cause such as a potter, through the particularity imparted by the operation of the instrument, even then how could that [specific] consequence follow? And when, in dependence upon mere conceptual determination (adhyavasāya), there is a pervasion of the specific by the general, even then this [consequence] is even further removed.

If, however, by this established rule, the apprehension of pervasion occurs specifically through the particular with respect to the universal, how is it that the inference of a potter from a clay object does not result in an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? For if an over-extension occurs even from something extremely dissimilar in relation to its effect, such as a jar, why would it not occur from something slightly similar? And likewise, if there is no inference even from a similar class when one considers the perceptual determination (*pratyakṣavyavasāya*) that follows internal subdivisions due to the lack of certainty regarding the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then what can be said of an inference from a dissimilar class?

The mention of "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*) is intended to show that this is an instance of the *daṇḍāpūpa* maxim (the stick-and-cake logic), namely: "for one who has observed the pervasion in something absolutely heterogeneous. If it is objected:

"Even under both interpretations, there is no inference because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); so how can this be considered an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? We reply: Deviation is actually a supportive factor for us according to the sequence already stated, not a subverting one. For, when there is a transgression of the operation of the two means of valid cognition, or when there is exclusion from the immediately preceding category, deviation serves precisely to establish the absence of certainty regarding the intended necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

Furthermore, there are three positions regarding what is called "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*): first, that it brings about the subversion of a pervasion grasped in a general sense with respect to a restricted object; second, that it demonstrates that the very apprehension of pervasion has not occurred at all; or third, that even when the extension of pervasion exists, it merely invalidates the inference itself. For this very reason, "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) is also declared to be a defining characteristic of a logical mark (*liṅga*).

In that regard, in the first position, there would be no confidence anywhere; for even elsewhere, the hope for the probandum would depend solely on that [inference], and since that [hope] might be shattered even when certain in some cases, doubt would not cease elsewhere either, and for that very reason, its apprehension would be useless.

In the second position, however, there is a distinction regarding consciousness. For just as the pervasion of the general category of "effect" by a potter is apprehended through perception and established as being impossible to misapprehend due to deviation, so it is also by means of mere consciousness; for in that case too, there is no difference in the operation of perception.

But in the third case, since pervasion exists only when there is deviation, inference is discarded; thus, this succession of fallacies is most grievous. In this position alone, the following consequence arises: that if this probans here, while deviating from the probandum, does not remain [there], then it establishes the probandum. And no one other than one who perceives all objects directly is capable of establishing such a thing, which is devoid of the probandum.

For he either takes that very subject (*dharmin*) which does not possess such a middle term as the locus of deviation for inference, or—if all counter-instances (*vipakṣa*) are not observed—he establishes that there is indeed deviation and that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is difficult to grasp; thus, a pervasion consisting merely of the effect is simply impossible with respect to the specific cause under discussion, even if it appears sound. Once the pervasion is grasped, if there is a contradiction, there is a lack of confidence; if there is no contradiction, then for a wise person, that is the grasp of the pervasion.
And if there is no distinction [between the two], then for the intelligent, that is the grasp of the pervasion.

When there is a requirement for non-obstruction, there is no perception of all opposing factors except through freedom from fear; therefore, indeed, the method of apprehension does not consist merely in the result.
This is the summary.

Furthermore, if it is held that one first grasps a pervasion (*vyāpti*) whose object is all things, and then, by the force of a sequence of subverting arguments (*bādhaka*), establishes its own pervaded (*svavyāpya*) status within each respective class (*tajjāti*), why is that [pervasion] not likewise inferred within those classes by the force of a sequence of proving arguments (*sādhaka*)? Why do the wise enter into such a position, which is a locus for the doubt of fruitless effort? [311]
This is an intermediate verse.

That which is called "unreckoned" (*aparigaṇita*)—meaning the domain of the operation of things that is most unreckonable—must be without [logical] scope. In that regard, who, having repeatedly observed the deviation of each individual member of a multitude of effects not belonging to [the cause], would be capable of exercising an unlimited operation to restrict the cause to its own specific classes of effects? Such being the case, a thing can only be an indicator (*gamaka*) when its deviation has not been directly perceived at that very moment.

If it is argued that [the pervasion] does not hold because doubt arises [regarding supersensible causes], we say no; for in that case, one might as well achieve certainty regarding some other supersensible object. If it is argued, "How can there be doubt concerning that which has been established by perception as having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, since perception was directed toward that very class [of things]?"—then, in this way, by following the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that opposes the occurrence of doubt regarding the higher and lower universals pervaded by that [universal], the point falling under the third quarter [of the verse] follows.
Therefore, it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion of all effects by a specific cause characterized by intelligence.
The passage beginning with "siddhaṃ yādṛg" (PV II 13) constitutes the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Alternatively, it summarizes what was stated previously—that it is not possible to apprehend the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of an effect by mere effort independent of a body, because such [effort] is refuted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), and so forth. Thus he concludes that very point.

“Siddham” means: such as that [proponent] who possesses a body and so forth, and is a controller. The rest is easily understood. The intention is that such a [controller] is the object of defects such as contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*). Now, one might argue: “Since sentience is observed even in one possessing a body, it is possible for it to exist elsewhere too; thus, just as the effect and so forth are established as being pervaded by a bodied [agent], they could likewise be established by one who is merely intended. To this, [the author] replies—shattering the desire for proof based on what remains, which is nothing more than a mere name—by means of the previously stated logic regarding the difference in reality (*vastubheda*) in the case of jars and the like: [The text continues: ...in the case of jars and so forth, which differ in their actual substance...

If the word "conscious" is merely a designation for well-known agents such as potters and the like, then it is not logical to infer [consciousness] from that alone—[a term] which, while intended to be non-different [from the agent], has been set aside in view of the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, regarding the phrase "from a thing considered to be pervaded," which is either the subject under discussion or implied by the context, he asks: "How so? and replies:
"Like fire from white substances and the like."

This is the intended meaning: if there were inference from that which is not distinct [from the subject] merely by similarity of word, then why would there not be an inference of fire (dhūmadhvaja) from a pale man (pāṇḍu), who is also not distinct [from it] by similarity of word? Or, if in that case [the inference] depends upon a specific effect-nature (*kāryasvabhāva*).

[312] It is not called inference because perception excludes the pervasion by another; for if that were so, why would perception not also exclude that [inference] by excluding mere sentience? By this, when perception sets aside even another visible effect, what need is there to mention [its exclusion of] mere sentience which lies beyond the range of sight? Let it be, then, that there is indeed a distinction based on the pervaded, since such is the common experience in the world and otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Anticipating the objection, "But what fault would there be if this rule did not apply with respect to the omnipresent [creator]? he renews the previously stated point by means of another reductio ad absurdum, beginning with the words "Otherwise," and so forth. "Of the anthill" (*valmīkasya*) means "of the creature that is the anthill. "Its making" (*tatkṛtiḥ*) refers to the making of pots and the like.

The meaning is this: if, having ascertained the pervasion even by means of a specific instance, one were to infer merely consciousness as a general property (*sāmānya*), then—since the agency of jars and the like is restricted to a potter who is a conscious being, yet that [agency] would terminate in mere consciousness—the anthill-creature would also have to be inferred as the maker of jars and such things. For just as when the pervasion of jars and the like is grasped with respect to a potter, there is an inference of him [the potter] based on his non-difference from mere consciousness, why should there not likewise be an inference of the inhabitant of the anthill, since he too is non-different from others in terms of consciousness? And when...

If the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through an embodied being (*śarīrin*), then there is the exclusion of any other [such] embodied being; at that time, what need is there to mention something entirely dissimilar? Nor is there utility here for plurality, since even a single self possesses consciousness; thus there is the designation "of the anthill" (*valmīkasya*). By this, the implication that smoke and the like would also entail the inference of stomach-fire (*jāṭhara*) and so forth is made clear. And in the discussion regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*), everything should be repeated as before.

Regarding what was stated—that the arrangement and so forth pervaded by an intelligent agent are not established in the case of oceans, mountains, and the like, and that which is established there [in those things] is not pervaded—this might be said: "Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), because it involves a conceptual distinction between different properties (*dharmabheda*)? For instance, when it is argued that 'whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot,' someone might say: 'If the state of being produced residing in the pot is the reason, then it is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of sound; but if the state of being produced residing in sound is the reason, then it is absent in pots, cloths, and other composite things that are impermanent.'"

This is contradictory. Now, if the view is that [the reason] does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) just as it does not in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then it is the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). Nor does the fact that [the reason] is produced (*kṛtakatva*) lack the capacity to prove impermanence (*anityatva*) in reality; this [other reason] is likewise. For instance, by the statement "that which is established is not pervaded," there is a contradiction with the non-occurrence in the similar instance; or, if one maintains its exclusion even from the dissimilar instance, the "uncommon" nature is thereby implied.

Now, if it is proclaimed that this is not a fault at all because it conforms to the subject matter at hand (*prakṛtakārya*), then it would follow that even "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and other such reasons would fail to be proofs, and there would be a contradiction with the author of the Sūtras; for he has declared this very objection under the name *kāryasama*. As he said:

"That which points out the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a slight difference in the nature of being an effect is *kāryasama*; and this is threefold according to the intention of the speaker."
[313] Thus, by virtue of being merely metaphorical, a slight indication of otherness has been stated, and the threefold nature [of this otherness] has been shown according to the speaker's intention.

Both of these [positions] are likewise without substance. First, regarding the initial position, it has already been refuted. For it was stated that when the nature [of the pervader] is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves pervasion (*vyāpti*), even if the related entities (*sambandhin*) are distinct, they do not constitute a sublation [of the pervasion], appearing as if their difference were shaken off. However, if that [nature] is distinct, then properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), which appear as if distinct even though they are non-different [from the pervader], cannot prove that [pervader]. Furthermore, two ways of apprehending pervasion have been shown.

In that case, if—by the force of a counter-inference that subverts the contrary, just as in the case of perishability and being produced—one were to grasp the invariable concomitance of "being an effect" and so forth with an intelligent agent, then since the means of valid cognition would have functioned with respect to mere coming-into-being after non-existence and mere structural arrangement, who could rightly find fault by differentiating the subject (*dharmin*)? Thus, it is appropriate to call this a "fallacious rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*).

If, however, by the force of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) were determined to be pervaded [by impermanence] just like "configuration" (*sanniveśa*) and so forth, then who could prevent the status of being a probans for sound as well, since the operation of perception and non-perception is finalized precisely through the delineation of a specific class (*jāti-viśeṣa*)? Otherwise, even properties such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) residing in smoke, if established as invariably concomitant with fire without being delimited by a specific class, would lead to an unavoidable over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), thereby destroying one's own position.

They might encounter [this difficulty]. Furthermore, the objection that there is deviation in other instances of the probandum (*kārya*) is a most trivial counter-argument; for in that case, precisely where no deviation is directly perceived, that very thing becomes the proof—so how much lightening of the burden of faults is there?

Furthermore, it has already been explained that for one who has previously grasped the pervasion of smoke by its sole effect, there is no inference [of fire] based on ashes and the like—even in a dream—since those are never found to deviate from fire. Therefore, in view of the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one must admit that the differences among the properties of the subject (*dharmin*) and its types (*jāti*) are indeed differentiators. How then can this be called a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*)? As for the author of the Sūtras, who speaks according to logic (*nyāya*), he says:

"But when the effect is the probans even in a general sense, because it follows upon the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), the fault of asserting a difference [in the probans] due to the difference in its relata is considered 'balancing the effect' (*kāryasama*). (PV II.16)

This is the meaning: when the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) concerns only a specific object, disregarding the operation of perception, then let the statement of a distinction in "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and so forth—based on the difference from other related universals (*jāti*)—be considered a fault, for it is logically established.

Even when the probans (*sādhana*) is employed by relying on a universal, such as the mere fact of "coming into being after not having existed," which is common to all things because of the sublation of the contrary (*viparyayabādhaka*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) such as "perishability," even then the fault of stating a distinction based on the difference of related entities arises; this is because, due to observation in certain cases, there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[314] It is said without due consideration that this is considered by our teacher to be equivalent to all other cases; however, at another time, this is indeed a fault of the proof (*sādhana*), and thus there is no fault [in our position]. Now, even so, it is established that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which includes all instances is not proven. But it does not follow from that alone that the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, provided that the apprehension of pervasion has been successfully carried out merely in accordance with the opponent's own view.

For us, however, it is only the form observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that is determined as being pervaded; just as, having determined smoke seen in a kitchen to be dependent on fire (*dhūmadhvaja*), one enters into the universal [of smoke] even while it resides in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), and then, perceiving smoke in the subject of the thesis, infers fire because fire is seen wherever there is smoke, as in the kitchen—so too, although the pervasion is established for the mere class of things such as pots produced by an effortful agent, wherever [such a thing exists]...

Since it is possible to state that "the state of being an effect is observed there [in the pot] because it was made by one possessing effort," and since the proof of the probandum is thus not contradicted even in this way, what is the point of insisting on grasping a pervasion that includes all instances? If you argue that this is for the purpose of proving the futility of the original means of proof (*maulasādhana*), then it follows quite clearly that one would be taking the pervasion from one class of things and performing an inference based on a completely different class of things.

If [the reason] were based merely on the similarity of names for the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the mark (*liṅga*), then in that case, a real mark would not have been stated; there would be nothing more than the mere occurrence of words such as "effect" (*kārya*). Showing that this is incorrect, he says: "Because of the observation of a commonality of words for that which is established in another class [of things], such as 'one who exerts effort,' it is not correct to establish [a property] through that, just as [having] horns [does not prove] that speech and so forth possess the nature of a cow. (PV II 17)

Furthermore, if that [universal] were established, it would again involve the same contradiction regarding its withdrawal; so what has been avoided or accepted by this [argument]? Therefore, we see that even for that [proponent], who introduces a distinction based on the difference between types of effects within the universal, there is no actual continuity of the entity; thus, he relies solely on a mere word as his proof. Consequently, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [proof] and the proof of horns for speech and the like by means of "go-ness" (the state of being a cow).

The same verse applies to the example as well. In that case, if one wishes to avoid the objection regarding the inclusion of all instances (*sarvopasaṃhāra*), the phrase "in another class" (*jātyantare*) should be construed as "of fire, which is well-known to arise from other smoke. However, when one determines the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by unifying every form of smoke through the force of a single uniform reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), then there is no mere similarity of words; that very [fire] is what is pervaded.

[315] Since the object [of the reason] is present here as well, there is no contradiction with the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is it possible to perceive the futility of the fundamental reason (*maulahetu*) in this way. For a cognition that functions in a general manner—namely, that "wherever there is a means of proof (*sādhana*), there is a probandum"—is not capable of taking as its locus specific distinctions of place, time, and so forth, which are intended [by the proponent]. Therefore, in order to take a particular instance as the object of engagement or exclusion, one cannot remain without relying upon the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). Thus, how could the fundamental member [of the syllogism] be fruitless?

Therefore, for one who avoids the universal application (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) when grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), even smoke would not be an inferent of fire; thus, while seeking a gain, there is the destruction of the very root. For fire is not observed to be active in the production of smoke in exactly the same way in another location; rather, there remains only a similarity of words, namely that "this too is denotable by the word 'smoke' and that too is. This is no different from proving horns from the word "cow" (*go*). Now, even so, what kind of proof of horns is this from the word? Since it is sublated by perception (*adhyakṣa*), it is indeed [invalid] by itself.

If you argue that [the reason] is rejected because it lacks a locus (*anāśraya*), we reply: True, but even such a vast possibility as this occurring to you is a great gain for us! It is strange that, while you thus negate [the reason], the hope for establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) should dissolve even on account of a mere name; and it is further remarkable that, despite your laborious study of the treatises, you perceive the proof (*sādhana*) upon the peak of your own prideful words.
Why is the accomplishment of what is to be accomplished desired through mere designation?

Since even cowherd women would find this unacceptable now, he—desiring that one should have faith even in such a thing—uttered a reply intended as a jest corresponding to that [objection], thereby characterizing the entire inference of horns from speech as nothing but an improper inference.

For when even in the case of fire and the like, inference can find scope even from donkeys and such, then what is not understood from what? This is the underlying intention: provided that there is no direct contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). But surely, in the context of the process where the ascertainment of a pervader follows from the application of a term common to both the pervaded entity and [other things], what scope is there for an inference of fire from a donkey? If you argue that words such as "smoke" or "ash," which are common to entities pervaded by fire, cannot possibly apply to a donkey, we say: no, because even by the word "entity" (*vastu*) and so forth, the identity of the word-form is established; and this is as follows: [The opponent objects: "But surely, in the process where the ascertainment of the pervader follows from the application of a term common to both the pervaded entity and [other things], what scope is there for an inference of fire from a donkey? For words such as 'smoke' or 'ash,' which are common to entities pervaded by fire, cannot possibly apply to a donkey. [The author replies: No, because even by the word "entity" (*vastu*) and so forth, the identity of the word-form is established. And this is as follows: [the argument continues].

Having already refuted this by the very statement "as in the case of white objects and so forth in the fire," he says the following to satisfy [the opponent] by means of another alternative, while implicitly including that point:
[316] "Because they are dependent upon the speaker's intention, words do not exist anywhere at all."
"But if the object were established through the existence of that [convention], then everything would be established for everyone" (PV II 18).

By this it is shown that even in the case of donkeys and the like, words such as "smoke" cannot possibly apply so long as there is no desire for a convention; therefore, the absence of inference is also strictly limited to the period before the application of words such as "smoke. But once they have been applied, who can obstruct the probandum? This has already been stated. However, this is not the case when establishing a real entity (*vastu*). For indeed, where there is the domain of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the occurrence of non-invariable concomitance is impossible.
Since they are dependent upon the speaker's intention, where indeed do words not exist?
The word "vā" has the sense of "yathā" (just as).
But if the object were established through the existence of that [nature], then everything would be established for everyone.

However, when the establishment of the probandum is intended not merely from the perspective of the conventional status of things as they appear, but rather from the standpoint of the reality of awakened objects, then—as in the case of sound and other phenomena—the establishment of everything would result in nothing more than a superficial victory; rather, the point is that the establishment of everything occurs through the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in its true nature. Thus, if one states a pervasion based solely on what is observed in the example, an establishment that depends merely on verbal similarity results in nothing but non-establishment (*asiddhi*). Therefore, by one who seeks the proof of the actual entity that is the basis for real establishment, a pervasion that encompasses all cases (*sarvopasaṃhārin*) must be demonstrated.

And neither of these two [types of evidence] constitutes a valid means of knowledge for inferring an intelligent agent from the arrangement [of the world] and so forth. Even if that much were established, the specific qualities we desire would not be proven; for what purpose would learned people who seek the highest good pay heed to the designation "God" being thus asserted? This, in brief, is the meaning of the treatise. Therefore, it is established that such [an inference], even if accepted as a means of knowledge regarding impermanent things, is not a valid means of knowledge [in this case].
The commentary on the Vārtika-saptaślokī in the section concerning the doctrine of God is completed.
The establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is accomplished through three kinds of perception and non-perception;
some maintain that the nature of cause and effect is established by means of the fivefold [method]. (1)

The logical principle is that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established by means of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). In this regard, some maintain that the proof for this is threefold: either two successive perceptions whose objects are both [cause and effect], accompanied by a general prior non-perception; or two successive non-perceptions accompanied by a general perception grasping both. Others, however, [hold a different view].

They say that the fivefold [sequence] has a fixed order, such that the triad exists only when the final dyad is present. For even if the first three are possible, a cognition free from doubt does not arise for the practitioner; however, once the final dyad is attained, [the goal] is established. Indeed, the relationship between cause and effect is characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); therein, positive concomitance is perceived through the triad, and negative concomitance through the dyad.
[317,11] Success is well-established by means of the pentad. The sense is that if either of those two is not ascertained, doubt is difficult to dispel.
[317,12] To this it is said:
[317,13] If the prior non-perception [of the cause] were due to something else, such as a connection [with an obstruction], etc.,...
[317,14] It does not negate; what is the use of that negation by the latter? ||2||

Indeed, non-perception is sought precisely for the purpose of establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by means of two types of non-perception. And that [negative concomitance] must be established by this [non-perception], which subverts the existence of what is considered an effect in the absence of what is considered the cause. Furthermore, that existence is conceived in three ways:
its persistence in that very same place, its arrival from elsewhere, or its arising from a collection of factors devoid of that [cause].

If it is asked: "What is the reason for this [reasoning] to depend on such an absence of sublation (*bādhā-vaidhurya*)? It has no utility regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Rather, it was already shown that it provides assistance to the perception (*pratyakṣa*) which grasps the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," [we reply: "Is it not understood by sense-perception (*akṣaja*) that 'when this exists, this comes to be'? For there is no positive concomitance other than the existence of one thing when another exists. And since that is established by perception, what is the use here of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)?"

[Is it] by way of assistance? But in that case, would this not also apply to another [object] that has arrived by chance, since there is the possibility of mere perception? However, if perception is qualified by the apprehension of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then it is the grasper of that [non-existence], and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Well then, is that [prior non-existence]—which is of the nature of the opposite of an entity divided into three types of distinctions—established as a mere non-existence through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), or is it established as a specific kind of non-existence? In the first case, this follows:
"When this exists, that comes to be;
otherwise, it is impossible"—this is precisely the negative concomitance (vyatireka). ||3||
It does not abide there, nor is it born from another, nor has it come from elsewhere.
If an effect could exist when something is present, it would not exist when that thing is absent; thus, it belongs to nothing at all. //4//

And this is established by perception preceded by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); therefore, there is nothing to be gained by the latter two [reasons]. For even that [non-apprehension] establishes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) precisely by subverting the persistence of an effect in the absence of its cause, its production from something else, or its movement elsewhere through another effort; it is not merely the latter two [reasons], because even with a hundred [of them], the effect would still be absent in the absence of that [cause's] operation. And that—
[318,12] Since it is produced by one person alone, there is no utility for another.
[318,13] Furthermore, if the view is that the initial non-apprehension cognizes mere non-existence,
[318,14] then even when mere non-existence is sublated, the prior [non-apprehension] remains useless.
Prior to this activity of his, what exactly remains? ||5||

If there is the cognition of mere non-existence, first of all, what could have a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with what? Even the cognition of positive concomitance in the form "when this exists, that exists" is merely an incidental occurrence that obstructs utility by leading to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If, however, there is the cognition "this is the non-existence of that," then the same threefold path arrives; what remains that might render the final non-duality fruitless?

If it is argued that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is followed because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), why is this not likewise asserted regarding the operation of mere perception (*pratyakṣamātra*)? (6)

That for the sake of which one would seek [the relationship] previously—namely, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—is indeed called the "relation of cause and effect" (*hetu-phala-bhāva*) precisely because each taken individually is subject to deviation. Therefore, the possibility of each occurring even where that [effect] does not exist is a non-refutation (*abādhaka*) for both of us; this is the same for both parties.
Thus it is established.
Therefore, it is established that the first [moment] has no utility for the last two, nor do the last two have any utility for the first. This is not established.

For although one may perceive through the first moment prior to its operation that "this [object] did not exist," one does not thereby ascertain that "its non-existence is caused by the operation of this [first moment].
However, it is incorrect to claim that this is ascertained by the final moment, because the lack of utility of the first moment remains exactly as it was.
Moreover,
because of the non-existence of that which consists of those [elements], there is a final determination through their subsequent non-existence.
Since that same logic applies equally, why was it not also accepted by the former? (7)

The statement "it did not exist prior to this activity" also indicates its non-existence solely by means of the absence of that [activity] itself, as has been stated through the implication of the refutation of the threefold nature of existence (*sattā*). Therefore, if there is no certainty by means of that [prior absence], let there be none by the subsequent one either. In that regard, for one who perceives that the former [absence] is merely the co-presence (*sannidhi*) of the non-existence of both, and not the cause (*prayukti*) of the non-existence of one alone, what confidence can there be even in the subsequent [absence]?

If it follows that [the effect] would arise even in the absence of those [causes] because it does not depend on them, then the impossibility of a second non-existence is the same. Now, if it is argued that although smoke arises immediately after the arrival of both fire and a donkey, its absence when the donkey is absent is experienced by the former [observer], then [one might say] that its departure when both have departed is also experienced by the latter; thus, one must follow a succession of ever-newer means.

[319,13] There would be the loss of the fivefold classification. If it is argued that this being the case, there are three [types of non-apprehension], not two—[we reply: it is stated merely that even by the latter [definition] it is not possible. But what does it matter whether there are two or three? If it is argued that there is a purpose for the two, because certainty is impossible even in the absence of the other [conditions]? Then, at the very moment when there is non-apprehension due to the mere absence of the reason (*hetu*), that is precisely when the former [definition applies].

[319,16] Why is it not accepted that [the cognition] is also capable? If it is not, it has already been stated that this is because it is entirely useless; otherwise, one could just as well say that perception consists of three [factors], not two. Furthermore, for the proponent of five [factors], since there is no distinction due to their occurring at the same time, only the first non-perception is accepted. And since that exists even when the fire and the donkey have departed, it remains [present] even now in relation to the subsequent non-perception of smoke.
[319,19] It is indeed duality.
[319,20] Furthermore, [319,21] having previously not seen it, one perceives it sequentially; thus one understands the state of cause and effect.
Or if it were seen, it would not be seen sequentially; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. ||8||

Because there would follow an endless search for successive perceptions and non-perceptions of each preceding and succeeding instance in order to refute those various doubts, one may establish the triad and so forth as one pleases. However, perception has no utility whatsoever in validating the middle term or the non-perception, since both lack reliability when another doubt arises; moreover, the distinction between them is established by perception alone.
Therefore,
when positive and negative concomitance are ascertained through perception and non-perception,
what kind of doubt could there be regarding the established relationship between cause and effect? (9)

If they were distinct entities, then those two alone would constitute the nature of that [non-apprehension], and there would be no restriction regarding their cognition, since it could be established in either way. It might be argued that such a determination arises precisely from the firmness of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); therefore, for the non-apprehension that grasps that [absence], it is entirely appropriate that it transcends the perception whose object is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For the necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatva*) itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the object of cognition (*prameya*).

[It] establishes firmness, not multiplicity, because [the reason] is seen even in fallacious proofs (*pramāṇābhāsa*). And since the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*) alone is sufficient to prove its absolute absence when that [object] is absent, what is the use of running further? For at that time, not even a scent of smoke is conceivable. [Objection: But surely, due to the absence of many [instances], in whose absence has smoke not occurred?

If it is argued that "it must be ascertained," then perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is required precisely for this purpose; for if the absence of this [subject] were necessitated by the absence of something else, one would not take its occurrence into account. Thus, even when ascertainment is preceded by the apprehension of positive concomitance, since many possibilities exist, there arises the desire to know: "Whose presence necessitates the presence of this? In response to this, it is established through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) that since the absence of this is necessitated by the absence of that [specific thing], its presence was also necessitated by the presence of that very thing previously. In that regard, whether in the addition or the removal of each individual instance, [the same principle applies].
Or rather, it is not possible to apprehend it in that way. And this being so, there is the capacity for establishing exclusion (vyatireka) either in the preceding or in the subsequent [instance];
however, it is established that in the case of multiple applications (upanaya) and so forth, there is no capacity for either of the two.
Furthermore, this arrangement of five factors is not universally applicable; for it is absent in cases such as ashes and fire, or a potter and his jar, since the latter is missing there.

Likewise, it is established even in the absence of the former in cases such as water and its container. For instance, when one perceives the stability of a flood of water behind a dam, the determination of the causal relationship between those two—based on observing that the presence of the one results in the presence of the other—is independent of the former factor.
It is exactly so. Likewise, it should be understood that in other cases as well, it depends solely upon a triad.
