Now, why is it not imagined that, having previously been unseen, when smoke is observed in the presence of fire, it produces something else by depending on the fire? Even in this case, the fire would merely be a cause, just like the fuel. If that were so, then anything else that happens to be present by chance would also [be a cause].
If it is argued that the donkey and so forth might be the cause, and consequently there would be the undesirable consequence of inferring even that [donkey] from smoke—[we reply:

Is it because fire is ascertained to be the cause that the same must hold for the donkey? Or is it because perception and non-perception operate there as well, such that neither [of these two means of knowledge] is applicable? Nor is the recourse to the triad [of conditions] for the purpose of negating anything else in that manner; rather, [it is for the purpose of establishing the causal relationship].

[321,4] For the sake of establishing fire; and since that [fire] is established, the non-prohibition of anything else is indeed not a sublation (*abādhaka*). Non-inference, however, arises precisely from the lack of certainty regarding causality. The doubt that "a donkey never produces [an effect] in dependence upon fire" is itself not a certainty, because of contradiction, as such a doubt is of the nature of uncertainty (*saṃśaya*). Even its negation occurs only through the examination of that [specific case] and not of anything else; thus, there is no room for such a thing.

[Regarding the charge of] "nonsensical talk": But even so, since the restriction that "fire alone is the cause" is untenable, the position remains flawed. For fire is not the *only* cause, because other factors are not excluded; furthermore, fuel is also a cause from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor is it the case that [fire] is *only* a cause, because smoke can occur even when it has not yet begun to arise. This objection is not valid, because both types of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) apply.
Because it is established; for thus, when there is a cutting of another in relation to the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*), it is in relation to the substance (*dravya*).
In the case of capability, there is the proof of incapacity; and this is established absolutely with respect to the action. ||10||

For when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) characterized by that [fire] is denoted in brief by the word "fire," then the phrase "that very thing" functions as an exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). But when it refers to the substance of fire itself, if "causality" means capacity (*yogyatā*), then the phrase "it is indeed a cause" functions as an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Furthermore, if it refers to the action itself, then the phrase "it certainly exists" functions as an exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).

[321,17] This is established. And since this much operation is possible only for the threefold direct perception and non-perception, it is correct that regarding this portion, the commentary of the venerable Bhaṭṭārcaṭa alone [is authoritative]. It is also [the view] of the Blessed Vārttikakāra himself.

The making of a jar by a potter, the production of ash from fire, and [the healing] of a wound by means of medical treatises and the like—this is precisely what is meant by one who speaks [of causality]. (1.11)

But how is it that, despite the lack of distinction in being an effect, there is no inference of fire from ash as well? It is not so, because [the inference] is intended with respect to place, time, and so forth. For instance:
every effect, merely by its arising, depends upon a cause.
Another [cause] exists for the persistence of the continuum; the knower of time [acts] in dependence upon that.

In that regard, from things such as a potsherd or ashes—which depend on other factors for their very production, and precisely because they lack a continuity dependent on other factors—the time of the past presence of the cause can be determined with certainty, but not the present; thus, there is no confusion regarding activity and so forth. Furthermore, from subsequent signs such as smoke or light—which may or may not depend on specific conditions and lack a continuity—[the cause is inferred through its] material cause (*upādāna*).

[322,4] It is even more deficient for the sake of interrupting the stream [of cognition], because it operates in the present without depending on others; thus there is no fault. With respect to this, however, the effort to rely on the latter two [definitions] by the Master Dharmottara might bear fruit. But the restriction to five [types of non-apprehension] remains subject to criticism even then. Since non-apprehension preceded by perception does not depend on anything else, the first [definition] alone is superior.
The establishment of the causal relationship, preceded by the three types of perception and non-perception as summarized in the eleven verses,
composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitrapāda, is hereby completed.
The Section on the Determination of Yogins [323,3]:

Whatever is meditated upon becomes clearly manifest at the culmination of the intensity of that meditation, just as the form of a beloved woman appears to a lover. And the properties of things, such as momentariness and selflessness, are meditated upon by one who seeks the supreme human goal.

In this regard, the following is considered: let it be granted that through cultivation there is a vivid manifestation (*sphuṭābhatā*) of the mind; however, since this is common to both real and unreal objects, how can there be validity—given that even for that clarity produced by cultivation, a rule of correspondence is untenable—and how, then, can the cognition of a yogi be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

If it is argued: "Since there is no suspicion of error regarding the cultivation of an object established by inference, how could there be any room for doubt concerning the cognition produced from that [cultivation]? Let us set aside for now any hope for the efficacy of inference; even through perception, having apprehended lightning, fire, or the like, there may arise—upon reaching the culmination of the intensity of cultivation—a cognition possessing a much more stable form of that object, provided that one does not reach the limit of application toward a contrary cultivation.

And since that object has set, how can there be confidence in correspondence even when the object falls within the scope of what is presented by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Or, even if it has not set, there is no certainty that fire will persist for that duration. The same applies to the ocean and other such things; furthermore, trees and the like are seen to undergo transformation over short periods of time, and mountains and the like are altered by fires, thunderbolts, and so forth.

However, since meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) occurs by becoming fixed upon a certain state, the manifestation of clarity is restricted to that single state; therefore, with respect to its object, it is an error due to the difference in its mental aspect (*ākāra*), and thus it possesses neither validity nor the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, when even a plowman, having inferred the fire-god’s food [the oblation], makes it manifest through cultivation, that would not be a cognition of a yogin because it lacks an ultimate reality as its object; consequently, it would follow that this is merely another type of direct perception.

To this it is replied: First of all, this immediate objection is not even possible. For would meditation (bhāvanā) arise spontaneously due to the onset of passion, grief, and so forth, or would it be undertaken intentionally by a discerning person out of regard for a purpose? In that regard, since there is an absence of any report of a supreme purpose, the mere burning and cooking are accomplished simply by approaching that location through fire inferred [by smoke]; moreover, meditation would be futile even in a place where [the object] has not been touched.

Furthermore, when that [object] is cultivated, an error arises in relation to its actual nature; the same applies to cultivation brought about by grief and so forth. Therefore, how could there be the consequence of it being another type of perception (*pratyakṣāntara*)? Or, let such cultivation of an object occur in some way, like the cultivation of a horn on one's head. Even so, in the case where it is not an error, it is included within the cognition of a yogin (*yogijñāna*). For yoga is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), characterized by one-pointedness of mind; thus there is no fault. However, when the form of the horn becomes vividly manifest—as in the case of the "earth-totality" (*pṛthvī-kṛtsna*) and so on—it is indeed not perception, because it lacks a real objective basis (*nirālambanatvāt*).

Or rather, that commentary which is authoritative and concordant with what was previously determined as a real entity— that perception born of meditative cultivation is accepted [as valid], while the rest are distortions. (PV II 286)

Furthermore, as for the cultivation of a thing even when it has ceased to exist, or of something possessing another aspect by way of a stable aspect—of which it has been established that all such [cultivation] is without an objective support—that too is appropriate within the framework of the cultivation of a thing (*vastu*), but not within the framework of the cultivation of the properties of a thing (*vastudharma*). And the properties of things, such as momentariness and so forth, have been undertaken for cultivation precisely because they become manifest through the development of dispassion toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

Now, one might argue: "Since we observe discrepancies even regarding an object that has been purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it comes to the clarity produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), what confidence can there be in any other case? For, apart from purification by a means of valid cognition, this [clarity] lacks even the cause for confidence, and that [purification] is incapable of guaranteeing correspondence. This is not so, because there is a distinction based on whether the object is stable or unstable.

For an unstable entity is consumed by destruction and transformation; thus, there is no correspondence [with a stable object]. However, the properties of an entity, such as momentariness and so forth, are never interrupted; therefore, the manifestation directed toward them is always possessed of an objective support (*sālambana*).

[324,8] But surely this too is not tenable. For there is no such thing as "momentariness" (kṣaṇikatva) that exists as a real entity; or, if it did exist as a reality, then that very thing would be eternal and unconditioned, whereby everything would perish without effort. And if it were a non-entity, then that itself would be the state of being without an objective support (nirālambanatva). Therefore, even in your own view, what is called "momentariness" refers to the aggregates of momentary entities themselves, spoken of as such by disregarding their distinctions and setting aside other differences.

And this being the case, even the so-called "cultivation of momentariness" has the same meaning as the "cultivation of the multitude of momentary entities. To that extent, those very same things being cultivated become manifest; thus, the same fault remains. Now, if it is argued that although momentariness and the like are non-different from the objects, they nevertheless appear as if they were different? Even so, because of the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), it is only the properties residing in the actual entities that are being cultivated; therefore, there is no escape from that fault, since it is impossible to cultivate them as something standing apart (*taṭasthatayā*).
And thus, the very form of the cultivation is that "this collection of entities is of a nature that is disintegrating."

[324,21] How, then, can there be an avoidance of contact with a real entity even when there is a cultivation that depends upon the reality of an entity? And if there were such an avoidance, it would be merely a cultivation of a non-entity, not a cultivation of the Dharma. True. Although an entity is generally implied by the cultivation of the reality of an entity, nevertheless, there is no manifestation of that entity, because the intent culminates solely in the reality itself. For it is the cultivation of reality alone, as it becomes manifest, that is the path for the removal of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

For it is not the case that the direct perception of a beloved woman’s body brings about the contraction of passion; rather, it is her very nature as impermanent, suffering, and so forth [that does so]. Therefore, because the intention (*tātparya*) is directed toward that [nature] alone, it is that [nature] which attains clarity through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), not the object itself. Now, one might ask: even if the intention is directed there, what is the connection between the claim that the property (*dharma*) of the object becomes manifest while the object itself does not, given that both are encompassed by meditative cultivation? Or, of what sort is the manifestation of a mere property that does not touch the substrate (*dharmin*)? This is merely painting the sky; indeed, it does not produce conviction even for a common plowman.

This is not a fault, because we observe that even without touching upon the manifestation of the substratum (*dharmin*), there is a manifestation of the mere property (*dharma*) alone. It may be argued that there is simply no vivid appearance without depending on proximity to the object. However, its manifestation consists in the sudden flashing forth of its respective form within the cognition of it, without depending on effort when that object is present; yet dependence on proximity to the object is not abolished, precisely because it is a property (*dharma*), just like "dearness" and so forth.

For instance, it is observed that even in the case of the juice of the *nimba* tree and the like, the cultivation of its agreeableness becomes clearly manifest. Yet, that [agreeableness] is not an inherent property of the *nimba* itself; therefore, through the cultivation of that [idea], the *nimba*—whether remaining in its place of origin or present on the tip of the tongue—does not vividly appear as such until there is an intensification of the application of the cultivation of its opposite.

Nor is this state of being dear perceived as something neutral or external; rather, it is not experienced independently of the experience of the neem tree and so forth. Instead, whenever there is an experience of the neem tree and so on, at that very moment the state of being dear suddenly becomes an object of experience. It is not experienced as something repulsive as it was before—this alone is the meaning of the manifestation of the quality (dharma).

For instance, even when an object such as a beloved woman becomes manifest, there is no manifestation of the reality established by convention; likewise, even through the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), there is no manifestation of the external object, despite the fact that both are invariably concomitant with one another—so what fault is there? If it is argued that "belovedness" is not an external property because it is unique and because it is produced by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then to whom does this property of belovedness and so forth belong? It cannot be denied, since it is personally experienced within each individual. If it belongs to cognition (*jñāna*)?

What logic is there in the claim that the dearness of an external object becomes manifest through knowledge as something not to be feared? Even the form of the mental cultivation "this neem tree is excellent" does not mean that the knowledge itself is excellent. Furthermore, if it were the case that knowledge itself becomes manifest as dear, no one would ever experience anything unpleasant; for unlike external objects, knowledge is not something whose presence is merely occasional.

If it is argued that even cognition manifests as pleasant only for some [particular individuals], then what is the cause of this distinction? If it is caused by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), then let that practice occur only with respect to external objects. If it were independent of those, then since there would be no proximity or distance for anything at all, the mind alone would become the substrate, and thus there would be no distinction whatsoever.

In the external world, however, there is no over-extension [of the argument], because specific species such as the *nimba* tree and so forth have been made objects of repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa*). In that case, even cognition is proximate only when it has the cultivated *nimba* as its object; this is the distinction. If this is so, then the following consequence follows: whatever object is cultivated in a certain form, that object is set aside and what is proximate to it becomes manifest. Thus, for one cultivating the image of a beloved woman (*kāminī*), the consequence would be that her father or someone else who is proximate to her becomes manifest, rather than the beloved woman herself.

Now, is there some specific proximity between the object and the subject—namely, cognition—such that this would be the case? Even so, when the neem tree (*nimba*) is repeatedly practiced upon as being pleasant, its cognition will manifest as pleasant; yet the neem tree and such objects would remain just as unpleasant as before. Therefore, just as the ascertainment of an unpleasant thing like a snake is itself pleasant because it serves as a means of avoidance, while the snake itself is not, so too is this [cognition]. Thus, enough with this cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

[325,26] Now, is it your hypothesis that through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), a cognition having that object as its domain arises in a pleasant form? If this were so, then since the neem juice (*nimbarasa*) is cultivated as being pleasant, it follows that the cognition having that as its object is itself cultivated as having a pleasant form. Furthermore, its vivid appearance (*sphuṭābhatā*) consists in the sudden manifestation of the pleasant form by the cognition grasping it when that object is placed nearby—without depending on effort—but it is not the direct presence of the object itself, which remains unapproached.

In this way, even mountains and the like are to be meditated upon as momentary; thus, it is the cognition of those objects itself that is meditated upon in the form of momentariness. Its manifestation as clear occurs when the mountain and so forth are present, through the arising of the aspect of momentariness in the cognition grasping them, and not through the manifestation of the mountain and so forth when they are absent. This very cultivation of the dharma (dharmabhāvanā) culminates in the word-meaning itself; therefore, there is no loss to the subject matter at hand.

In reality, however, what is called "dearness" (priyatva) is simply the quality of producing pleasure. In that regard, when there is a cultivation of dearness toward a certain object for someone, that object—acting as a cooperative condition—produces pleasure by depending upon the appropriation (*upādāna*) of that person's mental continuum which has been refined by such cultivation. Thus, not everything is dear; rather, the quality of being pleasing is a property (*dharma*) of that very object, and it is no fault that everything is not equally pleasing. Moreover, this [dearness] arises solely from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). This same principle should be applied to other mental qualities such as compassion (*karuṇā*) and the like.

The manifestation of the cultivation of "I shall rescue the suffering one" is that knowledge which arises instantaneously upon the presence of its object; it is the cause for the production of an action corresponding to that [knowledge]. Likewise, even in the case of the cultivation of the skull as pure, the manifestation of ruthlessness is to be understood as occurring upon the approach of the skull-bowl. It does not, however, flash forth simultaneously with either a relative who is nearby or anyone else.

As it has been stated in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*: "The excellence attained through awakening, compassion, and so forth does not require such effort when that object is present; rather, it unfolds spontaneously within each individual."

Therefore, even when the practice of the dharma of momentariness has reached its peak, for as long as it must be experienced by this [yogin], it remains a form that is fragmenting and distinct from the perception of those such as ourselves. Just as our own perception and conceptualization—though directed toward something extremely similar—suddenly conform to a very sharp distinction between different locations, and our practical application follows accordingly, so too are the perception and conceptualization of the yogin directed toward two entities that differ in each moment.

Furthermore, his mind is unstained by the blemishes of passion and the like arising from delusions such as stability; thus, its clarity reaches this much. Now, one might object: "This is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*), that its degree of excellence extends only this far. To say "because it has been seen so" is no answer. Even if it has indeed been seen in this way, it cannot be maintained in the present case that its state is limited to just that much. For perhaps the excellence, being further intensified, might become manifest together with the object itself; thus, the previous defect is not eliminated.

If it is argued that even regarding [the attainment of] beloved objects and the like, there might sometimes be a different ultimate result (*niṣṭhā*), we reply: let it be so; yet, by the very thought that "it shall be," there arises the apprehension of a manifestation that transcends the desired state. However, for one who acts with foresight and is devoted to cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for his own sake or for the sake of others, his purpose is accomplished by that alone. Why then would he enter into further exertion, given that such exertion is useless and [cultivation] is productive of the goal, just as in the case of food, medicine, and the like, once the desired cooking has been achieved?

Just as in this case, even though another degree of cooking is possible, the conventional usage of the "culmination of the excellence of cooking" occurs by means of that [initial] degree alone, so it is also in the present case; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Therefore, although the manifestation of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is the substratum (*dharmin*) is accompanied by non-correspondence due to the instability of the object, nevertheless, one should not suspect such a thing regarding the cultivation whose domain is the aforementioned property (*dharma*); this is established.

If this is so, one should not object that the example of the amorous woman is inappropriate, because what is intended to be shown is merely the clarity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). For this very reason, the *Vārttika* says: "like [the clarity of] disgust, detachment, and passion."

In that case, is that yogic cognition distinct from sensory cognition or non-distinct? And what follows from this? On the view of non-distinction, there would be no such thing as a distinct type of perception called "yogic cognition," because it would be subsumed under sensory cognition itself. Nor can its classification as distinct be established on the grounds that it arises in a mental continuum refined by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), for otherwise it would follow that other types of perception—such as those resulting from the refinement produced by elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like—would also have to be classified as separate types of perception.

Furthermore, on the view that there is a distinction [between ordinary and yogic perception], the claim that the knowledge which directly realizes momentariness arises from meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) while other knowledge does not, is a "virtuous" purification [of the system]. For if sensory perception itself were to realize instability at that stage, what would be the use of yogic knowledge? Moreover, its realization of momentariness is not accidental; rather, that realization occurs when clarity has been brought forth by meditative cultivation. And meditative cultivation does not apply to sensory perception, but rather to the mental faculty (*manas*). If direct realization were obtained even without such cultivation, then meditative cultivation would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, are those two [the subject and the property] at different times or at the same time? In that regard, their being at the same time is untenable. For the momentariness of the substratum (dharmin) presented by sensory cognition must be directly realized through an experience arising from meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). Otherwise, for one who directly realizes the property and the substratum independently, the refutation based on the substratum would be unavoidable. Moreover, it has already been explained that the function of the cultivation of a property does not lead to the direct realization of the thing itself, unlike [the cultivation of] a neem tree or similar objects.

Therefore, the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*) is indeed superior to the domain of sensory cognition. Thus, there is a fixed temporal distinction: first, sensory cognition grasps the substratum (*dharmin*); subsequently, mental cognition grasps its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*). If there is a difference in time, then because the latter, in relation to the former, grasps what has already been grasped, it lacks validity when the object is the same. However, if the objects are different, then mental cognition, proceeding toward something other than the domain of sensory cognition, presents the substratum independently; yet even so, there is no escape from the aforementioned defect.

To this we reply: First, regarding the first position, there is no refutation of the entity (*vastu*), because such a specific person who is to be proven is already established. Nor is there a refutation of the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*), because that specific state, being the very object of proof and transcending the nature of the world, is designated as distinct from the sensory cognitions common to ordinary people, in order to demonstrate the specific means for its realization.

Nor does the treatise achieve its purpose through a mere inclusion under the term "sensory cognition" (indriyajñāna), as if it were a specific state produced by elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like resulting from the purification of the bodily channels (*koṣṭhaśuddhi*). For this very reason, there is no mention of a distinction even in comparison with the specific states produced by collyrium (*añjana*) and so forth, because such a specific state would not transcend the nature of the world.

For, depending on the purpose, it is indeed accepted that even that which is generally subsumed under a single category may be specified according to its distinct types—as in the case of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), which, though included within the aggregate of formations associated with consciousness (*samprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*), are treated separately; or as in the case of the afflicted mental cognition (*kliṣṭamanovijñāna*), which, though included within conceptualization (*vikalpa*), is distinguished. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in the position that sensory cognition and the cognition of a yogi are non-different. That very same [cognition] is "sensory cognition" in relation to the form of the substratum (*dharmin*), and "yogi-cognition" in relation to the property (*dharma*), just as the direct perception of a substratum itself is termed "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*) in relation to a negation.

Even on the view that there is a distinction [between perception and conceptualization], there is no possibility of the objection based on the appearance of stability versus its opposite; for even sensory cognition, while grasping an object in its entirety, grasps it precisely as having a fragmented nature. Furthermore, the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) was previously difficult to obtain, whereas now it has been brought about by the mind, which has attained proficiency by relying on the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the distinction.

But surely, since even the sense faculty acquires an unsurpassed distinction at that time, who can prevent its experience of distant or subtle objects, as in the case of an external yogi? For even those devoid of supernatural powers may perceive things in such a way to some small degree due to the projection of certain karma. Furthermore, among existing moments, even the slightest dissimilarity must necessarily occur; otherwise, if there were similarity in every respect, it would follow that they are identical in essence (*tattva*). Therefore, since the goal is accomplished by sensory cognition alone—which is capable of discerning such subtle differences—knowledge of a yogi is useless.

By this, the direct realization of suffering, selflessness, and so forth, has been explained. Furthermore, since it is impossible for a sense faculty to exist without a human body, let it be that the cognition of a yogin is not produced. That too is incorrect; for a discerning person engaged in worldly conduct, relying on the power of the eye brought about by mere possibility, cannot abandon the path that takes recourse in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Or rather, it is precisely that [sensory cognition], aided by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), which establishes such a capacity of the sense faculty; thus, even though sensory cognition shares the same status as the cognition of a yogi—which is unavoidable—there is no fault whatsoever in it. If it is argued that one of them is redundant (*vaiyarthyam*), then which of these two, both of which possess the property of being brought forth by their own causes, should fear redundancy in its own operation and consequently cease? Just as in the case of seeds and so forth when they have reached their final moment.

If it is argued that one [of two cognitions] must be invalid (*aprāmāṇya*), then let one among the seeds and so forth also be a non-cause. If it is asked, "Since all possess equal capacity, which single one can be established as the non-cause?", then in the case of two cognitions possessing the power of discernment, why should one be rendered invalid? If it is argued, "Let neither be valid with respect to each other," then it is the same for the seeds and so forth: let not even one possess causality.

The so-called "apprehension of what has already been apprehended" does not exist at all. If it is argued that this is therefore a fault, we say no; for that [fault] is accepted only when there is a difference in time. Indeed, the term "apprehension of what has been apprehended" refers to that which was already grasped, not to what is being grasped. Just as one who performs an action already completed is not considered an agent, whereas one who performs an action while it is being done is indeed an agent—just like a seed and so forth. Therefore, this fault does not apply to the position that [the cognition and its object] are simultaneous.

If it is argued that even so, there would still be the undesirable consequence of the manifestation of two forms, we reply: True. First of all, the form of the true cognition is indeed co-spatial with the object, for otherwise the cognition would result in being an error. Therefore, who is capable of determining by what manner those two non-obstructive forms manifest? As it has been said: "The range of the yogis is inconceivable" (PV III 532).

Thus, since there is no supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no occasion for either [position]: "What is undesirable? or "What is not a fault? If they occur at the same time, then how is the fault of independence—which was stated regarding the lack of dependence on sensory cognition—to be avoided? It is not a valid answer to say that it will be avoided precisely by depending on the senses; for in that case, that [cognition] would also be nothing other than sensory cognition itself, because it would follow the activity of those [senses]. There would be no such thing as "yogic cognition" at all.

[329,10] Therefore, it is better to accept only one [of these]; thus, the position of their distinction is not tenable. This is not so; for let there be no dependence on the sense organs. Just as the visual faculty (*vīkṣaṇa*) proceeds toward the production of its own cognition by depending on a suitable location situated according to its own capacity, so too will the mental faculty (*manas*) proceed, because non-contactual operation (*aprāpyakāritā*) is common to both, and because at that time, even space (*namas*) is accepted as being possessed of an object (*arthavattā*).

However, the mental continuum of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) does not possess such power; for the mind, unlike the eye and the ear, cannot produce cognition by reaching an object located in a suitable place through such spatial restriction while depending on that object as a cooperative condition. Thus, there is no over-extension [of the principle].

In that state, however, who is capable of determining how far the proximity of the object extends even for the mind—just as it does for the ears and eyes? Only this much is said: to whatever extent an auxiliary object capable of imparting its own form can be apprehended by it, to that extent it becomes the object of that [cognition] through a form that is momentarily distinct from that of ordinary people. This being so, the form of the object is produced by the object itself and not generated by mental cultivation; thus, there is no suspicion of non-correspondence.

[329,20] If it is argued that while the capacity of the eye and so forth is indeed observed in making very distant objects their range, the mind does not possess such capacity by transcending the senses to take all things as its object—this is not so, because [the knowledge of others' minds and the like] is possible. If it is argued that even this is not accepted by some, we reply that it is improper to reject something merely on the grounds of it being unseen. If it is argued that there is no means [to achieve such knowledge], we reply that even in the absence of a means, there is no other means than the mere non-perception [of one].

Therefore, the point of this objection is that if it were so, then even on the position that there is a distinction between the sensory cognition and the mental cognition of yogins, there would be no successful resolution (*nirvāha*). However, a resolution has indeed been shown in another way. This being the case, there is no fault even on the position of a difference in time, provided that [the mental cognition] first functions as a mental cognition and functions by transcending the path of the senses. As for sensory cognition, it does not cause distress even if it lacks validity in relation to that [mental cognition]; so enough with this elaboration.

Thus, in the case of the knowledge of a yogin, because it pertains to the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), its appearance as an object is indeed produced by the object itself. Furthermore, through such cultivation, a certain extraordinary power is bestowed upon his mental continuum—just as a specific ointment is applied to the eye—by virtue of which he possesses a vision not shared by other people, as was stated previously. If, then, the knowledge of a yogin is produced solely by an object, what is the status of his thorough knowledge of the past and the future? This is the result of failing to penetrate the context of the discussion.

For the introduction to the cultivation of the nature of things was made by way of the authority of a *sarvajña* (all-knowing one) who knows what is necessary, not with reference to the position of an omniscient one regarding everything. Therefore, even the non-perception of the past and future does not constitute a contradiction, since the cessation of suffering is established by that much alone, and because it enables the introduction of unshakable teaching for others.

Furthermore, as for the objection raised against the cognition of a yogin—having first established its direct realization through the cultivation of the reality of momentariness and so forth within the central circle (*kaṇikā*), and then by cultivating all things that possess those properties (*taddharmin*) to produce a cognition having their form—that objection is indeed to be disregarded, because it falls outside the arguments found in the *Vārtika*, the *Bhāṣya*, and other such works.

Otherwise, if it were intended that the cultivation of eternal suffering and so forth has already been undertaken, and that this very cultivation bestows omniscience regarding everything, then how could its refutation have been undertaken with such effort in the *Vārtika*?

And [is this not stated] in the Bhāṣya with the words, "We cannot know [it], therefore contentment is desired"? However, if—upon reaching that state—the internal organ becomes free from obscuration, and due to an excellence of compassion, one becomes intent on praying for the welfare of others in all their aspects; then, in a mind that ranges over the entire field of experience and in which enthusiasm has long been firmly rooted, there will be the attainment of such a specific means that, by practicing it, a clearer cognition will arise—one that takes every object as its domain down to each individual atom, according to its location and time, and in accordance with each particular state.
In that case, there is no lack of correspondence caused by a deviation from the object, nor is there a lack of objective support (*nirālambanatva*), because it is the objects themselves that appear.

If it is argued that the determination of an objective support is based on both its production and its similarity [to the cognition], then [if one asks] "how can something belonging to a different time be an object of apprehension?", they understand that it is indeed the state of being an object of apprehension.

Because of the statement: "Those who know the reasoning [hold that] causality alone is capable of imparting the form to the cognition" (PV II 247), it follows that similarity (*sārūpya*) by itself is ineffective; how, then, can the objection regarding the lack of an objective support (*anālambanatva*) be avoided?

That is incorrect. Indeed, that definition—given in the context of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) with respect to external objects—is intended to negate the apprehension [of an object] by a cognition that arises simultaneously and is not assisted [by the object], as the present discussion proceeds in that manner. In reality, however, whatever appears in a cognition is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*). Just as in sensory perception there is an external object, whereas in other cases there is one's own form (*svākāra*), for the apprehension or non-apprehension of perception depends on what appears; such is the commentary on the first chapter.

In this context, what is called the "appearance of the external" is merely the arising of its form (*tadākāra*). For it is simply from the experience of the emergence of an externally distinct form that the thought "this has been seen" occurs. Indeed, at the time of its conceptualization, no further arising is required, because that [arising] is determined later either through the attainment of a result or through the absence of both. And that arising of its form occurs, in the case of sensory perception, from the object; in the case of an error, from a distortion; and in the case of conceptual construction, from latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

In that regard, with respect to external objects, there is correspondence when [cognition] is produced by the object, while elsewhere there is error; however, with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is a rule of correspondence everywhere. Therefore, since correspondence with the intended object does not exist in a cognition without being produced from that [object], nor is there a similarity of form (*tādrūpya*) [without it], one must seek production from that [object] in such cases. For this very reason, having the form of that [object] alone is the criterion of validity (*prāmāṇya*); and since both similarity of form and production from that [object] constitute the definition of what is cognizable, the two are not contradictory.

But where there is a cognition that possesses the form of an object and is inseparable from the true nature of the object—occurring as if in a true dream due solely to the power of a specific cultivation and the presiding influence of a deity—there nothing at all arises [from an external object]. As the *Vārttika* states:
"Thus, regarding form and so forth, and likewise the mind, this investigation of the grasped and the grasper is for those of impure intellect; the state of the yogis is inconceivable. (PV III 532)

Thus, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the persistence of the object of cognition occurs externally through both similarity and production; for a yogi, it occurs through similarity alone; and with respect to its own nature, it occurs through mere capacity—this is the logical principle. If, then, there were a manifestation of the own-nature of the future and the past, they would necessarily be present.

[331,16] Now, if it is argued that because the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is not present, cognition itself takes on that form and is therefore necessarily without an object (*nirālambana*), that too is not the case. For even when an object is not present, if cognition conforms to its place and time through the power of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), how could it be without an object? Because, through a specific mode of manifestation, there arises a conceptualization of temporal difference, and since one is restricted to an activity corresponding to that [manifestation], one attains it. As the *Bhāṣya* states:
"Just as it was seen as conjoined with the autumn season and so forth, so for that [cognition] there is no sublation" (PVA II 615).

Or rather, having intentionally entered meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*) for the sake of perceiving the nature of objects that possess temporal distinctions, there arises upon emerging from that absorption a determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding those temporal distinctions. As it has been said:
"Whatever he desires to know..."

And so forth. However, even effortless (*anābhoga*) cognition is not contradictory in this sequence. Furthermore, because cognition alone manifests in reality, there is no consequence of its being [restricted to] the present, just as in the theory of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*), where it is the very nature of the object that manifests. And although even in the case of the present, it is only the form of the cognition that manifests, nevertheless, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) therein occurs precisely as "present. The same should be understood regarding the distinctions of distance, proximity, and so on.

In that regard, validity exists when there is a necessary correspondence with the attainment of what was determined; otherwise, there is error, as in the case of a beloved in a dream and so forth. Furthermore, there is no need for consideration regarding the conceptualization of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice as a means to attain heaven through intuition, because there is simply no manifestation of the future object in its clear form. Nor is there, in such cases, any certainty for a discerning person engaged in worldly activity regarding the necessity of attaining [the result].

If it is asked, "Even when this has been introduced, what is the certainty?"—well, whose certainty is being considered here: that of the person in question, or someone else? If it is that of the former, then just as for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) there is a cognition of the means of proof from which all suspicion of error has been completely dispelled through repeated practice, so too for a yogin, why should the appearance of future, past, and other objects not occur due to extreme cultivation? If, on the other hand, it is the certainty of another, then this follows: as long as another's cognition of its validity has not occurred, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As long as [a cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so long there can be no non-erroneous realization of the validity of another; thus, nothing would ever be a *pramāṇa*. Therefore, one should not be subject to the tyranny of mere verbal assertion. Consequently, since the specific distinction of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) accompanied by particular means does not manifest directly, doubt arises only regarding the establishment of such [a state], but once it is established, it cannot be undermined by defects such as being "without a basis" (*nirālambanatva*).

Furthermore, having raised the concern that even if an external object is not grasped by conceptualization, it might nonetheless appear clearly as an object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), [the opponent] asserts: "That which is grasped by inference and that which is determined—both are exclusions of others (*anyanivṛtti*) and not real entities (*vastu*), because if they were to penetrate the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), an appearance capable of being associated with verbal expression would be impossible. This too is incoherent.

For instance, whether in one way or another, worldly practice proceeds under the influence of Buddhist tenets; just as in the cultivation of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the form of a beloved woman, the production of a final, pure moment of a grasped object characterized by momentariness is nonetheless unavoidable. If, however, you will argue that such a state of exclusion (*apoha*)—which rests solely upon the bed of the conceptualization of momentariness—does not cognize the conceptualization of a beloved woman and so forth, we shall accept it exactly as you say. Nor is the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) merely the negation of a non-entity;
for even in the view of Dharmottara, the established position is that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of determination.

[332,21] Is it not the case that the form of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is "fire is perceived by me"? And therein, the manifestation of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—this is a rash claim, because conceptualization and determination have the same object. True; however, it is not said that the particular characteristic is determined merely because it manifests therein. If there is no manifestation, then since there is no cognition, how can there be determination? Even if there is manifestation, that is merely an appearance (*pratibhāsa*); how then can it be determination? Furthermore, appearance and determination do not even have the same object.

For *pratibhāsa* (manifestation) is direct flashing forth; even when there is no flashing forth, it is the making of something an object of activity through the power of delineating a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). According to the Commentary, this is "determination" (*adhyavasāya*). Therefore, that which is suitable for execution is the "object of determination," and it is precisely that which has entered into conformity with the form being manifested. And that [object] is, in some cases, merely superimposed, while in other cases, it is the actual nature of a thing.

But as for the subject at hand, since it accepts the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must be of the nature of a real entity (*vastu*); so how can it be said that "mere exclusion (*nivṛtti*), which is a non-entity (*avastu*), is what is determined"? Let this persistent insistence on an irrelevant point rest for now. Furthermore, the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) in conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is of an excluded form, not of mere exclusion, provided one follows the dictates of experience; otherwise, anything whatsoever—such as a *rākṣasa* or the like—might appear at all times.

Furthermore, through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is a transformation into the determined aspect (*adhyavasitākāra*) which is uncontradicted; in that case, there is objectlessness (*nirālambanatva*) with respect to the mere superimposed object of determination (*adhyavaseya*). However, when [the transformation occurs], that very [aspect] is the objective support (*ālambana*), as was stated immediately above.

As for what you said—that the status of an object as an objective support (*ālambana-pratyaya*) with respect to consciousness is pervaded by its dependence upon a sense faculty (*indriya*), and that this [dependence], being withdrawn from it by the perception of its own contrary (*svaviruddhopalabdhi*), also withdraws the object's status as an objective support—this displays great cleverness, in that you clarify the "perception of the contrary of the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*) without having first established through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the relationship of pervasion between the status of being an objective support and dependence upon a sense faculty.

If it is argued that "it is because [the object] is seen thus," then let us simply abide by what is seen and not seen as our authority; why this obsession with adducing such a formal proof? Therefore, we see no subverting argument if an entity were to assume the status of an objective support (*ālambana*) even without depending on the sense faculty. Now, as for what was said here: "Indeed, a specific kind of fuel is not the cause of smoke; even without fire, it would produce smoke through thousands of refinements."

Otherwise, if that [cognition] were produced from the object alone, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the abolition of inference, which is the cause for establishing all effects. Therefore, cognition also possesses the property of arising from an object that is dependent upon the sense faculty.

If it is argued: "Since its existence is not present when there is an absence of sensory activity—even while all other causes are present—it is established that [the cognition] is dependent upon them; therefore, how can an object that is independent of the senses serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for its own cognition?"—this too is refuted by the possibility of knowing another's mind. Furthermore, those who know another's mind are accepted by everyone except the Cārvākas and Mīmāṃsakas. As for the Cārvākas and others, since they themselves harbor doubts [on this point], there is no other recourse.

And in the case of doubt, it is impossible for [the reason] to be invariably excluded from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). But surely, because the effect of cognition is necessarily dependent upon the sense faculty, there can be no doubt regarding anything else, just as smoke is dependent upon fire?

If such is the case—that the causal complex required for visual cognition to depend upon sight does not lack even a fraction [of its components] when it comes to the specific movement of footless beings like snakes that depends upon their feet—then why was the example of smoke not capable of negating the movement of those very snakes? Or else, how could the task of neutralizing poison and so forth, which for some is accomplished through a succession of forceful mantra-recitations accompanied by the activity of hands and other limbs, be achieved by another through mere meditative absorption (*samādhi*) alone? Furthermore, smoke is never observed to arise from fuel independently of fire, such that one might suspect the same here as well.

Therefore, external entities, insofar as they are perceived through the relation of cause and effect, possess a fixed mode of occurrence; however, the manifestation of the mental continuum is indeed diverse due to the power of the formative forces (*abhisaṃskāra*) of various karmas. Consequently, it is impossible to restrict that its effects depend on the same conditions in one case as they do in another.

How, then, could there be a total absence of the cognition of another's mind and so forth? Moreover, if the sense organ does not produce cognition independently—just as fire does not exist without smoke—then even with respect to its own object, the capacity for loud proclamation, observation, and the like would be utterly deficient. For instance, as long as the means such as smoke produced by burning fuel are perceived only within a certain range, they lack the power to extend beyond that range.

In this way, up until now, it has produced the perception of objects, sense-faculties, and so forth within our own location; how then could it produce such perceptions in vultures and other beings beyond that range? Furthermore, the causal complex based on the mental continuum is not capable of reaching the stage of burning fuel, nor is the cognition capable of reaching the stage of smoke.

Therefore, why is it not possible that even when there is a deficiency of auxiliary causes—as if they were excessively obstructed—something might still arise from some particularity? If it is argued that this distinction is produced by birth (*jāti*) and does not depend on the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), we say no; for birth itself has as its nature the bringing about of various forms precisely through the sovereign influence of diverse karma, and since karma is not other than the mind, the dependence upon the mind is not avoided.

Now, because the sense faculty functions by reaching its object (*prāpyakāritā*), it is said that the entire causal complex for the production of consciousness occupies a common location. Nevertheless, why is it that [the visual organ] reaches such a distant location in some cases—such as when there is contact with the rays of light entering the eye—and in other cases comes to rest at a much nearer point? What can be said here other than through the sovereign power of karma (*karmādhipatya*)? Therefore, the capacity of the mental continuum (*cittasantāna*), which is the basis of that [faculty], is indeed diverse.

For even externally, this is not possible. Otherwise, between two lamps situated in similar locations, one might have a mass of rays extending far away while the other’s rays move only nearby. If it is argued that this could happen through the power of a mantra, and that such a mantra also induces dullness in the sight of a reptile, then that power belongs to the mental continuum itself. Even in the case of a mantra, its efficacy is produced solely by the greatness of the person.

As established in the *Vārttika*, even though mantras are not of human origin, they do not possess efficacy independently of persons; therefore, it follows that it is the person alone who, by means of mantras and other such instruments, establishes the capacity of external objects. Given this, what is impossible in the present case? Furthermore, just as the status of an object as a cognitive support (*ālambana*) is observed to depend on the eye and is thus accepted as being restricted to that [condition], so too it is observed to depend on light; consequently, owls and the like would not be able to see in the dark.

If it is argued that there is no fault because it is observed to be so, then you are defeated precisely by the fact that it is observed to be so. For instance, although the eye and light are equal in terms of the logic of dependence on causal factors, we observe the transcendence of one [the eye] due to the inconceivable power of the mind; this observation casts suspicion upon the other [the light] as well. However, such a thing cannot be possible if it were not observed. Now, if it is said that even though effects possess the common property of being cognitions (*jñānatva*), they nevertheless partake of different specific classes (*jāti*) and therefore do not arise without depending on a difference in the causal complex (*sādhanasāmagrī*).

But by what means have you been deceived into thinking that even this extraordinary (*alaukika*) knowledge under discussion shares the same genus (*ekajāti*) with the knowledge of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)? If you argue that there is no difference in genus precisely because that [extraordinary knowledge] is non-existent (*asattva*), then [we reply]: since there is no difference in genus due to its non-existence, the restriction [of perception] based on the sense faculties would be possible; thus, there is a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*).

Therefore, for people like us whose experiences arise from common karma, the dependence upon the sense faculties—which is the pervader of being an objective support (*ālambanatva*) with respect to the differentiation of experience—is not capable of negating mere experience by its own cessation, because the establishment of pervasion occurs only with reference to specific [conditions].

Now, if it is claimed that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by unifying mere experience (*anubhavamātra*), then, because there is no subverting evidence for the contrary, pervasion itself is not proven. Furthermore, the basis for the necessity of cause and effect is destroyed, because it is impossible for [mere experience] to be common to smoke and so forth; for mere experience arises from a mental continuum possessing inconceivable power due to the impressions (*abhisaṃskāra*) of diverse karmas. Moreover, if one relies on a particular [instance], the pervasion does not include all cases; thus, that very same fault remains, namely, what is called "possessing particularity" (*viśeṣavattva*).

Furthermore, as for what he said: "Since it is observed that the capacity to produce clear cognition belongs to a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that has a non-existent object and is independent of an external object—as in the case of those afflicted by passion and so forth—it follows that even a cultivation with an existent object is capable of producing such cognition independently of it; thus, it is impossible to understand that an external object functions as an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*)."

In that regard, what is this "independence from an object"? Is it (1) not having an object as its domain, or (2) not appearing directly as an object, or (3) not having an object as its cause, or (4) deviating from an object? These are the possible positions. Regarding the first position, it is contradictory to claim both that [the cognition] has a real object (*bhūtārtha*) and that it lacks an object (*aviṣayatva*); for, just like the inference arising from it, it too has that object as its domain in terms of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

However, with respect to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), let it not be that the object of that [appearance] is the external thing; for it is desired that the object of the cognition produced by that [appearance] is indeed the appearance itself. Thus, the second position is also untenable. The third is impossible, because that [cognition] also has the real object as its cause, by way of the inference arising from itself. For this very reason, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is also established; thus, the fourth position is not tenable. Therefore, since the cognition produced by that [object] is invariably consistent (*saṃvāda*), how could the status of the object as the objective support (*ālambanatva*) be impossible to understand? Consequently, the objection is sound according to the ancient method, and the refutation has already been stated.

Furthermore, as for his effort to refute the cognition of past and future things by arguing that only those objective moments which are actually present can logically be grasped by him, and not those that are prior or subsequent—that has already been refuted. However, regarding the position of the Omniscient One under discussion, the proof of the thesis is established simply by this much: that however many things produce a cognition, they are experienced as falling within the scope of one's own knowledge precisely in the form of momentariness, suffering, and selflessness.

Regarding things that have passed away, there is recollection; regarding things yet to come, there is merely anticipation. If it is asked: "If there is only recollection regarding the past, how can there be a clear manifestation (*sphuṭībhāva*) of the aspects of origination (*samudaya*"? [The answer is: The five aggregates themselves are "origination" in relation to what follows. In this context, the very clear manifestation of the aspect of origination is a certain mode of radiance—a cause for the immediate production of corresponding conceptualizations, practical applications, and so forth—when those [aggregates] have become present in relation to what is subsequent, by which one becomes distinguished from ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), as before.

And in the same way, there arises a clearer recollection regarding past [moments]. However, the realization of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) occurs by means of its own nature alone, independent of anything else, through aspects such as momentariness and so forth. If it is argued: "Since conceptual cognitions (*vikalpa*) cannot occur simultaneously by their very nature, when there is the determination (*avasāya*) of the aspects of suffering, there can be no determination of the aspects of the Origin (*samudaya*); and subsequently, that determination would be without an object," this is true. Yet, even for each individual Truth, the conceptualization of its four aspects does not occur at one and the same time. And there is no fault whatsoever in this.

Indeed, it is the very particular mode of apprehension, when its entire form has become manifest, that constitutes direct perception (*sākṣātkaraṇa*). For from this arises the manifestation of the intended conceptual construction, which is interspersed with the seeds of conceptualization. Just as for a person seeing a blue lotus blooming on a mountain, there is no obstruction to the direct perception of all the aspects of that object through a sequence of conceptualizations, so too should it be inferred in the case of [the yogic] intuition (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Furthermore, the moments, though distinct from one another, are directly perceived by your very successive experiences.

Furthermore, conceptual constructions proceed according to one's inclination in the form of grasping and subsequent synthesis; it should be understood that the state of omniscience is established by experience alone. In this same way, regarding the truths of cessation and the path as well, everything should be inferred based on their being known through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Furthermore, as for the objection that seeing everything would follow from seeing a few things by way of the mutual relationship—whether direct or indirect—between all entities, that is already refuted simply by not accepting [the premise]. However, if there were a conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) whose object is the totality of all things by way of such a relationship, acting as a qualifier, and if at that stage it were possible to remember a succession of births, we see no fault in this.

Just as for one who has practiced [meditation], upon seeing fire and so forth, there arises an immediate conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that "this is the effect of fuel" and "this is the cause of the fire," so too let there be clarity (*vaiśadya*) even for those things grasped by conceptual construction when there is an intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). However, we do not maintain that from the mere perception of one thing, there follows the perception of another simply by virtue of their relationship. Or, let there be no clarity at all; for omniscience is fulfilled by the mere conceptualization of all objects, provided it is consistent with reality, even while remaining in that state.

Alternatively, [perception], which has as its object only its own objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), is the cause for the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object qualified by all things. Therefore, even though it is non-conceptual, it comes to have all things as its domain because its activity is followed by such a determination. As it is said: "Those of great intelligence determine all aspects from the very moment of perception" (PV II.107).

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Whence comes this power of an experience that takes only a few things as its object, such that there is a determination of all things? If it is argued that it is "due to the removal of the veil of passion and so forth," then one would simply perceive things as they truly are; however, it is not logical for him to possess, on this basis, the skill to produce a determination of all things without exception. For while impurities are easily found to obscure reality, they do not constitute an obstruction to the production of conceptual discourse.

In this regard, the inquiry is as follows: when an object is being perceived, is it simply that no conceptual construction (vikalpa) is observed, or is it that such construction is prevented by afflictions (kleśa)? Neither of these two cases exists. For nowhere is there a conceptualization of every aspect [of an object] as there is in direct experience; nor does the absence of such conceptualization occur without the intervention of afflictions. Indeed, when an agreeable object is seen—even if it possesses faults—the non-conceptualization of those faults is then said to have passion (rāga) as its cause.

Furthermore, when there is no conceptualization of qualities even toward an unpleasant object that possesses them, that is aversion (*dveṣa*). However, when there is no practice, the failure to conceptualize all real forms is caused solely by delusion (*moha*). Nor is this an obscuration like that of a blanket or similar objects; rather, it functions by instilling a defect in the mental continuum. Therefore, to the extent that delusion and the rest are overcome, to that same extent, through effort and the removal of defects, when the cognitions possess determinate ascertainment regarding those aspects, then—ultimately—if they were to occur regarding all aspects and all things, there would be no contradiction whatsoever.

Because memory is possible even for things previously seen or remembered through a succession of mental acuity, and because a more intense impression of memory is deposited when things are being perceived, and because birth is without beginning or end, and because a single type of certainty has the nature of determining all things of that same class, there is no fault arising from the non-arising of conceptualizations regarding all objects.

And as for what was said: "That [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because while it possesses extreme clarity, it is produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); for whatever cognition is produced by cultivation and possesses extreme clarity is not a valid means of knowledge, just like the clear cognition of an object cultivated after having inferred it. In that regard, since it has already been shown that there is no such thing as meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding fire after one has inferred it, the example is non-existent.

And as for this poetic composition of his: "There is here the application of the cultivation of the thought of fire by one whose body is extremely sluggish due to the cold accumulated by the weight of winter. In that case, if the emergence of the cultivation occurs through a mental absorption of one's own due to being afflicted by sluggishness, then what talk can there be of inference? For inference is sought as that which possesses the proficiency for purposeful action.

If one is thus incapable [of direct perception], what is the use of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)? Or rather, let there simply be the manifestation of that [object] as it is; where then is there room for inference? For it is not possible that a lover would fail to apply himself to cultivation until he has inferred the presence of his beloved. Therefore, let the example be merely the cognition of fire produced by cultivation in one afflicted by dullness. Even that is surpassed by the example of the beloved, which is adorned by its own poetic imagery.

Nor is it a logical principle that because one cognition arising from meditative cultivation is non-authoritative due to its being deceptive, another [cognition] that is non-deceptive should also be non-authoritative; for if that were so, it would follow that every instance of sensory perception would be non-authoritative, like the optical illusion of seeing hair-tufts and the like.

Furthermore, regarding that which was elaborated to establish the rule of correspondence between the cause—characterized by the excellence of cultivation—and its two effects, namely the example and the exemplified: why do you not perceive that the eye itself is the common cause for both the vision of two moons and the vision of one moon? If you argue that the distinction between the two eyes is caused by the impairment or non-impairment of cataracts (*timira*), then why is there no such distinction between the two types of cultivation based on their having real or unreal objects? Is it not simply some kind of modification produced by cataracts in the eye?

If it is argued that there is some difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) or its clarity, even though the object remains the same, we say no. Since a more powerful difference in capacity (*śakti*) can be established by the distinction between the causes of correspondence and its opposite, what is the use of anything else? This is like the case of food and poison, where the perceptions of color and taste remain identical; or like the cognitions of the probandum (*sādhya*) arising from a valid reason and a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), as well as the resulting activities prompted by them. Furthermore, the mere absence of a physical change in the eye is not itself a defect, even when a change is produced by the application of collyrium (*añjana*).

[Otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of establishing [the existence of] defects. Rather, it is by virtue of being a cause of error; thus, even in that case, the distinction is produced solely by capacity (*śakti*). Therefore, in this way, it is only the state of appearing clearly (*sphuṭābhatva*) that is established through the intensification of cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*), not its validity (*prāmāṇya*), because [only then] would there be room for defects such as the unestablished nature of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*). Validity, however, arises from correspondence due to having a real object (*bhūtārthatva*), and the status of perception (*pratyakṣatva*) arises from being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous (*kalpanāpoḍhābhrāntatva*); by this much alone, the entire system corrupted by ignorance (*avidyā*) should be understood as refuted.

The author of the *Nyāyaprakīrṇaka* has already refuted the apprehension of non-existent objects by means of the very proofs for momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth. Furthermore, regarding what he said concerning the conceptual nature (*vikalpatā*) of inference: "In that regard, everything presented by conceptual constructions is unreal, because it is associated with words."

And when that [unreal] is being cultivated—when the conceptual construction belonging to you has its clarity obscured by the practice of cultivation—the state of being conceptual, which is caused by the apprehension of an object conjoined with words, ceases. And upon the cessation of that, everything conjoined with all words regarding the apprehended object also ceases. Consequently, it follows that even the non-conceptual cognition of the yogin would be without an object.

In this regard, what is meant by this so-called "objectlessness" (*nirviṣayatva*)? Is it the absence of form (*anākāratā*) due to the disappearance of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyākāra*), or is it the presence of another aspect (*anyākāratā*), or perhaps, even while possessing that very aspect, there is a non-connection with the nature of that object? First of all, the first position is impossible, because it is untenable for cognition to be devoid of form, since through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding objects such as a beloved woman, one clearly perceives the very form of that object. For this same reason, the second position is also not tenable.

As for his claim that even for one afflicted by grief whose sensory faculties have ceased their activity, there would be the appearance of a father and so forth through the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a son—this is merely a confused prattle, having introduced the premise that when this [object] is cultivated in conjunction with another, the other form does not clearly manifest. For by this [cultivation], the very manifestation of clarity is entirely precluded, since cultivation is impossible without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

And since conceptual construction occurs without the association with words, where could its manifestation be made clear? Furthermore, for one who argues that the appearance of a father and so forth would follow from the mental cultivation of a son, the appearance of the son itself must indeed be admitted; otherwise, he would have to assert that even from the cultivation of a non-son, the appearance of a son would follow. Nor does a mere undesirable consequence suffice to deny what is observed.

And likewise, in the very case of the *kaṇikā* (the central dot), the lover confirms the clarity of the beloved’s form through specific words, gestures, and the composition of poetry. How else, then, would this statement—"in the state of clarity produced by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)"—be rendered meaningful? Therefore, since the manifestation of one thing does not occur through the cultivation of another, it is correct to establish their distinctness with respect to the object of conceptual determination (*adhyavaseya*).

There is no mutual [identity] between the form of conceptual construction and that which is intended as the object, because of the superimposition of oneness upon those two. For even the manifestation of what is intended as external is, in the end, merely the arising of a clear moment that is the material cause (*upādāna*) of conceptual construction. It is by means of this alone that the conventional usage occurs, namely, "that object was directly perceived by him. It has already been largely considered that a cognition bearing the form of an object is reliable only when the object exists, whereas it is unreliable when it does not.

For this very reason, the third alternative as well has been refuted; for it is impossible to define any contact with the nature of a real object by means of cognition other than through correspondence and direct perception. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the cultivation of the son" (*tanayabhāvanā*), what is the meaning of "cultivation of the son"? If you say it is the repeated placement of the son in the mind, even the meaning of "placement in the mind" is nothing other than the conceptualization of its form.

If it is argued that, in this case, what this person prattles—that while momentariness is being cultivated or superimposed, it is actually real momentariness itself that appears in the cognition of the yogi—is not so; for since there is no identity between existence and non-existence, if a true appearance were to occur despite the cultivation of something false when there is a distinction consisting in their lack of unity, then it would follow that even upon practicing the meditation on the Son of the Truth (Satyatanaya), there would be an appearance of the essential nature of some other distinct entity called "Son" due to the mere similarity of the word.

Therefore, the claim that even non-conceptual [cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it arises from the practice of an unreal object and lacks correspondence (*saṃvāda*), is also refuted; for there is simply no such thing as the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of a superimposed [object].

For just as there is the habitual conceptualization "son, son," so too, if there were a conceptualization "superimposed momentariness, superimposed momentariness," then there would be a cultivation of superimposed momentariness; but it is not so. Rather, it is "the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) are momentary. Therefore, just like the case of a real son, actual momentariness itself is cultivated. Or else, another aspect must be stated for the cultivation of a real son.

Since a conceptualization of a moment does not touch upon the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a moment, how can that conceptualization or its cultivation [be considered valid]? This is equally true for the conceptualization of a son as well. Furthermore, the determination of it being a "conceptualization of that" (the son) based on the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*) is exactly the same. For even in the conceptualization of a son, nothing other than the superimposed [mental image] appears.

Thus, this person—who, despite the appearance of a mental image conjoined with the superimposed word in the cultivation of a son, desires the clear manifestation of an actual son—rejects the subject at hand; what is this but being swallowed by the great demon of another's delusion?

And this has been stated as an equivalence in the cultivation of reality merely by way of externality, in relation to that which is superimposed as flashing forth in conceptual construction. However, from the perspective of actual external reality, the cultivation of a son by one afflicted with grief is nothing but the cultivation of what is unreal. For this very reason, that [cultivation] is invalid because it is unreal; furthermore, since at that time there is no such son, its appearing in the form of a son is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). But the cultivation of momentariness, because phenomena always have that as their nature, has a real object; thus, the clarity produced by it is a valid means of knowledge due to its non-contradiction.

Now, it may be thought that since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has a non-real object, even when one contemplates a son as a son, the clarity (*vaiśadya*) attained remains distinct [from that of direct perception]; this is not our view—such is the thought held in the heart. Let that too digest within the heart. For this *Yoginirṇaya* (The Determination of Yogis) has been commenced, and there is no harm to it regardless of either position.
