Since even in the case of exclusion (*apoha*), when it is purified by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), clarity is seen to belong precisely to the determined object (*adhyavaseya*); so what can be done here? If it is asked: "Since there is no manifestation of a real entity (*vastu-nirbhāsa*) in inference, how can there be purification by a means of valid cognition with respect to that?"—this is a different topic for another occasion.

Furthermore, this is it: cultivation (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated placement of the object to be cultivated within the mind. And that [cultivation], when practiced with devotion, for a long time, continuously, and through celibacy and austerity, becomes a firm ground and is held to produce the clarity of appearance for a conceptual cognition whose form was previously indistinct. Moreover, that [cultivation] cannot be established by one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness and selflessness. For instance, the very same kind of conceptual cognition that arises grasping the object to be cultivated ceases without leaving a trace (*niranvayam*).

And when that [preceding cognition] has ceased, a condition arising again is produced as something entirely new and unprecedented. Thus, by this reasoning, even over a thousand eons, because there is no difference in the production of what is unprecedented, no cultivation (*abhyāsa*) consisting of a formative tendency (*saṃskāra*) produced from that can arise. By this, the production of a distinguished consciousness through cultivation is explained.

For how could a preceding consciousness, having ceased without leaving any trace (*niranvaya*), produce a subsequent state that is distinct? In every way, it is only a persisting form that can be cultivated by conditions occurring in succession.

This is consistent. For there is no cause for a certain restriction other than the touch of a fierce deity that dictates: "The very same kind of cognition that grasps the object as it is—being devoid of persistence and ceased—must arise again exactly like that. If you argue that this is due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), then surely momentariness is contradicted by permanence, not by the arising of something dissimilar.

For if that preceding [moment], which ceases without a trace, gives rise to a subsequent moment that is similar to itself, then what harm is there if it produces a subsequent moment that incorporates a slight degree of distinction due to even a minute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? Indeed, you have no greater aversion to the momentariness of entities than we do; moreover, in this case as well, there exists a slight difference in the causal complex.

For instance, for one who is engaged in meditation with the specific intention of seeking the destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra—based on the mere restatement that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary"—that very intention produces a distinct result exceeding even an atom, until the final fruit is attained through a gradual sequence of degrees of intensity, just like a seed and so forth. However, if they were to remain in the middle due to distraction and the like, there would be only a gradation of dullness and so on. As the *Bhāṣya* states:
"When the formative force (*saṃskāra*) is powerful, distraction is removed."

"If distraction is more powerful, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would be turned away. (PVA II 500) If, then, there is destruction without any continuity (*niranvayavināśa*), how can the second [moment] acquire a specific quality (*viśeṣa*), given that the previous specific quality cannot be transmitted? If this is so, then even in another causal complex (*sāmagrī*), such a specific quality ought to arise, since this [quality] does not transmit itself there either. Therefore, just as that specific quality arose by the power of its causes even though it was non-existent [previously], so too is this [second moment]. If it is argued that this [second moment] is thus identical to that [first], we say no; for it is impossible to prevent a specific result from arising from a specific cause.

For instance, the first particularity arises devoid of such a particularity, whereas this one arises accompanied by such a particularity; how then could they be the same? Furthermore, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is simply untenable under analysis. For regarding that portion which has been transmitted from the cause, there is no further operation of another cause; and that very operation was previously non-existent. Thus, when a factor ceases, it does not persist; and what persists cannot cease.

How, then, can cessation and arising possess a common substratum (*sānvaya*)? If it is argued that this is because they occur together (*sahavṛtti*), then by that logic, one would have to conceive of space (*ākāśa*) as also possessing a common substratum; for there is no such thing as "togetherness" (*sahārtha*) produced merely by persisting through both times. Furthermore, that [togetherness] is not denied in the interval between a jar and its shards at the moment of their destruction.

As for the rest, it is merely the proclamation of a theoretical system (*prakriyā*) that opposes valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); so what is the use of it? Moreover, since the Self remains constant like the word "Hari," the aforementioned [notion of] excellence is untenable—this has been chewed over many times, so let it rest for now.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that practice is undertaken to settle the mind one-pointedly by abandoning distraction, yet for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), there is no such thing as a distracted mind because everything is one-pointed by virtue of being restricted to each respective object—that too is incoherent. For it is established by experience that for some, the mind brings reality (*tattva*) face-to-face; for others, the opposite occurs; and for another, it is merely a conceptual reflection upon effects and so forth.

In this context, every state of mind that is turned away from suchness—such as selflessness—is called "distracted. Since it has been stated that a mind focused exclusively on suchness is "concentrated," why is this not sufficient? Why must one necessarily seek out a single [mind] that functions within a manifold range of objects?

Nevertheless, because the apprehension of a single form as "I" is possible prior to the time of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkriyā*), that [apprehension] is also conventional (*vyāvahārika*). Even so, since the thought "the destruction of my own defects will come to pass" remains unimpeded, the engagement in the practice of the path proceeds; for the conceptualization of what is to be attained is the motivator in all cases.

If that is so, even when there is a departure from the actual state of things (*vastutathābhāva*), what prevents one from acting? If you argue that one acts because momentariness and so forth have been ascertained by such an inference, [we reply: this is not so, because certainty has not yet become second nature (*sātmībhāva*). For the mind, being dominated by the latencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless ignorance, continues to engage in conventional activity that is inconsistent with that certainty. It is for this very reason that it is stated in the *Vārttika* that even when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has been attained, there is still a requirement for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which remains to be investigated.
Therefore, prior to the attainment of that fruit, practice is accomplished by means of ignorance alone; and from practice, one becomes perfected as the omniscient one.

Furthermore, the critique of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa* from the perspective of the Yogācāra position is irrelevant, because that work proceeds with its proofs precisely by accepting external objects (*bahir-artha*). Even in that case, the sublation (*bādha*) raised against the position of universal omniscience is refuted simply by the fact that such a position is not accepted [by the author]. Moreover, that is not a genuine sublation at all, since it merely establishes a doubt.

For instance, as for what was stated to refute the status of past and future objects—that "there is no form whatsoever belonging to the non-existent"—this is indeed true for now. Consequently, it is also true that they are not apprehended by the cognition produced from them. However, it has been shown that even otherwise, the possibility [of their existence] cannot be denied, as in the case of true dreams and the like. Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no form whatsoever for the past and the future at other times, just as there is none now; if that were so, they would lack the very nature of being past or future, like a horse's mane. And the points regarding non-error and non-contradiction have already been considered previously.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāditva*) is not tenable even in your own view—since you intend non-contradiction to consist in either the perception of an object that is to be attained, or the indication of an object that is the locus of purposeful action, or the accomplishment of the manifest telic function (*arthakriyā*), none of this is possible for a cognition of past objects and the like; nor is it even tenable for a cognition of a present object under the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). That too is merely a display of envy, because it is devoid of logical justification.

If it is argued that such [non-existence] is stated because of a temporal separation between the future and the past, then this same consequence would apply even in the case of spatial separation; thus, even in a location suitable for activity, the indicator would be invalid. If you say, "That [object] at least exists [in another time]," but something else—whether future or past—is not present at that time, then it is the same: even if it were present in that location, it would not exist [at that time]. Furthermore, causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) is just as absent when one is not in proximity to that location as it is when one is not in proximity to that time; there is no distinction whatsoever.

Even though the present moment is instantaneous, there is no impairment of its status as a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) for conventional practice, because of the capacity for the superimposition of unity; for, from that perspective, the correspondence [of cognition with its object] is established.

Furthermore, as for the refutation undertaken by the followers of Kumārila—who, having introduced the non-perception of a cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*) regarding an omniscient being, proposed the alternatives that his cause must be either sensory cognition, mental cognition, or born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanābalaja*); and even within the latter, whether it be visual or mental—this merely demonstrates the weakness of their own hypothesis and does not result in the certainty of non-existence, as was discussed in the investigation concerning the dependence on sense organs and the nature of the objective support (*ālambana*).

Nor is the non-perception of a cause a ground for uncertainty; for that very reason, even regarding the objects of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), it is impossible to deny the power of that which arises from the force of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Consequently, the inference of the author of the *Kāśikā*—that yogis lack direct perceptual cognition of merit and demerit because of the absence of sense-organ contact, just like ourselves—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it is impossible to establish with certainty its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, what is called "knowledge of dharma and adharma" is merely the thorough comprehension of the relationship between actions and their fruits. And that [knowledge] is difficult to prevent when the recollection of past births (*jātismara*) is possible. Therefore, since such thorough comprehension is possible, once cultivation (*bhāvanā*) reaches its perfection, why would it not be tenable that a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) capable of instantly producing a conceptual determination—such as "this very gold, when employed in this way, is the means for achieving this"—should arise? One need only consider the case of the recollection of past births.

In this regard, since mere non-perception is not a valid means of proof, it is not correct to state a total negation [of such memory]. For just as even when there is the possibility of forgetting what has been practiced due to conditions such as a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*), memory is nonetheless observed in some individuals; likewise, even due to the pain of dwelling in the womb, for someone whose intelligence is exceptionally sharp, for whom merit has arisen, and for whom the pain is mild, the recollection of an immediately preceding birth (*jātismaraṇa*) occurs—and this cannot be denied in every respect by anyone who is not a Cārvāka.

Furthermore, since it is possible for this [meditation] to take multiple future births as its object, there is no contradiction in the possibility of gradually forming conceptualizations regarding all objects; thus, the fault of the non-arising of cultivation caused by a lack of comprehension of the objects is avoided, because cultivation is possible once the arrangement of the world has been correctly grasped from scripture.

Even if scripture (*āgama*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), why should it not be possible for one who possesses faith and perceives its corroboration by other profound means of knowledge? Furthermore, once the non-falsity of its object of cognition (*prameya*) is established, the point to be proven is accomplished. Indeed, the manifestation of even a part is observed through the conceptualization of the whole; thus, there is a gradual manifestation of the subtle and so forth.

By this, that [objection] is also refuted: namely, that one who has mastered a single treatise lacks the capacity for another, or that both are represented in many ways as being manifold and dissimilar, [and thus] the supreme human goal is not attained through words and so forth. For there is no disagreement on this point. However, this remains: the effort required for the initial study of a treatise is not the same as that required for another work, even if its subject matter is of a different kind. Thus, in a succession of increasing proficiency, there may be such excellence in someone regarding an unheard-of subject that it does not exist in another, even regarding a heard one.

Then, when the recollection of past lives occurs, through further practice, even with respect to objects not previously practiced, the possibility of *ūhāpoha* (inference and exclusion) arises; thus, one will not remain in a state free from afflictions merely by that much, but rather will become capable of acting for the sake of others. Alternatively, because all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*) are possible, yogis devoted to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) will manifest everything according to their own will.

For this very reason, the objection that meditative cultivation is useless under the view that all things are cognizable is also pointless; for it is established that once the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths—which must necessarily be accomplished—is complete, and the inference of all objects becomes possible, one’s own will is what brings about [the realization].

[343,10] Now, if one were to perceive that in the direct realization of all things there is indeed another kind of happiness or the accomplishment of the welfare of others, then for one in such a state there would be no weariness from meditation whatsoever, and the complete manifestation of everything would be easily accomplished. Thus, even Mahodadhi has not said anything more; by this much alone, the objection has been answered. Therefore, however one reflects upon it, the presentation of objections against the Omniscient One results only in doubt; it is not a definitive refutation.

But the proof for the omniscient being under discussion is absolutely certain. If it is argued that even there, there is no restriction regarding place, time, or person, we say no; for if such restrictions were required, the proof would be ineffective. Indeed, this proof is directed against one who denies [omniscience] in every respect, and it achieves its purpose even if there is no restriction of place and so forth. And thus, such a proof has been set forth by us in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
The chapter entitled "The Determination of the Yoginī" is completed.
The *Advaitabinduprakaraṇam* [345,3]:

Here, for one who is intent upon external objects, it is established that whatever is perceived in a certain way exists in that very way, just as a water-lily is perceived through its blue form. And since jars and other such things are perceived as having a form distinct from consciousness, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). There is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) here, because [the object] is perceived as separated from the factor of the grasper (*grāhaka*), as something capable of being pointed out by the index finger.
[345,6] Because the form of a jar or the like, which stands before one, is embraced through both its appearance and its conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*).

For thus, the cognition "this is a jar" or "this is not a jar" is personally experienced by all persons, even those who have not learned linguistic conventions; it is an internal mental event corresponding to that [external object], free from the explicit articulation of specific names (*saṃjñā-viśeṣa-ullekha*). Even an infant, having beheld the breast as a means of pleasure...

By directing the tip of the hand toward that [object], one extends the self outward, accompanied by the determination [of the object]. Consequently, the cognition of the form of a jar or the like, in a manner distinct [from the self], does not set out upon the path of unestablished proof (*asiddhi*). Nor is it contradictory to the probandum (*sādhya*), since its occurrence in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) has been demonstrated; for a contradictory reason (*viruddha*)—which is pervaded by the opposite—is impossible in that case.

For this very reason, there is neither a lack of exclusivity (*asādhāraṇatva*), nor is there a doubt regarding the positive concomitance (*sandigdhānvayatva*); and because it is not observed in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), it is not a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*). Nor should it be argued that even when one afflicted by jaundice perceives a conch shell as yellow, or when one with ophthalmia perceives floating hairs, there is no such established determination; therefore, the reason is indeed common (*sādhāraṇa*). For those perceptions are undermined by subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).

Because it is erroneous, it lacks the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, in the case at hand, since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) and error is not established, there is indeed the operation of direct perception. Nor can there be a lack of confidence based on the thought that "a sublation might occur here at some time," for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cessation of the operation of direct perception everywhere. Therefore:
When there is a subverting factor consisting of differences in place, time, or person, [cognition] is not born of the senses;
however, the cognition of the difference between a jar and so forth is perceptual because of the absence of such a subverting factor.

In that case, the objection—“If this is so, what is the use of inference when perception is already at work?”—is not valid, because it is the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is intended. For the possibility of dispute regarding the object of perception does not cease merely through the application of inference.

In that regard, just as even when a cow is perceived, a deluded person who, due to some superimposition, does not engage in its conventional usage [of "cow"], [is led to do so] by [pointing out] its nature as a collection of dewlaps and other such features; |||

[345,23] It proceeds; or, by means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), there is the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of non-existence. Likewise, even in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) is conventionally employed by one who follows other scriptures (*āgama*) because it is perceived as such; thus, there is no fault. And this conventional usage [345,25] is established solely on the basis of that [distinction], because it is set in motion all at once. For even in the case of a blue lotus (*kuvalaya*) and so forth, the blue and so on—

In conventional usage, there is no other or additional cause for [the cognition] than appearance and conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), because it would follow that activity could not occur based on that alone. For even the correspondence with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) is sought only upon the first instance of activity.
That conventional usage is indeed dependent solely on the appearing object; however, in the case of the present conventional usage of difference, it is everywhere rooted in beginningless habituation.
Those who possess proficiency are observed; for it has been said:
"Even a child," and so forth.
Therefore, for one who is proficient in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), such usage is dependent solely upon such a cognition.

When that [conventional usage] is to be proven, being cognized in such a manner is pervaded by independence from anything else. And if, despite there being such a cognition in some instance, there were an absence of such conventional usage, then it would be dependent on something else; thus, the fitness for that conventional usage—which is the probandum—is [established].

[346,11] Since its being perceived as such is negated in the absence [of duality] by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), it is pervaded by the very fitness for being established as such in a domain free from sublation (*apetabādhaka*). Thus, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, even the charge that the reason (*hetu*) presented has an uncertain exclusion from the heterologue (*sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika*) does not approach the case at hand. Therefore, it is proven that the distinction between cognition and the cognized, even regarding the object of direct perception (*adhyakṣaviṣaya*), is established by the aforementioned inference.
[346,14] "The state of being conventionally expressible is not to be taken away.
[346,15] To this it is replied: What is this so-called "cognition" (*vijñāna*), by means of which a distinct apprehension and, likewise, conventional usage could be established?

[346,16] For if it is "cognition" because one cognizes by means of it, or because it cognizes—under either interpretation, this definition is dependent upon an object of cognition (*jñeya*). And yet...

For those who deny the external world, it must be established that there exists some object of knowledge (*jñeya*) by virtue of which there could be a cognition that serves as the means for its apprehension. For instance, regarding the conventional usage "this is cognition" and "this is the object of knowledge," would this distinction be produced by a specific operation (*vyāpāra*), as held by the proponents of duality (*dvaitavādin*), or would it be determined by their respective intrinsic natures (*jāti*)? In the first case, does the operation belong to the cognition with respect to the object, or to the object with respect to the cognition, or to both mutually?

In this case as well, regarding the first position, there are the alternatives of whether it is productive (*nirvartaka*) or transformative (*vikāraka*). Among these, first of all, it cannot be asserted that the operation of cognition upon the object of knowledge is productive, because that would entail the consequence of destroying objects that are not visible. Nor is such an admission tenable, since at that very moment [the object] is seen by someone through that cognition.
Furthermore, if one accepts its production, then even though it is imperceptible, its continued existence cannot be denied.

And if that [object], being seen later by him, becomes the producer of that very cognition, it would not be the object [of that cognition]. If you argue that it is not perceptible to that [cognition], but rather something else produced by that cognition [is the object], then the impossibility of a single location arises. For if it were non-obstructive (*apratigha*), how could that which is of the nature of light and is to be personally experienced (*pratyātmavedya*) be [perceived] by another?

[346,26] The very nature of the object-field (*gocara*) as being of the form of consciousness would thus be established by another means. If it is argued that this is not so because it has the form of blue (*nīla*), [347,1] then by what means is the production of the blue aspect (*nīlākāra*) in consciousness denied? For that would entail the consequence of failing to apply a proof for the sake of establishing that [denial].
[347,2] Therefore, it is not logical for the proponent of duality to claim that what is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) is simply non-existent.

Nor is this an accepted tenet of his; thus, there is no insistence on this point. For even one who maintains that in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there is an absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), does not intend for that which is beyond perception to be non-existent in every respect; rather, he holds that while it exists, it must necessarily be the object of some means of valid cognition, albeit at a slight distance. Otherwise, it would be impossible to state: "When there is contact with existing objects, the arising of cognition occurs for a person through the sense faculties."

It might be argued that [the object exists] prior to cognition because of its absence [therein]; however, that further assumption is not logical, so what is the use of this? Since only that much was intended to be said, enough with this elaboration.

But in the case of the view that [the object] is modified (*vikāryapakṣa*), if one establishes that the object which is modified by a cognition is the apprehended (*grāhya*), then [regarding] grief and so forth—

If cognition were impaired, would the sense organ also be an object of apprehension, or rather things such as the reflection on a soiled face? If it is argued that this impairment is produced by suffering, we say no; for apart from the perception of the affected form itself, no other such thing is perceived. This has already been thoroughly examined in the treatise, so enough with this effort. Furthermore, such an excellence does not belong to the object of knowledge (*prameya*) through cognition; rather, it is the production of that which has the nature of illumination.

[347,12] In this case as well, that which has a single object would have to have all things as its object. Upon the cessation of the knowledge of that [object], because its form ceases, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-perception of anything else as well.

[347,13–14] If it is argued that this is not so because other things are also connected with the means for perceiving them, then for that person whose knowledge has ceased, the manifestation of those [other things]—

This leads to an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*). Even if that cognition ceases while its form does not cease, this same fault remains. For clay that has been removed from the potter’s effort does not become a jar for that very person; nor does fire, through its burning, cause the non-existence of a jar for one who is merely providing fuel for the fire.
If that were the case, then its nature as a benefactor (*upakāritva*) would also be common to all, yet it is not so. Therefore, just as in the case of being a jar...

Even if this [cognition] were common to all, it would not be so by virtue of its form that produces an object; likewise, why should it not be so by virtue of its luminous form? What is the force of this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*)? Or, if you argue that its capacity to assist specific beneficiaries is what makes it common, then its luminosity, which depends upon specific persons, would also be common to everyone—this is the same.

It is not the same. For what is called "being an auxiliary" (upakāritva) must be intended either as direct assistance or as mere suitability for activity. Regarding these, since mere suitability is common to all things, there is no dispute over that. However, in the first case—where it is defined as an effect characterized by assistance—why should its state of being a cooperative cause (sahakāribhāva) in one instance not also exist in another?

This is the meaning of the objection: this principle does not hold, because it depends on the absence of an interval (*avyavadhāna*) and so forth. Therefore, since assistance belongs to that very appropriation (*upādāna*) which exists within a continuum (*santāna*), how could there be nourishment (*puṣṭi*) from something remote and so on? Likewise, if even "illumination" were intended as a conventional usage by way of producing another effect, then this might indeed be the case. As some have said:

[348,1] Its manifestation (*vyaktatva*) consists precisely in its being the producer of the manifestation characterized as cognition. For then, that very [entity] for which cognition is the material cause—counted as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and not participating in the occurrence of another means of proof—is not logically manifest, because it lacks the provision of auxiliary causes (*sahakāra*).
[348,2–3] Furthermore, we shall state another refutation regarding that point as well.

And this is not tenable, because we are currently considering the position that the object, which is of the nature of light, arises from cognition itself. However, if the designation "manifested" is applied by means of another effect, then there is no damage to our fundamental point, namely that the object does not arise in that way [as light] from cognition. If it were to arise in that way, the undesirable consequence of its being common [to all perceivers] would be unavoidable. For even the state of being a benefactor (*upakārakatva*) exists only as long as there is a distinction...

The capacity to produce pleasure and so forth within a mental continuum is indeed common in relation to that [continuum] for that duration alone. However, if it were admitted that [the object] is of the very nature of pleasure and so forth, then who would be able to deny its commonality? If it is argued that even so, what is the pleasure of one is not the pleasure of another, [we reply: commonality belongs to the object (*artha*), while non-commonality belongs to the cognition (*jñāna*). Therefore...

It is logical that pleasure and so forth, being restricted to that specific self, are not common to others because they consist in the form of benefit and so on. However, an external form, even if it is accepted as the effect of that [pleasure], is indeed common [to all], because the benefit consists in the nature of a subsequent moment that is to be appropriated by the cognition of pleasure. If you argue that, in the same way, there is both commonality and non-commonality?

In this way, there is no such thing as "sonship" belonging to Maitra that is produced by Caitra and is common [to others], like fairness of complexion; rather, his sonship is designated precisely as being produced by him. And that generative activity of Caitra is not shared with anyone else. Likewise, the designation based on that [activity] also arises from the designation of being produced by him. But fairness of complexion—

[348,16] Even that which is produced by it is not *exclusively* produced by it, because it possesses other qualities; thus, it is correct that this is common [to others]. For he is not white only for his father, but also for others.

[348,17] Likewise, the manifestation (*vyaktatva*) of an object is not merely its being produced by cognition, since its form remains undifferentiated even when obstructed and so forth; rather, the accepted position is that there arises a manifestation-form (*prakāśarūpa*) that excels it. Otherwise, the object would not be said to be "manifested. Such is the linguistic usage (*tathāvyavahāra*).

That [external object] would be merely the cause for that [cognition], just as whiteness is for a person acting [on the basis of it] by virtue of being produced from it, or for a Sautrāntika by virtue of being its producer. And just as there is the consequence that the other cognition which is its producer would become its object, so too there is the consequence for this produced cognition. Thus, nothing more than a mere transgression of the convention regarding the causal relationship between cognition and its object is added; however, the avoidance of [the fault of] commonality applies to both alike. It is not [the case that one avoids it and the other does not].
[348,22] However, the accomplishment of this [cognition] is established from this [fact], namely the production of an object in the form of a manifestation.

[348,23] When there is the production of illumination, there is the possibility of being illuminated for everyone; [348,24] but when there is the state of not being illuminated despite being produced, it is not so even with respect to a single person.
Thus is the summary.

For just as one who asserts that the mere fact of being produced by fire constitutes the "manifestness" of both raw and cooked grains— which are covered by dense darkness— is not able to truly establish their perceptibility to the senses, so too this [proponent] cannot establish the production of knowledge [as a criterion for manifestness].

[349,1] Let it be seen thus. But if the production of that which has the nature of illumination is admitted from consciousness just as from a lamp, [349,2] then its opposite would result for an object such as a jar that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). Furthermore, a common fault is difficult to avoid.
[349,3] If it is argued: "In that case, even a jar manifested by a lamp would be an illumination for everyone," [we reply: such is the nature of the illumination produced by the lamp.

Luminosity is the state of being free from darkness; it consists in a capacity for generating cognition that depends upon factors such as being situated in a suitable location, and it is indeed common to all.
However, that which is restricted—consisting precisely of what is produced by cognition—is that which accomplishes activity and so forth through conceptualization, memory, desire, and the like.

If even that were manifested as being established in the same way as its luminosity, then alas, activity and the rest would be common to all, because of the pleasure and other sensations occurring at that time.
Or that it would be the means of proof for everything—this has already been largely stated. Therefore:
"In the mere arising [of cognition], or in some other excellence, there is no manifestation of an external mass by means of cognition."
But if there were the arising of that which has the nature of luminosity,
there would inevitably follow the consequence of its being common to all.
Therefore, the activity of cognition is not based on the establishment of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.

If it is argued that, therefore, the status of being an object (*grāhyatva*) belongs to the knowable because of its causal operation (*vyāpāra*) upon the cognition, we say no; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the sense organ (*indriya*) is also an object. Furthermore, if the status [of being an object] consists in being a producer of a similar form (*sarūpajanaka*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Moreover, since the qualification "provided it is external" (*bāhyatve sati*) could only be meaningful for one who asserts that very [external reality], this position is also not tenable. Let it not be so.

[349,16] Let there be the position that both [factors] possess causal activity: cognition, arising from an object with a form similar to it, is the grasper by virtue of its operation of apprehending that [object].

[349,17] In that case, due to the operation of the object, there is no grasping of those [objects] that are not active; and due to the reliance on the operation of cognition, there is no [grasping] of the sense faculty either.
[349,18] If it is argued that "cognition does not have the operation of apprehension with respect to that [faculty]," this too is not a valid principle. For that [apprehension]...

[349,19] Is comprehension (*adhigati*) of the same nature as the object, or is it something different from knowledge, or another instance of knowledge? In the first case, because it is established just like the nature of the object itself, there is an absence of any operation of knowledge. Alternatively, if the object likewise required the operation of knowledge, the aforementioned fault would apply. In the second case, however, it is contradictory to say that the operation belongs to knowledge itself, for the operation is nothing other than comprehension.

In this case as well, the same refutation applies, because the non-difference between the activity and its possessor is established. In this very manner, the conceptualization of [cognition] as having the nature of both the knower and the known should be seen as rejected.
Furthermore, if the object were a separate entity, what would that have to do with the sense faculty? For it is not the sense faculty that is seen when blue is perceived.

If it is argued that there is the attainment (*sādhigati*) of that [cognition], then what establishes the relation between the cognition and that [attainment]? If it is argued that this is due to the operation (*vyāpāra*) of that [attainment] as well, then, in that case, since the attainment of both is established through the operation of both, there would be a mutual relationship of being the apprehended (*grāhyatva*) or the apprehender (*grāhakatva*). And in this way, the objection regarding the consequence of the sense organ itself being apprehended is not avoided; for the operation of the eye—
[349,28] There is comprehension of form even without [the operation of] the sense organ.

[350,1] Now, if it is argued that the function of the sense organ lies only in cognition (*jñāna*) and not in comprehension (*adhigati*), whereas for form it exists even in that [comprehension], who indeed—unless out of sheer stupidity—is capable of making such a distinction? For there is no distinct entity other than cognition and the object of cognition.

Only a certain form of apprehension (*adhigama-rūpa*) is perceived, wherein the operation of cognition itself might be postulated; yet in that case, it belongs to the object as well and not to the sense organ—this is merely a desire for something auspicious. If it is argued that the relationship between the apprehension and the object is precisely characterized by the state of being object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayī-bhāva*), then is this very state of being object and subject not itself the operation?

It is examined by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And for one for whom that [conceptual construction] is not established in respect to both cognition and the object of cognition, how could it be established even in respect to the realization and its object? Or, if one accepts that the status of being an object belongs to realization based on a single [entity], how could one reject [the existence of] cognition? If it is argued, "This conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) at least exists," then we reply: if it exists, one must simply consider what its basis is—namely, the non-confused...

[350,9] Is it the establishment of the nature of its characteristics, or the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) resulting from the habitual practice of beginningless false conceptualization (*vikalpa*)?

[350,10] If one asks, "What is the seed of this?"—what does it matter? For even if the opponent does not understand it, we have nonetheless demonstrated the unmixed characteristics of these two. By this, the postulation of [the object] being a different cognition from the apprehension (*adhigati*) is refuted.

For its being an object of that [cognition] is likewise unestablished in that very same way. And it is a great absurdity to claim that an object is known by means of an apprehension that does not have that object as its domain. By this, the conceptual construction is refuted which holds that at the time of debate, the intellect—neither performing an operation upon nor transforming the object—is called "having that as its object" merely because it extends the simple apprehension of it. Therefore, it is not...
It is established that this conventional usage of "knower" and "known" occurs by way of functional activity (*vyāpāra*).
Nor is it restricted by genus (*jāti*), because a thing is established as being known by someone, somewhere, at some time, and in some manner.
For such a conventional arrangement does not belong to things like "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, which are fixed by their very nature; for even now, it must necessarily be explained.

[350,18] Since a distinction of characteristics is not possible, in the absence of that, the mere existence of either cognition or the object of cognition would be the cause of reality; thus, everyone would achieve the cognition of all objects, or else no one at all, because there would be no distance [between them]. But surely there is a proximity of the sense organs to the objects, characterized by conjunction, inherence, and so forth; cognition arising through the power of that [proximity] would [cognize] each respective object—

[350,21] It is established that [the cognition] is necessarily restricted and excluded from objects that are remote due to the absence of the sixfold contact (*ṣoḍhā-sannikarṣa*). So how can there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? This too is trivial. For by this [argument], a restriction regarding its arising would indeed be established, but not a restriction on consciousness being the apprehender (*grāhaka*) with respect to any particular object. To explain: through the power of contacts such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), cognition is produced by an object, and not by one lacking that [contact].

Let it be granted that [the cognition arises] from something obstructed and so forth; however, there is no certainty as to what its apprehender is. If you argue that it is "that very thing by which it was produced," then the self, the mind, the contact with the sense-faculties, and so on, would also be objects of apprehension; thus, the over-extension [of the definition] is not avoided. For even regarding that which is intended to be the object, no utility of this [cognition] toward the sense-faculties and the like is possible, by which a distinction between [what is] apprehended [and what is not] could be established.
[350,27] Has it not just been considered that there is either the production of a delimitation or another operation?

[351,1] If it is argued that in that case, it is simply the manifestation of that very [cognition], and therefore there is no over-extension [of the definition]? [351,2] While there is a manifestation that cannot be denied for the two parts regarded as the grasped and the grasper, if there is anything else based on the capacities of instrument and locus, then...

Let it be said: mere simultaneous manifestation is not the sole basis for the appearance of two moons; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that those two [moons] would perceive each other, or that blue and yellow would do so. Or, one might argue that one moon is false while the second part is insentient (*jaḍa*), and that because the mind cannot function toward both at once, and so forth—this would be appropriate only if one were established in the doctrine of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*). And this investigation has that as its purpose. But when...

Even in the case of two parts, there is no simultaneous manifestation, because it is not accepted that one cognition is experienced by another simultaneous cognition; thus, this path also does not exist. However, if adherence to ill-conceived tenets were not a subverting factor, then one might consider the following basis: that the forms of internal joy, distress, and so forth, as well as the form of the moon and so forth, are perceived at the very same time. But this is not the case.
It is established that [the pot] is perceived.

Furthermore, the fact that there is sensory contact with the pot and not with the cloth must be determined solely from the experience of that [perception]. And this being an experience of that [object] is due to its arising through contact with that [object];
thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Alternatively, if the experience of that [object] were established by some other means, then [contact] would be redundant.

Because it would be redundant. Furthermore, if [the cognition] were the experience of that object simply because it arises from contact with it, then the experience of the object would have an indistinct appearance established merely by conceptual construction and not a distinct one; this would result in the loss of what is observed, just as [one does not experience] Maitra’s son-ness or his fairness [merely through contact]. Therefore, this portion intended as the object, appearing with distinctness, [is so] because it is free from consideration of the operation of other causal factors.
One perceives the self as being known by itself, just like joy, distress, and so forth.
Even for one who thinks:
"The very same prior causal complex [produces] the cognition and the momentary object."
It would act like a visible form possessing light, by which there would be simultaneous cognition.
Thus it is said. Nevertheless:
"If the manifest object is produced by the causal complex, what is the use of cognition?
Furthermore, there would be the fault of commonality; and if it were not manifest, there could be no appearance of clarity."
Since this is established merely on the basis of dependence upon the same causal complex,
it would further follow that the sense faculty itself must be luminous.
But if stability were maintained, how could even a single object be produced by a single causal complex? And how could consciousness be experienced as flashing forth simultaneously with that object?
[351,26] Now, if cognition were non-cognition, then everything would indeed be well-spoken;
[351,27] but in the view that there is self-awareness, this external world is today difficult to perceive.

If it is argued that the capacity belongs to the causal complex itself, and thus the object of cognition and the cognizer arise as distinct from it— just like taste and color— who can be questioned regarding their intrinsic nature?
If the form of the object of cognition and the cognizer is determined and characterized,
then let it be said that the causal complex (sāmagrī) possesses the power to produce it through its pursuit of arising.
When health is established through a healthy form, the power of the physician must be stated;
yet the form of the knower and the known has not even now been definitively determined.
Therefore, when the intrinsic nature [of the object] ought to be stated, [to instead provide] a shift to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
or to state something irrelevant, or to act like a *ḍiṇḍika*— that is precisely what it is.
Therefore, there is no knower whatsoever, nor the known, nor the act of knowing;
rather, this world must be established as self-luminous in dependence upon that.
For blue and other such objects manifest, yet there is nothing else that illuminates them;
thus, their self-luminosity is established, and for us, that alone is consciousness.
Thus are the intermediate verses.

This being the case, there is no such thing as "consciousness" that is established as distinct, by virtue of which the cognition of the form of a jar and so forth could establish its difference from that [consciousness]. Thus, the reason (*hetu*)—characterized by the qualification of being perceived as distinct—is afflicted by the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*), because its qualification is unproven (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the probandum (*sādhya*), namely the conventional usage of difference based on that, does not serve the purpose at hand precisely because the qualification is unestablished. For even if the jar were of the nature of consciousness, since...

Since difference is established even from some other cognition, it is not useful for establishing mere difference. Therefore, since difference is to be proven with respect to a specific limit (*avadhi*), and you are unable to clarify that limit, your presentation is futile.
[Objection: But surely even for the Proponents of Cognition (*vijñānavādin*) there is the conventional usage of "cognition"; whether it be such or otherwise, it is the same for us as well.
It will serve as a refuge for establishing those limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Furthermore, there exists in the world that which is recognized as "some cognition";
it is precisely from this that we shall state the distinction. There is no need here for our own definition.
And if it is argued that in an inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta-anumāna*), there is no conformity to convention (*samaya*).
For the Vijñānavādins, consciousness-ness is indeed luminosity;
and that [luminosity] is the same for both parts designated as the apprehended and the apprehender.
Therefore, the distinction from cognition consists in its being a manifestation;
that distinctness is already sublated in these things such as jars by the very fact of their being perceived.
Furthermore, there is a non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), for jars and the like are indeed not unmanifest.
However, when the subject (*dharmin*) is something other than these, then the non-establishment of the property (*dharmāsiddhi*) is evident.
Furthermore, the essential nature of being known through differentiation is precisely unestablished;
moreover, for one who relies on manifestation, there are further issues such as the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).
Therefore, that [argument] is not tenable even from the perspective of the opponent's own view.
Furthermore, in the world, it is said that "this consciousness is vibrating within.
Consequently, what is the point of establishing its difference from that which is by nature unknowable?

If the conventional distinction between the blue object and its cognition is established as being proven through their forms as the cognized and the cognizer, then that distinction would be a product of human agency.
[353,12] Of those two which have the nature of self-luminosity, being devoid of the forms of the cognized and the cognizer;
[353,13] which are unique and touch upon internal and external determination respectively.
If you are satisfied by the distinction between the "I-maker" and the body,
as between a pot and its parts, then why is the distinction between two different mental continua not established for your pleasure?

If, on the other hand, there is no manifestation [of one consciousness] by that which exists in a different stream of consciousness, then why is it not observed that the relationship between the object and the subject is lost, even though [the object] appears?
If no one considers there to be unity between two distinct continua,
then even in that case, [the argument] would be valid by means of the proof of their difference.
Oh, how great is the prowess displayed by the outsider who speaks in opposition; it is indeed appropriate!
But when the Vedāntins and others assert that there is no difference between two cognitions even though their mental continua are distinct,
then there would be no other unity even for the two cognitions of blue.
In that case, what is this obsession with calamity?

For even among the proponents of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), there are various positions. To this end: In the world, a single mind appears as if divided into the portions of the grasped and the grasper;
or else, these two—the self-cognition of this [mind] and the cognition of coldness and so forth, or pleasure and so forth—appear as distinct.
Whether pleasure and so forth are the ultimate reality here, or whether blue and so forth are deposited [in consciousness] through the power of ignorance;
or whether [consciousness] is a single entity possessing diverse forms, or rather entirely formless.

And what is the use now of considering their relative strength or weakness for one who is intent upon proving an external object through an applied formal argument (*sādhana*)? Therefore, since the form of the jar—which is of the nature of consciousness as described, established as being individually cognizable (*pratyātmavedya*), and so forth—is being used to prove its difference from what is accepted as another consciousness, there is no fruit whatsoever in this; thus, the effort is futile. [Objection: But the form of the jar is not individually cognizable, because it is common to all. Consequently, although it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is in fact an external object (*artha*) due to its commonality.

If it is argued that even from this, a cognition of non-difference is employed to establish conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), we say no; for commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) has already been refuted previously. For it has been demonstrated that the manifest form cannot remain without inducing engagement or withdrawal toward those things whose causes and so forth are unimpaired, whether they are present or even remote. This being the case, if [the object] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇatve*),...

[354,12] In that case, it would not occur even for those things that are present. [Reply: It is certainly not the case that even for those things that are present, that form is one and the same; rather, [354,13] it is of such a kind (*tādṛśam*). [Objection: If there is indeed a difference, how then can there be a single cognition (*ekasampratipatti*)? [Reply: This is not a fault, because such a cognition is observed even in the case of distinct things like hairs and so forth.

If it is argued that [the cognition] is not valid because a sublation (*bādhaka*) is observed there, then why is a sublation not perceived here as well, given the consequence that activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth would occur even for what is obstructed? Even if such [activity] exists, the cause is simply activity and the like; however, when asked what the seed is for the fact that such a manifestation occurs for some but not for others, we say it is "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*). What is this habitual tendency?

It has been analyzed elsewhere that the mere capacity for appropriation—which has come down through a succession of preceding cognitions from beginningless time—is a single entity that, due to some perspective, is perceived as if it were diverse; this is conceptualized as the object. Because such a transformation of the seed occurs, some possess such a cognition while others do not; thus, there is no fault here, owing to the necessity inherent in the succession of the relationship between material cause and its effect.

It is like the hair and other objects seen by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Or rather, just as in that case, because of its resistance (*pratighatva*), there is the determination of it as being in one place; enough with this elaboration.
Why is it determined as one, even though it is distinct in each [instance]? It is because of the force of determination (*vyavasita-vaśāt*).
If you say it is because of sublation, then why is there no perception of sublation at present?
However, similarity is appropriate to manifest due to the sameness of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
since cognitions lack resistance (*pratigha*), even occupying the same location is not a fault.
Thus is the summary.

Therefore, it is established that [these qualities] are also to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedyatva*). If it is argued that hardness and so forth are not properties of cognition (*jñānadharma*), we say no; for all things are cognition by virtue of having the nature of luminosity (*prakāśarūpatā*). Furthermore, one cannot tolerate [the claim that] even blueness is a property of cognition.

"Hardness," say those of tender intellect. But surely, that very blue which is perceived is experienced as hard; and if it is argued that this is not tenable in the case of consciousness, we reply: even externally, because of the perception of error, blue is merely color (*rūpa*) and hardness is touch (*sparśa*). Nor is there anything other than these two that falls within the range of perception, since a quality (*guṇa*) is dependent upon a substance (*dravya*).
If this is so, what is this "reality of quality" (guṇatattva)? If it is merely dependence (pāratantrya), then the reason is indistinguishable from the probandum (sādhyaviśiṣṭa).

Or, if it is something else entirely due to a difference in exclusion (vyāvṛtti), even then, because it is impossible to establish a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates the contrary, the reason suffers from the fallacy of having an uncertain exclusion from the dissimilar instances (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika). As for this [which follows]:
He recites: "That which resides in a substance, possesses qualities, and is an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions.
In that regard as well, its status as a quality is established by its residing in a substance.
And when the existence of quality is established, its having a substratum follows;
thus, these two would be mutually dependent.
Therefore, for him, his own mere reasoning is the only refuge.

[355,15] It is of no use in debate to fail to regard that [external object] as a valid means of cognition; enough, therefore, with chewing what has already been chewed. Or, let there be some other external entity that serves as the locus of the two qualities; even so, if it is luminous (*prakāśa*), then it cannot exist without being included within cognition. [355,17] If it is non-luminous, the reason remains unestablished (*asiddhi*) as before. Furthermore, the simultaneous determination (*adhyavasāya*) of blue and hardness is nothing but an error. And its sublation (*bādhaka*) consists precisely in their mutual non-inclusion within cognition, according to the sequence already stated. Moreover, the seed of the cognition appearing as blue—

[355,19] Since there is no fixed rule that the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a cognition appearing as solid depends upon its engagement with an object, such jackal-like howls do not assail the lion of the Yogācāra.

[355,20] Furthermore, regarding what was said— that there is the cognition "I am not a jar"— in that case too, for those for whom this cognition of "I" has the self (*ātman*) as its object, [it would follow that they perceive the self as non-existent].

If it is argued that for them [the pot] does not exist, this would only negate its being a self (*ātmatva*), but not its being cognition (*jñānatva*). Even though it is based on being an object of consciousness (*vijñānaviṣayatva*), Maitra’s notion of "I" does not occur with respect to mere consciousness alone, because that would entail the same notion occurring even with respect to Caitra’s mind. If you say, "Caitra indeed has that [notion] with respect to it," then in considering why Maitra does not have it as well, the answer must be given that there is simply no prior cultivation (*anabhyāsa*) in another continuum (*anyasantāna*). That...

Furthermore, non-habituation exists even with respect to the forms of jars and the like that appear as external objects. Thus, this exclusion of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*), being established even otherwise, is not capable of proving that [consciousness] has the nature of cognition (*vijñāna*).
Moreover, it might be argued that whatever is cognition necessarily becomes the object of one's own or another's notion of "I"; however, it does not.

If it is argued that [the object] has the form of a jar (*ghaṭākāra*), we say no; for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the object by the cognition which possesses that object is not established. For the object is held to be distinct [from the cognition]; it is not an effect (*kārya*), though it might be a cause (*kāraṇa*). And since there is no necessary rule that the existence of an effect follows from its cause, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to doubt regarding its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣa*). Thus, this person, having brought forward the externality of the form, is a victim of the addiction to externalist theory (*bāhyavāda*).
The method for proving difference resembles the account of removing gold after it has been fashioned into a knot. It is not mere verbal assertion that is to be proven;

rather, what is intended in this context is the distinctness of the manifest object—such as a jar—which exists as a manifestation through the operation of the manifester from the manifester itself. Since such proof is not established, the proponent’s statement of a non-essential part of the proof is futile.

[This is] a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Or, even if it were not so, who can prevent the lack of certainty (*anaikāntya*) due to appearances such as those of one who is asleep or suffering from ophthalmia (*taimira*)?
If it is argued that "in all cases, the external object exists as the objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature is different in terms of place and time," [we reply: no.
In all cases, cognition has an object of perception whose nature consists in the alteration of place and form.
In that case, it can also be said:
"How is there a grasping of its own nature, and how is there a grasping of another?
Whether the cognition [is held to be] identical with or different from itself, the absence of activity is the same."
And just as it appears to be active in other cases, so it appears to be active within itself;
like a lamp, this conventional usage of the intellect cannot be denied.
These are the intermediate verses. Therefore, just as there is the notion that "it is otherwise-manifesting," so too:
"That which is not external appears externally, and that which is not blue appears in the form of blue."
If it is determined by oaths that cognition itself does not appear, [then what of it]?
What is the cause here for the failure of cognition, even though its nature is that of the object?
This objection regarding the restricted manifestation in a specific location applies equally to both views.
If an internal disturbance accompanied by a differentiation of capacities is manifested therein,
why can that very thing not be stated as the cause here as well?
Furthermore: "If it is argued that what exists appears otherwise, let that be the case when there is a difference in location;
but how can there be an appearance otherwise when there is a difference in time, given its non-existence?"
A living actor may indeed appear otherwise, but even so, he is not truly dead;
therefore, it is the mind alone that is capable of appearing otherwise in all circumstances.

Therefore, even in the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (the appearance of something as otherwise), there is no avoidance of the charge of inconclusiveness (*anekānta*). If it is argued that even when there is a difference in time, the object is not absolutely non-existent because it exists at its own time—what use is the mere existence of that object at another time when it is non-existent at the time of its manifestation? That which has no utility through the imposition of its own existence in a particular case cannot be effective there if it is long past, just as a burnt seed or a piece of cloth is ineffective toward a sprout or blackness, respectively. Furthermore, since the object manifests by way of the imposition of its own existence, this is a perception of a contradiction (*viruddhopalabdhi*), because:

[357,10] Even for that which has perished, there is the possibility of causal capacity; yet, utility through the imposition of its own existence (*svasattopadhāna*) is a contradictory property. Here, even a past seed situated in a granary is utilized for the sprout through a succession [of moments], but not by the imposition of its own existence; therefore, this qualification is for that purpose. [357,12] Furthermore, an object that is appearing must be said to be utilized in the appearance precisely through the imposition of its own existence, and not through a succession. Appearance—

For that [object], there must be either its nature (*dharmatā*) or its effect (*kārya*). In that case, if it were its nature, there would be coexistence; if it were its effect, there would be a necessity of immediate succession to its own existence.

Thus, not even a single moment of intervention can tolerate its absence. Therefore, the utility of the object is established only when it appears through the imposition of its own existence. And due to the absence of that [existence], the past cannot be manifested.
Therefore, this which appears does so while being non-existent,
because its own existence has passed away and has been shaken off by the act of superimposition.
Furthermore, even in the absence of that [external object], if there is an appearance, then the appearance of what is non-existent follows;
for by your own words, you maintain that there is an appearance despite the non-existence of the entity.

Therefore, even in the position that external objects exist, the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is unavoidable in the case of erroneous cognition. Or, let it be the theory of the manifestation of something else (*anyathākhyāti*); in either case, since it is merely a transformation of cognition (*jñānavivarta*), it cannot be refuted by mere dislike because it exists as such. Thus, due to the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the reason "being perceived as distinct" is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) for establishing the conventional usage of distinction.
[It has been] established. [Objection: Even if such a state exists only in the case of errors, what follows for the experience itself?

If it is argued that there is no inconclusiveness because the qualification "provided it is non-erroneous" is intended, we say no; for the status of being erroneous is dependent upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), and that [subverting cognition] is established here as well by the very sequence already stated.
To explain: from consciousness, which is self-luminous and possesses a unique nature...
If there were a difference [between the object and its cognition], the object would be cognizable by another; likewise, it would be common [to all].
And this restriction is not established in such a way by the reasoning already stated;
therefore, how could a jar be distinct from cognition, like hair and other such [illusory objects]?
When the establishment of a property does not occur in the absence of a certain thing,
then the positive concomitance (anvaya) of that property excludes its difference from that thing.

Therefore, this unique property of self-luminosity—which is the opposite of the common nature of being external and non-self-luminous—is perceived in jars and other objects; thus, by the force of sublation (*bādhaka*), the cognition of them as such is indeed an illusion. Furthermore, this sublation is a functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not merely a product of imagination; therefore, there is no fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As for what the Vijñānavādin [says]:
He establishes the proof:
whatever manifests is consciousness, like what is seen in a dream;
and the nature of blue and so forth manifests—this is the reason.
Even then, let this continuity exist for the sake of establishing the connection;
furthermore, any room for doubts regarding the succession of cognitions is far removed.
It is accepted that consciousness is self-luminous and unique;
and its pervasion by that nature [of luminosity] is established by others even in cases not produced by it.
If blue and so forth manifest by themselves and not by another,
then why do you not likewise consider that they manifest by themselves and not by something else?
If even a perceived operation of differentiation is not appropriate in the present case,
how can you postulate an unperceived one regarding the difference of the object to be established?
[358,21] But is it not seen that "that which is itself distinct from illumination," and so forth?
[358,22] Even there, it is not said that the nature [of consciousness] is pervaded within itself; rather, it is described in that way.
In this way, let it also be understood that cognition manifests itself;
just as emptiness manifests by itself in space, because it precludes the activity of anything else.
Likewise, the hearing of another's words serves to eliminate the delusion regarding the activity of a self;
for the occurrence of cognition does not depend on such an activity, but rather its form is simply as it is at that time.
Just as space is entirely devoid of obstruction and is itself luminous, so too is this [nature of mind];
and this has already been established previously as being unique.
Therefore, that which is called "manifestness" (prakāśatā), along with its commonality and its action upon others,
remains established only after being rejected, because it is equally subject to the same fault in all cases.
Therefore, through reasoning, contradiction with those two is established, and from that, the determination of their identity is obtained.
Consequently, because of this very contradiction, there can be no persistence of the reason in its opposite.
Since luminosity is established, coldness and so forth are of the nature of cognition;
the hope for them to have an external form is merely a vain hope.
If the forms are the very nature of the single cognition, how can there be variety? Or else, if the cognition were distinct for every atom, there would likewise be no mutual awareness of them.
Even if they are cognized as distinct from one another, just like external objects, their defining characteristic would be undermined.
If that is the case even when there is a difference between them, how could those cognitions be joined with illumination?
[359,15] Or rather, in this very way, the appearance [is known] by a cognition through a cognition of its own continuum;
or what other external cognition could there be for the mass of unreal forms? [359,16]
Furthermore, in the case of false cognition, there is neither manifestation nor anything else.
Therefore, this reason, being common to the opposing side, establishes doubt.
This other exclusion (vyāvṛttyantara) is said to be "otherness" (anyatva), which is false;
even though it possesses doubtfulness, its status as cognition remains established when it is manifest.
Thus, when it has been established that what is manifesting is cognition—
whether in some cases or everywhere— even if it is unreal according to the opponent's argument, it still possesses the nature of awareness.
Therefore, it is cognition alone that is real, whether it be true or false, but not the external object.
Or, let there be an external entity; nevertheless, let it be the luminosity itself that possesses the nature of consciousness.
Even the conceptual construction of difference and non-difference does not subvert luminosity;
nor is it [necessary] because of the pervasion with the aforementioned probandum—so what is the purpose [of such a distinction]?

For one who might falsely imagine that another person’s consciousness is perceived by another, the remaining [objections] might indeed constitute a fault; however, we maintain that this is not the case even in a dream.
Because it is devoid of both unity and plurality, this insentient world is without intrinsic nature;
as it is thus, there is nothing at all—how, then, could existence belong to that which is one?
Whether the manifesting blue and so forth be insentient or indeed non-insentient—
in this context, we state the reason for its being cognition.

In that regard, if the absence of being one or many were to impart some other property [to the object], what would be lost for us by that? For the insentience of blue and so forth remains nonetheless.
[360,11] Once existence has been established, is it not then either insentient or sentient?
[360,12] For the non-existence of things such as a horse's horn is certainly not inferred in the case of reality.
Nevertheless, this is irrelevant because of the absence of any inquiry into existence;
for it is only when existence is already established that a specific qualification is considered.
If there is doubt regarding existence, then if it exists, it is simply cognition;
consequently, there is no fault in the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), because neither the proof of non-existence nor its refutation is established.
Because it possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its form as a mere conventional reality, it is not without a basis;
otherwise, how could even the reason of "lack of intrinsic nature" have a basis?
If, in that case, there is not merely existence, but here there is merely the state of being cognition,
then the establishment of external objects is contradicted for both parties.

If you say that what is to be proven here by you is "the state of being a cognition qualified by a real entity," then why is such a qualification introduced when the discussion concerns the mere state of being a cognition?
If being a cognition were not pervaded by being a real entity, then in its absence there would be no such thing;
otherwise, where would the fault of "incompatible non-deviation" (viruddhāvyabhicāra) lie? Or rather, let there simply be realness.
Furthermore, is existence— whether conceived as distinct from the nature of mere luminosity or otherwise—
the intended object of negation by means of the reason of "lack of intrinsic nature"?

In the negation of something distinct [from manifestation], there is no exclusion of the nature of manifestation itself. If this very [nature] were excluded, by what could that which appears to the witness-consciousness be excluded?
If inference, being a means of valid cognition, sublates something for someone, why should perception not likewise establish something for someone, since it possesses that same status?
[361,7] Ultimately, the validity of direct perception must necessarily rely upon inference.
[361,8] And for that which consists of mere luminosity, sense-perception does not depend on inference.
Now, if this object of inference is distinct from that of sensory cognition, then since it is of a manifest nature, it is perceptual; how, then, could there be occasion for inference?
Now, that which is established by direct perception cannot be refuted;
for what difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) could there be here if it were unable to withstand analysis?
Let it be that this property belongs to consciousness alone, while the external object is like the horn of a hare;
or, in the absence of causal efficiency in an object, let that property belong to cognition itself.
The lack of causal efficiency and the inability to withstand analysis belong to cognition alone, not to the external object; what more than this could be required?
This reflection concerns only manifestation; its scent does not exist even slightly outside.
Since its similarity to a "snake's horn" is thus established, why is the goal not achieved?
The designation of a "heap of form" occurs among appearances that manifest as if external;
since feeling and perception are not distinct from formative forces, why are they not considered distinct from you?
The very root of that which is non-luminous is unstable, because its existence cannot be established;
however, for that which exists as luminous in nature, a further property (dharma) does not constitute a contradiction.
If, due to that same fault, existence is even further removed from manifestation,
then what else will non-manifestation establish regarding non-existence?
Non-existence belongs to that which lacks luminosity, but not to luminosity by its own nature.
Therefore, it has been said that this [non-existence] applies to the imagined, but it is not tenable in the case of [luminosity].
Furthermore, for that which is manifesting, its reality arises precisely from being manifest;
whereas the non-existence of even a hair is determined by a cognition whose nature is insentient.

For this very reason, even in the case of blue and so forth, which are considered to be manifest, it is precisely causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that has been stated to be the truth; without that, there is no distinction between the two.
And because it is followed by mere activity, consciousness too is impermanent;
however, when there is an absence of activity in this [consciousness], its existence is primary, since it appears as such.
At that time, its momentariness and existence are not subject to deviation;
since existence consists in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that proof is not flawed.
Or rather, even for that [cognition], there is no other state apart from its impermanence;
it is the perception of that very moment itself, otherwise there would be no distinction whatsoever.
If it is argued that this causal relationship has thus come about, then surely there is no negation here of the conventional; its momentariness, too, is merely conventional.
If it were eternal in reality, it would not exist even conventionally.
If you argue that it exists because impermanence is negated, even so, how could there be any comprehension of it?
One might utter distinctions or non-distinctions by putting some entity forward;
but what sequence could there be in one's own pure consciousness, which is devoid of distinctions such as place, time, and so forth?
The nature of cognition does not unite with nor does it divide from other things;
for the distinction between self and other is merely a decoration borrowed by the intellect.
The so-called "ineffability" of anything else indicates the existence of its own intrinsic nature;
that very form is the reality, and it is established in non-duality.
For the wise person, O learned one, necessarily attains what is certain;
activity and cessation do not occur merely through a mistaken cognition.
First, the aspect of the grasper differentiates itself from the grasped object by way of distinctions such as location and form, and likewise from other grasped objects.
