Otherwise, it is non-duality alone that, in the absence of that [duality], cuts through differentiation;
therefore, difference and non-difference are restricted to duality, and not so in non-duality.
And as long as one perceives a distinction of time for the sake of awakening from a dream,
this cognition is swallowed by another conceptualization through its own exhaustion, just like any other.
Therefore, that which is called "permanence" exists neither in reality nor conventionally;
yet, even though it lacks the nature of momentariness, let it be apprehended just as inference is.
Even the conventional usage of "variegated" and "one" is considered to be primarily for the purpose of excluding difference;
for here, only pure manifestation exists, devoid of both unity and plurality.
What is the use of a manifestation that, though existent, is devoid of all causal power?
Since there is no capacity for action, no effect can arise; yet where would its own nature go?
If even the nature of illumination is not found upon investigation, we recognize that investigation as inference; it is not sublated by direct perception.
If the errors regarding the gunja berry and fire were sublated even though they were produced by the sense organ,
then since the error concerns the form of another object, why would there be no delusion regarding the sense organ's own nature?
If you claim that a means of valid cognition is not a means of valid cognition, the occasion for inquiry is destroyed;
for by so speaking, you must necessarily be asserting something either to be proven or indeed to be refuted.
In that case, what kind of praise could there be for one who speaks unreasonably in an assembly?
There is no reasoning superior to inference; what is established if that [inference] is disregarded?
If it is argued that because she has been accepted by him, he is therefore awakened by her cognition,
then how can he not be awakened by the cognition of that [other woman], since he has likewise accepted her?
If it is argued that there is nothing to be proven (*sādhya*), then the sublation (*bādhā*) itself must also be something to be proven.
To say "that too is not" is a useless statement; what purpose is served by such a mere question?
If the fruit of words were nothing other than the awakening of understanding, then speech alone would be capable of producing comprehension;
it would not be fitting for sensory marks such as smoke and the like to be so.
If cause and effect are merely conventional, by what means could their existence be apprehended?
Certainly, the cognition of the cause arises from the effect; otherwise, vows and the like would be in vain.
Even one afflicted by heat approaches sandalwood and not fire;
yet, without relying on something, it is impossible for cognition to function.
If logical arguments are presented after having introduced some subject matter, why is there no taking of a position regarding that in the treatise? If not, by whom could it be grasped?
When asked about the path to liberation, if one were to explain the cultivation of emptiness,
then while awakening [others] to emptiness, how could one possibly censure the grasping at a position?
Therefore, whether the probandum or the proof depends upon consciousness, it is unavoidable; thus, the acceptance of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unavoidable.
If you claim that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is accepted from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), then this very investigation is also conventional.
If you do not accept it even from the perspective of conventional reality, then one who speaks thus is a victor in whatever manner.
Just as the cause and effect are conventional, so too is the corresponding cognition;
for one who accepts inference, there is no perception—what certainty is this?
If it is argued that there is a dispute regarding self-awareness, we reply: no, because it is established by means of conventional reality alone.
Therefore, even if it is not ultimate, cognition as it is apprehended serves as a sublater.

If it is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), where is its extraction? Let the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) be just that much. Consequently, how can that which is conventional be abandoned within conventional reality itself?
If it is argued that the conventional usage of existence for the mind follows from its luminosity,
then how can it be compared to that which possesses neither luminosity nor capacity?
Therefore, let that which possesses properties such as being unable to withstand analysis,
while not contradicting its manifest nature,
belong to the mind alone.
The establishment of the mind is based upon luminosity.
The non-existence that is asserted of that whose nature is luminosity is not a flaw, for it is in reference to an existence imagined by oneself;
whereas the other, being a real entity, is indeed luminosity itself.
The two are equal in the proof of worldly established entities:
that which has the nature of manifesting what is non-existent is not real, nor is it real in any other way;
by one there is no duality, and by those two there is no non-duality.
If the world were thus devoid of the four peaks,
what would be the difference between the system of the Commentator and that of the Madhyamaka?
For those for whom even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists only in the ultimate sense, and for whom even that which has the nature of luminosity is negated—
let there be a distinction between them; however, it is naturally difficult to overcome.
This path for the knower of the Self has as its essence the burden of daring.
This incidental discussion has arisen in accordance with the opponent's subsequent arguments; enough, then, with further elaboration.
It is established that, by virtue of being manifest, the three worlds are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
[365,17] Thus ends this treatise, the *Advaitabindu*.
Sākārasiddhiśāstram [First Chapter] [367,4] To him whose form is profound and vast, and who has shaken off the web of conceptual construction;
Homage to Samantabhadra, whose radiance shines everywhere!
May the author of the commentary on the *Vārttika* on the thought of the Lord of Munis prevail—
he who is the stage-manager for the drama of the eye of the *Sākārasiddhi*.
He possesses the glory of a valorous stride that is difficult for all enemies to overcome— a stride that first crushes the pride of those on the paths of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
This entire triple world exists as nothing but representation-only;
herein, the relative strength and weakness of its internal distinctions is now explained.
For it is thus, by way of refuting external objects and so forth:
first of all, this external object does not exist as such, because it is of the nature of luminosity, and because it is necessarily perceived simultaneously with its cognition.

[367,15] By means of reasoning, nothing else is possible here; even if it were possible, it would not possess the characteristic of being an object of apprehension. Therefore, this is mere cognition (vijñaptimātra). [72b]
The world has diverse forms, such as white, the *gāndhāra* note, sweet, fragrant, soft, pleasant, and their opposites. Thus, a sutra states:

"O sons of the Conqueror, that which is called the triple world is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). For this reason, the author of the *Vārttika* strives through a succession of efforts to illuminate the theory of forms (*sākāravāda*) specifically regarding external objects. If it is asked, "How then can this be said to be the original discovery of the author of the *Bhāṣya*?"

Because it has been formulated by others according to the direction of the aspectless (*nirākāra*), it is said that he has established it as if it were established merely as existence (*sattāmātra*); however, it is not his own original invention.
Regarding this, others say: "Let white, pleasure, and so forth have the nature of being solely luminosity; yet, their emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnyatā*)..."

[367,23] However, they are not able to transcend it. If the reasoning characterized by the absence of being one or many is brought forward to conceive of an external object that is impossible, [368,1] that reasoning does not fear white and other such things that possess the nature of consciousness. Therefore, the emptiness of all phenomena alone is superior, as has been proclaimed many times in the Āgamas. Also in the Vārtika:
"In whatever manner objects are conceptualized, in that very manner they fall apart" (PV III 209cd).
Thus, the principle of consciousness is merely conventional (*saṃvṛti-mātra*).

Regarding this, others offer the following resolution: because it sublates the entities produced by causal conditions, their unreality is established; however, mere manifestation (*prakāśa-mātra*) is real.

[368,7] There is no contradiction [in the self-cognition of light], because the cognition of that [light] is perception (*pratyakṣa*), given that it is impossible for it to be erroneous. Since the very nature of illumination is its own intrinsic form (*nijam rūpam*), that [nature] is not brought about by a distortion (*viplava*); therefore, the cognition of it could not be an error. Blue, however, being a different form (*rūpāntara*), may indeed be brought about by a distortion; thus, the cognition of it could be an error. Consequently, there is no room for a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) to arise with respect to blue and the like.

[368,10] Regarding illumination (*prakāśa*): it should be understood that the negation of both the imagined (*kalpita*) and the unreal (*alīka*) applies everywhere. (Cf. *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* 167b8–168a3; Kajiyama 1965) [368,11] Here it is considered: what is this so-called "illumination" that is distinct from blue and other [objects]? For if it were not distinct, there would be no cessation of the fear of contradiction (*bādhā*). Nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for something distinct. First of all, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [the object] has the nature of being illuminated...

Because it is impossible to perceive anything other than blue, and because there can be no inference—since for something that has never been experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is impossible to grasp a relationship (*sambandha*) with anything else. Furthermore, [368,13] Because it is impossible to perceive anything other than blue, and because there can be no inference—since for something that has never been experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is impossible to grasp a relationship (*sambandha*) with anything else. Luminosity within one's own continuum is cognized through inference regarding an object beyond the reach of the senses; what greater humiliation could there be than this?

It is evident that this view of Śabarasvāmin has been adopted as a refuge; what more need be said here? Thus, this perceptible self, being unperceived apart from jars and other such objects, cannot become the object of the conventional usage of "existence," just like universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.
Otherwise, there would be no negation of those [universals] either.
If it is argued that because permanence is accepted, [the object] is non-existent due to the absence of succession and so forth, we reply:
no, for there is no absence of the pervader of valid cognition (*pramā*) when one disregards the non-perception of what is perceptible.

Or how could there be a negation of the qualities, actions, and so forth of a horn? This is trivial. Now, if you argue that when blue is perceived in its nature as cognition (*bodharūpa*), the perception of both the blue and the cognitive self-nature is impossible to deny, and therefore non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not established; then, when a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) is being perceived, how can one who objects on the basis of perceiving both natures be refuted? For there is an absence of separate perception.

But that [non-difference] is common [to all]. If it is argued that "the non-separate mention of light and blue occurs due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*)," then the same will apply to quality and substance as well.

If there is a persistent insistence on the negation of inherence (*samavāya*), then the doubt remains whether the non-perception of them as separate is due to the power of ignorance or simply due to their non-existence;
such a doubt is possible for both cases. It is possible [to say] that the very perception of that [object] is the perception of its action and so forth, just as in the case of a blade of grass.
Or, regarding a hundred elephants:
if that form which has reached the state of being visible is not seen separately,
how can it exist in a blue object even when it is scattered in a hundred ways?
Therefore,
universal properties and the like do not exist, just as they do not exist in the case of distinct entities such as white and so forth, which appear as partless.
Likewise, since another manifestation is also non-existent, how could there be the possibility of non-sublation when white and other such things are sublated?
Furthermore:
If the difference in location were to differ according to the individual, then the appearances of two objects—
which are perceived by an identical cognition that is entirely the same— would likewise appear distinct because of their being observed in different places.

For, due to the extreme similarity between a magical illusion and a ball, there is indeed a single cognition even when they exist at different times; however, when they are in different locations at the same time, there is a sharp distinction in their appearance that is inseparable from the ascertainment of their difference. Therefore, when there is a difference in location, there is an unimpeded difference in manifestation and its subsequent ascertainment.
In a given location, there is only a distinct form and not another form, nor is there another location.

If it is argued that wind and sunlight possess a difference in intrinsic nature despite the non-difference of their location, we say no; for they arise as the forms of composite wholes (*avayavin*), and two things of a single solid mass that are resistant (*sapratigha*) cannot occupy each other's space. However, a collection of atoms (*paramāṇunikara*) does undergo intermingling.
[It] reaches [it]. And that being so, why is a collection of wind, heat, and dust, which has a distinct nature and occupies a distinct location, not [considered to reach it]?

Therefore, just as there is a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too is there a difference in location (*deśa*); thus, what is called "location" is not something other than the essential form itself. Consequently, when that [location] is non-different, the essential form of the manifestation (*prakāśa*) is likewise non-different.
Similarly, if one accepts the aggregation of atoms (*aṇu-saṃhati*), the same fault would apply.
Even in the case of a gross resistance, the same fault applies due to the differentiation of spatial locations.
Furthermore, pervasion here would otherwise be interrupted, since in a fragmented object there is the occurrence of appearing in different ways;
therefore, by virtue of that, the manifestation of white and so forth persists only as far as the manifestation itself.

For as far as the location of the form of blue and so forth extends, if there were an absence of pervasion over that extent, it would follow that blue and the rest would appear as fragmented, by virtue of their being perceived as separate manifestations. Therefore, for as long as there is the manifestation of white and so forth, there must be the persistence of that which is called "manifestation" over that same extent. Consequently, even for that [manifestation] which pervades that much space, when one considers its nature in terms of parts and atoms—just as in the case of blue—[it would likewise be subject to fragmentation].

Furthermore, there is no liberation due to common defects; therefore, when blue and so forth are negated, nothing remains, because difference itself is absent, and thus there is an absence of any distinction in appearance.

[370,10] Now, even if there is no appearance of difference between two moments, just as their difference is established through a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), so it is here as well. For just as the presence and absence of a particular effect, being otherwise inexplicable, establish the difference between those two, so too does the occurrence of a subverting argument through difference apply to manifestation (*prakāśa*) and blue (*nīla*) as well. Therefore, if it is argued that manifestation, which is not subverted, is indeed distinct from blue, which is subverted—[we reply: it is said:

Non-sublation (*abādhyatā*) is twofold, distinguished as *paryudāsa* (exclusion) and *prasajya* (absolute negation). Even *paryudāsa*, when its object is the specific individual under discussion—as in the case of "one who is untouchable" and so forth—would merely bring about another form of sublation, because it excludes a genus, like "a non-Brāhmaṇa" which excludes a Kṣatriya. If this so-called "non-sublation" is considered to be established by the force of valid cognition (*pramiti*), [then it is not a mere exclusion].
Not even a single valid cognition can prevail regarding self-awareness, which is by nature diverse.
Furthermore, since there is an absence of sublation due to its commonality when it does not exist,
how could doubt regarding the locus expand the distinction between the two cognitions?

For in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), the meaning of "non-sublation" is merely the non-appearance of sublation. And that is the same even when the existence [of the object] is doubtful;
how, then, could it establish that the manifestation has a nature distinct from blue and so forth?
If it is argued: "There is no doubt regarding the establishment of their distinct natures, since blue and so forth are sublatable while the manifestation is non-sublatable," this is not so.

Because non-sublation consists merely in the non-appearance of a sublater, when there is doubt regarding existence, it is impossible to establish a distinct nature for blue even from that which is sublated.
For this very reason, it was stated: "in the case of a word, there is doubt.
However, in the case of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), its avoidance is impossible due to the force of other sublaters; one should not harbor such hope for a proof of such a fragile [nature].

And it cannot be argued that the same applies here as well. For in that case, sometimes—just like the fetching of honey or water—the sequence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) is experienced by perception in relation to gross time; yet at other times, even if it is imperceptible in relation to moments (*kṣaṇa*), it is established by its own capacity and would reveal a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-existence in a moment where all activity has ceased, for one cannot perform again what has already been performed.
Because it is possible:

it is logical that this sequence of effects cannot transcend the sequence of causes. However, in this case, nothing established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is accomplished through mere manifestation, nor is anything established by implication (*sāmarthya*). Nor is there a determination of the distinction between effects based on abstraction (*apoddhāra*).

Furthermore, a real distinction between the self-natures (*ātmabheda*) cannot possibly exist in that which appears as non-distinct at once, except for what resides in mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), like the reddish form of light used for the purpose of tinting the space where darkness has been dispelled by a lamp. And this reflection concerns that which appears as non-distinct; there is no appearance of non-distinction among moments (*kṣaṇa*), because there is the manifestation of a form that pervades every fraction of time.

Because it would follow that everything would be perceived all at once at the very moment of its completion, throughout the three times. Furthermore, even if a distinction in the effect were not thus accessible to perceptual convention, it could not bring about a difference in the cause based on the states of existence and non-existence.
For if they are grasped as one, whatever state—be it existence or non-existence—the effect has in one moment, that same state must persist in the subsequent moment as well.
Because there is no separation [between them].

Therefore, just as its object is a producer by means of a form that lasts for only a single moment, so too this sensory cognition conforms to it and is the grasper by means of that very same form. However, the conceptual determination (*avasāya*) obscures its [the cognition’s] actual operation; but here, the manifestation—
Thus, it is experienced as even more clearly non-different. Nevertheless, what offense has been committed by a thousand limiting conditions (*upādhi*) if one still imagines a distinction?

Furthermore, it has already been stated that there is no other way to exclude [the object] than through non-perception. Therefore, this non-sublation, when asserted while the non-perception of the perceptible is possible, collapses of its own accord and does not require any further argument.
Furthermore, if there were two distinct appearances, there could be sublation here and not there.
If there is no appearance of that constituent part, how can there be a state of non-establishment with respect to it?
Even if the reason (hetu) were established there, it would not be capable of functioning.
Surely, that which is not connected to the probandum is not capable [of proving it], even in the case of its appearing form.
An object that establishes its own nature or its cause without deviation does not cease to be of that nature even when it contradicts someone's argument.
But surely, luminosity indeed appears to embodied beings within blue and other such objects;
why then is it not capable of being established as manifest when there is no sublation regarding that alone?
What is the point of stating that it does not manifest its own nature as blue?
For there is no effort here to state the absence of sublation for that very thing itself.

If it is argued that there is no manifestation of the blue [object], what could be more reckless than this? For if there were a manifestation of the blue, what further manifestation could there be beyond that?
Even if its manifestation were to arise from something else, it would still be impossible to prevent.

If its manifestation does not come from anything else, and if its manifestation were something entirely other than it, then that blue object would not be manifested; for what would the manifestation of something else have to do with it?
And because the relationship itself is sublated, there is no coordination expressed by "its";
even if the genitive case were obtained, a confusion of forms would be impossible in any way.
Therefore, its manifestation is undeniable from whatever source it may arise;
and if that manifestation were not sublated, there would be neither a result nor anything at all consisting of that alone.
However, let that which is intended and well-established be stated according to one's own conviction;
by this very means, the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is eliminated, and for this same reason, the logical reasons (*hetu*) are also established.
If it is argued that the objects established as being non-sublated are merely constructed by conceptualization,
then because they are identical in nature to those objects, there is no validity in establishing them through a formal injunction.
If existence is established only by non-contradiction, then that [non-contradiction] would be the reason for existence;
thus a circular argument arises, which refutes this illusion.
Moreover, even if there is no sublation, it is set aside when a sublation manifests;
but in its absence, such a state is established as being a ground for doubt.
But if a property of the class (*vargadharma*) is relied upon, it does not escape the charge of circularity (*cakraka*).
Let there be a substratum (*āśraya*), but let the cause that subverts the subverter be stated;
for it has been shown that self-cognition itself does not exist as something distinct.
Nor is it logical for you to maintain that there is even a cognition [of an object] based merely on self-awareness,
since even when there is self-awareness of blue and so forth, sublation may still occur.
If self-awareness does not belong to the blue object, why does it not appear? It is impossible to claim that it appears by means of something else; such a thing cannot be so.

Because the cognition of another by means of another has been refuted at length elsewhere. If it is argued that there is no "other" because of its non-existence, let there be no "otherness"; yet, by the mere fact that selfhood (*svattva*) is possible, the establishment of that cognition is achieved through that alone, and nothing further is required, since its nature consists solely in self-cognition (*svavinmātra*).
If it is argued that there is no fault because of an imagined identity (*kalpitatādātmya*), this is merely a deception of the ignorant; for [the cognition] exists simply due to its manifestation.
For the conceptualization of identity and the appearance produced by it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

If it is argued that the conceptualization does not arise from the appearance itself, but rather from the determination (*avasāya*) of the appearance— then let there be a circular argument (*cakraka*), since that determination of the appearance would likewise arise from the appearance, which in turn arises from the conceptualization of identity, and from that, the determination.

[373,5] Therefore, that is a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). If it is argued that even this conceptual construction does not arise from the conceptualization of identity (*tādātmya*), but rather from that identity which has been made an object of conceptualization, [we reply: no, because that [identity] did not exist prior to the conceptual construction; otherwise, its being a conceptual construction would be untenable. Furthermore, nothing that is a conceptual construction is ever observed to be effective in any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); if it were so, [it would be real].
Because it would necessarily follow that [the object] is truly real.
By this, the claim that it possesses the nature of being unreal is also refuted, since even unreality is untenable if there is some utility [for it].
Otherwise, there would be no insistence on negating it in the case of a mere nominal action; for even that which is manifest may be useful in certain instances.

If it is argued that falsity is not contradictory because of sublation (*bādhana*), then since manifestation (*prakāśa*) cannot be sublated, if a sublater does not even sublate its utility in any respect, why must a sublater necessarily be defined as such? From where, then, would there be an identity with falsity? Or, if it is argued that it sublates the causal capacity of the object by implication rather than directly—let it be so; what is the point of insisting on the sublation of capacity here?

Since it is established that identity is not applicable because it is unproven, this remains the case. Furthermore, as for what is said— that consciousness alone, being of the nature of luminosity, appears as luminous, yet due to being afflicted by the impressions of beginningless erroneous tendencies,
it manifests through false forms such as blue and so forth, like a dream— that too is refuted by this.
[373,17] This has been refuted.

[373,18] Since nothing called "consciousness" (vijñāna) is perceived apart from blue and so forth, this is merely a proclamation of a theoretical framework. Furthermore, the example of a dream is devoid of the probandum. Moreover, since there is an absence of causal power due to such falsity, when there is the intention to express something as being thus—as in "it is blue"—[the following applies].

Furthermore, since it has been clearly stated that an object is merely its simultaneous manifestation, the absence of its being manifested by something else is evident. Therefore, how can there be a transgression of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)? If it is argued that it appears in such a way due to the force of the latencies of ignorance (*avidyāvāsanā*), and thus it will indeed be manifested by that [ignorance], then in that case, ignorance would be the cause [of its appearance] rather than the illuminator. For that which is of the nature of illumination cannot [originate] from that [ignorance].

[373,23] Its arising is like that of a lamp, from its own cause; so how could there be the destruction of its self-luminosity? [373,24] Even if it were thus established as being illuminated by another, it would follow that experience itself [would be so]; therefore, nothing at all is called "self-luminous. Furthermore, because self-cognition is impossible, existence is not established anywhere. Thus, this is not a valid principle.

[373,26] In relation to that which produces the form of illumination, its "destruction" is self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*); thus, it is established that blue and so forth also possess self-awareness. [373,27] Now, if it is argued that because [the object] is not non-blue (or, because the non-blue is unreal), it lacks the status of being an effect, and therefore there is merely an illumination—whether by ignorance or by light—and that for experience (*anubhava*), since it is a real entity, only production by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is spoken of; even that is trivial. For experience too...

For, by self-awareness alone, the object is established; therefore, the so-called "unreality" of the blue consists in its non-existence, and its non-existence follows from its unreality, which acts as an obstacle to its being an effect.

Furthermore, whether blue is unreal or not, how can its status as an effect be denied? For an entity is called an "effect" when it depends upon the operation of another for the completion of its own nature.
Thus, because this blue exists only occasionally, its possession of a cause is established.
[374,7] There must be either constant existence or non-existence, because the cause does not depend on anything else.

[374,8] In this same way, the lack of restriction regarding place and so forth is also to be understood. Furthermore, there is nothing else that serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect" apart from dependence on another—namely, the state of being established through the restriction of place and time. Otherwise, even the experience [of such effects] would not exist.

Therefore, regarding this [objection]: since the production of something that is the object of mere faith is imagined from exactly such [a cause], why do you reject the non-arising of some other observed form from what is observed? What can we say to this? By this, the claim that there is no "being an effect" because of the absence of causal capacity even in the case of arising after non-existence (*abhūtvābhāva*) is refuted, because causal capacity is established according to the sequence already stated. As for that which is the object of faith, however, let it be considered that there is no observation [of its arising]; let there be no causal capacity.

[374,13] But what is excluded by the fact that [the thing] arises in dependence on another, such that its being an effect (*kāryatva*) is negated? For its exclusion from non-things (*atadvyāvṛtti*) remains intact. [374,14] Alternatively, if being an effect is a property of a real entity (*vastudharma*), and there is no reality (*vastutva*) without causal capacity (*śakti*), then let there be causal capacity as well; for we observe "being an effect," which is a property of a real entity pervaded by that [capacity]. [374,15] If it is argued that because of the absence of capacity, that very [effect] does not exist, we say no, because that is unproven (*asiddhatvāt*).

But there is no doubt regarding its being an effect, just like any other effect. Therefore, if there is an invariable connection (*pratibandha*) between capacity and being an effect, let capacity be inferred in some instance; it cannot be rejected on the basis of mere non-perception (*anūhamātra*). However, in the absence of such a connection, its status as an effect is established.
Consequently, how can it be said that "because blue is not an effect, it is not produced by causes consisting of mere manifestation," since [it is indeed an effect]?
[374,19] Regarding "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedana*):

[374,20] Furthermore, if there were the possibility of another unperceived material cause for the mere manifestation of something by means of something else, then—due to the determination of non-difference between preceding and succeeding moments—it might even be said, as in the case of a jar and so forth, that it is [manifested] by light. But what kind [of manifestation] could there be in the case of that which is admitted to be false?

[374,22] Is this a misconception? However, the arising of what was previously non-existent is not contradictory, provided it occurs through manifestation (*prakāśatā*) just as it does through blueness (*nīlatā*). Or, let there be no effect-ness (*kāryatva*) whatsoever; even then, if there were a restriction based on dependence upon another, there would still be the suspicion of being manifested by another. If there were absolute independence in every respect, then without doubt there would be an absence of self-awareness for all aspects (*sarvākāra*). And in that case, when sublation is observed here, it would apply elsewhere as well.
The absence of the assurance of existence is established. Alternatively:
If it is held that [the object] is distinct from blue because it is not sublated, then from where does the removal of sublation come?
If it is argued that it is due to the absence of superimposition, then if that absence of sublation is the result, there would be a mutual dependence on each other's existence.

They say that blue itself is superimposed when it is being sublated. In that case, how could the very state of being sublated—which has as its result the absence of superimposition—be capable of establishing non-sublation?
If you argue that this is the very nature of consciousness, then why is it not so for the nature of blue itself?

For just as the very nature of light is luminosity itself, and it is not said that this is brought about by a distortion (*viplava*), so too the very nature of blue is blueness itself; even if it were said that this is not brought about by a distortion of it, that would not cause one’s face to become distorted.
Nor does the operation of logic proceed by way of partiality, such that one thing would be to be accepted and another to be rejected. Otherwise, if it were apart from luminosity—
There is no persistence of blue; nor is there a persistence of manifestation even in the absence of blue. If it is argued that it exists in yellow, let it be so, but it is not a property of blue.

If you claim this is because of the commonality of the term "manifestation," then, in view of the manifestation of the property of yellow, the persistence of blue—even when devoid of manifestation—becomes an object of negation.

Therefore, the notion that "this very form belongs to it" is not a conceptual construction restricted solely to manifestation; for it is precisely because of its non-superimposed nature that one gains confidence in its freedom from sublation (*bādhā*). In that case, let the difference between the two be established without effort, since they are mutually inconsistent.

We recall the example of the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), because it is impossible to provide an example of cloth and water. This is because [the two] are characterized by stability and change, respectively.
[375,15] Indeed, since two contradictory properties designated as residing in the same substratum are not perceived, you yourselves are the authority in this matter.

[375,16] Therefore, enough with being under the sway of dogmatic attachment! For that which is to be believed in as having that very form—[375,17] if it appears in such a way to one whose mind is focused solely on conceptual construction, why would it not be so?
The blue object possesses reality; its only further fault in establishing its existence is that it appears as having a specific intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

Moreover, this is a novel method for dispelling sublation (*bādhā*), namely, that its very essence is its reality. For even that which is subject to sublation—such as *pradhāna*, *sāmānya*, and so forth—[is likewise established].
Whatever appears or is conceptualized in whatever form, that very thing is its reality (*tattva*).
By means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that [reality] may be either existent or otherwise; for in both cases, there is room for sublation (*bādhaka*).

Whether it be in the case of blue or in luminosity, if at most there is a distinction in the occurrence of defects such as non-establishment (*asiddhi*) through a division [of the object], yet that [reality] itself remains unchanged.
[375,24] On the grounds that it is reality (*tattva*).
Furthermore, [375,25] that which is superimposed is merely imagined (*kalpita*) and is sublatable; they say that which possesses manifestation is the false and is sublatable.
[375,26] Therefore, reality is established solely within the imagined; how could it not be restricted to the perceived alone?

The state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is spoken of only in conventional usage regarding that which is purely imagined (*kalpita*) and sublated, like water [in a mirage]. However, they designate even that which is manifest as false (*alīka*) when it is sublated, like a double moon. Therefore, if you must say that even the visible is superimposed, let it be said. But from what [source] does this follow that the visible itself is superimposed? Consequently, the imagined is not [defined] by the exclusion of superimposition.

[376,4] This is established as distinct from what is proven by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, it is only through valid cognition that proof or refutation can be properly determined. [376,5] However, the emergence of refutation or the establishment [of a thing] does not occur merely because its very nature is such [i.e., being sublated].
[376,6] Thus, this distinction is also made: blue and other such things are conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), because although they are perceived, they are subject to sublation.

However, consciousness whose very nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), appearing as blue and so forth, is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*) because it is not subject to sublation and because it possesses powers established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it appears as something merely constructed by the hand. For if luminosity were distinct from blue, then the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—just as in the case of blue—would not be withdrawn from the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) merely by one's lack of desire; this and more has already been stated.

[376,10] Furthermore, what kind of sublation could there be for that which is intended to be manifest, if it does not manifest? Moreover, as was stated immediately after, "Likewise, capacity too has only the form as its object.
[376,12] And this negative concomitance (vyatireka) appears as something brought about by mere conceptual construction, like the case of being produced and impermanence; it is not direct.

[It appears as distinct], like twin fruits or like two moons. And when the substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived as differentiated, it is possible to ascertain that "this property (*dharma*) is possible here, and that is not possible here. This is because, specifically in the case of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it is precisely a real property (*vastudharma*) that must be presented in its opposite form.

Furthermore, every means of establishing difference is merely a means of establishing conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), for nowhere can there be [a distinction] without the association of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*).

Because their difference is not established. Otherwise, how could there be such a thing as non-difference? Furthermore, two contradictory properties are not differentiated by mere conceptual construction alone.

They must be cognized through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having distinct substrates; for if they were cognized as being without a substrate or as having the same substrate, there would be no operation of either valid or invalid cognition, nor would there be the establishment of contradiction. And if those two are established as having different subjects (*dharmin*), what else remains?

[376,19] Is it an endeavor to prove a difference between the substrata (*dharmin*)? [376,20] Precisely for this reason, the establishment of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) has as its basis cognition and determination (*nirṇaya*). Among these, the proof of a difference between substrata occurs in some cases by way of spatial difference, like a physical sphere (*golaka*), and in other cases by way of temporal difference. Under this heading, it is said that for those two states, there is indeed a difference in the entity (*vastu*).

[376,22] "To be determined" means that even in that case, there is no such distinction as "this is the state of being in a granary" and "this is the state of being in a field. When the difference in time is not demonstrated, the distinction based on doing and not doing is impossible to specify.

[376,23–24] Since the establishment of the distinction is concluded by that much alone, the presentation of action and non-action serves merely as a means for conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*). Where...

[376,25] However, there is no delineation of difference by way of place or time; in that case, the only refuge is either a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*) or a difference in the sense faculties (*indriya*).

[376,26] This is like the color, taste, and so forth of a beverage, or like the Cārvāka’s own admission regarding the intellect and the body. For he [the Cārvāka], when forming a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a mountain and the like—which is dissimilar to the body with its hands, feet, and other features—by what form could it possess the nature of a conceptual construction of a mountain and so forth in the absence of an example? [376,27]

How could one distinguish them? Where there is not even a trace of a difference in appearance other than from the form of conceptual construction, as in the case of a blue lotus and so forth, there is indeed an ontological non-difference.
For that which is not thus—namely, where there is no unity of undivided cognition—is possessed of difference.
If it were established that there is no means of proof, on what basis could difference and non-difference depend?
This is an intermediate verse.

Therefore, the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by sublation and non-sublation cannot effect a conventional distinction of the substratum (*dharmin*) without a difference in its manifestation. A proof of difference alone does not incur the three types of logical fallacy, because its nature is that of a proof for existence (*sattā*).
[377,8] It oversteps [the logical rule]. As for what is also said: "Whatever is neither one nor many in a certain form, that is not real in that form;
just as suffering is not real in the form of pleasure. And consciousness is neither one nor many in the form of blue and so forth"—this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
[377,9–10] That too is refuted by this very [argument] and is merely a matter of personal satisfaction. For it is not understood, or rather, it does not cognize.
The nature of consciousness is held to be based on its functional activity (*vyāpāra*), because that is what is negated elsewhere; however, its essential nature is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*).

And since that luminosity does not exist in that [inert] form, what is intended is not merely the negation of identity (*tādātmya-niṣedha*), but rather that it simply does not exist by its own nature.

By this, the argument that "the fault does not apply in that case" is also refuted. Otherwise, there would be no establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with respect to the son of a barren woman.

[377,15] This would also follow as a consequence merely by way of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Therefore, since the distinction is established solely through sublation (*bādhā*) and non-sublation (*abādhā*), no additional object is apprehended by us; thus, this point is already understood by that alone. Nevertheless, something will be said here. In this context of proving that manifestation is distinct from form (*ākāra*), manifestation must be established by inference even while it remains unmanifested.

That which appears must be established as distinct from its form; however, in either case, within the context of establishing a positive proof (*vidhisādhana*), what occasion is there for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)? Even if it exists with a nature imparted by that [form], if there is no cessation of the suspicion of its non-existence in its own right—as in the case of a horn—how can its difference be established?

[377,21] Now, if the non-existence of those two is intended to have the very nature of another entity, then a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) must always be employed, because the subject matter of the dispute pertains to a positive affirmation (*vidhi*). [377,22] However, when someone might doubt that it could exist even in the absence of that [other entity], then the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is appropriate with respect to that alone. Furthermore, there is no occasion for the suspicion of existence (*sattvaśaṅkā*) even when there is a separation from being one or many. It is not so.

And if there is an intention to state the opposite, then it is secure. For in that case, it must be shown that whatever exists in a certain form is either one or many with respect to that [form]. However, neither an example nor the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) can be established here. Indeed, mere luminosity is not established anywhere because nothing else exists; so how could there be an example, or where could there be an application of the property of the subject, given the absence of any other means of proof?
Or, if it were the means of proving that, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if one holds the position that "manifestation (*prakāśa*) exists as having the nature of manifestation," then at the time of applying the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there is no avoidance of the charge of perceiving something irrelevant (*aprakṛtopalambha*).

For there is no dispute regarding unity or plurality in terms of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*); rather, the dispute concerns whether there is difference or non-difference with respect to the form (*ākāra*). This is for those who dispute unity and plurality.

Or how could there be the establishment of existence? In that case, since it is precisely because of the impossibility [of being either one or many] that blue and so forth are non-existent, what is the point of the effort to present that [argument]? For even in the absence of that [argument], existence would be established through the force of negation (*prasajya-śakti*).
Otherwise, if there were doubt regarding it, how could one establish [existence]? And that will be considered later.
Now, if you mean that "being one or many" refers to its own nature (*svarūpa*), and therefore existence is intended to consist in that very [nature],

even then, when asked what this nature of it is by which there is a connection with oneness or manifoldness— if it is replied that "this very thing is fit to be pointed out by the forefinger," then the claim that "this cognition is one or many because it is blue" collapses.
If it is something else, that is not established. Or, if it were established, what would be the point of this? Furthermore, that very objection remains in its original state.
For dispute occurs only when there is a difference; once that [identity] is established, there is no occasion for the question, "Does it exist even in the form of another?"

[378,12] Now, if it is argued: "This subject (*dharmī*), namely manifestation (*prakāśa*), is indeed established; once its non-existence in the form of blue and so forth is proven, its differentiation is obtained by implication (*sāmarthyalabdha*). Since the intended point is established by that much alone, there is no need to conform to a positive affirmation (*vidhi*); therefore, it is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) alone that is useful for the present context. [378,14] This is a great display of cleverness! However, if manifestation itself were not non-existent even as blue and so forth due to ignorance (*avidyā*)...

In that case, since it is likewise [established] by its own nature, how can there be an establishment of difference? Surely, there is no suspicion of its non-existence, because it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), and because there is no error regarding its own nature. For the dispute concerns only difference. How then could such an establishment of blue be sublated? It has already been stated in passages such as "the nature of manifestation is manifestation itself. And it is possible—

One might say that the nature of the manifestation of blue is simply the manifestation of blue itself, and so forth. Therefore, even if one were to reject the distinction [between them], if self-awareness, by not providing an occasion for contradiction, were to establish the existence of manifestation, what would be gained by this?

Likewise, even if it lacks such power, what is the point? For, just as with the blue object, the distinction remains unestablished there as well, since the rejection of the "hand-off" (the transfer of the burden of proof) has not been avoided.

[378,21] Now, if for the opponent manifestation is established as ultimately real and is indeed differentiated, then there is a dispute; from that, it follows that manifestation exists, but not as having the nature of blue—thus the probandum is established. In that case, what kind of cleverness (*vaidagdhī*) is this, which exhausts all means and brings the logical process to its conclusion? [378,22–23] This deserves to be treated with contempt, according to the logic of establishing the selflessness of a jar by one who asserts a self. Furthermore, in this proof, regarding the two things that appear as non-different...

The intended meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is the distinction between the experience and its form; the reason (*hetu*) is the absence of being one or many in that nature. Furthermore, it is not possible to demonstrate in an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this with the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*). This is because, even in that case, a manifestation distinct from the forms of suffering and so forth is unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if it were established, one could not say "just as the pleasant is by means of the unpleasant," nor "just as the experience of suffering is by means of the form of suffering and so forth."
This is logical.

Otherwise, if a manifestation apprehended through one form were to be shown as non-existent by means of another form, that difference would exist only in relation to that [other form]. Consequently, at the time of the probandum, the difference of the blue form from the experience of yellow would be established. Therefore, if...

A distinction dependent upon self-luminosity cannot be demonstrated in the example; how then will it be established as the probandum (*sādhya*), given the total absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?
If it is argued that positive concomitance is stated here in a general sense—that "whatever is neither one nor many [is not self-luminous]"—that is incorrect. For:
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by inquiry is considered to be the probandum (*sādhya*), just like one's own self-interest.

This same logic applies to the proof of the eyes and other sense organs being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*). Alternatively, regarding the statement "that which is neither one nor many," one may intend to mean "that which appears as non-different" by means of "that which causes it to appear"; or else, one may distinguish this by considering it in terms of a universal (*sāmānya*).
[379,9] There is no concomitance with respect to a particular, and with respect to a universal, it is a proof of what is already established.

[379,11] Just as in the case of pleasure and pain, because the experiences of blue and yellow lack each other's form, their difference is established by the non-existence of that [common] nature; however, there is no impairment of perception—which grasps non-difference—in either case. The rest is as in our *Bṛhadīśvaravāda*. Moreover, when...
And "illumination is neither one nor many, like blue and so forth" is the application of the reason to the thesis. In that regard, what is this so-called "illumination"?

Is it the act of illuminating (*prakāśana*), or that which is illuminated (*prakāśate*)? Or is it some distinct entity denoted by the word "illumination," established in dependence upon such operations as "it illuminates" and so forth?
This latter view has already been refuted.
In the first position, this so-called "manifestation" of manifesting blue, yellow, and so forth is merely a property (*dharma*).
Even though it appears as if distinct by excluding other differences, it is not capable of remaining neutral when the conceptualizing intellect analyzes the form of the substrate (*dharmin*).
Therefore, how can a real distinction be established? For properties are never found anywhere apart from the form of their substrate.

[379,19] There exists a sentient being (*sattva*), just like the qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth. However, in the view that it is the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*sādhana*), it is only blue and the like that appear; thus, as before, that very thing is empty of that form. [379,20] Furthermore, in the view that it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), if the word "appears" (*prakāśate*) is used in its primary sense (*anvaya*), then there would be no appearance of that which is distinct from blue and the like. [379,21] And if it is used in a secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*), then since it is not established that blue and the like are perceived by another, it follows that they themselves are what appears. Thus, the consequence remains the same. [379,22] Moreover, if one were to say that the self (*ātman*) is what appears, then because the self is eternal, it would follow that all objects are perceived simultaneously. Therefore, this too is untenable. [379,23] Furthermore, if one says that the self is what appears, then since the self is unitary, it would follow that blue and the like are unitary. Or, conversely, because blue and the like are manifold, it would follow that the self is manifold. Consequently, the self is not established. [379,24] Moreover, if one says that the self is what appears, then since the self is eternal, it would follow that it is always manifest. Or, if it is said that it is not manifest at other times, then because it is not manifest at those times, it would follow that it is impermanent. Therefore, this too is untenable. [379,25] Furthermore, if one says that the self is what appears, then since the self is unitary, it would follow that blue and the like are unitary. Or, conversely, because blue and the like are manifold, it would follow that the self is manifold. Consequently, the self is not established. Or, if it is said that it is not manifest at other times, then because it is not manifest at those times, it would follow that it is impermanent. Therefore, this too is untenable. Or, conversely, because blue and the like are manifold, it would follow that the self is manifold. Consequently, the self is not established. Or, conversely, because blue and the like are manifold, it would follow that the self is manifold. Consequently, the self is not established. Or, if it is said that it is not manifest at other times, then because it is not manifest at those times, it would follow that it is impermanent. Therefore, this too is untenable. [379,47

Even if that which is sublated by the non-perception of the perceptible is non-existent in its own nature, there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). Furthermore, even in the position of total destruction without residue (*niranvayanāśapakṣa*), there is no establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasiddhi*). And although the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) might be avoided by relying on a relationship of probandum and probans between two mere exclusions (*vyavacchedamātra*) therein, this does not serve the purpose at hand. Now, if it is argued that this very perceived illumination (*prakāśa*) is the subject (*dharmin*); but surely, "perceived" means appearing (*pratibhāsamāna*).

And that [manifestation] is indeed blue; there is nothing whatsoever distinct from it. If it is asked: "Is this not an effort precisely for the sake of establishing something distinct from it? Why, then, is that sought at the very outset?"—[the reply is:
Let whatever be your thesis to be proven; however, if there is such a thing as manifestation, its basis—the established nature of the means of proof—must be shown.

A subject (*dharmin*) that possesses the nature of a real entity (*vasturūpa*) is possible. However, if the subject were a non-entity or one whose status as an entity is doubtful—merely out of deference to the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) between the probandum and the probans—then this rule would not apply; and the establishment of the matter at hand would be far off. Now, if, in deference to the establishment of the matter at hand, the subject is light (*prakāśa*) as a real entity, then, being accepted as having a determinate intrinsic nature, it would necessarily be blue itself. In that case:

It follows that form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; nevertheless, this does not establish the point at issue. Nor can there be a persistence [of form] by means of an emptiness that is other than it, for there is no hope for such a state of being without an aspect (*anākāra*). Lest there be the suspicion of proving what is already established—namely, that one thing is empty of another through its being of a different nature—the phrase "by that" (*tena*) remains meaningful even with that much [qualification].

Or, according to the theory of cognition with aspects (*sākāravāda*), this is a negation of the external object as it is apprehended, just as there is an emptiness of the form of two moons in the case of one with cataracts seeing two moons. For everywhere it is only that which is superimposed that is negated, and in all cases, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) merely superimpose externality upon their own internal aspects; otherwise, reality would be lost. Therefore, the probandum is not established in the subject (*dharmin*) "blue. Now, what is the point of this insistence on a specific qualification?

[380,10] That which is called "manifestation" (prakāśa) is considered the subject (dharmin) in a general sense. For if it were restricted to a specific [quality], there would be the undesirable consequence of obstructing the presentation of the proof (sādhana), since the probandum (sādhya) would already be established [prior to the argument].

[380,11] Furthermore, no one employs a proof without having an intended probandum in mind. Nor is a subject ever presented with its probandum already excluded, as that would be equivalent to proving what is already established. Therefore, the emphasis is not placed on a restriction to a specific [quality].
Or let it be so;
this very thing is that which is called "the manifestation in front" (puraḥprakāśa), with respect to which you were doubtful regarding its distinctness from the blue.

Let your longing cease. And the relationship between property and property-bearer (dharmadharmibhāva) is observed through a distinction in exclusion (vyāvṛtti), just as in the case of the essential nature as a logical reason (svabhāvahetu), where there is identity with that.
[380,16] "Exclusion is the property-bearer; the state of being distinct from another is what is to be proven—thus there is no fault. That too is incoherent, because:
[380,18] "The establishment of the probandum and the probans is tenable by means of mere exclusion."
However, it is precisely the substratum (dharmin) as perceived through its distinctions that is useful.

For, since it is impossible to understand the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) without a universal form (*sāmānyākāra*), the establishment of the reality of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)—which are both floating in nature—is based solely on their being grounded in the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*). It is not, however, based on the mere exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) while the nature of the subject itself remains floating; for this [exclusion] is not cognized as "this is such" unless the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word "tree" and so forth is presented. This is the distinction of exclusion.

However, it is required for the purpose of conventional linguistic usage regarding distinctions, not for the sake of establishing the existence of the subject (*dharmin*); for if it were not perceived as residing in a specific individual, there would follow the consequence that the subject itself remains unestablished. Just as, even when a subject characterized by its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*)—such as this sound "pot" which possesses branches and so forth and is perceivable by the ear—is understood, one proceeds with the proof because there is no contradiction in the presence of doubt regarding the tree's momentariness and so on, so too is it here.

There is no room for this in the present context. For, as soon as this subject (*dharmin*), which is suitable to be pointed out by the index finger, is presented as being blue, at that very moment the doubt regarding its difference is eliminated; it is not the introduction of a formal proof (*sādhana*). This is because, in the absence of that blue form, it is impossible for the manifestation to be established as having a specific form.

For the attainment of its own nature occurs when mere exclusion of non-manifestation culminates in a particular manifestation, as in the case of the exclusion of non-wordhood (*aśabdavyāvṛtti*), and not through the exclusion of each individual [non-instance]. Therefore, because of the suspicion that it might be a non-entity (*abhāva*), a real subject (*dharmin*) is not established as desired. Consequently, since every universal possesses causal efficacy only in the form of a particular, and thus has the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), it is the blue object itself that is the subject.

The procedure for investigating difference and non-difference has been concluded with this introduction. However, the nature of momentariness and so forth would remain a subject of doubt, as it has not yet been refuted.
But here, this very same subject (*dharmin*) is manifested; since its blue form has already been shown by the proponent himself, what remains now?
Should this be understood by the members of the assembly? Or is there no fault in subsequently applying the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)? There is indeed a fault;

for even if it is stated later that "manifestation is neither one nor many," since [the statement] culminates precisely in the nature of blue—asking "what is this manifestation?"—it is impossible to demonstrate any other distinction. Furthermore, in the absence of a perceived particularity, it is impossible to establish the subject as having an existent nature.

And although, in the case of a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), both entities are indeed excluded from what is not that nature, nevertheless, it is not only this [reason], such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), that is so;
rather, this too is so. Therefore, because it is common to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is called a "universal" (*sāmānya*) and not the form of the locus (*dharmin*).
This is because it must be relied upon for the sake of engaging in or desisting from activity precisely through its non-common form, [thinking] "this is thus."

For this very reason, even regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the desire for further particulars is eliminated by means of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Let it not be that non-existence follows from being devoid of all individuals;

for ultimately, even in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no absence of individuals due to its possessing those characteristics. Even in the case of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and so forth, these are precisely the distinctions of individuals.

However, by relying on an imagined distinction, the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) holds, even when there is a factual separation through exclusion (*vyatireka-viveka*). Thus...

If the status of being a subject (*dharmibhāva*) were to exist through an imagined distinction, then let its reality (*vastutva*) be established by that very form. Since you yourself have accepted this, what effort is there to deny it? Or how could another person respect anything else that has already been refuted by the very determination of the nature of the subject? For this very reason, just as you exert effort for the sake of proving your own point, so too does the other person exert effort precisely for the sake of proving theirs.

[381,21] The investigation into the nature of the subject (*dharmī*). This person, like one who is grandly indifferent toward that [subject], does not perceive the requirement for critical examination when seeking its production. Therefore, enough with that inference which results in a contradiction precisely through the determination of the specific nature of the subject of the probandum (*sādhya*).
[381,22-23] Only a property (*dharma*) that is doubtful once the subject has been established deserves to be the means of proof (*sādhana*).
But when the ultimate limit of the specific nature of the substratum is reached, it is truly destroyed, truly destroyed.
For this very reason,
even the rebuttal regarding the distinction established by convention applies to the subject (*dharmin*);
for if the subject were established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such [conventional] impossibility would not exist.
Even when [the object] is established through inference, the form is postulated as qualified in accordance with it, depending upon the knowledge of the relationship.
Likewise, even if it were possible, since one is unable to say that this manifestation is "thus" (tathā), the fault of abandoning the subject matter (*prakṛtahāni*) remains as before. Furthermore,
there is sublation (*bādhā*) of what was accepted regarding the blue subject (*dharmin*).
[382,6] It is established that nothing else is accepted as true, and it is in vain;
[382,7] for when form reaches its ultimate limit in possibility, there is only non-duality in reality,
[382,8] just as it was stated in the proof of the *kekā* (the cry of a peacock).

Furthermore, in the formulation beginning with "in whatever form," if the application of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) is that "it is neither one nor many by means of the cognition of blue and so forth," then what fault is there? And thus, it can indeed be stated as follows:
"In whatever form something is neither one nor many, in that form it is not real."
Just as pleasure is obscured by pain, so too is light obscured by darkness.
Who can prevent the fact that illumination, like blue, pervades such an extent of space and is devoid of the nature of gross or subtle atoms?
Therefore, blue exists, but not as having the nature of illumination; thus, the existence of a distinct, insentient form is established. However, the essence of illumination is unreal.
And this is logical.
An illumination resembling a flash of lightning appears somewhere to someone at some time;
in relation to that, external illumination is considered stable, and therefore its unreality [is established].
Just as the capacity of cognition is held to exist for the production of a false blue,
so too the capacity of the intellect is held to exist for the production of a false consciousness.
"It is not possible for you to say, 'This is not desired by you either,' because my lack of desire arose from not knowing such a proof."
Nor has mere luminosity ever been perceived by anyone anywhere.
Furthermore, pleasure and the like are forms of the object to be known; therefore, the intellect is distinct from them.
Pleasure is the recognition of a manifestation and so forth; that exists even for one who is cold.
Even when there is a manifestation, the manifestation of coldness also occurs without differentiation.

[383,1] Now, if you argue that because of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), one is unable to introduce [the notion of difference] therein, then in that case, suffering (*duḥkha*) as well would be of the nature of manifestation itself, and thus it could never be abandoned. Furthermore, since this would entail the resurrection of the "whole" (*avayavin*) and so forth, everything would have been shattered from the very beginning. Therefore, where there is an appearance of non-difference, difference is not established. For this very reason, everyone...
It has been stated that the cause of differentiation is the means for establishing conventional usage.

As for those who say: "The subject (dharmin) appearing as duality is necessarily a delusion because it is unreal, just like the appearance of two lunar discs to one suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika)," their hope is based on the assumption that delusion is defined as the manifestation of what is non-existent.
And that [notion of permanence] has already been refuted for this very reason. In the same way, the claim that "the manifestation called illusion is unreal" and so forth is also refuted.
Furthermore, no so-called "illusion-maker" is established as distinct from the self-luminous form [of consciousness]. Moreover, it is accepted that one cognition arises from another cognition.

Even those who claim that there is a distinction based on the nature of the inclusive and the exclusive, for them too this is a mere conceptual construction, because— as was already largely stated in the discussion on cloth and water— there is no establishment by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for such a universal. Thus,
this [cognition] "blue light" is based on distinct limiting conditions (upādhi).
Just as the cognition of one who wears earrings arises through the nature of a specific condition.

This is the conclusion of the argument. Therefore, with respect to the various manifestations such as blue, yellow, and so forth—which arise from their respective immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*)—that which is called "manifestation" has a nature established merely through the exclusion of others (*parāpoha*). This is a mere conceptualized property (*kalpita-dharmamātra*) belonging to them.
[383,] The notion that [the cognition] is unimpaired even in the case of error is a gross delusion.

[383,17] Now, if the relationship between property and property-bearer is established as being the reverse, even in that case there is no operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for there is indeed a misconception (*viparyaya*).
The subject (dharmin) is that which possesses experience, while the property (dharma) is that which is conceptually constructed as genus and so forth.
Why, then, is the reverse held to be true for the trustworthy and the blue?

[383,21] It is only because this world, weak in discernment, relies upon the distinction between positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it employs conventional designations such as "clay" and "shape," and even the reversal of the relationship between property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Therefore, one should not be dogmatic here. Nor is it possible to accept that these two possess a separate status as distinct substrata.
If blue and so forth are luminous, what need have you for another luminosity?
If blue and so forth are not luminous, what need have you for another luminosity?

Indeed, that which is not self-luminous cannot be made manifest by another, according to the statement beginning with, "for whatever is the intrinsic nature of something... Now, if the view of those who hold to the conceit of falsity is that this is not so because there is no other intrinsic nature, then—precisely because of the absence of any other intrinsic nature—is its intrinsic nature merely luminosity? What then is the use of another luminosity? Upon what is that "falsity" mounted?

The claim that [the object] "becomes an appearance" is equivalent to the doctrine of a self (*ātman*) that serves as the substratum for cognition and so forth. However, there is this distinction: since the self, as an object of knowledge (*prameya*), remains unmanifest, its persistence is not contradictory and thus requires another blow [to refute it]; but for that which is of the nature of light (*prakāśātman*), even the mere utterance [of such a claim] is untenable—so what is the use of these burdensome and futile efforts? Let there be no exclusion of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*) on the grounds of its being unreal; therefore, for that which is not the self...

What kind of offense has been committed by the external object in its manifestation? If it has the power over the false, how could it fail to destroy the real? Therefore, Dharmottara’s desire is established without any obstacle.
If that [cognition], depending on assistance, manifests only with respect to the object,
then it is logical that the object alone is the locus for the conceptualization of identity.
And when there is the manifestation of an unreal differentiation, the form does not have a basis as it appears;
likewise, when there is the illumination of external differentiation, what is the use of a [real] form?

[384,14] Now, if it is not accepted that the external and the other [the internal] share the same security and well-being (ekayogakṣema), [384,15] then let sublation (bādhā) belong to the external alone; how, therefore, could there be falsity [of the internal]?
Just as the establishment of the external world is produced by the intellect, so too is its sublation;
this is what is appropriate, and it has been observed repeatedly.
Just as there is no establishment of one's own intellect by another's intellect, so it is not otherwise.
Even sublation does not destroy its own nature, even when it is considered external.
Thus is the intermediate verse.

Furthermore, because that which is false has no real form, it possesses no causal capacity whatsoever; therefore, even the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), which depends upon being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), is shattered without effort despite having been laboriously established. This sequence is accepted for the purpose of introducing one to the system of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavāda*). And thus, since this is the case:

Furthermore, in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, there is a persistent insistence on establishing the reality of duality; therefore, if it is maintained that cognition is in fact formless (*nirākāra*) in its ultimate nature, then let alone the establishment of the causal status of forms, since the external object—just like the form—is not denied in experience, how can the proof of "cognition-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) be established? Thus, the attempt to prove that forms are false is like raising a weapon for one's own destruction.

[It follows that this occurs] "with effort. However, when the form is undivided, because of the capacity of the determination—based on the specific nature of its own essence—that "blue was seen, not yellow," the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is at least accomplished through mere conceit (*ābhimānikī*), even though there is no external object.

Consequently, for the investigation already undertaken, since there is an absence of the definition of a graspable object (*grāhyalakṣaṇābhāvāt*), there is no obstruction to the establishment of self-cognition alone (*svavedanamātrasiddhi*). For this very reason:

At the end of that [passage], one might think it would be appropriate for someone to say: "This [cognition] has blue and so forth as its form, and it is that very thing which is the experience" (PV III 328; NBhūṣ 139,27), and so on. Yet, even so, because there is subsequently an absence of a pervader, the external form or the [external] object lacks substantial reality.

Do you mean to say that we shall set aside mere luminosity and establish [something else]? If so, why this elaborate effort from the very beginning to propitiate the demon of "forms"? Just as it is your own view that this cognition is formless while the external correspondence possesses form, let the accomplishment of the goal be achieved by introducing the non-perception of such a fixed state. Therefore, whence the consideration of the definition of the apprehended object? It is not [necessary].

Alternatively, two reasons must be stated for the simultaneous perception of the manifestation [of the object] and [the cognition], because of the fault [inherent] in proving the form [of the object] by way of [that manifestation], and because the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) must necessarily be relied upon;
thus, it is well established according to the intention of Dharmottara.
And we see that this very threefold method is the direct means for the Master [Dharmakīrti] to prove "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) in all cases.

The intent of the demonstration lies precisely here; however, regarding the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) discussed by the former masters, it is merely inferred, like a coarse object, because there is no refutation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Therefore, if Dharmottara’s lack of attention toward the rebuttal of atoms is due to the statement that "their form is neither one nor many," we observe that this is established as the primary point without effort; thus, everything is resolved.
