The view of the Teacher (Ācārya) is adopted here; yet there is no harm whatsoever in this, provided it possesses even a scent of logic (*nyāyagandha*).

On this point, something has already been stated. Furthermore, do not think that because the external object is unreal—being known through manifestation—the status of the grasped and the grasper is established in some other way.
For if it were not manifested, the consequence would be that self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) would have to be admitted; so what is the use of another manifestation?

Therefore, forms, sounds, and so forth are established as being of the nature of cognition by virtue of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), since we have already demonstrated in the refutation of external objects that they are indeed unique (*asādhāraṇa*). Here too, one should not be terrified by the "frightening specter of the ignorant," namely the objection that mere self-awareness is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and that its reality (*tāttvika*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for what is imagined (*kalpita*) is untenable, and it is only the real that exists.
Since this has been established, there is no room for the two-fold conceptual alternative.

For this very reason, when proving the falsity of consciousness as well—on the grounds that its forms are not distinct from it—it is impossible to charge the argument with being unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, as for what is stated by way of a counter-argument: "Whatever form is non-sublatable belongs to the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of that thing; for example..."
“The essence of awakening (*bodhātman*) is the nature of all phenomena; and the fact that the form of the essence of awakening is unassailable constitutes a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
This too is refuted by the very same [argument]: because a distinct subject (*dharmin*) is not established, and because blue is subject to sublation.
Therefore,
there is no functioning of cognitions apart from the distinction of their forms; thus, victory belongs to the illustrious Middle Way, which is powerful in refuting that [position].
If this faultless, non-dual, and variegated [reality] does not exist,
then what room is there for one who maintains that the mind is devoid of form?
The first chapter, the Refutation of the Formless, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.
The Second Chapter [387]:

If, then, the non-existence of a formless consciousness is [asserted] in reality, there would be a collapse of the established order of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*). For the collection of forms is a delusion (*bhrānti*), arising from grasping at that which is not [the case]; thus, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is precisely this. When the mass of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) produced by that [delusion] is completely eradicated, the delusion vanishes, and what remains is Nirvana: a stainless, non-manifesting mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*). Thus, there is no fault. Otherwise, if a consciousness possessing forms were sublated, purification would be untenable.
But if there were no contradiction [with perception], the difficulty of establishing the nature of affliction (*saṅkleśa*) would arise.

For, since sentient beings themselves clearly experience their own natures without error, there would be an absolute absence of delusion (*bhrānti*). Consequently, all sentient beings would be eternally liberated and eternally perfectly awakened Buddhas. If it is argued that "delusion is conceptual cognition (*vikalpikā buddhi*), because it superimposes an object onto its own appearance, which is not an actual object," then how is it that the object being determined by that [cognition] does not appear [in it]? Or, if it does appear, how could that [object] not appear in that [cognition]?

If, on the other hand, it were indeed manifest, then it would follow that the object is identical with it; furthermore, that [manifestation] would not exist when the object is absent. Moreover, there would be a determination in its entirety such as "Māndhātṛ existed," "Śaṅkha will exist," "the self exists," or "sound is eternal. And it would be manifested through its own distinct characteristic as "cow"; and since a convention is impossible regarding a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that cognition would not be conceptual at all.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the cognition of a cow (*gobuddhi*) appears through a distortion (*viplava*) associated with verbal expression, by means of "cowness" (*gotva*) which is common to all individual cows without exception; such an appearance is what constitutes the determination of the object "cow. For in this way, these faults would not arise, since there is a mistaken determination (*bhrāntavasāya*) of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), even though it does not actually appear [in the cognition].

Just as the unreal universal *gotva* (cowness) appears in the cognition of a cow and is identical with it—and because it is not distinct from that [cognition], it possesses either reality or non-superimposedness—so too, in the manifestation of blue and so forth, the identity of the unreal blue and so forth is established by the very fact that their manifestation is established. This is because there is no contradiction between being unreal and being real when these properties reside in different forms, even within a single entity. Furthermore, if that identity alone were the reason (*hetu*) to prove reality or non-superimposedness, then it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the presence of] universals such as *gotva*.
If, on the other hand, "non-superimposed identity" is the reason, then that is unestablished (*asiddha*). To this, it is replied:
If it is universally accepted that error consists in the apprehension of something as what it is not,
then [the theory of] a false mental image being perceived as real is not tenable.

[388] In the world, the perception of water in a mirage where there is no water is known as an error (*bhrānti*); and in the treatises, it is stated in many ways that inference is erroneous because it proceeds by determining an object (*artha*) within its own appearance (*svapratibhāsa*), which is not an actual object. Thus, the apprehension of something as what it is not is recognized as error. If this [error] is untenable in the theory of "possessing aspects" (*sākāravāda*), then consider how it could possibly be tenable in the case of a purely false aspect (*alīkākāra*).

For knowledge indeed arises with some aspect, whether real or false; however, as for the superimposition of an external object upon that aspect, it might be produced by that [knowledge] itself or by something else. If it were produced by that [knowledge] itself, then at that very moment another operation would have to be experienced—so how could there be such a superimposition? And at a later time, being non-existent by its own nature, of what could it be the operation?

In the second case as well, even another cognition cannot perform any function whatsoever toward anything else through any other operation, except by way of an arising that is colored by the form [of its object]. Thus, even when making the form of a prior cognition its own object, this [subsequent] cognition does not touch upon any further operation of superimposing the external, apart from merely imitating a fraction of that [prior] form; for even the form of the word is included within its own essential nature.

And if another operation were possible for the sake of superimposition (*āropa*) rather than [the manifestation of] the form, one would have to state that [that operation] is the means of proof even in inference (*anumāna*). If it is argued that "it is the means of proof for the sake of apprehension (*adhigati*), not for the sake of superimposition," we say no; because the manifestation of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is rejected in inference, this [manifestation] is indeed a superimposition. If it is argued that "superimposition has an unreal object (*asatyaviṣaya*)," then surely there would be the apprehension of the very form of fire established by inference. Therefore, "superimposition" (*āropa*), "ascertainment" (*avasāya*), and "conceited cognition" (*abhimāna*) are synonymous terms.
However, there is a distinction based on correspondence and its opposite, because it would follow that conceptual construction alone is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, there is no operation of cognition other than its form (*ākāra*). And if that external object being superimposed appears in that cognition by way of its own nature, then this is simply a true perception; what, then, would be the purpose of the superimposition? Furthermore, if it were to appear, it would entail the consequence of perceiving a second form. If it is argued that "the appearance of that [external] form is itself the appearance of the [object]," we say no, because that [external object] is the objective domain of the superimposition. For the appearance of a mirage is not the same as the appearance of water, even if they are unified with it. If it is argued [that they are unified] because of their being identified with one another...

What is this meaning of "unification"? If it means being the cause for the attainment of oneness, then that is impossible, because there is never any actual unification between the object of superimposition and its locus; for instance, there is no cause whatsoever for a rabbit's horn. Nor is it tenable for a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) to claim that what was previously manifold attains oneness, for that would merely be the arising of a different entity, and even that is not within the range of perception apart from the locus of superimposition. Furthermore, since the object itself undergoes no change by that much, how could there be a superimposition of it?

Now, "single cognition" means unification. Even so, it does not apply to two things, because there is no experience of the superimposed object. Nor is mere cognition of two things itself a superimposition, as in the case of blue and yellow; for that too must be rejected, since there is not even a trace of the cognition of an object to be superimposed. For if an external object were to appear, it would be logical to speak of its cognition as being either as one or as many, or as existent or non-existent.

If it is argued that this cognition is a "single cognition" because it occurs by way of obscuring the true nature of those [individuals] in all their aspects, then, if their true nature is obscured, they would simply not appear at all. If it is argued that this is not so because some part [of them] does appear, we say no; for since a real entity is partless, it must either appear in its entirety or not appear at all. This has been explained at length in the treatise regarding the opponent's position.

If it is argued that this is due to "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), we have already essentially stated that this too—being synonymous with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—does not know even a report of the external object apart from its own internal form. Furthermore, if it is claimed that there is a cognition [of the object] as non-different [from the cognition], then even under the view of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), what has been said is simply a restatement of the cognition of identity, and that has already been refuted. Even if one merely negates the cognition of difference, no cognition of the external object has been stated; so how could there be a superimposition (*āropa*) of it?

It is useless to define [the relation] as "not by way of difference," because there is an absence of any established cognition of identity through non-difference, and because it is impossible to deny the mere cognition of the object of superimposition itself; for one who merely restates that much has not stated any specific distinction at all.

Therefore, as long as something is being conceptualized, there is no such thing as "superimposition" (āropa), because there is an absence of contact with that which is to be superimposed. Even when an error is established through some manner of designating it as a manifestation and thus superimposing it, there is an obstruction [to truth] regarding the form—even if it were real—as if it were false; however, by that much alone, its ultimate reality is not asserted. If that is so, then even when its own nature appears, it would certainly not be an error; how then can there be the status of an illusion? It is not possible in any way, provided one has regard for critical inquiry.

Relying upon conventional usage—which is pleasing so long as it is not investigated and is established even among children—we employ designations such as "person" (pudgala) and the like; yet, when subjected to investigation, these utterly fall apart.
Just as the self [is established], so too is external [reality] known through correspondence as valid cognition;
thus, the two types of error, which are intent upon conventional practice, are manifold.
In this regard, as long as there is non-investigation, so long is there saṃsāra; and as long as there is the culmination of the discernment of one's own nature, so long is there nirvāṇa.
Full comprehension of existence itself is said to be nirvāṇa.

Such is the logical principle. How, then, is there the full comprehension of existence (*bhava-parijñāna*), or how can there be activity and so forth through delusion regarding that which does not exist in reality? We shall explain this later. For now, let us consider how the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākāravādin*) establishes the status of delusion in terms of ultimate reality. In that case, for him as well, let there be no delusion consisting of the imposition of something external (*parāropa*). What is incorrect about the claim that delusion is simply the association with a false aspect (*alīkākāra*), and that its removal constitutes liberation?

First of all, there is the transgression of both worldly convention and scientific treatises. For a person employs the term "error" (*bhrama*) regarding a rope due to the superimposition (*āropa*) of a snake; however, cognition does not touch the person in any such manner. Furthermore, when that superimposition of a snake is investigated, there is no effort [to reach its limit], nor does another have the power to carry it to its conclusion. Thus, it is established that one employs this error characterized by such [superimposition].

In the treatise as well, activity based on the determination of an object within one’s own internal appearance is called an error; it is not, however, because the internal appearance itself is devoid of an object. Likewise, the meaning of the unification of the perceived and the conceptualized is precisely this: it is not that the conceptualized object is unreal in itself, but rather that it is so because of the superimposition of the perceived upon it. Even in the case of non-conceptual [cognition], where two moons appear, it would be "delightful only so long as not investigated" (avicāritaramaṇīya), because the conceptualization superimposes its own operation onto that very [appearance].
Error exists even in the non-conceptual because of conceptualization; there is nothing beyond that.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] comes to rest in the non-conceptual by first resting in the conceptual.

Therefore, since the persistence of error occurs everywhere solely through the imposition [of something] by another, why is it improper to call this a mere technical term (*paribhāṣā*) that does not resolve the issue? If you argue that there is no fault because the avoidance [of the problem] follows simply from its impossibility, since you have already admitted the incapacity of your justification—then if that is so, there certainly exists an error established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), and investigation acts as its subverter. By this much alone, the desired point is proven; any further distinction is merely a trace of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*).

For that conventional delusion is indistinguishable from the positions of either the real or the unreal; since I have accepted that even the mental aspect (*ākāra*) is unreal, I have brought about its status as a delusion simply so that it does not persist in the final analysis—this is a mere insistence, for both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are established otherwise.
As long as the fall of delusion occurs through investigation, that is excellent;
but to say it is "non-existent in every respect" is even more excellent than the excellent.
Therefore, it is appropriate to apply effort toward investigation;
for even the wise might occasionally have doubts regarding the removal of what truly exists.
These are the two intermediate verses.

Therefore, what is the point of this claim that error is the appearance of the unreal? Even for one who does not accept that [definition], this is merely a failure to adopt the opponent's position; it is a transgression of the logic observed therein. As for the statement that "error is the manifestation of the unreal because of a lack of connection" (*ayogāt*), for one who perceives that lack of connection, what kind of "connection" could there be such that one would say "error is the manifestation of the unreal"? For instance, by "appearance of the unreal," do you mean the cognition of something unreal such as God (*īśvara*) and so forth, or that the appearing form itself is unreal, or that some real thing simply does not appear?
Regarding these:
[391] How could that which has the manifestation of its own nature be non-existent?
If it is because of sublation, then surely that sublation is also either perceptual or inferential.
If there is no trust in perception in one case, what recourse is there in another?
How then can inference, which is preceded by that [perception], be an object of trust?
Perceptuality consists in the direct realization of its own nature, and there is no other [perceptuality].
In the treatise as well, perception is defined precisely as the direct realization of the thing's own nature;
for this very reason, its status as a ground for conceptual construction or error is refuted.
If it were not perceived by direct perception, its appearance as a form would not exist at all;
therefore, the claim that God and so forth appear [in consciousness] while being non-existent is incoherent.
If its form were to appear, then that [form] would indeed exist;
but since it appears as non-existent, for you, only the non-existent appears.
(These three verses may also be found at RNA2 133,17–22.

By this, the second position should also be understood as refuted; for since existence is established by mere appearance, there is no room for sublation. [Objection: But is it not observed that even in the case of the appearance of two moons and so forth, there is indeed sublation?
Since it is observed [to exist], there is no lack of logical consistency; thus, what was stated previously is also incorrect.
That too is incorrect; for that which is sublated does not appear [in cognition], whereas that which appears is not subject to sublation. To explain:
The appearance of the form of cognition is the sublation of the external object;
for just as there is the appearance of color-form, there is likewise the sublation of touch and so forth.
(Cf. RNA1 125, RNA2 133,14f., where the second half reads:
"Even when there is manifestation, if there is no conviction, where is there conviction? Thus it is proclaimed.")

For that which appears as mere form is determined as a specific aggregate of color, taste, smell, and touch. For this very reason, the possibility of actions such as grasping with the hand occurs in relation to hair and the like; likewise, sublation applies only to that form which is accompanied by [the other qualities], not to form alone. Indeed, one who seeks a specific causal efficiency (arthakriyā) attends only to the establishment or sublation of its means, and not to just anything.
What is the use of a lustful woman examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch?

[392] However, it is precisely those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*) who, out of regard for other purposes, examine even universals (*sāmānya*) and the like. In that context, regarding both that which appears as mere form and those four concomitants which are determined as having the nature of a composite whole, people—due to the absence of discernment and the conceit of non-difference between them—conventionally designate this [composite] as "non-existent" or "unreal."

Therefore, due to that very conceit (*abhimāna*), whatever injunction or prohibition exists here terminates only in what is conceptually determined (*adhyavasita*), because its true nature is concealed by the superimposition of something else. Consequently, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of it in reality, just as in the case of the meaning of words. And it is established that for that complex (*kalāpa*) which is subject to sublation, there is no appearance (*pratibhāsa*).

Therefore, even if there were an obstruction caused by mere conceit regarding that which appears—whether it be real or not—there would be no harm; for such diverse conventionalities are indeed experienced in the world. For this very reason, one enters into the investigation of reality (*tattva*). However, if it does not manifest according to the aforementioned method, how can there be a determination of it? Thus, it follows that there is the manifestation of the non-existent.

Likewise, regarding the conceit of non-difference (*abhedābhimāna*), there is the appearance of a non-existent non-difference; and even the "concealment" (*pracchādana*) through the superimposition of something else cannot occur without the manifestation of that other thing—this would require one to open one's mouth wide in laughter. In this regard, if one were to close one's eyes and reflect upon it, one would only mock oneself. For it has been said: even in the case of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), there is no other mode of superimposition of another [object] apart from the vivid delineation of a specific form; nor is there a cognition of what is not the self.

Nor is the negation of its own form intended by people, nor is it possible, because it contradicts the negation of that which appears as its own nature. Therefore, what was prattled in the theory of "having forms" (sākāravāda)—that permanent entities and so forth must exist—has fallen back upon oneself. "If there is sublation even when there is an appearance, then non-existence is not considered [the case] for things that do not appear; for there is no negation of perceptions that have not been negated. (81b)
If that whose own nature appears is not real because of a sublater,
then what confidence can there be even in the sublater, since it too appears as having another nature?
The exclusion of its own nature occurs through the introduction of another nature;
even in that case, doubt arises because of the perception of a prior sublation.

If this very sublation occurs upon grasping [the object] and there is no other for that which is born of the senses, then let the former alone be its [sublation]; the manifestation of form is the same in both cases.
There is no proof for you that [cognition] does not manifest anything other [than itself],
even when there is the possibility of a sublation regarding the manifestation of its own nature.
Therefore,
when there is no appearance of its own nature due to the failure of the purification of the cause, [393]...
If this were so even when there is no appearance of a suspicion of sublation, then there would be a great confusion.
(Quoted in RNA1 129,
RNA2 137) These are the intermediate verses. Therefore,

what further cause for ridicule is there than this frantic effort to revive— in every respect already refuted— the theory that the unreal is manifested, merely by hearing a word when there is no determination of an object that has been ascertained?
The resurrection from the word of one who has been refuted by valid cognition is as remarkable as the revival of one bitten by a serpent through the power of a mantra.

Therefore, just as in the case of the employment of words such as "self" (*ātman*) or "cowness" (*gotva*), it is correct that the wise attend only to the mere investigation of the determination [of an object] and its cognition—whether from themselves or from another. This is the ultimate truth here: due to the force of various beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), arising in a certain form in dependence upon a specific awakening condition, establishes a continuous stream of purposeful action, memory, and verbal expression conducive to outward-directed activity.

Consequently, for a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), there arise activities and abstentions that correspond to external objects. Such is the cause of the moments of cognition within the mental continuum of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), because the nature of things is determinate. Even at the time of conceptualizing an object whose relationship [to reality] is uncertain, there occurs the production of activity based on the determination of existence, non-existence, and so forth.

In this context, that capacity of the means of cognition (*sādhana*) which functions in both ways—having come to it by the power of its own cause—is precisely this superimposition (*āropa*) of the object as the domain of activity, which has the other name "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*). For example, whether a cognition of the moon and so forth is erroneous or non-erroneous, its very operation of grasping consists in the production of an ascertainment based on the perception of that [object].

According to the principle that "this [cognition] must be seen as having an object through its functional effect (*kārya*) even in some respect," so too, for a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in a form such as "there is fire here," its very capacity to impel activity (*pravṛtty-ākṣepakatva*) constitutes the determination of the external object (*bāhyādhyavasāya*). Just as for non-conceptual perception, its very possession of the form of the moon and so forth is what effects the determination, so too for conceptual determination, its very possession of such a form is what effects the activity directed away from other objects.

Consequently, even though its appearance in that form lacks the status of being the cause for an unapprehended object, it is established as if distinct by virtue of being the locus of superimposition, as is the cognition of what is superimposed. If it is argued: "In that case, those three alone are established as non-existent, and since establishment is a form of cognition, there is no escape from the cognition of the non-existent," this is merely shifting the burden within the same stream. For it has been said: "Superimposition is simply the implication of an activity corresponding to that [object]; it is not some other thing called 'cognition'."

[394] Therefore, even today, there is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a non-existent triad; thus, there is no fault whatsoever, because the result is merely a cognition corresponding to that [determination]—a conventional usage based on the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asad-pratīti-vāda*)—and the cognition itself has the form "this is non-existent," characterized by its beginningless state (*anādy-avasthā-lakṣaṇa*).

In this way, one should infer similar minor disturbances elsewhere as well. This kind of error—consisting in the apprehension of something as what it is not—is common to all conceptual constructions and follows from direct experience. This very process is designated as the "unification of the perceived and the conceptualized. It is the capacity to engage with another object based solely on the awareness of one's own internal representation; and it is the concealment of one's own nature by means of that [external] form.

However, with respect to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*), it is said that the form of another is concealed by its own form, because only that [own-form] is manifested. Even though the external object exists, it is in reality devoid of an object (*nirviṣaya*) precisely because of this manifestation. Furthermore, because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) has the nature of the self, and because there is no conceptual determination (*anadhyavasāya*), for these very reasons, the threefold establishment of exclusion (*apoha*) occurs: according to conceptual determination, according to appearance, and according to reality.

If that which is excluded from other classes is what is denoted by words, then let it be so in external conceptualization; however, my friend, since this has been established as a limb [of the system], now, by means of this primary cause, both [the external object and the internal image] are [excluded] through the exclusion (*apoha*) of the appearance and the mental determination (*adhyavasiti*).

If it is argued that because of the non-existence of the external object there is an absence of appearance, and because there is an absence of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an aspect (*ākāra*) resembling a real entity excluded from heterogeneous things produced by sound, then nothing at all would be denotable; so what, in reality, is the meaning of *apoha*? [The response is: This *apoha* is clearly that which is "nothing at all. The connection [of the words] is "it is not denotable," just as in the preceding sentence. The meaning is this: when it is said that *apoha* is the denotable, the meaning is that, in reality, there is a negation of the very thing that would be denotable.

Just as "non-existence comes to be" means that "existence does not come to be," so it is established that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the object of words. Regarding the Sūtra passage beginning with "by whatever dharma," let as many branches as there may be emerge from such a root for the proponents of Apoha; we have no insistence on this point. And since the property of conceptual thought known as "ascertainment of the external"—which is defined by its nature as the cause for outward-directed activity—is established, then even the resulting ascertainment of all aspects must likewise have its essence established through its utility in producing corresponding subsequent cognitions.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the capacity of a conceptual cognition—which delineates a single form—to function with respect to another form is beyond the scope of experience; therefore, it is logical to ask: how could there be a dependence on other means of valid cognition, such as verbal testimony?

In this regard, although non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is erroneous, it is established as a means of apprehension by virtue of its clear manifestation. Conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), however, because its nature consists of reflective deliberation (*vimarśa*),—even though it functions independently of anything else—is the locus of conventional designations such as "superimposition" (*āropa*), since it delineates a single, indistinct exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). Every conceptual cognition, without actually touching the external object, is said to be erroneous because it prompts activity toward something external, whether that external object exists or not. But when the external object does not exist, it is settled that the error of non-conceptual cognition consists in its connection with a form that contains within its womb the capacity to produce such a conceptual cognition.

Every conceptual cognition is indeed devoid of an external object; yet, following various distinctions of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and fashioned by its own internal form, it produces recollections of perceived results and so forth,
thereby inciting the activity of worldly people just like perception, even though it is independent of anything else.
The superimposition of a real entity is said to be like the superimposition of water upon a mirage, as in the case of [imagining] waters where there are no waters.
Thus is the summary.

This being the case, that which was determined to be an external aggregate of parts—brought to a state of readiness for practical engagement and yet sublated according to the aforementioned sequence—does not appear [in cognition]. And it is established that there is no sublation of the form that actually appears.

For there is no dispute whatsoever regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). It is simply that the subsequent conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) follows upon what is endowed with causal efficiency, and there is no impairment of that [efficiency]. Any impairment, however, pertains only to that which is to be accomplished by a specific complex of conditions (*kalāpaviśeṣa*); thus, it is only that [specific capacity] which is absent. Therefore, how can it be said that there is a sublation (*bādhā*) of that which is appearing? And when one relies on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), everything previously mentioned recurs.
In the consideration of the absence of the pervader, there is neither a boat nor an ant;
yet, even without [the presence of] a fault, there is the investigation of affliction and so forth within the theory of cognition with forms (*sākāra*).

It has begun. In that regard, even though there is the self-awareness of the true nature [of cognition], no impairment of the defilements occurs by relying on the status of error—which, although established in worldly convention for all cognitions, is produced by beginningless time. And just as there is the establishment of error in some cases when an external object exists, so it is everywhere in the case of determination. It is merely said that, with respect to activity directed toward the external, there is no error whatsoever regarding the self;
for "in whatever way a cognition appears, that indeed is its form."

Thus, in the association with words, because there is a determination toward the external, there is conceptualization and lack of clarity in that very [cognition]; for, in relation to another cognition, that same object exists as solitary and clear. But regarding its own nature (ātmarūpa), since such a form is subject to deviation, how could there be such a determination for that cognition which is born from a specific causal complex?

Even when this very [cognition] is intended to be connected with another object by means of a word without being made the object of that other cognition, even then the connection occurs only with respect to the other and not with respect to itself; this is what must be considered according to the treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, it is not the case that it would not be conceptual (*vikalpikā*) in relation to itself—this is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—but rather, it is indeed conceptual with respect to the other, by virtue of the force of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) and conventional establishment (*vyavasthā*).

Now, if it is argued that this is said solely by the force of the manifestation of the thing's own nature (*vastusvarūpa*), then even to assert this in the context of the theory of "cognition with form" (*sākāravāda*) is a great rashness. If it is claimed that [the external object] is drawn forth by conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), we say no; for that [determination] has been established otherwise. Indeed, when that [object] manifests, there is no such thing as "determination," because only the appearance itself is obtained. For this very reason, the claim that—despite the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) not appearing—there is a determination of it therein due to error (*bhrānti*), is not tenable.

When there is contact with the cognition of that [object] through a determination (*avasāya*), what other appearance could there be? To say "because of its indistinctness" is not tenable; for if there is a cognition of that very form, that [indistinctness] itself is unestablished.
One should recall such statements as: "A different basis indeed arises" (PV III 235a).

And at that time, it cannot be an error, because it appears as the very form of a real entity; if you argue that it is a cognition of the unreal (*alīka*), then how can that [cognition] itself be the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object? If you say that "that [cognition] itself is it," no, for one who knows "this is unreal" lacks the established determination of an external object. If you say that it is not a verbalization of the unreal, but rather the awareness of that [unreal thing] which constitutes the determination of the external, even so, there would be a mere difference in terminology, and there would be no manifestation of the intended object.

For as long as it is said that there is "cognition of a false form" due to the absence of contact with an external intrinsic nature, so long is it said to be "ascertainment"; thus, no distinction whatsoever has been stated. And this being the case, just as the cognition of a false form does not admit a connection such that "it belongs to the external," so too ascertainment would not possess the connection such that "it belongs to the external. For the genitive case [expressing "of"] is dependent upon the conceit of cognizing that [external object]; in its absence, how could it exist?
If that [cognition] is false because it has come down through a tradition, then there is no error on that account alone; for this would apply equally even to a cognition that is not false.

Therefore, that which was stated—that this "determination of an object by the cognition" is merely a specific manifestation capable of being associated with verbal expression—is refuted, because the connection [expressed] as "of the object" (arthasya) is untenable, and because there can be no error regarding the cognition itself. Furthermore, let the determination simply be that the manifestation is false; what is the use of the qualification "capable of being associated with verbal expression"? If it is argued that this is for the sake of excluding non-conceptual [cognition]:

If this is so, then even in the case of non-false (analīka) discourse, it is only cognition qualified by those specific attributes that is an error, not all [cognition]; thus, there is no total absence of affliction and purification. For even when error ceases, it is only a specific class of cognition that is relinquished. Furthermore, in both systems, the connection with verbal expression is dependent upon something else, so there is no harm. The only fault is that if that [object] is not perceived, the determination of its conceptual resolution is difficult; and that [fault] is common to both of us.

Therefore, even for one who runs very far away from cognition, it must be accepted that a determination (*avasāya*) regarding the external object—by means of a specific capacity alone, even without [direct] cognition, and by metaphorically designating it as its apprehension—rests upon a function that establishes a connection; for at that time, there is no distinction whether the mental form (*ākāra*) is false or real.

Thus, having attributed the state of being manifest through the process of being determined (*avasīyamānatva*) to the object for the sake of its determination, [you argue that] the identity of the object [with its cognition], its non-existence when the object is absent, and so forth, are logical; however, all of this is untenable. That the cognition functions without having perceived the object—this alone is the cognitive distortion (*viplava*). For this very reason, since there is no contact with the object even when the exclusion (*apoha*) in the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the denotable [meaning], where is the fault of the consequence that [the cognition] would grasp all aspects?
Thus he says: "And because the cognition of a universal is a cognitive distortion, it is therefore not a flaw. (PV I 169)

Thus, because it implies activity toward that very [object] by way of having the form of the exclusion of others (*ekavyāvṛtti*), and because the person attains satisfaction with just that much, they do not investigate anything further. However, regarding the failure to obtain that alone, he states the contradiction: "That which, despite being existent, does not appear to any conceptual cognition—how can it be called non-existent? This is far removed from reason. Nor is there non-existence for that which is appearing. Therefore, how can blue be manifested as non-existent by means of the example of "cowness" (*gotva*), and how can there be a conceptualization of identity (*tādātmya*) between them?

By this, [the objection] beginning with "between those two which abide in different forms" is also refuted. Furthermore, the claim that there is a contradiction between the non-existent and the manifest is incorrect because of the proof of their opposition; moreover, the phrase "in a single entity" is improper, since there is no entity of manifestation distinct from blue. Nor is there any purpose in postulating a difference, because what is intended to be expressed is merely the negation of one of two things. And that [negation] would exist either when one thing is manifest and the other is imagined—as the nature of a cloth [is absent] in a jar—or even when both are manifested separately, as in the case of a hare and a gadfly.

Furthermore, this principle is not established anywhere for two things that have an identical appearance but whose difference is established merely through the exclusion of what they are not (*atadvyāvṛtti*).

If it is argued that even though color and shape appear identically, the shape is non-existent, we say no; for in that case too, what is negated is only a conceptualized shape called "the conjunction of the arrangement of parts" which is distinct [from the color]. How could the essence of the color, denoted by the word "square" and arising from the exclusion of states that are the objects of conventional usage such as "circular," be negated?

Likewise here too, only the differentiated and imagined [nature] is negated; it is impossible to negate the blue as being either identical with its manifestation or identical with the manifestation itself, precisely because they appear as non-distinct. Consequently, if the probandum is "being a real entity" or "not being superimposed," the blue exists [as such].

Furthermore, with respect to the form of cognition that has become manifest, there is no absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*). For the manifestation of the form of "cowness" is not a superimposition (*āropa*) by anyone else, because there is no superimposer distinct from the existence [of the cognition itself], and because the manifestation of the very form of "cowness" is produced by its own cause. Nor is there a superimposition of a self upon itself, nor a superimposition of one thing by another; rather, there would merely be a naming [of it]. Consequently, since the nature of manifestation is entirely non-superimposed everywhere, there is not even a scent of the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Furthermore, that which is superimposed ought to be indistinct, like water and such; however, the luminosity (*prakāśatā*) of the blue is experienced as being even more distinct. It is not as if there were a separate luminosity [distinct from the object], like a separate blueness; for if it were distinct, then luminosity, being existent, would have to appear just like the blue.

Thus, wherever there is the cognition that something appears as non-existent or false according to reasoning (*tarka*) and scripture (*āgama*), provided it is other than the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra, that [cognition] occurs only with respect to what has been determined (*adhyavasita*), or from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyāvahārika*). For he employs terms such as "false" based merely on the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for an external object to be accomplished, which is imagined through its form. This negation of the external is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [conventional view]. In reality, however, the non-existent (*asat*) is simply another kind of existent; and it is called "false" because it is other than what is intended. Or rather, it might be so.

When cognition has a permanent form, then because it arises as pervading multiple times, it would follow—though this is trivial—that it must be eternally existent just like its form; however, its possession of that form is merely by way of imitation (*anukāra*) and not through identity (*tādātmya*), for otherwise there would be the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of burning occurring through the mere conceptualization of fire. Therefore, just as a banyan tree, which pervades a vast space, is imitated by a reflection on the surface of a mirror that can be contained within a mere leaf due to some difference in form, so too is the permanent [entity] imitated by a momentary form.

And here, experience [confirms this]: at the time of conceptualizing a permanent self and so forth, there is a resemblance to that [object] even without a pervasion of all time, which would otherwise obstruct the opportunity for other cognitions. For even if it is false, it need not be a false thing that possesses the form of permanence by virtue of pervading time; otherwise, it would lack the capacity to prompt the engagement in investigations into existence and non-existence that correspond to it. Therefore, it is logical that there is a partial resemblance to it even without a pervasion of time. This is just as when a representation of an upright staff or the like is attended to at some particular time.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that for an eternal entity, an effect produced in all its states could occur in only a single state—by means of the "upper," "lower," and "intermediate" parts which characterize the forms of the past, future, and present—it is shown that there is likewise no contradiction in the arising of even the intellect (*buddhi*) in a single moment when it assumes that form. Therefore, that which is non-existent does not manifest; however, it may be merely determined (*adhyavasita*). As was stated previously: "And that which manifests by its own nature is established as being non-existent [in that respect]."

Consequently, the manifestation of the non-existent cannot be the definition of error, because that is impossible. For this very reason, the third alternative—that what is existent does not manifest—is also untenable; for existence is pervaded by manifestation, and that which is unmanifested is swallowed up by non-existence (*aprakāśasyāsattayā grasteḥ*; the meaning is "because of the pervasion").

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that what is called 'manifestation' (prakāśa) is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes an object? And there is no absence of an object merely because a means of valid cognition is absent. Furthermore, the reality of an entity consists in its capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā-śakti), and this is not incompatible even with that which is unmanifested"—this is true in the context of the theory of external objects (bahirarthavāda), since even an unmanifested object is admitted there. However, in the case of the appearance of [illusory] hair and the like, the object as determined by conceptualization is devoid of causal efficiency.

[399] For in this way, non-existence is established. But if there is an absolute absence of external objects, since cognition is never dissociated from its manifestation, its existence is accounted for by that alone; what then is the use of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? If it is argued that its existence is not established by manifestation alone because it belongs to another's mind, then neither is there causal efficiency for anyone. If it is asked why it does not appear to everyone at all times, [the answer is: why should it not manifest to someone somewhere?
Moreover,
even in the case of an external object, its existence is asserted in reality by virtue of its manifestation.
The classification of sentient beings is established according to the practitioner's intention and capacity.
Since even a capacity is not established as existing without manifestation,
if one were to claim it exists by the power of another capacity, there would be an infinite regress.
Power is known through its effect, and being an effect implies dependence on something else;
even if there is no certainty regarding that power, it exists provided there is a distinct exclusion [from others].
If its capacity is not ascertained, how indeed can it be an effect?
For being an effect is a property of the thing itself, even though it partakes of distinct exclusions (vyāvṛtti).
Otherwise, why is it that hair and the like do not possess the status of being effects?
If you say they indeed possess the status of being effects, then let existence itself be nothing other than manifestation, because of its non-deviation [from it].
If it is argued that superimposed things have no causal function, then why is luminosity not likewise [without such function]?
If luminosity is due to their being unified, then how can they also possess causal function in that same way?
Just as there is no member [of a causal complex] due to the absence of the result, so too there is no result due to the absence of the members;
therefore, when there is doubt regarding its being a real entity, there is doubt regarding its being an effect and so forth.
Therefore, through the power of practice, there is a definitive certainty regarding that capacity:
luminosity itself is existence, or its effect is cognition itself.
Nor does its existence depend on another effect; rather, it is [known] through self-awareness.
For cognition never deviates from its own object.
If someone has doubt in that regard concerning an action, certainty arises from repeated practice;
therefore, in reality, existence exists even outside [the mind] solely through manifestation.
[400] Nor is there any loss of momentariness in this way, because cognition grasps [the object] in a single moment;
and that cognition, occurring only occasionally, serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the exhaustion of the power of the cause.
And it is stated in the treatise: "Cognition is existence; non-cognition is also the non-existence of the perceptible.
This [non-existence] is devoid of dependence on the loss of designation, purposeful action, and so forth."
Even incapacity in that regard does not constitute a sublation;
moreover, this much is the distinction: visibility and invisibility are declared to be existence and non-existence.
Sometimes, for someone, there is illumination somewhere by means of inference;
however, the absence of illumination is to be understood as false when one attends to external objects.
Even in the absence of inferential cognition, there is manifestation through conceptual construction alone;
let manifestation be of the same nature as the existence of such things.
Everyone seeking purposeful action attains the status of a real entity only through its result;
and it is precisely therein that one deposits the appearance, making it the locus of activity.
And thus there is no impairment of the commenced conventional pride;
power has been described, and from that follows existence, which is indeed pure by nature.

Therefore, even in the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda), although from the perspective of conventional usage there is a twofold status— namely, that power (śakti) is [conventional] existence and manifestation (prakāśa) is the ultimate reality.
These are the intermediate verses.

Now, if it is argued that existence (*sattva*) should not be denied even to the appearing form (*ākāra*) because it lacks causal efficiency (*śakti*), and that for this reason existence is defined as causal efficiency—then what kind of proof of our desired conclusion is this? For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that [existence] is distinct from that [causal efficiency]. Furthermore, it is impossible to deny that the form possesses causal efficacy, since it has been demonstrated that the moment of the material cause (*upādeyakṣaṇa*), the determination (*adhyavasāya*), and the continuous series (*prabandha*) initiated by it—which persists until the present through the form of determinations such as "existent" or "non-existent"—possess a state of necessary antecedence (*niyataprāgbhāvitva*) toward their own production.
Otherwise, the relationship of cause and effect could not be established anywhere. If it is argued that the cause in this case is a distinct, pure luminosity, [we reply:
"The form is seen to possess causal power through positive and negative concomitance;
it is another that acquires causality"—this is the established principle of the royal court.
[401] If its status as a cause is not denied even in the case of the mental aspect (ākāra),
then fire does not deny its status as a cause with respect to smoke.
Furthermore, the agency of the other depends upon each of them;
thus agency belongs to both, due to the capacity for the persistence of their existence, just as in the case of fire and fuel.
If it is determined that a distinct manifestation dependent on blue produces [the cognition],
then it follows that a *piśāca* (demon) dependent on fire is a constituent part of smoke.
For this very reason, ignorance alone cannot be established as a [causal] factor;
for dependence upon the observed totality of conditions is never negated anywhere.
Otherwise, the entire variety [of the world] would be produced by karma alone;
there would be an elimination of other causes, and human effort would not bear fruit.
If existence and non-existence do not conform [to one another], there is no relation of cause and effect anywhere;
and if they do conform, there is likewise no relation of cause and effect anywhere.
And the determination of a blue perception does not arise from seeing a non-blue form;
for the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl occurs despite the absence of a deviation in color.
When there is a confusion in the apprehension of the distinction from a similar class of material objects,
the superimposition of "materiality" occurs upon seeing a part, because that [distinction] is not seen.
Or let there be a perception otherwise, even by chance or through fate; in that case, the distinction of genus would be inferred from it, like smoke created by a yogi.
Just as the external seed is associated with being the cause of a sentient being,
so too is the cognition in the form of a seed [the cause] for the arising of the form of a sprout.
Thus, setting aside the external object and indicating that cognition exists in its place, he declared:
"Dependent conditions arise and cease."
If its property were pervasive, then since being earthen and so forth would be the cause, let there also be luminosity; thus, "it is not a manifestation" is a sound conclusion.
[402] Therefore, since only the external blue is observed as having a result,
that which is seen in cognitions such as those of [illusory] hair lacks reality due to the absence of such a result.
In that case, since it lacks that activity, let its very reality be negated;
for there can be no denial of the mere fact of being an entity for something that is engaged in some other activity.
When one emerges from the interior of a mountain cave due to the illusion of a waterfall,
what is there in reality that is not merely a thing, given the transgression of its actual activity?

Because the activity of determination has been abandoned, a person seeking that object would again describe the form of the cognition as non-existent through the appearance of existence in that very place.

Therefore, in accordance with that [convention], when a cognition is intended to be non-erroneous, statements such as "the appearance of the non-existent" (asadbhāti) are made for the purpose of negating what is merely imagined.
For that [universal] is not self-cognizable by that cognition; rather, it is something else, and that [other thing] is not real at all.
Therefore, the universal such as "cowness" is indeed non-existent, because its form is not manifested.
Just as a pair of moons is not even a single moon, so too here, the absence of an apprehended nature [is to be understood]; this is the general direction.
This arrangement is established according to conventional determination; however, in reality, place and so forth are not universals, because they do not involve an adherence to non-existent objects.

Thus he says: "But it is not because they are non-objects," and furthermore, "the appearance of clarity [is established] because, by virtue of being of the nature of cognition, they are objects; however, there is the notion that they are hairs and so forth."
That which has a universal as its object, which appears as hair, and which is devoid of reality—
though reckoned as sensory cognition— is non-existent because it is a determination of something external.
Likewise,
if it follows that the universal is an object by virtue of having the nature of cognition,
there is no fault, because that is accepted; for there is equality in its having the nature of an object.
And it has been stated more than once that the referent of a word is a phenomenon that is not subject to rejection.
Therefore, this referent of a word is described according to how it is perceived; it is not non-existent.
And it has been stated by [the author] himself in the *Bhāṣya* that [cognition] is of the nature of knowledge;
if existence were according to appearance, then appearance would have to be manifestation.
That very existence [of the object] is not a sublater of its being known as if it were external;
nor is there a sublation consisting in the absence of a pervader, for incapacity and so forth are considered [to apply] to the external object within the cognition.
The meaning of a word is properly [understood] as dependent origination, because that very form appears in verbal cognition;
and for embodied beings, there is a determination of their own internal form precisely as something external.
Therefore, just as the expression "sentient being" is firmly established as the reality even when there is no sentient being,
so too the notion that the three realms are merely mind is considered to be a diverse [and conventional] view.
The effort expended regarding terms such as "all-empty" is exactly the same:
that very mind, possessing its own form, is said to appear as an object.
For the negation of the external object as it is conceptualized is indeed self-evident;
moreover, its being afflicted by latent impressions (vāsanā) is held to follow from the arising of forms that are not [ultimately] desired.
Because it contains within it the capacity to give birth to the volitions projected by [worldly] activity,
there are neither engagements nor cessations from activity upon ascending to the pinnacle of non-duality.
How could those very [appearances] be accepted as saṃsāra by one who knows them,
except through the conceit of the ignorant that "a form is seen in a mirror"?
Just as there is the removal of the superimposition [of externality] onto the form of sensation,
so too is the state of being an entity [removed] from entities, and the state of being external [removed] from the forms of cognition.
Just as the moonhood of two moons seen by one with cataracts is unreal,
and because it lacks the depth [of the actual object], there is no identity between the external [moon] and that which appears in the mirror.
The nature of consciousness is not perceived as distinct from the appearances that have entered within it,
nor through entities characterized by forms or mental representations.

The universal is reckoned as cognition; for this very reason, it is spoken of separately. In common worldly usage, cognition—which is like a mirror—is treated as if it were distinct [from its object].
The mental aspects have the appearance of reflections; that which is imagined in both cases is not real.
There is no identity between cognition and external objects, because it has attained a state devoid of their own intrinsic nature.
There is no otherness because it is not perceived [as distinct], nor is there existence for that which does not manifest;
and by the logic of the king’s sequence, it is devoid of both unity and plurality in the mirror.
Thus, it is either logical or not that phenomena are joined as being like a mirror;
the yogi is said to abide in the non-manifest, for manifestation is considered to be conceptual construction.

That which appears slightly as external within that [consciousness] through the exclusion of others (ekāpoha) is a manifestation due to its all-pervasive shining; it is a proliferation (prapañca), like a kadamba flower.
That which is mounted upon diverse conceptual constructions is to be abandoned, even in a mind that is variegated.
The rest is the same. Alternatively:
even when there is the abandonment of the external object of apprehension, one must prevent the persistence of the act of apprehending itself.
Thus, by abiding in suchness (*tathatā*), one transcends "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).
As he said: "In that case, by the absence of even one [of the two], etc. (PV III 213).

Lest there be the fall of the superimposition along with the removal of what is superimposed— and thus the ruinous gaze of nihilism regarding the variegated world— there is the warding off of non-appearance.
And so,
just as variegated forms persist in the world exactly as they are, in this same way the wise lead others to the truth.
(In this way, indeed, the wise lead others to the truth.)
And so forth. And the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna says:
"The great elements and so forth are said to be established within consciousness;
when that consciousness is known, they vanish. Indeed, they were falsely conceptualized."
Therein, the conviction that there are no sentient beings, the obstruction of objects, and [the realization] "it is the knowledge of that" occur in the heart consisting of reflection;
and the exhaustion occurs in the direct realization of the nature of that knowledge.
Even when [the object] is sublated, there is no harm to the names, the causes, or the forms;
let the phenomena of the Sage be merely names, whether they exist by way of an imagined nature or not.
In this same way, other cases should also be inferred.
Then, through the destruction of adventitious stains, it is like the surface of space;
its equality with the object of knowledge is manifest by virtue of its being non-distinct from that object.
This [consciousness] is mere luminosity, similar to the continuum of a lamp-flame;
it is not [luminous] because of the absence of non-luminous parts, but rather due to the manifestation of its own form.
Even for that which possesses not even a particle of luminosity, there was no possibility of existence even previously;
rather, the state of being stained or stainless depends upon the determination of error.
In that very [dependent nature], which consists of various forms dependent on causes, that which is imagined— the act of grasping and the grasper— is non-existent.
For one who discerns the distinction between those two, that very [nature] is of a single form.
"That very [reality], which is of a single nature for one who discerns that duality—
[it is] perfected," said the Prince, the King, on all sides.

Therefore, in the theory of aspects (*sākāravāda*), there is no contradiction whatsoever with the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or with the scriptures (*āgama-śāstra*). Nor is there any falsity (*alīkatva*) of the aspects, because the causal efficacy (*arthasāmarthya*) of objects has been established. Or, even if they were false, or even if they were merely designated as "error," there would nonetheless not be a connection to affliction (*saṃkleśa*) in reality, because there is no loss of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and because there is an absence of any establishment based on the imposition of something else (*parāropa*).

The notion that all embodied beings are always already liberated is a hindrance resulting from a long-continued habituation. For once something has arisen from its own cause in the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), it cannot be altered by anything else, even by something possessing power, let alone by that which is considered false. Furthermore, when [cognition] arises as a unity with its own cause, let its nature be non-differentiated awareness; what is the point of resorting to this repetitive twisting of limbs? That entities arise from their own causes and are experienced as having that very nature—this is the great affliction for those who maintain the doctrine of [ontological] unity.

[406] If it is argued that these two—arising and appearance—exist thus due to ignorance and are therefore not reality, that too is not sound, because: "Let there be birth from some cause or other; what is the use of a conceptualized cause?
Even if born from something undesirable, that which is undesirable remains exactly as it is."
Thus, one must with effort offer a final libation to the proponents of non-aspectarianism,
if they maintain that the ultimate is accessible through faith, thinking that some distinction [between them and the proponents of aspectarianism] will eventually arise.
If it is argued that there is an apprehension of oneness—like milk and water—even when [the objects] arise as distinct, this is not so;
for there is no apprehension by means of something distinct, nor is there an apprehension otherwise by means of itself.
For just as the grasping of a self by the self is the self itself, so too is that [grasping];
the conceptualization of a single entity is merely an error of manifestation arising from the intellect’s dependence on something else.
If there were no sublation even in other cases, the possibility of error would not arise;
how much less so in the self-awareness where not even a trace of sublation exists?
If there is a subsequent determination of non-difference, there is no harm by that either;
for, like indeterminate cognition, this too consists for the self-cognizer in mere falsity.
Nor is there the imposition of another [concept] there, for that [imposition] is false and self-cognized;
what other peace could there be than the cessation of the engagement with and withdrawal from that?
That which is merely false, even if it exists, does not act as an obstacle anywhere;
for if it were to act as an obstacle, it would follow that its falsity is abandoned.
Movement to another sphere of experience is certainly not desired; where, then, could bondage be produced?
Furthermore, in its own self-awareness, there is no bondage for it even by a hundred [means].
For if an insentient entity were to be both bound by its own cognition and luminous by virtue of its own cause,
such an untenable position would make even cognition through its own distinction impossible.

For it is not logical that self-awareness—which arises from its own cause as something luminous by nature—should possess an insentience imposed by an obstacle through the power of false forms. Therefore, it is also impossible to claim that this [cognition], being false, would cognize itself as distinct from itself, precisely because of such a contradiction. Indeed, when that which is being produced is mere self-awareness, any alteration of it into something other than that is contradictory, given that its production consists in the very nature of cognizing that [object] and nothing else.

If there is an obstacle to the realization of that which consists of nothing more than this, then that very obstacle is itself a merit; for if it were not so, it would merely be a formal assumption of discipleship.
If [the two] are of an identical nature, then their identity is unshakable;
even if they are distinct, provided that the distinction is unreal, there is no harm whatsoever.

If it is not held that there is a superimposition of the external—whether one reflects in such a way or otherwise—once the two, the false and the non-false, have been understood as distinct; [then how can this be so?]
For one who regards external objects as the object of action, the occurrence of activity and so forth is not possible.
The mind is necessarily fixed upon its own cognition; therefore, because it is unreal and permeated by unreality, there is no engagement with or withdrawal from other superimpositions.
Thus, for embodied beings, what need is there for direct exertions toward liberation?
(86b) What loss is there even in abiding in the form of the daughter of Śravaṇa?

Consequently, because all sentient beings would always be in a state of liberation, there would be no need even for the state of a perfectly enlightened Buddha (samyaksambuddha); thus, no one would ever undertake the practice of skillful means (upāya). Therefore, this delusion—characterized by the apprehension of something as what it is not—is, in its own nature, devoid of rational inquiry. If it were not established as having the capacity to impel such activity, then there would be no fault even if it were merely unreal; thus, the rebuttal of the aforementioned objection would not hold. "If that unreal [delusion] exists without impelling activity, then behold the audacity displayed by the unreal's incapacity!"
Its engagement occurs through false appearances and never through the qualities of true forms;
thus, this Yogācāra is one who delights in the contrary and is not ultimate.

Therefore, [408] it is not merely the unreal that is functional in existence, for its nature is delusion; nor is the determination of that [unreal] elsewhere [in the external], as that is charming only to critical inquiry.

However, the conceptualization of conventional usage appropriate to the external is equal in both cases—whether one holds the view of having forms (*sākāra*) or being formless (*nirākāra*). Thus, how can the minds of the wise be so habituated to an adherence to the formless alone by abandoning the "having forms," out of fear of collapsing the established order of affliction and purification?
If, however, there is an application [of the term] to "comprehension" (parāmarśa),
then the establishment of the connection with powers and so forth is appropriate for the proponents of the theory of forms (sākāravāda);
but for the proponents of the theory of formlessness (nirākāravāda), it applies to internal affliction and purification.

Thus, there is a great difference. For instance, if the form (*ākāra*) were a real entity, then experience, by perceiving a particularity either through identity with it or through connection with it, would produce a corresponding determination (*adhyavasāya*). And that determination, being colored by the particularity of the object, would result in purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*); thus, there would be no confusion of activities. This is because a certain object, through the application of a particularity inherent in its own nature, [induces action], like a blue lotus held in the hand.

Consequently, identity and causal efficacy are established as being tied to real entities (*vastu*). Furthermore, if the mental image (*ākāra*) were not a real entity, there would be no distinction between the mind perceiving water and the mind perceiving fire; thus, it would follow that even from the experience of water, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of fire would arise.

In this way, from the conceptualization of fire, there would be an inclination toward one who desires to drink or bathe. However, one who thinks "there is no fire here" does not act out of a desire for a drink. What difference is there between [the cognition of fire] and an experience that, due to its clarity, surpasses the rays of a crystal gem by means of an unreal form? For the crystal itself is not the cause of the distinction in the activity of perception apart from the assistance of objects such as blue or yellow. If it is argued that there is a distinction in power due to association with that which possesses the designation "light" because of the appearance of even a non-existent form, that is incorrect; for: [The verse follows: *na hy asaty api bāhye ’rthe buddhir dṛṣṭā vinākṛtā / tenākāreṇa tasmāt sā saṃvṛtyāivopapadyate //* For indeed, even when an external object is absent, a cognition is not seen to be devoid of that form; therefore, it is established as being merely conventional (*saṃvṛti*). If it is argued that the form is real because it is perceived, that too is not so, since it is sublated by the cognition of the thing as it truly is. Furthermore, if the form were real, it would follow that the cognition is non-erroneous, and thus the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions would be lost. Moreover, if the form were real, it would have to be either different or non-different from the cognition. If it were different, it would follow that the cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), and thus it could not be the perceiver of that form. If it were non-different, then the cognition would be manifold, or else the form would be unitary. Therefore, the form is merely a manifestation of the mind’s own nature, appearing as if external through the force of beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Thus, the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous is based on whether or not there is sublation by a subsequent cognition. This has been extensively explained in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. Therefore, the claim that the form is real is untenable. Consequently, the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous is established solely through the presence or absence of sublation. Thus, the entire system of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its results (*phala*) is established as being conventional. This concludes the section on the refutation of the reality of forms. Now, the following is said regarding the refutation of the theory of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*): [text continues].

If it is argued that there is non-existence even when there is an appearance, then what kind of meaning does "conjunction" have here? Even the designation "unreal" is not capable of denying existence.

Therefore, for one who speaks thus, it would indeed be worthy of belief that an entity whose nature is entirely undifferentiated becomes capable of plunging into water through contact with a sky-lotus, yet becomes a giver of burning pain through the proximity of a suddenly enraged son of a barren woman. If it is argued that there is a distinction because those two [the sky-lotus and the son of a barren woman] are not perceived despite their non-existence, while the form [of the entity] is perceived, we say: no, because even when it is perceived, its non-existence—which is opposed to any effort toward assistance—is brought to light.

Furthermore, for that which is non-existent and incapable of having any excellence added to it, no distinction whatsoever can arise from anything; nor does any distinction belong to that [non-existent thing], nor even to the manifestation [of it]. Moreover, the claim that "the form is merely an indicator" (upalakṣaṇa) is also incoherent, because the status of being an indicator is only possible in the case of a real entity, as in the case of a crest-lock and so forth.

Furthermore, even if illumination (*prakāśa*) is thus characterized, it cannot by itself—given its lack of differentiation—be conducive to a distinction in action. If it is argued that it possesses such a power due to the efficacy of the object (*karman*), we say no; for a power is not observed in an object without depending on a perceived means. Nor is such a distinction in action observed without a distinction in form (*ākāra*). Even so, if one were to merely postulate its status as a witness (*sākṣitva*), it would follow that one could likewise postulate such a status for the cook and others in the case of cooking and similar acts.

Consequently, the capacity of the form (*ākāra*) therein is impossible to deny. Nor does anyone maintain that [the form] is established by a distinct experience. Therefore, because it "shines forth," the light (*prakāśa*) is the form itself. As for the statement that "light is the act of shining forth," this is merely a property (*dharma*) of that [form], intended to exclude any other distinction; such is the established position.
For external activity is indeed restricted to the form itself; how could there be a state of error regarding that [activity] in the absence of such a form?
Therefore, since the view of those who deny forms has been thoroughly refuted, this undertaking is established; thus, the doctrine of the existence of forms alone prevails.

If that were the case, then as long as there is cognition, so long is there a mental aspect (*ākāra*); and as long as there is a mental aspect, so long does the state of delusion established by the externalist persist; thus, purification would never occur. However, if mental aspects are unreal, then through the total destruction of the collection of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) from which they arise, when they have utterly ceased, only a manifestation devoid of appearances (*nirābhāsa*), resembling space, remains; this is called purification. If it is argued that this is difficult to achieve under the view that mental aspects are real, let it be so—what can such a person do about it?

Indeed, for one who is greedy for the destruction of the *saṃbhogakāya* through great undertakings, let there be no false conceptualization at all, nor any outward activity; or rather, let even the mental image (*ākāra*) not be undesirable. What fault could there be in the arising of a desired specific mental image through the power of cultivating a particular form of the mind and the application of the accumulation of merit?

Nor is there ever a constant restriction to that [pure] form due to the removal of defects, because an absolute difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is possible; otherwise, even the occurrence of the false would be eternal. Therefore, the mind—which is variegated by the splendor of the primary and secondary marks—reaches a certain pinnacle of transformation through the abundance of practice characterized by the full-blown manifestation of hundreds of virtues.
The self is connected [to the world] and is a treasury of qualities; it is bound by unreal latent impressions, yet it is devoid of a collection of pure forms, though not entirely formless.
If conventional reality were to cease, there would be the destruction of the Dharma-body;
and if its forms were to cease, there would be the ruin of the Enjoyment-body.
The state of the Buddhas who traverse the ten stages is likewise established through that very mode of appearance;
it is clearly like licking one's own hand after letting go of a morsel of food.
When even the lords of the earth, who are like fully awakened Buddhas, have their inner senses rendered utterly formless,
then those wretched ones who perceive only emanations would find it better to emaciate themselves or lick their own hands.
