Through the sovereign power of the Buddha, such awakening for the ten worlds is the supreme gain; whereas for those wandering like atoms, the burden of delusion brings no happiness, even when compared to the filthiest of things.

If it is argued that because of the direct realization of those dharmas, there is the vision of the *dharmakāya*, then while the vision of the *dharmakāya* would follow, the vision of the *saṃbhogakāya* is not established for him.
Because it has that form, the intellect arises with that same form;
this experience of it, which arises from the accumulation of merit, belongs to those on all stages.
The clear teaching of the Dharma arises from the manifestation of pure worldly conceptualization;
alternatively, even the cognition of all things [arises] from the maturation of the exalted vow, according to their respective objects.

Even in the absence of an apprehended object and so forth, because it is possible for those seeking various objects to have a correspondence with those respective objects, the establishment of omniscience is also merely the play of the forms within one's own cognition. Or rather,
just as the manifold state of experience for all embodied beings throughout the three times consists of all forms that correspond to it.

Through the ripening of his resolve, the All-pervading Lord, by the very splendor of his own nature at the stage of origination, manifests as a single form through the intermingling of various appearances.
Covered by a layer of exceedingly fine clouds, this form is invisible to those who lack divine vision;
yet these ten directions perceive all of this as its own true nature.

And therein they desire that which possesses an unmoving, incomparable portion to be the very sphere of the body—this is the case even for the remainder in its entirety. How is it that this rule whereby the manifold is one is established? How is it that this rule whereby "this king is one" is established?

If that state is established by resorting to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), then this great excellence arises from the vast burden of the merit of knowledge. And for this mass of diverse forms, which has the nature of an unassailable, ultimate reality, there can be no subversion by misconceptions, even if the intellect exerts effort, because of its partiality toward that [reality].
For it is thus: (PV II 212–213, also quoted in NKan 107,22f., with *bādho 'yatnavattve* in the second half). To explain:

Born from the practice of the accumulations, this stage—whose unique consciousness is the object of unsurpassed delight; which is the ground of light like the expanse of space, familiarized by the removal of adventitious conceptual proliferation;
and which, through various hosts of emanations, never ceases its mass of activities for the sake of the world—is the tenth.
By whom should that [duality] be abandoned, for which, at best, conceptualization alone is the appropriate emergence?
Thus ends the second chapter, the "Establishment of Defilement and Purification," in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
[The Third Chapter]

But how, while abiding solely in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), can the relationship of cause and effect be established, so that the sequence of causes and effects under discussion may become an object of focused attention? For indeed, neither a preceding cognition, nor a subsequent one, nor even a cognition consisting of a synthesis produced by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of both can enter into the empirical usage of experiencing the relation of cause and effect—expressed as "this [effect] arises from that [cause]"—because all cognitions consist solely of self-awareness, and thus it is impossible for them to have any acquaintance with the discourse of another.

Even if today a mere limit (*avadhi*) has been apprehended by the intellect, it is not that which possesses the limit (*avadhimat*); and by a subsequent [cognition], it is only that which possesses the limit, not the limit itself. Yet, by even a single synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-dhī*), neither is [apprehended]; so who else could be the cognizer? Even the notions "the limit" and "that which possesses the limit" arise solely through the power of that [synthesizing cognition], because not even one of them is the object; for the object of both is only their own pure intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

By this, the relation of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparabhāva*) is refuted, because priority and posteriority are themselves apprehended in some manner; thus, the fulfillment of the [opponent's] desire—that the causal relation (*hetuphalabhāva*) consists precisely of that [priority and posteriority]—is established. For perception has no operation here, since priority, posteriority, and so forth are excluded when there is a state of distinct cognition. Nevertheless, it might be argued: "Since they arise sequentially, priority and posteriority do indeed exist; therefore, the cognition of priority and posteriority makes itself its own object of experience as something prior and posterior."

However, because it lacks the form of reflective discernment (*vimarśa*), it is merely the word that has been set in motion. Yet, by that much, there is no loss of the experience of the object; for indeed, the name is not the thing itself, even though that [name] also proceeds subsequently through a conceptualizing cognition (*anusandhānabuddhi*). Nor is its self-awareness (*svavedana*) impaired by that much. For it is precisely as something self-cognized that it establishes an obstacle against another; and the cognition of cause and effect is simply the awareness of a fixed sequence of prior and posterior states, mediated by the specific latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by each preceding moment. To this, it is replied: [The text continues: ...it is said: * *vimarśākāravirahāt tu śabda eva paramapravartitaḥ |* But because it lacks the form of reflective discernment, it is merely the word that has been set in motion. * *na ca tāvatā vastvanubhavahāniḥ,* And by that much, there is no loss of the experience of the object. * *na hi nāma rūpaṃ vastūnām,* For the name is not the very nature of things. * *tad api paścād anusandhānabuddhyā pravartate |* Even that [name] proceeds subsequently through a conceptualizing cognition. * *na ca tāvatā tasyāḥ svavedanakṣatiḥ |* Nor is its self-awareness impaired by that much. * *svasaṃveditaiva hi paratra bādhakam upasthāpayati,* For it is precisely as something self-cognized that it establishes an obstacle against another. * *pūrvapūrvāhitaviśiṣṭasaṃskāradvāreṇa niyatapūrvāparabhāvabodhaka eva ca hetuphalabodha iti |* And the cognition of cause and effect is simply the awareness of a fixed sequence of prior and posterior states, mediated by the specific latent impressions deposited by each preceding moment. * *atrocyate,* To this, it is replied: (87b) ...it is said: (Note: The provided text fragment ends with "atrocyate," indicating the beginning of a formal response to the preceding argument.)
At the time of the conceit of non-self-awareness, all of this is fit for conventional usage;
but when one is intent upon the awareness of one's own true nature, where is the application of distinctions such as prior and posterior?
Just as it is fit to be grasped by a divided intellect externally, so too is its mutual distinction;
likewise, there is also the relation of priority and posteriority. If this were not so, the external would not exist at all, yet it is indeed being perceived as external.
Just as there is priority and posteriority in external objects, so too is there the apprehension of cognitions themselves;
yet memory is concordant in both cases. Otherwise, experience would be incapable of producing any effect whatsoever.
Therefore, that which was established by the intellect through synthesis is indeed self-established even for one who lacks valid cognition;
yet, in the descent of valid cognition where there is no communication from another, such a state is clearly like painting a picture in the sky.
Nor can such a state be established even by the purity of the internal organ (*koṣṭha*), since it has never been within the scope of direct apprehension;
for if it were ever seen by anyone at another time, it might perhaps tolerate an uncontradicted doubt.
Therefore, even sequential order cannot determine a method without [direct] perception; like a blind man, it too is incapable of knowing another.
Consequently, it is entirely deluded regarding external objects and is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*); yet, being undeluded with respect to itself, there is no sequence therein.
Likewise, the sound itself is not established; thus, even that which is perceived as being both prior and posterior is unreal.
There is no cognition of another, nor is there delusion regarding oneself; even in the case of delusion, one's own [nature] is not intended to be so.

But how can even you establish the negation of the relation between cause and effect, given the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For perception is not determinative, because it is non-conceptual; nor is mere conceptualization [determinative], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that a determination—whether born of perception or born of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—is determinative of its own cause, the object, due to an invariable connection (*pratibandha*), then the relation between cause and effect is indeed established by a means of valid cognition; how then could it be sublated?

That is incorrect. For in this way, the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not demonstrated; because when the apprehension of the causal relation (*hetuphalabhāva*) by perception is negated, it implies the negation of its activity. And if there is dependence on the opponent's admission, there is no independent establishment, since a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is not a proof. This presentation would merely bring about an obstruction to the opponent’s negation.
[414] If there were some sublation of the cause, then the status of cause and effect would remain;
but if that very cause does not exist, then the status of cause and effect is not established.

And likewise, [the opponent] says, "There is no cause," while [simultaneously] asserting that [the world] is "caused" (*sahetuka*), and so forth. Nor does the establishment of one's own conventional usage of "existent" follow merely from having established a negation of another's position. If you argue that for the opponent as well, there is only a blockage of the establishment of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), and that the relationship of cause and effect is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus the conventional usage of "non-existent" is not established either—this is not so, because the opponent has initiated that very [discourse] alone.

For even the conventional usage of "existence" is established as dependent upon a proving means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, if there were some means of valid cognition regarding the relation of cause and effect, that relation would exist; in its absence, how could this [relation] be? Thus, this relation of cause and effect—when devoid of the possibility of perception at any time or place—brings about a state of unshakeable friendship with the external object.
If it is argued that [the relation] is not equal [to the existence of external objects] because other defects are possible in the case of the external, [we reply:
another refutation has been stated here by the author of the *Bhāṣya* in accordance with the text.

Even when there is no entry into the mere measure of the *vinaya*, the words of the *sūtra* and the *vārttika* likewise project the reflection of their own independence through the force of the *bhāṣya*.
Or rather, why is this fault not considered to apply exclusively to the external as well?
Otherwise, how could there be an effort [to prove it] such as, "if the external were experienced," and so forth?

Therefore, let this rule or prohibition established by his benevolence be heeded by the wise; what is the use of anything else? But surely, even so, when one concludes that "this follows from this logical ground," the reason (*hetu*) has already been employed. Furthermore, one must ultimately rely upon non-perception (*anupalambha*) as well. Thus, how can there be any presentation of reasoning devoid of a reason? For in such a context, it is not possible to remain mute.
When one speaks, something must necessarily be either established or refuted;
in that case, how can there be a cognition for one who asserts that [the act of speaking] is causeless, given that it pervades itself?

Therefore, this grasping of causes by an existent is indeed difficult to abandon. Furthermore, this position is contradicted by its own words; for if one says, "From this statement, there shall be a comprehension of the meaning," then the utterance of that statement is directly inseparable from the acceptance of a causal relationship. How, then, could one deny it? Moreover, since all systematic arrangements are produced by the relation of cause and effect, the very life-breath of this doctrine has departed. This too is inconsistent.

For it is not that the relationship of cause and effect does not exist even when established through conventional determination in every respect; rather, [it does not exist] from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Therefore, as long as there is no interruption of conventional practice which is by nature delusive, there is no fault in adopting causes in whatever way may be appropriate.
Just as one accepts a reason for the sake of establishing one's own cognition alone,
so too does one accept its two inseparable concomitants when denying cause and effect.
If it is established by worldly convention, let the relationship between cause and effect remain; but if it is established by direct perception, then let self-cognition be relinquished.

Indeed, it is not a matter for the respect of the wise that self-awareness—which is incompatible with the apprehension of a distinction pervading the state of prior and posterior—should simultaneously abide therein and cognize the nature of cause and effect as being sequential; rather, it would be more appropriate to abandon this addiction to the doctrine of consciousness-only and simply accept the direct apprehension of cause and effect.

Therefore, just as causes such as illumination serve to establish the absence of an external object (*nirālambana*) by relying on conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) for the purpose of reminding one of worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), so too the statements of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish causal potency (*śakti*) are not contradictory. Furthermore, the relationship of cause and effect is known by the person engaged in worldly practice (*sāṃvyavahārika*) as being preceded by the apprehension of difference. Once direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises which grasps non-difference, this [notion of difference] dissolves of its own accord; at times, it may not even grasp difference at all.

In this regard, as long as the operation of the reason (*hetu*) is manifest for both disputants, so much is well, because the dispute occurs only between those who abide in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). And in that context, where could there be any talk of proof without a reason? If it were the case that the absence of a reason is to be proven by means of a reason, then the meaning would be that the reason negates itself; yet this is not a contradiction, because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the reason simply does not exist.
Thus, even the dissolution of all established conventions is not a sublation, since it is precisely the gradual subsiding of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) that is auspicious (*śiva*).
For all connections between entities proceed by way of cause and effect; [in reality],
there is only the state of dependent origination, which is impartite and realized through self-knowing.

But in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), even that which is a cause establishes that which is to be established, and even the established order remains intact. Where, then, is the charge of "killing the self"?
Just as the external object of apprehension exists together with its preceding state, so too does it extend the memory that apprehends it.
When one strives to investigate the root of these afflicted states, how could this diverse phenomenal world possibly withstand such a denial?
Thus is the summary.

How, then, is the absence of a cause established by means of a cause? This is its meaning: in a conceptual construction that conforms to the form of ultimate reality as it has entered through the door of the cause, there is an appearance of being devoid of prior and subsequent forms; this very [appearance] is the absence of the apprehension of the relation between cause and effect. Consequently, although it is devoid of activity, this self-appearance—by virtue of being perceived as possessing activity—is observed as if it were active. Thus, it appears as "the cause" and "the cause of the absence of a cause."

And there is no means for attaining reality other than the specific transformation of the forms of conceptual construction. However, when one is established in the ultimate reality characterized by self-cognition alone, there can be no dispute for anyone anywhere, nor any occasion for the application of proofs or refutations. And regarding conventional reality, even though that [ultimate] is far removed, the mere manifestation of its form in some way is our only recourse.

Therefore, for one who knows that the comprehension of meaning arises precisely from such a statement, the formulation "there is no reason" requires the qualification "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*). Thus, there is no contradiction; however, this fault would indeed arise in the case of a total denial, as in the statements "sound is non-expressive" or "inference is not a valid means of knowledge. Even in those cases, because of the qualification "in reality," there is no inconsistency anywhere: inference, like sensory perception, is a valid means of knowledge only from the standpoint of conventional practice (*saṃvyavahārataḥ*), not in reality.

Because it depends upon the apprehension of a relationship (*sambandhagrahaṇa*) and so forth, and because mere self-awareness alone cannot accomplish that [apprehension]—since even in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), the positive and negative concomitances (*anvayavyatireka*) must be established through distinct cognitions—and because validity arises from correspondence (*saṃvāda*), yet no correspondence exists with respect to any distinct object; therefore, the validity of anything beyond self-awareness is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Likewise, the conventional discourse of cause and effect (*hetuphalavyavahāra*) is also merely conventional, because both are apprehended by a single cognition; for as there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding another [external] object, so too there is no [validity] regarding cause and effect.
And just as there is the relation of cause and effect in this world, so too is it established in the other world.
Upon what, then, can one rely for the establishment of the mind to be spoken of here?
Since, in reality, no other [external] object is established, its establishment in conventional terms is merely proving what is already proven.
Conventional reality (saṃvṛti) is that cognition which is pleasing only so long as it is not subjected to analysis;
true reality (tattva) would be that which is apprehended by each successive cognition, up until the non-dual [reality].
And as for the notion that "this is born from that," this conceptual construction arises for one who knows the supreme through a logical mark;
thus, this is merely conventional reality, and there is no such activity here for one who knows the self.
Likewise, even the cognition of synthesis would be a mere conceit;
therefore, whatever is established from that mere conceit is merely conventional.
As long as there is conventional reality, the fixed order of causes and so forth remains stable;
and proceeding by way of avoiding what is undesirable is not faulty.

Now, if [the object] could not exist without causal capacity (*śakti*), then when that very capacity exists, the talk of its being "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*) is false; what is the point of this difference in terminology?
It is not merely that the externality of cause and effect is untenable;
rather, this cognition in the form of a sprout must arise from a cognition in the form of a seed.
In that case, for one who knows the causal relationship between those two cognitions,
what is the purpose of a verbal distinction, since he already possesses knowledge of the difference external to them?
In the absence of difference, there is no establishment of the relation between cause and effect due to the lack of duality;
or else, those two cognitions themselves would be mutually exclusive and contradictory.
There is no prior cognition, nor a subsequent one; there is no self, nor any other grasper thereof.
Later, the conceptualizing grasper arises—this thorn shall defeat the Pāṇḍavas.
If the apprehension of the word's power is [admitted], let there also be the apprehension of the external object; what is the use of shame here?
Or, if you desire liberation through the light of logic, then let there be the apprehension of the power as well.

If it is argued that the determination "it is seen" exists even with respect to the external object, then the sublation of the external object consists solely in its being established within self-cognition; that [sublation] alone is the result and the constituent factor.
And thus says the Sūtra:
"The turning away from causes and conditions, the negation of a [substantial] cause, and the establishment of Mind-only—this I call non-arising. (**)

[418] "Non-arising" is the negation of the fruit. The mere existence of mind alone is the explicit negation of cause and fruit. If your activity occurs solely through a cause, it lasts only as long as there is external conceptual determination; as long as the notion of a self persists due to a lack of realization, there is no engagement with anything other than that.
There is no certain conclusion apart from inference, and there is no inference without supreme knowledge;
just as that [knowledge] destroys both oneself and others, so too do my reasons destroy both myself and others.

What logic is there in this: that those who, by means of an inference produced from a proof purified by the determination of the three forms of evidence—which by its very nature functions toward external objects and is invariably concomitant with another cognition—employ it as a means for establishing the understanding of another, yet in some context challenge the very person restating that meaning with a refutation based on contradiction? What kind of principle is this?

Just as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), due to their adherence to duality, is unable to live without relying on the validity of inference, so too [the yogin] cannot do without the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the truth established in that state. And that very resolute conviction in the truth regarding the mere nature of one's own realized awakening is itself a disregard for external inference. Yet it is not possible to remain in such a state; otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of abandoning the effort characterized by practice, since the goal would have been accomplished at that very moment.

Therefore, when those very [cognitions] proceed from the power of delusion—as if from a mental resolve directed toward a self—and when direct realization is attained, the all-pervading *dharmadhātu* is established; thus, there is no returning to the denial of inference, any more than there is ash remaining after the fire has consumed its fuel. For this very reason, the meaning is that the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*), designated as "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*), bows down as being without objective support (*nirālambā*). This same point is restated in the context of the investigation into cause and effect; nothing further is prescribed.

To the extent that there is external mental inference, this alone constitutes the acceptance of cause and effect; for at that very time, it is the mark (*liṅga*) which is its basis, because it makes known what is imperceptible, and because it acts as the producer upon the cognition of that [object]. And as for that subsequent sublation when one abides in the mere self-awareness (*ātmavedana*), that itself is the relation of cause and effect—so what is the point of attachment here? How then is the distinction between the producer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*) established by the author of the *Vārttika* within the Vijñānavāda? True, this is merely a provisional internal arrangement.
For this very reason, there is the method of expression stating that "it should be postulated by relying upon the intellect. However, when the ultimate reality is being extracted, it is said:

"Everything is incapable" (PV III 4), and so forth. This is the meaning: prior to non-duality (advaita), an arrangement may be made in whatever way suits the differences in the dull, middling, or superior intellects of those to be instructed; through the gradual sharpening of the mind, confidence in non-duality is established as one moves from stage to stage.

Therefore, although conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) possesses a multiplicity that is progressively higher in terms of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the entry into the relationship of cause and effect in dependence upon it consists precisely in the possibility of the three types of perception and non-perception; this alone is the truth. Lest there be deception even regarding one's own intended [convention], this very convention is to be adopted over another convention, and not some inferior one—even if there is no difference in their lack of ultimate reality—because they differ in terms of whether or not they accord with one's intention.

Therefore, this is not even a subject for inquiry: how can there be the establishment of an object (*arthasiddhi*) from a mere cognition that lacks a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), much less from one that is sublated by investigation? For in such a case, there is no establishment of an object other than the mere satisfaction of the person [involved]. Whatever kind of cognition it may be, it is simply a cognition; likewise, the non-establishment of an object is itself the "establishment of an object"—this is a "sacrificial offering corresponding to the spirit" (*yakṣānurūpo baliḥ*).

If one follows the perspective of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), then everything exists according to our own [conventional] heart; however, a discerning cognizer should understand things in such a way that they might be deceived even by mere satisfaction. Therefore, he says: "And this is stated to be the nature of conventional valid cognition" (PVin I 100,20), and so forth.

Consequently, there is no fault of following a specific means of proof for the conventional [cognizer]; where, then, would there be dissatisfaction for another? Now, according to our view, everything indeed exists, but for those who have directly realized reality (*tattvasākṣātkārin*), it does not exist—so what is the final position?
It is true that to one who has realized the truth, this world is like a dullard, a madman, or a ghost;
and even though he has realized the truth, he appears to the world like a dullard, a madman, or a ghost.
Thus, in this regard, there is the sovereignty of will.
If the world were a manifestation of what is non-existent, let its determination proceed from that [will] and not directly.
For there is no manifestation of causes and the like other than through the conceptualization of its own appearance.

Therefore, although from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*) there is no relation of cause and effect, since it cannot be avoided within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), how could it be disregarded? The production of the intended result arises from the accumulation of causes; for one who desires to engage in that practice follows it precisely because it is merely conventional. However, for one who has realized ultimate reality, just as the relation of cause and effect is not established anywhere, so too is there no engagement in practice anywhere.

If it is asked, "How can that which performs no purposeful action possess existence? We say: No, because from our perspective, there is no interruption in the continuity of its stream of performing the welfare of others, which does not diminish even for a single moment. However, in reality, it has been established that luminosity itself is the true existence; thus, it remains settled that this belongs to the variegated form alone.
But even so, if it is argued, "That variegated thing is one," then this is even more marvelous than that! (PV III 200cd)
And then there is this most wondrous thing: their mutual division.

For a variegated (*citra*) thing is designated as having various forms (*nānākāra*); therefore, how could there be non-difference among these forms that are superimposed with mutually contradictory properties? But then, how could there be difference either, since those forms contained within a single cognition do not cognize one another—like distinct mental continua—and thus it would follow that only some single [form] would appear? That is incorrect, because the superimposition of contradictory properties remains as it was.

Therefore, this [cognition] is indeed manifold; however, because it is produced from a non-different material cause (*upādāna*), its nature consists in the appearance of simultaneity and mutual perceptibility. There is no over-extension [of the definition] to cognitions arising in other mental continua, as they lack a non-different material cause. Here it is considered: does their state of having a single material cause exclude their multiplicity?
And precisely because of their distinctness, mutual cognition among them is not admitted.

For one consciousness does not enter into another consciousness; rather, the denial of mutual cognition between one's own and another's cognitions occurs solely through the removal of the bolt of a single consciousness. And since that [denial] remains unshaken even in the case at hand, there is no distinction. Now, if the appearance of coexistence (*sāhitya*) is what must be established, what is the use of the entry into a single consciousness? For there is no harm in doing so, as it contradicts the probandum even without it. But is it not well known that "coexistence" is merely concomitance, defined as being restricted to the same place and time?

Furthermore, since their "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*) consists in the direct realization of their own respective natures, it has not been established that there is mutual cognition, just as in the case of several men who are present together but do not perceive one another. Therefore, it is only the mutual penetration of consciousness (*saṃvid-āveśa*) that serves the purpose of the conventional usage of "mutual cognition"; what is the use here of mere "concomitance" (*sāhitya*)? If, on the other hand, by the term "appearance of concomitance" you mean the appearance of all [objects] everywhere for everyone, then even when the appearance of concomitance is the probandum, the reason "penetration into a single consciousness everywhere" is contradictory; thus, this verbal formulation is empty. For if that were its meaning, this would simply be a synonym for "assistance" (*sahāya*).
If there is no mutual understanding in a single cognition, then when that [cognition] is denied, there is simply no mutual comprehension; in this case, the fault regarding the object is unbearable.

Or, let there be no such assistance; however, if the appearance of a collection (*sāhityapratibhāsa*) consists in the mutual appearance of its members, then even if they share a non-different substratum (*abhinnopādānatva*), their difference cannot be denied. For we do not understand what answer has been given to the objection that "one's own cognition does not enter into another's cognition," since merely proclaiming synonyms does not nourish any specific distinction.

For even when they share a single object of appropriation, those [cognitions], though occurring together, do not enter into one another's awareness; otherwise, what indeed would constitute their difference?
Immersed solely in their own consciousness, they do not touch the consciousness of another;
yet they perceive one another—how truly marvelous this is!
Furthermore,

if it is argued that there is a complete familiarity [of the object] due to the non-difference of its appropriation (*upādāna*), then it would be better for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) itself to be non-different; however, experience does not occur even when [the objects] are distinct.

Likewise, if a single causal complex were to produce a cognition capable of apprehending a restricted object, what fear would there be? For in either case, the definition [of the object] would be destroyed.

This being so, there is no fear whatsoever regarding the refutation of that which possesses the characteristic of being an object (*grāhya*) by virtue of its arising and its similarity [to consciousness]; for for one who maintains the existence of external objects (*bahirarthavādin*), the relationship between the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) is easily established in quite another way. In that case, because there is no difference in their material cause (*upādāna*), there is mutual experience, since all things have experience as their intrinsic nature (*anubhavasvabhāvatva*). However, if they were produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrījanyatva*), then insentient matter (*jaḍa*) and experience would possess their respective restricted states of being the object of cognition (*vedyatva*) and being the cognizer (*vedakatva*). And due to that restriction, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, since even an insentient thing manifests at that time, how can there be a fixed restriction? [If you say: "The object is that which has an insentient material cause, while the other is the subject"—[we reply: no, for this would over-extend to the sense organ as well. If it is argued that [the distinction] arises from the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) such that only blue arises as the object of cognition, [we reply:
there is a lack of mutual assistance due to their simultaneous existence, and both of you alike fail to escape the consequence of identity (*tādātmya*).

Now, if it is argued that there is the fault of commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) regarding the arising of manifestation (*prakāśa*), [we reply: its arising is as "being cognizable" (*vedyatva*), not as "manifestation" (*prakāśatva*). If it is asked, "What is this 'being cognizable'?", [the answer is: the question "What is this mutual cognition between two things known by themselves? is the same [for both sides]. If it is further argued that "being cognizable" is nothing other than the arising of manifestation, even so, the fault of commonality will be avoided precisely through the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Now, since an entity is of a single nature, just like its blueness, it cannot—by virtue of its unique character—exist without manifesting, even through non-manifestation; for it is indeed possible by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), so let this matter rest.

[422] Now, since this object is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), where could the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) be applied? Furthermore, regarding that which does not even require entry into that [complex] and dissolves of its own accord upon the determination of its own nature—how can there be an indication of non-difference in its material cause (*upādāna*)? For it is not the case that when two illuminations have arisen, one is illuminated by the other; nor does one appear to the other, nor is there any logical consistency in saying "in one."

For just as the self-illumination of a lamp is somehow known and understood by following that [knowledge], so too no mutual illumination among lamps is ever perceived. Therefore, just as the notion that "one lamp is illuminated by another lamp" is an error, so too is the notion that "one cognition is illuminated by another cognition. Thus, for what purpose should the answer be given that there is a single material cause (*ekopādāna*)? By this, even the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) regarding "self-cognition" is addressed.

If you argue that even for the exclusion of non-conjunction (*ayogavyavaccheda*), the avoidance of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is achieved simply by not denying [the existence of the object], this is easily refuted; for the very object of another's cognition cannot be established. If you say that the illumination of another is indeed observed, we reply: even that occurs only through the production of a subsequent moment of illumination by means of taking non-illumination as its material cause; thus, there is no occasion for such a claim regarding cognitions, lamps, and the like.

But he who maintains that even in that case light, which co-exists with the cloth, is its illuminator—his position is also untenable. For the determination of reality does not rest on mere worldly convention; if one were to rely on the production of a cognition as the basis for the inferential determination of "this belongs to that," then, since the object co-existing with the cognition would have to be admitted as being illuminated by it, the determination [of the relationship] would be undermined. Alternatively, if it is argued that here too there is parity in view of the subsequent conceptualizing cognition (*pṛṣṭhajavikalpajñāna*), then this [subsequent cognition] alone would be the apprehender, not the preceding one. Furthermore, since this [subsequent cognition] is simultaneous [with the object], this is the entry point into the Sautrāntika doctrine.

Now, if it is argued that light does not possess the quality of being an illuminator merely by producing cognition—even though cognition itself arises simultaneously with it, and that this simultaneity occurs simply through arising together from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—then it would follow that the sense organs existing at that time are also illuminators, since they too arise simultaneously. If you say this is not so because they do not have the nature of illumination (*aprakāśarūpatva*), then let illumination itself be illumination; but how can it be an illuminator? For a blue object cannot become yellow merely by being simultaneous with something yellow.

Therefore, nothing that is ineffective can occupy the path of relationship with anything. However, by way of causal assistance, a lamp is seen to participate in the conventional usage [of "illumination"] regarding objects such as jars, which are not of the nature of light; thus, when it is understood that the cognition of that [object] has another cognition as its illumination, one might indeed refrain from employing the genitive case where there is a single shared material cause.

It is not, however, with respect to perceptibility; for instance, in the case of "Maitra is more beautiful than Caitra," this is with respect to the beauty as it is understood (*gamyamāna-saundaryatā*), and not with respect to perceptibility, because both beauties reside in a single substratum (*ekātmaniṣṭhatva*).

If it is argued that no one would employ [such a statement] in this way, [we reply: if he were a disparager, how could he even employ it? For the logic is the same. Thus, by means of the absence of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper, the proof of non-duality through the "logic of the blind man milking a cow" has been established for the Leader of Logic (Dignāga). Nor is this a [new] logic; so why this futile agitation out of hatred for the Vārttikakāra (Kumārila), like the trampling of Śubhagupta?

If it is argued that, like many lamps, cognitions then appear as both conjoined and distinct, and thus what is the point of [positing] a single *vedana* (cognition), we say: no. For the conventional usage that "they appear conjoined" is made in relation to a cognizer who is distinct [from them]. But surely, even in the absence of such a [distinct] cognizer, the manifestation of the conjoined [cognitions] is not exhausted. This is true; however—

[423] It may be argued that even a single entity can be the illumination of another; however, since the nature of self-illumination exists even for those things covered by a water-tight jar, the point at issue is not established. Therefore, the establishment of the conventional usage of "mutual cognition" occurs only through the inclusion of one consciousness within the other. For there is not even a rumor that lamps originating from a single source illuminate one another.
If you claim that the atoms there are indeed distinct, then life (the individual soul) is all the more dear [to us];
for it is clear that the cause [of such mutual perception] is uncommon, as it is never observed elsewhere.

If it is argued that, just as a lamp is seen to be self-luminous and yet manifold, so too is the case here— then this would be well-said provided that a mutual manifestation were observed there due to the non-difference of the seeds.

Thus, this occurrence within a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīsambhava*) may, by way of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), enable the inference of one thing upon the perception of another in certain cases, but not for the sake of perceiving the other directly—as is the case with taste and color, for instance. Likewise, the fact of having a single material cause (*ekopādānatā*) would establish a greater degree of homogeneity (*sajāyīyatā*), but not the manifestation of another thing as established by the confusion of intrinsic natures (*svabhāvasaṅkara*). Otherwise, in some instances, even one thing might be insentient (*jaḍa*) in relation to another.

By this, the hypothesis that mutual manifestation consists precisely in having a non-different material cause (*abhinnopādānatva*) is also refuted; for it would follow as an absurd consequence that even insentient things, which have a single material cause, would possess mutual insentiency. For their insentiency, just like their luminosity, exists in the form of their own self-nature (*ātmarūpa*).
Moreover,
it is not by way of producing form that the existence of a thing is established; rather,
let it be so designated through the fact of having a single material cause.

For just as, according to the Sautrāntika, being an object of cognition consists solely in the production of a form similar [to itself], and not even in its manifestation, so too the manifestation of one [form] would be the manifestation of another, and there would be no perception of a variegated [image]. Furthermore, this [notion of] having a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*) must also be understood in its pure sense, because it is determined that in both the states of dreaming and waking, the cause is precisely the variegated form; for even at a time of confusion, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is a transformation (*vivarta*) of multiple forms, and even when conceptualizing a single object, the form is variegated due to the difference in spatial locations.

Even if one assumes that the production of a [visual] mass arises from a [prior] mass, and that the capacity for this belongs to only one [of its constituent parts], then the fact that multiple things act as producers—conforming to the presence or absence [of the effect]—is the same [as in the case of a variegated cause]. Since we observe the arising of a blue form even from a broken [or partial] blue form, there is no answer for one who maintains that a variegated [effect] arises from a non-variegated [cause]. Furthermore, because it is impossible to count [the parts], there can be no state of deficiency or excess. Moreover, even if there were deficiency or excess—as in the case of a banyan tree—something might still be a single entity producing many;
however, if there is a state of deficiency, a variegated [whole] cannot be a non-dual unity.

That cognition is like that; likewise, after states such as deep sleep, from the *ālayavijñāna* itself, another variegated [cognition] arises from a variegated [precedent] through a distinction of its specific aspects (*pradeśabheda*). Or rather, let it be that from a single, coagulated form, a variegated [cognition] sometimes and somewhere arises either successively or non-successively.

First of all, as long as one remains unobstructed by torpor (*middha*) and so forth immediately after waking, there would be no mutual experience of moments other than those belonging to the first instant, because their material causes (*upādāna*) are distinct. If it is argued that this is due to their being awakened from that same [initial] state through a continuous succession, then, to whatever extent there is an interval, to that same extent there would be a gradual loss of mutual illumination due to the increasing degree of dullness, such that it would cease after some small distance.

Furthermore, the non-destruction of the manifold luminosity is experienced through waking and other states for many days, nor is there any gradation in its intensity. If you argue that this is not possible in the case of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), then how can it be possible to have the perception of something distinct from a single uniform perception? Even if there were no difference in the material cause (*upādāna*), this would be so because it is the internal difference or non-difference itself that is the determinant. Moreover, in the case of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), the truth lies in the opposite conclusion, as it leads to the subversion of the opponent's position.
Furthermore, if the apprehension of the effect (*upādeya*) occurs simply because of its connection with the material cause, [then the same would apply to external objects].
The connection "what is not [the cause] of grasping" is not the determining factor.

For cognition is by nature remote from its object; yet, having transcended that limit, proximity manifests its own power. And since this [proximity] is primary only in relation to the material cause (*upādāna*), the experience of a distinct co-existent entity would have to occur solely through the medium of the apprehension of the cause, as in the case of an inference dependent on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*). If it is argued that this is not so because [the object] is past, we reply that there is no difference between remoteness of nature and remoteness of time.

Now, both of these [proximity and remoteness] belong to the *upādāna* (the material cause), whereas for that which co-exists [with it], there is merely a spatial remoteness of its own nature (*svabhāvaviprakarṣamātra*). In this case, then, even proximity would be diminished; however, in the case of the *upādāna*, it is predominant—this is the "logic of the lizard and the rabbit" (*godhāśaśanyāya*). Furthermore, the persistence of perception occurs by the power of proximity. If, therefore, there were a manifestation of the past, it would indeed have to be present; how then could it be past? Consequently, there is no manifestation of the past.

If such were the vision of reality—that the other, being perceived by consciousness which has become one's own self, were merely one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*)—how could there be the cognition of another?

In that case, let the proclamation of "proximity" (sannikarṣa) apply even elsewhere for one whose eyes have not been opened. Like a yogi, there might also be the grasping of what has passed away. Thus, if the process were to proceed in such a continuous stream, there would be the consequence of perceiving every preceding moment, either until reaching a single material cause or without limit. Just as there is a gradation in the degree of intervention, so too there is a gradation in the intensity of proximity. Likewise, if it follows that even its own effect should appear [to the sense organ], then everything would be subject to that same consequence.

Moreover, if there were indeed a difference between the various appearances [within a single cognition], then there would also be a difference between a blue fragment and a yellow one, just as between blue and yellow [in general]. Consequently, since one perceives things down to the level of atoms, there would be nothing whatsoever perceived as a single unit that could serve as the single material cause for another; thus, the entire world would fall into an unobstructed blindness. Or rather, this doctrine culminates in the conclusion that "nothing exists at all."

[425] Therefore, if this is precisely what you intend to say, why this trivial wrangling? It should simply be stated directly: that even the multiplicity of entities does not exist. If you argue that the unreality of the forms (ākāra) is already accepted, even so, why resort to this which fails to withstand logical scrutiny?
Furthermore, because the forms are unreal, a single material cause (upādāna) is impossible;
however, for mere luminosity (prakāśamātra), there is no harm even in the absence of differentiation.
Furthermore, if a distinction were admitted, one could not tolerate their mutual manifestation;
for if mutual manifestation were tolerated, then the state of being apprehended object and apprehending subject would follow as a consequence.

Thus, there is a collapse of the established tenet (*siddhānta*). Consequently, this non-difference of the material cause (*upādāna*), even when explained independently of the Teacher, fails to bring about a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is therefore incapable of manifesting the mutual experience of these forms (*ākāra*).
If it is seen thus, let it be seen; however, one must investigate whether [this occurs] due to non-difference, or rather, of the seed itself. This is what deserves deliberation.
If there were unity, there would be an absence of variety; if there were plurality, this [absence] would be even more extreme.
Neither unity nor plurality is logically tenable for cognitions.
What, then, is the ultimate truth here? For instance:
if the various forms are indeed the very nature of the mind, how can it be manifold?
Or if the mind itself is manifold, where can you establish its unity?
The intellect, bearing the form of atoms, is neither capable of nor able to perceive them individually; yet when they are combined, they appear [as objects].
What kind of magical process is this, whereby they manifest through their mutual interpenetration?
Therefore, this follows from the force of reality itself, as the wise declare: "In whatever way objects are analyzed, in that very way they fall apart. (PV III 209)
That form by which entities are conceptualized does not exist in reality,
because neither a single nor a manifold form is found among them.
[426] These [entities], being defiled by the investigation of their parts, do not maintain their existence; for it is better to regard things while closing one's eyes like an elephant.

Thus, it is the emptiness of all phenomena—like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or a reflection—that is established by reason; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Now, one might object: "The investigation was undertaken with reference to the Blessed One; so now, is even the Buddha, the Blessed One, like an illusion or like a dream?"

Who, then, can here offer a critique? For it was the Blessed One himself who proclaimed it thus, and the Noble Ones have illuminated that utterance with joy; furthermore, because they accepted that there is no distinction between a Tathāgata and an ordinary person by virtue of suchness (*tathatā*), and because of the excellence of profundity and magnificence celebrated in the scriptures, [who could object] except for others? But surely, since it is sublated by the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) and because the aspects of characteristics and so forth are unreal, where is the magnificence? Moreover, there would be the consequence of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).
Since its nature is a cognition in which the non-existent appears, it is erroneous; where, then, is the profundity? That is incorrect.
The grasping of that [reality] in what is not that is delusion; other forms of delusion have been refuted.
Furthermore, he does not perceive the unreal by means of an unreal form.
Just as this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) exists, so does the Tathāgata exist through knowledge;
even from the perspective of mere conventional designation, there is no delusion regarding him, because the seed [of such delusion] is absent.
Since engagement and withdrawal arise from conceptual construction, which is born of latent predispositions,
the state of abiding in the immutable reality follows from uprooting those two along with their roots.

In this system, the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) is not undesirable, because everything appears here as non-existent in its true nature; nor is there anything else that remains uncontradicted.
Because this has already been refuted in detail previously,
even so, due to its association with the path of higher dharma, this very thing—
which is devoid of forms such as 'da' and so forth, yet internally throbbing with suffering, pleasure, and the like— is accepted as a constituent part.
"It is said that here [in the case of internal cognition] there is no occurrence of a subverting factor because of the absence of spatial extension. That too is erroneous; for:

"Internal sensation has pleasure and so forth as its object, while external sensation has cold and so forth as its domain; each takes on the form of its respective [object], and is indeed seized by a subverting factor."

[427] For we know that the form of cognition is indeed a particular individual (vyaktiviśeṣa). As for the absence of spatial extension, it would mean either a smallness of space or its total absence. In that regard, the first position—that a defect which applies even to a space the size of an atom would be obstructed by how much of a small [space]—is not tenable. The second position, however, is impossible; for what is possible must necessarily exist somewhere. If it does not exist anywhere at all, then its absolute non-existence is established.

Furthermore, unpleasantness, mental pleasure, and so forth are experienced as being delimited from locations outside the body, manifesting within the limits of the body. Otherwise, if there were no difference [between them] and blue and other objects—as there is none with light—the same fault would apply. And in that case, what is the point of asking how much space they occupy within the body? Or what is "having spatial extension" (*sadeśatā*), since even in the case of color, nothing distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*) designated as "space" is ever perceived anywhere? Nor is the "location" merely the support (*ādhāra*), for if it were, it would follow that wind and sunlight would also lack a location. Moreover, the application of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) does not occur in relation to that [support], but rather in relation to the object's own nature.

Just as an essential nature (*svarūpa*), though devoid of parts, appears in the conceptualizing intellect as if surrounded by distinct attributes, so too "space" (*deśa*)—which is constructed by a cognition opposed to the awareness of time and form in the manner of "this is here"—enters into linguistic usage only as the counterpart to the movement through space (*nabhogati*). Furthermore, it has already been stated that this [conceptual] movement is not remote from the internal experience of pleasure, mental well-being, and so forth, just as the experience of touch is not.

Now, if you think that whereas in things such as blue [objects], a state of having clearly discernible parts—such as upper and lower—as well as being delimited by measurements such as a *vitasti*, a *hasta*, an elephant, or a man, is perceived, this is not the case for pleasure and so forth; then what follows from that? It would merely mean they are not known to possess spatial extension. For in that case, it would follow that even odors, tastes, sounds, and so forth—which are perceived by non-tactile senses—would lack spatial location. Furthermore, it is impossible to establish a fixed spatial location even for fire and other objects that are beyond direct perception.

Now, if it is argued that the two [qualities] existing in a fruit where fragrance and taste arise can be inferred as having a restricted location—since they are perceived at the time of grasping by the portion of the front part and so forth, and by the remaining dimension of the sense organ—then why can pleasure and the like not also be apprehended through their spatial dimension based on their experience within the body? However, a lack of pervasion is observed in the case of fragrance and taste in the fruit. If it is argued that there is the perception of the enjoyer in a restricted location, [we reply: ...

Even that [cognition], being a gross apprehension, is not capable of determining a location with atomic precision; therefore, in this case as well, it is the same insofar as it exists by pervading some extent of space. Likewise, at the time of perception, there is indeed a determination of the specific restriction of that which is measured by the location of the sense faculty. This same principle applies even to pleasure and the like, including those produced by seeing and hearing. For the eye itself, scorched by the sight of what is unpleasant, is experienced as becoming cool upon the sight of what is pleasant.

In the case of plunging into a pond when heated by the hot-rayed sun, there is indeed a manifest distinction in measurement or a division into upper and lower parts. Even if one were to imagine the rising of another location there, it would still be that very same location. A restriction of measurement is appropriate for kings upon the earth; and this alone is human happiness—that which is verbal cognition—thus there is no establishment of difference, or rather, because of the clear manifestation.

However, because mental joy (*saumanasya*) is of the nature of the mind, even when its manifestation is indistinct, it is possible—by following that [feeling]—to establish it in a general sense as existing somewhere in this very place; thus, there is no obstacle [to its existence]. Nor is insistence useful in that regard, for it would entail the consequence that the probandum (*sādhya*) itself would be conceptual.

Furthermore, if there is no determination of a fixed dimension, and if the negation of spatial location applies only in some cases, let it be that temporal location applies to everything, since it is impossible to determine the dimension of a single moment. Nevertheless, the coarse intellect establishes a specific temporality by noting that "it did not exist previously" and "it does not exist afterwards. Here too, the certainty remains established: that [the feeling] is not outside the body, but exists right here within the mind, such as in the case of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*).

Furthermore, the connection with time is indeed accepted for mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and the like; otherwise, the fact that they never occur at all would constitute a valid subverting argument (*bādhakayukti*). Moreover, that very [connection with time] brings about spatial location, because something that does not exist anywhere at all can only come into existence at some particular time. And wherever it exists, that is its location—whether it be gross or subtle, what does that matter? As for time, the establishment of a restriction is made in view of other requirements.
Just as the restriction of time is clearly evident, so too is the restriction of place;
however, this spatial restriction occurs either through atomicity or through extreme minuteness.
Yet, in neither case is there an end to the contradiction regarding pleasure and the like.
Therefore, what need is there for a specific refutation when [the object] has already been rejected by the mere statement of its negation?

Thus, since spatial extension is necessarily concomitant with existence just like temporal duration, it cannot dispel the fear that the non-perception of a pervader might occur anywhere; nor can one say "let it not be so," for how then could the conventional usage of existence itself be established in the case of pleasure and the like? Just as the proof of its being neither one nor many is not established for you, so too is it not established for me, having set aside the locus of the cognition of the "one" or its opposite, as if it were measured.

For just as, because pleasure and so forth do not appear with a form situated before one like blue, it is impossible to apprehend their exclusion from being either unitary or manifold; likewise, for that very same reason, the possibility of either of those two [unitariness or manifoldness] is also [impossible], since one finds that the determination "this is one" or "this is many" occurs only when something is manifesting before one.

Even regarding an imperceptible object, if its status were established in accordance with what is seen, then even though the form is not manifesting before one, its non-existence could be established—due to the restriction of location following the manifest form—just as in the case of sparks from a fiercely blazing fire.

If it is argued that existence must necessarily be of one kind [either eternal or non-eternal], we say no; because those two [categories] are mutually exclusive, when there is doubt regarding either one, there is doubt regarding existence itself. As for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cast away its efficacy just as you would a white cloth or similar object; do not remain placing your hopes in it. Furthermore, even for one who points out the "doubtful unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddhi*) fallacy of another by claiming that no other means of valid cognition exists, there is no personal conventional usage of "existence," because when there is an absence of both a proof and a refutation, doubt is logically established.

Furthermore, regarding the mass of the nature of cognitions such as "blue" which is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), the very non-observation of sublation (*bādhā*) is the powerful basis for its validity. If it is argued that, for this reason, let there be invalidity for self-cognition, while validity exists in the absence of sublation—this is not so; for the non-existence [of sublation] is not established by mere non-observation. Since everything external has been examined and there is the possibility of a prover for the absence of sublation, there is no other [means of establishing it] than the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*). However, this doctrine of non-sublation has already been considered in the *Śāstra*; let it rest for now. In this same way, even stories and the like produced by the Veda would possess the status of valid cognition.
The claim that the status of being a means of valid cognition is established by general presumption is also refuted by subsequent arguments.
They know that even where validity is intrinsic, it is the fruit of repeated practice; for everything practiced externally is unreal at its core, yet it is contemplated [as real].

If it is argued that the manifestation of the aggregate of the apprehended aspect, though false, is impossible to deny because of the power of the apprehending aspect—just as pleasure and so forth [are undeniable]—we say no.
This is because both parts possess the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*).
What, then, would be the apprehended and what the apprehender? Nor can one thing manifest another.

Thus, since this has already been established previously in the refutation of external objects, the state of reality does not arise from mere conceit. Furthermore, in this view, if the entire host of afflictions— attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, and so forth— is innate, being of the nature of formless cognition just like suffering and the rest, then, my dear friend,
what distinction could there be between the "desirable" and the "undesirable," and what would constitute detachment in the view that [cognition] possesses forms?

For you, the association with the aspect of light (*ālokākāra*) is an error. Due to its absence, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [afflictions] would exist as the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those subject to existence; for if they were unreal by way of their objective support (*ālambana*), it would follow that pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest would also be so. Therefore, the rejection of what is undesirable and the adoption of what is otherwise—this is stated in different words within the position of "having aspects" (*sākārapakṣa*). As for the disagreement regarding the conclusion that the circle of aspects (*ākāracakra*) is limited to what is seen and touched, this is of no consequence.

Just as something may be abandoned by some because it is undesirable even though it is an error, so too, let a specific aspect (ākāra) remain because it is desirable even though it is unreal; thus, the thesis (*sādhya*) is undermined. Furthermore, these mental factors (*caitta*), such as pleasure and so forth, are accepted [as real], whereas the mind (*citta*), being the nature of the aspect through its grasping of objects, is to be abandoned, and the mental factor is said to be enduring; thus, there is a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) in claiming this is not a concomitant dharma (*samprayukta-dharma*).

Moreover, if there is no difference [between the mind and its aspects], they must be unreal just like the mind, or else the mind itself must be real like them; how then can an aspectless (*anākāra*) thesis be established?

[Objection: Surely, whatever is meditated upon manifests in that very form; thus, even if the mind is meditated upon as having the form of space, it will manifest as such. Furthermore, since it is devoid of any established form, it is itself formless (*nirākāra*). How, then, can the probandum be established? [Reply: No, because there is no purpose [in doing so]. For it is said: "If you desire to abandon this physical body—which is untouched by the defects of *saṃsāra* and radiant with the primary and secondary marks—and instead [attain] the state of space, [then meditating on the mind as space is appropriate]."
Is it not the case that this *sambhogakāya* is indeed accepted by the sons of the Arhats?
One who desires to attain the *dharmakāya* should resort to a body comparable to space.

If this is argued, then that [cognition] is not first of all the *sādhya* (the thing to be proven), because the intended object is fully established by the aforementioned [cognition] itself. Nor is it a means (*sādhana*) for establishing any object, since the establishment of an object from a formless [cognition] is unproven. It has already been stated that the establishment of an object for another [person] is likewise strictly bound to a specific form. Now, who—other than a proponent of *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness)—would believe that the establishment of an object occurs from a form [in one case], while in another case it occurs from a formless [cognition]? If you say, "It is so because of scripture (*āgama*)," [we reply:]...

Where an object is contradicted by reasoning, what refuge can scripture provide? (93b) Since the capacity of an object is distinguished by a specific mode that is a synthesis of merit and knowledge, at the ultimate limit of its excellence, that [capacity] must itself abide at the ultimate limit of excellence; how could it be severed from that, or how could it possibly arise from anything else?

For whom could even the possibility of cognition ever be non-existent? Nor does the scripture itself have such a primary literal meaning; rather, recourse to another interpretation might occur through the boldness of reasoning, and that [boldness] has been exhausted—this is what was considered. Nevertheless, out of fear of sublation (*bādha*), that very form must be accepted; and since it is not sublated, let it also be established that it alone is capable of conveying the meaning. And if it is argued that for this very reason, even previously, the power of the meaning resided solely in that means—[we reply:
there is no kind of convention (*samaya*) wherein sublation does not strike down what stands upon it.
For instance: if this [fire] has the form of the sky, then if it were all-pervading like space, its refutation would be exactly like that of space;
this remains true even when compared to moonlight, lightning, gems, flames, sparks, and so forth.

The connection is "in exactly that same way. For how could there be a comparison by anyone of that which is to be established with those very things that were not previously perceived either in their own nature or through the medium of an example?

It will come to pass. For one who is dispassionate toward form, that knowledge arises through the very cultivation of the Noble Path by means of the cognition of purity; it is not through the mere meditation upon that [object] alone, for such a person is free from the danger of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Furthermore: "In that which has parts, there is the fault as in the case of a composite whole; in that which is partless, there is the fault as in the case of an atom.
There is no other entity here, for emptiness devours everything."

Therefore, even one who foresees the ruin caused by the fear of contradiction must accept that [the scripture contains such things], for it is impossible [to avoid]. If you argue that it must be accepted because it was spoken in the *pravacana* (the teaching), then why now drink the salty water from your father’s well? Or is it that the paths of the elements, the destinies, the wombs, the Śrāvakas, and so forth, were not taught by him? Furthermore, even that which is indicated here as something to be abandoned is not abandoned out of ignorance; rather, it is due to the inclinations and desires of those to be trained (*vineya*). For the Blessed One is an authority precisely because he teaches the way to heaven.

Therefore, since there is an absence of the cognition of utility therein, and because there is no demonstration of the manner in which that which is itself invisible transcends sublation, how could there be any accomplishment consisting of meditative cultivation? Thus, the culmination of the activity lies in enjoyment alone; the qualities are restricted to that alone, the inclination is restricted to that alone, and the measure restricted to that alone is equal to sublation itself.
Alas, those for whom the Victor is merely an external object have lost even their own Teacher—
that [Teacher] who is grasped through the straightforward method and who shines with the characteristics derived from the scriptures.
Emptiness is nothing other than consciousness, and profundity resides within it;
however, it has been deliberated whether this [profundity] pertains to all imagined phenomena.
Even in the scriptures, it is not heard in one's own words that a subject devoid of form possesses the nature of the *dharmakāya*; nor has any other explanation been made [to this effect].
If it is desired that the mind, by way of its own example, be partless and thus void in every respect, then let it indeed be so;
but if not in every respect, then why is the abandonment of partlessness not also dear to you?

For it was shown previously that the similarity to space is due solely to the departure from adventitious stains and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). For this very reason, the analogy of space is applied everywhere according to the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) specified in the *Mahāyānottaratantra*, such as "free from conceptual construction, like the sky," and so forth. Therefore, [the state of reality] is not [defined] by the absence of form (*ākāra*). As for the statement:
"In that which is nothingness, without appearance, without support, and without basis;
when the eye has passed beyond, it is formless and invisible..."
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, everything is seen even among the Buddhas, yet it does not exist there in that way.

[432] Thus, it is clear that the qualification "possessing nothing" (*akiñcana*) and so forth is intended to demonstrate the non-existence of even the perceived "elevations and depressions" caused by dust, mist, and the like, in the case of space itself. By using the locative construction *buddheṣu* ("among the Buddhas") instead of saying *sambuddhe 'pi* ("even in the Perfectly Awakened One"), there is an effort to employ a plural number as an indicator of contradiction. However, regarding the Blessed Sugata, the intention is merely this: that even when one perceives the "elevations and depressions" characterized by underestimation (*apavāda*) and overestimation (*samāropa*), there is no such existence in the Blessed One who possesses the aforementioned nature.

Or let it be that, by changing the wording, this [epithet] is also applied to the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). Just as the venerable teacher Vasubandhu, in the *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga* during the section on the definition of non-conceptual knowledge, distinguished [the object] as "formless" because it cannot be determined through the duality of apprehended and apprehender, and as "without appearance" because it possesses an object, so too may it be understood here when the term "Buddha" is employed. Furthermore, his state of possessing nothing (*akiñcanatva*) should be understood as the departure of adventitious passion and the like. The remainder is not contradictory.
For this very reason, in that same *Dharmadharmatāvibhāga*:
Since error is established as being either the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*) or non-appearance (*akhyāti*),
it should be understood without confusion that "appearance" has the sense of "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*).
"How do you see it? It appears and manifests in this way"—such statements regarding conceptual construction (vikalpa) are not contradictory, as they express how [an object] appears.
And because [this] is very clear in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*:
"If, however, manifestation were intended to be the non-existent form,
then the enjoyment of the Sage would be like that of a crown prince or a king, which is non-existent."
Why did he not state that its manifestation as something else occurs through its sovereignty over it,
just as he clearly distinguished the meaning of "eternal" and "pervasive"?
Therefore, this determination is said to be the manifestation of the non-existent;
hence, out of fear of losing your wealth, do not cast away this heap of jewels.
If this same principle applies even to the abandonment of the *dharmakāya* as taught by him, then who, indeed,
having gone for refuge to the Buddha, would disparage it?
The universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of a thing (vastu)— that is, of that which has the nature of a substrate—
is considered to be the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), known as emptiness (śūnyatā), which delivers those who are cowardly.
This nature, known as the "essential nature" (svābhāvika), is proclaimed by such terms as emptiness, suchness, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the peak of existence (bhūtakoṭi).
[433] According to the Yogācāra school, the perfected nature is also proclaimed;
as the absence of duality, it is the emptiness of all things on the Middle Way.
The revolution of the outflows is itself the untainted realm;
it is reality and the ultimate truth, and because of the awakening to that, one is called a Buddha.
When there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose fruit is the ascertainment of that [object], the qualities which depend upon its power cannot be denied,
just as one cannot deny a distinct subject (*dharmin*).

For this manifold world, which necessarily appears, must be directly realized as emptiness; by that alone is the perfection of awakening achieved—what need is there for anything else? Furthermore, there is no direct realization other than self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And since that suchness (*tathatā*) is a mental quality (*cittadharma*) common to both the states of affliction and purification, it is designated as "essential," "innate," and "nature" (*prakṛti*); yet, with respect to purification, it is the domain of the conventional usage of the *dharmakāya*.

In that regard, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatā*), when cultivated independently of specific forms, penetrates whichever form happens to be present; thus, it takes as its basis that very final form brought forth by the auxiliary cause of the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasambhāra*) which produces the specific characteristics and so forth of that particular subject (*dharmin*). In its prior state, that which is dependent upon those [forms] is said to be "variegated" (*citram*); it is also called "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).

However, in the final analysis, it is precisely the *citra* (the variegated) that is not so designated, because it is not the cause for false conceptualization; rather, it is said to be devoid of that form. Furthermore, even if there is the mere possibility of dependence on causes, if there is an absence of dependence on unreal habitual tendencies (*asadvāsanā*), it is not called "dependent" (*paratantra*), but rather "enjoyment" (*sambhoga*), both because of the enjoyment of the Dharma and because it is enjoyed by those on the ten stages. Or, from the perspective of ultimate reality, since there is no relation of cause and effect, where is there dependence? Therefore, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is indeed the very nature of the Dharma. But, [one might object]:
The nature of those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects is the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the Sage.

Such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). How then can it be said that the nature of phenomena (*dharma*) called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the form described by others? That is incorrect. Indeed, no nature of phenomena other than emptiness is found in the path of the scriptures (*āgama*). However, it should be understood according to one's inclination (*adhimukti*) through a distinction in its mode of presentation.

For instance, some understand selflessness (*nairātmya*) as the absence of a Lord (*īśvara*) and so forth; some [understand it] as the absence of an eternal self (*ātman*), even one that is inexpressible; and some [understand it] as the absence of the conjunction of insentience and luminosity.
