[434] Furthermore, others maintain that because even external atoms are absent, form—like a dream—is incapable of being defined as it is not established even by self-cognition.
And because, through the process of reasoning and reflection, the mind gradually becomes exclusively inclined toward that [object].
For the establishment of entities does not occur through either perception or inference;
rather, it is by means of these two alone that they are sublated, because their primary purpose lies therein.

Nor do we say that "dharma" refers merely to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; rather, it refers to all those modes of mind (*cittaprakāra*) that bear their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are comprised within the categories of body and intellect. The nourishment and sustenance of all these is merely an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), and even that is set aside for the sake of awakening to enlightenment. And in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*:
"The nature of those dharmas which have attained purity in every aspect..."

Because it is taught in this way in general terms, there is no abandonment of the *sambhoga* [body]; rather, it is established as a distinct body (*kāya*). Since it is enumerated up to the limit of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), it is counted separately. Therefore, having distinguished them by way of the relationship between property and its possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*), these two bodies are established. Thus, its relationship with the Blessed One is one of identity (*tādātmya*), whereas that of the *nirmāṇa* [body] is one of origination from it (*tadutpatti*). However, when that form is intended as being eternally present in the aspect of all pure qualities (*śukladharma*), then even in that case, it is simply an origination from it. As it has been said:
"Qualities are manifested by the *dharmakāya*.

This being so, although that [the *dharmakāya*] is indeed the means (*sādhana*), nevertheless, one does not pay regard to it merely as such; rather, one regards it solely as the reality (*tattva*). If it is asked why there is no mutual inclusion between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), it is because the direct realization of reality itself is the goal, and the cultivation of that [realization] alone is the means; for in the absence of that [cultivation], or if there were uncertainty regarding it, those two [goal and means] could not possibly be lost.

And since its purpose is fulfilled by the very appearing subject (*dharmin*), only the search for the validating cognition (*niścāyaka-pramāṇa*) remains; thus, the human goal is accomplished. That [object] must be cultivated as having the nature of a universal (*sāmānya-rūpa*) alone, like momentariness and so forth; therefore, another essential nature (*svabhāva*) is established. Since the designation "Buddha" depends upon the realization of that [nature], that alone is the primary form of a Buddha, or he alone is called "the Buddha," just as in the expression "the king himself is valor."

For the *Uttaratantra* states that the variegated nature consisting of the marks and so forth belongs to the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). Moreover, even if some other entity were to exist in this way, it would serve no purpose whatsoever. Consequently, even the designation "Dharmakāya" for this [entity] is merely a borrowed ornament; thus, there is no adherence at all to a vision of formlessness. For this very reason, [it is said]: "In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, distinguished by its specific body, enjoyments, and abode, situated above the Pure Abodes—therein the Perfect Buddhas awaken. Otherwise, how could they do so in the Formless Realm?"
Therefore, the Protector, having directly realized the *dharmakāya* through his own experience, abides precisely as the *sambhogakāya*.
For if there were a difference between the two states, that very [realization] would be what is to be accomplished; but if it were sublated, various efforts would be in vain.
And this being so,
consciousness is ultimately real because it is devoid of the grasped and the grasper; yet,
due to its lack of being either one or many, even consciousness is empty.
Even conventionally, that form does not belong to those who revolve within the three realms;
nor is such vastness accepted [for them], because it would transgress the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
If you have endured momentariness on the grounds that it is unreal, why should unreality not be endured? Or, if momentariness is endured, how can death not be endured?
For one who has no fear of death, how could there be fear of anything else?
Indeed, every form of abuse is terrifying only because it culminates in death.
Better than death is constant weakness, for that alone is dear to us;
better is the non-attainment of a desired object than its attainment followed by its loss.
Therefore, this very nature is not intended to be transgressed;
nevertheless, it is the established position that some excellence is desired to be attained.

And since this [reason] is common to both the momentary and the unreal, there is no fault whatsoever. Just as with momentariness, dependence on causes and so forth should also be understood in the same way. Therefore, enough of this misplaced timidity. Furthermore:
Let the sky itself be devoid of its false stains in order to remove them from the surface of the sky; let it be free from movement in order to pacify motion.
If there is no transgression of the properties of a real entity when established by valid cognition, then this [same logic] applies equally even to the doctrine of the unreal.
The third chapter, the Entrance into the Middle Way, from the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.

[The Fourth Chapter] Alternatively, what is this "falsity" (alīkatā) of that which has experience as its very nature? If you say it is due to sublation (bādhaka), then what is sublated by what? Is it the mass of variegated forms [that is sublated] by the non-perception of a pervader? This is like the case of watching a cow after it has already been sold;
for you have merely established a conventional (sāṃvṛta) relationship between the sublated and the sublator.
Because in the Bhāṣya, the contradiction of the theory of "existent manifestation" (satkhyāti), which is pervaded by that [theory], has been established.

Furthermore, cognition does not subvert itself, because self-awareness (*svarūpasaṃvedana*) is inherently powerful. Subversion by another [cognition] would have to occur either through a cognition that has the same object or a different object, and whether it occurs simultaneously or at a different time. In that regard, it is incoherent to say that a cognition with the same object subverts it. As for a cognition with a different object, what kind of subversion could it effect? If you claim it is merely by presenting its own object, why would that not constitute a subversion of this [first cognition] by that very [second one]? Nor can there be subversion by a simultaneous [cognition].

When multiple things—whether of the same or different classes—appear simultaneously, what could invalidate what? But if there is a difference in time, there is even less room for such invalidation, as this would lead to the absurd consequence that even Mahāsammata and Śrīharṣa [could invalidate one another].

Now, if the demonstration that one cognition is objectless by means of another cognition is for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*), and that sublation is not contradictory between two cognitions occurring at different times: if that object appears in that cognition, then it exists; how, then, could there be sublation? But if it does not appear, it is non-existent by its very nature—what is the use of a further negation? Nor has it been stated that the sublation has that [object] as its domain. If it is argued that it is the negation of what has been superimposed (*āropita*):

Since it has been established that even superimposition is established as mere conventional usage, the sublation based upon it likewise does not transcend the conventional. Now, just as error—characterized merely by the production of another cognition—is based on a particularity within dependent origination, so too will sublation consist simply in the arising of a cognitive form such as, "This is thus and not otherwise."

If this is so, then it is established that [the cognition] does not sublate [its object] in reality. This cognition has arisen by way of assuming a certain form, but nothing whatsoever has been sublated or established by it, just as the cognition of sweetness [arises] immediately after the cognition of blue. If it is argued that there is a distinction because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of sublation elsewhere, [we reply: that which is established merely through determination is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛta*). Therefore, the demonstration of the emptiness of the objective support (*ālambana-śūnyatā*) does not have sublation as its purpose.

Furthermore, this [distinction between] sublation might occur even in a dualistic system where there is a division between cognitions with objects and those without; however, in a non-dualistic system, it is a great audacity to claim that cognitions—which abide as awarenesses restricted solely to their own essential nature—could mutually sublate one another. And it has been said: "Just as there is no establishment of another's cognition, so too there is no sublation. (**)

Thus it is said. Now, one might object: "But the proof of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is also established only through something external; likewise, there will also be a sublation [of that proof]. This is without substance. For one who is established within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) cannot remain without relying upon inference (*anumāna*). Otherwise, one would not engage in any activity such as proceeding or desisting from action. And when inference is relied upon, the proof of consciousness-only necessarily follows by force. However, there is no room for inference in the final determination of ultimate reality (*tattva*).

Likewise, if the acceptance of sublation (*bādha*) occurs only within the conventional level (*saṃvṛti*), then since this [object] is determined as being external while it is appearing, the sublation would have to occur in that very [external object]. Whether it be some [mental] cognition or something insentient, the establishment of sublation must occur in that very [object]; even then, the operation of the proof (*sādhana*) does not proceed by bypassing the external form. Now, what is the use of this conceptualization? If one takes the diverse mental form itself as the subject (*dharmin*), then there is no operation of the proof regarding the external [object].
This [position] merely resembles the story of a man on horseback who forgets his own horse.
With reference to any sensation whatsoever, that which is external is indeed merely external;
and the inquiry as to whether that cognition might be insentient is pointless.
Thus it is established that, in every respect, the sublation [of an object] is inseparable from the determination of an external apprehended object.
Now, if it is argued: "Is this not precisely the object intended by the sublation of blue and so forth?
And since that cognition might be either non-insentient (jaḍa) or [insentient], such deliberation is pointless."
Nor does the fear that "this is the form of a cognition" arise there for the sublater;
nor, subsequently, would there be a "loosening of the bolt" regarding the capacity of that knowledge.
Furthermore, there is no rule of necessity regarding the dependence on the distinction between external objects and internal apprehension;
for this [distinction] is sublated, whether one says "this blue exists externally" or "it is the mind."
Or let that distinction be granted; nevertheless, there is still this subversion:
does a blow delivered by one with a mind of enmity not cause the death of a kinsman?

If this is argued, we reply once more: it is the established position that there is no room for a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the proof of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). In that case, when a subverting argument is established as being inseparable (*nāntarīyaka*) from the determination of the grasped and the grasper, nothing undesirable is entailed; for just as there is a distortion (*viplava*) regarding that [determination], so too is there one regarding the subverting argument, and thus the probandum is established. Nor is it possible to avoid that inseparability. Furthermore, there can be no subversion of that which has not been made an object of cognition, because the determination of subversion occurs in the form: "this is subverted by that."

Regarding the objectification of that which is sublated, there are the following alternatives: it may be objectified by something other than the sublater; by the sublater itself; by another sublater; or by itself or by something else. First, if it is objectified by something other than the sublater, then it is simply not sublated at all.

Even if it were made an object by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), what room would there be for subversion? For being made an object consists in the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*). If it is argued that the nature manifests precisely as something being subverted, this is contradictory: "manifestation of nature" implies the existence of the nature, whereas "being subverted" implies non-existence. If it is argued that both occur sequentially, it is not so; for subversion cannot occur first, because the related term (*sambandhin*) has not yet been cognized.

Now, if it is the manifestation of its own nature (*svarūpa*), then since the existence [of the object] is established by that alone, where is there any sublation? Indeed, even if [the object] were to exist at a later time, there could be no sublation of that [manifestation], because at that time the [manifestation] itself has ceased to exist. Or, if it were still present, nothing could be done even by a hundred sublaters. But if both [the manifestation and the later state] are made objects of cognition, then there is simply the establishment of correspondence; how could there be even a scent of sublation? Furthermore, it is not logically possible for one thing to be made an object of another—whether by that [cognition] or by something else—since we have already begun this inquiry on the basis of the establishment of consciousness. Nor does making it an object of itself leave room for sublation.
When that which is manifesting by itself is made an object by another through a subverting cognition,
its own head must be crushed by that stronger force.

Furthermore, the conceptual construction—which functions by terminating in its own mere form, thinking "this blue has been sublated by me through this reasoning"—does not even touch upon the matter of difference; nor is it a rash claim that, even in the case of non-difference, it sublates itself. Moreover, regarding the cognition of both self and other, there is simply consistency as before. However, if one were to sublate what has not been made an object of cognition, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). But if there is an inclination toward grasping the external, then even when a cognition arises that does not touch that [external object], there might be the hope for the conventional usage of "sublation" based on what was established therein.

And since that [notion] is a distortion regarding resolve (*adhimokṣa*), the affliction caused by it is likewise a distortion. For when the establishment of external objects is overcome, everything is submerged in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); thus, what action could there be, for whom, or by what means? Even then, it is not possible to say, "This is exactly this. If that were the case, duality would arise once again, as it has been said:

"Even when one thinks, 'All this is indeed mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*)', because of the very perception [of that thought], one who posits something before oneself does not abide in that mere-consciousness alone."

(Thakur adds *triṃśikāyām* in the corrigenda). Now, one might object: "Even when there is certainty regarding reality (*tattva*), for one who has not yet attained direct realization (*asākṣātkaraṇa*), a sublation (*bādhaka*) may still find scope, just as it does in the case of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. Even so, there is no fault. For just as activity and the like proceed solely through the external domain of innate ignorance (*sahajāvidyā*), thinking "this is to be known" or "this is to be attained," so too would the sublation fall upon that very summit [of ignorance]. However, when there is reflection on pure consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), there is the cessation of all activity.

Therefore, this relationship between the sublated and the sublator is merely conventional; it finds no occasion at the time when the true nature of reality is being revealed. And at that time, while it is true that even the means of proof (sādhana) has no application, its non-application does not constitute a sublation, because the probandum (sādhya) is already established.

If that [reason] is unestablished, the other [refutation] cannot even enter; what purpose does it serve, except for the mere satisfaction of the opponent? If, then, the application of the refutation depends upon the operation of a proof establishing that [reason], then this fault indeed follows. But who would delay in such a manner? Let the application of the refutation occur right from the beginning. This [objection] is merely like the ritual rinsing of the mouth by one who is already terrified.

For when it is established that there is no entry for this [objection] upon the realization of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), then, since its application depends precisely on the absence of that nature, once consciousness-ness is established through the very act of defining it, the entry of any sublation (*bādhaka*) is dispelled; or, if such a sublation were to occur, it would have to do so in the form "this is not consciousness. Therefore, as long as there is sublation, it is established that [the object] exists only externally and does not possess the nature of consciousness. If one asks, "What, then, is the fault in the proof?"—it is as follows:

No, for in the proof of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only), since there is no arising of inference at all, where is there room for proof or refutation? To explain: inference and the like are means of knowledge regarding external objects, not regarding one's own singular self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*). But when one's own singular self-awareness is established, that [external object] exists only through the apprehension of it.
Nevertheless, if satisfaction is found in stating these faults, then since the nature of the other [the probandum]— namely, the subject and the nature of the reason— is unestablished,
there is neither establishment nor pervasion; what, then, is not a refutation?

Furthermore, this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), or any other subverting argument (*bādhaka*) such as that called "investigation" (*vicāra*), is not something other than inference (*anumāna*) that could serve as a subject of possibility. For every statement advanced by one engaged in a dispute must, in order to be relevant to the matter at hand, necessarily imply an inference through the manifestation of the thesis (*sādhya*), the reason (*sādhana*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It is for this very reason that we have demonstrated in the *Advaitabindu* that one must necessarily accept the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).

Otherwise, by mere restatement in whatever manner, what purpose could be established for anyone? Nor can inference be considered "in accordance with reality" (yathārtha) by disparaging perception, because it is produced by that very perception through its indispensable utility in the apprehension of relations and so forth, even if only indirectly. Thus, to claim that this [inference] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when that [perception] is not a means of valid cognition, is like aspiring to noble birth when one's progenitor is of low birth.
Furthermore, since this awareness of the form [of the object] regarding its own nature is perception—being free from error and conceptual construction—how could there be any occasion for sublation?
If self-awareness alone is not a means of valid cognition because it is not produced by another [means], then what here is a means of valid cognition?
Therefore, regarding those things established or sublated by that [self-awareness], no other [means] has the power to either sublate or establish them.

[441] Now, if it is asked: "At the time of establishing cognition, how can there be a self-defeat through direct perception of one's own source? We say: No, because when the probandum is established, there is defeat for oneself as well. Just as a fire that consumes its own support burns the tree from which it was produced by friction against its own mass of branches, if even this *parivitti* (the act of superseding) were to destroy itself, who here would be at fault?

Indeed, the proof of cognition does not hope for its own validity by subverting another's perception; rather, the inquiry is raised in that manner because of the commonality of perceiving others—just as fire is a burner for everyone, it is not the fault of anyone in particular. Furthermore, the non-perception of a pervader (vyāpakānupalambha) requires its own validity only through the subversion of perception; thus, it is not logical [to claim otherwise]. However, the proof of cognition possesses a validity that is indeed superior to the validity of another's perception.

Furthermore, when one does not engage in such conventional usage because the object—whose existence is established by the cognition of its capacity for causal efficiency—is not perceived due to a lack of reflective awareness (*avimarśa*), that is not a fault of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), since there is no sublation from one's own side; yet from the perspective of another, the stick [of the logical reason] remains the same. For indeed, there is no manifestation of the capacity within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

But when the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) itself is the leading factor, then it is not even capable of subverting the validity of another form of perception, let alone that of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which by its very nature has cast far away the stain of the suspicion of error and conceptual construction. Therefore, there can be no injury from any quarter to that which is protected by self-awareness.
[Objection: But if the sense-faculty lacks validity, then inference cannot possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*).
Likewise, it can also be argued that if inference lacks validity, the sense organ [likewise lacks it].

When an inference is invalidated because of a defect in the mark (liṅga) that was apprehended as a constituent part of it, the fault lies in that very [mark]; for how could the invalidation of what is produced from that [mark] be caused by anything else?
Therefore, even if both [the cognition and its object] possess validity, nevertheless,
let consciousness manifest its own persistence within itself, since error is impossible therein; yet how can this cruel [opponent's] denial of unity and plurality be prevented?

Who knows whose power is superior— this interplay between perception and inference, which possess equal force and glory, since the existence of one is necessarily dependent upon the establishment of the other?

[442] That too is not a valid means. For let there be parity between the non-perception of the pervader—which is restricted solely to the cognition of another—and the direct perception that grasps the pervasion and so forth, since the validity of one is necessarily concomitant with the validity of the other. But self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is the substratum for both of these, whereas neither of those two is its substratum; so how can it be weighed against them?

Furthermore, because inference has as its object that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), it does not apply to what is perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, where is there any occasion for considering their relative strength? For this very reason, it is stated that the thesis (*pakṣa*) must not be contradicted by perception and the other means of valid cognition.

Is it not the case that even in perception, inference is indeed accepted for the purpose of bringing into linguistic usage a distinct nature (*svabhāvāntara*) that was previously unexpressed? Furthermore, neither affirmation nor negation ever applies to that which is merely appearing. For the application of words such as "cow" occurs with respect to a specific arrangement of features like the dewlap and hooves when they appear; and the linguistic usage of negating a jar occurs when only the bare ground is perceived; likewise, the negation of an external pair of moons occurs with respect to the form of two moons present within cognition.

However, affirmation and negation do not apply solely to that which appears. Likewise here, in the context of negation, as many imagined properties as belong to the appearing form of blue and so forth are to be negated—such as self, other, the grasped, the grasper, the made known, the maker known, permanence, momentariness, unity, plurality, and so on; or substantiality, quality, being composed of the three *guṇas*, and so forth; or even down to the nature of atoms, the accompaniment by other forms characterized by touch and so on, and causal efficiency—all these are denoted by the term "proliferation" (*prapañca*), because they are all merely imagined.

Therefore, when a subject (*dharmin*) is manifest, the negation or affirmation of another property (*dharmāntara*) that is not itself manifest occurs by relying on conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). This is because even in the absence of verbal or other such usage, the capacity for such usage exists in what is suitable for it, yet that capacity remains of a hidden nature. There is, however, never a negation of that which is manifest. As stated in the *Nyāyabindu*: "When that [subject] is to be proven as being devoid of a certain entity, its non-perception is the reason; it is not the non-existence of that very thing, because of the employment of words. (PV I 208)
Thus [it is said], and also: "The reason, when isolated, lacks a locus" (PV IV 91).

If, then, affirmation and negation regarding that which appears are both useless and incapable, and the same negation applies even to that which does not appear—being likewise incapable and useless—where, then, is the operation of words? Nowhere in reality; this is merely a conventional practice based on dependent origination, wherein by means of words something is either affirmed or negated.

For just as the affirmation of the existence of a tree by means of a word consists merely in the production of a conceptual construction that projects an activity corresponding to it—by virtue of the convention that "the tree exists"—so too, the negation of it consists merely in the production of a conceptual construction that projects an exclusion of those who seek that object, [expressed as] "the tree does not exist. However, when neither the negative particle nor the verb "to exist" is employed, there occurs merely the production of a conceptual construction of an aspect possessing branches and so forth, which is incapable of either prompting engagement or withdrawal.

This is what is meant by the non-performance of injunctions and prohibitions. In the proximity of a word, that very same tree appears as if augmented by its existence; thus, compared to the previous [perception], there is merely the delineation of a specific form. Even when joined with the negative particle (*nañ*), it appears as if diminished; thus, in relation to the experience of the positive injunction, there is only the delineation of a diminished form. From that follows activity and so forth corresponding to that [delimited form].

The same applies to an inferential mark (*liṅga*): when fire is inferred from the perception of smoke or clouds, there is a distinction based on whether it is invariably concomitant with a corresponding reality or not. Thus, neither affirmation nor negation applies to the manifest form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*), nor to an external object that does not manifest, whether it exists or does not exist in reality. Nevertheless, through the gateway of the arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the practical application of affirmation and negation pertains solely to the external object as it is conceptually constructed; for that which manifests vividly before one cannot be negated even by a hundred "nots."

And conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is distinct from external objective apprehension (*parāmarśa*), because it involves the suspension of the state of attention required for determining existence or non-existence when there is a mere conceptualization of a tree. For this very reason, the form (*ākāra*)—superimposed as an external reality—is called "exclusion" (*apoha*) and the denotation of words, since it is that alone which appears in verbal cognition. However, it has been explained previously that through determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*), it is regarded as being "external" and excluded from other classes. Therefore, there is no negation of the form nor of the external in reality;
for while [the object] is external only conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), it is not so even conventionally in the case of the form.
(See JNA 229; RNA2 65.20: *vidhisādhanam*:

*pratiṣedhanam*) Because people do not desire that [liberation] and because they are by nature extroverted, when there is no room for negation even regarding external objects as they manifest, how could there be any for the self? Therefore, there is no possibility of protection through logical reasons against what has been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that which is established by self-cognition is indeed established in reality.

Even though the relationship between the probandum and the probans is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), it must nevertheless be based upon a valid convention (*sat-saṃvṛti*). For if, for each individual, the establishment of various means of proof and so forth were distinct, then everything would be established for everyone. Furthermore, there is no possibility of rescue by means of other conventions once a reason has been sublated by [valid] reasons. If others have a disagreement regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), then in that case, it is not possible to live by means of [other] instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) apart from self-awareness;
this has indeed been determined in the treatise (*śāstra*) by the destruction of the means of knowledge, just as in the case of the world at large.

Therefore, since [existence] is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the proposition [that it does not exist] leaves no room for inferences such as the non-perception of a pervader; thus, the proposition is sublated by direct perception. Alternatively, what kind of existence is intended to be refuted by these proofs? In that regard, if it is an existence well-known in other systems—characterized by its connection with "Being" (*sattā*), its nature as "intrinsic existence" (*svarūpasattva*), or the three criteria of a valid definition (*trilakṣaṇa*), and so forth—or some existence imagined by oneself, then there is no dispute.

[444] Now, that which is well-known in the world is also characterized by capacity (*śakti*) and characterized by manifestation (*prakāśa*). For it is said that what is fit to be perceived, yet is not perceived, does not exist.

In that regard, if [existence] is defined as causal capacity (*śakti*), then refuting it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Even if it is defined as manifestation (*pratibhāsa*), the same logic applies if one refutes that which lacks ungrasped capacity. Alternatively, at that time, manifestation is not the defining characteristic; rather, it is simply capacity—thus there is no fault. However, how can existence (*sattā*) in forms and so forth be denied, given that their nature is mere luminosity devoid of adventitious conditions such as imagined capacities? This is because it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*); thus, the thesis is contradicted by direct perception. In this way, these entities are without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Thus, even though there is a difference in the manner of expression, if the object denoted by the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is something other than manifestation (*prakāśa*) as previously stated, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, it should be understood that there is simply no capacity for it to appear. However, the absence of being one or many is indeed intended, because the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is what is sought to be expressed. For if it were otherwise, it would be undesirable due to the fear of losing its intrinsic nature. Moreover, since existence is established through appearance, what is the point of this [argument]?
Is this not contradictory? If it is asked, "How then can there be non-duality in diversity?

[the answer is: This is non-dual because of the abandonment of the grasped and the grasper; or else, because of the transcendence of insentience, and because of the destruction of unity and plurality, it is diverse through its having form, and thus wondrous.
The manifold non-duality is known as such, and like the word of a king, it is a conventional single sound;
multiplicity does not exist in reality, and therefore there is no fruit that is truly existent conventionally.

The word "variegated" (*citra*) has the sense of a marvel, since existence is possible even in the absence of being one or many. Whether the Blessed One is "one" from the perspective of conventional truth, as stated previously, there is no utility in the conventional usage of "many. For just as the activity that determines oneness—thinking, "That Blessed One is to be taken as my refuge, and I too must become exactly like him"—is purposeful, so too there is nothing whatsoever [to be gained] by way of multiplicity.

[444,19] We consider the result: because activity in respect to any distinct entity is unestablished, therefore, since both are in reality untenable, oneness is conventionally designated with respect to the result and nothing else, just as impermanence is [designated] by virtue of being conducive to pacification. But surely even this [cognition], extending from the interval between blue objects to its periphery, is conventionally designated by you as a single variegated wheel of cognitions, consisting of those of the same and different classes; that—
How is it said?
To the very extent that there is external conceptual attachment, to that same extent this and that appear as distinct.
But that mind is complete;
for he himself possesses such hands, feet, and so forth, which consist of gnosis.

Indeed, Caitra is not merely his hands and other limbs apart from the mental transformations (*manovivarta*). Therefore, just as with other transformations, because they are included within what is denoted by the term "Caitra," there is a single conventional usage solely when one reflects upon the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). Even in that case, it should be remembered that a distinction in the portion of the objective sphere has been stated, just as in the case of the Blessed Lady. Or, in reality, the word "one" (*eka*) is intended merely to exclude a plurality, just like the word "non-dual" (*advaita*).
Therefore, the summary is this: blue and so forth exist precisely as manifestations, yet they are devoid of being either one or many.

"In a variegated cognition, blue and so forth have cognition as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and do not appear as anything else. For it is impossible to perceive them while distinguishing them from the object; [if one were to do so], one would fall [into error]. (PV III 220)

In this context, "variegated" (*citra*) is the negation of unity; "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to a single cognizer. Because it is included within a single cognition by virtue of appearing as such, there is a negation of multiplicity. By the phrase "having cognition as its limiting adjunct" (*jñānopādhi*), there is an absence of sublation because it is of the nature of cognition through its exclusion from insentient matter. By the statement that one cannot perceive another form, such as yellow and so forth, without partaking in it, there is shown the lack of purpose for the conventional usage of difference.

He says: For if one [entity] could be apprehended separately from that [collection], and if the accomplishment of what is to be established by it were possible—as in the case of Caitra, Maitra, and so forth—then the conventional usage of "many" would be appropriate. But since this is not the case, only a single [entity] is appropriate. By the words beginning with "For him...

(taṃ hi), he explains the meaning starting with "externally" (bahir) and so forth. For when there is a reflection upon the nature of cognition, the single term "Caitra" and so forth is applied to the collection consisting of cognition and its other factors.

In that case as well, one should proceed in the same manner. While discerning and analyzing, one would again fall back upon the object itself, or rather, the arising and grasping of the object alone would be distinct, not that of the cognition. For:
"In whatever way a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way."

[445,16] Thus, there would be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. [445,18] "Name" (*nāman*) means a word that expresses a designation (*saṃjñā*). That single nature is not real. "Appears" (*bhāsate*) means "is born" (*jāyate*), because the intention is that birth belongs only to that which is manifesting. Therefore, it is indeed devoid of both a unitary and a manifold intrinsic nature. (98b)

[445,20] Knowledge is a non-dual manifold, free from sublation; and it has been shown that even within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), it is the very object of a single linguistic usage, just like momentariness and so forth.
[445,21] But even so, how can that which does not exist and yet is pervaded by it be an object of conviction? Nor is there any such confidence anywhere in this manner.
[445,22] Furthermore, when one thing is negated and another is affirmed, since there is no third category, why would the "neither" [option] regarding entities be any less than the two sides?

[445,23] What is the possibility? Therefore, at the very time of establishing the definition, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established by both modes. But for the opponent, the absence of both [modes] due to the nature of the thing (*vastusvabhāva*) does not constitute a sublation; thus, this [objection] is irrelevant. [446,1] True, it is irrelevant, because existence is established even without those two, since pervasion itself would be impossible [otherwise]. Where?
And is it thus? Is it not right here, in this very body of cognition (*buddhi*)? Then why now [claim] a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) merely because it has been made the subject (*pakṣa*)?

Or what fault is there if the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*) involves deviation? For even in another locus of properties (*dharmyantara*), by that very same [operation], it is rendered "inconclusive due to being common" (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
And if there is protection here merely by making it the subject, then what is the obstruction in that case as well? And when—

Even if there is direct observation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is no impairment of the probandum (*sādhya*); at that time, mere doubt is ineffective, and thus the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) does not apply for now.
Nor is there non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth, because the reason is established from some source, out of respect for the sublation by perception (*adhyakṣabādhana*). And thus:

Even if there is no confidence in a reason because its probandum has been refuted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no fault; for what room is there for suspicion in other cases? For that very reason, even at the time of defining [the reason], pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established. When one [alternative] is negated and the other is affirmed, the negation of a third category occurs only externally.
Indeed, even in that case, it is impossible to demonstrate a sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), for this [entity] is neither different nor non-different in relation to that.

Because it is impossible to say so; and self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is inherently difficult to fathom, for if there were neither difference nor non-difference regarding external objects, it would follow that all conventional practice (*saṃvyavahāra*) would be abolished.
As it has been said: "For one who does not see fire... (*na hy analaṃ paśyan* [***])

And so forth. Therefore, this principle is restricted to the external alone; however, if the intellect (*buddhi*) is also established in accordance with that, let it be a mere conventional establishment (*vyavasthāmātra*). As it has been said:
"Just as the external is the object of apprehension..."
And so forth. However, even then, it is not direct (*āñjasas*).

As for what was stated in the *Buddhi-adhikāra* [of the *Pramāṇavārttika*], beginning with "Otherwise, of a single entity" (PV III 358), that was intended from the perspective of a specific Madhyamaka school.

[This is] for the purpose of clarifying the statement: "In whatever way objects are conceived" (PV III 209). If that were so, one might also say: "Just as it is neither one nor many, so too it is neither luminous (*prakāśa*) nor non-luminous.
But this is not the case, because the negation of luminosity is sublated by luminosity itself. Such a thing is not possible regarding unity and plurality for the opponent.
Furthermore, there is no utility in the argument introduced by the words "but" (*tu*) and so forth.
For the abandonment of both unity and plurality is preserved by their being non-entities (*avastutva*).
But who could preserve a thing from being devoured by its own cognition if it were a non-entity?

Therefore, one who distinguishes between the "one" and the "many" has no authority over the cognition for the purpose of proving non-existence, because the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) depends upon a specific object; thus, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). Furthermore, if you maintain that the determination of the establishment of pervasion occurs through generality alone, then since existence—the pervaded—is established, there must be either oneness or manyness by means of a single [entity], and not manyness.
Let it be that "tolerance" (*kṣama*) is one and only one. For if there were multiplicity, then until the atom is split down to its constituent parts, there ought to be an appearance of atoms;
yet this is not the case. Therefore:
"In whatever manner a cognition appears..."
The meaning is: by way of the exclusion of many [factors], due to its lack of atomic form.
That is experienced exactly in that manner;
it is "followed" (*anugamyate*)—that is to say, it is "approached" (*upagamyate*)—because it has the sense of being attained.

[447,12] Thus, there would be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. [447,14] The word *nāma* is an indeclinable used here in the sense of "admitting" (*upagame*). And this is not possible for that which is insentient, because consciousness itself would be non-existent; this is what is shown by the term *jñāna*. However, when even an atom of cognition is logically untenable due to its division into spatial parts, then a composite whole cannot be formed from partless atoms.

[447,16] In the case of the position of manifoldness (*nānātva*), the very commencement would be without appearance; therefore, this appearance comes to rest in oneness alone. [447,17] In whatever manner and from whatever kind of non-dual characteristic (*abheda-lakṣaṇa*) cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way, existing as nothing but non-dual, according to the principle that "experience is existence" (*anubhavaḥ sattā*). Thus, the passage beginning with "nāma" is easy to understand. The word "nāma" is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*). By this—
[447,19] Consequently, its lack of established proof follows from that very admission.

[447,20] But is it not contrary to experience to say that a variegated thing is one, since blue, yellow, and so forth appear only as distinct? Furthermore, [447,21] "variegated" is synonymous with "not manifold," and since that [term] is established by the exclusion of "one," how can that which is variegated be one? Otherwise...

If it is argued that light would then be insentient (*jaḍa*), we say no; for the function of cognition (*saṃvedana*) consists in being blue and so forth, not in difference. The determination of difference or non-difference, however, must follow its basis. If it is asked: "Is this 'this is blue' and 'this is yellow' not itself the cognition of difference, since they are perceived as having mutually distinct natures?"—this is indeed so in the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*). But due to the force of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is superimposed even upon the intellect (*buddhi*). In the intellect...

One ought to consider whether these forms are distinct or non-distinct. If it is argued that even in the case of cognition, the determination follows precisely that [distinction], we say no; for not all [cognitions] are so. For instance, regarding the state of being stable or otherwise, it is necessarily determined by another.
That which is to be manifested exists externally through causal efficiency;
due to the difference in its forms, it is utterly of a different nature.
Internally, however, it is certainly not the opposite, owing to the force of habitual practice.

The term "internal" refers to the mind (*citta*), while its opposite is external. Furthermore, why is it that the nature of cognition (*buddhi*) is not determined as being either stable or unstable? Because, in reality, there is no perception of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparāpratīti*).
For if priority and posteriority were perceived, there would necessarily be either permanence or motion.
Because that [duality] does not exist through the resolve upon it as either one or many, the two are non-existent.
In that case, if there were differentiation, the consequence would be the absence of the appearance of gross objects, and the consequence of non-appearance would be difficult to avoid.
Alternatively, if there were unity, blue would have to be yellow itself. As it has been said:
"Even in the absence of differentiation, unity would be contradictory to variegation. (* ***)
And yet, it does not appear in that way. Nevertheless:

"In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is accepted as being exactly so; thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind possessing variegated forms. (PV III 221) — this corresponds to Prajñākaragupta’s version.

The word "nāma" is used here in the sense of concession (*aṅgīkāre*). The meaning is this: it is true that a single entity could not exist as something manifold; however, let there be no denial of the existence of that which is manifesting—thus, nothing undesirable follows. This is the intended point:
if consciousness were real, its manifoldness would be established, and [the claim of its unity] would be sublated.
And if there were identity, your own position would be undermined; for us, however, neither case results in a contradiction.

If existence is established, we have not failed in anything even by [asserting] multiplicity; we merely teach unity in accordance with reason (*nyāya*). For, because it shares the same acquisition and preservation (*sāmānayogakṣematva*) as existence, there is no injury to its unity.
But multiplicity is its opposite; therefore, that [multiplicity] ceases within it.

As for what is said—that if there were identity, blue would be yellow itself—that is a fault only from an external perspective, because those who seek the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of that object would still engage with it, and because the [undesired] consequence of such activity would follow. If it is asked: "Even if one does not exclude the desire for causal efficiency, how could that which is blue possibly become yellow?"—then why should it be deprived of its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*)? It is better to accept it as it is.

[449,4] If you ask why, it would indeed be so if there were a state of being beyond perception (*parokṣatā*). Therefore, if they were external, there would necessarily be a plurality between blue and yellow, lest there be a confusion of activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. But if they are cognitions, there is indeed oneness. However, due to the long-standing habit of external conventional usage, this [oneness] is as unbearable as the midday sun facing one directly; what can we do about that? Thus, in this case, there are contradictions with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so on.

Even these [cognitions] are indeed floating [in error], because the conceptual construction that "blue is other than yellow" proceeds by disregarding the operation of self-awareness (*svavedana*), since it flows spontaneously as a single following of the operation of sensory cognition. For this very reason, there is no contradiction in [the claim that] the variegated is one; for it is variegated by way of being blue, yellow, and so forth, but not by way of being manifold. It is only due to the conceit of pervasion by way of manifoldness [that such a notion arises].

Thus it is said: pervasion exists only in the external world. Alternatively, the statement that "the manifold is merely a restatement" means that which you accept as being diverse is, in reality, a single form of cognition; thus there is no fault, like that of a man already mounted on a horse.

Now, it may be argued that the superimposition of contradictory properties is what defines difference, and there is no restriction here as to whether this applies to the external object or to cognition.
If you ask why, it is because of necessity itself. For if there were no distinction between external objects, there would be no specific determination of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*);

and if that were disregarded, there would be no distinction based on mere appearance, and thus that [causal efficiency] would simply be absent. However, in the case of cognition, if there were a distinction [between its aspects], there would be a loss of its own nature, because its existence consists solely in its manifestation, independent of causal efficiency. Furthermore, if there were a distinction, it would follow that there is an absence of manifestation for that state [of cognition]. Even if...

Furthermore, if one insists on a distinction between the two, both would suffer a loss of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Nevertheless, without going so far as that, just as the external object—reckoned as an aggregate of atoms—endures even when divided, and maintains its status as an object of apprehension through even a slight degree of correspondence with a cognition that possesses a single, solid, gross form despite lacking any delineation of the atomic shape, it is said that cognition does not do so; nor, for that matter, is there any loss of the external object itself.

It causes affliction, because it is established merely through overestimation (*abhimāna*). Or rather, it might proceed outward solely from overestimation. But as for cognition (*buddhi*) established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could both of those [affliction and proceeding outward] possibly exist? For there is a necessary loss of its own nature when there is a distinction resulting from the attainment of a reflection upon an external form. As it has been said:
"For one who discriminates that [appearance] falls upon the object" (PV III 220).
Just as an appearance devoid of causal capacity for the object resembles [an illusion such as] hair-threads and the like,
so too the discrimination "this is other than that" occurs only with respect to the external.

This is not a consequence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), but rather the mere play of external habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Therefore, just as the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of cognition is unique to the external world by virtue of properties such as being independent of another [cognition], so too it is logical that its distinction is established by the sublation of the imposition of contradictory properties through the force of reasoning (*nyāyasāmarthya*). If, then, it is only external...

[450.2] If difference is produced by contradictory properties and non-difference is not of the nature of experience, what is the recourse? For even in that case, the establishment of "the Blessed One is one" is accepted; for in the absence of a restrictive cause, there would be the undesirable consequence of non-difference even with respect to another continuum. Thus he says: "Blue and so forth [are present] in variegated cognition" (PV III 220).
And so forth.

[450,7] What is called the "unity" of cognition (*buddhi*) would be an essence that cannot be analytically separated into a plurality; or rather, this name "cognition" would apply to it and not to the insentient (*jaḍa*). When the counter-correlative is incapable [of being perceived], the word "name" (*nāma*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). And in whatever way a manifold (*citram*) appears, [it is so].

Even that which is contained within a single cognition is experienced in exactly that way; thus, there may be a unity of the mind, which is the object of the designation "single continuum. However, this kind of impossibility of being distinguished—which is what the opponent intends—is not present here, so there is no fault. Therefore, in this way, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the independent [argument], because the unity of the forms of cognition is indeed established. Furthermore:

[450,12] What is this unity or plurality, and where do they reside? What is the pervasion of these two with respect to being a real entity (*vastutva*)? [450,13] To this, the answer is: that very thing is both partless and one, and it is also a plurality when combined. In the world, the existence of a real entity is established precisely through its unity and plurality. [450,14] Now, if it is argued that what is perceived by oneself is useful for inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), [we reply: this is so within the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) which serves as the basis for investigation.

[450,15] "Is there no fault in saying that it was perceived by itself in that very way? To this it is replied: even in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), only that which is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is said to be seen. And nowhere is a partless entity within the scope of perception by these two. Therefore, even though it is manifold in the form of a collection of those [parts], it is not perceived; so how can the pervasion of real entities (*vastu*) be established by these two? Nor does anything [partless] exist at all.

[450,18] As for the entity (*vastu*), however, the admission by another (*paropagama*) is not employed as an independent reason (*svatantra-hetu*). And since a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*) results in the opposite conclusion, there would be a contradiction with the probandum (*sādhyavirodha*). Let this penalty apply to one who maintains that an entity is pervaded by unity and plurality; but for one for whom being an entity consists merely in being manifest, what need is there to conform to such a restriction?

Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be established by oneself. Furthermore, if the cognition of a relation between an entity and its oneness or multiplicity occurs in some instance, then that very thing is not empty; thus, the proof of the emptiness of pervasion is undermined. Now, one might object: "The actual state of things—the conventional usage of 'one' and 'many,' as well as the determination established by valid cognition—indeed exists in the world. However, it does not exist upon critical investigation. This is precisely what [is being addressed].

If it is asked, "How can our probandum (sādhya) possibly constitute a sublation?"—no; for what you intend to prove is the absence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), not merely the absence of being one or many, since that is what has been presented as the means of proof (sādhana). Nor is this a case of pointing out an unestablished reason (asiddha); rather, it is the lack of pervasion (vyāptyasiddhi) that is being asserted. Furthermore, the pervasion of the contrapositive (viparyayavyāpti) relies upon the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha) and so forth, and that [pervasion]...

In some cases, because the pervaded and the pervader are not established, the reason is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*), since they are not made objects even by conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvṛta-pramāṇa*). Nor is mere worldly convention (*vyavahāra-mātra*) a valid cognition, nor is it a separate definition [of valid cognition]. Even in the case of what is not a valid cognition, there is no fixed rule for the establishment of valid cognition.
If you claim that the means of valid cognition (māna) is accepted within the conventional (saṃvṛti), then this very analysis is also conventional.
If it is not accepted even conventionally, then one who speaks thus would be a victor in either case.
This is an intermediate verse.

Therefore, if you intend that the non-existence of all things follows from their absence everywhere because you have conceived a pervasion based on a form that has been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the separation from the son of a barren woman would also be a non-empty means for proving that; thus, [your position] is excellent!

The hope for proof is thus lost. Therefore, when the perception of the pervaded and the pervader occurs—whether in the form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) based on the apprehension of pervasion, or in the form of inference designated as a "sublater of the contrary" (*viparyayabādhaka*)—and when, due to the absence of that [perception], the certainty of the non-existence of the other [the pervader] arises in some cases, it is logical [to conclude that the pervaded is absent]. Consequently, the proof of the pervasion of existence by momentariness is necessarily concomitant with the ascertainment of the existence of momentariness.

[451,11] Thus, that very apprehension belongs to this [subject]. But in the present case, just like that, if their existence were implied even by way of a commonality, then a reason that is invariably concomitant with that would be a contradictory reason (*viruddha*) because it would subvert the intended [property]. Even if there is no such implication, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

[451,14] Therefore, why is there a negation of the cognition of variegated forms? If it is asked, "Why then is there no external object either? [The answer is: Precisely because it does not manifest in reality (*tattvataḥ*). For it is well-established that non-existence is nothing other than non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). Nor is it characterized by partlessness and unity; what, then, would be the obstruction to the power of the non-apprehension of the pervader regarding an external object? Furthermore, what is this characteristic of unity, from which—

Is it not possible to level this objection? [The objection is that] the inability to demonstrate [the parts] through analysis [is the definition]; however, that does not apply to the external [object]. Since that [external object] does not exist, its composite form—though manifold—is likewise non-existent. If it is argued that there will be a manifold [entity] that is capable of being analyzed, then if there were some final [part] that was incapable of being analyzed, only in relation to that would there be mutual capability for analysis; otherwise, there would be none.

And it is thus, because even an atom would lead to an infinite regress. However, in the case of a variegated cognition occurring within one's own mental continuum (*svasantāna*), there is an impossibility of its being analyzed into parts;

he shows that this is not the case when it is associated with another continuum. By this, it is clearly stated that the establishment of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader occurs in the cognition, whereas elsewhere it functions through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

For this very reason, even by the venerable teacher Vasubandhu, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) was set forth solely with reference to external objects, not with reference to cognition. If it is argued that, by virtue of the same logic, [the objection] might still find scope there as well and thus be difficult to ward off, we say no; for it has already been refuted through that same logic in the passage beginning, "This is indeed consciousness-only" (*vijñānamātram eva*). Therefore, due to the non-existence of the duality of grasped and grasper...

[451,26] And by means of the existence of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), which has the characteristic of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) of the three realms, the cessation of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) has been accomplished; it was not stated that there is the non-existence of other entities. If it is argued that it was not stated because it could be inferred from that, then the refutation of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) has been stated directly; therefore, its very absence is not what is to be expressed. Consequently, it is precisely that [unreal imagination] for which the refutation has been stated.

Thus, enough with this elaboration. Likewise, having analyzed it, one should understand that "being neither one nor many" is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) because it is observed as the very nature (*svabhāva*), characterized by mutual exclusion (*anyonyaparihārasthitalakṣaṇatayā*). It is not "the state of being a partless mass," for the consideration of parts is undertaken only out of deference to others. Alternatively, it should be understood that through that means, the absence of the impossibility of differentiation is what is actually revealed.
"Like another continuum. But surely for one who maintains the doctrine of a single reality through self-cognition, there is no basis for the establishment of multiplicity;

if this existence of another continuum is not established, it is like a factor that does not serve as a result. Is the establishment of another continuum then merely conventional, however that may be?

[452,8] What is the point of insisting on this matter? For even in this way, let there be no multiplicity of cognitions at all; since the non-perception of a pervader is established even by means of a single [cognition] as being one, [the reason remains unestablished]. Furthermore, the word "one" will apply through the exclusion of the imagined multiplicity for as long as conventional usage persists. Therefore, there is no distinction in cognition—as there appears to be externally—caused by the superimposition of contradictory properties.

Let it be so; however, what is the proof for that? And what is the proof for their being one? Direct perception itself. If you argue that it is not so because it is followed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this is merely the fault of conceptual construction. Why is it not the fault of direct perception itself? No, because it appears precisely within the internal awareness of the mutual [perception]. Furthermore, blue, yellow, and so forth have been seen by me.

[452,14] Thus is the apprehension of a single agent; and because of the relation of "this variegated appearance is mine," there is a single possessor of that relation. This very perception-conceptualization (*pratyakṣa-vikalpa*) possesses the form of experience as non-different from a cloth. In this way, is the intellect itself one, or is its conceptualization—the conceptualization of the three worlds—one? Even the statement "there is a variegated appearance in a single intellect" is like the body of a stone-son (*śilāputra*); for [the term] "body" [is applied to both].
Or, it is like the case of hands, feet, and so forth. This is indeed a single determination; however, due to the conceit of externality, it is merely spoken of as a collection.

In the absence of that [conceit], however, this very oneness is delineated. Thus, even in the case of trees, mountains, and the like, when they are mere cognitions, there is the conventional usage of "one" in both instances.

Therefore, there is no fault in perception; nor is it established that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) exists as a real entity. Thus, it is proven that direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) grasps non-difference. If it is argued that even in the case of difference, direct perception alone is the refuge, we reply: in cases such as "the cognition of a single mountain," there is no lack of conformity with conceptual construction due to its arising erroneously, because it has been observed repeatedly. Why, then, should both be accepted? Therefore, the [objection] is a delusion resulting from the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Thus, at the outset of establishing emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by means of the negation of both [existence and non-existence], he has proceeded to illuminate the doctrine of "maybe" (*syādvāda*) by establishing both; this is a fatal blow. Now, if each individual proof is intended merely to refute its opposite and not to establish its own position as a finality—since even that [position] is subsequently refuted in turn—then, when unity is established by perception, the refutation of the second [alternative] has already occurred.

How can there be a sublation of another based on that [substratum]? For there is no revival from anything of what has already been sublated. If such were the case, and if there were a portion of revival for that which is being sublated by this [second cognition], what kind of fulfillment of one's desires would that be? Furthermore, because of the lack of cessation in the succession of sublation and revival by the other [cognition], the substratum (dharmin), being accompanied by each [instance], would never [be established].
[453,2] The possibility of the non-perception of the pervader [is as follows].
[453,3] This is the meaning: it is said that cognition is not, first of all, a single form, because blue, yellow, and so forth appear without being intermingled;

nor is it manifold, because that would entail the consequence of their mutual non-cognition. In that regard, when the difference in appearance is cited as a refutation to negate unity, [it is as follows:]

In that case, if this [unity] is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), by what means could it be negated? If that [self-awareness] were not firm, how could there be a sublation even of unity? The same should be said regarding the claim that it is "not manifold" either. Furthermore, if the defeat of the opponent were achieved through another means of proof (*sādhana*) independent of the possibility of a counter-position (*pratiyogin*), then there would be no fault; however, [this is not the case] for that which is itself accepted as established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The term "refutation" (*prativahana*) is incoherent; furthermore, there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could overturn the [distinction between] unity and plurality. Even if one were to have the conceit of its possibility, there is not the sublation of even a single thing established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Because it is not a real entity, even a single thing does not exist—this is mutually dependent. Since two contradictory things cannot coexist in one place, there is no negation of both. Therefore, in this case, let that very thing which can be demonstrated to lack awareness be non-existent.
[453,11] "But the claim that there is no cognition of either [subject or object] would only hold if there were a total absence of cognition; however, that is unestablished.

[453,12] Now, it might be argued: "This is merely the imposition of an undesirable consequence upon the proponent of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*); therefore, this fault belongs to him alone and not to us, since we do not accept that [self-cognition].
[453,13] If this is your position?
This avoidance by the great, known as "the undesired," is a great abandonment;
for if it were so in all instances of attachment to misfortune, one's purpose would be accomplished.

[453,16] For it has been stated that for one who asserts the acceptance of a pervader, the acceptance of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) follows by necessity. Therefore, [453,17] if direct perception were established as being non-different, then even in the case of difference, the avoidance of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda) would not be possible. And if no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is accepted, then even if everything were established according to one's whim, what would be the avoidance of that [doctrine]? If this is so, then:
If both difference and non-difference were established, the doctrine of "maybe" (syādvāda) would be fully attained;
however, the Vedānta doctrine, which maintains absolute unity, is an unavoidable subversion of reality.
To this it is replied:
although this wheel of one's own mind is a single self, it is nevertheless not all-pervasive like space or wind.
If it were to manifest for the Tathāgata in that way,
then the excellence of mental concentration would not be the ultimate reality.
Indeed, such pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is not the very essence (*tattva*) of cognition, because at one time it is one thing and at another time it is absent.

However, this is a specific established quality (*siddhiviśeṣa*) of the Blessed One. Since there is contact with prior and subsequent forms through direct experience (*saṃvedana*), how can there be permanence?

By this, the objection regarding its own nature (*svatāntaparihāra*)—or rather, the objection regarding its shortness (*hrasvatāntaparihāra*)—is refuted; for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) never experiences itself as ceasing.
[454,2] However, the avoidance of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism through the gateway of continuity is indeed accepted as depending upon intermediate distinctions.

[454,3] It is a gross delusion on the part of the world that the Commentator [Vasubandhu] maintains non-difference even with respect to the past and so forth; for he merely negates the conceptualization of the past and so forth regarding that which is currently manifesting. [454,4] Therefore, mere identity does not entail the flaw of being as all-pervasive as space, nor does it imply the perception of permanence.

Thus, how can there be any doubt regarding the established doctrine of the Vedānta? Furthermore, if this [space] pervades all locations, how can there even be the cognition that "this is one way and that is another"? If it were so, then just as with time, there would be no perception of spatial extension; how much less, then, could there be eternal omnipresence? To claim the establishment of both [time and space] is the talk of nothing but a shameless person.

[454,8] But surely the Digambara also maintains that there is an external [object]; and even in that case, there is some kind of identity-in-difference (*bhedābheda*), and things are neither exclusively external nor exclusively internal. Even if such objections as these are set aside, what relevance does the Digambara doctrine have here, given that we are concerned merely with the unity and multiplicity of the cognition established by perception? Indeed, it is impossible to avoid every point of similarity; however, their mutual contradiction has been refuted.
[454,11] This is due to the appearance [of objects] by virtue of the predominance of cognition. Therefore, [454,12] in whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
[454,13] since it appears as having a dual nature, its state always remains exactly so.

By the mention of "cognition" (*jñāna*), this is what is meant: there is no manifestation anywhere of an external object as having a dual nature as a unity, because even an error is possible—just as in the case of two moons and so forth—since it is observed that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) subsequently applies to it. So how can there be unity for a variegated form (*citrākāra*)?
It is said in reply:
Because you lack a sense of shame, there is no liberation for you when the meaning of the fundamental reality is examined;
that which ought to have been practiced by us has instead been practiced by you.

If even one of the two—oneness or manyness—is established, whatever is desired is achieved; what need is there to mention when both are established? Even a single [entity] would be difficult to refute.
[454,21] Regarding the objection concerning the unity of the variegated, the reply is: [454,22] Since both unity and multiplicity are established, that unity is indeed established;
[454,23] thus, there may well be a state of oneness even in a mind possessing variegated aspects.

[454,24] This is also the meaning: regarding form (*rūpa*) which has variegated aspects, whether of a single or multiple nature—[454,25] even if there were a state of unity in the mind (*cetasi*), which is nameless and insentient (*ajaḍe*), it would not be a state of unity alone. For it is not logical to say that what is blue and square is not blue.
[454,26] Or alternatively:
A single [entity] cannot be variegated due to contradiction, nor is there contradiction because it is perceived;
thus, the mind possessing a variegated form would indeed have a unitary nature.
[455,3] In that case, there would also be multiple conventional designations. But if there is a purpose, who can prevent it?
For just as the Blessed One is called "one," so too we see such things as the "four grounds of self-confidence" and the "thirty-two marks" and so forth;
what loss is this to us? For you, however, this is like raising a weapon for your own destruction. Let it be, then, that this is a refutation of the opponent's argument.

But how can the proof of the variegated non-duality (citrādvaita) desired by you be established, given that unity is refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since there is a confusion of appearances between blue and yellow? Furthermore, as for the claim that they are "incapable of being distinguished" (*aśakyavivecanatva*), even that is a cause of difference based on non-deviation due to being produced by a common causal complex (*samānasāmagrījanyatva*); since, however, neither the whole nor its parts are objects for the opponent because they consist of the nature of cognition (*buddhirūpatva*), what is this "unity"?
Suppose it is so:
if the unity [of the self and cognition] is merely figurative due to the inability to distinguish between them,
how could it truly be that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished?
As for what is said—that the appearance is inseparable from unity—that too is incorrect: for an appearance characterized by spatial extension could not belong to a single entity;
why then do you not accept that the appearance is likewise inseparable from its diversity?
Just as the non-separability of the appearance is observed, so too is its dependence upon blue, yellow, and so forth; and that very [dependence] is what constitutes difference.
Therefore,
why does that very teaching of the identity of caustic alkali and curd— which causes such horror and shame— not also apply to you who produce molasses from milk?
To this it is replied: If difference is also stated to exist by this much, what is the harm?
By the exclusion of non-connection, identity has been stated immediately thereafter.
In the same way, it has also been shown that variegated non-duality (*citrādvaita*) is the primary [reality];
for otherwise, there would be only oneness, and variegation would not be logically possible.
For one who fears the confusion of forms due to their mutual contradiction, unity must necessarily be asserted; therefore, let the distinction be abandoned on account of the appearance.
When there is an appearance, there must be either difference or non-difference from that form.
Since there is no appearance of multiplicity, unity alone is real.
The pervasion of space is possible only for that which is manifold and insentient;
but how could it apply to that which is self-cognized when each [cognition] appears as a single unit?

Let it be that blue, yellow, and so forth possess causal dependence; yet they are not distinct from that [single entity], because that very single thing, having been accepted as such, arises in that manner from its own causes.
Just as unity is accepted, so too is difference not accepted;
because a second [entity] does not appear, it is indeed mastered as non-different.
And in the position that they are mutually contradictory, there is no support for a second [nature];
even if contradiction is not admitted, the non-duality of the variegated has been established.
Therefore, the impossibility of distinguishing between cognitions is not the proof for non-duality;
rather, once this [non-distinction] is established through a single cognition, that very state is called "oneness."
In this context, what is the meaning of the statement that "there would be a single nature"? It means that oneness is the impossibility of [the object] being analyzed apart from its cognition.
Thus: "In this way, the single nature of this [object] is indeed one thing, while the cognition is another;
where is there any use for a lack of conviction in that which is established by the power of the thing itself?"
When an external object exists, the cognition appears as if it possesses a distinct white [quality] from the whiteness itself;
therefore, one who asserts their identity while seeking the external must be refuted due to the confusion regarding the external.
By this non-difference, the rejection of direct perception is established.
Furthermore,
if perception itself were to differentiate white from cold,
would it differentiate that which is already being differentiated, or that which is undifferentiated?
