Since there is not even a trace of another in a difference, how could one differentiate? And for whom would it even be possible to say, "the mind differentiates," when the mind is itself undifferentiated?

For even externally, it is only by being differentiated that cognition differentiates objects; and in this case, regarding the nature of cognition itself, there is no room for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) except for self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And it is contradictory to say that it is one and yet differentiates. Externally, however, even if cognition is not differentiated under the view that it is formless (*nirākāra*), it is nonetheless perceived as having a differentiated nature due to the firm conviction arising from the differentiation of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) and so forth.

One might distinguish between objects; however, consciousness itself, whose very nature consists of its own attributes, does not differ between blue and yellow. To claim that it distinguishes these two is a great audacity. If it were to distinguish them by differentiating within itself, then—since there is merely an absence of any communication between one thing and another—the appearance of a variegated form would be impossible at that time; so how could there be an establishment of difference? Or rather, from what source [could such a distinction arise]?

[Objection: Does it differentiate [itself] because its limit (*avadhi*) is not perceived? [Response: And what is to be done here by the perception of a limit, since the very fact that it is not perceived is precisely what establishes its differentiation from that [limit]? Furthermore, even when another is apprehended, an entity is not differentiated by way of the other's form;
rather, it is the perception [of itself] as identical [to itself] that constitutes the perception of its difference from the other, and that occurs even when the other is unperceived.
[457,10] "If it is not incomplete, there is no damage to the cognition of difference.

[457,11] To this, the reply is: if this is stated with reference to the position that even what is not being cognized exists, then this is appropriate only within the framework of the externalist doctrine (*bāhyavāda*); it is not so in the system of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). For instance:
That existence belongs to those who have transcended the senses and that they abide in mere self-cognition—
this which is asserted by others is pleasing, and here I am truly amazed.

Therefore, because it is unmanifest and non-existent, there can be no establishment of difference based on dependence upon it. Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot even be an object of dependence; for there is no establishment of non-difference for anything in relation to a rabbit’s horn. There could only be a mere negation of unity, and that is precisely what is accepted. If one asks, "If it is not excluded from that, what then would it be—namely, a jar?"—it is simply a mere negation of unity.

We reply: Is it not the case that "being" (sat) is defined as that which is excluded from the non-existent (asat)? And that which is excluded from the non-existent is also excluded from the son of a barren woman;

yet it is not logical to say that what is excluded from a tree is not excluded from a *plakṣa* tree. Therefore, how could a jar not be excluded from a donkey’s horn? If this were so, then the distinction of even a sky-flower from jars and the like would be all the more difficult to deny. For it is not the case that something is not [excluded] from something else...

That which is excluded from that is itself characterized by exclusion. Consequently, it cannot be said that for the son of a barren woman there is neither difference nor non-difference from the Vindhya mountains;
for since the negation of both is necessarily determined by non-existence, it cannot be adduced as a proof for the non-existence of universals, persons (*pudgala*), and so forth.
Indeed, whether taken as the meaning of the nominative or the ablative in the phrase "it is excluded from that," the sense is common to both, as it is a property of real entities.

Or [it may be understood] by way of imagined nature (*kalpitadharmatā*). This is the true reality of the object here: if the speaker’s intention is merely the negation of a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāvatā*) such that "this is distinct from that," then let there be a mutual exclusion between a jar and a horse-horn; what harm is done?

Likewise, if the existence of "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*) as real entities (*vastu-rūpa*) is intended, then that would apply only to things such as jars and cloths, and not to a human being and a donkey’s horn, nor to a human being and a donkey’s horn taken together, because only one of these would possess the status of a real entity. This being the case, the intended meaning is that the person (*pudgala*) is not different from the aggregates (*skandhas*), and thus neither of these two exists in the form of a self or what belongs to a self; nor, however, are they identical.

There is no fault in saying that it experiences a state equal to the son of a barren woman. However, regarding existence and non-existence, it is said that they have characteristics established through mutual exclusion by relying on the imagined nature (*kalpita-rūpa*) of non-existence, but neither of the two possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*). For this very reason, it was stated that there is an establishment of the nature of entities such as self and what belongs to the self. Therefore, as long as something does not appear [as a conceptual construct], it does not transcend the status of being a real entity.
[458,5] Thus, it might be thought that even from non-perception, there is the apprehension of difference when there is mutual non-confusion, provided that existence (*sattā*) is being established.

[458,6] Otherwise, however, even then there would be only doubt. But for that which has the nature of light alone (*prakāśaikasvabhāva*), being cognized as existent, it is neither one nor many. As for the appearing entity (*pratibhāsī bhāvaḥ*), since it is not a non-entity (*abhāva*), the meaning of "difference" is indeed intended. And that is expressed by way of the convention of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*).

However, there is no mention of the aspect of non-existence (abhāvāṃśa), which is negation; for if it were mentioned, its identity [with existence] could not be avoided, so how could it be non-existence? For this very reason, even by way of being both existence and non-existence, duality is not established. Therefore, since there is no cognition of even a trace of what is intended as "other," it is rightly said: "How can it be distinct from non-existence itself? For this same reason, regarding the preceding and succeeding [moments]...

[458,11] Even if there is non-perception [of the object], the distinction [between them] is certainly established; thus, this is clearly nothing more than self-deception. For priority and posteriority are not manifested, and manifestation cannot be associated with priority and posteriority. Therefore, because it does not exist, there is no such thing as the cognition of the past and so forth; for manifestation alone exists. And thus:
In this delusion, the conceptualizations and imaginings—
such as pleasure, pain, white, black, and so forth, which arise from all the sense organs—
are cognitions that are non-different, because they are perceived together.
But priority and posteriority are simply not cognizable at all.
Thus is the summary.
Alternatively, the meaning is: "From what could it be divided? because the limit of division does not appear at all; what is the use here of considering existence or non-existence? For instance:
"If this [notion] 'it is different from that' refers to the intrinsic nature of the object to be apprehended..."
The appearance of this [object], which has a limit, may or may not exist; it cannot be apprehended in its own nature.
If it is argued that even when another related entity does not appear, there is still a cognition of a related entity such as a father and so forth, we reply:

even in that case, we recognize that the state of being related is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*), because if it were an actual reality (*vasturūpa*), every related entity would depend upon the cognition of [its counterpart].
For even a limit (*avadhi*) is simply a particular kind of related entity. Therefore, the cognition of one among cause and effect is devoid of the cognition of the other.

Being directed toward objects that possess a pure intrinsic nature, it merely establishes what is constructed by the artisan of conceptual thought—the delusion regarding the relationship characterized by mutual dependence.

Therefore, the notion that "the cognition of the delimited object arises when the delimiter is not cognized" is nothing but a misconception; how could perception, which grasps difference, apprehend that which does not appear? Surely, blue must necessarily be accepted as distinct from non-blue, and by that which grasps it...

[459,3] It is not apprehended by perception in that manner; thus, blue is indeed not apprehended. We too say this: if there is no apprehension of non-blue, then since it is not apprehended as distinct from that [blue], how is blue itself apprehended? If you argue, "Precisely because there is no apprehension of it, there is the apprehension of its difference from that; otherwise, both apprehension and non-apprehension would not be established," [we reply: as follows—

In that case, just as there is no perception of that [entity], how can there be a perception of the difference that has it as its limit? Consequently, what is called the "apprehension of that" contradicts its unity just as much as it contradicts the apprehension of the difference delimited by it. Or, if it is argued that the very cognition of this form is itself the cognition of difference, then this is equally true even when the cognition of difference is denied.
For how can that which is perceived as distinct without a limit of distinction be considered a distinction?
If it is argued that the word itself should not be so, let it appear in that manner.

For when both appear (*ubhayābhāsane*), it is said that its very nature, which depends upon them, does not manifest; this is not a mere rejection of conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Therefore, just as the appearance of a form unmixed with another is called the manifestation of difference (*bhedapratibhāsa*), so too, a perception independent of such [other forms] is called the loss of the manifestation of difference, because there is the manifestation of its own nature alone. If this is so, then...
An object is not known through the appearance of division because of its limit, nor through non-division because of the lack of confusion;
nor is it anything other than division and non-division. How, then, can there be a cognition of a real entity?
If this is correctly considered, it is indeed so:

for if there is no distinction in the object, how could there be a distinction even from the cognition? And if there were a distinction, then even when the object of knowledge is distinct, everything would be within the range of everyone.
[459,19] This reflection is made solely under the compulsion of attachment to external objects; and in that regard, this same refutation applies equally.

[459,20] For just as there is no apprehension of difference for one who does not admit the grasping of difference, so too there is no apprehension of difference for the second when there is an absence of the apprehension of a limit (*avadhi*), which is the basis for grasping difference.

[459,21] In that case, if the establishment of the apprehension of difference for one were to occur even without the apprehension of a limit—just like the apprehension of an external object with the eyes closed—then [the eyes would have to be...]

[459,22] Why should another not also have the established determination of grasping a real entity (*vastu*) even in the absence of the apprehension of difference (*bhedagraha*), just as in the case where there is no mental representation of the form of atoms (*paramāṇurūpa*)?

For there is no real entity other than the atoms; therefore, in that case too, for one whose eyes are closed, the established determination of grasping the real entity occurs even in the absence of its representation. Thus, there is no fault even when difference is not perceived.

How, then, is there a grasping of difference? Not in any way whatsoever. Rather, there is merely the conventional establishment of the grasping of difference with respect to a subsequent ascertainment (*niścaya*). For that [ascertainment], by distinguishing the blue and the non-blue mass—which have been made objects of appearance corresponding to itself—through their mutual opposition, casts its own activity even within perception itself, such that one thinks: "This blue has been seen, not the non-blue."
In dependence upon that [subsequent cognition], it is established that perception itself grasps the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the other, or else that [perception] is itself a memory;

just as a subsequent cognition in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) is considered to grasp what has already been grasped, even though [the object] was not previously grasped by that specific instance, in view of the determination of identity.

By this, the lack of contradiction regarding such statements as "it delimits that" is explained. Therefore, by means of this mere internal distinction, there is no connection between perception and the grasping or non-grasping of non-difference.

[460,5] In that case, should there now be identity between apprehension and non-apprehension? No, because what is intended is merely the negation of the grasping of difference. However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whether through the simultaneous or successive cognition of a counter-correlate, or through mental synthesis (*saṅkalpa*), may employ the conventions of either difference or non-difference; yet with respect to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which does not appear is neither one nor many.

If it is asked, "What is the status of that which appears?"—in that case as well, if there were a distinction between the two apprehenders (*grāhaka*), then, because no other object is delineated, it would be merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) grasping at difference, just as before. If, however, there is no distinction, then the doctrine of variegated non-duality (*citrādvaitavāda*) is established; for the very form of cognition (*buddhirūpa*) is the apprehender of non-distinction, and thus it is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is the summary (*saṃgraha*).
Whether external objects exist or do not exist, there is no perception of their difference;
rather, the perception of non-difference occurs within cognition by virtue of its own appearing nature.
Therefore, difference is solely dependent upon conventional usage.

[460,14] But surely, how can another deny that which appears as a distinct form, superimposed with contradictory properties such as blue, yellow, and so forth? This is not denied; for this very reason, it is called "variegated" (*citra*). Regarding that which is designated by the term "variegated"—namely, the blue, yellow, and so on—it cannot ultimately tolerate a distinction between each of its parts; this is what is called "self-awareness" (*svasaṃvitti*). And therein lies the superimposition of contradictory properties.

Are they two contradictory properties, or are they two things that are themselves contradictory? Regarding the first alternative, is it by way of their locus (*āśraya*) or by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*)? If it is the case of the locus, then since the status of being a substratum is established through cognition itself, the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) remains unestablished; for there is no room for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to intervene regarding that which is accepted through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). If, on the other hand, it is by way of their own nature, then mere [contradiction of nature] does not cause distress, since the two [properties] appear while their locus remains non-different.
For one who brings about loving-kindness (*maitrī*), opposition is destroyed, just like the case of the produced (*kṛtaka*) and the eternal (*nitya*).

If it is argued that the difference between those two is merely conceptual (*kalpanākṛta*), whereas here it is produced by appearance (*pratibhāsakṛta*), this is an illustration based solely on the difference in their substrata (*āśraya*). If it is then argued that in that case there is no difference in the substratum because there is no difference in appearance, then it is the same here as well.
Because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is non-dual. If it is asked, "In that case, why is there not indeed a distinction based on the difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*)," we say no.

For regarding external objects, appearance—which is synonymous with form (*ākāra*)—is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, in the absence of that [external object], the object is merely the manifestation itself. Since the means of valid cognition is self-awareness, how could that which is unified by it be divided? As for the claim that these are two contradictory properties (*dharma*), that has been cast far aside.

Since difference itself does not exist, where is there contradiction? Therefore, there is no means whatsoever for establishing difference. On the contrary, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the means for establishing non-difference and the subverter of difference; as for external conventional practice, it merely presents [the appearance of difference]. This has been established.
He also says this:
"In a variegated cognition, blue and so forth are attributes of the cognition that do not share in anything else.
For it is impossible to perceive them while distinguishing them from the object; they fall [into the category of the object]. (PV III 220).

"Not sharing in anything else" means not sharing in another nature. Blue and so forth, not partaking in the nature of yellow and so forth, cannot appear as distinct when situated within a variegated cognition.
[461,7] It may be possible to perceive [the object] as solitary, because the appearance—which has acquired that property—is restricted to each [quality] individually, such as yellow and so forth.

[461,8] The meaning is that only by relinquishing its mutual nature can it be capable of appearing. For, by discerning and separating that [nature], one would necessarily accept that the appearance has not acquired that property; thus, one would fall into the very position of the proponents of external objects (*bahirarthavāda*). And this is a qualification of cognition (*jñānopādhi*).
Blue and so forth; therefore,
"in whatever way a cognition appears" (PV III 121)—

that is, by appearing as blue, yellow, and so on— it is experienced in that very [form], because it is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*) as having the nature of yellow and so forth, and thus as being mutually identical.
This is the meaning. The remainder is easy to understand. Therefore, the author of the Commentary rightly said:
"Or rather, that is not surprising, because it is impossible to establish [it] as distinct from what is non-variegated" (PVA 290).

For here, there is no establishment of [the variegated] as distinct from what is non-variegated—that is, from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) which is not of manifold form—due to its non-difference [from it].

The intended establishment [of the distinction] culminates in a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), and that has already been proven by [the author] himself. Previously, "oneness" was described as the characteristic of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) consisting in the impossibility of differentiation; however, now it is said to be simply the state of being contained within a single cognition (*ekasaṃvidantargatatva*). This is the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*). By this, even the possession of variegated forms is said to exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*); but in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the sense is that there is only non-duality (*advaita*). Having thus postulated the meaning:

That was stated with the intention of merely negating the cognition of difference. [But it is argued: "If that is so, then it is not non-dual (*advaita*), because it does not appear as distinct from duality; likewise, it is neither knowledge nor self-cognition. This is refuted. For duality is indeed difference; and where could there be an appearance of that [duality]? Therefore, even if there is no appearance of difference from that [non-duality], how can there be unity? [For unity] consists in the inclusion of the one within a single cognition.

Because it has already been established? Likewise for the rest: for if there were an appearance of everything, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva-bhaṅga) of all error.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that even the distinction [between appearances] is worthy of being established here as variegated (citra), by way of the conventional reality of manifestation (udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti), because of the [monolithic] nature of experience.

Because it establishes the arising [of the manifold] through the contradiction of difference, the statement that the variegated (*citra*) is non-dual (*advaita*) by means of mere blue, yellow, and so forth, is merely a conventional designation for the purpose of manifestation;

it is not a statement of actual difference. However, for one who has not yet realized the reality, the statement of difference—which is cultivated through repeated practice—does not obstruct the truth.
In reality, however, these expressive syllables are purely a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*); the notion that they serve to establish oneness is an error.

[Regarding] the world: this is the meaning. Alternatively, that which is intended as the apprehended and the apprehender—such as blue, yellow, and so forth, or what is denoted by the word "variegated"—is not variegated, nor is it manifold. Because it cannot be established as distinct from the non-variegated self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the mere negation of manifoldness is intended; and since the opponent’s negation of unity is also based on perception itself, manifestation is indeed free from both [manifoldness and unity].
It is stated that momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is as if existent; this is what has been expressed, just as was first proclaimed by us.

Precisely for this reason, because there is no other insentient entity—neither a grasped object nor a grasping subject—this term "non-duality" (*advaita*) signifies a positive state (*kevalārtha*), and not a mere negation of duality (*dvaitaparyudāsa*) nor a simple synonym for "one" (*naikārtha*). Demonstrating this, he says:
Therefore, self-awareness alone is non-dual because of the absence of anything else.

Thus, that which was previously stated by way of an objection—"Now, how is it that what appears does not exist simply because of the conceptualization of it as one or many?"—is addressed: even while being conceptualized, it indeed appears. If it were non-existent, how could there be an appearance? If there is an appearance, how can it be non-existent?

Thus? And here, the *Ṭīkā* states that because there is perception by way of the nature of perception even for that which is devoid of the forms of unity and plurality, according to the principle that "existence is perception," it is indeed existent (*sad eva*). That very point has been clarified as another established tenet (*siddhāntāntara*). Thus, the doctrine of the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaitavāda*) characterized by the attribute of unity is seen to be the primary view of the author of the *Vārttika*; however, for the author of the *Bhāṣya*, it is characterized by the exclusion of both. But in reality, for both of them, it is one.
This is the intended meaning: however, the distinction between the primary and the secondary is established based on the difference in the manner of manifestation.
Therefore, without having reflected upon the diverse establishment of the non-duality of the manifold,
for whom would the refutation of the Teacher on the pretext of his commentary be an ornament?

If the Teacher’s intention is one thing, while the Commentator’s intended meaning of the words is another, then it is not impossible; alas, this is a plain contradiction! Thus, since the unity of the mind is established even in the case of a variegated form (*citra*), the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished. Furthermore, the claim that "there is no utility for the non-duality of the variegated for those engaged in worldly discourse" does not constitute a refutation.
Because it is the domain of the Buddhas, like emptiness.
If you argue that there is indeed a fault because there is no distinction between the realization of reality and its opposite,
then the owl lives happily without even looking at its own face.
For indeed,
there is no contradiction regarding a mind that possesses form,
because the mind itself is not established as something manifest.
But it is non-existent by its very conceptualized nature;
this is the distinction, even though it is manifesting.
And by what nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is this wheel of cognitions ever liberated?
Nor is there an experience of its own nature,
because that would entail the over-extension of the consequence that it is of the same nature as the mind.
Consequently, there was no certainty regarding that [object] at all; and even that [certainty] was not distinguished by a difference in its mental aspect (*ākāra*).
Furthermore, this [cognition] does not follow either ultimate reality (*tattva*) or conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
There is a distinction in the absence of dependence on another.
And indeed, there is no cognition of another anywhere;
moreover, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is equal for both.
Therefore, it is conventional at one time and not so at another.
By what means is this distinction established even for you?
Alternatively,
there is never an absence of emptiness,
nor is there any other supreme realization whatsoever.
When conventional reality is investigated through the lens of causal efficacy, there is neither the destruction of faults nor the arising of virtues.
Therefore, in this regard, as long as the possibility of analytical investigation has not arisen, this principle holds:
"This existence is one thing, and peace is another. But when the mind is stirred by the play of analysis, [this distinction no longer applies].
Tell me, what is existence or peace here? What is it that is called "here"?
And likewise, in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
"In this world, there is no difference whatsoever between these two—
the state of peace and birth— when considered in terms of their functioning as ultimate reality."
Nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds, the attainment of peace is ordained through the exhaustion of birth.
By way of the existence of the true object—that is, by way of the ultimate mode of being—the remainder is by way of the conventional. In the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* as well, it says:
"Because all phenomena are like a dream, there is no conceptualization of existence or peace" (AAĀ 440), and so forth. Consequently, this is established by its very nature.
"Nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist. The thorough understanding of existence itself is called 'nirvāṇa'. (Nāgārjuna).
This refutation is like the murder of one's own innocent mother; such is the meaning of this treatise.

Whether distinction or non-distinction, whether in two ways or not in two ways—let it be as it may regarding the nature of cognition; there can be no falsity in manifestation, for that which is opposed to it is contradicted by even a scent of sublation.

“Consciousness is that which cognizes”—thus, emptiness of all such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) exists everywhere. And so it is said: “Indeed, those phenomena do not exist in their own-being (*svabhāva*) in the way that unlearned, ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) are attached to them,” and so forth in detail.
For even mental factors (*buddhidharma*) exist only by way of forms imagined by another consciousness, and not because they possess existence through being self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*).

By this, the Blessed One’s being like a dream or an illusion has been explained. For even in the case of examples, it is only that which is conceptually determined (*adhyavasita*) that is negated, not that which is appearing (*pratibhāsamāna*). Therefore, it is established that the proof of the Blessed One as possessing an aspect (*sākāra*) is inseparable from its non-sublation. And thus, the meaning of the verse of salutation is established.
That which has attained magnificence through its own nature, characterized by both food and condiments;
which is profound because it is not the domain of others, being empty of the waves of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
and from which the rays of gnosis radiate throughout the world in the form of emanations—that is not unreal.
Therefore, O Blessed One, the body of the Sage is stained on all sides.
Furthermore:
Just as gold, endowed with a perfection of qualities and form, reaches the ultimate limit of excellence and is inexhaustible;
Just as the body of embodied beings is liberated from the suspicion of the stain of falsehood, so too is the Buddha-body.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the Non-duality of the Variegated, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great paṇḍita Jñānaśrīmitra.
(Fifth Chapter) [466,2] But surely this entire preceding elaboration is but the play of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), and as for this so-called self-cognition, it simply does not exist,
because it is refuted by both reasoning and scripture. [466,3]
In the absence of that, from where could the manifold establishment of non-duality arise?
Nor would there be the state of Samantabhadra, because of the failure to abandon the unreal.
Here is the question:
Is it that cognition itself does not exist? Or, even if it exists, how can there be a means of knowing if it does not itself destroy the object of knowledge?
The heart exists in its own cognition or even in the cognition of another;
all this is not established in the final determination.
For instance:
"It is not possible for me to manifest that 'this is not my consciousness' by means of distinct earthen objects;
nor does this [consciousness] arise from another anywhere, and even when it is manifest, it is not non-existent."
If it is argued that manifestation is itself real, then how could it be real if known by another? Since it is not real in either case, it is improper to say that it exists by itself.
This is the meaning:
even one who is insentient would say, "There is no consciousness at all.
If there were neither speaker nor listener, this [consciousness] would still appear as its own manifestation.

As for the claim that "there is cognition of another," it has been refuted elsewhere; let that matter rest for now. Now, if it is argued that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is not denied in every respect, but rather it is said to be merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtī*), then, since there is no total rejection of it, its status as conventional must depend upon a sublation (*bādhaka*).

And this sublation occurs either through a difference from the object of cognition (*prameya*) or through the experience itself. By the very sublation of the object of cognition, the existence of that [self-cognition] is not established.
In that regard:
If there is experience through differentiation, how could there be self-experience because of that differentiation?
Furthermore, the sublation of the object of cognition cannot be accomplished even by Śakra himself.

For it is not possible to determine that what possesses a manifest form simply does not exist. Now, if there is no negation of the manifest in every respect, let it be that which is cognized by another; but let it not be that which is self-cognized. This is not so;
for if there is no confidence even in self-cognition, what can be said of cognition by another?
For if self-awareness is absent, awareness of another is also non-existent.

If that which is perceived by another were to exist as something other, how could that "other" itself be real? Furthermore, that which is non-existent cannot be the cause for the conventional usage of the existence of another.

If it were perceived by another while existing, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If you argue that the existence of the other is likewise established in this very way, then let it be the same for the object of cognition (*prameya*) as well.
And if existence were self-evident, then even the insentient would be luminous by itself;
for the contradiction of acting upon oneself is equal for both of these.

[467,11] Now, if it is argued that even the cognition of another is accepted by someone, let that person alone bear the fault; as for me, there is nothing that is self-cognized or cognized by another. [467,12] If this is said, one who possesses intelligence ought not to speak thus. For it is not possible to negate an object—whether it manifests from itself or from another—merely by means of an undesirable position or by words alone. If one were to follow valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then:

[467,14] Having first taken perception as the basis, there is an enumeration of the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is in inference and the like that one observes the acceptance or rejection [of objects], but not in perception. [467,15] And regarding the domain of the imperceptible, the remainder—whether it be total or partial—is not capable of either establishing or subverting [an object] within its own domain. [467,16] That alone is said to be established by perception, namely, the direct manifestation of the thing's own nature. Whether that [manifestation] occurs through itself or through another—what does this matter?
If its own nature is not known even in the absence of any activity by another, then that very loss of its own nature occurs; what then is the use of other subverting factors?
Precisely because it has the appearance of a self, it is not sublated;
precisely because it manifests its own object, even that which would sublate it is itself sublated.
Let it be understood that he too is a merchant with that very same merchandise;
therefore, for that which is manifest, there is no such thing as sublation.

[467,23] Would it not be the case that protection would come from that very external illumination? Self-manifestation, being without a protector, would be sublated by another possessing power. To this it has been said: even the other is useful only through the manifestation of its own nature, not by its mere existence, nor by warding off a blow by stretching out an arm; if that manifestation of its own nature were possible for the [object's] own nature as well, nothing else would be required.
On the contrary,
he who is strong by his own power alone is weak in the presence of another; just as one who is intent on guarding himself is, for that other person, merely an "other."

Likewise, [theories such as] the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), the manifestation of the contrary (*viparītakhyāti*), the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*), and the deception of vision (*dṛṣṭimoṣa*)—
these various conceptualizations of error observed by others do not prevail in the production of the manifestation of its own cause.
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is established exactly as such;
a cognition does not appear otherwise by superimposing another form upon it.
Whenever whatever form manifests, it is indeed that very [form] which,
through its unification with its own internal aspect, is called an "error" even though it appears externally.

But when, through repeated practice, a cognition that manifests its own nature arises even regarding external objects—free from any suspicion of error—then where is there room for the suspicion of sublation? How much less so in the case of one's own self-experience? It remains only to ask: how could such a cognition arise, or how could it be ascertained?

Just as birth occurs by way of its own nature as blue through the essence of cognition, so too does it occur for the intellect from its own cause, just as a lamp occurs by way of its own nature as yellow light.

But how is it that this is only self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) and not cognition by another? It has been stated elsewhere: "The point at issue is simply that a form appearing as either self-known or known by another is indeed non-sublated (*abādhya*). And that is established, for there is no sublation of one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by another means of valid cognition."
How much more so, then, for self-awareness, which is of the nature of direct perception?

Even for inference, which arises from the awakening to the purity of the three marks (*trairūpya*), no sublation by another means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*) is possible, nor by verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth, as the case may be. For it is virtually self-evident that it is impossible for two properties that are mutually contradictory to be established with respect to the same subject (*dharmin*) at one and the same time. However, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) would occur only if one of them lacks firmness regarding its own object.

Regarding one's own object, whether there is firmness or lack of firmness in the two extremes belongs to perception alone, through its failure or otherwise. And the failure of perception with respect to its object is nothing but an error (*bhrama*). Since error is necessarily restricted to the cognition of another, what rival can there be for self-awareness (*saṃvedana*)?
If there is no sublation even externally for that which has cast out the suspicion of error, how could it be sublated by an inference of non-duality arising from itself?

[Objection: Is there not a contradiction here? [Response: It has been stated in this regard that this is a distortion (*viplava*) of the cognition of another; it cannot be so, because even when there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*), it is possible to assert that this is a distortion of one's own cognition (*svavitti*), since the operation [of the former] does not conform to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognition of another.

Even then, to claim that existence exists merely by way of its being (*sattāmātreṇa*) is a power of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), like the washing away of impressions (*saṃskāra*) by what has been heard.

If it is argued that there can be a lapse even in the absence of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), then, since there is no lapse in the absence of life, death itself would be the remedy for the lapse; such is the excellent Buddhist position! Furthermore, since self-awareness (*svavedana*) is all-pervasive, its absence is impossible to perceive; thus, for one who asserts that even this distortion arises from beginningless ignorance, the proof by the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*)— [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

Even with respect to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), [errors such as] the superimposition of intrinsic nature or passion are distortions; thus, they are not far removed [from the object]. However, the aspect of being an adversary (*pratyanīkākāratā*) is common to both. Therefore, utility is not established by mere existence; nor does the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*)—if it is not produced by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that conforms to the operation of that [utility]—have power over it. For one who does not have power over it fails to invalidate even the cognition that grasps the relationship and so forth.

Therefore, by virtue of having the same object, it would be only the cognition of another that would be touched by the fault, not self-cognition, because their objects are absolutely distinct. Consequently, just as in that proof, if one were to accept the validity of the cognition of another, one would have to accept even inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) since it would invalidate itself; yet if one does not, then the goal to be established by inference is nonetheless accomplished—thus it is for that very reason...

The error becomes manifest through the arising of an inference; it does not do so through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) regarding self-awareness (*svavitteḥ*), because it is impossible to state the aforementioned capacity [of such a reason].

However, by one's own whim, a cognizer might even take self-awareness as the subject (*pakṣa*); yet, because it is sublated by a specific perception (*pratyakṣaviśeṣabādhitatvāt*), the rule is that no effort should be made toward a proof [for such a case].

[469,18] In that case, this logical principle applies only to the proof of *vijñaptimātra* (representation-only); however, it is even more impossible to establish it when the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) has already arisen.

[469,19] It is not so; for at the very moment one asserts that blue lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is simultaneously rejected by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svavedana-adhyakṣa*), according to the sequence already stated. [469,20] If this were the case, it would follow as an absurd consequence that [the blue] is devoid of the means of proof such as its being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*). This too is not so.

Because it serves merely for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of cognition. Now, even so, if self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) is being established by negating the state of being illuminated by another (*paraprakāśyatā*), would that not establish the conventional usage of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)? Furthermore, if there were an absolute absence of being cognizable by another, or if there were a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there could be no such thing as a proof or a probandum;
how then could even the establishment of conventional usage occur?

That is incorrect, for the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) exists only at the level of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*). At that time, neither of the two realities is established.

In that context, for one who—despite blue appearing with other adventitious attributes—still harbors doubt regarding its being revealed by another due to the force of innate formative ignorance (*avidyā*), the presentation of a proof capable of withstanding logical reasoning (*nyāyasaha*) is offered to awaken him. And at that time, it is precisely that [proof] which [is subject to] sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) and so forth.
He will investigate this. And once that has been established, there is the conventional usage of "representation" (*vijñapti*).

By this much alone is the task of the Proponent of Cognition (*Vijñānavādin*) completed. As for the opponent, however, the very fact of perceptual sublation (*pratyakṣabādha*) precludes their application of the means of proof.
Furthermore, the operation of perception never depends upon the non-arising of inference; rather, inference always functions precisely where perception does not reach its object.

Therefore, it is established that even if [the object] were sublated, just as if it were proven, no room for objection is found. Consequently, the self-cognition [of consciousness] does not become merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) by virtue of the sublation of its object. Likewise, this too should not be suspected: that if blue is established through self-cognition, then that self-cognition must also be established through another self-cognition, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding that...

If [cognition] is established by itself, then what need is there for blue to be self-cognized? For indeed, if one says that even blue must have cognition, then it follows that cognition itself must be self-cognized; this is precisely the doctrine of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and thus it is like the maxim of "the rider on the horse.
However, if that [cognition] were distinct [from the object], then one would not transcend an infinite regress, nor...

Regarding the statement "the touch of the doctrine of self-cognition": if, then, it is not a separate entity but exists merely as a designation (*prajñapti-sat*), and if this is nothing other than that very phenomenon (*dharma-mātra*), then when that [designation] is sublated, it is not capable of remaining neutral by itself; how, then, could it be capable of protecting another?
That too is something of no consequence.
The blue possesses luminosity, and luminosity also possesses blueness;
the establishment of the distinction between property and property-bearer is not considered to be restricted to a single essence.
In this case, protection is indeed non-differentiation; differentiation here is purposeless.
For the protection of others is either necessarily concomitant with the protection of oneself, or it is not.
Precisely because it shines by itself, it is not sublated;
thus the reality of things is communicated by whatever verbal expression may be used.
Furthermore, as for what is said out of pride in one’s own logical reasoning— that there is no self-cognition because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself,
just as the tip of a finger cannot touch that very same fingertip— even in that case: if the fingertip were not to be touched by its own tip, how could it be smooth?
If this [body] is itself smooth, why is there no contradiction now?
Why does the intellect not itself shine forth? Or rather, why is it that one perceives, "this has arisen as something smooth by itself"?

Since the meaning of the sentence culminates in such a cognition, there arises a contradiction regarding its causal function (*kāritra*). Consequently, statements such as "it goes by itself" or "it is white by itself" must not be asserted at all by proponents of such views, either in principle or in the presence of those who hold them, because they involve the rejection of factors such as instigation (*preraṇā*) or coloring (*aṅgarāga*).
"To be [known] by another" is a great calamity. Furthermore, in an action that possesses an object, it is not appropriate for there to be both a single object and a subject;
yet the action of cognition has an object, as in "Caitra cognizes blue. If that is so, then let us remain silent regarding such statements as "consciousness illuminates itself."

Furthermore, regarding the expression "it is perceived" (*vedyate*) and so forth, which others employ with the intention of expressing [the relationship between] object and agent (*karmakartṛ*), we have merely assigned this to the very same meaning as "it appears" (*bhāsate*); thus, there is no difference whatsoever. Now, by the passage beginning "the Blessed One is self-existent" (*svayambhūr bhagavān*), there is simply a demonstration that such a nature arises from its own causes alone, through the exclusion of the operations of Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), and so on; it is not, however, seen as a distinction [between subject and object].

It is said that here the conventional usage of action and agent is intended; however, since cognition also arises from its own cause in the form of luminosity and is not illuminated by another, what is the cause of this aversion to such a consensus?
This very nature of being non-inert is its self-awareness.
However, its self-cognition does not occur by way of the relationship between action and agent.
This is an intermediate verse.

Furthermore, as for what was said here—that the world itself will be the subverter of one who speaks thus—that is refuted by this very point, because such an intention is observed in the world. Even if it is not observed in the domain of the intellect, it is nonetheless present in the conventional usage of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*).

[471,12] This is because it is observed that there is a desire to express both self-illumination and other-illumination, as in the case of a lamp and a jar. [471,13] Although both are seen in external objects, with respect to the nature of cognition (*buddhi*), since being illuminated by another is sublated, self-illumination alone is established; however, it is not the case that such a distinction does not exist at all in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). [471,14] Thus, it is only in the context of the nature of cognition that other-illumination is refuted, while self-illumination is established. It is not that such a distinction is non-existent in all respects.
Indeed, it is known that "the lamp shines," and this is expressed by means of cognition;
but who, as a friend, could say that "cognition itself shines"?
Whether manifest or unmanifest, when it is not perceived by anyone,
it is as futile as describing the playful dance of a barren woman’s daughter.
If this is so, is this not without foundation? For it has been established that this very blue and so forth is cognition whose nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśasvabhāva*);
how then can this be stated by a well-wisher? Regarding an object that is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*), instruction from another is not authoritative;

otherwise, who could be a subject (*dharmin*) for [arguments such as] the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) and so forth? If that is the case, then how is it that even in the instance of a lamp, there is only cognition?
[471,23] Is this an example? True; it is intended to dismiss the objection that, from the perspective of the world, the world itself would be the subverter.
This, however, is merely a resting place for one whose reasoning has failed, and offers no protection; otherwise, if everything were empty, what could the world possibly subvert?

[471,24–25] If you argue that it is because everything is accepted conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), then the very claim that "nothing exists in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is precisely what the world cannot tolerate.

If it is argued: "Let it be that [the object] does not exist conventionally; however, even if it does not exist ultimately, what is it that we are proving? For we intend to transcend both existence and non-existence. [We reply: No, for there is merely the negation of existence, and this is not the meaning of "non-existent. If there is no being of blue and so forth, by whom is its non-being prevented?
And in the doctrine that "it is non-existence," existence itself remains established.
Since those things established through mutual exclusion possess such a nature, the negation of one entails the affirmation of the other; it is not otherwise merely by virtue of one's lack of desire.
Or else, a third alternative must be stated here regarding these two:
that for the wise, they are established in one and the same place; there is no other possibility.

It might be argued as follows: "We do not establish the affirmation or negation of anything; rather, it is demonstrated that for those who maintain the positions of existence, non-existence, both, or neither, the respective definitions of their own tenets are untenable. In that case, if the prior absence of existence [of an entity] follows simply from the untenability of the definition of existence, then what have we removed that was not already there?"

And when, due to the impossibility of a characteristic of non-existence, there is an absence of non-existence even prior [to an entity], then how could there be what is called "existence" for anyone through the absence of non-existence,
and from what source? For just as a maiden experiences joy or dejection through the birth or loss of a son.
Due to the conceptualization of a son in a dream, it does not exist for one who is awake.

If that [statement] does not achieve the falsity of its own continuity in order to dispel her remaining sorrow, then what has been done by it—either an affirmation of the non-existence of a son or the like, or a negation of the existence of a son or the like?

Is there a negation of the existence of someone through the negation of the birth of a son, or an affirmation of existence through the negation of death? For from the very beginning, the son himself was non-existent.

[472,19] For one who is awake, however, there is merely a restatement of that [which was previously perceived]. In this same way, it should be inferred for both the noble and the non-noble. And this very state of being primordially peaceful (*ādiśāntatva*) and natural purity (*prakṛtipariśuddhi*) is proclaimed in the scriptures.
[472,20–21] To this, it is said: What kind of injunctions and prohibitions are you avoiding—those characterized by production and destruction?

Is it by grasping with the hand [the objects] whose natures are bringing near or removing away? Or is it an affirmation characterized by proof, or a negation characterized by sublation, regarding some dharma that has become the subject of dispute?
In that regard, first of all, even for another [opponent], the first two positions do not exist.
Even by you, the third [objection] cannot be refuted.

For others also maintain that it is not the case that the validity of the Blessed One, which was already established, is later removed, nor that something non-existent, such as a creator god (*īśvara*), is subsequently attributed to him. Likewise, it is not that duality, which was already established, is removed, nor that non-duality is now newly attributed;
rather, an already established intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is merely restated by another, and demonstrated through some form of reasoning.
Thus there is universal consensus. And since that [consensus] exists for you as well, what kind of distinction is being asserted here?

This very process of affirmation and negation—namely, the demonstration that "this exists" and "this does not exist"—has necessarily come to the one engaged in speech, especially to one who has entered into debate out of a desire for victory or a disposition toward the welfare of others. However, this inquiry would not apply to one who remains silent. Furthermore, the example of the dream is common to all; for whatever property of an object is acknowledged by anyone...

Someone might be refuted; through the establishment of that [refutation], there is joy due to the attribution of its merits, or despondency when another demonstrates its non-existence. However, for one intent on dispelling that [despondency], it is equal [to the former case] because, from the very beginning, he has merely repeated that "it does not exist" in that manner.

In this regard, the example of a dream is under one's own control only for that person who is capable of providing the proof. Likewise, even in the doctrine of non-duality (*advayavāda*), just as at the time of waking one experiences joy and so forth by superimposing a realized son upon what is merely one's own mental form, so too in the waking state there is no harm [to the argument], as it is merely the form of cognition that is superimposed as being external. This applies to both states as well.
It has been stated that although the non-conceptual appearance terminates in its own nature alone, it is obscured by conceptualization through the superimposition of the unreal.

And that [conceptualization], having concealed its own nature, joins the perception with a form other than that [nature]; for it is precisely because of this that one says, "I saw my son today in a dream.
For upon some reflection, there is no such thing as "seeing a son," but rather: "a mere cognition arose in me in that manner."

[473,17] Therefore, with regard to that determination (*vyavasāya*), it is said that she sees her son as both born and dead; however, in reality, where else could there be the perception of a son except for the arising of a mere cognition possessing a specific form capable of producing an adherence (*abhiniveśa*) due to the power of beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*)?
What, then, is the actual reality here? [473,19] It is simply this.
What is the use of the habit of scrutiny for one who can grasp [the truth] with his own hand?
Let the application of effort be directed toward the *Kīrti-vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya* with joy.
Even if one is under the sway of faith, it is better to rely on the way of the crown prince,
wherein even the noble Nāgārjuna and others are established.

This will be demonstrated [below]. Furthermore, scriptural passages are causes for the production of mere merit only for one who is not skilled in investigation. In the course of investigation, however, the affirmation of the second follows by implication when there is a statement negating one of the two—existence or non-existence; thus, it cannot be avoided merely by a lack of desire. For instance, the non-existence of a son in a dream is expressed as "there was no such thing as a son."

Since existence has indeed been established and negation refuted, how is it that for one who is awake neither affirmation nor negation is performed? However, the fact that the Noble One does not perceive things in that way is simply the arising of a cognition of a form contrary to the perception of those specific forms; it is by no means a total loss of consciousness.
Let this matter rest for now.

Now, if the intended meaning is the negation of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of existence and non-existence, there is by no means an abolition of mere appearance; this is precisely what we accept, because conceptual construction is inherently erroneous by nature. If, on the other hand, the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is simply the inability to withstand analysis, then analysis itself relies upon the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and in that case, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) necessarily enters into it, there is nothing apart from self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).

It is neither another perception nor inference, because that would entail the consequence of its being devoid of its own essential existence (*svarūpasattā*). Nor is there the apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*), a property (*dharma*), and so forth;

for, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) possesses a determined form within the conventional (*saṃvṛtti*), and since—just as in the case of other objects of cognition and means of cognition—no sublation is possible, it remains established. Thus, there is no occasion for the qualification "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*).
In whatever way objects are reflected upon and analyzed, in that very same way,
self-cognition— like the shadow of one who runs— is difficult to escape.

And therefore, what kind of incapacity for analysis could there be in that which has the nature of self-cognition? For how many analyses can possibly be applied? Indeed, the luminosity of the manifestation of blue, or its blueness, is not a mere passing away; nor is it another non-luminous property that becomes an object of familiarization. And that very [nature], which—
The experience of the mere intrinsic nature is the defeat of imagined things;
that itself is it.
And therefore, equality should be understood between non-perception and perception. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.8)
Such is the principle.
This very state of being primordially peaceful and naturally pure,
however, is the purity of stainlessness, which is the exhaustion of all unreal conceptual constructions.

This has already been stated. As for the claim that, by accepting that very [definition], the definition itself is untenable—even by that much, there is no disparagement of the nature of experience. For: "Even if definitions imagined by the ignorant are refuted, there is no harm to the true nature of reality, which is free from all limiting conditions. (The same verse is also quoted in ATV p. 530)
Having observed an elephant at the king’s gate,
he spoke to the cloud-dragon from his urine-stream, which was a darkness reaching to the very foundations with its tusks:
Someone [might see] a door with four pillars and a polished architrave, made from excrement that resembles a mass of food offerings.
"He who stands at the king's gate or in the cremation ground is a kinsman"— thinking thus,
the fool, whose mindfulness is firm, regards even such a person as a true relative.

Therefore, let even those intrinsic natures (svarūpa) imagined by others—like those of the materialists (bhauta)—melt away; for one who is illuminated by another, what harm has come to him? Consequently:
"If this very position is established, then there is no difference between us two."
But if there were sublation in every respect, how could there be no sublation by the world?
If it is said that even out of regard for the world, the wise do not speak of its non-existence,
then why is the distress caused by the thought that it does not exist at all in reality not taken into account?
Therefore, whether the world is terrified or not, how can the exposition of reality—which is useful for human goals—be avoided?

If this is your own intention, why do you needlessly confound others with falsehood? For who would believe that there is an obstruction to your power even when a valid response exists? Moreover, since the conventional usage of "self-luminous" (svaprakāśa) exists in the world as well, where is the contradiction with worldly experience?

If it is argued that [the object] is not directly perceived while cognition alone holds sway, what is the point of this? Even if an entity is self-luminous, there is no contradiction with its causal efficiency;
for the example has already been established on the basis of a commonality. Furthermore, why is it that such thoughts as "this cognition is manifesting to me" do not occur?
And here, in this resolve that touches upon your virtues, there is my own direct experience.
Therefore, enough of this deception of foolish people.

Furthermore, as for the objection that memory establishes the existence of experience—on the grounds that memory and experience both refer to the object itself, and that the object is what is called "knowledge"—even in that case, it is simply the cognition bearing the form of the object that is remembered, and since that [cognition] is remembered as having manifested of its own accord, there is no harm. Moreover, regarding the claim that memory is directed toward the object, it cannot occur with respect to something not previously experienced, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And if the object has been experienced, yet that experience itself is not experienced...
Thus, how is this understood here by the heart?
For if there is no awareness of cognition, there can certainly be no linguistic usage based on its limiting conditions; yet if it is known by another, an unavoidable infinite regress ensues.
By this very [reasoning], even when [the object] is set aside, there is an absence of a logical mark (liṅga) for one who infers;
nor is an unperceived mark [sufficient], and there is doubt regarding the establishment of its comprehension.
Thus is the intermediate verse.
How, then, is this cognition being experienced not designated by way of its limits? Is it not already designated thus:
"Internal is the object such as pleasure and so forth; external is the sphere such as cold and so forth;
sensation has those respective forms; there is nothing else beyond that"?
This phenomenon called "vibrancy" (sphurattā) is personally experienced and cannot be denied.
Thus, that very capacity is the means of knowledge, the self is the object of knowledge, and self-awareness is the result.

Therefore, while a fault would certainly arise in the case of the position that [cognition] is formless (*nirākāra*), there is not even a suspicion of one in the case of the position that it possesses form (*sākāra*). Indeed, the position that it possesses form is the one favored by the venerable Śāntideva. As he said:
"That which is seen, heard, and known is not at all negated here."

"Therefore, it is conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) regarding this that is prevented as the cause of suffering" (BA 9.26). For here, what is seen and so forth is not denied in terms of reality (*satyataḥ*) or in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*). Thus, by the mention of "what is seen" and so forth, it is stated that the blue, soft, and other qualities appearing [to consciousness] cannot be denied.

To the question, "To what, then, does selflessness belong? he replies: it belongs to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) itself—namely, to the unreal [entities] such as the grasped, the grasper, cause, effect, and so forth; this is the meaning. Conceptual construction arises from words alone. For conceptual construction occurs with respect to that which is not perceived. And because it is not perceived, it cannot exist in reality (*tattvataḥ*); this [phrase] is also to be connected here. Therefore, even in statements such as "all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*), there is a negation of a conceptually constructed form in terms of reality.
Such is the meaning. For what purpose, then, is there the warding off of unreal conceptualization? Because it is the cause of suffering.
For that alone projects *saṃsāra*, which is characterized by engagement, withdrawal, and so forth; for without it, the mere arising of its form would be ineffective therein.
As for those who connect "as real" (*satyataḥ*) with "the conceptualization as reality" (*satyatvena yā kalpanā*), if in that case too—

Even if [the object] were real, the purpose would be to prevent the conceptual construction that "this is real"; what fault would there be in its being perfectly established (*pariniṣpatti*)? Alternatively, if the meaning is that even now one prevents the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in its reality because of its non-existence, then it is contradictory to say that "perception and so forth are not negated. For while it is being reduced to unreality, perception and so forth are not being negated; thus, it is precisely the reduction to unreality [that is occurring].

Because it has the sense of negation. Now, if it is not negated conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), then there is a prohibition from the perspective of reality (*tattvatas*). But even that is not established by the literal meaning of the words.

The word "in reality" (*satyataḥ*) is employed otherwise as a qualifier for "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*); yet at that time, the word "conceptual construction" is not appropriate, because it is intended that only a single thing—such as what is perceived—is the object of affirmation and negation in relation to both the conventional and the ultimate.
For it is thus:
that which is seen, heard, and known is not at all negated here;
rather, from the perspective of conventional reality, this cause of suffering is prevented from the standpoint of ultimate truth.

Thus it is appropriate to say. Therefore, in this context, why do the great ones obscure the literal meaning by repeating the word *śabda*, supplying the word *saṃvṛti*, and assigning a different meaning to the word *kalpanā*? It is clear that the forms (*ākāra*) intended as the objects of the six sensory consciousnesses are not being negated, because they are self-cognized; rather, it is only the imagined (*kalpita*) [form] that is negated.
[477,10] Regarding the term "negation": how then is there a negation of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) for these [cognitions]? It is as it is for the Blessed One. How is it for the Blessed One?

[477,11] Because of the negation of distinct objects; even in a single variegated form, the state of grasped and grasper exists directly, even in the subtle, with the intention of the relation between action and agent. And this is not an object of doubt, nor is it a matter for any effort at refutation.
It should be understood as follows: for just as the conceptualization of cause and effect occurs even with respect to a single entity,
so too would the cognition of the grasped and the grasper occur within a single consciousness.
Just as it was for the Blessed One:
"And this sprout is not made by itself," so too for the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna.
There is an effort at negation through such statements as, "Not from itself, nor from another" (MK I.1), and likewise:
"The mind does not perceive the all-pervading. (**) (* ***)
And so forth. This is logical. Furthermore, the superimposition (samāropa) regarding cyclic existence—such as the notion that "the aggregates themselves are the self" and so on—is limitless;

for a compassionate one, even such a view must not be neglected, since the superimposition of subject and object is the primary fault. Therefore, its negation by way of the relationship between action and agent is appropriate.
However, the arising of that which has the nature of self-cognition is indeed praised.

As it is said in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "Maitreya, there is indeed no one there who discerns any phenomenon; rather, that mind has arisen in such a way that it appears as such. Even the statement that "the mind proceeds as the appearance of an object" indicates nothing other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because the perceived and the perceiver are unified. Likewise, when a person possesses the cognition of blue, it is said that "he knows the blue."
Because the root *ag* has the sense of "going," it carries the sense of "knowing. By the statement, "being one who experiences the cognition of blue," it is clearly stated:
"For one whose apprehension is not perceived, the seeing of the object is not established" (PVin I 55cd). "One who experiences that" means, in short, "one who experiences blue."

And in the *Uttaratantra*, there is the very syllable: "The Dharma is to be personally realized" (UT 10). For one who asserts that the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) exists, there is no refuge other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, it is not...
When one's own realization is established through both reasoning and scripture, there is no obstruction.
Let it be granted that there is self-cognition; however, let it be understood that the object itself is false.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition, just as in the perception of a momentary blue object.

[478,17] Even when there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that which is qualified by an exclusion established through inference (*anumāna*), there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because, just as in the case of momentariness, no certain cognition (*niścayapratyaya*) arises regarding its falsity. Furthermore, the difference in their objects (*viṣayabheda*) is evident. That too is trivial. For there is no contradiction, since the proof of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)—which establishes a particularity of existence (*sattāviśeṣa*)—is indeed a proof for the perception that apprehends the existence of blue. [The proof] that subverts existence...

However, [to claim] that "knowability is like a tortoise's hair" is indeed contradictory; furthermore, it is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).
For instance:
what object could possibly cognize itself as being false?
The meaning is that it manifests as having an existent nature (or rather, a non-existent nature). And since its very existence has been said to be its manifestation itself,
how can there be both negation and affirmation of it?

By this, even the status of being dependently originated— which is intended as a "reason based on essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*) for the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), like a reflection— is refuted. Furthermore,
that which is called "dependently originated" refers merely to the state of being an effect.
And since that [impermanence] is eternally opposed [to permanence], let it indeed subvert permanence itself.
[479,6] "For intrinsic nature is non-artificial and independent of anything else";
[479,7] with this intention, there is the sublation of precisely such an intrinsic nature.
Therefore, when such a [conceptual] form is superimposed upon a real entity, it is that very [superimposition] which is sublated; the establishment of momentary destruction remains uncontradicted.
In this way, it follows that the Sautrāntika himself is a Mādhyamika; this is a great feat!

Furthermore, where an unconditioned nature (*akṛtrimarūpa*) is accepted, as in the case of space and so forth, the arising through dependence (*pratītyodaya*) is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Jars and the like are perceived as being capable of performing the desired purposeful action;
however, there is no cognition whatsoever that "the self and so forth do not exist, while jars and the like do exist," which would be the reverse of this.
If it is argued that they do not exist precisely because they are not perceived, then perception must be the proof of existence;

how then could mountains and the like be non-existent? If it is argued that neither perception nor non-perception is a proof of existence, this is merely a response from another school. What does it depend upon for establishing [non-existence]? If it is argued that this [non-perception] proves non-existence, then since existence is never established in any way at any time, [non-existence cannot be proven].

Non-existence is indeed established. This non-apprehension of mine is not the reason for non-existence; rather, it is presented because it has been accepted as such by the opponent. If it is argued that existence is not established through non-apprehension, we reply: no, for the proponent of the self (*ātman*) and so forth does not accept non-existence based on mere non-apprehension. Even if another person accepts it, the fault is not stated against him by virtue of his own admission; therefore, this [reason] is independent (*svatantra*).
Non-apprehension is to be established as the logical reason.
Existence is established by cognition; non-cognition, however, is subverting.
And since that [non-cognition] does not depend on a qualifier, it is an endless succession of impossibilities.

Furthermore, there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) that establishes a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the state of being an effect and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) through their contrapositives;

nor is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established merely by observing both [the property and its absence] in some instance. Moreover, the absence of intrinsic nature as conceived by you is not possible in the case of a reflection, because its appearance cannot be denied. This is because, once the probandum has been established, there is no other means of proof to avoid the charge of being devoid of a probandum.

[480,2] There would be an infinite regress; furthermore, since the pervasion of appearing things is established by that very [negation] when demonstrating the negation of what has been determined, it is a case of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*). Moreover, since the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanaśūnyatā*). If it is argued that the probans, as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), is established by relying on the world (*lokāśrayāt*), then [the conclusion follows] by relying on the world.

One must offer a final farewell to emptiness. For one cannot adopt the "half-old-woman" approach, whereby the world is relied upon as the basis for the means of proof (*sādhana*) but not for that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).

If it is argued that emptiness is perceived even in a reflection by relying on the world, then it is not so in the case of the original object (*bimba*), because of the perception of its opposite there.

[The proof: It is a logical principle that one cannot take as a thesis (pakṣa) what has been refuted by valid cognition (pramāṇa). If you argue that this is merely a conceit of seeing when there is no actual perception of the opposite, then even in the case of a reflection, your conceit of seeing occurs despite the non-existence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva).

It is only the world that relies on valid cognition; regarding the opposite in the case of the original object (bimba), the world itself is the authority, whereas in the case of the reflection, it is not an authority.

[480,11] Even in the case of a reflection, how could there be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that the very absence of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) in a reflection is itself the means of valid cognition, then in cases where correspondence does exist—such as with trees and the like—the absence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) would be unavoidable. If it is argued that this is merely a conceit of correspondence, then one must state what the object of correspondence is, since it must be something other than what is commonly established, given that it occurs in the case of a reflection.
Its absence is cognized.

If it is argued that [the absence of the object] consists in the mountain and so forth being incapable of withstanding the scrutiny of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and being non-correspondent (*asaṃvāda*), then in response to the question "By which valid cognition do you pursue such scrutiny?", one must state whether it is perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), comparison (*upamāna*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), or something other than those.

[480,17] However, since not even a single thing is established without self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), one would fall into a great delusion. Therefore, [480,18] even when other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are set aside, mountains, oceans, and so forth are established through self-awareness alone. And if, in some case, there were the apprehension of correspondence (*saṃvāda*) through the investigation of a means of valid cognition, then it might cease due to the absence of that [correspondence]; but that is not the case. Furthermore, [480,19]...

[480,20] What logic is there in the claim that "service to another's feet alone is the refuge"? For it would be permissible to accept that [refuge] merely on the basis of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum). Yet, there is not always a *prasaṅga*. Indeed, the application of a *prasaṅga* is for the sake of establishing the opposite [of the opponent's position]; nor is it ever permissible to present these [reasons] as independent reasons (*hetu*). Or, if they were permissible, would they be conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) or ultimate (*tāttvika*) means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
