The phrase "to be relied upon" does not establish a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with things such as mountains; rather, for anything else, there is merely the conventional usage of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*), but no establishment of a necessary connection with the appearance of a form. Furthermore, if the inability to withstand analysis constitutes the non-correspondence (*asaṃvāda*) of mountains and the like, then that itself is their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*); so what is the use of dependent origination (*pratītyotpāda*)?

Furthermore, dependent origination is inseparable from causal capacity (*śakti*), and causal capacity itself is existence; thus, there is the fault of contradiction in establishing the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). If it is argued that there is no fault because empty phenomena arise precisely from empty phenomena, then is the avoidance of this fault achieved now merely by reciting a tenet? For in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It might be so;
for that very thing which is capable of producing a result is indeed that [result] itself.
What use is there in imagining a lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) even in that which is capable?
But for another, the very absence of a prior and posterior state is the cause for obstructing that conceptual construction; thus, this is faultless. Furthermore:
Because it is the foundation of all cognition, the law of the stability of cause and effect is subverted by this method for those who desire emptiness through effort.
Therefore, this so-called dependent origination is itself causeless with respect to the absence of intrinsic nature.

[481,9] Now, if dependent origination itself is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), and it is merely intended to establish conventional usage (*vyavahāra-mātra*), [481,10] even then, emptiness would be stated as being merely the state of being an effect; thus, this results in nothing more than falling back into the lower position. Or, for one who is merely following a convention, there is no obstacle whatsoever—so what is the use of this? Or else, having oneself imagined that there is intrinsic nature in something artificial, [one would then negate it] by means of its non-existence.

For one who asserts the loss of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even by means of a horn, one would have to conceive of the state of being a horse; yet, due to the absence of that [horn], one would also have to understand that "it is not a horse. How then [is it so]?
That which is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself considered by you to be emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

this abbreviation is not explained in JNA) [481,16] This and so forth is connected [to the context]. With reference to the entry into emptiness by means of that many members in relation to a lower state of existence, such proofs as these may, in some cases, not possess utility for the speaker of the present argument, just like the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

It is established that [the self] is not arrived at through the investigation of its parts, being devoid of human agency and free from the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the claim that self-awareness is established in any way whatsoever by virtue of being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is refuted, because there is no scope for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it, and because there is an absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) and so forth with respect to direct perception;
furthermore, if establishment were possible without a means of proof, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, in the case of that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśin*):
The state of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is precisely that which is established as such without depending on anything else.

As for what is also said—that the nature of being insentient (*jaḍasvabhāvatā*) is not established for anyone against the proponent of Madhyamaka, such that self-awareness would be non-insentient by virtue of being excluded from that—this too is merely a repetitive prattle and does not provide protection. For it is thus:
For the practitioner of yoga, there is neither ignorance nor is the middle way non-empty for one who possesses knowledge;
nevertheless, the conventional usage of terms such as "knowledge" and "emptiness" is not contradicted.

If there is a negation of the word that serves as the basis for the exclusion [of an object] on the grounds that it does not exist in any way whatsoever, then alas! from the very beginning, by uprooting words such as "momentary," "selfless," "not created by God," "not consisting of primordial matter" (*aprakṛtimaya*), and so forth, one arrives at a state of total non-communication.
For one who asserts that a negative particle has no application when it lacks an object [to negate].
How could one who is himself disregarded by his own words awaken another?
An intermediate verse:
Let this, which is so utterly loathsome, be set aside for now. Therefore, not even a grain of a fault can possibly apply to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

Consequently, by removing the qualification "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*), the establishment that self-awareness indeed exists is consistent with reason; provided, however, that the mind is not possessed by the obsession of dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*).
If there is the operation of a sublater even with respect to your own awakening,
then what kind of satisfaction do you have regarding that specific [object] presented [to you]?
Or, if somehow it does not apply there, why not directly?
In experience, that non-sublation is self-awareness, which is the foundation of awakening.
But as for the cognition of another, although it does not exist in reality, even if it is sublated by another inference once it has been established through mere conceit, let it be sublated;
however, since perception—which terminates in its own intrinsic nature—is incapable of protecting itself, it is simply not capable at all.
Therefore, every investigation here is appropriate only within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
In some cases, sublation by experience is not permissible even within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*).
Nor is there anything experienced that is ultimate; when that cognition is sublated, let this conflict be destroyed like Kali by Kali—let there be peace.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Self-Cognition, in the *Sākārasiddhi* composed by the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra.

(Chapter Six) [483,2] Now, having begun with the Madhyamaka, which is the object of such praise, one might ask: "What is this sequence, that this *Yogācāra* system is presented as being fully established? This is not a fault, because even this [system], though spoken by the Blessed One himself, is treated here for the purpose of distinguishing between the definitive (*nītārtha*) and the interpretable (*neyārtha*).

Because it has been accepted by the Noble Ones who have received predictions—from the beginning down to the Crown Prince—and because it has been established by the Teachers as something praiseworthy and free from defects, this *Sākārasiddhi* (Proof of the Manifestation of Aspects) has been undertaken. [Objection: Even so, would not both [theories], being mutually contradictory, be unreal? In that case, even though the Blessed One, the Teacher himself, was of one heart [regarding the truth], he might have taught even this [theory of aspects] out of consideration for those to be trained (*vineya*). But how could those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) and perceived the truth [accept such a view]?
Is it because they each fall into one side by teaching only their own respective views? For if this were taught as something distinct [from the truth], it would be due to compliance with others.

Moreover, since the commitment (*samaya*) of the mantra system is supremely profound, how can there be peace of heart—even for one who is *Samantabhadra*—given that such a great contradiction exists between those two who rely upon these very [positions]? It is said in reply:
In this case, there is a contradiction regarding a human author, for a single entity cannot abide in both states;
indeed, the teaching of the Sage has declared that it lies between the extremes of superimposition and denial.
For here, within this mass of variegated luminosity, it is not permissible to superimpose even a particle of non-luminosity, nor is it permissible to deny even a trace of luminosity;
just as when a thorn has entered the body, whether it be being pierced or already cut out.
In this world, with respect to a manifest form, there is distress through superimposition and denial.
If negation does not exist conventionally and superimposition does not exist ultimately,
and if both of these do not exist in reality, then what contradiction is there?
Likewise, in the *Sadasallakṣaṇanirdeśa*, the Noble Master [Maitreya] says:
Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there.
But emptiness exists here, and within that, it too is found. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.2)

"But the unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms" (MV I.9). By stating this, he expresses the negation of denial regarding that which appears, while simultaneously establishing the negation of the superimposition of the grasped and the grasper. In this context, "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*) refers to that by means of which, or in which, the duality of the grasped and the grasper is imagined; it functions as the door for the subsequent conceptualization (*pṛṣṭhajavikalpa*). That very [unreal imagination]...
Demonstrating it in detail along with its commentary, the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"Just as an illusion is described, so is unreal imagination;
just as that which is produced by illusion, so is the delusion of duality described."
Just as a cause of delusion, such as wood or a clod of earth, when seized by the spells of illusion, is so,

should the construction of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*) be understood in relation to the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*). Just as the forms of elephants, horses, gold, and so forth— which are produced by illusion— appear within that illusion despite being non-existent, so too within that construction of the unreal, the delusion of duality appears as the grasped and the grasper.

The nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) should be understood as follows. In this commentary, the mention of "wood, clods of earth, and so forth" refers to the forms of elephants and the like fashioned by skilled artisans, as well as painted images; this has been correctly explained. A "clod of earth" (loṣṭa), through the influence of mantras and the like, is surrounded by the appearance of phenomena such as distorted sensory cognitions or yellow colors. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), clay, stone, and other materials are included. It is just like that which is produced by illusion (māyā).

This is an explanatory restatement (*vyākhyeyānuvāda*). "In that illusion" refers to the magically created elephant and so forth. This is an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*), including the clod of earth mentioned previously. The "form" (*ākṛti*) of the elephant and so forth is their color and configuration. By way of that—that is, by way of being an elephant and so forth—they appear and are conceptually determined (*adhyavasita*); for there is no experience of what is non-existent. It is merely a conceptual determination, like water in a mirage.

The meaning is that what was stated there regarding the elephants and so forth is that they are produced merely as an illusion (*māyāmātra*). Thus, it is connected with the phrase "the error of duality.

Its explanation is as follows: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is precisely the grasped and the grasper; its aspect (*ākāra*), its delineation (*ullekha*), belongs to this unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) because of the appearance of two parts. Its state (*bhāva*), its suchness (*tattā*), is the determination (*adhyavasita*) based on appearing as the grasped and the grasper.

Just as there is the determination of an elephant and so forth in relation to illusions and the like, so too is there the determination of duality in relation to unreal imagination; such is the meaning.
And thus: "Just as that thing does not exist in it, so is the ultimate reality intended."
Just as there is the perception of that [object], so too is there conventional truth.

Just as there is no reality of that [elephant] in what is produced by illusion—the absence of elephant-ness and so forth—so too is the ultimate truth (paramārtha) held to be in that dependent nature (paratantra): it is the absence of the imagined characteristic of duality. Just as that which is produced by illusion is perceived as having the form of an elephant and so forth, so too is that unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) perceived as conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya). In this context, "that which is produced by illusion" refers to...

It should be understood as something fashioned by illusion (*māyā*). The meaning is that cognition (*jñāna*) is the apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) of things such as elephants and so forth. Conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) consists of the grasped and the grasper; the apprehension and determination of them as such is [conventional truth]. By this root object, the indication of the subject is shown.
Just as the manifestation of that which has it as its cause is obtained when that [cause] is absent,
so too is the manifestation of the unreal imagination obtained upon the revolution of the basis.
Just as when the illusory creation has ceased, the real object consisting of wood or other materials that served as its cause is perceived,

so too, upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because of the absence of the delusion of duality, the real object of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is perceived. In the root text, "unreal imagination" (*asatkalpa*) refers to the *abhūtaparikalpa*, while the "real object" (*bhūtārtha*) is the discernment of duality (*dvayaviveka*).
Just as one who is undeluded might act at will in the world with respect to its signs,
so too the ascetic, having undergone transformation and being free from inversion, acts according to his will.

Just as the world, being undeluded regarding that sign (nimitta) such as wood and so forth, acts according to its desire and independently, so too the noble one (ārya), having undergone the revolution of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), becomes undeluded, acting according to his desire and independent. In this regard, it should be understood that this is merely a mechanical device made of wood and so forth, or simply the form of a deluded cognition;
for there is the certainty that "this is not an elephant, nor is it gold."
The appearance of that exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like.
This verse has its meaning already explained.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in the case of illusions and the like.
Therein, existence is not non-existence; that which is the existence of its form is not non-existence. And non-existence is indeed existence;

for that which is the non-existence of the elephant and so forth is not non-existence. Furthermore, no distinction is established between those two—existence and non-existence—in illusions and the like.
That very existence of its form therein is itself the non-existence of the elephant and so forth; and that very non-existence of the elephant and so forth is itself [the existence of its form].
It has the appearance of that form;
likewise, there is the manifestation of non-duality, yet its substantial existence is not found.
Therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates.

Likewise, here in the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), there is the appearance of non-duality and the absence of duality. Therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other [objects], which have the unreal imagination as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). And herein, that which appears as if it were duality is the "appearance of duality" (*dvayābha*); its state (*bhāva*) is the intrinsic nature that manifests as internal and external forms.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed not existence;
yet, the distinction between existence and non-existence is predicated of form and the other aggregates.

Therein, existence is not non-existence, which is the appearance of duality; nor is non-existence itself existence, which is the non-existence of the cultivation of duality (*tad-dvaya-bhāvanāstitā*).

Furthermore, the distinction between existence and non-existence is established with respect to form and the other [sense-fields]. For that very thing which exists as the appearance of duality is itself the non-existence of duality.
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial,
and also for the purpose of negating the vehicle of the Hīnayāna.

For what purpose, then, is the absolute nature and the lack of distinction between existence and non-existence asserted here, respectively? It is asserted for the sake of refuting the extremes of superimposition and denial, and for the sake of preventing one’s departure via the Lesser Vehicle. For, having understood the non-existence of non-existence, one does not engage in superimposition; having understood the existence of existence, one does not engage in denial. And having understood the lack of distinction between the two, [one avoids falling into either extreme].

One does not tremble at existence; therefore, one does not depart by means of the Hīnayāna—such is the detailed explanation. Likewise, the essential meaning in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* is: "The existence of phenomena and the exhaustion of obscurations regarding the knowable."
"That which is said by others regarding the Teacher— herein I am amazed"—

having thus spoken with the intention of negating imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-dharma*) as in other contexts, he says this for the purpose of narrowing the scope of the doubt that the negation of illumination might apply generally due to the general nature of the statement.
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added.
Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
Thus, in this context, "from this" refers to the manifold luminosity, which, with respect to the time of affliction, is designated by the term "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Because it is self-cognized, there is nothing whatsoever to be removed.
If you ask, "What has been removed by us here, since it was non-existent even previously?"—
what kind of denial could there be other than the establishment of its non-existence?

Nothing whatsoever—whether the non-manifest, the grasped or the grasper, the formless, or the self and so forth—is to be added; rather, that which is real must be apprehended as real and not as unreal. This is the negation of denial (*apavāda*). Furthermore, that which is real must be resolved upon (*adhimoktavya*) as real and not as unreal.

This is the negation of superimposition (*samāropa*). However, in order to lead to a definitive conclusion regarding the distinction of whether that is real or unreal, [it is explained] in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.

Following the characteristics of existence and non-existence, one understands that duality is unreal, while the substratum (*dharmin*) which is the emptiness of duality is real, because they share a single agent. Here too, by the reference to "this" (*ataḥ*), there is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the collection of aspects; since it is not subject to rejection, its reality is established. As for the other, however, it is unreal because it is merely imagined (*kalpita-mātra*). Consequently, the reality of its emptiness is also clearly indicated. Therefore—
One who has direct realization of reality is liberated, as is one who grasps reality; the meaning is that one is liberated through the sequence of practice based on hearing and reflection.

Furthermore, the middle way is free from both superimposition and denial, and this is precisely the Yogācāra view; thus, there is no difference in the underlying substance. For it has been stated that appearance itself is not superimposition, nor does it imply the negation of the object. As for those who [hold that] even here, although it appears...

Those who superimpose a person (*pudgala*), formlessness, sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, as well as the state of being an object (*grāhyatā*) and so on, and those who deny everything—even that which does not appear—whether in its entirety or in part: the contradiction based on these two types of persons, which consists of mutual refutation, leads to ruin. Therefore, this alone is the method of emptiness (*śūnyatānaya*), as stated in the *Uttaratantra* (UT 75):

In this regard, those whose thoughts are distracted by emptiness are described as follows: Bodhisattvas who have set out in the vehicle are not those who are deluded regarding the principle of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Rather, they are those who desire the bliss of the liberation of emptiness for the sake of destroying existing entities, thinking that *parinirvāṇa* is the subsequent cutting off and destruction of what is currently existent; or those who, through the apprehension of emptiness, resort to emptiness [as a thing], thinking:
"There exists some dharma called emptiness apart from form and so forth, which we shall realize and cultivate."
Thus, what is this method of the emptiness of the *tathāgatagarbha* that is spoken of?
Nothing is to be removed from it, nor is anything at all to be added. Reality is to be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated. (UT 1.154; AAĀ 499)

[487,19] Such is the detailed exposition. In this regard, because one maintains that the very aspect which exists is unreal, and because one does not subsequently admit its annihilation, there is no first deception concerning the meaning of emptiness. Nor is there a second, because—unlike formless sensations and so forth—it is perceived as something distinct.
[487,21] Indeed, in this case, nothing whatsoever is to be removed from the *tathāgatadhātu* as a cause of affliction, nor is anything whatsoever to be added to it as a cause of purification.

Thus it has been explained. It is true; however, because a phenomenon (dharma) is taught by means of another phenomenon, by the term "tathāgata-element" (tathāgatadhātu), it is precisely the emptiness-phenomena that is to be grasped as the object of the mind’s transformation (*cittavivarta*). This is because there is no room for the suspicion of adding anything whatsoever to the mere emptiness that resides within conceptual construction (*kalpanāniveśin*). Consequently, by way of negating the cessation and arising of the existent and non-existent causes of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*), [the nature of reality is established].

It is precisely the negation of the aforementioned denial (apavāda) and superimposition (samāropa) that is intended; for immediately thereafter it says: "In this way, one sees that whatever is not present in a certain place is empty of that. Furthermore, whatever remains there, one understands as it truly is that it exists here as a reality.
By thus avoiding both superimposition and denial, the characteristic of non-erroneous emptiness is elucidated by this.
Therefore, there is no negation of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśa*). This indeed is the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamārtha*). Alternatively:
"Everything is designated as empty, nor yet non-empty; because of existence, non-existence, and existence again, that is the middle way. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.3)
By this [verse], he stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*: "And that very same thing is called the Middle Way practice."
Since the crown-prince himself is directly non-conceptual,
what is the use here of the exertion of scholarly erudition?
Therefore, this very middle way is the Yogācāra system in reality.
And with reference to this very point, the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna also said:

"The teaching of the aggregates, elements, and so forth, was given for the purpose of eliminating the grasping at a self; even that has been demolished by the Greatly Fortunate Ones through the establishment of mere representation (*citramātra*). (***).
Thus is the praise. However, by way of casting out the other directions:
"This entire world is mere representation"—this teaching of the Sage is for the purpose of removing the fear of fools; it is not from the perspective of ultimate reality. (* ***)

Thus it has been said: "Generally, people have come to regard even the mind as having existence through the power of external objects themselves; and thus, until this day, despite the efforts of the authors of the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*, they do not attain awakening, but rather proceed by means of refuting the intentions of others.
The general statement "mere representation" (*citramātra*) is for the most part intended as a provisional indication, and not as a total negation.
For it would follow that there would be no occasion for praise. Nor is praise possible for these things apart from their being mere appearances that are unarisen and unceased, like a dream.
No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does any phenomenon whatsoever cease.
"Only conditions arise and cease.

Because of this statement, their system is indeed one that maintains the existence of mental aspects (*sākāra*), and because of the description of the *saṃbhogakāya*, whereas others do not describe the conventional [body] and so forth.
How, then, is it?
Was it not stated that "He is neither red, nor green, nor madder-colored" (*rakto harinmāñjiṣṭaḥ*) and so forth? This was said with reference to the *dharmakāya*. And likewise immediately thereafter:
"Homage be to You, the non-dual! (*advayāya namo 'stu te*).

Thus it has been stated by resorting to the *prasajya* (non-presuppositional) mode of negation. Furthermore, even though there is a respect for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) in the statement, "I bow to the *dharmakāya*, which is to be personally realized," there is still the suspicion of error; alas for this independence, since self-cognition finds its rest solely in the manifestation of variegated forms. And since that has been firmly established, nothing is gained by the lamentations of those who deny the *dharmakāya* and so forth. Therefore, the view favored by the Crown Prince alone is the one accepted by the Noble Ones.
It is established as the Middle Way.
By this, those who also maintain that, based upon the form-body (*rūpakāya*), because of the state of natural delusion,
the cessation of mind and mental factors is asserted as the attainment of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); (***).
It has been demonstrated that their systematic arrangement is also untenable; for instance:
where could there be a basis consisting of mere form, since it is established everywhere as being of the nature of self-cognition, which is incompatible with the existence of error?

Therefore, even knowledge (*jñāna*) is not able to withstand analysis from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). However, since conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) all five aggregates (*skandha*) exist, one should not say: "Why is there the negation of one and the establishment of another? Furthermore, what is this so-called "convention" (*saṃvṛti*)? If it is a cognition that is pleasing only when not analyzed, alas, since conventions are infinite, where would the restriction to five aggregates lie? [The same applies to] the cognitions of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*), and so forth.

Furthermore, various [cognitions] involving innate or produced delusions—even in the case of a child—would, at the end, have as their objects such things as the lunar disc; these would be inferred from actions like reaching out or stretching forth the hand, and thus they would cause one to grasp those respective things as conventional truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
If you say, "Let it be so," then what is the use of seeking the Path for the sake of cessation (*nirodha*), since one would likewise have to seek the Vedas, Īśvara, and so forth?
[489,25] (114a) Now, if even within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), one does not rely on existence because satisfaction is found only in certain specific instances, then in that case,

the conventional must be relied upon precisely in the form of perception and inference characterized as previously defined. And such being the case, this designation of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) is merely an intermediate conceptual arrangement.
Neither through direct perception nor through inference is there any proof for the existence of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha);
rather, by those very two means, it is sublated, and therefore all cognition is indeed [of the nature of consciousness].

[490,5] It is said that even in that case, inference alone is the sublater; thus, it is certainly not established there either. That being so, [490,6] consciousness alone is conventionally real (saṃvṛtisat), not form. Therefore, it is logical that consciousness alone persists throughout the cycle of existence by way of convention, [490,7] because it continues to manifest even when sublated, whereas the other does not. Or, let all five aggregates exist by way of convention;

Would it be through the cessation of cognition itself, or by means of an effort toward its cessation? Not the first position, because the mental continuum has been proven to possess a stable nature. If it is argued that it ceases when it is without an object (*nirālamba*), then what fault is there? For "peace" (*śānti*) is said to mean the absence of affliction (*anupadrava*). If you intend "destruction" (*nāśa*) by this, even then, if the object (*ālambana*) refers to a sense-object (*viṣaya*), it exists even now.

[490,11] How can that which is truly without an object proceed as a continuous stream? Conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), however, there is never an exclusion of an object. [490,12] Now, what about its support (*ādhāra*)? It has no support whatsoever, because it lacks weight (*gaurava*). Now, what about its cause (*kāraṇa*)? Even now, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the cause; even then it is not interrupted, especially when accompanied by compassion for the entire world. Because of the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*), it does not [cease].
If it is argued that there is an attachment to rebirth, then let there simply be no saṃsāra characterized by the desire for welfare and happiness and the falling into impure states;

however, who can prevent its occurrence as a mere continuity, especially in the case of one who is compassionate? Therefore, cessation does not occur spontaneously; rather, effort would be required from one who perceives the virtues and faults of either maintaining one state or abandoning the other.

In that regard, what kind of quality belongs to the mass of insentience (*jaḍarāśi*) that does not belong to consciousness (*caitanya*), or what kind of defect belongs to this [consciousness] that does not belong to the mass of insentience? If you argue that it is because the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are inherently deluded, then why is it not said that [this is so] for matter (*rūpa*) because it is a mass of insentience? And if you hold such high regard for that alone, then clods of earth, bricks, and the like would be better for you!

What further must be done beyond this? And what indeed is this so-called "error" (*bhrānti*)? It cannot be mere falsity (*alīkatā*), for that would entail the same consequence for form (*rūpa*) as well. If it is argued that even though it is false, the designation of error does not apply to form, but rather to consciousness alone—then in that case, this is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā*). Furthermore, the distinction between rejection and acceptance is made solely in accordance with one's own linguistic conventions. This being the case:

Having thus refuted form as well, its abandonment would follow. If, however, one who maintains the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavādin) intends that only that [consciousness] ceases and not form—contrary to the Blessed One’s position—even so, what is the point of bolstering the notion of delusion? Let there be no possibility of delusion through proximity to insentient form.

If it is argued that error (*viparyāsa*) is perceived in consciousness (*vijñāna*) and not in that which is of a single insentient nature, [we reply]: surely "error" and "delusion" (*bhrama*) have one and the same meaning; and since this is merely a definition of its very nature, how does this answer apply? Furthermore, if the meaning of delusion is established according to convention as the apprehension of something as what it is not (*atasmims tadgraha*), then by its opposite, non-delusion (*abhrānti*) is likewise perceived in consciousness.

It might be argued: "The error is indeed an error, as it is established for both parties; yet, in my analysis, even that is merely an error. If that is the case, then everything is an error, and thus even the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) would be an error. If you object, "But surely there is no such thing as the knowledge of emptiness in reality," we reply: let it be that it does not exist in reality; however, the claim that the knowledge of emptiness is an error is some kind of arbitrary convention. Moreover, [491,2] It might be argued: "The error is indeed an error, as it is established for both parties. In this regard, even that [knowledge] is merely an error according to my analysis. If that is so, then everything is an error; consequently, even the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) is an error. If you say, "But surely there is no such thing as the knowledge of emptiness in terms of ultimate reality (*tattvena*)," then let it be that it does not exist in reality; however, the position that the knowledge of emptiness is an error is some sort of formal establishment (*vyavasthā*). Furthermore, [text continues].
In reality, nothing exists; this is what is called "emptiness.
In reality alone, there is only delusion here—there is no non-delusion; such is the direction of the teaching.
Since the state of all delusion arises from that very investigation,
is that itself delusion or is it non-delusion? If it is delusion, how can all this be delusion?
If not, then that very thing is devoid of the nature of error.

If it is argued that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no such thing as even an error that is not non-error, this may indeed be logical. However, within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), just as there are the five aggregates (*skandha*), one must necessarily accept that some cognitions are errors and some are non-errors. For even then, the cognition of blue regarding what is blue is not an error, whereas it would be an error regarding what is white. Likewise, cognitions such as that of silver must be described in these two ways; otherwise—

There is no such thing as a "form-aggregate" (rūpaskandha) in reality; it is intended [by the Buddha] that, conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), the cessation of mind and mental factors is the persistence of the form-aggregate, yet in that regard there is only delusion. There is no correct awakening to that [conventional state], because all undertakings are for the sake of that [ultimate goal].
Conventionally both exist, but in truth (*tattvataḥ*) both are non-existent.
If everything is indeed nothing but an illusion, to what can this statement be applied?

[491,19] Now, if it is argued that error is sometimes observed in cognition alone and not in form, then one might as well say that it is observed in the aggregates (*skandha*) alone. Or, if one perceives faults even in those things accepted by the Teacher, it would lead to the abandonment of the Blessed One as well. However, internal distinctions are common to all. If by "error by nature" you intend to mean that it does not apply to every individual instance, then for that very reason—

This has already been answered. Now, if it is argued that even when an error occurs in some cases, it is merely a transformation (*vikṛti*), even so, how can this certainty be reached, given that both states are observed? In this regard, scripture repeatedly declares that the mind is pure by nature (*prakṛtipariśuddha*) while defects are adventitious (*āgantuka*); furthermore, experience shows that the mind is tormented by the suspicion of error until there is correct thorough knowledge.
And that it is "obstructed" has been analyzed in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
Nor can this be stated with reference to either the conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or the non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), because both are observed in both cases.

Alternatively, if such a state exists in one case, let there be the abandonment of that very [state]; or, if there is no perception of the distinction, another treatise must be sought for the sake of its perception.

[492,1] Thus, this is a groundless objection, namely that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are inherently deluded. Furthermore, the cessation of the mind and mental factors and the realization of the *dharmakāya* are contradictory, because realization is a property of the mind. If it is argued that this is a metaphorical designation for realization, from what [source]? If it is argued that it is because there is no other possibility (*gaty-antara-abhāva*), then in that case, there would be the abiding of a realizing mind.

Let it be so; what is the point of the effort to turn back [the objection]? How is there an absence of any other alternative? This attempt to amuse oneself with the curiosity of sight by plucking out one's own eye is not acceptable to those who possess discernment.
If you argue that clods of earth and the like are the ones who directly realize the *dharmakāya* because they lack any superior power (*prabhāvātiśaya*), [we reply as follows]:

Indeed, the direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) of the *dharmakāya* does not occur by that much alone, but rather through a specific excellence of realization; otherwise, since mantras and the like would also be identical [to it], they too would possess Buddhahood. If this is so, what is to be accomplished by direct realization when an excellence of non-existence (*abhāvātiśaya*) is possible, as in the case of a jewel and so forth? If this is so, then what is to be accomplished by the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)? [They serve] for the sake of a specific capacity (*sāmarthyaviśeṣa*).

Since it is possible otherwise—as in the case of jewels, mantras, and so forth—it follows that neither the *dharmakāya* nor the *saṃbhogakāya* exists; such is the perfectly pure state of the Buddha. Alternatively, since even for one who has attained realization there is seen an excellence of radiant fruit, let it be that form alone is to be dispelled, or rather, it is to be established;
for in either case, the accomplishment of some purpose is achieved by someone through something.

If it is argued that all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) can only be superimposed upon form (*rūpa*), then let the opposite be the case—that it can be superimposed upon consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone; "no" is not a valid proof, as it would be like drinking from a jar [of poison]. Even so, if one were to establish [capacity] in only one thing, it might belong only to the mental portion (*cittabhāga*); thus, there is no restriction to form alone. Furthermore, because we observe that the capacity of knowledge (*jñāna*) itself is greater than the capacity of form.

In that very context, the relinquishing of the burden is appropriate. Otherwise, how could it be understood that the world is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Therefore, even within the conventional position of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhaka*), the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) is not tenable; nor is that same conventionality [tenable] within the position of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*).
The final conventional reality cannot be spoken of as being conventional;
and that final [reality] is of the very nature of gnosis, otherwise even substance, quality, and so forth would be [conventional].
Therefore, the abiding of the mind itself with its mental aspects is the Dharmakāya, established through self-cognition.
If this is so, since self-awareness has a real entity as its object, how can the designation "emptiness" be merely a conventional reality? How, then, can it be the Dharma-body of the Blessed One?
Therefore, the knowledge other than the enjoyment body (sambhogakāya) is indeed formless.
Others, the wise, understand that the Dharma-body has emptiness as its objective support.
In this case as well, since it is distinct from that which is designated as the Buddha of Enjoyment (sambhoga),
how could it possibly be his essential nature?
If that [body] were also of the nature of a Buddha, there would be two Buddhas with distinct characteristics;
if it were indeed of the nature of a Buddha, then the Dharmakāya would be something other [than him].
If this very Buddha is the Dharma, then there is no possession (samanvaya) expressed by "his";
neither as the relationship between a substratum and its attribute (dharmidharmabhāva), nor by way of universal and particular (sāmānyaviśeṣataḥ).
If the Buddha were the dharma of enjoyment, then the Buddha would be merely a conceptual construct.
Furthermore, if the self-nature of the dharma were something other than that, and if it were a substantial entity, then there would be an infinite regress.

If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) were not consciousness, then, like blueness and so forth, it would exist within consciousness; yet, if it were formless, how could that which lacks enjoyment be the very nature of phenomena? Or rather, how could it be the nature of phenomena for one who does not enjoy others?

[493,11] But then, how is it shown in the *Uttaratantra* (UT 40f) that "this very same *dharmakāya*, through the increase, decrease, and ultimate exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*), is called the 'constituent of sentient beings' (*sattvadhātu'), the 'bodhisattva,' and the 'buddha'"? That which is stated in that very same work [is as follows]:
[493,13] "The *dharmakāya* is to be known as twofold: the utterly stainless *dharmadhātu*..."
[493,14] And that [is its outflow], as well as the teaching of the profound and manifold methods [of the Dharma].
[493,16] Thus, this is called the *dharmadhātu*; and that alone is the subject under discussion, not what is termed the teaching of the profound and manifold methods which constitutes its outflow.
[493,17] What, then, is the *dharmadhātu* itself? Study the *Madhyāntavibhāga* for this very purpose. That which...

“Suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena—these, in brief, are synonyms of emptiness. (Madhyāntavibhāga I.15) Thus it was said, in order to dispel such delusion. Likewise, if there is a misconception even regarding this point—that emptiness is merely a phenomenon (*dharmamātra*)—then [it must be addressed].

"The non-existence of duality is indeed the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness" (Madhyāntavibhāga I.14). Following such various formulations, one might therein—by means of that very [negation]—posit some formless entity as what is expressed by the term "dharma-kāya. This is an arbitrary assertion. But surely, mere phenomena (*dharmamātra*) exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*); how [then can they constitute the ultimate]?
Is it the object of self-awareness?
Or how is its perpetual absence from the preceding [moment] established?
Thus, in some cases, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of an affirmation (*vidhi*). It is said in reply:
The existence of all things is twofold, through the modes of absolute negation (prasajya-pratiṣedha) and relative negation (paryudāsa).
In every case, when there is an absence [of a property], it is accepted as a means of valid cognition (māna) regarding the subject (dharmin).

First, regarding the case of *paryudāsa* (presuppositional negation), as it has been said: "For that very existence which is the absence of duality is itself the absence of duality. In that case, there is no suspicion of the non-apprehension of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because "duality does not exist therein" (Madhyāntavibhāga I.2).

And so forth; even in the case of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapakṣa*), there is no cognition of the absence of duality other than the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) itself that produces the conceptualization of the absence of duality.
Therefore, in the treatise, the discussion regarding the negation of identity and the negation of being the locus of a jar in a particular place must be considered.

In either case—whether by way of implicative negation (*paryudāsa*) or non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—it results in that very same single form of the entity; thus, it is merely a matter of conventional usage.

[494,15] This is the insistence. Or, just as the entry into the Digambara doctrine was refuted by the author of the *Ṭīkā* even when there is a negation of absolute difference and non-difference based on the mere existence of an entity, so too must it be negated in the case of that which has a positive form appearing in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because even that—such as the form of "permanent" and so forth—is not a real thing (*avastu*). And this systematic arrangement is for that purpose, as was stated previously. Or, just as that very same...
Regarding the term *dharmakāya*: otherwise, there would be no purpose whatsoever for considering it as being with stains, without stains, all-pervading, and so forth.

Having introduced the commentary on the meaning of the "supreme outflow" (*niṣpandāgra*)—on the grounds that the word of the Buddha is characterized by the *dharmadhātu*—it is stated that [the teaching] proceeds through the sovereign power of the *dharmadhātu*, which is called the *dharmakāya* and is pure in every respect. Therefore, it exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).

The *dharmakāya* is not an object of fear for those possessed of intelligence, because it is established in that very way through both reasoning and scripture. Alternatively, where there is the ultimate negation, that which is the finality of the positive form (*vidhirūpa*) is indeed a real entity (*vastusad*) in relation to its substratum (*dharmin*).
Thus, "the Blessed One is the *dharmakāya*"—let fear be abandoned. For just as the absence of a jar in a certain location is true as a mere [positive] state.
"Region" (*pradeśa*) means the culmination of the object; likewise, "the absence of duality here" means that the nature of cognition is devoid of duality or the state of being dual.

It is with this very intention that there is the exclusion of the two-fold [nature], and its culmination lies in the form of the real entity (*vastu*). For it is the established conclusion in the treatise that "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which apprehends the subject (*dharmin*) also [establishes] the property (*dharma*). Therefore, regarding the property and the subject...
Relying upon the conceptualized distinction between them, both the Buddha and the Dharma are established;
the Saṃgha is the manifestation of the transformation body—thus is the abiding of the Three Jewels.
In reality, however, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*) between the Buddha and his qualities. By this, that which is explained in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* is addressed:
"The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) is considered equal, subtle, and connected.
The essential body of all Buddhas is equal because it is without distinction."

It is subtle because it is difficult to know; thus, it is connected with that body characterized by effortful application (*sābhogika*). In this context, one should understand that the actual relationship is one of identity (*tādātmya*). If it is argued: "In that case, since there is the statement that it is the cause of the *saṃbhoga*-buddhahood, let it be simply its origination," [the answer is:

no, because in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (116a) it is said that the *dharmadhātu* is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*), for the noble qualities arise from having that as their objective support (*ālambana*).

By this statement, because the power of bringing that [object] to presence exists therein, the meaning—that such conventional usage occurs—is made clear. Likewise, in the *Ṭīkā* on the occasion of the discussion of the intrinsic nature of emptiness, it is stated that the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness begins with the attainment of the two states and extends up to the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha; the excellence of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) for oneself and others results from the cultivation of emptiness.
Thus, it is the same with other cases as well. Alternatively, the establishment of the predominance (*adhipatya*) of that factor (*aṅga*) therein is in relation to its previous state, as in:

"His valor accomplishes all aims," and "momentariness" (*kṣaṇikatā*). Furthermore, no purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is ever perceived apart from a form (*ākāra*), since its very capacity is observed in the production of all pure and impure phenomena, and in the manifestation of reality (*tattva*) during the arising of pure qualities.

[495,15] "There is the state of being a cooperative cause. If it is argued that everything arises from that very formless [cause], we reply: no scripture supports this, as has been shown, nor is there any logical reasoning.
Furthermore, even though this world arises from the absence of dependence," [495,17] people...
One relies on a mode of activity that is performed by another while remaining face-to-face;
what kind of darkness is this, such that one perceives existence and non-existence without seeing?

[495,21] From the root *kṛ* (to do), when there is a desire to express the agent or the object, the suffix *ṇic* is applied; the meaning is "caused to be done by another" or "the action performed by another. [495,22] It is better that one does not perceive the existing relationship between cause and fruit, which is merely a semblance of form (*ākāraleśa*), rather than perceiving something non-existent that belongs to another domain. Is this not a verse from the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* in the section concerning the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*)? What else could be called the "doctrine of self" other than this? [It refers to] permanence and omnipresence.
If it is argued that this is not so because [the self] is not admitted [by us], we say no, because the proponents of the self (ātmavādins) are diverse. For:
The agent and the enjoyer, distinct from the perceived [objects], is the sphere of the "I"-conception (ahaṃkāra);
it is stainless, and for yogins, liberation consists in its remaining as the sole residue.

Furthermore, since you do not experience any utility in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) when there is no manifestation of a distinct intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), you would certainly not accept its momentariness. Therefore, this [permanent entity] is the object of such statements as: "Like that which consists of non-conceptualization (*niṣkalpātman*), it is incapable even of performing the function of mere cognition. However, when the *dharmakāya* is established in scripture as being both eternal and omnipresent, then...

What is the answer? It is not the permanence of a continuum (*pravāha-nityatā*), because it is precisely the permanence of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti-nityatā*) that is being taught. And so it is said in that very same work: "Permanence exists both through the non-destruction of the fundamental nature and through continuity.
Regarding this, the commentary states: "The permanence of the fundamental nature belongs to the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), because it is permanent by its very nature."

The enjoyment body (*sāmbhogika*) is non-ceasing because its enjoyment of the Dharma is uninterrupted; the emanation body (*nairmāṇika*) is continuous because, even after vanishing, it repeatedly displays emanations. And its mastery has already been explained according to the *Uttaratantra*: "Just as space, being non-conceptual, is omnipresent everywhere," so too is that [Buddhahood].
The element of the stainlessness of the nature of the mind is likewise all-pervading.
(I.49) What does this demonstrate?
It is the universal characteristic that pervades its defects, its qualities, and its ultimate state.
"In the inferior, mediocre, and superior [objects], like space within those things that have taken form" (UT I.50).

Regarding the phrase "within those things that have taken form," the commentary states: "in vessels made of clay, silver, and gold. Furthermore, the word *gata* should be understood as having the sense of "kind" (*prakāra*). Patañjali [states in the Mahābhāṣya]: "The suffix *kta* [is used] after the root *hṛ* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*). [Note: This specific line does not appear in the extant Mahābhāṣya; this is Kaiyaṭa’s interpretation of Patañjali’s intent, as explained by Kaiyaṭa and others in the *Pradīpa* on *Pāṇini* 1.3.21. Thus, *gata*, *vidha*, and *prakāra* are synonymous.

Thus, the conventional usage [of the suffix] is "having attained that nature. The instrumental case in "by way of non-conceptuality" (*nirvikalpatayā*) is used in the sense of "being in such a state. The very natural dejection of the mind (*cittasya prakṛtivaimanasyam*) is the element (*dhātu*), which is suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, its primary permanence and omnipresence have been stated. Consequently, if the *dharmakāya* were indeed a substantial entity (*dravya*), how could there be an avoidance of the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*)?
[496,21] However, the permanence, omnipresence, and so forth of the *dharmatā* are conventional;
even though it possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), they are established according to conceptual construction, just like momentariness and the like.

In this context as well, "among those who are inferior, middling, and superior" is the specification of the subject (*dharmin*). Nor is there a doctrine of selflessness (*anātmavāda*) due to a lack of pervasiveness, as held by the Digambaras; nor is there any insistence on a doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*), for one who lacks insight perceives neither existence nor non-existence.

Thus, because the fault remains unrefuted in exactly that same way; even if there were such a thing as the "aspect" (*ākārabhāga*) of that which is to be trusted (*śraddheya*), it would be difficult to deny that it is at least real (*satya*). This is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptimātra*) of existence, whereas only that which is to be trusted is substantially real (*vastusat*). Therefore, the claim that the nature of the Enjoyment Body (*sambhogātmā*) is false, yet not distinct from it because it is the manifestation of its basis, and thus not unrelated—this is mere poetry devoid of scripture and logic. And that...
The meaning of the name "Buddha" is unreal; that which is the *dharmakāya* is the truth—this is a sound conclusion.

Furthermore, if the Buddha were merely subordinate by virtue of being simply dependent [on the *dharma*], then the direct designation "the Buddha is the *dharma*" would be appropriate, as the Buddha is the master of the *dharma*. Alternatively, if both together constitute the Buddha, then in the alternative analysis of whether this refers to each individually or to the aggregate, [only one...]

It is also well said that the Buddhas are "partless," "unreal," and "erroneous," because of the contradiction between error and awakening. And how could he be unreal while being accepted as the cause of the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) within the nature of the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)? As the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"The fulfillment of the two aims for both [bodies] is established in every aspect."

Thus it is said. Regarding this, the commentary states: "The enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) is characterized by the perfection of one's own welfare; the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*) is characterized by the perfection of the welfare of others. This perfection of the welfare of others is established, respectively, in the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the enjoyment body. And this being so, the fruit belongs to the dharma-body, while the cause belongs to the emanation body for the sake of the perfection of the welfare of others. Furthermore, this perfection of one's own welfare appears even though it does not exist."

All of this is a delusion. Therefore, this claim that there is the fulfillment of one's own purpose within the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) contradicts the thesis of its unreality regarding the mental aspects (*ākāra*).
By this, the conceptualization that the enjoyment body is respected for the sake of a specific effect—even if Buddhahood or truthfulness were indeed trustworthy—is refuted.
For, by that [conceptualization], not even an atom of a fruit exists, and because it would be of the nature of a blemish.
Someone, disregarding a minor fault, persists in an action out of regard for a greater purpose; yet that [action],
being devoid of true benefit, is a swarm of bees consisting of major defects.
How could one who is more senior show such respect?

It is not tenable to say that its arising is due to the power of karma; for karma alone is the cause of that which must be abandoned absolutely, and it does not merit being undertaken, just like other sins. It has been well said that such an error on the part of the Tathāgata arises from a lapse in karma; thus, his [error] would necessarily result in a total cessation [of omniscience]. Furthermore, what is the use of those called "bodhisattvas"?
If it were devoid of form, it would be entirely unfit for human service;
if one admits that it possesses form, this would be a literal "bathing of an elephant."
The thesis of formlessness is for the sake of establishing formlessness;
yet, to accept a form is its own refutation—what else could be more so?
These are the intermediate verses.
As for the obstruction of that [power] due to a longing for some object, what resistance to power can there be for one who is worthy of trust?
If he possesses power in one instance, let it be proclaimed as power everywhere.
For positive and negative concomitance are not the refuge for establishing the nature of causes.

Therefore, for those who maintain that there is no mental aspect (*nirākāravādin*), the form [of consciousness] must be established as possessing all powers, resembling a pure, infinite, and empty sky;

let this be another philosophical system—what is the use of further attachment to others? For if one transgresses the method of the leader, the noble Maitreya, what kind of establishment of Buddhist reality could there be?
In brief, he [states]:
Regarding the mind within the three realms, he declared it to be manifold; herein, the duality of the perceived and the perceiver is indeed false.
Thus, dispelling [that duality], he drove away [the mind] which is fixed upon superimposition and denial.
[498,10] The glory of one’s own welfare, which is the cause for the benefit of others through the enjoyment [of the Dharma].

Furthermore, in no discussion concerning the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) or secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), has it been shown that this form of the Buddha does not exist in reality, or that it is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Even when the conventional designation "Buddha" is discussed with emphasis on the *dharmakāya*, non-existence itself has not been established, nor has it been treated as merely figurative;
for it is observed that the primary marks and so forth belong to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) as well. This is also stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:
[498,14] "His body is adorned with all various marks" (MSA***).

Regarding this, the commentary states that the inclusion of the word "various" (*citra*) is for the purpose of distinguishing these from the marks of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and so forth; this is indeed a reinforcement.

Furthermore, even though this has been written, because the Blessed One has abandoned the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), error is impossible, and he is of the nature of mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśanajñāna*).

Because the images of all objects of knowledge arise within it at every moment, its nature is that of a single wheel of cognition (*jñānacakra*); for this very reason, it is marked by the symbol of the wheel (*cakracihna*).

The direct experience of the reflections of all objects of knowledge is itself its awakening to all objects of knowledge. For this very reason, because he possesses superior intelligence (*buddhi*) through the realization of the true nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), he is called "Awakened" (*buddha*). Consequently, only his own self is dissolved, and likewise that of the objective form.

Because of the establishment of error, where could there be a connection with excellent cognition, or where could there be the abandonment of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)? Since one perceives the unreal as being precisely unreal, there follows the consequence of the doctrine of error consisting in the apprehension of that which is not [the object] as being that. This has been refuted in the case of the cognition of a form (*ākṛti*).
Neither the way of mantra nor the system of the perfections;
let that very state remain, free from fault,
delightful, and adorned with the jewels of celestial virtues.
This is an intermediate verse.

Now, even if the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) is accepted as being merely false, it is nonetheless capable of accomplishing that purpose. Or, even if it possesses such capacity, because of its very purity, through its withdrawal there arises another state characterized by the direct realization of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is like the sky.

Is there no fault? No; for even so, one has not avoided the transgression of the doctrine of non-decay and permanence. Furthermore, it follows that the Blessed One, acting for the sake of the world, would be devoid of the *dharmakāya*. And that contradicts what the *Uttaratantra* says:
"Having surveyed the entire world with great compassion, the Knower of the World..."
"Without wavering from the *dharmakāya*, through emanations of diverse forms...
(UT II 53). Thus, the connection is explained in detail as "he displays [the deeds] beginning with the *jātaka*s and ending with *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore:
"In every celestial realm, without wavering from the state of Brahmā..."
Just as Brahmā displays his manifestation without effort, so too does he appear.

In the same way, the Sage, without effort, through emanations within the realms of sentient beings, appears to those who are worthy while remaining unmoved from the *dharmakāya*. (UT IV 53–4) And so forth, as explained in detail further on. Now, if it is said that there is no movement from the *dharmakāya* with respect to its intrinsic purity (*prakṛtipariśuddhi*), then...

[499,15] Since this is equal for every living being, what excellence is expressed by the Blessed One in saying this through such a continuous discourse? [499,16] Therefore, this distinction is made solely with regard to purity through the removal of stains (*vaimalyaviśuddhi*). At the time of the direct realization of the *dharmakāya*, there is no performance of the welfare of the world that depends on effort and the like; hence, this effort is intended to dispel the doubt that "that [activity] occurs only upon arising from meditative absorption," and so forth. Thus:
And it has also been stated: "by effortless emanations. Thus, by the relinquishing of the body, the refutation of the proponents of a self who claim to have attained reality is established.
Furthermore, even if movement is intended here as the repeated arising from and entering into meditative absorption (*samādhi*), what follows from that?
Is it through exertion? Indeed, [it is said]: "Beyond the *sambhogakāya* lies purity;
from that, the *sambhogakāya* exists for the accomplishment of the goal."
When will the Sage attain such composure as mine, whose body is so habituated to sinking and surfacing?
And thus, the welfare of others is not one whose method is unimpaired, nor is there eternal purity; let this matter rest for now.

Let there be no recollection of the story of Tundi. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "the Dharma itself is the Buddha"—since even in that case there is an absence of any conceptualized distinction, and because it is sufficient [as a designation] despite having different grounds for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), like the terms *ina*, *muni*, and *indriya*, how [could there be a contradiction]?
What is the distinction between the different bodies (*kāya*)? Furthermore, how can there be no contradiction between the Dharma and the Victor (*jina*) given their synonymous nature?

It is said that he "does not waver from the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*), and so forth. For it is not logical to say that one is a Sugata by not wavering from the Buddha; rather, it is indeed logical to say it is because of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*). This is because they are one.
And he speaks of the persistence of designations (*prajñaptisthiti*), as in that statement: "Just as Brahmā does not waver from his Brahma-state.

For in that case, Brahmā alone is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*); that state, however, is merely conventionally real (*prajñaptisat*), for it is not some other distinct entity, since the designation of a "state" refers to a particularity of the basis, the requisites, and the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Even when the very intrinsic nature (svarūpa), depending on specific limiting conditions (upādhi-viśeṣa), is denoted by the word *pada*— just as in the case of the term *ācāryapada*— nevertheless,

that which is indicated as if separate from the substratum (dharmin) through conceptual construction (kalpanā) exists only as a designation (prajñaptisat). Likewise, in this case as well, it follows that one of the two things denoted by the terms "Muni" and "Dharmakāya" possesses existence only as a designation.
[500,13] Let it be so for the Dharma alone, but not for the Sage, because of the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

[500,14] If that existence is also devoid of form (*nirākṛti*), how can the arising of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) be spoken of? (***) Thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words. Furthermore, in this way, even the "Sage" would be entirely formless; and consequently, from the Dharma-body...

[500,17] To say that "it does not move" would be a misconception, for it would imply that the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) itself—being a mere conceptual designation—is what is expressed by the term "dharma-body.

[500,18] If you argue that the emptiness of duality is the dharma-body, even then, how can the birth of the enjoyment body be spoken of? For it has been established that the purpose is fully accomplished by that alone.
[500,19] Thus it is concluded.
[500.20] Now, if it is argued that there is some distinction between the category of activity—namely, that of enjoyment (*sambhoga*) and that of the formless (*nirākāra*)—[we reply]:
no, for such a distinction is untenable regarding the nature of activity, because both are equally matured, and thus the analogy of the terms "Brahman" and "That" (*tat-pada*) is inappropriate;
furthermore, this is not how it is taught even in the various contexts (*prakaraṇa*), whereas in the case of enjoyment, it is like the *dharmakāya*.

The reason has been stated and has already been demonstrated in that manner. Or, let there be some activity of the formless [cognition] toward the enjoyment body (*sambhoga*), or toward other groups of effects; however, the existence of the enjoyment body itself remains unestablished. Consequently, one must further connect the argument that both would be non-illusory (*analīka*). So how can the illusoriness of the enjoyment body, or the establishment of supramundane non-manifesting cognition (*nirābhāsajñāna*), be proclaimed? [This is because it is contradicted by] the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*).
If it is argued that [the enjoyment body] is false—[we reply:
if, by means of the analogy of Brahman, one sets aside reflections and the like, then the falsity of the enjoyment body would be established; however, its power of sublation has been considered.
[501,3] Through the uninterrupted continuity of appearance and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the previously mentioned status of being subordinate is thereby refuted.

Furthermore, [501,4] when both are established as having functional capacity, if one should desire the emptiness of duality itself to be the *dharmadhātu*, which has another name, the *dharmakāya*— either out of deference to the Crown Prince as shown previously, or just now by means of the analogy of the state of Brahmā— then:

And the body would be the fourth, for it is indeed to be trusted due to the distinctness of the emanation (*nirmāṇa*). Furthermore, that emptiness of duality belongs specifically to the enjoyment (*sambhoga*), because of the mention of its connection and because it demonstrates the uninterrupted enjoyment of the Dharma belonging to that very [body]. For there is no enjoyment other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
In the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* as well:
"In some places he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways;
in some places he manifests birth and disappearance, and in others, various supreme magical transformations."
In some places he displays complete enlightenment, and in others, repeatedly with his emanations;
yet he does not move from that state, and he accomplishes everything.
Thus: "From the station, from the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu)," according to the Bhāṣya. And that untainted realm is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Its direct realization and stability are for the sake of immovability; such is the meaning. Alternatively, it may be the fourth body.

Thus, a fourth nature would follow from the three natures—imagined and so forth—whether conceived as formless or with form, because it would be distinct from the manifold wheel of mind called unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*). If it is argued that this very mind is indeed unreal imagination, we say no; for this point has not been disclosed even by the masters of the means (*upāyakāra*). Nor can it be that the mind is non-luminous, or that what is non-mind is luminous.

And it was stated previously: "in the case of form and so forth, which have the nature of unreal imagination. Thus, the discussion concerning form and so forth as the imagined, the conceptualized, and the true nature (*dharmatā*) should be followed in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*. If it is argued that the explanation is otherwise, let it be; however, it is said that it does not conform to the logical words [of the text]. Furthermore, even in this way, the aggregate of mental aspects (*ākāra-rāśi*) alone would be a distinct intrinsic nature termed "unreal."

[501,23] It might be argued: "It is included within the imagined (*kalpita*). If so, where is there an imagination of what? If it is argued that it is the imagination of a form (*ākāra*) within that which is formless (*nirākāra*), [we reply: is that which appears within that which does not appear imagined, superimposed (*āropita*), or is it the perception of an effect? However, in the case of luminosity (*prakāśa*), that which is non-luminous, or within a form, that which is formless, is superimposed as if it were something else; thus, its inclusion is indeed within the imagined. Therefore, [501,25]...
That which is devoid of difference and identity, appearing as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) through the form of conceptualization,
and which follows the dependent nature (*paratantra-dharman*), is considered the perfected nature (*niṣpanna*) called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That is said to be the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) of the Blessed One at the arising of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
This body, designated as "dharma," is conventionally expressed by the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) of phenomena.

Such is the meaning of this section. Therefore, if the compilation of the scattered meanings of the teaching is indeed the policy of the Crown Prince, then this [work] provides a much clearer understanding of the meaning of the words;
such is its connection with other treatises.
The power of the distinctions between means of valid cognition has been reflected upon;
as for the commentaries, let them be according to one's preference.

Therefore, there is not even a mention of the doctrine of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*). Now, in the *Uttaratantra*, with reference to the unsurpassed qualities of a Buddha, there is this verse (the reading in the *Uttaratantra* is "subsequent analysis of the qualities of a Buddha"):
"The welfare of oneself, the welfare of others, and the nature of the ultimate body (*paramārthakāya*), as well as the nature of the conventional body (*saṃvṛtikāya*) which is based upon that."
"The fruit, because it consists of dissociation and maturation,
is thus divided into sixty-four qualities" (UT III 1).
In that context, having referred to the bodies of enjoyment of the Dharma for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others, there is the ultimate body and the conventional body.

When established in their respective order, as well as in their nature as the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) and maturation (*vipāka*), the demonstration that the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is conventional is stated as follows:
"How can it be said that there is no talk of formlessness (*nirākāra*) when it establishes the ultimate (*paramārtha*) as being without form? And thus, the commentary on that very point states:
The ultimate body is the basis for the perfection of oneself;
the conventional body of the Sage is the basis for the perfection of others.
"The first body is endowed with the qualities of dissociation, such as the powers (*bala*) and so forth;

the second, however, consists of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) which are the results of maturation (*vaipākika*). (III.2–3) Thus, this explanation is merely a presentation motivated solely by the desire for benefit, and it has already been refuted previously regarding the *dharmakāya*.

In the investigation of the nature of substantial phenomena, how could the Lord, having begun to speak of the qualities of a Buddha for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, cease until he has described the uncommon *nirmāṇakāya*? Or else, how [could he do so] when it is said therein: "The pure *svābhāvikakāya* is to be known as like a jewel-body"?
Because the nature is unconditioned and because it is the locus of the jewels of the qualities.
Because of being the great sovereign of the Dharma, the Enjoyment Body (*sambhogakāya*) is like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);

and because of being like a reflection, the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is like a golden image. (UT I 151–152) By this, the conventional nature of the Emanation Body is clearly stated; for, having been brought forth from the Dharmakāya—which serves as its source—it exercises great sovereignty over the Dharma.
[503,7] How should one apply this to the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is exalted as equal to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)?
[503,8] As the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said:
[503,9] "I here prostrate to that *saṃbhogakāya* established in the great kingdom of Dharma. (***)

Thus, this is the meaning of the verse: having referred to the enjoyment of the Dharma for one’s own sake and for the sake of others, the conventional designation "ultimate body" (*paramārthakāya*) is prescribed, because those two are the objects of supreme gnosis and are the supreme goals to be accomplished. Having thus stated the non-duality of desire as subsumed within the ultimate, he states the third: "and the state of being a conventional body based upon that. This is because an emanation is like a reflection.
Because it is established as being conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Furthermore, it was previously established that dependence (*āśritatva*) is direct in the *saṃbhogakāya* and indirect in the *dharmakāya*.

In the *vivṛti* as well, having restated the first two bodies denoted by the term "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), their status as the basis for the perfection of self (*ātmasampatti*) is prescribed. In that regard:

He who, in the midst of the assembly, displays his own great and manifold majesty—which transcends the senses, is inconceivable, and is the fruit of hundreds of his own deeds—for the sake of bringing joy to the wise;
of that majesty, the *saṃbhogakāya* is clearly the empowerment and the basis (*āśraya*). The *dharmakāya*, however, is the support of that.

It has already been shown. He states the third [point] with the latter half [of the verse]: therein, by way of the analogy of a reflection and through worldly convention, the conventional state is established in the root text. However, in the commentary (*vivṛti*), it is explained that "Buddha" is merely a designation in the sense of an emanation (*nirmāṇa*) according to reality; it is not that he is the Buddha himself, for such is a conventional term. Furthermore, his fruit of human effort is well-known as being common to external yogins, and thus it is not discussed separately. As for its essential nature, however—
It has been stated that all three are also uncommon qualities.

[503,24] Now, if the term *paramārtha* (ultimate reality) is thus applied to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), how is it explained in relation to the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) as well? [503,25] It is not so, because the meanings are different. For emptiness is the *paramārtha* by virtue of being the object of supreme gnosis (*paramajñāna*), whereas the *sambhogakāya* is the *paramārtha* because it is the supreme purpose (*paramaprayojana*) consisting in the fulfillment of one's own welfare (*svārthasampatti*). And so, while the word *svārtha* itself was shown to apply to the *sambhogakāya*, it is now further stated to apply to the *dharmakāya*.

It is considered "one's own object" (*svārtha*) because the object (*artha*) is for oneself. Consequently, there is no fault due to the distinction of objects. [Objection: But is it not also said that the *dharmakāya* is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*)? And in that case, since it is one's own object, there is no harm [to the definition].
