[Response: True; however, this is merely a conventional designation (*vyavasthāmātra*). It does not possess the status of being something to be accomplished by way of being produced (*nirvartyatayā*), as is the case with the *saṃbhogakāya*. Thus, the distinction of objects is established. Likewise, the state of being for the sake of others (*parārthatā*) is direct in the case of the *nirmāṇakāya*, whereas in the case of the *saṃbhogakāya*, it is through that [nirmāṇakāya] as a medium; so it is stated in the scriptures (*āgama*). Alternatively, the word *paramārtha* alone has been made a synonym for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), [referring to] the *paramārthakāya*.

Thus, since this is stated as being based on the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), there is no contradiction. Or rather, how much can one insist upon regarding such playful manifestations of faith? Let it be for now. This remains established: that not even a whisper of the theory of formless cognition (*nirākāravāda*) exists here.
How then did the venerable teacher Dignāga state the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*)?
"This is the negation of the imagined" is the summary view:
every aspect that has ascended to the state of being an object of knowledge is considered imagined within the mind.

Thus, the meaning here is as follows: every aspect (ākāra) that has ascended into cognition is conceptually constructed as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). The negation of that which is conceptually constructed as an object of knowledge means the negation of its status as a graspable object (*grāhyatva*). As it is said:
"Because of the absence of that, this too is non-existent. (*tadabhāvāt tad apy asat*) (* ***)

Regarding this, the master Sthiramati [states]: "Because of the non-existence of objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is non-existent in its capacity as a cognizer, but not in its appearance as objects, sentient beings, self, and representations (*vijñapti*).

For if that [appearance] were non-existent, it would follow that [consciousness] is entirely non-existent, since no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness is described apart from those [appearances].
Or, if it had an intrinsic nature distinct from them, how could it be consciousness, or how could it be differentiated from them? In this regard, then:
What is to be done?
Since that which appears is indeed non-existent, it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). For that power which manifests the non-existent is designated as "ignorance."
Thus,
this very story of the courtesan’s death has arrived;
it is a difficult-to-cross entanglement from which one can somehow escape alone.
Let it be so; however, even in this case, the error belongs to you alone, due to a failure to consider what precedes and follows. For it is said:
"I do not see that Buddha or that awakening through the primary designations. From here until the conclusion, the refutation of imagined things is to be understood.

In this regard, what could even you do if the negation of manifestation (*prakāśa*) itself were intended anywhere? Therefore, by the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) alone is denoted; the meaning is that it is precisely an unreal external form that is fashioned and displayed by it. For this has already been stated in the context of refuting the difference or non-difference between form and emptiness; thus, there is no fault. Consequently, this is *khyāti*...
The meaning is that of determination (*adhyavasāya*).

Having concealed its own innate nature (*nijaṃ svarūpam*), it is brought under the sway of ignorance (*avidyā*); it appears otherwise, like an illusion (*māyā*)—in this regard, the term "appears" (*bhāti*) is used according to common understanding.

For it is not that an elephant appears in an illusory elephant; rather, it is merely apprehended as such. If one were to accept it otherwise, then even silver and the like would appear [as real], and thus the twofold classification [of appearances] would be lost. And because it is so, the teaching in the *Prajñāpāramitā* relies upon three [bases].
The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected.
By all such terms as "it does not exist" and so forth, that which is imagined is refuted;
through similes such as "like an illusion," the dependent nature is taught.
The perfected nature is proclaimed through fourfold purification;
for in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is no other teaching of the Buddha.

Thus, because one follows the meaning of the method of the unimpaired perfections (*pāramitā*), it is stated here that even for the dependent nature (*paratantra*), its aspect (*ākāra*) is not non-existent; rather, mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*) is existent. By this, there would be no difference from the method of the perfections and so forth. Nor has he clarified his own intended position and made an extension (*atideśa*) stating that "the meaning of that should also be viewed in this way. Furthermore, there is no demonstration of a specific distinction regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) by which [the two systems] might thus differ.
[It] would be led away. The non-dual gnosis of the perfection of wisdom—that is the Tathāgata.
This is because it establishes the emptiness of the mere grasped and grasper as that which is to be realized; otherwise, one would have to speak merely of "absence of appearance."

Furthermore, that very same aspect cannot be both the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), because it lacks the defining characteristics of those two; thus, reality would be merely imagined as divided into the apprehended and so forth. Moreover, the *saṃbhogakāya* would have to be specified as either worldly or metaphorical, since this treatise has begun with the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) of the *Bhagavatī*, and such a distinction is not stated elsewhere. What further [purpose] is there for these commentaries (*vārtika*)? That is the point.
What is the point of smearing oneself with the impurity of another? Or rather, it is one's own.
In some cases there are only virtues and not excellent form;
and in other cases there is form, but specifically not virtues.
But these qualities and this form, which consist of the perfection of uncommon yoga, have taken refuge in you.
Thus, because the distinction is made manifest, enough with further elaboration. Nor is it our intention to exert effort in supporting the author’s intent beyond what is possible.
However, these [masters] are considered to belong to a single lineage; for instance:
when the lord of kings, who carried the doctrine of the Conqueror free from passion (Anaṅgajit), ruled over Ārya-Asaṅga...
The teacher Vasubandhu, possessed of lofty intelligence, shone forth by his command; then Dignāga,
who rendered extraordinary assistance to Kumāranātha,
[established] therein a faultless position through the efforts of the authors of the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya*.
However, it has been demonstrated that even though the lineages of the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna differ, their established position regarding the reality to be proven is indeed common;
this is because they accept uncontradicted self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, in this way:
some understand the Buddha to have a body of false form, devoid of consciousness.
The nature of consciousness is formless, resembling the sky, and non-erroneous; yet others hold that the nature of consciousness has a beautiful body that is false, though it is free from error.
Still others maintain that this [consciousness], being devoid of falsity, should be accepted as that which appears.

Therefore, since the enjoyment-dharma (*sambhogadharma*)— that is, the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)— is established through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), what need is there for anything else? For even if it were to exist, how could that which is perceived as distinct due to its differentiation be its own nature, even if they occupy the same location, like the beings of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

[506,18] But surely the Blessed One has been described in the Pāramitā system itself as having the nature of the fourfold gnosis, such as the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśana-jñāna*) and so forth. Therefore, [506,19] if it is asked: "How can there be any doubt even regarding the present topic?"—in that case too, the resolution is achieved precisely through the state of non-dual diversity (*citrādvaita*). For, in the case of the formless (*nirākāra*), any mutual distinction is indeed difficult to establish. As it has been said: "Or how could they be distinguished from one another? Even if there were a distinction...

If there is no mutual awareness [between cognitions], that very same fault remains. And if one accepts the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaita*), what is the need for anything else? If it is argued that even the non-duality of the variegated has not been stated [by the author], we say no; for, as a proponent of cognition with forms (*sākārajñānavādin*), he depends upon that [non-duality], just like his formal proof (*sādhana*). Indeed, even the entire mass of subjects in the *Vārttika* was not stated therein solely for the purpose of proving that [non-duality]. Therefore, just as in the case of that [proof], its conclusion is reached precisely through that very statement.

That too has already been refuted. This is like searching for a lamp by means of a lamp; for while the Blessed One introduces the idea that he alone is of the nature of the four gnoses, one nevertheless seeks a manifold non-duality. The same arguments should be applied to the characteristics of a painting and so forth.
For this very reason, as it is stated in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "Those very conceptual constructions proceed, but they do not proceed as appearances of duality. Thus...
Regarding the statement that "purification is to be sought," even there, the meaning is simply that there are appearances of duality and determinations of duality.

Furthermore, the word *vikalpa* does not mean "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*), but rather "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*). For this very reason, the plural number is used. And this is logical;
for nowhere else has another meaning for the word "duality" been stated apart from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). Nor do those two appear directly.

But it is merely a conceptual determination (*avasāya*), like the case of an illusory elephant being treated as an actual elephant. Otherwise, since purification (*vyavadāna*) would occur at the very moment all mental aspects (*sarvākāra*) are extinguished, how could there be the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) as the fulfillment of one's own welfare? Thus, all systematic arrangements (*sarvavyavasthā*) would be destroyed.

Furthermore, since there is no demonstration of the unreality of aspects and the reality of the aspectless, how can that [objection] be avoided? If you say, "Therefore, let it be inferred," [we reply:]...
No, because it has a different meaning. However, when it is explained in that way, there is no assumption of another meaning. And thus, in that very same [text]:
"Having realized that objects are mere mental chatter, he abides in mind-only which appears as those [objects]."

Regarding this, the commentary states: "Having understood that objects are merely produced by the mind, one's abiding in 'mind-only' which appears as those [objects] is the bodhisattva’s stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Thereafter comes the direct realization of the *dharmadhātu*, which is free from the two characteristics—the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper. This is the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore, even the stage of the aids to penetration is not present here [in the latter case].
The loss of that aspect is said to occur during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and not at any point on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

However, the exhaustion of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper occurs everywhere. Therefore, the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) consisting of the grasped and the grasper does not arise again; this is the meaning of the search for purification.

[507,17] But has it not been stated that on the seventh stage, which is comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is effort (*sābhoga*) and lack of effort (*anābhoga*), and on the eighth stage, the avoidance of signs (*nimitta*)? And since a sign (*nimitta*) is indeed a mental aspect (*ākāra*), is this some kind of "Nāga-world dialect" or an "instructor’s fist" [i.e., a secret concealment]? [507,19] Or rather, is it that the aspect (*ākāra*) is called the sign of error (*bhrāntinimitta*) or the sign of conceptual proliferation (*prapañcanimitta*), because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of error? Let us set that aside for now.
To that extent, even for an external object that exists, there is no necessity that its form be the cause of error, because that [error] is bound solely to latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).

Furthermore, although it has been stated that similarity is also a means of establishing stable error, nevertheless, in the case of a non-noble person (*anārya*), only a specific latent predisposition remains as the basis. And if, at some time, there were an avoidance [of error] due to dwelling with error, let that first apply to the formless [cognition] alone.

Or rather, whatever can be established as a cause of error—such as the perception of non-existent forms—that very thing is what is to be negated as the referent of the word "cause. How, then, can there be confidence in this statement? Furthermore, you yourself deny the causal relationship among those phenomena that are conceptually constructed, on the grounds that they are unreal (*alīka*). And yet, regarding the form (*ākāra*) which is itself accepted as unreal...

It is well-established that there is a capacity within error. If you argue that its capacity is spoken of by way of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that has that [object] as its objective support (*ālambana*), then let the conceptual construction itself be what is to be abandoned. Furthermore, since for you that very mental aspect (*ākāra*) is itself the error, what is the point of mentioning a cause (*nimitta*)? Moreover, if one considers the continuity [of the stream of consciousness], it would follow that all things to be abandoned must be indicated solely by the word "cause. This is because [the object] is without an objective support (*nirālambana*).

Furthermore, its having an erroneous object is not established from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Even if it were to exist conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), it would not be a cause for that which is to be abandoned; so what is the use of this [concept], which is like a rotten pumpkin?

Therefore, the factor dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—recognized as a real property of things (*vastu-dharma*) and serving as the cause for the conventional usage of distinction—is precisely what is intended by the term "sign" (*nimitta*).

Let it be understood that what is called "apprehension" (*udgraha*) is both a conceptual designation (*saṃjñā*) and something to be abandoned, because that which is differentiated has no existence. If, then, even that [apprehension] must be accepted as the cause for the conventional usage of differentiation solely by way of its own object-discriminating thought (*vikalpa*), then discriminative thought alone is what is to be abandoned. True. That itself is its abandonment, because—like a mental image (*ākāra*)—it lacks any self-manifestation. And if there is the relinquishing of the mental image, then from this...

On this very stage, the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*) becomes even more predominant, because one penetrates all signs (*nimitta*) as being signless (*animitta*), yet does not cease the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) resulting from that [penetration]. Thus, there is no contradiction with the explanation. For the conventional usage resulting from that is shown in both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Ṭīkā* to be precisely the conventional usage of differentiation (*bhedavyavahāra*). And that [differentiation] is [the object] even of a mental wish devoid of any form (*ākāra*).

[508,11] It is not an object. Furthermore, it is not the case that the mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*) of the Blessed Ones arises only when forms (*ākāra*) have been discarded. To claim that it is mundane is merely a display of one's own fancy, because there is no such thing as "noble recollection" (*āryarājasmṛti*). How then is the mirror-like gnosis described in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*:

"It is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge, yet it does not manifest toward them"? Regarding this, the commentary states: "And it does not manifest toward them, because it is without form (*anākāratvāt*)."
[508,14] This is not a fault, because it was stated with the intention that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is that the "aspects" (*ākāra*) are the modes of the cognition of the object.

[508,15] The meaning is that it is not called a "face" (*mukha*) because there is an absence of the mode of grasping that [face], even though the reflection of the object of knowledge arises. And this is very clear precisely because it is mirror-like cognition (*ādarśajñāna*). And thus, immediately thereafter:

Regarding the passage, "And because of the arising of the reflection of the wisdom of the Sambhogakāya-buddhahood, that [is so]," the commentary states here: "It is the Sambhogakāya-buddha, and because of the arising of the reflection of wisdom, it is called 'mirror-like wisdom' (*ādarśajñāna*). Therefore, in the phrase "because the appearance of objects and sentient beings is without aspect," it is also logical to understand this as "because it is without a grasper."

This has been analyzed by Ācārya Sthiramati. Likewise, it has already been demonstrated that the venerable Master Vasubandhu himself explained elsewhere that even the term "non-appearance" (*anābhāsa*) has the meaning of being "without an object."

How, then, is it that the non-existence of the knowable is itself the arising of the reflection of the knowable? It is said: in whatever manner one previously adhered to the universe as being external or as mere consciousness, for one whose intention is to accomplish the welfare of others through great compassion, there arises a vow to know all aspects and everything at every moment and in every atom; in that very same manner, the arising of knowledge occurs. And therein, in the absence of external objects—

Even so, there exist various distinct forms due to the differentiation of the transformations within the continuum of consciousness; the perception of that form is itself the perception of the object. Nor does this consequence apply even to external insentient things, because we have established that existence belongs to manifestation alone.

Therefore, another mental continuum, although not manifest to the other, exists as self-manifesting. But this is not the case for the insentient, for that would entail the loss of its very nature as insentient.

This is logical; however, what assurance is there regarding the very existence of another continuum? Is it not for that very purpose that the establishment of another continuum occurs? But in this case, that is irrelevant to the subject at hand.

[Objection: Is it not the case that your intention (*āśaya*) therein is profound and not capable of being grasped by us? Furthermore, the perception of that reflection (*pratibimba*) is precisely what constitutes omniscience (*sārvajñya*), which is the very subject under discussion. [Response: For an aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) depends upon the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of another's mind. Whether that other person actually becomes so or not, it is simply through the cultivation of a fixed form—thinking, "I shall become one of such a nature, with such a retinue, vessel, and requisites"—that the arising of that mental aspect occurs. That itself is...

And when there is cognition of everything, then there is no harm. But when the form of another's question arises, then the very vow—"O, may I have the form of a response"—is the means; in that case, it is appropriate only when that [other person] exists. Even so, there is no harm to the vow because of the possibility of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). And when another continuum (*santānāntara*) exists, it will be established accordingly; even when it does not exist, there is the perfection of the equipment for the superimposition of its own nature.

Thus, there will be no impairment of the thesis for the minister Śubhasañjaya; and those very [cognitions] are what are designated by the term "knowable reflection" (jñeyapratibimba), because they superimpose a knowable object upon their own internal forms (svākāra).
[509,11] But how can there be a vow if there is no certainty? [It arises] from the instruction of others, from conviction regarding sentient beings, and because there is no subverting factor.

[509,12] Nor is there any fault; indeed, this very [conviction] constitutes the totality of the conditions for one's own welfare. And in this regard, according to the opinion of the Commentator—who, as a proponent of the non-duality of the variegated, rejects the existence of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth—how could there be instruction from others? This is due to his adherence to the position that [cognition] is devoid of aspects (*nirākāra*).
For some, it acts like a venomous serpent of hatred. In this regard, the recitation of the mantra is as follows:
"One who is devoid of partiality toward dharma and adharma, who devours all, thrives in happiness;
he who is empty of deliberation on what is proper or improper, and whose speech is according to his own whim."
For instance, this was directly challenged and stated by the Crown Prince and others through their advocacy of *sākāravāda* (the theory of cognition with forms).

Furthermore, this doctrine of the non-duality of the variegated (*citrādvaitavāda*) was established by the author of the *Vārttika*, while its commentator is being refuted. This is like the punishment of Māṇḍavya due to the crime of a thief. Or rather, [it is as follows:]
One who stands directly facing the sun with impaired vision indeed overcomes the sun; however, one with healthy vision does not perceive the path or the non-path because of that glare.
By speaking thus, neither reality (*tattva*), nor conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), nor your own position, nor the position of others has been considered. For:
Even though one has established a footing in self-cognition due to the conceit of being a Yogācāra, one still perceives the existence of other things.
What further insult could there be for us than this? Indeed, from that, even doubt becomes difficult to find.
If there is doubt, what fruit could there be for you? And if there is even something, why not have certainty?
If there is no expectation, how can there be doubt regarding self-awareness? Cast aside this blindness of ritual injunction!

For there is no human effort whatsoever on its part such that, by means of it, it could bring about the cognition of another, since that would entail the consequence of the loss of its established nature.
Nor is the absence of difference in the material cause possible here for one who asserts that [cognition is] formless; the rest is the same.
If [it is argued that] the dependence on conventional reality is for the sake of doubt...
Why is certainty regarding that not sought?
If [it is argued that] even inference is impossible for a manifold non-duality,
then manifold non-duality is indeed proclaimed as the ultimate reality.

And the manifold non-duality of the variegated has been demonstrated. In that regard, if one mental state is inferred elsewhere through the representation of speech and so forth by means of a single common condition (*ekopādhi*), why indeed would one draw it back [to the side of the opponent] out of hostility toward the doctrine of images (*sākāravāda*)? For in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), that single common condition is simply non-existent. And yet, you seek inference within conventional reality? Or else, [what else could it be?]

As long as conventional reality exists, it is a real convention because it is not sublated by inference. Even if this [convention] is sluggish regarding external objects, it does not function without the existence of another cognition. Therefore, until the end of saṃsāra, the Teacher is an object of inference; thereafter, however, [he is not].
Since perception has self-awareness as its very nature, what other means of knowledge could there be for it?

This would be most clearly demonstrated by the principle that "that which is seen by oneself is indeed seen. At that time, there is no dependence upon the instruction of another; when there is such dependence, then inference is unavoidable. The very cessation of that [inference] is called the direct realization of non-duality.
That too is not far for us; for you [merely] exceed [us] in the state of becoming like space (*ākāśībhāva*).

Nor can there be inference from it, nor anything else. Therefore, this object is indeed profound; even when it is not ascertained, how can one avoid the conventional practice that proceeds by relying on the instruction of a trustworthy person, having examined it to the best of one's ability while resolving upon its existence? This same principle applies even in the Middle Way system (*madhyamā-naya*), because self, otherness, and so forth are merely conventional (*saṃvṛta*). Furthermore, in that context, even an "other" does not appear within the conventional.

To that extent, it is possible; for even then, one must rely solely on inference. Furthermore, it has been established that there is no difference in reality between the Madhyamaka and the Mātravāda positions. Moreover:
Some know everything to be like an appearance, while others know it to be appearance alone.
[510,23] For some, how much of a difference is there here regarding that which is devoid of the capacity for any object whatsoever?

If it is argued that this teaching of emptiness is unprecedented, [we reply: when it is demonstrated by a single crown prince, even the corroboration by an intermediate authoritative person (*pramāṇapuruṣa*) is more than sufficient; what need is there for the assistance of others? And it is said in the *Candrapradīpa*:
"Many people speak of the emptiness of the aggregates."
And they do not understand that things are selfless;
not understanding this, being indeed incited by others and overcome by anger, they speak harshly to a person.
Thus, analysis is the refuge; therefore, it has indeed been performed in some manner or other.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the fourfold establishment of stability maintained? it is said: There is no difference between these two in terms of substantial reality (*dravyataḥ*) as there is in external systems; rather, with respect to a single undivided reality to be demonstrated, conventional usage is made by way of affirmation and negation. And this is due to the difference among those to be trained (*vineya*). Briefly, those to be trained are of two types: those who habitually engage in superimposition (*āropacarita*) and those who habitually engage in denial (*apavādacarita*).

In this regard, for those whose disposition is characterized by the tendency toward denial (*apavāda*), the Blessed One’s teaching is presented by way of affirmation (*vidhimukha*), delineating the existence of things as being limited to mere appearance; by that much, the system of consciousness (*vijñānanaya*) is established. However, for those whose disposition is characterized by the tendency toward superimposition (*āropa*), the teaching of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) is presented by way of negation (*pratiṣedhamukha*); this is called "abiding in the Middle Way. For even when all superimpositions are excluded, there remains nothing but the manifold appearance itself.

This is now impossible to deny, as it is established by its own implication: even for one whose conduct is characterized by nihilism (*ucchedacarita*), when grasping at the existence of consciousness, its existence is likewise nothing but the nature of mere appearance; thus there is a single conclusion regarding the tenet, just like statements concerning similarity and dissimilarity.
For one whose conduct is characterized by reification (*āropacarita*), the detailed teaching is primarily given from that perspective, in view of what is generally possible. To explain:
In that which is naturally pure and free from all superimpositions and conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*),
whatever slight thing is projected here shines forth as something utterly unbearable;
yet this limitless burden cast upon it is thus rendered in vain by others.
Just as if the self of an entity had long since descended from palm to palm.
For this very reason, even the statement that "everything is non-existent," regardless of conceptual qualifications, is well-suited for one whose nature is to engage in superimposition (*samāropa*).

For he, like a lazy man, will remain fixed against a wall when strongly impelled; such is the sense. Therefore, because these two are of the same lineage and are in fact kinsmen, their dispute is groundless. As it is said:
What is the use of a manifestation that exists yet is devoid of all capacity?
Due to the absence of capacity, there can be no effect; but where would its own nature go?

And there is no difference in the object of cognition (*prameya*) here, other than the mere conceit regarding the application or non-application of the word "existent. Furthermore, since there is neither increase nor decrease resulting from the use or non-use of a word employed according to one's whim, it is easy to prevent disputes. As for those who deny even that which is manifesting, who superimpose a variegated form that is unmanifest yet designated as "manifest," and who [posit] the power of the object and so forth—

Or rather, the goal (*sādhya*) is unprecedented; for they have strayed far from even those Vijñānavādins who postulate the mere power of objects (*artha-śakti-mātra*), and thus they do not share in kinship. Furthermore, "conflict culminates in a single point. Therefore, in reality, even the Madhyamaka is non-duality alone. Nor is there any difficulty in establishing the fourfold state of stability, because there is no contradiction anywhere in the state of being Samantabhadra.
Nor is there non-extinction.

As for what was said: "If not, then this non-dual is indeed eternal"—this is a witty remark intended to refute the proponents of formlessness (*nirākāravāda*), or else it is with respect to other Mādhyamikas. However, in reality:
"It is not non-existent, because its nature is luminosity; nor is it existent, because of those others."
If the world were thus devoid of the four peaks— neither one nor two, nor non-dual, nor both—
then what would be the distinction between the views of the Commentator and the Middle Way?

For those for whom even causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) exists only from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is indeed a negation of even that which has the nature of manifestation.
Let there be a distinction among them; however, it is naturally difficult to overcome.
This path for the knower of the self has as its essence the burden of daring.
And there is the refutation of the commentator, who stands in the position of a rival king, either by means of what is established for the opponent or through his own admission.
Furthermore, it is clearly evident that the author of the *Vārttika* alone is the leader here in this section concerning the establishment of the policy of a crown prince. Moreover, what is more?
Even while entering the Middle Way, he does not overstep his own experience;
he expresses his own preference regarding the forms of things,
and he refutes the notion of cause and effect as possessing intrinsic qualities.
Therefore, that very same style is established even for the treasury of the eyes.
What praise can there be for him who, like the manifest majesty and power of the Teacher himself, protects the Teaching from the mouths of the rākṣasas of cruel and innumerable adversaries?
Or rather, what praise can there be for him who, having undertaken the task of the Mandara mountain in its vigorous churning, [has stirred up the ocean of the Dharma]?
For the fortunate who possess the perfection of the ultimate truth, this immeasurable ocean of hardships is for their joy.

"Even by a mere statement, 'What one desires is obtained in the ocean,' a child, out of the force of his own restlessness, began [to enter it], for fear arose even upon hearing it. He would have reached the edge of that shore and met his destruction had he not entered this primary ocean of nectar."
This is its quality: that it causes the sky to tremble, adorned with garlands of the ocean's waves.
Since this state has been attained even while mimicking the play of a child, toward the Teacher Mañjuśrī— who is honored as having manifested in the form of a youth—
may all these people everywhere thereby attain the highest good.
The sprout of the single root of supreme bliss, brought forth by the mastery of the glory of knowledge consisting of unimpeded loving-kindness.
The sixth chapter: The Determination of the Duality of Both.
[513,8] And thus is completed this treatise on the Proof of Cognizance (*Sākārasiddhiśāstra*), which was commenced by way of an examination of strengths and weaknesses [513,9],
the work of the great scholar Jñānaśrīmitra-pāda.
Sākārasaṃgrahasūtram,
First Chapter:
Wisdom, having dragged down our beloved who had reached the state of being like the sky, has indeed been brought low by whom...

While those of celebrated fame stand in this assembly, this Duḥśāsana—who consists of cruel injustice and the method of repudiation—has now fallen into the cage of my arms; let him be guarded, O Kauravas! (1)

Having raised up various displays of prowess by the learned masters regarding the *Sākāra*, *Anākāra*, and *Madhyamaka* systems, this burden now rests upon me concerning the elucidation of the system of the Leader, the Crown Prince [Maitreya],
as described in the final verses of the commentary on the venerable Nāgārjuna’s authoritative position.
The effort of one with a neutral mind toward investigating whether those [qualities] are deficient or excessive is fruitful. ||2||

The fact that cognitions possess forms, the restriction of existence and its cessation, and the beautiful form of the Buddha—these do not exist as real entities because of the loss of the cause and the pervasion; rather, let them simply be "existent" by virtue of self-cognition.
This avoids contradiction with the noble Teacher, constitutes a thorough acquaintance with the principles, and represents the Dharma-body and the two systems.
The *Sākārasiddhi* teaches that the supreme [state] is the non-difference between liberation and abiding. ||3||

He whose stainless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is attained through self-awareness of a form as beautiful as the ornament of all unique and complete qualities; he who is the sole bulbous root for the multitude of vines that benefit the three realms.
May Kandarpaketu, who dwells in the highest heaven of Akaniṣṭha, protect us. ||4||
Through the lineage of treatises devoted to its proof,
and by the effort to establish it for the world of diverse intellects,
the entire flood of non-Buddhist outsiders who deny it has been destroyed.
But those who are renowned for the virtues of union with that path are indeed irresistible. ||5||
Even when it appears, this manifold variety of forms is indeed unreal, for it is devoid of the nature of either one or the other.
Even in that case, another reality— self-cognition— is accepted.
Where is the Protector, when only that [deed] remains as a pure legend? //6//
This path follows the method of the Crown Prince, which consists of the statements of reason and scripture; thus, this proclamation is established within the system of the Sākṛtinaya,
just as a formal debate proceeds according to the sequence of the disputants' positions.
But that method of writing has become scattered. ||7||
In brief, he will compose this treasury of sūtras that summarizes that meaning;
for otherwise, this practice for the benefit of others would not exist.
But one's own welfare is unavoidable through the practice of reality. ||8||
That which is called "manifestation" is never experienced as being without an aspect, even in a dream.
Therefore, the non-perception of the object does not invalidate the sense faculty; rather, it establishes it. //9//
Because qualities and so forth are insentient, their non-perception is accompanied by a qualification;
it requires sublation, and thus there is no delay in self-cognition. (10)
When the white essence of awakening is manifest, the cognition of awakening is thereby established;
for when "non-birth" is being perceived, why is there no comprehension of "cowness" in what is not a cow? (11)
Furthermore, if the location were distinct, then the determination of that distinction would be uncontradicted;
however, if there is no distinction in the location, then that [determination] is simply the non-distinction of its own nature. (12)
There is no spatial distinction between wind and sunlight, nor between two collections of atoms that possess resistance; yet the cognition conforms to them in such a way as to appear grosser.

Whether there be no distinction of location due to the end of the obstruction, or whether it be white, the same refutation applies to the alternative views that the whole is either identical with or different from the atoms. (14)
Just as there is a distinction between two moments despite the appearance of non-difference, due to a subverting proof.

Because they appear as non-different, there is no distinction between two moments; however, there is a clear distinction between two cognitions of blue. Otherwise, unity could never exist anywhere. (16)
There is no sublation when there is a non-presuppositional negation (paryudāsa), for there are two means of valid cognition that establish it;
as for the case of absolute negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), the loss of sublation is, for now, difficult to maintain.
Because it is sometimes sublated by something else, that [cognition] is indeed known to be like [the cognition of] blue;
however, the mere appearance of sublation exists even in the case of a false object when there is doubt. (18)
Therefore, since difference is not established by itself as a property, difference cannot be a constituent part of its proof;
for two moments that exist simultaneously, their difference would consist only in the distinction between the time of cause and the time of effect.

And thus, even when the difference between effects is abstracted away, there is no such thing as a single time for that which manifests without distinction, like the light of a lamp and its yellowness. //20//
Furthermore, if there were a sublation here but not there, it would imply a duality between the two, because that which possesses a nature incapable of being sublated is perceived as distinct. (21)
Furthermore, for that which lacks a distinct aspect, there is no separate appearance apart from its blueness;
however, the determination of spatial pervasion serves as a proof for this very point when it is challenged by an opposing argument.

Even if a reason is established therein, if it is not considered capable, then surely there is no connection with the probandum; therefore, it is not competent even with respect to the form [of the object]. ||23||
The quality of "shining" (bhāsa) exists in the shining blue object;
because it constitutes its very nature, both sublation and non-sublation are equal for the two. [24]
If there is no manifestation of the blue, what could be more reckless than this?
Even if its manifestation were to come from something else, it would be impossible to prevent. (25)

If its manifestation does not come from anything else, and if its manifestation were something entirely other than itself, then that blue would not be manifested; for what purpose would there be a manifestation of something else? (26)
Therefore, its manifestation is undeniable from whatever source it may come;
for when a jar or the like is illuminated by a lamp, is it not indeed manifested? (27)
The statement of its sublation is fruitless because there is room for the sublation of the locus (*dharmin*);
for while that which appears is its manifestation, that manifestation itself is not perceived as such. (28)
If blue and so forth are luminous, what need have they for another luminosity?
If blue and so forth are not luminous, what need have they for another luminosity? (29)
For illumination by another is destroyed, and nothing else is established; whose sublation could there be, and for what reason? Because everything is subject to doubt regarding its basis. (30)
Now, if there is indeed a manifestation, that is considered to be the property of "blue";
since its distinction is established by the fact that it is not sublated, what was intended is proven. (31)
For a blue object that is appearing, there must necessarily be a property expressed by speech; for otherwise, the claim of its distinction would be contradicted by a clear [cognition]. (32)
Furthermore, if that mere appearance is not sublated by self-awareness, why does blue and so forth not likewise rush toward sublation even within self-awareness? (33)
If self-cognition does not belong to the blue, why does it not appear? To say, "Let it be made manifest by another," is refuted in such a manner. (34)
If it is argued that there is no "otherness" because of non-existence, then how can there even be a notion of "self"?
Furthermore, the incapacity for appearing [as an object] is stated while closing one's eyes. (35)

[518,17] Now, if it is argued that this mutual doubt arises from the imagined identity [of the appearance with the object], [518,18] then from the appearance there is the imagined identity, and from the appearance there is the conceptualization of identity. (36)
It is generally accepted that a conceptual construction (kalpita) is of no use regarding any object;
yet for this long time, even this has been held as something to be believed. (37)
Therefore, since nothing else is possible, the claim that the mind appears with false forms due to the affliction of the latencies of error is merely a bolstering of a conceptual construction. (38)
Furthermore, in this case, the example of "dreams being false" is devoid of the probandum;
for how could there be an appearance of any other object by means of something that is not distinct from its own [subjective] experience? (39)
Even though they are not manifest due to ignorance, let the forms produced by it exist;
however, the illuminations arise just as a lamp does from its own cause.
Nevertheless, if it depends upon a cause, its self-luminosity is undermined.
Even if an experience is distinct from another, does it not cognize itself simply by arising? (41)
Therefore, since self-cognition is absent in some cases, there would be no conventional usage;
for the same logic applies even to a collection of letters. (42)
Whether it be manifesting by itself or by another, this consideration applies to blue and the like; however, it does not apply to that which is non-manifesting and formless. (43)
Nor is mere appearance [of form] a product by means of causes;
for that which depends on the operation of another for its own arising is called a "product. (44)
Furthermore, due to the absence of causal capacity, the absence of being an effect is sublated by that very same fact;
therefore, let this be considered elsewhere, since the production of form from a configuration is observed. (45)
Or rather, the white effect is not capable [of being produced]; why? Because it arises without depending on anything else.
If you say that it is pervaded by capacity, then let capacity also be inferred. ||46||
For there is no doubt regarding its being an effect; however, its causal capacity is what is to be proven, because of the presence of doubt.
Even the appearance of hair is not something that is not an effect, yet it is devoid of capacity when it is merely superimposed upon [the visual field].
And it has already been observed that in the absence of an object of appropriation (*upādāna*), what could possibly be manifest?
Therefore, one must accept that this blue thing, which possesses the nature of manifestation, is born [from something else]. (48)
If there is a difference due to non-sublation, how can the absence of sublation be accepted?
The capacity of self-cognition has just now been refuted. (49)
If it is argued that there is no superimposition because its nature is not superimposed, from where does the cognition of non-superimposition arise?
If it is argued that there is no superimposition due to the absence of sublation, this involves mutual dependence.
The luminosity of light is not a superimposed form; it is that very nature itself.
Likewise, the blueness of the blue is not a superimposed form; it is that very nature itself. //51//
Blue does not exist without manifestation; yet if it were to exist even without that manifestation, then what other pervasive property imagined by you would not be similar? (52)
Furthermore, illumination does not remain as blue even when [the object] is yellow;
otherwise, why would a universal be arbitrarily excluded? //53//
And if there were otherness, just as blue does not exist without illumination, so too this illumination would not exist without blue; thus it would possess illumination and possess form. (54)
If difference is established through mutual deviation, what is the point of a blue lotus?
Is there not a difference even between a cloth and water; for what is it that is not determined by the perception of form?

Even in the case of a seed, when its distinct forms are delineated by the index finger according to temporal differences, there may be distinction or non-distinction by means of measurement; however, such is not the case for blue and its manifestation.
The blue object and its manifestation are not distinct;
rather, that very essence which belongs to the imagined [blue] is said to belong to the luminous as well—is this not so? (57)
[520,13] Why is it that its imagined form, such as birth and so forth, is not that very thing?
[520,14] Rather, by means of valid cognition, it is investigated whether that is real or unreal. ||58||
Therefore, even though it appears, why would the distinction be made that blue and so forth are unreal while being considered real entities, on the grounds that there is no subverting cognition? (59)
Alternatively, its establishment as a means of valid cognition is not possible, nor is its connection with causal capacity;
for such capacity is perceived only in the form of a specific configuration, and never in the absence of configuration. (60)
Furthermore, because of the imposition of contradictory properties, there can be no proof of difference without establishing that the two contradictory properties reside in different substrata. (61)
A distinction based on place, time, form, and locus is not possible for two cognitions of blue; therefore, where could there be such a thing as a contradiction between properties? (62)

If, for you, that differentiation is established even in the absence of differences in place, time, or appearance—as it is, for example, in the case of a blue lotus and so forth—[then your argument holds]. (63)
If the mind is that which is self-cognized as the very bliss and so forth throbbing within, and is considered to be formless because it is devoid of forms such as blue; 64.
If cognition exists because of its appearance, then that [cognition] exists for the white as well.
If the manifestation is non-different [from the object], then it belongs to the white just as much as it does to pleasure. (65)
Just as blue is distinct from pleasure, so too is pleasure distinct from blue;
just as "I" am not considered to be blue, so too "I" am not considered to be pleasure. (66)
If the cognition is "I am happy" and not "I am blue," then the presence or absence of conventional usage does not constitute the establishment or sublation of the object. //67//
Even that state would not exist through the conceit of commonality;
nevertheless, it certainly exists in some cases, as in "one who possesses cows," "one who possesses a staff," or "one who possesses fine silk."
Internally, sensation has pleasure and so forth as its object; externally, it has cold and so forth as its domain.
That sensation possesses those respective forms and is indeed seized by a subverting factor.
[521,13] It is said that because of the contraction of its spatial extension, there arises the possibility of an obstruction;
[521,14] even if the defect occupies only a minute portion of space, it is thwarted by even a very small amount. ||70||
For that which does not exist anywhere at any time can never come into existence;
thus, its existence, such as that of pleasure and so forth, has been properly established. (71)
If that [self] were to exist anywhere at all, it would indeed be located in that very place;
however, pleasure and the like are experienced as being non-different from the body. (72)
If measurement by the hand, the span, and so forth were not known with certainty, then what would be the point of the unrestricted land-ownership of kings alone? (73)

Since there is no restriction regarding the means of knowledge (māna) with respect to objects and sense-faculties other than touch and the tangible form, why would there be no sublation even in that case? [74]
Even where a determination is possible regarding a measurement, it cannot be established even in the slightest degree;
for even when there is a determination of fingers and so forth, from that [determination], there is no measurement in reality. //75//

When plunging into a pond, the measurement of pleasure for one who is heated [by fire] is clearly manifest from above, below, and so forth; it is superimposed there through its vivid appearance, and not from anything else. //76//
"The cognition that [the object] is in that location occurs through the door of the tactile faculty" — this too is refuted by the fact that, because it is an error, its attainment is not clear. (77)
If you claim this is merely a sensory illusion and not a different kind of pleasure, then for us, this very thing is happiness: that which is clearly felt as a pleasant sensation. (78)

Alternatively, why not establish a limit even for form and the other [objects], since they too are perceived as such and can be described as being equal to others by virtue of their dependence on the sense faculties such as the eye? 79.

If pleasure and the like were not located in space because their manifestation is restricted, then the entire world would be timeless due to the lack of knowledge regarding their momentary nature. (80)
Just as there is necessity regarding time, so too is there necessity regarding place;
because it cannot be subverted by any contradiction, what is the use here of words that deny it? (81)
Or, even if there were an absence of sublation, on what basis could one have confidence in existence?
For neither identity nor difference can be established as residing in a single locus, since they do not occupy the same place. (82)
Moreover, the absence of a subverting proof is not established by mere non-perception;
for even when one subversion is absent, another subversion might still arise. (83)
If a proof is offered to establish that [the subject] is not sublated by inference, it cannot in any way avoid the refutation of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). (84)
In this same way, suffering, hatred, and so forth are also the inherent nature of all embodied beings.
If it is argued that their abandonment is undesirable even to oneself, then by that very desire, they would persist even if they were non-existent. (85)
In whatever manner the mind is cultivated, it becomes manifest in that very way;
even if it were to take the form of space, there would be no loss of its purpose. (86)
If you desire to leave the sky, you must first abandon this physical body—which is untouched by the defects of saṃsāra and radiant with the primary and secondary marks. [87]
If it were all-pervading like space, then the same refutation would apply to it as well, even when compared to light, lightning, jewels, flames, sparks, and so forth. (88)
If it has parts, there is the same fault as with a composite whole; if it is partless, it is like an atom.
There is no other alternative; thus, your proclamation of the teaching is in vain. //89//
The qualities are restricted to that alone; the inclination is restricted to that alone;
the measure is restricted to that alone; and the other is equal only through sublation. (90)

Those for whom the Victor is merely another have lost even their own Teacher—[the Teacher] who is grasped through a straightforward method and who shines with the characteristics derived from scripture. (91)
That which, by its very nature, is neither one nor many is not real;
just as pleasure is not [identical to] pain, and light is not [identical to] white. //92//
For it has already been stated that a property cannot be separated from its substratum;
nor can the manifestation of something distinct be established by this reasoning. (93)
Even if the blue object has no reality apart from its manifestation, by what means can the reality of that which appears as distinct be established? (94)
The son of a barren woman is neither one nor many in the form of fire; therefore, he does not exist by that means.
Consequently, how could there be any reality for him according to your own criterion of existence? 95.

The son of a barren woman is not established as existing; yet, if it is argued that his manifestation is established even while he himself remains unestablished, and that it is only this difference of his that is being proven, that too is incorrect. 96.
If it is held that the establishment of difference exists by way of its true nature as a reality, that is not established;
for there is no absence of pervasion in a non-entity. (97)
If establishment is merely a matter of conventional cognition, then even that which is distinct is not ultimately real.
Yet, why do you not likewise accept the conventional distinction between yellow and white? 98.

If one were to establish both the existence of manifestation and the absence of an occasion for sublation, then by that much alone the difference would be proven; this [separate] means of knowledge is redundant. //99//
Even if that [capacity] were impossible, this display of arrogance would be in vain;
for how could the opponent's current admission serve as a valid basis? (100)

Since the blue color and its luminosity appear as non-different, yet a distinction is being asserted; and since such a positive concomitance (anvaya) is impossible, how then can the probandum (sādhya) be established? [101]
That by which something is neither one nor many is the general positive concomitance (*sāmānyato 'nvaya*).
Let it be that what appears blue is neither one nor many because of its yellowness; it does not exist by virtue of that. (102)
Even if not explicitly stated, that which is pervaded by the [proponent's] intention is considered to be the probandum (sādhya), just like the self for its own sake.

Therefore, a positive concomitance (anvaya) with respect to a particular is [unestablished], whereas [a concomitance] in general results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). //103//
Just as pleasure is distinct from pain because it is of a different nature, let the appearance of blue likewise be so [distinct] from yellow, precisely because they belong to different classes. (104)

When it is said that there is neither a single nor a multiple illumination by means of the blue, then what could be the meaning of "illumination" if it is held to be a mere property (dharma-mātra)? 105.
Since that [cognition] is non-different from the nature of the substrate (dharmin), its stability is established by that very [substrate].
Thus, the [alleged] identity or non-identity of the manifestation with the blue object is unproven. (106)

If even for that [universal], neither oneness nor manifoldness is accepted—if you desire even non-absolutism (anekānta)—then why not let the real entity "cowness" exist as a real thing that is neither one nor many by way of its mass? (107)
Even in the position that [the self] is the agent (*kartṛ*), the fault is indeed difficult to remove:
for emptiness would then exist as that very nature which is the form of luminosity. (108)

If that which is called "manifestation" were a distinct entity possessing a continuous nature, it would neither exist as something separate from blue and other such objects, nor would it have any result. (109)
And since there is no continuity [of the subject], for you the substratum of the reasons is unestablished here;
furthermore, even if a mere exclusion were established, it would be useless for the matter at hand. (110)
If this luminosity, which is to be directly realized, is the subject (dharmin), then no subject that is the object of direct perception exists apart from blue and so forth. (111)
If "otherness" itself is what is to be proven, how can that which is already established be sought?
Let whatever be your probandum; the subject (dharmin) must, however, be your effect. (112)
When an object is considered to be an already established entity, there would be no result for you if there were no dependence on the two types of exclusion (vyavaccheda). (113)
[525,5] But surely, luminosity is a universal (sāmānya) that is the locus of properties (dharmin); what is the use of its being restricted to particulars?
[525,6] And since the probandum is already excluded by the restriction to particulars, there is no effort toward it. ||114||

Even though its specific nature is already established, that which is the subject (*dharmin*) becomes a point of dispute; it is merely a single exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), while the other is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), as in the case of "sound. (115)

The establishment of the probandum and the probans is based merely on their exclusion; however, the nature of the subject (dharmin) must be perceived through its distinction [from others] to be effective. //116//
Pervasion is only possible to be cognized between two general properties (*sāmānyadharma*).
However, in every case, the locus (*dharmin*) is characterized by particularity, such that "this is thus. (117)
Wherever there is reliance upon a universal, one must necessarily depend upon the perception of its particular; the establishment of the universal occurs only in this way, and not otherwise. //118//
Nowhere is there an establishment of a universal without a particular;
otherwise, there would be an equality between it and the exclusion of the son of a barren woman. (119)

The distinction between the probandum in the example and that in the subject and similar instances must necessarily be taught even for a universal; however, the locus (dharmin) must be indicated as "this very thing. (120)
These very same distinctions among individuals are accepted for momentariness and so forth as well;
and the subject (*dharmin*) is a word whose individual instances are well-known, as is any other such case. (121)
In the same way, let the transformation of non-manifestation be shown here:
if it were to be shown as "this" right before one's eyes, it would be nothing other than a mental form (ākāra). ||122||

[525,23] Therefore, for one who asserts that the universal is nothing other than the manifestation of blue and so forth, [525,24] the critic maintains that various [faults] are admitted because it is accepted as having its own nature. //123//

When the locus (*dharmin*) is established, a property (*dharma*) that is yet to be proven is what requires proof; but if the specific nature of the locus itself is settled, then the argument is destroyed, utterly destroyed. (124)
Likewise, if even momentariness and so forth were established in the subject (*dharmin*), who would refute it? For what purpose would one establish that which is already proven? (125)
That which, by its very nature, is neither one nor many is not real;
just as pleasure is not [real] in relation to pain, so too is darkness [not real] in relation to light. (126)
An illumination resembling a flash of lightning appears somewhere to someone at some time;
in relation to that, external illumination is considered stable, and therefore its unreality [is established].
Just as the capacity of cognition is held to exist for the production of a false blue, why is there not likewise a capacity for the production of a false awareness in an external object? (128)
[526,11] "It cannot be maintained that you do not accept even a single [entity]," for this statement is untenable;
since my non-acceptance arose from not knowing such a proof as this. [129]
Nor has mere luminosity ever been perceived by anyone anywhere;
therefore, the hope for inference is merely a hope indeed.

If, therefore, there is a loss of both unity and plurality because of its own [nature], then its persistence by way of its own nature must be established; yet even so, your reason remains unestablished. (131)
If you intend to express the opposite: "Whatever exists by whatever nature, that exists as one or many by its own nature, and an appearance also exists by its own nature. (132)
In the first case, there is no existence of an example, for that is admitted to be a mere appearance;
nor is there an application to the subject (*pakṣa*) because of the dispute, and the original point is not established. (133)
All this delusion is like the appearance of two moons; others, however, maintain that this delusion consists in the appearance of duality while being attached to reality. (134)

What is intended [by this] is that birth occurs as having the form of two parts, or there is the manifestation of duality, or rather, there is the determination of the forms of the grasped and the grasper. (135)
When there is an object of cognition that is not that [object], yet possesses the appearance of that [object], the cognition is an error.
However, when the object of cognition is entirely absent, there is in reality no such thing as an error. (136)
Whatever is not as it truly is, yet is conceptualized as being so—what kind of fault could there be in that? It is rather appropriate to find fault with the one who conceptualizes. (137)

If there were no such thing as an eon (*kalpa*) and no such thing as delusion (*bhrama*), then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if delusion exists by way of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), [the reason is not unestablished]. (138)
How could there be an error regarding that which is non-false according to worldly convention, even though it exists only externally?
But when there is a superimposition upon what is not external within the sphere of conventional discourse, then it is an error. (139)

Since, upon the transcendence of superimposition, there is a firm establishment in reality itself, that [cognition] which is an error due to its falsity because of sublation—how can that too be an error? (140)
If it is said that there is falsehood in the expression, how could there be error?
For there is no apprehension of that [object] in what is not that, as in the case of a cognition that is not false.
Even in the appearance of two moons, that which is renowned as error belongs to the mind that perceives the two moons, and not to the two moons themselves. (142)
When the two parts of cognition are conceptualized as the apprehended and the apprehender, how can there be validity in the apprehending part and error in the apprehended part? (143)
When both the state of being the object of cognition and the state of being the cognizer have passed away, there remains a mere manifestation;
even though this is swallowed by the cognizer, it would be unreal, yet it is not an error.
Error is held to be pervaded by the state of being conceived as a cognizer;
since non-cognizingness is the opposite of that, error is utterly excluded from it. (145)
If, however, there were determination otherwise, then non-conceptual cognition would be an error; it is not an error, and therefore let it indeed possess a connection with reality. (146)
Whatever departs when something else remains is distinct from it, as in the case of a cloth and its threads;
others maintain that blue and other colors depart while illumination remains. (147)
Whatever departs while something else remains is distinct from it, like a cloth from its threads;
likewise, let it be proclaimed that while "cowness" remains, variegated color and other qualities depart. (148)
[528,3] Now, if "cowness" is the exclusion of non-cows, how can that be a positive concomitant (anvayin)?
[528,4] Furthermore, is even the appearance (bhāsa) the property of appearing things such as blue and so forth, and if so, is it a concomitant? ||149||
[528,5] Thus ends the first chapter, the Determination of the Absence of Proof for the Proponent of Formlessness, in the *Sākārasaṃgraha*. [528,6]
[Second Chapter] Nor can the mind, being formless, be understood through scripture;
nor can there be the application of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to that which has already been refuted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). (1)
And even within the teaching, there is no primary syllable that makes this [reality] known;
rather, the world merely reflects its own subjective attachment upon that very [teaching]. //2//
"In the scripture it is said that the mind, stirred by latent impressions (vāsanā), appears as an object;
here the root *luṭh* means 'to adhere,' not 'to be shaken' (*loṭhita*) in the sense of being struck. (3)
Regarding the question, "How can cognition appear as an object in the absence of an object?", it is said here:
"Due to the connection with latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)," that is, by virtue of the power of the immediately preceding [moment]. (Verse 4)

The description appears as if it were a distinction, yet it does not indicate any actual difference; for what is the statement "one makes gold into the form of an earring" not [an expression of identity]? (5)
And being afflicted by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) is considered to be due to the arising of undesirable forms;
for it possesses within it the capacity to give birth to conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), which impels one toward active engagement (*pravṛtti*). //6//
Upon ascending the pinnacle of non-duality, there is neither engagement nor withdrawal;
since these alone constitute saṃsāra, how can they be accepted as its cause? (7)
This statement is made in consideration of the state of the minds of those to be trained.
Therefore, the phrase "appearing as an object" is a general term established upon its specific instances. (8)
Based on the conceit of the foolish that "a form is seen in a mirror," [the sūtra] restates this and then prevents the superimposition [of reality] upon that appearance of sensation. (9)
Likewise, the substantiality of entities exists within the forms of cognition, just as the non-existent moonhood of two moons is seen by one with cataracts. (10)
Because it is devoid of high and low, there is no identity with the external object in the mirror;
nor is there any difference for the observer, since there is no appearance of having entered within. //11//
The nature of awakening is characterized by entities or by the notions of their forms;
for this very reason, that which is reckoned as "knowledge" is a universal (sāmānya), and thus it is not spoken of as something separate. ||12||
In the world, knowledge is conventionally established as if it were distinct, resembling a mirror; the forms appear like reflections, yet that which is imagined in both cases is not real. //13//
Cognition is not identical with external objects because it would thereby lose its own nature;
nor is it something other than them because it is never apprehended as such; furthermore, that which does not manifest itself cannot possess existence. (14)

And by way of a direct sequence, it is logical that [the reflection] in a mirror is devoid of oneness and multiplicity; thus, while entities are not tenable as being like a mirror, they are nevertheless comparable to a mirror. //15//
All phenomena abide as nothing but one's own cognition within a concentrated mind, because they rely upon emptiness, which cannot be subverted by imagined phenomena. (16)
Because they are of the nature of that very illumination, these [phenomena] such as white and so forth are the mind itself.
However, because they are imagined and lack luminosity, they are neither phenomena (dharma) nor the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). //17//

Just as that which is called emptiness appears in conceptual construction as if it were differentiated, so too, by means of that [emptiness] which is [in fact] undifferentiated, these phenomena are empty of those very phenomena. (18)
Even when the grasped object is abandoned, one must prevent the persistence of the grasper;
by abiding in the objective support of suchness, one transcends mind-only. ||19||

Lest, by the removal of the superimposition, there should also be the removal of the object of the superimposition—lest there be the fall into the view of nihilism regarding the manifold world—it is necessary to prevent its non-appearance. //20//
"The yogin abides in the non-manifest; manifestation is considered to be conceptual construction.
That which appears slightly as something external within that [construction], by means of the exclusion of the one, [is what is meant]. [21]
Because it shines forth everywhere, appearance (ābhāsa) or conceptual proliferation (prapañca) is like a kadamba flower;
even when the mind is variegated, that which is mounted upon diverse conceptual constructions is to be abandoned. //22//
Then, through the destruction of adventitious stains, it is like the expanse of space;
equal to the object of knowledge, it is manifest by virtue of being non-distinct from that object. //23//
This is mere luminosity, similar to the continuum of a lamp;
it is not [a self-luminous entity] because it lacks non-luminous parts, since it manifests its own form. (24)
Even for that which lacks the capacity to illuminate, there was no prior existence;
however, the state of being defiled or stainless depends upon the determination of error. //25//
Even if names are sublated, there is no harm to the causal signs or to the form;
let the phenomena of the Sage be mere names, whether they exist by way of an imagined nature or not. //26//
Even when there is the form of conceptual construction, those things called "seen" appear as non-perception;
O sir, how do you perceive number when it appears in what has been cultivated? 27.
For one who abides in the state of non-appearance, even that is considered to be non-conceptual abiding.
By this much, the delusion consisting in the appearance of the existent and the appearance of the non-existent has been explained. (28)
[531,11] And this non-appearance of the existent must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, what else could it be?
[531,12] For there is no delusion in the non-manifestation of another, nor is there a lack of mind in the non-manifestation of itself. //29//
Therefore, for that which exists, there is no abiding in the state of being neither grasped nor grasper;
thus, the determination of a non-existent grasped and grasper is likewise an error. (30)
Thus, the unreal imagination exists; duality is not found therein.
Nothing other than the grasped and the grasper is expressed by the word "duality. //31//
Unreal imagination, however, consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms. Apart from these various forms, what could the establishment of the three realms be? (32)
And nowhere has a part of the mind been established as something exceeding its aspect;
for this position stands far beyond the Vaibhāṣika school. //33//
That wherein or by which the unreal is imagined through discursive conceptualization—this is unreal imagination; it is appropriately understood as a manifold cognition. (34)

Because there is a connection with a positive concomitance (anvaya) based on the superimposition of a non-existent duality, there can be no such thing as superimposition regarding an invisible, additional portion. //35//
Furthermore, the imagined duality is not blue itself because it does not appear as such;
therefore, that which is called "intrinsic nature" must also be discussed in relation to the imagined and the other [natures]. //36//
To say that the imagined is itself what flashes forth—what could be more reckless than this?
Even in the case of the certain perception of a mirage, let it be that the imagined water is what flashes forth; what else could it be? (37)
If it is accepted in that way, let it be stated that milk is the effect produced by that [cow].
If you say, "It is not so because it is non-existent," then how can that which is non-existent be milk? (38)
If it is argued that [the manifestation] is due to superimposition (āropa), then let it be a mere superimposition;
however, it is not a manifestation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), because if there were such a manifestation, the activity of that [nature] would necessarily follow.
[532,9] Reality itself would follow as a consequence, and likewise, sublation would be rendered powerless.
[532,10] For if its activity were lost through sublation, it would no longer possess that activity; indeed, milk does not possess that activity. //40//
How is it said that its appearance manifests within superimposition?
Thus, the manifestation of superimposition belongs to the grasped and the grasper, but not to the [object] itself. (41)
Since both parts have the nature of self-luminosity, what could be the grasped object and what the grasper? For that would entail the loss of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). //42//

Therefore, let the very form that is manifest be the fourth nature; for the notion that "there is a conceptualization of the visible within the invisible self" is merely some kind of mental construction. (43)
Therefore, the dependent nature is manifold; thus, the intellect is both imagined and conceptualized.
Observe clearly this very point in the determination of the form of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā). //44//
Since superimposition and denial regarding the imagined duality—which appears as the dependent nature—have been refuted, they are thus eliminated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*. (45)
Reflect upon the noble *Sūtrālaṃkāra* together with its commentary, wherein form and the other [sense objects] are explained as being clearly manifest as the dependent nature (*paratantra*). //46//
In that case, its appearance exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like. //47//
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in the case of illusions and the like.
Likewise, there is the appearance of non-duality, yet its substantial existence is not found;
therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates. ||49||
Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed not existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in respect to form and the other [sense objects]. (50)
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial, and also for the purpose of negating the vehicle of the Hīnayāna. //51//
And regarding "in form and so forth," this means "in that which consists of unreal imagination.
See the commentary (*bhāṣya*) for its detailed explanation, or look at the extensive exposition itself. //52//
Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, and he who sees reality is liberated. //53//

If this deliberation is held to have as its object a thing perceived through direct perception, then there is no direct perception other than the variegated [cognition]; such is the effort made in both philosophical systems.
In the statement analyzing the *dharmadhātu*, the subject (*dharmin*) is expressed by the word "phenomena" (*dharma*);
likewise, this has been clearly stated by the immediately preceding words. (55)
And for this very reason, the cessation of a phenomenon after its occurrence is indeed *nirvṛti* (extinction);
this fault has been accepted by those who, under the false name of "emptiness," long for the destruction of forms. //56//

[533,19] That there exists a dharma called "emptiness" distinct from form and so forth, [533,20] which is to be cultivated—this is the reproach incurred by the proponents of the absence of mental aspects (anākāravādins). //57//
Having realized that objects are merely mental discourse,
he abides in mind-only which appears as those [objects];
thus it is said regarding the path of penetration and the vision.
[533,24] Indeed, it is the attainment of direct perception of the dharmadhātu. ||58||
That which is devoid of duality in the form of grasped and grasper—its distinction is such, yet its aspect is never exhausted anywhere. (59)
The abandonment of the two characteristics is clearly evident everywhere;
for this very reason, there is no state of grasped object and grasping subject among the forms.
The appearances of duality proceed, yet they are not conceptual constructions;
furthermore, they exist for the sake of purification. In this regard as well, there is both appearance and the state of being determined.
"Not deluded regarding all objects of knowledge, yet never directed toward them"—the reason for this state, as explained here, is its being "without mental aspect" (anākāratā). //62//
The meaning is "by way of the absence of the modes of the apprehended," even when the reflection arises;
this will become clear immediately upon examining the root text and the commentary. (63)

Thus, regarding such a root text and commentary of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the meaning of "due to the excellence of the beginning and the end" has been correctly analyzed by means of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*). //64//

And likewise, when the author of that commentary himself proceeds with the definition of non-conceptual cognition in the context of inferring the nature of phenomena and their true reality, [verse 65].

The term "formless" is used because it cannot be determined as either the grasped object or the grasping subject; and this term "non-manifest" is described because it is beyond the range of sensory perception. //66//
But if it is so because of the absence of appearance and the absence of an object to be grasped, then what is the use of this effort? It would be more appropriate to speak directly. (67)
