"Nothing whatsoever that is considered an object of perception appears within this"—this is the etymological derivation intended here, and it is likewise accepted in the *Uttara-tantra*. (68)
In that which is nothingness, without appearance, without support, and without basis;
which has transcended the range of vision, is formless, and is invisible. (69)
Just as depressions and elevations are seen in the sky, yet they do not exist there in that way;
so too, everything is seen even in the Buddhas, yet it does not exist there in that way. //70//

In this case as well, if the excellence of the qualification of the example resides in the omnipresent [subject], then it must necessarily be applied [to the subject], for its nature is indeed non-appearance, just like that [example]. //71//
The abandonment of both the objective support and the basis is equal to the higher stage through comparison;
it is "nothingness" because of the separation from all adventitious defects without exception. ||72||
However, the first verse has fulfilled its purpose through its own mere qualification;
thus, the plural number in the word "buddheṣu" (among the Buddhas) serves as a differentiator from that [first verse]. ||73||
Because of their equality in being empty, there is no lack of nature, nor is there a lack of intrinsic character;
for they are equal through the abandonment of the high and low positions of superimposition and denial.
The conception of high and low states may occur regarding things that have the nature of entities;
however, since there is not even a suspicion regarding that which has the nature of a non-entity, it is illustrated as being like space. //75//
If non-conceptual cognition is non-erroneous and conceptual form is erroneous, then the conventional discourse of the three bodies would cease, because the enjoyment body would be sublated. (76)
As long as this collection of forms is an error, so long there is no Buddhahood;
since awakening is the antithesis of error, how could it be the nature of a Buddha? ||77||

Nor is this merely conventional reality, for conventional reality is indeed conceptual construction; nor can it be called a "body" through metaphorical designation, since it is logically established as being nothing but relinquishment. //78//
[535,17] Due to the sovereign power of the Buddha, it is not fitting that those who are fortunate should have a mere appearance of him;
[535,18] for they are more devoid of form, whereas the Buddha is superior in his manifestation. ||79||
[535,19] The sovereignty of the Buddha and their blessedness in various stations—this is the arising of such a gross delusion for those who are wandering in the egg. [80]
And just as pervasion and eternality have been described according to his own intention, so too is the explanation not applicable to the Sambhogakāya; this is his great sovereignty. (81)
Because his self is adorned with all the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he is called "Citravāk" (the One of Varied Speech);
the author of the Commentary states this because he is distinguished from the multitude of characteristics belonging to the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*). (82)

In order to demonstrate that the Dharmakāya is primary, [the author] stated in the subsequent passage that this will also apply to the Lord of the Mandala (cakreśa); thus, he did not describe him as being unreal or the like. (83)
Furthermore, this *Sūtrālaṃkāra* would be contradicted if there were falsity:
"The fulfillment of the two aims for both is established in all its aspects. (84)
The Enjoyment Body is the perfection of one’s own welfare, while the Emanation Body is the glory of the welfare of others;
both are established within the Essential Nature and the Enjoyment Body—such is the teaching of the Commentary. (85)
Thus, the body of the dharma-body is the cause for emanation;
the manifestation of the perfection of one's own welfare is called "enjoyment," which is a conventional designation. 86.
[536,9] In the doctrine of space, because it possesses the nature of a body, there is no plurality for the Sage;
[536,10] plurality is not pervaded by form, as in the case of the mind, mental factors, and the self. ||87||

But the Commentary says: "Because the Sage lacks the grasping at a self and because he has abandoned both himself and others, there is no 'ground' (bhūmi). Thus it speaks; for it clearly states that the body is the grasping at a self. (88)
One's own welfare, the welfare of others, the nature of the ultimate body (*paramārthakāyatā*),
and the conventional body (*saṃvṛttikāyatā*) which is based upon that;
the fruit consists of the state of dissociation and maturation.
Thus, what is the meaning of "it" in the subsequent supreme tantra? ||89||
For us, the self-benefit is considered to be the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), while the benefit for others is the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*);
however, in this context, it is the establishment of their ultimate reality that is intended. (90)
Whether indirectly or directly, the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) relies upon those two conventionalities; and it is taught that the emanation is the conventional fruit. 91.
While praising the qualities of the Tathāgata, how could one possibly abandon the emanation body?
Having thus referred to those two bodies in the commentary as being ultimate, [the author says: 92.
And the rule regarding the basis of self-perfection is not contradicted;
self-perfection is twofold: through the accomplishment of form and through worldly prosperity. //93//
In the first [verse], one should establish the beginning; in the second, the second [part], characterized by many distinctions such as "inconceivable" and "transcending the world. (94)
Alternatively, their power resides in the self, in the enjoyment, and in the perfection;
the pure essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is to be known as being like a jewel-form. //95//

Because its nature is unconditioned, because it is the locus of the jewels of the qualities, and because it possesses supreme sovereignty over the Great Dharma, the Enjoyment Body is like a universal monarch. //96//
Because its nature is that of a reflection, the emanation is like a golden image;
thus it has been asserted by those who take pleasure in their own position regarding the Teacher as the speaker. (97)
The enjoyment body is conventional, excluding the emanation body; fie upon its independence!
Having surveyed the entire world with great compassion, the Knower of the World— 98.
"Without wavering from the *dharmakāya*, by means of emanations of diverse forms"—this and what follows in this very context constitute the demonstration. (99)
Furthermore, it has been stated regarding the Jātakas and other tales ending with his final nirvāṇa:
that he remained everywhere in the celestial abodes, never wavering from the state of Brahmā.
Just as Brahmā might manifest an appearance without effort, so too does the Sage, through effortless spontaneity, manifest emanations throughout the world-systems. //101//
"Without wavering from the dharmakāya, he comes into the sight of those who are worthy.
Thus, and so forth, it is explained at length there that [the Buddha] is distinct from the dharmakāya by means of speech. (102)
If the one whose nature is enjoyment does not exist, what other Sage could bear the burden of the task? 103.
In some places he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways;
in some places the disappearance of his wisdom, and in others the method of various ointments;
in some places the entirety of enlightenment, and in others, repeatedly, with its emanations.
And yet, he does not move from that state, and he accomplishes everything. //104//

Thus it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* as well: "In this regard, the locus is the untainted realm (anāśravadhātu) proclaimed in the commentary; that is precisely the immovability of the Dharma-body. (105)
Nevertheless, it is held that the self and its form are indeed false and an error;
that the burden of causal efficiency arises from something other than these is nothing short of a shameful shamelessness. (106)
Furthermore, if it is accepted that the error exists as a false entity, then the burden of mental images would be useless regarding the gross object;
however, this burden of images must necessarily be abandoned if it is so desired.
Because it leaves behind nothing but the knowledge that has the appearance of a cloudless sky,
this supreme state has emerged, having cast off the attainment of the three bodies.
If the enjoyment body were to perish, its property—the dharma-body—would not exist;
nor would there be the emanation body which is its effect. Such would be the flawed conclusion regarding the nature of a Buddha. (109)
[538,9] Let it be that the enjoyment body (sambhogakāya) has set; let the dharma-body (dharmakāya) be formless.
[538,10] And from that very [dharma-body], the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) [arises]; thus, the Buddhist conclusion is excellent. //110//
Precisely because it is illusory, having abandoned the enjoyment body, it takes recourse in the state of being bodiless;
for that is indeed the culmination of purification—why then would there not be a union of those three? (111)
[538,13] It has been demonstrated that this is contradictory according to the method of the Crown Prince;
nevertheless, if there is some curiosity regarding the investigation, it shall be stated. [538,14] ||112||
If the *dharmakāya* is defined as a manifestation without mental aspects (*anākāra*), then what is the Buddha’s *sambhogakāya*, which is not fit to be abandoned? (113)
Even if he remains for the sake of the task, how can the Sugata be subject to error?
If he were to be employed for a task, that would only nourish the charge of his being false and unreal. (114)

And that being so, there is neither delusion nor the abandonment of non-delusion; therefore, for one who is free from delusion, there is the establishment of equality and the removal of all dogmatic tenets. ||115||
Therefore, that which is the cause of this [defilement], which must necessarily be abandoned, does not deserve to be undertaken;
for that reason also, he is not the Sugata if the Dharma alone is the Victor.
The conventional expression "the dharmakāya of the Jina" is not established, because even by way of the distinction of exclusions, it is a designation for that which is one and the same. //117//
Otherwise, there would be hundreds of bodies for the Jinas and so forth due to their non-differentiation;
furthermore, the conventional expression "the Buddha of the Jina" does not exist anywhere. //118//

But the word expressing the property of the substratum is indeed distinct [from the word for the substratum], as it participates in conventional usage; just as one says "the fruit of the *dhātrī* tree" or "the fruit of the tree," but not "the *dhātrī* is the tree. (119)
If the Buddha is considered to be mere phenomena (dharmamātra), then it is logical that the Buddha possesses the Dharma;
for if the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) belongs to the Buddha, then the Dharma is his quality (guṇa).
That being so, your body is formless and equal to the fourth state; the triad of bodies is not to be reckoned as distinct from the enjoyment body, for there is no diminution. (121)
"The essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is considered equal, subtle, and connected"—if this were explained by the term "connected," it would contradict the objection [stated above]. //122//
It is said to be "connected with the enjoyment body" (sāmbhogika-kāya) because, when the enjoyment exists, its qualities deserve to be connected with it. //123//
In its absence, there is no identity; even if it exists, there is no identity due to absolute difference.
This is because it is proclaimed in that very context as the cause of the *sambhoga*-buddhahood. (124)
If there is a causal relationship, the effect cannot be a non-entity for anyone.
If it is argued that the cause must likewise be merely a property of a non-entity, how could that be? (125)
In the Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya, it is not stated that [the ālayavijñāna] arises by having that as its object;
rather, it is stated that it is the cause of phenomena. Such is the commentary in various places. (126)
Or, having isolated that part which exists even previously, it is described as such;
just as the valor of this king alone is the accomplisher of all his aims.
It has not been stated anywhere that something arises from a formless [cause] within itself;
however, the refutation set forth in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* applies equally here. (128)
Even though the arising of existence occurs through dependence, people resort to the notion that it is produced by another, acting as if it were directly perceived;
thus it says in the *Mātṛkā*: "It arises from that."
What kind of darkness is this, such that even one who possesses insight perceives both the existent and the non-existent? ||129||
The agent and the enjoyer, distinct from what is perceived, is the sphere of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
it is stainless, and liberation for yogins consists in its being the sole remainder. (130)
Thus, this is merely the doctrine of a self, and yet it is not eternal, as it is characterized by inactivity;
furthermore, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) would result in being eternal by virtue of its being the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). //131//
Even through the non-lapsing of its intrinsic nature, there is no permanence in the continuum;
for here, in this case of the intrinsic nature, that meaning is applied by means of the commentary. //132//
In the determination of the delusion regarding effects, that which is indeed intrinsic is proclaimed as the *dharmakāya* with reference to purification. (133)

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Dharma, and the Sambhogakāya Sugata himself—by dividing these into their internal and mutual qualities, the fourfold body (*kāyacatuṣṭayī*) is established. (134)

The mention of the *dharmakāya* among the three bodies expresses the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*); within the fourfold aspect of the *saṃbhogakāya*, the *nirmāṇakāya* is included, and the remainder is likewise contained herein. (135)
Just as space, by virtue of its non-conceptuality, is omnipresent everywhere, so too is the element of the stainless nature of the mind all-pervading. (136)
Thus, by means of the *Uttaratantra*, the primary all-pervasiveness has been proclaimed;
this doctrine of the Self is fully evident as that of the Vedāntins. (137)
[540.19] However, the permanence, omnipresence, and so forth of the *dharmatā* are conventional;
even though it possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvya*), they are established according to conceptual construction, just like momentariness and the like. [138]
Without a distinction, there is no logical justification; for this [distinction] is lost from the perspective of the actual state of things (*vastu*).
Therefore, in the context of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), that doubt is warded off by the All-pervading One (*vibhu*). (139)
Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because of the non-interruption of that very [activity], he is also said to be eternal. ||140||
That which is to be applied here is not that very same thing; permanence is not asserted of it by its own nature.
For, in the context of intrinsic nature, it is not the form of a real entity. (141)

When there is the performance of universal activity in the state of enjoyment (*sambhoga*), purity exists; yet when that is absent, as before, there is contradiction. Furthermore, both complete purification and the welfare of sentient beings are not eternal. (142)
"If there is no formless [reality], and its equality with the self [is not established], then this very thing is the Dharmakāya"—thus the King began. (143)
Through the destruction of the accumulation of afflictions and their ultimate cessation, what remains superior?
That which is revealed in the Tantra as the nature of sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and Victors. (144)

The Dharma-body is to be known as twofold: the utterly stainless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and its natural outflow, which is the teaching through the methods of profundity and diversity. //145//

Thus, the explanation is also found in that very same place; however, while the term "dharma" refers to the "possessor of attributes" (dharmin), the "Dharmakāya" under discussion here is the utterly stainless Dharmadhātu. ||146||
Suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena—these, in brief, are the synonyms of emptiness. (147)
Thus, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the dharmadhātu has been described:
it should be known as the perfected nature, reality, and the untainted realm. (148)

Emptiness is said to be twofold; therein, by virtue of the state of affliction, the quality of the dependent nature is to be known as existing when the impurities of the enjoyment body have been eliminated. //149//
Those untainted phenomena which have attained purity in all its aspects—the essential body of the Sage has their nature as its characteristic. (150)
In this regard as well, it is not contradicted by the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, because intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is established as the cause and as reality (*tattva*). (151)

Alternatively, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is their very emptiness; this is the intended meaning of all [the Buddhas], for it is the pure word arising from the context of the Buddha. //152//
Even though it is comprised within the pure [realm], the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) is not reckoned as part of the assembly;
for that must be declared a separate body—how then could it be the Dharma-body at that time? 153.
Because it is primary, however, it does not have that very thing as its subordinate retinue;
for, since they consist of a single cognition, it is apprehended precisely by the apprehension of that [primary object]. ||154||

Although enjoyment and the form of its basis are not distinct from it, nevertheless, the conventional distinction between them, like that between other things, is a differentiation from the person. (155)
Thus ends the second chapter, the determination of the words of the noble Asaṅga, the Crown Prince, concerning the investigation of the essential nature of the Dharmakāya to its ultimate limit.
If one is liberated by isolating mere *dharmatā* as either "the Buddha" or "the Dharma," how can there be self-cognition in the absence of duality? (1)
Because of the awakening to that, he is called "Buddha," and not because of the radiant marks and so forth;
for one who loves all pure qualities does not abandon that objective support.
The realization of that is common to all Buddhas; it does not belong to anyone else.
Recollection of that is the worship of the Protectors; its certain fruit is the object of knowledge. //3//
Therefore, the Buddha is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and the Dharma is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Since Buddhahood consists in the predominance of these two, how could there be a distinct category [of Sangha] apart from them? (4)
For this very reason it is said that the Buddha is indeed the Dharma; just as one says "the king is his majesty," there is an identity between the two in reality. (5)
And as it was said by the Master: "The object of the word 'Buddha' is the purified continuum of mind; this is also what is called the 'Dharma' of the Great Sage. (6)
In that regard as well, through the direct realization of the *dharmakāya*, that sound is the Dharma itself, just as the Victor is the Dharma; and likewise, he is the Victor himself. (7)
For one who is formless, there is no doubt regarding the *Āryanītisūtra-vivṛti*, which describes the non-appearance of the formless realm and proclaims the abandonment of the mere duality. (8)
Even when there is effort toward the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), that very [consciousness] is not eliminated;
otherwise, how could its cessation be said to occur in the state of Arhatship? (9)
If there were a cessation [of the world], there would be no distinction of states; it would be non-manifestation, and the proof [of the goal] would be destroyed.
For it is said that perfect awakening occurs in Akaniṣṭha, not born from the formless realm. //10//
The commentary also states: "It is nowhere stated in the scripture that there is no cognition of the form [of the object];
this follows the scripture as established by the renowned teacher Sthiramati. (11)
If it is argued that this has been stated as being indeed formless, then certainty is destroyed;
for what need have we for further reflection, since the subject at hand has been established? (12)
Let some systematic arrangement be established in the scriptures by the Victors in some way, or by the Primordial Teacher; this which has been introduced now is not that.
Because the mode of equanimity (upekṣākāra) exists, there is no destruction of form even in the formless realm (ārūpya);
for an aspect (ākāra) is a manifestation of cognition, since some kind of form persists.

If the manifestation of the class of cognition is its form, why is it not similar to space? Or rather, if cognition were possible, what would there be to exclude now? For there would be nothing at all. (15)
But in the case of blue and so forth, a cognition distinct from that form is denied;
for even in a dream, no such other cognition is observed, though some [cognitions] may otherwise appear. (16)
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is established exactly in that way;
if one desires it to possess various forms, then it has been offered as the vessel for this [desire]. (17)
The formless realm arises from detachment from the form of delusion and from the intention for tranquility;
therefore, blue and so forth are the very self of the Buddhas, and duality does not exist at all. //18//
The establishment of the non-existence of everything occurs in two ways, through negation by implication (*prasajya*) and negation by exclusion (*paryudāsa*).
Here, the exclusion of the duality is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*). (19)
[544,17] First of all, its status as a real entity is not contradicted by self-awareness;
[544,18] for it is established that the cognition of the substratum itself is a direct perception even in the absence of anything else. //20//

The absence of a jar on the ground is established by the perception of the ground; likewise, the absence of duality in the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga) is established by the perception of the enjoyment body. ||21||
The Noble One, considering that, said: "Homage be to You for this non-duality!
You did not describe [the self as] 'red,' 'green,' 'mañjiṣṭha,' and so forth. (22)
"Thus, 'to be personally realized' is spoken by one's own voice as one's own experience;
for even when that conceptual construction is excluded, the basis remains the same. [23]
The finality of that which is to be determined has also been clarified by Saṃbhoga;
for this very reason, they have made manifest the acceptance of cognition with an aspect (sākāra). //24//
No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does anything whatsoever cease;
it is only conditions that arise and cease. (25)
Thus, because the mind is applied to the place of the sprout, the seed, and so forth, there arises a clear appearance of them, which is the imagined destruction of the continuum. (26)
The great elements and so forth are said to be fully contained within consciousness; when that consciousness is known, they vanish—surely they were falsely conceptualized. //27//
In that regard, the conviction of non-existence is the comprehension of the meaning through hearing and reflection;
"the knowledge of that" refers to the destruction [of obscurations] upon the direct realization of the nature of that knowledge. //28//

The teaching on the aggregates, elements, and so forth is for the purpose of eliminating the grasping at a self; even that [teaching] has been discarded by the fortunate ones through the establishment of [everything as] mere representation. (29)
Thus, from the removal of praise, there is certainty even regarding preference (*ruci*).
If this distinction is made in view of the two states, it is as has been stated. (30)
The teaching of the Sage that "all this is mind-only" is for the purpose of removing the fear of the foolish; it is not [the truth] from the perspective of ultimate reality. //31//

This is a gathering [of disciples] by granting their wish to those who are intent upon nihilism; it is not so here because of the removal of fear, yet in terms of ultimate reality, there is no cutting off. //32//
[545,19] Otherwise, the fear of fools and the loss [of purpose] would be equal in both positions.
[545,20] What difference is there here, such that there should be praise or rejection in such a manner? ||33||

And regarding the statement beginning with "There is nothing to be removed from this," since it has already been explained, why should it be further explained by oneself? What more remains beyond this? (34)
"An element is to be seen as an element by means of the self that is an element, and indeed by the self that is an element itself"—is this not the meaning of the statement being proclaimed here? (35)
For in the doctrine of universal non-existence, there would have to be some unreal thing that is to be seen as having a real form; this is the extreme of negation. (36)
[546,3] "The same applies to you regarding superimposition (*samāropa*)," because superimposition is not conceptualization (*kalpanā*).
[546,4] When that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) manifests, superimposition therein is indeed the conceptualization of duality. //37//
If negation does not exist conventionally and superimposition does not exist in reality, and if neither of those two exists in reality, then what contradiction is there? (38)
Conventionally, there is no denial; for in reality, it is indeed a denial.
Thus, the doctrine of universal non-existence follows, and its refutation has already been stated. (39)
If emptiness is real, it is excellent; for whatever is absent in something, by that [absence] is that [thing] empty.
Just as a house is empty of men, there is no contradiction between the substratum (dharmin) and its property (dharma). //40//
Unreal imagination exists; duality is not found there.
But emptiness exists here, and this [unreal imagination] also exists in it. //41//

The doctrine of universal non-existence, however, is indeed to be refuted by the force of valid cognition. For this very reason, the Noble Ones will consider [this matter], and thus it is not the case that they do not perceive anything at all. (42)

Or else, this negation is similar [to the previous case] when there is an examination of conceptual construction based on what is imagined as the relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer. (43)
Just as their power of merit [operates] in the arising of variegated cognitions, so it is said by those engaged in conventional discourse that "they see this and that. (44)
We perform the negation of existence, but not the affirmation of non-existence;
for that too is subject to negation—this is a grand ambition indeed! (45)
The very negation of existence is designated as non-existence;
because the negative particle lacks another referent, it does not establish the affirmation of anything else. (46)

Of two things whose natures consist in mutual exclusion, the negation of one is the affirmation of the other; it is not possible for either to remain for even a moment without setting aside its opposite. (47)

When the intrinsic natures of things—whether elemental, imagined, or conceptual—are non-existent, there is no injury to the nature of the real entity, which is free from all adventitious conditions. //48//
Therefore, the finality regarding the two types of form does not reside in either affirmation or negation alone.
Consequently, let the denial of what appears and the superimposition upon what does not appear be abandoned. (49)
Just as there is pain when a thorn enters the body or when it is being cut out,
so too here, in this flickering form, there is suffering through both exaggeration and denigration.
Therefore, the pure primordial state does not differ from the Yogācāra;
for liberation from the extremes of superimposition and denial is indeed the Middle Way. //51//
It is neither empty nor non-empty; therefore, everything is so established.
Because of existence, non-existence, and again existence, that is the Middle Way. (52)

This statement regarding emptiness, which in the view of others has the meaning of non-existence, has been rendered futile by those consumed by dogmatic views; this is the effort of the Noble King. (53)

Therefore, regarding the removal of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) from sentient beings through these very dharmas, there is no cause for astonishment, because it is proclaimed repeatedly in the treatises with reference to what is conceptually constructed. //54//
[547,15] The Vijñānavādin himself might raise this objection using the word "other.
[547,16] What greater calamity could there be than for a Vijñānavādin to say this? //55//
If the Perfectly Awakened One were to become his own master, where would there be liberation?
Even those deceived by him alone, the wise, partake in splendor.
The method of knowledge of the Protector arises from the intentions of others; likewise, why would there not be other teachings for that Noble One?
Indeed, it is according to those who are to be trained by him.
Even those such as you are his disciples in that same way. //57//
He expressed praise for the noble lord of the earth, who had not mentioned his own personal intentions nor those common to others.
But there is effort, and that is the middle way. ||58||
Even if there is equality in the attainment of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is no further fault in the purpose of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If, then, with respect to a single truth that is similar, there were two [distinct] ways;
Better is entry into the mouth of a lord of the earth than [entry into the mouth of a dog]. ||59||

If you are a follower of the Dharma through reasoning (*dharmānusārin*), you should be solely devoted to the authoritative treatises (*pramāṇa-śāstra*); but if you are a follower through faith (*śraddhānusārin*), you should follow the great multitude.
The crown prince is worthy of being honored by the assembly. ||60||
Alas, even regarding the person (pudgala), there is nothing more than the mere word of the Victor;

there is no attainment of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) through the unraveling of the intentional mystery (*saṃdhi-nirmocana*). But if one disregards that, [the definitive meaning is not attained].
[548,14] When the Buddha himself is the speaker, what is the distinction? ||61||
Intermediate verses: [548,15] *antaraślokāḥ* ||

By dividing the single [teaching] according to the differences among those to be trained, through its profundity and ultimate meaning, and by way of affirmation and negation, its fourfold establishment is proclaimed. //62//
For some are intent on denial, while others are intent on superimposition;
with reference to the former, the first [extreme] was taught, and the latter for the latter. (63)
Having refuted attachment to those who are intent on their own negation, the establishment of the Yogācāra system occurs through the formulation of the existence of thought. (64)
Furthermore, regarding those things colored by superimposition, the middle way proceeds by way of sublation;
and through that, there is frequent expression of negation that is free from qualifications.
Like a lame man, they will stand by themselves upon the wall of the expressed and the implied;
why would the identity of meaning between the words "similarity" and "dissimilarity" not be a distinction? 66.
The pure Middle Way does not differ in reality from the Yogācāra;
therefore, it is excellent that even the Noble One is said to abide in the Noble One’s system. //67//
Because a superior capacity is observed, and because others are drawn in through that means,
as well as because of encouragement, the manifestation of joy is not contradictory.

Therefore, even according to their system, as long as there is a negation of what has been stated, that should be understood as referring only to the imagined nature, just like the second master’s method. //69//
This is the summary view: "This is the negation of the imagined.
Every form established as an object of cognition is considered imagined within the mind. (70)
The aspect mounted upon cognition is conceptualized as having the form of the object of knowledge; it is also characterized in some way by its nature as cognition. (71)
The negation of the imagined nature should be understood as the non-apprehension of it as a graspable object and so forth;
just as this has been analyzed in the commentary, that [imagined nature] is also non-existent due to its absence. //72//
Since that which appears is indeed non-existent, it is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); for it is called "ignorance" because its power consists in the manifestation of the non-existent. (73)
Alternatively, manifestation has the sense of conceptual determination as it flashes forth within conceptual construction;
it is held to be produced by that [conceptualization] while one remains in the state of imagination arising from the latencies of ignorance. //74//
For the teaching of the *prajñāpāramitā* indeed relies upon three [natures]:
the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). (75)
By all such terms as "it does not exist" and so forth, that which is imagined is refuted;
by means of similes such as "like an illusion," the dependent nature is taught. //76//
The perfected nature is proclaimed through fourfold purification;
for in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is no other teaching of the Buddha. //77//
Thus, because the sequence of meanings in the system of the *pāramitās* is inexhaustible, the stainless doctrine of *sākāravāda* shines forth within that very [system]. (78)

Therefore, if another meaning alone were the primary, literal, and real one, then it would be a reasonable statement that this very meaning should also be accepted according to the system of the Noble Ones (Āryas). //79//
[550,3] Now, if there is a distinction regarding the sense of "from that," even so, what is gained? [550,4] By the mere negation of both, has the goal been achieved by the wise one? //80//
The negation of appearance must also be expressed as appearance itself; it is not a duality.
Because of the absence of defining characteristics, the fact that existence is uncontradicted has already been indicated previously. //81//
Furthermore, in the *Sambhogakāya*, practices such as the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) are described in clear syllables;
this is because the Noble One has revealed them either for the sake of the primary purpose or for his own realization. (82)

For when the Blessed Lady engaged in speech concerning the summarized meaning, what was not accomplished by her words, which made the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted easy to perform? (83)
[550,11] Or is it self-praise by means of the excellence of its qualities and form; otherwise, what else?
[550,12] Or is it a commentary (*vārtika*) on that system, as seen by another? ||84||

In this regard, the author of the *Vārttika*, having with great effort established that even the external object possesses a form (*sākṛti*), leaves only that [consciousness] remaining, because of the sublation of the apprehended object. (85)
That experience belongs to that very self, and it does not belong to anyone else;
its being directly perceived is also due to its identity with that self. (86)
Thus speaking, the Noble Lord, even while the author of the Vārttika speaks in this manner,
if he acts otherwise even in our presence, he does not become an object of conviction.
If, even after entering into the mental aspect, the mind is found to be formless, then why is it desired that this false appearance be inserted within? What would be the fruit of this? (88)

The mind is established as being without form for both parties—the proponent of self-cognition and the opponent—because even when external objects are superimposed, the refutation of the mental image is identical to that of cognition itself. (89)
Therefore, why such great effort? It would be better simply to wash it away and abandon it;
for the continuity of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) in the case of false appearances is established without effort. (90)
When the form is refuted by the acceptance that the object of cognition is devoid of form, then the proof of the form is logical only upon the conclusion that consciousness possesses a form. (91)

Since it is perceived as nothing other than light itself as the instrument of apprehension, the mind—though possessing forms—is established as the substratum of hundreds of conflicting perceptions. (92)

Having established with persistence the logic of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results, one still remains unsatisfied; for even at the end, the effort expended toward that purpose is indeed great. //93//
For one who vainly establishes a presently unreal form, that very [non-arising] would be the example for the beginningless proximity in perception. (94)

Therefore, since the mind is established by its very nature as possessing the power to manifest itself as non-self, the consideration regarding the destruction of the characteristics of the apprehended object is fruitless. //95//
Enough with the two reasons expressed through the phrase "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*);
let it be said, as Dharmottara did, that this is merely subservience to a second teacher. //96//
And this refutation of the one and the many is not intended for the ignorant;
even regarding external objects, it is a refutation of something other than the atom, since the atom itself remains unrefuted in certain respects. //97//

Having established that the object of apprehension is refuted within the system of those who maintain a representation produced through effort, the Sautrāntika is described as superior to the Vaibhāṣika because of his proximity to reality. //98//
Therefore, regarding everything, it is determined that it is either false or non-existent;
for it is not grasped in its own essential form as an aspect, but rather as something external. //99//
That pair of moons was seen, yet the statement "it does not exist" is not [a negation] of the mind;
nor is it that the perceived form is false, for it is not actually two moons. (100)
Due to the fault arising from the superimposition of water, the mental aspect is indeed logical;
however, a manifestation that appears uniquely to oneself cannot belong to another. (101)
This establishment according to conventional determination is not, however, from the perspective of ultimate reality;
for things such as hair-tufts are not universals, because they are based on an attachment to non-existent objects.
"In some cases" refers to the *Mātṛkā*.

Thus he says: "But not because of being non-objects," and furthermore: "The appearance of clarity exists because, by virtue of having the nature of cognition, it is an object; however, the notion that 'it is hair and so forth' [is mistaken]. (103)
The appearance of hair, which has a universal as its object, is devoid of external reality; it is classified as sensory cognition because it determines what is non-existent as being external.

If it is argued that because it has the nature of cognition, the universal would follow as being an object, there is no fault, for such is accepted; thus, its commonality consists in having the nature of an object.
And it has been stated more than once that the referent of a word is a property-bearer that is not subject to negation;
therefore, the referent of a word is said to be as it is conventionally perceived, even though it does not exist [ultimately]. //106//
Even though the object of a word does not exist, there is the determination that "this is the object of a word";
this has been shown because when a word is heard, it appears as a form within cognition. (107)

However, there is the determination that the external object of a word exists according to its conceptual determination, because it is established as the mere thing excluded from what does not possess that form. ||108||
If existence were according to how it is perceived, there would be no determination here;
rather, that very appearance is the existence of the entity, while the dependence on external capacity belongs to the object. (109)
Therefore, it is established that the form is called an "object" precisely because it is cognition.
What is the point of the labor involved in the commentary provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya* on that matter? (110)
If the mind indeed possesses an aspect, then even at its limit there is no excess;
thus, both affliction and purification would be one, and not two. (111)
Defilement is simply the presence of mental aspects (*ākāra*), while purification is their cessation;
thus, in the doctrine of aspectlessness (*anākāravāda*), the establishment of both would be possible. (112)
Because one grasps that which is not as being that, there is error; conceptual construction is its exhaustion, and it is equal.
If conceptual construction were also equal, how could it be an illusion, given that it possesses the form of reality? (113)
[552,23] In the act of ascertainment there is manifestness, and in manifestation there is identity with that [object].
[552,24] If the object were lost, there would be no such thing as the cognition of "name" and so forth. //114//
There would be certainty regarding the entire essence, and the object would be clearly manifest as "cow";
furthermore, since there is no linguistic convention regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), cognition would be purely conceptual. (115)
Therefore, the cognition shines forth through the universal of all individual cows; it appears as such because of the unreal, verbalized "cowness. (116)

Let it be that there is a determination of "cow"; therefore, these faults do not arise, because even in the absence of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is a determination of it through delusion. (117)
Just as there is the manifestation of a false "cowness" in the cognition of a cow, so too there is identity, non-distinction, the absence of superimposition, and even substantiality. (118)

Likewise, when there is the appearance of blue and so forth, let it be accepted that the identity with what is unreal—such as whiteness and the like—is established simply by the establishment of the state of manifestation. (119)
When there is no superimposition upon reality, the logical mark (liṅga) consists in identity with the genus;
[otherwise], the superimposition based on the non-exclusion of "cowness" and so forth would be unestablished. (120)
All of this is trivial, because for those who maintain that cognition possesses a form (sākāravādins), even an existing object does not appear; how much less so could one that is non-existent? (121)
Because it is the very nature [of the cognition] that appears, even a child has this certainty;
indeed, the faults that would follow for him based on the appearance of an external object are not applicable here. (122)
[553,17] Where is the application of convention for a word that is its indicator? [553,18] Of what is the word the indicator, wherein the act of convention-making occurs? ||123||
What kind of verbal artifice is this that you perceive?
Show me, too, where the relationship between the signified and the signifier exists anywhere at all. (124)
If its form is false, how is it any different from that? If the convention applies to the false, why does it not apply to the true form as well? (125)
Even if the aspect exists, the fruit is not truly found in what is false;
if [the fruit is denied] because of the superimposition of an object onto the false, by what means is it denied in the case of the true? ||126||

What is the superimposition of an object? Furthermore, what is it like even when truth or falsity is involved? Is the form true or false? And by what is the superimposition of a real entity produced? (127)
For if there is no appearance of the real cow-nature, what is the point of the appearance of a real form?
If the form is real even though it is real, then the form must also be unreal even though it is real. (128)
Since superimposition is logical when there is the appearance of what is non-existent, how could it occur in the case of the real?
But surely, even regarding the non-real, if the convention is determined to be non-real, how [could it be established]? (129)

Therefore, regarding the body of that which consists of the superimposition of an entity capable of causal efficiency, the making of a convention makes no difference between the real and the unreal. (130)
In the state of suchness, no determination of the word exists; nor is there the manifestation of an object. Therefore, in reality, what is there that can be expressed? ||131||
Whether there is non-appearance or appearance, there is no superimposition of anything whatsoever;
such a thing is merely a conventional designation based on the distinction of dependent origination. //132//
When conceptualization arises from the non-conceptual, following a mere trace, it occurs due to the words of those who establish conventions, directed toward a specific mental image. (133)

The convention is established based on the conviction that such a word exists; furthermore, the determination of the denotable object occurs within the nature of the cognition that projects its own activity.

Thus, when the arising of the form of a conceptualization that projects such activity occurs, there is the superimposition of water and so forth; and this [superimposition] is equal in status to both the real and the unreal.
Therefore, although in reality there is no superimposition of anything upon anything anywhere, this [superimposition], which is established by conventional usage, cannot be denied. (136)
As long as there is the conceptualization of a self in that which is not-self, like water in a mirage, that very delusion is saṃsāra; nirvāṇa is the firm establishment in reality.
Therefore, in this matter, as long as there is no possibility of investigation, this principle holds: "This is existence; that is another, which is peace.
But when the mind is stirred by the play of investigation, let it be told: where here are existence or peace? (138)
And thus:
"In this world, there exists no interval whatsoever between these two—the state of peace and birth—when considered in terms of their ultimate reality (*sad-artha-vṛtti*).
Nevertheless, the attainment of peace is established through the cessation of birth."
[This is] for those who perform virtuous deeds. ||139||
Likewise: "Both nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist.
The thorough understanding of existence itself is called 'nirvāṇa. (140)
In the cognition of water, the falsity of the appearance is not the cause;
likewise, in the establishment of error, there is a confusion regarding the grasped object and the grasper. (141)
Whether the object is real or unreal, there is no fault on the part of the mind, provided that no external superimposition arises to impel its activity. (142)
Therefore, even knowledge that possesses the aspect of truth is conceptualizing with respect to its object;
it is flawed because it projects activity, since activity is cyclic existence. ||143||

If it is argued that activity occurs neither in the absence of conceptualization nor in the presence of conceptualization, then why is this not also the case regarding the recollection of distinctions? Therefore, what is the point? (144)

Just as something is capable of performing a certain function in a certain place due to practice beginningless in time, so too is this capacity of conceptual construction established as a means of proof. (145)
For this very reason, the afflictions exist within the conceptual constructions of Bodhisattvas;
therefore, effort must be applied to destroy those latencies as long as the state of cause and effect persists. //146//
The appearance of the unreal form of "cowness" is not established for one who possesses the cognition of a cow;
even though it is a conceptual construction with a real form, it is an ascertainment because it impels action. (147)
Just as the real form of "cowness" appears in the cognition of a cow, so too does identity, non-distinction, non-superimposition, and substantiality [appear]. (148)

Likewise, when there is the appearance of blue and so forth, the manifestation of the real white and so forth is established by that very fact; therefore, let identity with that be accepted as real. (149)

Whatever is the nature of a real entity, that entity is not the form [of the object] in the conceptualization of a cow; and blue, which is the nature of a manifest entity, is not otherwise than its manifestation. (150)
Since identity and difference have been eliminated, sublation is established as real;
and nothing other than white perceives it, thus there is no proof of superimposition.
But how can a false form—which is capable of neither benefiting nor harming, which appears only occasionally, and which does not possess causal efficacy—be anything other than deceptive? (152)
For when its own nature is thus understood, even an adversary becomes its servant;
therefore, it is self-luminous by nature, whether pure or afflicted. (153)
That which is merely false, even if it exists, does not act as an obstacle anywhere;
for if it were to act as an obstacle, its falsity would itself result in being false. (154)
Movement to another object of experience is not at all desired; where, then, could there be bondage?
Furthermore, even with a hundred [arguments], there is no bondage for that which is self-cognizing. (155)

For it is illogical to claim that what is insentient is luminous by virtue of its own cause within the bond of self-cognition; therefore, cognition is impossible even through identity with itself. (156)

Arising in that manner from its own cause and being experienced as having that very nature—[if] oneness were thus accepted by entities, it would be a great affliction for the proponents of philosophical views. (157)
Therefore, this hollow form does not touch it, even though it vibrates;
yet, by that much alone, why would there be no affliction for it through another mental continuum? (158)
Even if it were a real entity, the difference in mental continua would not be an obstacle for that [cognition].
But since the aspect is unreal, how can it possibly be an obstacle? //159//
Apart from the occurrence and cessation of that [consciousness], there is nothing else called saṃsāra.
When the obstruction regarding the various determinations of reality has been established, [verse 160].
Furthermore, there is no distinction among determinations beyond their mental aspect;
because of the non-conceptualization of the aspect of water, one proceeds toward water itself. (161)
Even the conceptualization of the form of water does not arise from the mere form of water; though it does arise, it is accompanied by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). //162//

When those latencies have been completely eradicated, there is no longer conceptualization of the unreal—such as the state of grasped object and grasping subject—from that which is non-conceptual and solitary. //163//

Even if non-conceptual cognition is the cause because it is the basis for latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then upon the destruction of that [cognition], there would be the destruction of the arising of the aspect as it has proceeded. (164)

From the moment of taking up the thought of awakening, through the gradual practice of generosity and the other perfections, there arises the manifestation of the forms of the universal body, enjoyments, and the environment. (165)

For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others and one's own welfare without resting until the end of saṃsāra, because of the singular devotion to that alone, the exertion toward its cause is peerless. (166)
Then, through the glory of merit and wisdom endowed with great compassion, he accomplishes the stability of the continuity of the bonds of purified latent impressions. ||167||
In that regard, non-existent conceptualization is time; it is affliction, and purification is subsequent.
Since consciousness possesses aspects (sākāra), this systematic arrangement is established. 168.
This form of the wheel of ornaments consists of the essence of the common substratum and the objects to be established, filled with hundreds of variegated qualities of non-duality;
yet, having discarded that which is to be accomplished, even the continuity of existence is not the core.
The principle of "possessing aspects" (sākāra) is the life-force of the person of the principle. //169//

It is observed that even for women and others who are drawn by the flavor of pleasure, cultivation arises in such a way that it becomes dependent upon the means for achieving a superior state of well-being;
and likewise, upon its completion, it takes on a form that is to be celebrated as a continuous flow of bliss.
In the process of establishing what is sublated and what is not sublated, let there be the sole remainder of bliss through the exclusion of both; what need is there for anything else? (170)
[557,23] Two intermediate verses:

Thus ends the third chapter, which is the determination of the consensus among other authors of treatises regarding the entirety of the Dharma-body, from its beginning through the limits of affliction and purification.
Let it not be something else; let there be the very possession of forms (*sākāra*) as the basis for the distinction between the proven and the other.
But by the exclusion of being one or many, who can prevent its falsity? (1)
Let there be the exclusion of being one or many, but not the unreality of that which is manifest;
for sublation occurs only when a form has been determined, never regarding the object of direct perception itself.
Even in the case of a double moon, the appearance of mere form is not sublated;
however, there is sublation of touch and so forth, as well as of the form that accompanies them. (3)
Likewise, even in a dream, a son or the like, though imagined, is not a physical body;
nor does the appearance of yellow in clods of earth and such, due to the influence of mantras, cause any harm. //4//
[558,10] That which is imagined as gold and so forth is sublated; however, there is no appearance of a clod of earth and the like.
[558,11] And because there is no determination [of it], there is neither its affirmation nor its sublation. //5//
The theory that this is a "misapprehension of something else" (anyathākhyāti) is flawed because such a manifestation is impossible;
however, the "manifestation of the non-existent" (asatkhyāti) is well-known, being conceived in relation to what is real.
[558,14] Is it not also the case that, according to the intention that "it is the clod itself that appears otherwise," [the error] does not exist?
[558,15] One insists on this from the perspective of conventional usage, but in reality, those two do not exist. //7//
Even though they are devoid of that form, they appear in quite another way;
because this has been stated, the actual meaning here should be understood as it was explained. (8)
Likewise, because those [errors] are not seen by one whose vision is unimpaired, the reality of the imagined nature is stated by him with respect to the appearance of gold and so forth. (9)
There is no sublation of anything in reality; however, there is sublation of that which is imagined within conventional reality.
If even that which is manifest were subject to sublation, then how could there be any confidence even when it is sublated? (10)
If it is argued that the invalidation by inference does not have a real entity as its object, [we reply:
this [invalidation] must necessarily be grounded in the nature of a real entity; otherwise, it would not be a valid cognition (*pramā*). (11)
Even in the case of a positive operation, it is only that which has already appeared as an object that is determined;
even a negation, though having the nature of an intrinsic property, ultimately results in the same. (12)
[559,3] Two intermediate verses:
It is held that the subsequent [cognition] makes known the absence of the object;
how could a cognition that is active toward its own object bring about the understanding of non-existence? (13)

If [the cognition] invalidates other objects by means of establishing its own object-domain, why does it not also invalidate that [other cognition], since that [other cognition] likewise abides in its own object-domain? (14)

If purposeful causal efficiency is distinct because of the abandonment of that [specific] object and action, then why would the abandonment of one thing not entail the abandonment of another? Yet, if there is no difference [between them], how can this [abandonment] manifest?
Having observed that color, there is the sublation of touch due to the cessation of burning and so forth;
yet touch does not manifest here. That very sublation belongs to it—what is the use of others? (16)

If something else were to be sublated first, once it has been made an object of cognition, how could that which is still manifest be sublated? And if it is not manifest, what would the sublater do? (17)
There is no sublation when there is a difference in time, because each thing manifests at its own respective time;
likewise, even when there is no difference in time, as in the case of blue, yellow, white, and so forth. (18)
Therefore, sublation is like a superimposition due to the difference in dependent origination;
it is conceptualized, but not in reality. As for that which is mere self-cognition, what talk can there be? //19//
If it is argued that as long as the non-establishment of self-cognition has not been proven, there may be sublation;
then, once the non-establishment of self-cognition has been demonstrated through analysis, let sublation proceed.

If, at the outset when beginning the argument, one were to say that the contradiction of one's own thesis has not been incurred, [thinking]: "In the negation of another's cognition, my own cognition is established. (21)
In whatever way objects are reflected upon and analyzed, in that very same way,
self-cognition remains like a shadow, never departing even from one who runs.
For this very reason, even though he was engaged in a negation, the Teacher declared:
"If this is pleasing to things themselves, what can we do about it? (23)
If there is no sublation by another, let there likewise be no establishment by another;
how then can even the establishment of self-awareness come about through a further means of proof? (24)
The establishment of anything from something else occurs not in reality (*tattva*), but rather in conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*);
just as this establishment of fire and so forth from smoke and so forth is accepted, so it is here. [25]

If self-awareness is established as non-reality, then for as long as the establishment of the factors of the proof persists, that alone is reality which is established by the power of the means of proof. //26//

Once that which is to be proven is established through the power of its own proof as mere self-cognition, there is no longer any room whatsoever for further establishment or sublation from any source. (27)
One who does not awaken to anything else is incapable of abandoning what is under discussion;
nor is one who abandons what is under discussion capable of apprehending another thing from something else. ||28||

For this very reason, another's cognition, when being apprehended, constitutes a sublation of one's own [position], because there is also room for the cognition of the three-fold criteria (trairūpya) which is the cause of self-awareness. //29//
But even if those forms are not cognized, their abandonment does not constitute a contradiction;
for the manifestation that establishes the probandum exists through another [means], and not otherwise. //30//
If it is argued that [the manifestation] should not exist even by itself, provided that the appearance is not [established] in every respect—this may be logical;
however, since the illumination exists, why should it not exist by itself? (31)
There is manifestation, but it does not arise from itself; if it were not from something other than that, how could it be?
Otherwise, just as there is a subverting argument [against the former], so too there is none for [the claim that] cognition arises from itself. (32)
[560,19] Furthermore, there is no obstruction of an action within its own self by means of two streams through their own interruption;
[560,20] why then is it not stated by the wise man that even a sharp stream is itself [the agent]? //33//
If that [faculty] is produced as sharp solely from its own cause and not from anything else, then cognition in the form of light is also produced solely from its own cause. (34)
Let it not be that manifestation is produced by the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary;
rather, the form itself, which arises with that nature, is designated by the word "manifestation. (35)
Just as illumination is seen to result from the mutual assistance between a lamp and a cloth, why is it not likewise observed that the lamp illuminates itself? 36.
If the lamp depends on the sense organ, why does that dependence not also exist in the jar?
Even when the jar exists, the jar requires the lamp, but the lamp does not require anything else. //37//

Just as, even when effort and so forth are present, the statement that there is "coming of its own accord" serves to exclude being impelled by another, so too does it serve to exclude that which belongs to the same class with respect to self-manifestation. (38)
Even in scripture, that which appears as self-cognition despite sublation is the negation of that subtle state of the grasped and the grasper. (39)

Just as the state of being both cause and fruit in one and the same thing was refuted after being raised as a doubt, so too has the state of being both grasped object and grasping subject in one and the same thing been refuted after being raised as a doubt. (40)

Therefore, it is held that the mind is self-luminous, not by way of being an object and an agent; rather, having arisen from its own causes, the mind shines forth in dependence upon other factors. //41//
[561,13] It is made clear in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* because that meaning is demonstrated there;
[561,14] it is also indicated by such statements as "the arising of the appearance of objects" and so forth. ||42||
Therefore, self-awareness is not contradicted by either reasoning or scripture;
that very same fault which contradicts the knower of another is like fire [consuming] a tree. //43//
Nor is it desired that the apprehension of another's cognition involve the operation of one's own cognition;
for it is through the merits and defects of one's own cognition that [the latter] is evaluated. (44)
The fault does not lie in mere existence, but rather in its functional activity;
for earth and the other elements are not to be censured when they remain in a state where they have not yet performed their function.

Therefore, there is no fault regarding self-awareness; however, because of the extensive nature of its manifestation, luminosity is itself determined as being excluded from awareness of anything other than that. 46.
If there is no appearance either from itself or from another, then there is no appearance at all;
and it is not appropriate to say this of something that is like a clod of earth or similar objects. (47)

If it is maintained that there is an appearance even when there is exclusion from both itself and others, then let there be for you the existence of a thing despite its being devoid of both unity and plurality. (48)
If an entity is held to be real even when it is devoid of being one or many, then why do you not accept that an appearance exists even in the absence of both self-nature and other-nature? (49)
Nevertheless, although these appear, they cannot be denied as being entities;
because their appearance is unique, they will also possess the nature of cognition.
The appearance of form possesses a real nature of perceptibility, and there is no fault in its self-cognition; therefore, nothing at all is undermined.
But how could it be that "the self-cognition of blue" exists?
For this [cognition] does not know itself as a single entity, by virtue of which there would be self-awareness. (52)

Since internal forms such as pleasure and so forth, and external forms such as cold and heat and so forth, appear, for whom could there be cognition by what, and how? Nor is there oneness [of subject and object]. //53//
[562,13] First of all, these [cognitions] do indeed have manifestation; therefore, it is impossible to deny that.
[562,14] If that [manifestation] were not possible in the case of difference, then let there be non-difference of the cognitions at that time. //54//
How could there be non-difference among these things which possess distinct forms?
Is it therefore intended that there is an absence of duality, or rather that duality itself is a real entity? //55//

Whether distinction or non-distinction, whether in two ways or not in two ways—let it be as it may regarding the nature of cognition; there is no unreality in manifestation, for it is opposed even to the mere scent of sublation.
For there is no sublation of one's own direct experience by any logical arguments;
for it is that very experience which is the source of those arguments, and they find their finality in it alone.
Let there be only the consideration of difference and so forth; there is no exclusion of manifestation.
Wherever there is repose in manifestation—whether it be one's own or another—it is that very thing which truly exists.
When the self-cognizing subject is established as existing in the sentient being, what is the use of deliberating whether it is one or many?
For it is said that the establishment of its result occurs through the non-existence of that [object], due to the absence of the [subject]. //59//
Even if mere manifestation is established, how can self-awareness be asserted? And if the object is established by that much alone, what need have we for the term "self-awareness"? (60)
For the opponent's intended thesis is indeed sublated by perception;
moreover, that [thesis] is established even when its own nature is revealed by the opponent.
Perceptuality arises from the direct realization of its own nature, and there is no other;
even by another, that very form of illumination first shines forth. (62)
Nevertheless, self-awareness certainly exists; however, it is not "self" in the sense of belonging to itself.
Thus, there is no damage to the argument even if one asserts that cognition is known by another, provided that sublation is not established.
Neither the cognition of another nor self-cognition is established;
therefore, what kind of thing is this so-called "perceptuality" by which [the opponent's position] could be sublated? (64)
It has been stated that the nature of direct realization is perception;
nor is there any impairment of its specific definition even in the absence of conceptual ascertainment. //65//
Just as there is a pervasion of particulars by a universal, so too is this [universal] established by them;
when the particular is established, the universal is established, and when the universal is established, that [particular] is established.
Whether it be a hero or someone else, one must cultivate certainty regarding being human;
yet, there is no defeat for a human being due to doubt concerning those two.
If that non-duality were established, there would be a loss of humanity;
however, whether humanity is unestablished or established, there is no loss of duality. (68)

Therefore, regarding an object that is beyond the senses, when its existence as a twofold appearance is undermined, let the loss of the appearance be determined; however, regarding the appearance itself, there is a single status for both.
There is no doubt regarding what is manifest; rather, doubt concerns the distinction and the non-distinction.
Either distinction or non-distinction must necessarily be concomitant with what is manifest. (70)
Just as the persistence of difference and non-difference depends upon logical justification, light is not like that; for if it were dependent, how could it be called "light"? //71//
If the pervasion of light were to occur by means of two [factors], there would be a coexistence of the two;
yet such pervasion is not established anywhere. Nevertheless, it has been stated that there is no impairment [of the argument]. //72//
Since one does not know through a feeling that is either non-different or different, how can there be sublation by perception? This [argument] is sufficient for the pervasion itself. //73//

If it is argued that perceptibility must be established by the proponent of the sublation, then for one who accepts a means of valid cognition, what kind of perception could there be for another? (74)
Even when there is a non-perception of the pervader, in the determination of the three forms [of the reason], perception must necessarily be involved, either indirectly or directly. (75)
In that case, what kind of direct perception do you have if it does not exist for us?
If that [perception] is conventional, then let there be sublation as well from the conventional, just like [the establishment of] proof. //76//
[564,11] When form is attained, conventional cognition is capable; how can there be no sublation? [564,12] Whatever kind of thing is established, let that very same kind be the sublater. ||77||

If the conventional nature of both the means of cognition (*māna*) and the object of cognition (*meyya*) is due to conventionality (*saṃvṛti*), then that very conventionality is still being investigated even now; how can it serve as a proof when it is not yet established? (78)

If the apprehension of the pervasion of the final cognition—which lacks awareness of another—is effected by something else, let that other apprehension be erroneous; what loss is there to self-awareness? (79)
For one who lacks valid means of cognition, silence is indeed better;
for by speaking, one will necessarily either contradict something or merely restate what is already established. (80)
If you claim that pride is accepted as conventional, then this very analysis is also conventional.
If it is not even accepted as conventional, then one who speaks thus is a victor, just as [the Buddha was]. (81)
Nor is there such a possibility of sublation even in the case of causes such as light, because the reversal of the unique appearance has not been established. [82]
By this direct perception as well, there is merely the act of making [the object] its domain;
there is no establishment of its existence—so why is there not an occasion for sublation? (83)
Because it is made an object by a means of knowledge that establishes through affirmation, there is nowhere any capacity to establish existence; rather, existence is merely worldly. //84//

In all cases, it is logical that the proof of a difference in existence is established by means of what is produced by human agency; however, that which contradicts existence—such as destruction—is a subverter of existence and is therefore inconsistent [with its own premise]. (85)
Therefore, whether it be one's own or another's, that which possesses the manifestation of the object's own nature is alone the domain of direct perception. 86.
Even in the doubt as to whether it has that form or not, the nature of the object of awakening is stable;
for it is precisely through the presentation of the cognition and the cognizable that there is proof or refutation. //87//
Form should not be sought in its own nature for the sake of pacifying delusion;
for when form appears as it manifests, there is no possibility of delusion.

[565,11] Let it be simply "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha); what then is the purpose of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta)? [565,12] If you argue that the insistence on establishing the two types of error is also futile, [we reply: 89.
[565,13] It is true that it was indeed composed by the venerable teacher Dignāga;
[565,14] however, in the *Vārttika*, it was done by superimposing externality upon the form of the world. ||90||
If people were to know the form as being merely a form, and the mother-of-pearl as being merely mother-of-pearl, how could there ever be delusion for anyone anywhere? (91)
At that time, the determination of identity regarding two things that do not possess that nature is to be averted precisely by the elimination of conceptual construction; this is logical. //92//
But when the apprehension of an object by all embodied beings is seen, specifically in the form of knowledge, as having an extremely clear and distinct appearance; 93.
Then, the apprehension of an unreal object would be perception because it is free from conceptual construction;
this would result in the second qualification being redundant, like the apprehension of what has already been apprehended. //94//

It is said that this [cognition] is "accompanied by obscurity" (sataimira) only in consideration of worldly understanding; and another [type of cognition] is taught for the sake of removing the delusion regarding the conceptual nature of this [cognition] which appears clearly. //95//

At the time of investigating reality, that determination of error occurs only in relation to the imagined; it does not occur through the observation of its own form when there is a clear appearance. (96)
Even though it is non-conceptual, it possesses the nature of error because of conceptualization; there is nothing beyond that.
Therefore, although it rests in the non-conceptual, it is said to be "resting in conceptualization. (97)
If conceptual construction were erroneous, there would either be another error or none at all; if conceptual construction were non-erroneous, then error itself would not exist. //98//
[566,7] Two intermediate verses:
The fact that something appears before one excludes its unreality;
therefore, falsity belongs to the object alone within the manifestation, and not to the cognition or the person. 99.

Therefore, even amidst disputes regarding difference and non-difference within cognition, the state of being an object of perception is established for that which is manifest; and existence is precisely that.
This non-duality is considered variegated because it is devoid of the grasped and so forth; the conventional designation of "one" for what is manifold is as futile as the notion of a person. (101)
As long as there is external conceptual attachment, so long does this appear as distinct from that;
but when that cognition is complete in its entirety, it is indeed that very thing which possesses hands, feet, and so forth, through knowledge. //102//

In a variegated cognition, blue and other such colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else; for it is impossible to perceive them as distinct, since one who attempts to differentiate them falls back upon the external object. (103)
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind, even though it possesses variegated forms. (104)
[566,20] Summary verses:
By these two [arguments], "the variegated cognition" and so forth, the refutation of the one and the many occurs respectively;
for it is sublated by its being a mental adjunct (*jñānopādhi*) and by its being incapable of being perceived as such. (105)
The inclusion of the remaining cases is by means of the verse beginning with "For that [object], multiple sounds are in vain" (mudhānekadhvaniḥ).
The logical proof is by means of the verse beginning with "Whatever [is perceived] in whatever manner... (yad yatheti); the identity of a single designation is the oneness of that [object]. (106)
Even when there is a contradiction between perception and inference, there is no doubt regarding their respective capacities:
inference is always dependent upon the senses, whereas that which is born of the senses is never dependent upon inference. (107)
Just as you avoid contradiction with direct perception while accepting inference, so too it is not possible for perception to arise without avoiding contradiction with inference. (108)
And since inference applies elsewhere than to what is imperceptible, what kind of contradiction could there be?
What object is sublated by the sense-faculty? This [inference] is not a means of valid cognition regarding that [sensory] domain. (109)

In the case of the subsistence of its own existence, [the object] is other than a quality [known] through perception or inference, because it is not engaged by direct perception and because its status as being beyond the senses is established. ||110||
Therefore, even by means of another perception, there is no inference whatsoever for comparison;
but as for that which is established through self-awareness, what kind of inquiry could there be regarding it? (111)
If self-awareness alone is not a means of valid cognition because it is not an external source, then what here is a means of valid cognition?
Therefore, regarding those things established or sublated by that [self-awareness], no other [means of valid cognition] has the power to either sublate or establish them. (112)
An intermediate verse:
Even when the categories of being one or many are excluded, by what could this manifestation be prevented?
Nor is there a pervasion of these two [categories] by existence, because that is sublated by direct perception itself. //113//
By this [argument], the pervasion regarding the operation of a characteristic at the time of its activity is destroyed;
this restriction exists only externally by virtue of its functional capacity.
Even in the case of dualism, not every external object is common to all cognitions;
just as there is stability and instability, so it would be in non-dualism—if this were not so, there would be no fault.
Stability and the like, being pervaded by the relation of priority and posteriority, do not exist in the absence of that [succession].
Stability is not pervaded by oneness or manifoldness; this is true for cognition, but not for consciousness. (116)
[567,22] Furthermore, there is pervasion; moreover, because that [pervasion] exists, there is a single [cognition] of these two.
[567,23] For indeed, the determination of all aspects does not occur even with respect to an object that is directly perceived. //117//
When blue and so forth appear, the appearance itself is the direct perception;
therefore, there is no suspicion of a difference from yellow and so forth. (118)

In that case as well, the establishment of non-difference is due solely to the appearance of interpenetration; for if there were difference, there would be no manifestation, just as in the case of cognitions belonging to distinct continua. (119)
