If it is argued that the distinctions such as the appropriated [aggregates] and so forth are mutually manifest, this is incorrect;
for even the designation "appropriated" does not eliminate their distinction. (120)
Even if there is proximity, what could be the purpose of apprehension? If that very [proximity] were the direct manifestation, it would indeed be the manifestation itself. (121)
And by virtue of that power, why is there no perception of the cause and effect within the grasping?
However, the gradation of proximity exists therein only in relation to that very [grasping]. //122//
If, in this context, the manifestation of concomitance has the purpose of mutual apprehension, then why is there not also a manifestation of proximity even when there is no mutual apprehension? (123)

Therefore, there can be no variegated appearance; for consciousness cannot tolerate differentiation, because it is characterized by the non-difference of its own nature due to the mutual penetration of cognitions.
If [the effect] arises always from the variegated [cause] alone, how can there even be a single material cause?
Furthermore, even during a state of contraction, there is no certain determination of it as being exclusively one. (125)
As long as the birth of a variegated [effect] is perceived from a variegated [cause] itself, so long is it not tenable for there to be a mutual manifestation of distinct material causes. (126)
If even a variegated object of appropriation were to abide as a unity, why would that not also apply to the appropriated? Thus, the non-duality of the variegated remains unrefuted. (127)
Or how could even a single blue object appear as atoms?
Therefore, when the existence of many [atoms] is subverted, by what means could there be stability and unity for anything? (128)

If it is thought that the absence of both unity and plurality follows for this very reason, let it be so; however, it has already been explained that the sublation of existence cannot be established. (129)

But this is relevant to the case of difference: it is not logical for there to be a mutual appearance, because the latter has no power over the former, since they are distinct in terms of their material cause (*upādāna*). (130)
Therefore:
"Because they are necessarily perceived together, blue and yellow are non-different. For their very nature is consciousness, which is non-different; so how can there be a distinction? (131)
There is no restriction of simultaneous cognition for two distinct things, such as blue and yellow; for in this way, each one might be seen by the two persons individually. (132)
Regarding this, it is said:
In a variegated cognition, blue and other such colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else.
For it is impossible to perceive them [as distinct]; indeed, one who attempts to differentiate them falls into [the error of perceiving] the external object. (133)
In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature even in a mind possessing variegated forms. (134)
For even when there is sublation, as in the case of external objects, there is no perception of a single [nature] by persons;
because since it is apprehended otherwise, the restriction is destroyed. (135)
Whatever appears as a single entity is like the white form in a painting;
and the entire variegated picture appears as yellow, cold, pleasure, and so forth. (136)
This has been stated with reference to a single intended cognizer;
therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason] on account of what appears to another mental continuum. (137)
In the example, there is no lack of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnyatva*), because there is no subverting evidence for the contrary.
For appearance is pervaded by grossness; it does not, indeed, break down into atoms. (138)
Because each individual atom is submerged [in its own particularity], there is no mutual cognition of them;
nor does the manifestation of a single atom exist, for it is only the gross [object] that appears. //139//
The appearance of external atoms is a single, more massive cognition; but what will the appearance of the atoms of consciousness itself be? 140.
Even in the case of a manifold whole, there is a single cognition of a variegated form; it is suitable for practical usage in fragments, but what is the recourse when it comes to the intellect? (141)
In one case as well, the cognition of a single part has been established as possessing a form;
since conventional practice cannot otherwise be explained, the grossness of cognition is difficult to abandon. //142//
Therefore, the appearance, which is pervaded by grossness, ceases because that [grossness] is removed;
for you, O Vinaya-master, it ceases from being manifold into oneness.
Just as there is the exclusion of difference from a portion of a similar cognition through the consequence of non-appearance, so too [is it excluded] from a dissimilar cognition. (144)
Therefore, let there be no probandum, no example, and no doubt or misconception;
nor can there be sublation of the probandum by perception, because perception itself lacks a firm foundation. (145)
Self-awareness is neither conceit nor the apprehension of another, nor is it that which grasps at difference;
the conceptual construction that "this is different from that" follows from latent predispositions. ||146||
Just as this [subject] independently imagines the external to be distinct from itself, so too does it itself imagine the external to be distinct from the internal. 147.
Even though external objects exist, perception does not cognize their difference from anything else;
for if it did, there would follow the apprehension of everything else as well, since they are apprehended as being qualified by that [difference].

If this "distinct from that" were the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of the object to be apprehended, then there would be no appearance of this [object] with its limit (avadhi), nor would it be apprehended in its own form. (149)
For if difference is perceived even without a formal rule [of distinction], why would non-difference not be so?
Consequently, there would be a mere metaphorical designation of difference; therefore, difference does not exist in reality. (150)
[570,19] Indeed, the apprehension of a form unmixed with others is what constitutes the cognition of difference.
[570,20] "Unmixed with others" means distinct from another; such is that which has a single referent. (151)
But when one thing is mixed with another, the apprehension of the other is not appropriate;
for if the other is not apprehended, how can that unmixed, solitary thing be apprehended? (152)
Since this [object] shines forth as something solitary, it is not joined with anything else;
for if another [object] were also manifest, how could it be apprehended as solitary? (153)

Just as there can be no apprehension of a thing in its isolation when another is manifesting, so too, even when another is not manifesting, that which is "isolated" is indeed mixed with something else. (154)
Just as the mental transformation [appears] as "this is unmixed with another," if experience were likewise [unmixed], by what could that primary intellect (*pradhī*) be prevented? 155.

Just as, my dear father, having excluded the other, the apprehension of a mixture does not exist; so too, my dear father, having excluded the other, the apprehension of a distinct entity does not exist. (156)
Therefore, it is logical that perception grasps only the thing-in-itself;
by means of it, neither a distinct nor a non-distinct [entity] can be grasped. (157)
An object is not known through the appearance of difference because of the limitation [of perception], nor through the suspicion of non-difference;
nor is it other than difference and non-difference. How, then, can there be a grasping of a real entity? (158)

If everything is indistinguishable from its object, how could there be any distinction even from cognition? And if there were such a distinction, then even when there is a limited measure, everything would be within the range of everyone. ||159||
[571,13] However, when there is an adherence to external apprehension, the refutation is equal in the case of reflection;
[571,14] just as it is when the apprehension of difference is not accepted, so it is when there is an apprehension of a real limit. (160)
Therefore, let the perception of external objects occur however it may, even with the eyes closed;
but how can one who knows reality be subverted when he merely describes the non-apprehension of difference? (161)
Perception does not create differentiation; rather, conceptual construction (kalpanā) acts as the thief here that does so.
It is this [conceptualization] that casts its own fault upon perception; such is the established nature of differentiation. (162)
If it is argued that this [cognition] is one, just like the blue [object], how can this be consistent? For how could it be coherent that the blue and its other parts are one and the same? (163)
If even that [atom] is not one, then how can there be an appearance when the atom is divided?
Furthermore, since the atom is incapable of withstanding analysis, how and of what could there be division at that time? (164)
Or, lest it be non-substantial, even that would result in the destruction of oneness;
for when oneness is established through manifestation, the substantiality of self-awareness is secured. (165)

Furthermore, for that which is devoid of another name, the attainment of spatial extension is impossible; nor can it be said that there is "appearance" when the manifestation of space has ceased. (166)
It is not logical for one's own nature to be different from another's nature; that [difference] belongs only to the external.
For consciousness, which culminates in self-cognition, what recourse is there for that which is other? (167)

Even though an external object is perceived by the intellect as divided by spatial location, by what means can the intellect itself—being divided by spatial locations—be the basis for conventional usage? (168)
Even though it occupies a large space, cognition cannot admit of differentiation because of its identity with that [object];
just as there is no differentiation within it despite its non-difference [from the object], so too it is with respect to the form. //169//
If it is argued that this single entity is variegated, then this is even more variegated than that;
and this is most variegated of all: that there is a mutual perception of distinctness. (170)
When there is the manifestation of a single cognition of variety, there may or may not be an external object;
for if it were not manifested, there would follow the consequence that neither external objects nor cognitions exist. (171)
Whether atoms exist or do not exist, there can be no coherence for the appearance in cognition;
therefore, the appearance of cognition is incompatible with both atomicity and its absence. (172)
Regarding this, it is said:
In a variegated cognition, the blue and other colors are attributes of the cognition itself and do not belong to anything else.
Indeed, one who attempts to discern them as distinct from the cognition falls into the realm of external objects, for such a distinction is impossible to perceive. (173)
"In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is understood exactly in that way;
thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the mind, even though it possesses variegated forms. (174)
In the experience of a variegated [cognition], this blue and so forth is distinguished by its nature as cognition;
not having attained mutual individual forms, it cannot be perceived as something gross. (175)

Because the distinction [of parts] would apply to every atom, or else there would be only a heap of blue and so forth; for it is impossible to perceive [it as such], since the intellect perceives each individual [atom] as it has arisen. //176//
Therefore, a single experience must be admitted as having multiple aspects, from which the mind subsequently constructs the notion that "this is distinct from that. (177)

For this very reason, when one differentiates an object such as blue and so forth, one should discern it [as external]; it is not the form of cognition itself. If that were different [from the object], there would be neither cognition nor an object of experience. ||178||
Therefore, in whatever manner and by whatever means the cognition shines forth, it is accepted as being qualified precisely by that—namely, by its gross unity. (179)

Furthermore, the superimposition of contradictory properties serves to establish difference in that case where difference is established by perception for the sake of accomplishing conventional usage. (180)
In this case, self-awareness alone is perception, and it is not distinct from that [awareness].
When there is the state of being blue and so forth, conceptualization follows after it; it is not distinct from that [perception]. (181)
If it is argued that the difference [between cognitions] arises from a difference in their manifestations, then that very manifestation is called the "aspect" (ākāra).
When the object of cognition is external, that [manifestation] is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); with respect to that object, self-awareness (svavid) is the result of cognition (pramā).
How can that which has been made one by self-awareness be differentiated externally through division?
Just as the apprehension of cognitions occurs from the sense organ, so too does their differentiation occur through self-awareness. (183)
If radiance were appearance, it would not exist as self-cognition; for the determination of difference produced by the form of the object of cognition is destroyed by wisdom. (184)
For if a cold [object] were to split a cold [object] through direct perception itself, then that which is being split would either be already split or not split at all.
If it is already split, how could it be split further, since there is not even a trace of another [part] to be split? How then could it split it?
Who could possibly say, "The mind was broken" or "It is broken"? [185]

The external object does not perish, whether through division into atoms or through non-difference; for in the case of non-difference, there would be a confusion resulting from the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). It is merely a portion [of it].
But the cognition perishes precisely through its difference, since its existence consists solely in being known.
Therefore, even though it is variegated, it does not undergo differentiation; what can we do about this? //186//
Even so, if you claim that the distinction exists merely in accordance with the cognition of the ignorant,
then even by this much, your reason remains unestablished (*asiddha*). Furthermore, there would be the loss of oneness, or else the contradiction of the requirement of cognition.
"But even that [substantiality] does not exist for us"—this is what has been stated by the opponent. (187)
Intermediate verses:

If the pervasion of entities by unity and plurality were established anywhere, then at the time of the proof of universal emptiness, that reason would result in the subversion of what is intended. (188)

Furthermore, even if something is well-known in the world, not everything imagined by the world constitutes the establishment of reality; rather, that which is consistent with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the refuge. (189)
Neither through perception nor through inference has anything partless ever been observed anywhere; for that which would have multiple parts could not be a single entity at all. (190)
[574,12] Each gross object is perceived individually; it is not determined as being either one or many.
[574,13] But in reality, how could there be a single thing? Nor is there any such thing at all. //191//
For the wise, the acceptance of another's position is not valid when establishing an independent proof;
nor does the primary meaning apply in a *prasaṅga* (reductio), for if it did, there would be a destruction of one's own tenet. //192//
Let that person be defeated whose definition of existence is pervaded by either one or both of these;
however, the proponent of existence [defined] as mere non-erroneous cognition is the victor. (193)
In all cases of a reason, pervasion depends upon the establishment of valid cognition;
and that [pervasion] is to be known through the non-perception of the pervader and so forth in the contrary case. //194//
When the subject is not established, there is no pervasion, nor is the pervaded admitted by oneself; it is proclaimed that what is known by another is sublated only by the cognition of another. (195)
Furthermore, the acceptance of intrinsic nature does not necessarily entail being a single attractor;
for its pervasion remains unestablished even now, and it is contradicted by valid cognition. (196)

If, by taking up the pervasion through the exclusion of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one negates that [existence], why would things not then be of the nature of non-existence, like the transcendence of a donkey’s horn? (197)
[575,1] In that case, how is even the external object refuted by the negation of being one or many?
[575,2] Because it is not perceived in reality, its characteristic as a graspable object is lost. ||198||
Nor is there a partless unity; rather, it is the perception of things as distinct from words.
And that [perception] does not exist externally because of the non-existence of those [external objects]; therefore, their synthesis [is also absent]. //199//
Even in the case of an atom, unity is impossible to demonstrate when analyzed;
since that [impossibility] applies equally to variegated cognition, where would a lack of interest be of any use? (200)
But in the case of a cognition that has a variegated form, it is impossible to perceive it as distinct from a single [unitary] nature;
through the distinction from the minds of others, that [cognition] possesses the characteristics of being both one and many. (201)
Regarding this, it is said: "Blue and so forth... and so on. The distinctness of one cognition from another is evident;
how could that [distinctness] be established through inference? If it is argued that it exists conventionally, let it be as it may. (202)

Nevertheless, just as momentary states are conceived in dependence upon a permanent imagined entity, so too do cognitions depend upon a single object that is firmly conceptualized by another mind. (203)

In that case, even if there is no single entity whose distinction is impossible, there would still be a plurality of things capable of being differentiated from it by virtue of their otherness; so what is the point of a single collection even in the external world? (204)
It is not the case that when a composite whole is destroyed, a single atom remains;
therefore, a multiplicity consisting of an accumulation of those atoms is refuted by that very same fault. ||205||

Likewise, when this semblance of that [unity] has been refuted as being neither one nor many, this collection which is accepted by the proponents as "many" is shown to be nothing but a single [entity]. (206)

It can also be explained in this way from the perspective of external objects; however, the analysis of the whole (avayavin) and the atom (aṇu) was undertaken out of consideration for the views of others. [207]

And when, by the very cognition of variety, there is the sublation of both unity and plurality due to the removal of other sublaters, why is the establishment of those two not achieved by that same cognition? [208]
If there were unity, there would be an absence of variety; if there were plurality, it would be even more so.
Just as there is no unity because of its variegated nature, so too is the status of being both one and many.
Without the introduction of a contradictory [reason], there is no sublation of the counter-entity;
likewise, tell me how there could be [sublation] when one [entity] is destroyed by many, since it is included within its own nature. (210)
And in that case, there would be a collapse of the pervader’s absence due to the maintenance of your own position;
however, for us, this fault does not apply if both are established by means of cognition. (211)
If all particularities are abandoned, how could there not be something uniform anywhere?
That [reality] is accompanied by both unity and multiplicity, as well as by their two modes of manifestation. (212)
Granted that there may be unity within that variegated painting consisting of both difference and non-difference;
nevertheless, the proof is for the sake of establishing one [aspect], not for the purpose of subverting the other. (213)
Even for that person, after the sublation, such a great hope remains:
"If the establishment of the one [entity] is through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), how could there be a subsequent sublation? (214)
If a single entity is not established by means of valid cognition, how could there be the negation of another?
If contradiction were inherent, the negation of one would not be the affirmation of another. (215)
And a positive cognition, being diverse, would negate another by way of introducing a contradiction;
if it were capable while being uttered, oh, what a state for those who rely on valid cognition! //216//
[576,15] At times there is no loss of either, yet there is the persistence of each one;
[576,16] at times it appears as unity, and at times it appears as multiplicity. ||217||
Nevertheless, the existence [of the reason] in one instance is unestablished due to the absence of the pervader. [218]
If existence in the form of causal efficiency and so forth is what is being negated, what loss is there? For that which has the nature of mere appearance is not sublated even by Brahmā.
Even if there were a sublation of that subject (*dharmin*), there would still be no sublation of it in itself;
just as this [object] appears blue, so too it may appear real or it may not. (220)
If it is argued that there is doubt regarding the subject because of doubt regarding its properties, then from what source [does this arise]?
If it is because of identity in reality (*tattvataḥ*), then this is the same as [the case of] the nihilist and others. ||221||

[576,24] Now, if it is argued that certainty regarding one thing destroys doubt even when it has arisen with respect to another, [576,25] that too is the same in the present case, because of the distinction between exclusions (vyāvṛtti). ||222||
When even in the external world existence is in reality nothing but cognition, then where is there sublation, and where is there doubt regarding the appearing subject? (223)

Sometimes that which has been seen by someone is an object of inference at another time; since it is established that what is unfit for perception is never so, how can that which is fit for perception be considered real? (224)
Even in the absence of inference, there is the manifestation of conceptual construction itself;
whatever the nature of the existence of such things may be, their cognition is likewise of that same nature. (225)
Making clear that existence is nothing but cognition, the skillful author of the *Vārttika* established that there is only consciousness, without any dependence on an external object. (226)
The status of substances and so forth as appearing [as such] is in vain, since they appear merely in the form of that [mental] manifestation.
In a painting, there would be only the state of being a single manifestation; there would be no manifoldness through qualities and the like. (227)
For in the system of consciousness, stability is both real and a constituent part of the fruit;
oh, what shamelessness! Or rather, everything belonging to the great is indeed great. (228)
The apprehension of that [object] occurs through the thorough knowledge of what precedes and follows, and through the knowledge of another;
for how could it occur when there is a finality in self-cognition, since both [of those conditions] are impossible? [229]
In the absence of appearance, there is no cognition of priority and posteriority, not because of a deficiency in cognition;
nor is there cognition of priority and posteriority in the presence of appearance, due to its union with non-duality. //230//

Because the two do not exist within its own singular nature, there is no state of being a fruit or a factor for either itself or another; yet, through the exclusion of others, it is known as "other" in two ways. (231)
Therefore, just as there is the cognition of another, so is the establishment of cause and effect;
just as there is the repose of self-cognition, such is this conventional truth. //232//
Therefore, they declare that the establishment of "mind-only" is without production;
for this reason, even dependent origination is not established, and thus it cannot serve as a proof. //233//
Dependent origination itself is not what is to be expressed as emptiness;
because they abide together on the same level, there is no such distinction—[to claim otherwise] is merely futile exertion. //234//
Let non-arising itself be the cause; it cannot be so because of the previously mentioned refutation.
Even if cause and effect were abandoned, where could the manifest form go? (235)
Therefore, every phenomenon is empty of imagined forms; there is no part whatsoever that possesses manifestation.
This is the manifold non-duality, this very wheel of variety.
That which is to be cultivated should be cultivated by means of those things to be cultivated, free from conceptual proliferation, for the sake of auspiciousness.
Direct realization does not occur for those who sustain existence as long as there is a lack of familiarity with the great multitude of things to be abandoned and adopted within this state;
therefore, when the two accumulations have reached maturity through repeated practice, by means of the qualities of form and mind—
That yogi is a lord of yogis, renowned for having attained awakening in the incomparable abode. ||237||
Just as gold, endowed with the perfection of qualities and form, reaches the ultimate limit of excellence and is inexhaustible,
so too it is free from the suspicion of the stain of falsehood.
In that very same way, may the body of a Buddha belong to all embodied beings. ||238||
[578,15] Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Determination of the Non-duality of the Variegated.
The Sākārasaṃgraha-sūtra is completed.
This work is by the great scholar and master, the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra.

The connection [is] with *saṅgati* in A and *saṅgiti* in Ā; it comes to rest (*viśrāmyati*) in A and Ā (J), and that [resting] occurs in A and Ā (J₁) (where J reads *tatra*).
In every respect, [the property] is possible (A); and everything is impossible (Ā). There is no non-pervasion (A, Ā);
there is no suspicion of non-establishment (asiddhi) either by way of its own nature or by way of its locus (A, Ā).
For one who examines it, there will be [the realization] that in some cases it is not so; [this applies] to both A and Ā.
(The emendation *bhaviṣyaty a-* is supported by A; *bhaviṣya...* is found in Ā.
[The word *kva cit* appears in A (it is missing in J); it may also appear in Ā?]
Because it is not established through proof, and because [the opponent] accepts it;
since there is no establishment [of the probandum], such as God and so forth,
and because inference operates everywhere [in relation to the probandum].
— the establishment [of it],

°tvad Ā: This is not so, because there is no specific reason [to restrict it]. For the proof of dependence upon a mental subject, which applies to a specific effect, also applies to effects in general; this is because there is no difference when one accepts that the proof of the general probans and the general probandum consists in *tadutpattiḥ* (origination from that).

This occurs when perception and non-perception are present. Just as one observes that an effect such as a material object has a material cause, and thereby determines another effect to be likewise, so too, since an effect such as a material object...

Once it is established that [a product] has a conscious creator, one may infer that even an effect whose conscious creator is not perceived likewise has such a creator; for the creator, just like the material cause, possesses both positive and negative concomitance with respect to the effect.

Therefore, just as one cannot doubt whether an effect can exist even without material causes (*nirupādāna*), likewise one cannot doubt whether there is an effect that is without an agent; for there is no difference in the proof of the arising of a mere effect based on a mere agent, just as there is none in the proof of [the aforementioned case].

CHEMPARATHY 1963: 123. My translation: “Just as by the sight of smoke, through the fact that [the probans] is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), the particularity of fire—namely, its being located in a thicket—is recognized even though it is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*), in the same way, the particularity of the creator is recognized.”

Therefore, there is no error. Consequently, God—who is precisely such a specific characteristic of the human being—is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why, then, would the teaching of the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) not be undermined by valid cognition for one who asserts that the world is without God?
